text: The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge and forming a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. A single iodine atom is attached to one of the carbons in a ring position adjacent to the fusion point, placing it at the alpha position of the naphthalene core. Because the fused aromatic framework is rigid and planar, the molecule has little conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity of the rings. Neither the iodine nor the aromatic carbons provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a fully aromatic, rigid, planar scaffold with no fused rings. Two nitro groups sit on the ring, each a strongly electron-withdrawing group with oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the two chlorine atoms are attached at the remaining carbons. The substitution pattern is asymmetric: the nitro groups and chlorines alternate around the ring so that the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis matching a simple pattern. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are aromatic C–H and no N–H or O–H groups are present.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents at the meta positions (1,3-substitution). One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. The other is an ether linkage connecting the ring to a benzyl group, a second phenyl ring attached through a flexible CH2 unit. The two aromatic rings are not fused, so the scaffold consists of two separate benzene rings joined by an oxygen and a methylene spacer. Because of the meta arrangement and the rotatable ether and benzylic bonds, the overall shape is asymmetric and moderately flexible. The ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents at meta positions: a hydroxymethyl group (a benzylic alcohol, CH2OH) on one side and a benzyloxy group (an aryl ether linked through CH2 to a second phenyl ring) on the other. The two aromatic rings are not fused; they are joined through a flexible ether linkage and methylene spacers, so there is no bridged or fused ring system. The scaffold has no internal symmetry beyond the local rotational freedom of the benzyl groups, and the ether and CH2 linkers give it considerable conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzoic acid, with a single benzene ring serving as the scaffold and a carboxylic acid group attached to one ring carbon. The ring carries four halogen substituents: two fluorine atoms, one bromine atom, and one further fluorine, arranged so that the ring has only one remaining hydrogen, located between the carboxylic acid and a fluorine. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the halogens contribute weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings or additional ring systems. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a bromine atom on the neighboring carbon. Because the substituents sit on adjacent and nearby positions without any symmetry, the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational axis and is essentially planar and rigid. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond and the pyridine nitrogen can accept one, while the bromine and methyl groups contribute only lipophilic bulk.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and the remaining ring positions carry a fluorine atom and a bromine atom on adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character. The aromatic framework is rigid and planar, and the substituents are directly bonded without rotatable linkers, so the molecule is conformationally inflexible. Overall it lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different.

The molecule is a cinnamic acid derivative built on a benzene ring bearing a trans-configured acrylic acid side chain, with the acid carbonyl and hydroxyl group separated from the ring by a conjugated C=C double bond. The benzene ring is trisubstituted: the side chain sits at one position, a fluorine atom at the para position, and a bromine atom at the meta position relative to the side chain, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the conjugated alkene extends this rigidity into the side chain, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate slightly. The carboxylic acid functionality provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The halogen substituents contribute electron-withdrawing character but no hydrogen-bonding capability of their own.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a propanoyl group, meaning an ethyl chain attached to a carbonyl carbon that bonds directly to the ring, so it is an aryl ketone. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no fused ring systems. Two halogen substituents sit on the ring: a fluorine and a bromine on adjacent carbons, both positioned para or ortho to the ketone group in a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents differ, and it is fairly rigid overall, though the ethyl chain and carbonyl bond allow some rotational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries four substituents: a methoxy group, a bromine atom, a hydroxyl group, and a trans-acrylic acid side chain. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with the hydroxyl and methoxy groups adjacent to each other on one side and the bromine positioned meta to the acrylic acid chain. The C=C double bond in the side chain is in the E (trans) geometry, which makes that linker rigid and extended. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability. The phenolic hydroxyl adds a further donor, while the methoxy oxygen and carbonyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group, and a bromine atom. Taking the carboxylic acid as the reference position, the hydroxyl sits para to it on the ring, and the bromine sits ortho to the hydroxyl, meta to the carboxylic acid. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered system with no ring fusion, and the molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with only the carboxylic acid and hydroxyl O-H bonds free to rotate. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor oxygens, and the phenolic hydroxyl adds another donor and acceptor site. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring that is broken by the asymmetric bromine placement.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents: a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) at one position, a phenolic hydroxyl group (–OH) at the position para to it, and a bromine atom on the carbon between the hydroxyl and the hydroxymethyl groups, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 across the ring. The compound has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the three substituents are all different. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl group adds some conformational flexibility. Both hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the bromine offers a weak halogen-bonding site.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, arranged as a single aromatic core with no fused or additional rings. A methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits at one position, a nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond) sits para to it, and a bromine atom sits ortho to the methoxy group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The overall framework is planar and fairly rigid, with only the methyl of the ether showing rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a potential mirror plane through the aromatic ring, since the three substituents are all different. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen and the nitrogen of the nitrile act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine-type ring that contains a nitrogen atom bearing an oxygen, making it an N-oxide. Positioned on this ring is a nitro group, which consists of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, and a bromine atom attached to a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring itself is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the substituents occupy positions that break any mirror symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric. Its rigidity comes from the flat aromatic core, while the nitro and N-oxide oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, carrying four substituents around the six-membered aromatic core, so there is no ring fusion. Starting from the carbon bearing a hydroxyl group, one neighboring carbon carries an ethoxy group (an oxygen linked to a two-carbon ethyl chain), the other neighbor carries a bromine atom, and the position across the ring carries an aldehyde group. This 1,2,3,5-type arrangement leaves the molecule without any mirror or rotational symmetry, because the four substituents are all different. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the ethoxy tail adds some conformational flexibility. The phenolic hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen and aldehyde oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom, so there is no ring fusion. It carries two substituents on the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and a bromine atom, placed at positions meta to each other, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy group adds a small degree of rotational freedom about the carbon-oxygen bond. The pyridine nitrogen and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on positions that are meta to one another: a carboxylic acid group, a bromine atom, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the bromine and nitro groups sit at the two other positions spaced evenly around it, giving a 3,5-disubstituted pattern relative to the acid. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring itself, while the carboxyl and nitro groups can rotate only slightly out of the ring plane. The substituent arrangement gives the molecule an approximate mirror plane through the carboxyl carbon, the ring carbon bearing it, and the carbon opposite it, so the bromine and nitro groups are arranged symmetrically. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the nitro group contributes two strong oxygen acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which is attached directly to the ring and contains a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl group that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The other substituent is a bromine atom on the opposite meta position, which contributes a halogen that can serve as a weak halogen-bond donor. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or additional rings, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate somewhat around its single bond to the ring. The molecule has a lack of rotational symmetry, since the two substituents are different, though it retains a mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a hydroxyl group (–OH) that makes it a phenol, and a bromine atom. Because the two groups sit next to each other, the pattern is ortho-disubstituted, which breaks the ring's symmetry so that the molecule has no rotational symmetry axis beyond a mirror plane through the substituents. The ring is rigid and planar, while the hydroxyl oxygen can donate one hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds through its lone pairs. The bromine can act only as a weak halogen-type acceptor and contributes no hydrogen-bond donation.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a bromine atom and a cyanomethyl group attached at positions that are meta to each other (a 1,3-disubstitution pattern). The cyanomethyl group consists of a methylene carbon linking the ring to a nitrile, which carries a carbon-nitrogen triple bond at its terminal end. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker gives the side chain some rotational freedom. Overall the structure has no symmetry axis beyond the mirror plane of the ring framework. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine-type ring in which the nitrogen carries a formal positive charge and an attached oxygen bearing a formal negative charge, making it an N-oxide with a dative N–O bond. A bromine atom is attached to the ring carbon at the meta position relative to the nitrogen, giving a 3-substituted pattern on the ring. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion, no stereocenters, and no rotatable bonds beyond the bromine substituent. There is no internal symmetry apart from a local mirror plane through the nitrogen, oxygen, and the bromine-bearing carbon, so the substitution makes the ring asymmetric. The N-oxide oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent positions of the aromatic core: a methyl group and a bromine atom, so it is a disubstituted aromatic compound. The six-membered ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no additional rings fused to it. The methyl group is a simple alkyl substituent, while the bromine is a halogen attached directly to the ring carbon. The molecule has no stereocenters and only mirror-plane symmetry through the substituted carbons, so it is essentially rigid apart from free rotation of the methyl group. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine offers only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a boronic acid group, and a fluorine atom. The carboxylic acid and fluorine sit on adjacent carbons, so they are ortho to one another, while the boronic acid is positioned meta to the carboxylic acid and para to the fluorine. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, rigid and planar, with no stereocenters and no internal symmetry, since the three substituents are all different. The carboxylic acid group carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The boronic acid contributes two donor O–H groups and two acceptor oxygens, while the fluorine acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents placed meta to each other, giving a 1,3-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and attached to the ring), and the other is a carboxylic acid group. The benzene core is a single flat six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern gives the molecule a mirror-plane symmetry through the ring. The aromatic ring and the planar carbonyl groups make the structure fairly rigid, with only limited rotation about the bonds linking the functional groups to the ring. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites, while the aldehyde oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, so its scaffold is a monocyclic aromatic core with no ring fusion. It carries one primary amine group (an NH2 attached directly to the ring), which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The remaining ring positions bear three halogens: two bromines, one chlorine, and one fluorine, arranged on adjacent and nearby carbons, so the substitution pattern is dense and asymmetric. Because the ring is aromatic and fully substituted apart from one C–H position, the structure is essentially rigid and planar, with the halogens and amine lying in the ring plane and little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing five substituents and one hydrogen. Going around the ring, it carries a methyl group, a bromine atom, an amino group, a second bromine atom, and a chlorine atom, with the hydrogen sitting between the methyl and bromine positions. Because the two bromines and the chlorine flank the amino group, the substitution pattern is crowded and asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl group is the only freely rotating part. The primary amine supplies two hydrogen-bond donor sites and a lone pair acceptor, and the halogen and nitrogen atoms add weaker acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying an aldehyde group, two fluorine atoms, and one chlorine atom, so it is a substituted benzaldehyde with no fused ring systems. The aldehyde (formyl) carbon is attached directly to one ring carbon, and the ring bears fluorine atoms on the adjacent carbons flanking that aldehyde, with a chlorine atom positioned para to the aldehyde-bearing carbon. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity of the aromatic ring. The rigid, planar aromatic core and the directly attached aldehyde leave little conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to one ring carbon, with the remaining ring positions carrying a trifluoromethyl group, a chlorine atom, and a fluorine atom. The carboxylic acid sits adjacent to both the trifluoromethyl group and the fluorine, creating a crowded ortho-substitution pattern on one side of the ring, while the chlorine is positioned para to the trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry because the substituents are all different. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the halogen and fluorine substituents act only as weak acceptors and contribute no hydrogen-bond donor capacity.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the ring, and it is the principal functional group. The halogens sit on adjacent carbons, with fluorine positioned para to the carboxylic acid and chlorine positioned meta to it, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system, although the carboxyl group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the halogens act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a substituted phenylhydrazine built on a single benzene ring. The ring is a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, and it carries three substituents: a hydrazine group (–NH–NH2) on one carbon, a fluorine atom on the carbon para to it, and a chlorine atom on the carbon ortho to the fluorine and meta to the hydrazine. The hydrazine group is the main functional feature, contributing two nitrogen atoms with hydrogen-bond donor capability through their N–H bonds and acceptor capability through their lone pairs. The halogens lend the ring a polar, asymmetric substitution pattern, so the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the planar aromatic framework. Overall, the structure is largely rigid because of the aromatic ring, with only modest flexibility from rotation about the bond linking the ring to the hydrazine group.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a methoxy group, and a chlorine atom. The carboxylic acid sits at one position on the ring, with the methoxy group positioned para to it, while the chlorine is located ortho to the methoxy group and meta to the carboxylic acid, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, so the scaffold is rigid, with the methoxy and carboxyl groups offering some rotational freedom. The molecule has no symmetry because the three substituents differ and are arranged asymmetrically. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor capability (the carbonyl oxygen), while the methoxy oxygen can act as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern. One ring carbon bears a methyl group, its neighbour bears a chlorine atom, and a carbon across the ring carries a sulfonamide group, meaning a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to an NH2 group. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the sulfonamide and methyl groups can rotate freely around their single bonds. The sulfonamide supplies two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 hydrogens and two acceptors through its sulfonyl oxygens. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the three substituents differ from one another.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, bearing a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a sulfonyl chloride group in a 1,2,4-pattern. The methyl group sits at one ring carbon, with the chlorine on the adjacent carbon, and the sulfonyl chloride group located para to the methyl group. The sulfonyl group is a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a chlorine, creating a highly electron-withdrawing site. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with only the sulfonyl chloride and methyl groups offering limited rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the full structure onto itself because the three substituents are different. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, but the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around the ring: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) and two halogens, one fluorine and one chlorine. Judging by the SMILES, the nitrile sits at one position while the fluorine and chlorine occupy meta positions relative to it, placed on opposite sides of the nitrile carbon. The nitrile is linear and rigid, and the aromatic ring is planar, so the whole scaffold is essentially flat and conformationally inflexible. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is an acetanilide-type compound: a benzene ring bearing an acetamide group, with a chlorine atom attached at the meta position relative to the nitrogen. The core is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the amide linkage (a carbonyl bonded to an NH that connects to the ring) is the main functional group. The substitution pattern is 1,3 (meta), which leaves the molecule without any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond a rough planar arrangement. The aromatic ring and amide plane are largely rigid, while the methyl group offers minimal flexibility. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the chlorine contributes only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a substituted phenylboronic acid, built on a single benzene ring with no fused or additional ring systems. A boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups, is attached directly to one carbon of the aromatic ring. A chlorine atom sits on the ring at the meta position relative to the boron-bearing carbon, giving a 1,3-disubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry plane that includes both substituents. The two hydroxyl groups each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the chlorine contributes only weak acceptor character. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the molecule has little conformational flexibility beyond rotation about the carbon-boron bond.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom, making it a strongly electron-withdrawing group. The other substituent is a single chlorine atom attached directly to the aromatic ring. The scaffold is a single, fully aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings, giving the molecule a flat, rigid framework. Its overall shape has a local mirror plane through the ring, but the substitution pattern gives it no higher rotational symmetry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzothiophene scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiophene ring that contains a sulfur atom, giving a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic core. A carboxylic acid group is attached at the carbon adjacent to the sulfur in the thiophene ring, and a chlorine atom sits on the neighboring carbon of that same five-membered ring. The substitution pattern is therefore contiguous on one side of the thiophene ring, and the molecule lacks any significant symmetry. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the sulfur and chlorine add weaker acceptor character.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone built around a central carbonyl group that links two benzene rings. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries a single chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the carbonyl attachment, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. Each aromatic ring is a flat, fully conjugated six-membered carbon ring with no fused rings present. The carbonyl carbon is sp2-hybridized, so the two aryl groups are conjugated with the ketone and the scaffold is fairly rigid, with rotation possible only around the single bonds joining the rings to the carbonyl. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing a chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the carbonyl-containing substituent, giving a 1,3-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. Attached to the ring is a ketone carbonyl that links directly to a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group, so the overall framework is an aryl ketone with a cyanomethyl-type terminus. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the carbonyl and nitrile groups add linear, polar character with limited conformational freedom along the short chain. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the carbonyl oxygen, the nitrile nitrogen, and the halogen, which together provide several polar contact points.

The molecule is a short, straight-chain carboxylic acid with three carbon atoms in the backbone, so it has no ring systems and no ring fusion. Its single functional group is a terminal carboxylic acid, where a carbonyl carbon bears a hydroxyl group, and a chlorine atoms sits on the carbon farthest from the acid, giving a halogen substituent on the terminal methylene. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the chlorine and carboxyl ends are chemically distinct. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the chlorine offers only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, with a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle serving as the scaffold and no fused or additional ring systems. It carries two substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group and a chlorine atom, which places them in an ortho relationship on the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl group contributes only minimal conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the chlorine atom is at most a very weak acceptor, so its hydrogen-bonding capability is essentially negligible. Its overall shape has only approximate mirror symmetry across the axis through the two substituents.

The molecule is a diaryl ether built from two aromatic rings joined through a single oxygen bridge. One ring is a pyridine bearing a nitrile (cyano) group at the 3-position and the ether oxygen at the adjacent 2-position, while the other is an unsubstituted benzene ring. The pyridine nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the ether oxygen provides a weak additional acceptor site, with no hydrogen-bond donors present. The two aromatic rings are fully planar and conjugated, but the ether linkage allows some rotational freedom, giving the scaffold moderate flexibility around the C–O–C bridge.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents placed meta to each other, at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, and the other is an isocyanate group, where a nitrogen is attached to the ring and double-bonded to a central carbon that is itself double-bonded to oxygen. Because the aromatic ring is rigid and the two groups lie in roughly the same plane, the overall framework is flat and largely inflexible. The nitrile nitrogen and the isocyanate oxygen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement lacks any internal symmetry that would make the two substituents equivalent.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring carrying a nitrile (cyano) group on one ring carbon, with the ring nitrogen oxidized to an N-oxide, so the nitrogen bears a formal positive charge and an adjacent oxygen bears a negative charge. The nitrile sits at the meta-type position relative to the N-oxide, and the ring is fully planar and conjugated, with no stereocenters or flexible side chains, making the scaffold rigid. The molecule has no symmetry axis that maps the substituent pattern onto itself, so it is asymmetric. The N-oxide oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen offers a further weak acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it lacks N-H or O-H bonds.

The molecule is an acyclic amino alcohol built on a straight three-carbon chain. A tertiary amine sits at one end, where the nitrogen carries two methyl groups and is bonded to the chain, and a primary alcohol sits at the other end of the chain. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic character, so the scaffold is entirely flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The molecule has no stereocenters and possesses an approximate mirror plane through the chain axis when the conformation is averaged, giving it a simple, nearly symmetric overall shape. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary nitrogen, with its lone pair, can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents, so it has no fused ring system. An aldehyde group (a formyl group, C=O attached to the ring) sits at one position, which makes it the principal functional group. Two adjacent ring positions carry an ether: a methoxy group and an ethoxy group, the latter reached through an oxygen linked to a two-carbon chain. The pattern of substituents is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry in its overall arrangement. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the ethoxy and methoxy side chains and the aldehyde carbonyl have some rotational freedom. Its hydrogen-bond capability is limited: it has no donor groups, but the aldehyde oxygen and the two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. An ethoxy group (a two-carbon ethyl chain bonded through an oxygen atom) sits on one ring carbon, and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, sits on another carbon at the meta position relative to the ethoxy group, giving a 1,3-disubstitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl chain of the ethoxy group adds some conformational flexibility. The ring has no internal symmetry once the two different substituents are present, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane. The boronic acid group contributes two hydroxyl hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms of both the ether and the hydroxyls act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. An ethylamino group (a secondary amine, NH bonded to an ethyl chain) sits on one ring carbon, a hydroxyl group occupies the position meta to it, and a methyl group sits ortho to the amine, giving a trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The phenol hydroxyl and the secondary amine N-H each act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs serve as acceptors. Apart from the aromatic ring, the ethyl chain provides modest conformational flexibility, whereas the benzene core is rigid and planar.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions. It has a bromomethyl group (a CH2 attached to a bromine atom) on one carbon, a trifluoromethyl group (a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms) on the neighboring carbon, and a single fluorine atom on a third carbon next to the trifluoromethyl-bearing position. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring with no additional ring systems. The substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted, which leaves the molecule without any internal symmetry axis. The ring is rigid and planar, while the bromomethyl group contributes some rotational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine and bromine atoms, along with the aromatic system, offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on a single six-membered aromatic core, with no fused rings. A fluorine atom sits on one ring carbon, a bromomethyl group (a CH2 linked to bromine) occupies the position meta to that fluorine, and a trifluoromethyl group (CF3) is attached para to the bromomethyl carbon and ortho to the fluorine. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor character comes from the weakly basic fluorine atoms.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits at one ring position, a fluorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, and a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur is doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to chlorine, sits on the ring carbon opposite the methoxy group. The molecule is a single benzene ring, so it has no fused ring system and is built on one aromatic six-membered scaffold. Three substituents sit around the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a fluorine atom, and a chloromethyl group (a CH2 carrying a chlorine). The methoxy and chloromethyl groups are para to each other, while the fluorine sits ortho to the methoxy, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the fluorine is a weak acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) attached at one position, a methyl group, and a fluorine atom. Taking the acetyl carbon as position 1, the methyl sits at position 4 (para to the acetyl) and the fluorine at position 3 (meta to the acetyl, ortho to the methyl), giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. Its rigidity comes from the aromatic core, while the acetyl group retains limited rotational freedom about the ring-carbonyl bond. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a cyano (nitrile) group, and a fluorine atom. It is a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no fused rings, and the ring is fully planar and conjugated. The methyl group and the fluorine sit on adjacent carbons, while the nitrile group lies para to the methyl group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. Apart from the rotation of the methyl group, the structure is essentially rigid and lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are different. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorine offers weak acceptor character and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and separated positions: a nitro group (NO2) at one carbon, a sulfonyl chloride group (SO2Cl) at the carbon para to the nitro group, and a fluorine atom on the carbon ortho to the nitro group. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid and essentially planar. The two strongly electron-withdrawing groups, nitro and sulfonyl chloride, sit on opposite sides of the ring, while the fluorine occupies the position between them. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, whereas the oxygen atoms of the nitro and sulfonyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Three substituents sit around the ring: a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one drawn as a formal positive charge with the other as a negative charge) carries strong electron-withdrawing character, a fluorine atom sits ortho to the nitro group, and a bromomethyl group (a CH2 carrying a bromine) occupies the position para to the nitro group. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the bromomethyl group contributes some rotational flexibility about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no O–H or N–H groups. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two oxygens of the nitro group and the fluorine atom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitro group, a hydroxyl group, and a fluorine atom. The nitro group and the fluorine sit next to each other on adjacent carbons, while the hydroxyl group is located on the carbon directly opposite the nitro group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is a single planar, fully conjugated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is rigid and flat. The molecule has no symmetry element that maps it onto itself, since the three different substituents occupy unequal positions. The phenolic hydroxyl is both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the nitro oxygens and the fluorine atom act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a mandelic acid analogue built on a two-carbon backbone: a carboxylic acid group and a secondary alcohol share a single alpha carbon that is also bonded to a phenyl ring. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused benzene ring carrying one fluorine atom at the meta position relative to the side chain, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The alpha carbon is a stereocenter, so the molecule is chiral. The carboxylic acid can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, the hydroxyl can donate and accept as well, and the fluorine atom is a weak acceptor. The side chain has several rotatable bonds, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility around the aromatic core.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a hydroxyl group (–OH) attached directly to the ring, making it a phenol-type aromatic alcohol. The other is a fluorine atom on the carbon next to the hydroxyl-bearing carbon, giving an ortho-substitution pattern with no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the substituted carbons. The ring is planar and rigid, with the substituents lying in its plane, and the molecule has little conformational flexibility apart from rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogen. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atom is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta relationship: a fluorine atom and a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linker attached to a carboxylic acid). The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no fused ring systems, and the fluorine sits at position three relative to the side chain. The carboxylic acid group, with its C=O and O–H, offers both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites, while the fluorine adds a weak acceptor. The methylene linker gives the side chain some conformational flexibility around its single bonds, so the overall structure is only partly rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local planar symmetry of the ring because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered heterocycle containing a sulfur–sulfur bond, with the carbonyl carbon sitting in that ring adjacent to the fused aromatic carbon. The five-membered ring holds a thiocarbonyl-type ketone (C=O) bonded to one sulfur, and the second sulfur carries two oxygen atoms as a sulfonyl group, making it a sultone-like scaffold. The benzene ring is unsubstituted apart from its two fusion carbons, so the substitution pattern is simply ortho-fused. The fused framework is essentially planar and rigid, with the aromatic ring and the heterocycle sharing a single bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local arrangement of the benzo ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons next to the nitrogen. One substituent is a hydroxyl group, which can donate a hydrogen bond through its oxygen-bound hydrogen and accept one through its oxygen lone pairs. The other is an iodine atom, a heavy halogen that contributes steric bulk and can act as a weak halogen-bond donor. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the orientation of the hydroxyl hydrogen, and the substitution pattern gives the molecule no internal symmetry. The pyridine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the molecule offers both donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is a small oxygen-containing heterocycle built on a six-membered pyranone-type ring, with one carbonyl group and one ring oxygen forming the core scaffold. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group is attached to the adjacent carbon, so the substitution pattern is contiguous and places the methyl and hydroxyl groups side by side. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, which makes the scaffold rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl and hydroxyl groups. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the methyl and hydroxyl substituents occupy different positions on the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid and nitro group sit on opposite sides of the ring, while the hydroxyl sits adjacent to the nitro group, giving a trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The ring and its directly attached groups are essentially planar and conformationally rigid, with only the carboxylic acid and hydroxyl rotating about single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl together provide two hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, hydroxyl oxygen, and nitro oxygens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group is attached to a carbon positioned meta to the nitrogen, with the two substituents adjacent to each other on the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the scaffold is rigid and essentially flat, with only the small rotation of the hydroxyl group available. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on an adamantane-type cage, a rigid tricyclic hydrocarbon framework of fused cyclohexane rings in a diamond-like arrangement. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached to one bridgehead carbon, and a tertiary hydroxyl group (–OH) sits on a second bridgehead position across the cage. The substitution pattern is 1,3 across the cage, which gives the molecule a high degree of three-dimensional symmetry, with the cage carbons forming several equivalent sets. The rigid, compact skeleton leaves little conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the hydroxyl group adds one further donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent-to-meta positions: a formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO) and a hydroxyl group (OH) placed in a 1,3 relationship on the ring. The aromatic six-membered carbocycle is a single, unfused ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the phenolic hydroxyl serving as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror plane or rotational symmetry that would make the two ring halves equivalent. Only the aldehyde C–C bond and the C–O bond of the hydroxyl offer limited rotation, giving the molecule modest conformational freedom overall.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta relationship: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) and a hydroxyl group. The aromatic six-membered carbocycle is a single planar, fully conjugated ring with no ring fusion, and the scaffold is essentially rigid, with only the bond to the hydroxyl oxygen permitting rotation. The substitution pattern lacks a true symmetry axis through both groups, so the molecule belongs to a low-symmetry arrangement with a mirror plane lying in the ring plane. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrile nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrazole-type ring, giving an indazole-based scaffold. The five-membered ring contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, both bearing hydrogens, and a carbonyl carbon adjacent to one of them, so the ring is a pyrazolone-like lactam. The benzo portion is unsubstituted, with four aromatic CH positions and no appended side groups, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule has the planar, fully conjugated, rigid framework expected of a fused aromatic system. The two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, so the scaffold contains a phenolic OH that can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond. The other substituent is an iodine atom on the neighboring carbon, which is a large, polarizable halogen that adds steric bulk next to the hydroxyl. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, so the core is rigid while the single bond to the hydroxyl oxygen allows modest rotation. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents are different, and it has no additional hydrogen-bond acceptors beyond the oxygen.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a flat six-membered aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents placed meta to each other: an isothiocyanate group (N=C=S), a linear, cumulated functional group attached through nitrogen, and an iodine atom. Because the two substituents sit at the 1 and 3 positions of the ring, the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring carbons, giving it a relatively symmetric, rigid, and planar shape with few rotatable bonds. The isothiocyanate carbon is electrophilic, while the sulfur and the nitrogen can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents, making it a disubstituted aromatic compound. The six-membered aromatic ring is a single, unfused ring system with no additional rings attached. One substituent is a methyl group and the other is an iodine atom, and they sit on carbons separated by one intervening carbon, a meta arrangement. Because the two substituents differ, the molecule lacks a mirror-like symmetry axis through both groups, though the ring itself is planar and rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom is the iodine, which can act as a weak acceptor.

The molecule consists of two five-membered imide-type rings joined by an ester linkage and a two-carbon ethylene bridge. One ring is a maleimide, a planar unsaturated pyrrole-2,5-dione with a carbon-carbon double bond between its two carbonyl-flanked positions. The other is a saturated succinimide ring, and it is bonded through its nitrogen to an oxygen atom that forms an N-O ester linkage with the carbonyl of the propanoyl chain. The scaffold has no stereocenters and little symmetry beyond the local ring geometry, and the chain provides some conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the four carbonyl oxygens and the ring oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methoxy group, three fluorine atoms, and a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid sits on the ring at one position, and the methoxy group is flanked by two adjacent fluorine atoms, giving a crowded, highly halogenated arrangement with a single unsubstituted ring carbon between two fluorines. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry because the substituents occupy positions in an unequal pattern. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, while the methoxy oxygen and fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Only the methyl of the methoxy group and the carboxyl rotation add conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Attached to the ring are three substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a methyl group on the neighboring carbon, and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, positioned meta to the methoxy and para to the methyl. Because the ring is fully substituted in a 1,2,4 pattern, the molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond what the planar aromatic core provides. The aromatic ring and the boron center make it largely rigid, though the methoxy and boronic acid groups can rotate about their single bonds. The two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyls and the methoxy ether each serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent carbons: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a hydroxyl group, and a second hydroxyl group, forming a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The two hydroxyl groups sit next to each other, so they form a catechol-like pair, while the methoxy ether oxygen sits at one end of the substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the methyl group on the ether oxygen adds only limited conformational freedom. The two hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the three oxygen atoms can all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic compound built on a short linear chain with no rings. A methoxy group, consisting of a methyl joined through an ether oxygen, is attached to a two-carbon ethylene spacer that terminates in a nitrile group, which is a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen. The ether oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen is a second, weaker acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond local conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms and three carbon atoms, with no ring fusion. A methyl group sits on one of the carbons of the ring, creating a simple substitution pattern. The nitrogen atom that carries no hydrogen is bonded to a carboxamide group, a carbonyl attached to an amino group, which is a urea-like unit. Because the ring is flat and the scaffold is small and compact, the structure is rigid, with only limited rotational freedom around the bond linking the amide to the ring. The amide NH2 and carbonyl oxygen allow hydrogen-bond donation and acceptance, while the unsubstituted ring nitrogen can also act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one methyl group and an amino group, with three bromine atoms distributed around the ring. Reading the SMILES, the carbons carrying bromine sit at three positions, with the amine and methyl flanking the arrangement, so the substitution pattern is fully asymmetric across the six-membered aromatic ring. The scaffold is a single aromatic benzene ring with no ring fusion and no additional heteroatom rings. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site on the nitrogen, while the bromine atoms contribute only weak halogen-bonding character and no hydrogen-bonding ability. The rigid planar ring limits conformational flexibility, leaving only the orientation of the methyl and amino groups as rotational degrees of freedom.

The molecule is a small aromatic heterocycle built on a single five-membered furan ring, which contains one oxygen atom and four carbon atoms with two double bonds in the ring. A methyl group is attached to one ring carbon, and a carboxylic acid group (a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl) is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring oxygen, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pattern with no ring fusion. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with only limited rotational freedom around the bond linking the carboxylic acid to the ring. Its carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through the hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at the carbonyl oxygen, while the ring oxygen offers a weak additional acceptor site.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a methyl group, and a nitro group, which is a nitrogen bearing a charge-separated N=O and N–O⁻ arrangement. The nitro group sits between the methoxy and methyl substituents, giving a crowded 1,2,3-substitution pattern on the ring. The overall framework is largely planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and methyl groups able to rotate. The ether oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered heterocyclic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, placing it in the pyrazolone family. The ring carries a methyl group on one of its carbon atoms, which sits on the carbon-nitrogen double bond, giving a substitution pattern with no additional fused or appended rings. A carbonyl group occupies a position adjacent to one of the ring nitrogens, forming a cyclic amide-like unit with a hydrogen atom on the neighboring nitrogen. The ring is small and largely planar, with limited conformational freedom and no stereocenters or internal symmetry beyond the basic ring framework. The N-H group can donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygen and the other ring nitrogen can accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it an aromatic monocyclic scaffold with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents: a methyl group, an amino group, and a nitro group, arranged so that the nitro group sits directly beside the methyl group and the amino group occupies the position para to the nitro group. The nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group with its formal charges written as a zwitterionic N-oxide style, while the primary amine acts as a hydrogen-bond donor. The ring is planar and rigid, and the methyl group is the only small flexible element, so the overall framework has no symmetry beyond its local planarity. The nitro oxygens and the amine nitrogen provide hydrogen-bond acceptor and donor sites respectively.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. The hydroxyl and nitro groups sit para to each other, with the methyl group placed meta to the hydroxyl and ortho to the nitro group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. Overall it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because of the asymmetric arrangement. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro group's oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a benzofuran scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a furan ring, with the fusion sharing one C–C bond between the two rings. A methyl group sits on the five-membered furan ring at the carbon adjacent to the fused junction, while a carboxylic acid group is attached to the carbon next to the ring oxygen on the same furan ring. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the carboxylic acid able to rotate about its single bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the furan oxygen adds a further weak acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the methyl and acid groups occupy distinct positions on the furan ring.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined directly by a single carbon-carbon bond, giving a biphenyl scaffold. One ring carries a methyl group at a meta position relative to the bond connecting it to the second ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The two rings are not fused; each is an independent aromatic six-membered ring, and the unsubstituted ring is attached by a simple bond that allows rotation, so the molecule is only moderately flexible. It contains no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its overall shape is largely nonpolar and hydrocarbon in character.

This molecule is a small, saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane skeleton, bearing two adjacent carbonyl groups, so it is a cyclic 1,2-diketone rather than a simple ketone. One ring carbon adjacent to a carbonyl carries a methyl substituent, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The single ring is fused to nothing else and is not aromatic, and its sp3-rich framework gives moderate conformational flexibility, with the adjacent carbonyls restricting rotation locally. Both oxygen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are attached to carbon.

The molecule is a five-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopentanone, bearing a single methyl substituent on a carbon adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing ring carbon, which places it at the 2-position relative to the ketone. The ring contains one ketone (C=O) group, which is the only functional group present, and no ring fusion or additional rings are involved. The scaffold is saturated apart from the carbonyl, so it is a compact, relatively rigid cycloalkane framework with some puckering rather than a planar aromatic system. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl group breaks the ring's symmetry, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its single carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a symmetric acyclic anhydride, with two identical 3-methylglutaric-type halves joined through a central carboxylic anhydride linkage (–C(=O)–O–C(=O)–). Each half is a branched chain carrying a methyl group on the carbon beta to the anhydride carbonyl, with a free terminal carboxylic acid at the opposite end. The scaffold contains no rings, so the structure is fully flexible, with rotatable single bonds along both chains. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the two terminal carboxylic acid OH groups, while the four carbonyl oxygens and the anhydride ether oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and an amide-linked side chain at positions that are meta to each other (a 3-methylphenyl arrangement). The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the attached carbonyl-amide-methylene-carboxylic acid chain is flexible and can rotate about its single bonds. A secondary amide (–C(=O)NH–) connects the ring to a terminal carboxylic acid group. The amide NH and the carboxylic acid OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis or mirror plane of note because the substituents are unsymmetrically placed.

The molecule is a single saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, bearing one methyl group on a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring contains no double bonds and no fused or bridged rings, so the scaffold is a simple monocycle with no aromatic character. The only functional group is the secondary amine within the ring, and the methyl substituent sits at the 2-position relative to nitrogen, which breaks any mirror symmetry the bare ring would have. The chair-capable ring gives moderate conformational flexibility, with the methyl able to occupy either axial or equatorial orientations. The nitrogen carries one hydrogen, so it can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a pyridine ring is fused to a benzene ring along a shared edge, giving a fully aromatic, planar framework. A single methyl group sits on the pyridine-type ring at the carbon adjacent to the one bearing the fused junction, on the carbon meta to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that is not part of the aromatic sextet, making it a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The fused aromatic system is rigid and flat, with the methyl group as the only freely rotating element.

The molecule consists of a thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, bearing a single long unbranched alkyl chain of sixteen carbons attached at the 3-position. The aromatic ring is unfused, so the scaffold is a simple monosubstituted heteroaromatic core with no additional rings or fused systems. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the saturated hexadecyl tail is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the substituent breaks the symmetry of the ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, because it has no N-H or O-H groups, and the sulfur atom is only a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a nitro group, and a trifluoromethyl group. The carboxylic acid is attached at one ring carbon, with the nitro group and the trifluoromethyl group each placed at the meta positions relative to it, so the two outer substituents sit on carbons separated from each other by one ring carbon. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, which is planar and rigid, while the carboxylic acid, nitro, and trifluoromethyl groups add little conformational flexibility beyond rotation about their bonds to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that fully maps the substituents onto one another, since the three groups are chemically distinct. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the nitro group contributes additional hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with two substituents placed meta to each other, which gives it an asymmetric substitution pattern. One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group, attached directly to the aromatic ring. The other is a nitro group, with its nitrogen bearing charge-separated oxygen atoms, also attached to the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the acetyl group offers a degree of rotational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen and the two nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring at positions meta to each other: a carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) and a nitro group (–NO2). The carboxylic acid is a planar, conjugated group that can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Because the substituents are not related by any symmetry that makes them equivalent, the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the ring itself. The scaffold is largely rigid and flat, with only limited rotational freedom around the bonds linking each substituent to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with fully conjugated pi bonds. Two substituents sit on this ring in a meta relationship, meaning they are separated by one intervening carbon: a nitro group (an nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged, giving a strongly electron-withdrawing N-oxide-like arrangement) and a trifluoromethyl group (a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms). The overall shape is planar and rigid, with the nitro group able to rotate slightly about its bond to the ring while the trifluoromethyl group is essentially fixed in place. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the ring's own local symmetry, since the two substituents are different. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, but the oxygen atoms of the nitro group are capable of acting as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a nitro group, a nitrogen atom bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged and one double-bonded, attached directly to the aromatic ring. The other is a bromomethyl group, a single saturated carbon carrying a bromine atom, linked to the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the bromomethyl group adds a degree of rotational freedom around its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the two substituents. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no hydrogens are attached to electronegative atoms. The oxygen atoms of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) is attached to one ring carbon, and a chloromethyl group (a CH2 carbon bearing a chlorine atom) is attached to a second ring carbon. The two substituents sit in a meta relationship, separated by one carbon on the ring, which gives the molecule a lack of the full symmetry seen in para-disubstituted analogues. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and can accept hydrogen bonds through its oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The rings and the single sp3 linker give limited conformational flexibility, with the chloromethyl group able to rotate freely around its bond to the ring.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) attached at a position meta to the bond linking it to the second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. The nitro group contributes hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its oxygen atoms, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two rings can rotate relative to one another about the central single bond, giving moderate flexibility, while each ring is planar and rigid. Overall the structure lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the local symmetry of each individual benzene ring.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a five-membered imidazole-like ring sharing a bond with a six-membered pyridine-like ring, forming an imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine scaffold with a bridgehead nitrogen common to both rings. The five-membered ring carries a nitro group (-NO2) on one carbon, and the bicycle is planar and fully aromatic, making it rigid with no rotatable bonds beyond the nitro group. The ring nitrogen that is not at the bridgehead can accept hydrogen bonds, and the oxygens of the nitro group are also acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bicyclic framework has no internal symmetry because the nitro substituent breaks any mirror relationship across the fused system.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no fused or additional rings. Two methyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, forming an ortho-dimethyl pattern, and a nitro group (–NO2) is attached to a carbon next to one of those methyls, placing the three substituents on three consecutive positions of the ring. The nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group with its two oxygen atoms able to accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement has no rotational or mirror symmetry, since the three substituents are not identical in position. The core ring is rigid and planar, though the methyl and nitro groups can rotate about their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring that contains a central nitrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups. The benzene ring carries a single nitro group (-NO2) attached to the carbon adjacent to one of the carbonyl-bearing ring-fusion atoms, which places it in the position next to the imide carbonyl. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the nitro group also largely coplanar with the aromatic ring. The molecule has no symmetry because the nitro group sits on only one side of the ring system. The imide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on an adamantane cage, a rigid, highly symmetric tricyclic framework of fused cyclohexane rings in chair conformations. A single carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached to one of the bridgehead carbons, so the substitution pattern is monosubstitution at a tertiary cage position. Because the cage is rigid, the scaffold has very little conformational flexibility, and the carboxyl group is the only region with rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The remaining hydrocarbon cage is saturated and carries no additional heteroatoms.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with a straight-chain scaffold of eight carbon atoms, with no rings and no aromatic groups. A single carbonyl group sits at the third carbon from one end, flanked by an ethyl group on one side and a pentyl chain on the other, so the substitution pattern is unbranched and unsymmetrical. Its flexible, freely rotating alkyl chains make the molecule conformationally flexible. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a short, acyclic aliphatic chain with no rings, so it has no ring fusion or aromatic character. Its backbone is a three-carbon ethyl-ketone unit: an ethyl group (CH3CH2) attached to a carbonyl carbon, with a cyanomethyl group (CH2–C≡N) on the other side of that carbonyl. The two principal functional groups are a ketone and a nitrile, separated by a single methylene carbon. The nitrile nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen both carry lone pairs, so the molecule can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at two sites, while it has no hydrogen-bond donor (no N–H or O–H groups). The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is a diaryl ether built from two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom, so the skeleton is a flexible C–O–C linkage connecting two planar aromatic rings. One ring is a plain unsubstituted phenyl group, while the other carries a primary amino group (–NH2) positioned meta to the ether oxygen, which defines its substitution pattern. Neither ring is fused to another, and the molecule has no stereocenters. The aromatic rings are rigid and planar, but rotation about the two C–O bonds gives the overall shape some conformational freedom. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl group (a –CH2–COOH unit) on one carbon and a phenoxy group (a second benzene ring linked through an ether oxygen) on the carbon meta to it, so the substituents are 1,3 on the first ring. The two aromatic rings are not fused; they are joined by a single flexible C–O–C ether linkage, giving a diaryl ether scaffold with a moderate degree of conformational freedom around that bridge. The carboxylic acid is the principal functional group and can both donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept two through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The ether oxygen provides a further weak hydrogen-bond acceptor site, while the overall framework has no rotational symmetry and is asymmetric.

The molecule is built around a five-membered cyclic carbamate, an oxazolidinone ring, in which a carbonyl carbon sits between a ring oxygen and a ring nitrogen. The nitrogen is attached directly to a benzene ring, so the phenyl group is an N-aryl substituent with no further substitution on the ring, giving a simple monosubstituted pattern with no symmetry-breaking extras beyond the ring's own geometry. The oxazolidinone ring is largely planar and rigid, while the attachment to the phenyl ring allows some rotation about the nitrogen-carbon bond. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ring oxygen and nitrogen can also act as weak acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all N-H and O-H positions are absent.

The molecule is a five-membered heteroaromatic ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom adjacent to each other, with a carbonyl group on the carbon next to the oxygen, forming an isoxazolone-type scaffold. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the two rings are joined by a single bond and are not fused. The ring nitrogen carries a hydrogen, and the exocyclic carbonyl oxygen is an additional acceptor site. The phenyl group is unsubstituted, so the overall framework has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom about the biaryl-type bond. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen can serve as acceptors.
