This molecule is a five-membered pyrazolone ring, containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, a carbonyl carbon adjacent to one nitrogen, and a carbon-carbon double bond to the other nitrogen. The nitrogen bearing the methyl group is an N-substituted amide-like center, while the ring carbon directly attached to the C=N unit carries a bulky tert-butyl group. The ring is non-fused and essentially planar, with a conjugated C=N and C=O system that makes it fairly rigid, and the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk but no symmetry beyond local features. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since both ring nitrogens are substituted or part of a double bond.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolone ring, a non-fused heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a carbonyl group and the other a phenyl substituent. The C=N double bond sits in the ring, giving it a partially unsaturated, fairly rigid core. A tert-butyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the imine nitrogen, which provides bulky, nonpolar steric bulk. The N-bound phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene that can rotate relative to the heterocycle, adding a degree of conformational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local rotational freedom of the tert-butyl group. The ring carbonyl oxygen and the imine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond attached directly to the ring), and the other is a carboxylic acid group, which contains a carbonyl and a hydroxyl. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, so the scaffold is rigid, while the vinyl and acid groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the two substituents onto each other, and it is not fused to any other ring. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the vinyl group contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring. One position carries an acetamide group, with the acetyl carbonyl attached to an NH bridge that connects to the ring. The opposite position is bonded directly to the nitrogen of a 1,2,4-triazole ring, which is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing three nitrogens and two carbons. The two rings are joined by a single bond and are not fused, so the molecule is largely planar and fairly rigid, with limited rotation about the aryl-aryl and amide bonds. The amide NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the unsubstituted nitrogens of the triazole act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One position bears a primary amine group (–NH2), which acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The opposite position is occupied by the nitrogen of a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, a fully saturated, non-aromatic ring that adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The piperidine nitrogen is tertiary, bonded to the aryl ring and two ring carbons, so it can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but not a donor. The overall scaffold is a rigid aromatic core linked to a flexible aliphatic ring, and the para substitution gives the molecule an approximate linear, elongated shape.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries an acetyl group, a carbonyl attached directly to a methyl, which acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen. The opposite side carries a pyrrolidine ring, a saturated five-membered nitrogen heterocycle joined to the aromatic ring through its nitrogen, so that nitrogen is an aryl amine with no N–H and therefore no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The para pattern gives the aromatic core a roughly linear, symmetric shape across its long axis. Overall the molecule is largely planar and rigid around the phenyl and carbonyl portion, with the saturated pyrrolidine ring adding some conformational flexibility at its edge.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a two-carbon chain ending in a primary amine, giving a flexible ethyl linker that terminates in an NH2 group. The opposite side carries a sulfonamide group, in which a sulfur atom is double-bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to an NH2 group, forming a polar, strongly electron-withdrawing unit. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the aminoethyl side chain adds conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local para-symmetry of the ring. Both the primary amine and the sulfonamide NH2 can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfonyl oxygens and amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzoic acid derivative, consisting of a single benzene ring bearing two substituents at opposite (para) positions. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a hydroxyl group, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The other is a two-carbon chain ending in a chlorine atom, a flexible alkyl linker that adds rotational freedom absent from the aromatic core. The para arrangement gives the molecule an approximately linear, elongated shape with a two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring's long axis, though the chloroethyl tail breaks any mirror symmetry. The aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar, while the chain and acid group can rotate about their single bonds.

This molecule is an α,β-unsaturated methyl ketone (an enone) in which the carbonyl is conjugated through a C=C double bond to a thiophene ring. The core scaffold is a short linear chain: a methyl group attached to a carbonyl carbon, followed by a trans-configured alkene, which connects to a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom. The thiophene ring is attached at its 2-position, leaving the ring otherwise unsubstituted. The conjugated system from the sulfur-containing ring through the alkene to the carbonyl makes the arrangement largely planar and comparatively rigid, with limited rotation about the alkene and the ring-to-chain bond. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on carbon.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a four-carbon carboxylic acid chain attached at one position, with two methoxy groups on adjacent carbons of the ring, giving a 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern relative to the alkyl chain. The aromatic core is a single unfused benzene ring, flat and rigid, while the saturated propyl linker between the ring and the terminal carboxyl group adds conformational flexibility. The terminal carboxylic acid functions as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two ether oxygens of the methoxy groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is a thiosemicarbazide, built around a central thiocarbonyl carbon that bears a free hydrogydrazine-type NH-NH2 group on one side and an NH linking to a substituted benzene ring on the other. The aromatic portion is a single benzene ring carrying one chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the nitrogen attachment, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The thiourea-like core is largely planar and can adopt a few rotational conformations about its C-N bonds, while the rest of the chain is flexible. The terminal hydrazine NH2 and the two NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom along with the nitrogen lone pairs serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a para-substituted benzene ring carrying an acetamide group (a CH3-C(=O)-NH- unit) on one side and a 2-aminothiazole ring on the other, linked directly by a single carbon-carbon bond. The thiazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom, and it bears a primary amino group on the carbon between those two heteroatoms. The acetamide provides a hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H and an acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the amino group on the thiazole adds further donor capacity and the ring nitrogen acts as an acceptor. The two aromatic rings are conjugated through the biaryl bond, giving a largely planar, rigid scaffold with limited conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local symmetry of the para-disubstituted benzene ring.

The molecule is built on a pyrimidine core, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 relationship. At one carbon of this ring sits a morpholine group attached through its nitrogen, a saturated six-membered ring containing both nitrogen and oxygen. Adjacent to it on the ring is a benzyloxy group, an oxygen linking the pyrimidine to a CH2 bridge that terminates in an unsubstituted phenyl ring. A bromine atom occupies the remaining open position on the pyrimidine, giving a fully substituted heteroaromatic core. The molecule has no stereocenters and is largely planar in its aromatic region, though the morpholine and benzyloxy linkers add some rotational flexibility. The morpholine oxygen and pyrimidine nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl group bridges two aromatic rings. One ring is a pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing a nitrogen atom at the position para to the carbonyl attachment. The other is a benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom at the position para to the carbonyl. Both rings are planar and aromatic, and the carbonyl carbon links them through single bonds, giving a moderately rigid but not fully fixed framework. The molecule lacks a plane or axis of symmetry overall because the two rings differ, though each ring is individually symmetric about its long axis. The ketone oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a linear five-carbon chain whose two ends carry a carboxylic acid group and an aryl ketone, so it is a 5-oxo-5-phenylpentanoic acid type scaffold. The aromatic portion is a single benzene ring, not fused to any other ring, and it bears one fluorine atom at the position para to the carbonyl attachment, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern with a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. The chain is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds, while the aromatic ring and the ketone carbonyl add rigidity to that end of the molecule. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the two oxygens), and the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule consists of a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement: a four-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid on one side and a fluorine atom on the other. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the three-methylene chain linking it to the acid group is flexible and free to rotate around its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, whereas the fluorine atom is a weak acceptor only. The overall structure has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the long axis of the molecule, but it is not a symmetric molecule as a whole because the two ends carry different functional groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused rings, giving it a planar aromatic scaffold. Three substituents sit on that ring: a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons, and a four-carbon side chain bearing a ketone at the terminal end, all arranged in a 1,2,4-substitution pattern. The phenolic hydroxyl can donate a hydrogen bond, while the ether oxygen and the ketone oxygen can each accept one. The aromatic core is rigid, but the saturated chain connecting the ketone to the ring adds some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry because its substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built around a para-disubstituted benzene ring bearing an acetyl group (a methyl ketone) on one side and an ether oxygen on the other. That ether oxygen links through a methylene bridge to a second benzene ring, which carries a nitro group para to the bridge, so the two aromatic rings are connected by a flexible CH2–O linker. The scaffold is a diaryl ether-like framework with no fused ring systems. The ketone carbonyl and the nitro group are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall shape is elongated and fairly linear, with the rigid aromatic rings flanking a rotatable linker.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a flexible ether linkage (an oxymethylene bridge), giving a non-fused, two-ring scaffold. One ring carries an aldehyde (formyl) group, and the other carries a nitro group, each positioned para to the bridging ether oxygen or methylene, so the substitution pattern is symmetric in arrangement but the two ends differ chemically. The molecule has no stereocenters and is largely planar within each aromatic ring, with rotational freedom around the ether and benzylic bonds that makes it moderately flexible overall. Hydrogen-bond acceptor sites include the aldehyde oxygen, the ether oxygen, and the nitro oxygens, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a nitro group, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and has two oxygen atoms available as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The opposite side carries a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen, a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen, which adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the morpholine adds a degree of conformational flexibility. The overall scaffold is largely unsymmetrical, though the para pattern gives the aromatic ring a two-fold axis of pseudo-symmetry. The ring oxygen of morpholine serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a para-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is an ethyl ester group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to an ethoxy oxygen, and the other is an isothiocyanate group, a linear N=C=S unit attached directly to the ring. Because the two groups sit opposite each other, the structure has a symmetric elongated shape with a flat, rigid aromatic core and relatively flexible ethyl tail. The ester carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries an ethylsulfonyl group, a two-carbon chain attached to a sulfur atom that is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms, forming a sulfone. The opposite side carries a boronic acid group, a boron atom bonded to two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic core is a single, unfused, planar ring, and the sulfone and boronic acid groups are strongly electron-withdrawing relative to the ring. The molecule is largely rigid, with only the ethyl chain offering rotational flexibility. The two hydroxyl groups on boron can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. A carboxylic acid group (-COOH) is attached directly to one ring carbon, and a hydroxymethyl group (-CH2OH, a benzylic primary alcohol) sits on the carbon directly opposite it, giving a para (1,4) substitution pattern. The two substituents are identical in size and shape at the ends of the ring, so the molecule has a high degree of symmetry about its long axis. Its rigidity comes from the planar aromatic core, while the single bonds of the hydroxymethyl and carboxyl groups allow limited rotation. The carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the hydroxyl oxygen of the alcohol adds a further donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a carboxymethyl group, a methylene linked to a terminal carboxylic acid, which provides a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor oxygens. The other substituent is a hydroxymethyl group, a benzylic CH2 bearing a primary alcohol, adding a further donor and acceptor site. The para-disubstituted pattern gives the aromatic core a roughly linear, centrosymmetric-like shape around the ring axis, though the flexible CH2 linkers allow rotation of both polar tails. Overall the scaffold is largely rigid in its ring but flexible at its two side chains.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methyl ester group, consisting of a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methoxy oxygen, and the other is a boronic acid group, in which boron carries two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat shape with no ring fusion. The para substitution pattern and the two polar groups produce a linear, roughly symmetric overall layout along the ring axis. The ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the two boronic acid hydroxyl groups can serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving a flat, rigid, and highly symmetric aromatic core with no ring fusion. One substituent is a methyl ester group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to an oxygen that is in turn bonded to a methyl group, so the ester acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its two oxygen atoms and has no donor capability. The other substituent is an isothiocyanate group, a nitrogen bonded through a double bond to a central carbon that is itself double-bonded to sulfur, which is linear and electrophilic at the central carbon. Overall the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and only oxygen and sulfur acceptors, and its only real flexibility lies in rotation about the ester and isothiocyanate bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit opposite each other on that ring, giving a para substitution pattern. One substituent is a methylsulfonyl group, a sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens and a methyl group, which acts as a strong electron-withdrawing unit. The other is a carboxylic acid, a carbonyl group with an attached hydroxyl. Because the two groups are placed symmetrically across the ring, the structure has a two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the sulfonyl and acid groups have limited rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, and the sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement on the six-membered aromatic core, with no fused rings. One substituent is a methylthio group, a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group, attached directly to the ring. The other is a formyl group, a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen, which makes it an aromatic aldehyde. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methylthio group has some rotational freedom around its bonds to the ring and the methyl. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring when the methylthio group is oriented in its preferred conformation. The aldehyde oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It bears two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methylthio group (an S-linked methyl, a thioether) on one side and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, on the other. The boron carries two hydroxyl groups, so the boronic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O-H groups and an acceptor through its oxygen atoms. The thioether sulfur is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor and the methyl group is a small nonpolar appendage. Overall the structure is planar and rigid apart from rotation about the bonds to the substituents, with a symmetric para substitution pattern that gives a roughly linear, elongated shape.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring in a para (1,4) arrangement: a methylthio group (a methyl attached to sulfur, which is bonded to the ring) and a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen). The nitrile is linear and strongly electron-withdrawing, while the thioether sulfur is a weak donor through its lone pairs. The structure is planar and largely rigid, with only the S-methyl bond providing rotational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the nitrile nitrogen can act as a weak acceptor, the sulfur is a poor acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship on a single six-membered aromatic ring, with no fused rings present. One substituent is a methylthio group, consisting of a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl carbon and attached directly to the ring. The other is a hydroxyl group bonded to the ring carbon directly opposite. The molecule has a planar, rigid aromatic core with a degree of conformational flexibility arising from rotation about the sulfur-to-ring bond. Its hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the sulfur atom is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with one position bearing a tert-butyl ether group (an oxygen attached to a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups) and the opposite position bearing a free hydroxyl group. The aromatic ring is a single unfused six-membered system with no additional ring fusion. The two substituents sit on opposite carbons, giving the molecule an approximately linear, symmetric-looking arrangement along its long axis. The bulky, rigid tert-butyl group contrasts with the small, planar aromatic core, and the molecule is largely rigid apart from rotation about the ether and hydroxyl bonds. The phenolic OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries an acetic acid group, in which a carboxylic acid (-COOH) is joined to the ring through a flexible CH2 linker. The opposite side carries a trifluoromethoxy group (-OCF3), an ether oxygen bonded to a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker and the carboxylic acid add conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid is both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the ether oxygen and the fluorine atoms act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is an acetophenone derivative: a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) on one carbon. A trifluoromethyl group (CF3) sits on the carbon directly opposite the acetyl group, making the substitution pattern para across the ring. The benzene core is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the two substituents are linked to it by rigid, planar bonds, so the scaffold is largely flat and conformationally restricted. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through both substituents. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are attached to carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on the ring in a para (1,4) relationship: a primary amino group (-NH2) and a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3). The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The para arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring, and the ring itself is rigid and planar, with the substituents adding only limited conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which serves as a rigid, planar aromatic scaffold. A primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached to one carbon of the ring, supplying both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. A trifluoromethyl group (–CF3) sits on the carbon directly opposite, giving a para substitution pattern that lends the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. The CF3 group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes no hydrogen-bond capability, since fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors. Overall the structure is compact and largely inflexible, with the only notable rotational freedom arising from the amide and trifluoromethyl substituents.

The molecule is a diarylmethanol built around a central sp3 carbon that carries a hydroxyl group and is bonded to two separate benzene rings. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other bears a trifluoromethyl group at the position para to the carbinol attachment, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern on that ring. There are no fused ring systems, and the two aromatic rings can rotate about the central carbon, so the scaffold is moderately flexible. The molecule lacks rotational symmetry overall because the two rings differ, though each ring is internally symmetric. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group serve only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para arrangement, giving it a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which carries a carbonyl oxygen that accepts hydrogen bonds and a hydroxyl group that can both donate and accept them. The other substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, where a carbon bears three fluorine atoms; this group is bulky, electron-withdrawing in character, and largely non-polar in its hydrogen-bonding behavior. The 1,4-substitution pattern gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry along the axis running through both substituents. Overall, the structure has limited conformational flexibility, with rotation possible mainly around the bond joining the carboxylic acid to the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a hydrazine group, with two nitrogen atoms joined by a single bond, attached directly to the ring through a terminal NH. The other is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically compact. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the hydrazine unit has rotational freedom about its single bonds. The hydrazine nitrogens can both act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H bonds and as acceptors through their lone pairs, whereas the fluorines contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the aromatic ring, making it a phenol. The other is a sulfur atom bridging to a trifluoromethyl group, giving an aryl trifluoromethyl thioether. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, so the scaffold is rigid, with only limited rotation around the aryl–sulfur and aryl–oxygen bonds. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the two substituents. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the sulfur and fluorine atoms offer only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a macrocyclic polyether built around a 24-membered ring that contains two benzene rings linked by oxygen-containing chains. Each aromatic ring carries a tert-butyl group in a para-like relationship to one of its ring oxygens, and the two halves are related by a two-fold symmetry axis running through the macrocycle. The benzene rings are fused into the macrocycle through their ortho positions, with ethylene-glycol-type segments (–OCH2CH2O–CH2CH2–) bridging the two aryl ethers. Because the aryl ether linkages and the ring itself are constrained, the scaffold is relatively rigid across the aromatic portions while the polyether chains provide conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all heteroatoms are ether oxygens, but those oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors and can coordinate cations within the ring cavity.

The molecule is built around a single central quaternary carbon that bears two para-hydroxyphenyl rings and two trifluoromethyl groups, giving a bis(phenol) scaffold with no ring fusion. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring carrying a hydroxyl group at the position opposite the point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is para on both sides. The two halves are related by a mirror or twofold symmetry through the central carbon, and the bulky trifluoromethyl groups restrict rotation about the central bonds, making the structure fairly rigid. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single sp3-hybridized central carbon that bears a hydroxyl group and three para-methoxyphenyl rings, giving a triarylmethanol scaffold. Each aryl ring is a simple benzene ring with no fusion, and each carries one methoxy (–OCH3) ether substituent at the position opposite the attachment point. The three aryl arms are arranged around the central carbon in a propeller-like fashion, which gives the molecule a near three-fold rotational symmetry about the C–OH axis. The bulky triaryl core makes the framework fairly rigid, with rotation limited mainly to the bonds linking the aryl rings to the central carbon. The free hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the three ether oxygens serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries two methyl-free substituents: a methyl group, a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, and two para-hydroxyphenyl rings, making it a diarylalkanoic acid. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring with a hydroxyl group at the position opposite the attachment point, so the two phenol groups are symmetrically placed. The carboxylic acid terminus and both phenolic hydroxyls can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The two aryl rings are bulky and flexible about their bonds to the central carbon, while the aliphatic chain adds conformational freedom. The structure is largely symmetric across the central carbon apart from the acid-bearing chain.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl carbon bonded to two para-substituted benzene rings. Each ring carries a diethylamino group at the position opposite the carbonyl, so the two aryl halves are mirror-related and the whole scaffold has an overall symmetric, roughly linear arrangement. The benzene rings are not fused to each other; they are connected only through the ketone carbon, which gives a fairly rigid aromatic framework. The nitrogen atoms are tertiary amines whose lone pairs conjugate with the rings, and the carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor site in the structure. Because the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, its flexibility comes mainly from the four rotatable ethyl groups.

This molecule is built on a benzanilide-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a central amide linkage, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to one ring and the nitrogen bonded to the other. Each benzene ring is para-substituted, carrying a primary amino group opposite the amide connection, so the overall arrangement is linear and symmetric about the central amide axis. The amide group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the N–H) and an acceptor (the C=O), and the two terminal aromatic amines each add an additional donor pair. The aromatic rings are planar and conjugated with the amide, making the core fairly rigid, with only modest rotational freedom around the amide and ring-to-amide bonds.

The molecule is a diarylmethanol, with a central tetrahedral carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and two identical para-chlorophenyl rings. Each benzene ring carries a single chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment to the central carbon, giving a symmetric substitution pattern that mirrors across the central carbon. The two aromatic rings are not fused to each other; they are joined only through the sp3 carbon, which allows some rotational freedom about the single bonds while the aromatic rings themselves remain rigid and planar. The hydroxyl group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors and contribute to the overall lipophilic character of the scaffold.

The molecule is built from two para-fluorophenyl rings joined through a single sp3 carbon that also bears a hydroxyl group, giving a diarylmethanol scaffold. Each benzene ring is unfused and carries one fluorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is para on both rings. The central carbon is a stereogenic center, but the two aryl groups are identical, so the molecule as drawn has no stereochemical distinction and possesses an approximate two-fold symmetry through the C–OH bond. The aromatic rings are rigid while the bonds linking them to the central carbon allow rotation, giving moderate flexibility overall. The secondary hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is a bipyridine: two pyridine rings joined by a single bond between their 2-positions, giving a biaryl-type scaffold with no fused ring system. Each pyridine ring is a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, and the two nitrogens sit on the same side of the molecule, adjacent to the inter-ring bond. Each ring carries one methyl substituent, with one methyl at the 4-position of one ring and the other at the 4-position of the second ring (relative to the nitrogen), so the two halves are arranged in a pseudo-symmetric pattern. The rings can rotate about the central bond, making the molecule moderately flexible, although the nitrogen lone pairs prefer a planar, syn-oriented conformation. The two pyridine nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone built on a central carbonyl group flanked by two para-substituted phenyl rings. Each of those rings carries a second phenyl ring at the position opposite the carbonyl attachment, so the scaffold is a linear, extended arrangement of four benzene rings joined by a ketone bridge and two single bonds. There are no fused ring systems, and the only functional group is the diaryl ketone. The structure has approximate two-fold symmetry through the carbonyl carbon, and the biphenyl linkages allow some rotation about the single bonds, though the overall shape remains largely planar and rigid. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from two para-substituted benzene rings joined through a single methylene (CH2) bridge, giving a diarylmethane scaffold. Each ring carries a dimethylamino group, N(CH3)2, positioned para to the bridging carbon, so the two halves are mirror-related and the molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry through the central CH2. The aromatic rings are planar and fully conjugated with their nitrogen substituents, while the methylene linker allows rotation about its two single bonds, so the overall shape is moderately flexible. The tertiary amine nitrogens have no N-H bonds, so the molecule offers no hydrogen-bond donors, but each nitrogen lone pair can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, and two bromine atoms occupy the two carbons next to each other on the opposite side, giving a 1,2-dibromo-4,5-dimethyl substitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully rigid, and the substituents are small and non-polar, so the molecule has no conformational flexibility. It carries no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its symmetry is limited to a single mirror plane passing through the ring's axis that bisects the two methyl and two bromine pairs.

This molecule is built on a five-membered thiophene ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom. Attached to the sulfur-adjacent carbon (position 2) is a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to a chlorine. Two bromine atoms occupy the adjacent ring carbons at positions 4 and 5, so the substitution pattern is contiguous and leaves a single ring C–H at position 3. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the sulfonyl chloride and the bromine substituents are distinct. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors; the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the electron-withdrawing groups make the ring electron-poor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, with nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 and the ring carbons bearing the substituents. The nitrogen at position 1 carries a methyl group, so it contributes no hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the unsubstituted nitrogen at position 3 can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, one at the 4-position and one at the 5-position, giving a contiguous dihalogenated substitution pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only conformational freedom is the rotation of the methyl group. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the methyl group and the two different chlorine positions break any mirror plane.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Going around the ring, it carries an amino group (–NH2) and a nitro group (–NO2) on adjacent carbons, with the nitro group placed ortho to the amine, and two chlorine atoms on the two adjacent carbons opposite that side, giving a 1,2-dichloro arrangement that is para to the amine. The substitution pattern is therefore unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a trivial one. The aromatic ring and its directly attached substituents are essentially planar and rigid, with few rotatable bonds. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H groups, while the oxygens of the nitro group and the ring nitrogen-free positions act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, containing two nitrogen atoms separated by one carbon, with one nitrogen bearing a hydrogen atom and the other left unsubstituted. Two nitrile groups, each a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, are attached directly to the ring at adjacent carbon positions, so the substitution pattern is a 4,5-disubstituted arrangement across the ring carbons. The ring itself is planar and fully conjugated, and the linear nitrile groups extend the rigid, flat geometry outward, giving little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry that would make its two substituents equivalent, since the ring NH breaks the symmetry. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and both nitrile nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) sits on one carbon, a nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond) sits on the carbon directly across from it in a para-like relationship, and two fluorine atoms occupy adjacent positions on the opposite side. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring and nitrile are essentially rigid, while the methoxy group can rotate about its bonds. The oxygen of the methoxy and the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries four substituents: a methyl group, two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons, and a carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the methyl group sits ortho to it, so the two groups are adjacent on the ring. The two fluorines occupy the positions that sit meta and para relative to the methyl group, giving a 1,2-difluoro arrangement on one side of the ring. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: two methoxy groups at adjacent positions, a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile), and a nitro group. Its scaffold is therefore a single, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The two adjacent methoxy ethers and the nitro group are electron-withdrawing or donating groups arranged on one face of the ring with no symmetry element beyond the plane of the ring, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical. The flexible CH2 linker and the methoxy groups give some conformational freedom, while the aromatic core is rigid. Oxygen atoms in the methoxy and nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every attached hydrogen sits on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, which contains one sulfur atom in the ring. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached at one of the carbon positions adjacent to the sulfur, while two methyl groups sit on the ring at the other remaining positions, giving a trisubstituted pattern with no ring fusion. The planar aromatic core is rigid, though the carboxylic acid can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a trivial one, because the substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the sulfur and the aromatic ring contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a central five-membered 1,2,3-thiadiazole ring, which contains one sulfur and two adjacent nitrogen atoms in an aromatic arrangement. Two phenyl rings are attached to adjacent carbon atoms of this heterocycle, one on each carbon flanking the sulfur, so the two aryl groups sit side by side with a single bond to the core and no ring fusion. The molecule has no conventional hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. Its nitrogen atoms can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the scaffold is largely planar and rigid, with the rings able to rotate somewhat about the single bonds linking them, and it has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the sulfur atom.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two pyridine rings joined by a single bond between their carbon atoms, forming a 4,4'-bipyridine-type scaffold with bromine atoms on each ring. One ring carries a bromine at the position adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and the other carries a bromine at the 2-position relative to its nitrogen. Each pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aromatic rings are fully conjugated and planar, with a single rotatable bond linking them, so the overall shape is rigid apart from modest twisting about that bond. The structure lacks symmetry because the two bromine atoms sit in different positions on their respective rings.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions. A methylthio group (a sulfur atom bearing a methyl group) is attached to the carbon between the two nitrogens, and two chlorine atoms sit on the ring carbons at the remaining positions. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds other than the methyl rotation on the sulfur. Its substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the two chlorines are not equivalent, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the ring plane. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the two ring nitrogens can act as weak acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups present.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions. It carries three substituents: a methyl group on one ring carbon and two chlorine atoms on the carbons flanking the ring nitrogens, giving a 4,6-dichloro-5-methyl substitution pattern. The fully conjugated ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the methyl group breaks the potential mirror relationship between the two chlorinated positions. The ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and two chlorine atoms, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The two hydroxyls sit meta to each other on the ring, and the chlorines occupy the remaining positions so that each hydroxyl is flanked by a chlorine on one side. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has only a limited degree of symmetry, since the substituent arrangement is asymmetric across the ring. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor character and no donor capability.

The molecule is built on an isatin-type scaffold: a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing an amide nitrogen (lactam). The five-membered ring carries two adjacent carbonyl groups, one as the lactam carbonyl and one as a ketone at the position next to the aromatic ring. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the benzene ring at positions flanking the fused junction, giving a symmetric-looking substitution pattern on one side. The fused bicyclic framework is largely planar and rigid, with few rotatable bonds. The N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a thiosemicarbazide, built from a thiocarbonyl group flanked by a hydrazine unit (NH-NH2) on one side and an NH linked to a phenyl ring on the other. The aromatic ring is a single benzene ring carrying a trifluoromethyl group at the meta position relative to the thiourea nitrogen, giving a 1,3-disubstituted pattern with no ring fusion. Two sp3-like nitrogen NH groups and the terminal NH2 act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the thiocarbonyl sulfur and the fluorine atoms of the CF3 group serve as acceptors. The aryl-thiourea linkage is somewhat flexible, with rotation possible about the C-N and N-N bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a piperidine scaffold, a six-membered saturated ring containing one secondary amine nitrogen. Carbon 4 of that ring carries both a hydroxyl group and a phenyl ring, making it a tertiary alcohol with a quaternary center. The phenyl ring bears a trifluoromethyl group at the meta position relative to the attachment point, a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. The piperidine ring is non-planar and flexible, adopting chair-like conformations, while the aromatic ring is rigid and planar. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because of the substitution pattern on the phenyl ring. The hydroxyl group and the ring NH can each act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen and nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolone (pyrazol-3-one) heterocycle, with a second ring formed by a phenyl group attached to one of the ring nitrogens. The core ring contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries an N-methyl group and the other a phenyl substituent, while the carbonyl sits adjacent to the phenyl-bearing nitrogen. A methyl group is located on the ring carbon next to the methylated nitrogen, and an acetamide group (an acetyl group bonded through nitrogen) is attached to the remaining ring carbon. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and rotates relatively freely about its single bond to the heterocycle, giving the molecule moderate flexibility at that position while the fused core remains planar and rigid. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring carbonyl oxygen and the amide carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a vinyl group (a C=C double bond attached directly to the ring), and the other is an ester oxygen linked to an acetyl group, giving an acetate-type functional group. The ring is planar and aromatic, and the vinyl and acetate groups are both fairly rigid, with the ester linkage allowing limited rotation. The para substitution gives the molecule an approximately linear, symmetric-leaning overall shape. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ester carbonyl oxygen and the ester ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated carbon chain built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a methyl group, a ketone-bearing acetyl unit, and two separate three-carbon arms. Each of those arms terminates in a carboxylic acid group, so the molecule contains two –COOH groups and one ketone carbonyl. Because there are no rings, the structure is highly flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds. The two carboxylic acid groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ketone oxygen serves only as an acceptor. The two acid arms are structurally similar but attached at the same central carbon, giving the molecule an approximate, though not perfect, mirror-type symmetry about that center.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond with no fused ring system. One ring carries an acetyl group, a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group, attached at the position para to the biaryl linkage, giving a linear, para-substituted arrangement. The other ring is unsubstituted. The ketone carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The biaryl bond allows some rotation, though the overall framework is largely planar and rigid, with the carbonyl group extending the aromatic system's shape along one axis.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain aliphatic compound with a four-carbon backbone bearing two terminal functional groups at opposite ends. One end carries a primary amine group (-NH2) attached to the first carbon, while the other end carries a primary alcohol group (-OH) on the fourth carbon, so the substitution pattern is linear and unbranched. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroaromatic systems. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the trivial, since the two ends carry different functional groups, and its chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds. Both the amine and the hydroxyl group can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N-H and O-H bonds, and each can also act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is 4-aminopyrazole, a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms in the ring. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to a carbon at the 4-position, which is the carbon two atoms away from both ring nitrogens and therefore the one that is not directly bonded to either. One ring nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so the ring is an NH-pyrazole tautomer. The scaffold is planar and fully conjugated, with no stereocenters and no rotatable bonds apart from the bond to the amino group, which makes the structure rigid. The ring NH and the exocyclic amino group act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the unprotonated ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms, a primary amino group, and a nitrile (cyano) group. The nitrile carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the ring carries the substituents at positions that leave the ring with one open CH position on each side of the amine. The two fluorines sit on carbons flanking the amino group, and the second fluorine lies meta to the nitrile, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The scaffold is a rigid, planar aromatic core, with only the amino group and nitrile being essentially fixed in plane and little conformational flexibility. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as an acceptor through its lone pair, while the nitrile nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered pyridine ring, an aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom in the ring. Two substituents sit on this scaffold: an amino group (-NH2) attached to one ring carbon, and a bromine atom attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the structure is rigid and lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy different positions. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as an acceptor through its lone pair, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile group, a primary amine, and a trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered unit with no ring fusion, and the three substituents occupy positions that form a 1,2,4-substitution pattern around the ring, with the amine and trifluoromethyl groups adjacent to each other. The nitrile carbon is attached linearly to the ring and carries a triple bond to nitrogen, while the amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as an acceptor through its lone pair. The nitrile nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the three fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group provide weak acceptor character. The molecule is largely rigid and planar, with only the rotation of the trifluoromethyl group adding a small degree of flexibility, and it lacks any internal symmetry beyond local features.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring, one at a carbon adjacent to the amino-bearing carbon and one at the carbon beta to the ring nitrogen, while a primary amino group occupies the remaining substituted position next to the first chlorine. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the ring plane. Being fully aromatic and fused to nothing, the scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds other than the C–N bond of the amine. The amino group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a carboxylic acid group, and an amino group. The carboxylic acid is attached to the ring at one position, the amino group sits para to it, and the methyl group is ortho to the amino group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no internal symmetry, so its three substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and amino groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, so it is a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: a methyl group, a primary amino group, and a nitrile (cyano) group arranged around the ring in a 1,2,4 pattern. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the amino nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring and the nitrile are essentially rigid and planar, with only the methyl group having free rotation. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on the ring at opposite positions, a primary amino group and a hydroxyl group, giving a para-disubstituted pattern. The arrangement has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the two substituent carbons, and the aromatic ring is rigid and planar while the substituents themselves are small and conformationally simple. The amino group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds through its nitrogen lone pair and two N-H bonds, while the hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond through its O-H and accept one through its oxygen.

The molecule is built from three benzene rings connected in a linear chain: an unsubstituted phenyl ring is joined through a methylene (CH2) bridge to a para-substituted central benzene ring, which in turn bears a second unsubstituted phenyl ring directly attached at the para position. Each ring is a fully aromatic, planar six-membered carbocycle, and there are no fused ring systems. The only functional groups are the aromatic rings themselves and the sp3 methylene linker, with no heteroatoms, so the compound has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The 1,4-substitution on the central ring and the symmetric end groups give the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry axis, while the single CH2 linker and the biaryl bond permit some rotational flexibility around those bonds.

The molecule is built on a pyrimidine core, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon between the two nitrogens, while a bromine atom is attached to the ring carbon at the 5 position. At the remaining ring carbon, next to the bromine, an oxygen links to a benzyl group, meaning a benzene ring joined through a flexible CH2 spacer. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The pyrimidine ring is rigid and planar, while the benzyl ether linkage adds conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any significant symmetry because the substituents are placed asymmetrically.

The molecule is a benzaldehyde core, a benzene ring bearing a formyl group (CHO) at one position. At the para position relative to the aldehyde sits an ether oxygen linking to a benzyl group, which is a CH2 bridge attached to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. The structure therefore consists of two separate aromatic six-membered rings joined by a flexible –O–CH2– linker, with no fused ring system. The para-disubstituted central ring gives a linear, elongated shape, while the rotatable ether and methylene bonds add conformational flexibility. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to the ring, which provides two hydroxyl groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds. The other substituent is a benzyloxy group, an ether oxygen linking the central ring to a CH2 unit that is itself bonded to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. The scaffold is therefore a flexible diaryl ether-type framework with two aromatic rings separated by a single rotatable methylene-oxygen linker. The molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry because of the different substituents on each end, and the flexible ether linkage permits considerable conformational freedom.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone: two benzene rings are joined through a central carbonyl carbon, with one ring attached directly to the C=O and the other ring bearing a benzyloxy group. The second ring is para-substituted, with the ether oxygen opposite the carbonyl attachment point, so the substitution pattern is linear and symmetric about the ring axis. The benzyloxy unit consists of an oxygen linking the para position to a CH2 that carries a third phenyl ring, making the molecule a three-ring aromatic framework. The ketone oxygen and the ether oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is largely planar and rigid around the aryl ketone core, with flexibility concentrated at the ether linkage and the benzylic CH2 group.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring that carries two oxygen-linked substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears an oxyacetic acid group, a carboxylic acid (–OCH2COOH) that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The other side carries a benzyloxy group (–OCH2–phenyl), so a second, unsubstituted benzene ring is attached through a flexible ether linkage. The two aromatic rings are not fused; they are connected by a chain of ether oxygen and methylene units, which gives the molecule a relatively extended, elongated shape with moderate conformational flexibility. The overall structure has an approximate two-fold relationship between its two ends but lacks full symmetry because the terminal groups differ. Its hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated in the carboxylic acid, which is both a donor and an acceptor, while the two ether oxygens serve only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring. One position carries an isothiocyanate group, in which a nitrogen is double-bonded to a central carbon that is itself double-bonded to sulfur, giving a linear N=C=S unit. The opposite position carries an ether oxygen linking to a benzyl group, a CH2 bridge attached to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. The two aromatic rings are not fused; they are connected through the flexible ether linkage, so the structure has several rotatable bonds and can adopt multiple conformations. Overall it is largely planar within each ring but otherwise adaptable in shape. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens sit on aromatic or methylene carbons.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a hydroxymethyl group (a primary alcohol, CH2OH) at the position para to the biaryl bond, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The substitution pattern is therefore para on one ring and unsubstituted on the other, giving the molecule an overall elongated, roughly linear shape with no true mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local symmetry of each phenyl ring. The aromatic core is rigid, though the biaryl bond permits some torsional rotation between the two rings. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak, non-classical interaction capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing four substituents. Two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, making the pattern ortho to each other, and a bromine atom sits on the carbon directly opposite the fluorine-bearing carbon that is para to one fluorine. The ring is planar and rigid, and the halogens are the only functional groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its halogen substituents can act only as weak acceptors, and the overall shape lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a modest pseudo-symmetry around the ring axis.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a substituted phenol. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a bromine atom occupies the position para to that hydroxyl group on the opposite side of the ring. A trifluoromethyl group is attached at the position ortho to the hydroxyl, adjacent to it on the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the substituents lying in the same plane as the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group are only weak acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that includes all substituents, since the three groups occupy distinct positions.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, so its scaffold is an aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries two primary amine groups? No — it carries one primary amino group (-NH2) and three halogen substituents: two fluorine atoms and one bromine atom, distributed around the ring. Taking the amine carbon as position 1, the substituents sit at positions 2, 4, 5, and 6 in a pattern that gives the ring no symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric. The ring is planar and rigid, while the amino group can rotate slightly around its carbon-nitrogen bond. The amino group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, whereas the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Four of its six positions carry substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), two fluorine atoms, and one bromine atom, arranged in a fully substituted pattern around the ring. The methoxy oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring and substituent positions are occupied by carbon, halogen, or oxygen with no N–H or O–H bonds. The rigid aromatic core and the lack of asymmetric flexible chains give the molecule little conformational freedom, aside from rotation of the methoxy group. The substitution pattern is not symmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry across the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, which consists of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom. Three halogen substituents sit on the aromatic ring: two fluorine atoms and one bromine atom, arranged in a pattern that leaves the ring with an asymmetric substitution layout rather than any mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with the sulfonyl chloride group the only substituent capable of significant conformational rotation. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups, while the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The halogen atoms contribute additional polarity and weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. It carries a hydroxyl group on one ring carbon, with fluorine atoms on the two carbons flanking that hydroxyl, so the phenol is di-ortho-fluorinated. A bromine atom sits on the carbon directly opposite the hydroxyl, para to it, with the remaining positions bearing hydrogen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric overall, since the three halogen-type substituents are not arranged in a mirror-symmetric way, though the ring itself is planar and rigid. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Three substituents are attached around the ring: two methyl groups and one bromine atom, along with a primary amino group. The amino group sits between one methyl group and the ring carbon that is adjacent to the other methyl, so the two methyls flank it on opposite sides, while the bromine is positioned meta to the amine. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane through its substituents. The amino group offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N–H bonds and one acceptor site through the nitrogen lone pair, while the bromine and the aromatic ring contribute little to hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold. The ring carries a hydroxyl group, which is the only hydrogen-bond donor and also acts as an acceptor through its oxygen. Two tert-butyl groups are attached at positions flanking the hydroxyl, creating a crowded, sterically shielded environment around the phenol oxygen, while a bromine atom sits on the ring at the position opposite the hydroxyl. The substitution pattern is therefore 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-bromophenol-type, with the bulky alkyl groups giving the molecule a bulky, largely nonpolar outline. The ring framework is rigid and planar, while the tert-butyl groups rotate freely, and the arrangement lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the molecule fully symmetric.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying three halogen substituents. Starting from one carbon, a fluorine atom sits on the ring, a bromine atom is placed at the meta position relative to the fluorine, and an iodine atom occupies the ortho position adjacent to the fluorine. The three halogens (fluorine, bromine, iodine) are all attached directly to the aromatic ring and act as electron-withdrawing, weakly polarizing substituents with no hydrogen-bond donor capacity. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three different halogens occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring. The rigid aromatic framework gives it little conformational flexibility, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites beyond the weak halogen interactions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an amino group, a bromine atom, and a fluorine atom. The amino group and the fluorine sit on adjacent carbons, so the fluorine is ortho to the nitrogen-bearing carbon, while the bromine sits para to the amino group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The core is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substituents are small and rigid, so the scaffold is essentially planar and conformationally inflexible. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair acceptor site, while the fluorine acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ from one another.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A hydroxymethyl group (a carbon bearing an OH) is attached to one ring carbon, so the molecule is a benzyl alcohol derivative. Going around the ring, a fluorine atom sits ortho to the hydroxymethyl group and a bromine atom sits para to it on the opposite side, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring and its substituents are largely rigid, with only the C–CH2–OH bond allowing rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine offers weak acceptor capability and the bromine contributes little to hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Reading around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits at one position, a methyl group sits on the adjacent carbon, and a bromine atom occupies the position para to the methoxy group. The aryl ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and methyl groups add only limited conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no overall mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local rotation of the methyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a nitro group. The methyl group and the nitro group sit on adjacent ring carbons, and the bromine atom is positioned para to the methyl group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, so the scaffold is fully planar and rigid. The nitro group, drawn as a charge-separated N-oxide-type unit, is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms and has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring, and it contains no hydrogen-bond donors at all.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. A hydroxyl group (–OH) is attached to one ring carbon, and three halogen substituents are placed around the remaining positions: two fluorine atoms and one bromine atom, with the bromine sitting between the two fluorines. This gives a 1,3,5-type arrangement of substituents on the ring, with the hydroxyl group opposite the bromine. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms serve only as weak acceptors. Apart from the rotation of the hydroxyl group, the rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, and the substitution pattern gives the molecule a mirror-plane symmetry through the hydroxyl carbon and the bromine-bearing carbon.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Its scaffold carries three substituents: an amino group (-NH2) on one carbon, a bromine atom on the carbon para to it, and a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the bromine, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no molecular symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the amino group contributes two N-H hydrogen-bond donors and its nitrogen lone pair acts as an acceptor. The halogens are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and add steric bulk and lipophilic character to the otherwise compact, flat framework.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a bromine atom, and a chlorine atom. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring and defines one end of the scaffold, while the halogens occupy adjacent positions on the ring, with bromine para to the carboxyl group and chlorine meta to it, ortho to the bromine. This 1,3,4-type substitution pattern leaves the ring with no internal symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the carboxyl group can rotate only slightly relative to it, giving the whole structure limited flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the two oxygen atoms), while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is an aryl ketone built from a benzene ring bearing a bromine atom at the position para to the carbonyl group. The carbonyl carbon links the ring to a three-carbon chain in which the terminal carbon carries a chlorine atom, giving a flexible alkyl tail attached to a rigid aromatic core. The benzene ring is a single unfused six-membered aromatic system with a para-disubstituted pattern, which gives the aromatic portion approximate two-fold symmetry along its long axis. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen substituents contribute only weak polar character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, making it an aniline-type aromatic amine, and a bromine atom and a fluorine atom are attached to adjacent carbons on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. Because the three substituents differ, the molecule has no rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic ring is rigid and flat, with only the amino group capable of limited rotation about its bond to the ring. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine atom is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor and the bromine is essentially non-participating.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a bromine atom, and a fluorine atom. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the aromatic ring and serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its hydroxyl) and an acceptor (through its carbonyl oxygen). The bromine and fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, forming a 1,2-halogen pattern that is ortho to each other and meta or para to the carboxylic acid. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the carboxylic acid hydroxyl able to rotate. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, making the molecule asymmetric overall.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no ring fusion. Three substituents sit around the ring: a methyl group, a carboxamide group, and a bromine atom, with the methyl and bromine on adjacent carbons and the carboxamide on the carbon meta to the methyl and para to the bromine. The carboxamide carries a primary amide, which can both donate two hydrogen bonds through its NH2 group and accept one through its carbonyl oxygen.
