The bromine and methyl groups are non-polar and contribute no hydrogen-bond capability. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the molecule has no stereocenters and only limited conformational freedom around the amide bond.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring bearing three groups: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a primary sulfonamide (–SO2NH2). The sulfonamide sits para to the bromine, while the methyl group occupies the position adjacent to the bromine, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern on the aromatic core. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the scaffold is largely rigid apart from rotation around the sulfur–carbon and sulfur–nitrogen bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the three substituents are different. The sulfonamide group supplies two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 unit and two hydrogen-bond acceptors through its sulfonyl oxygens.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a sulfonyl chloride group, arranged in a 1,2,4 pattern. The sulfonyl chloride, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to a chlorine, sits para to the bromine and meta to the methyl group, while the bromine and methyl are adjacent on the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the substituents giving the molecule no internal symmetry, since each position around the ring is distinct. The sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall, the structure is compact and fairly rigid, with its flexibility limited to rotation about the bonds linking the sulfonyl group and methyl group to the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its substituents are a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a bromine atom, and a nitro group, which are arranged on adjacent and nearby carbons around the ring in a trisubstituted pattern. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the methoxy oxygen is a weaker acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since none of its substituents carries an N–H or O–H bond. Because the ring is rigid and planar, the overall framework is largely inflexible, with only the methoxy and nitro groups able to rotate about their bonds to the ring.

This molecule is an acetanilide derivative: a benzene ring bearing an acetamide group (CH3C(=O)NH–) on one carbon and a bromine atom on the carbon directly opposite, giving a para-disubstituted pattern with a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, and it is the only ring system, with no ring fusion. The secondary amide linkage is the principal functional group, containing both an N–H that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and a carbonyl oxygen that can act as an acceptor. The aryl bromide is a weakly polarizable halogen substituent that adds electron-withdrawing character to the ring. Overall the structure is compact and fairly rigid in the aromatic core, with some rotational freedom around the amide C–N and N–aryl bonds.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement: a bromine atom and a hydrazide group, -C(=O)NHNH2, attached directly to the ring through the carbonyl carbon. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic benzene with no additional rings. The hydrazide unit contributes a carbonyl oxygen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while its NH and terminal NH2 groups act as hydrogen-bond donors. The para-disubstituted pattern gives the molecule an approximately linear, elongated shape with a two-fold axis of symmetry running through the ring. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the C-N and amide-like bonds of the hydrazide allow some conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents placed opposite each other, at positions 1 and 4 on the ring, giving a para substitution pattern. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which is linear and strongly electron-withdrawing. The other is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring. The rigid aromatic core and linear nitrile give the structure limited conformational flexibility, and the para arrangement lends it a high degree of symmetry along its long axis. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on positions that are para to each other. One substituent is a thiol group (–SH) attached through its sulfur to a CH2 unit, giving a benzylic thiomethyl arm, and the other is a bromine atom directly bonded to the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered, fully conjugated ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is planar and rigid apart from rotation about the CH2–S bond. The molecule has a mirror plane through the ring axis and is therefore symmetric about its long axis. The thiol sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond and a weak acceptor through its lone pairs, while the bromine is a halogen that can participate in weak halogen-bond interactions.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic compound built on a four-carbon backbone with no rings, so its scaffold is fully acyclic and flexible. At one end sits a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydroxyl, and at the opposite terminus a bromine atom is attached to the terminal carbon through a single bond. Because the chain is unbranched and the two functional groups sit at opposite ends, the molecule has no internal symmetry and no stereocenters. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the bromine contributes only a weak halogen acceptor character.

This molecule is a bicyclic aromatic heterocycle built from a fused benzene and pyridine ring, forming an isoquinoline-type scaffold. The two six-membered rings share an edge, producing a flat, fully conjugated, and rigid framework. A bromine atom is attached to the pyridine-side carbon adjacent to the ring carbon bearing the fused junction, giving a single substitution on the nitrogen-containing ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the bromine breaks the overall symmetry of the fused system. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since it bears no N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) sits at one ring position and serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Directly across the ring, a bromomethyl group (–CH2Br) occupies the para position relative to the acid, while an ortho-positioned nitro group (–NO2) sits adjacent to the bromomethyl carbon, which introduces a strong electron-withdrawing character and a planar, polar nitro moiety. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The carboxylic acid and nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, with only the acid providing a donor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a carboxylic acid group attached through a single methylene (CH2) linker, so the acid is not directly bonded to the ring. The opposite ring position carries a bromine atom. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker and the carboxyl group add some conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The bromine is a weak halogen acceptor, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the two-fold axis through the para-substituted ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with two substituents placed para to each other. One substituent is a terminal alkyne, a carbon-carbon triple bond bearing a hydrogen, which makes the group linear and rigid. The other substituent is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring. The overall scaffold is planar and fully aromatic, with no ring fusion and no stereocenters. Because the two groups sit opposite each other, the molecule has a high degree of symmetry about its long axis. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors in the usual sense, though the terminal alkyne C–H is weakly acidic, and it offers only weak acceptor character from the pi system.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two carboxylic acid groups and one bromine atom, arranged on adjacent ring positions for the diacid and a third position across the ring from one of them. The two carboxyl groups sit ortho to each other, so they are placed next to one another on the aromatic scaffold, which is a single fused-free six-membered ring with no additional rings. The bromine is attached para to one carboxyl group and meta to the other, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The planar aromatic core is rigid, while each carboxyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring. Each carboxylic acid group supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), so the molecule has two donor and up to four acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to one ring carbon is a vinyl group, a carbon-carbon double bond terminating in a CH2, which makes the substituent a simple alkene. A bromine atom sits on the ring carbon directly across from the vinyl group, giving a para (1,4) substitution pattern that yields a symmetric, elongated shape along the long axis. The ring is rigid and planar, while the vinyl group contributes limited rotational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the pi electron clouds of the aromatic and vinyl systems, with the bromine acting as a weak halogen acceptor.

The molecule is a biaryl built from a phenol ring linked directly to an isoxazole ring. The phenol ring is a benzene bearing a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a chlorine atom para to that hydroxyl, while the isoxazole is attached at the position ortho to the hydroxyl. The isoxazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, joined to the benzene ring through a single carbon-carbon bond, so the two rings can rotate relative to each other. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry axis, since the substituents on the phenol ring are arranged asymmetrically.

The molecule is a small heteroaromatic compound built on a single six-membered pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned in a 1,3-relationship. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. A methylthio group (a sulfur atom bearing a methyl group) is attached at the carbon between the two ring nitrogens, while a chlorine atom sits on the carbon farther around the ring, giving a 2,4-disubstituted pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-plane approximation of symmetry, and its rigid planar framework allows little conformational flexibility apart from rotation of the methyl group. The ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, at one position, a chlorine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group, CF3. The boronic acid and trifluoromethyl groups sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other), while the chlorine is located para to the boronic acid, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the CF3 group providing a bulky, strongly electron-withdrawing feature. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms can serve as weak acceptors. Overall, the structure has one rigid aromatic scaffold with a flexible-rotating B(OH)2 unit.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Around that ring are four substituents: two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms each bonded to a methyl group), one chlorine atom, and one primary amino group. The substituents sit at non-adjacent positions in a pattern that makes the ring asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy groups add modest rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, and the oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups can accept them, as can the nitrogen of the amine.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, with no fused rings. It carries two primary amino groups, one at each of the two carbons flanking the ring nitrogens, and a single chlorine substituent on a third ring carbon, giving a 2,4-diamino-6-chloropyrimidine-type substitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, so the scaffold is rigid, while the amino groups can rotate slightly about their bonds. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the chlorine breaks the arrangement of the substituents. Each amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the ring nitrogens provide acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying a nitrile group on one carbon, with the remaining ring positions bearing halogen substituents. Two fluorine atoms sit on the carbons immediately flanking the nitrile, and a chlorine atom occupies the position para to the nitrile, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-difluoro-4-chloro around the nitrile carbon. The ring is aromatic and fully planar, with no ring fusion, and the overall scaffold is a rigid, flat framework with no rotatable bonds beyond the bonds to the substituents. The molecule has a local mirror plane through the nitrile and the para chlorine, giving it a symmetric appearance. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an amino group and three substituents: two methyl groups and one chlorine atom. The primary amine sits on one ring carbon, with a methyl group on each of the two adjacent ring positions, so the amino group is flanked on both sides by methyl substituents. The chlorine atom occupies the position para to the amine, which gives the ring a 2,6-dimethyl-4-chloro arrangement around the amino group. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no fused rings, and it is essentially rigid and planar. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane running through the amine nitrogen and the chlorine-bearing carbon, so it is roughly symmetric. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the chlorine and the ring π-system offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, so its scaffold is one aromatic six-membered carbon ring with no ring fusion. Four of the six ring positions carry substituents: an amino group (-NH2), a fluorine atom, a chlorine atom, and an iodine atom, arranged around the ring in a 2-iodo-3-fluoro-5-chloro-aniline-type pattern with the amino group flanked by the iodine and one ring hydrogen-free neighbour bearing fluorine. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planarity of the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amino group offers two N-H hydrogen-bond donors and its nitrogen lone pair acts as an acceptor; the halogens are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile, C#N), a chlorine atom, and a fluorine atom. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat geometry with no stereocenters. The chlorine and fluorine sit on the ring at positions that place them meta and para relative to the cyanomethyl carbon attachment, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The only notable flexibility comes from rotation about the single bond linking the methylene carbon to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Three substituents decorate that ring: a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl sits on one carbon, the methyl on the adjacent carbon, and the chlorine on a carbon meta to the methyl, giving a trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl and hydroxyl groups add minimal conformational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the chlorine contributes only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, with no fused rings, carrying three substituents on adjacent and separated positions. One substituent is a methyl group, another is a chlorine atom, and the third is an isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S), which is the key reactive functional group. The methyl and isothiocyanate groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, while the chlorine is positioned meta to the methyl and para to the isothiocyanate, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the linear isothiocyanate group adds a small, relatively rigid extension. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the sulfur and nitrogen atoms of the isothiocyanate group, together with the chlorine, can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on the ring: an amino group (-NH2), a nitro group (-NO2) on the carbon adjacent to the amine, and a chlorine atom positioned para to the amine. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, so it contains no fused ring systems and no heteroatoms within the aromatic core. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group) and a fluorine atom. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para arrangement. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on positions para to each other: a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) and a fluorine atom. The molecule is built on a three-carbon acrylic acid chain, with a carboxylic acid group at one end and a double bond conjugated to a benzene ring at the other. The molecule is built on a naphthalene core, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic scaffold. The molecule is a diaryl ketone in which a central carbonyl group links a para-fluorophenyl ring to a thiophene ring attached at its 2-position. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. The molecule is an aryl ketone built from a benzene ring bearing a single para-substituted fluorine atom and a pentanoyl side chain attached through a carbonyl group. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and the fluorine sits directly opposite the carbonyl-bearing carbon, giving a symmetric 1,4-disubstitution pattern across the ring. The C=O group is a hydrogen-bond acceptor with no donor sites anywhere in the structure, and the fluorine adds a weak acceptor character. The linear four-carbon alkyl chain attached to the carbonyl is conformationally flexible, while the ring-carbonyl unit remains comparatively rigid and largely coplanar.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a 1,2,3-triazole ring, forming a benzotriazole scaffold. The five-membered triazole ring contains three adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries an N-H hydrogen and is directly bonded to the fused carbon framework. A hydroxyl group sits on the benzene ring at the position adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon, placing it next to the triazole portion of the molecule. The fused aromatic system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule lacks symmetry because the hydroxyl substituent breaks the mirror relationship of the parent ring system. It offers two hydrogen-bond donors, the phenolic O-H and the triazole N-H, and several acceptor sites on the nitrogen atoms and the oxygen.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered piperidine ring bearing a secondary amine nitrogen at position 1, with no aromatic or unsaturated components. Four methyl groups sit on the two carbons flanking the nitrogen (positions 2 and 6), creating a symmetric 2,2,6,6-tetrasubstitution pattern. The N–H and O–H groups both act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen and oxygen lone pairs serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents. One position bears an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3), which contributes a carbonyl acceptor. The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents arranged in a 1,3,4 pattern. The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused ring system. The phenolic hydroxyl serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the carbonyl oxygen and nitro oxygens act as acceptors, and the intramolecular proximity of the hydroxyl and nitro groups creates a potential for internal hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid), a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid OH and the phenolic OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the nitro oxygens serve as acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no symmetry elements beyond the identity operation.

The molecule is an acyclic, unbranched-chain compound built on a four-carbon backbone with a methyl group at one end and a ketone carbonyl two carbons along. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group para to a vinyl linkage. The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with no fused ring system. The molecule is an acyclic, linear chain of four methylene units connecting a terminal acrylate ester to a terminal primary alcohol. The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single secondary amine nitrogen, giving a diarylamine scaffold with no fused ring systems. Rotation about the two C–N bonds gives moderate flexibility, but the aromatic rings themselves are rigid. The hydroxyl oxygen and the amine NH together provide two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs serve as acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries an NH group. The pyrrole N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the phenolic oxygen can act as both a donor and an acceptor, and the aromatic nitrogen's lone pair is part of the ring system and is not available as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is an iodine atom, a heavy halogen attached directly to the ring. The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a hydrazine group (-NH-NH2) on one carbon and an iodine atom on the carbon directly opposite. The hydrazine group offers hydrogen-bond donor capability through its N-H bonds and acceptor capability through its lone pairs, whereas the iodine contributes a polarizable halogen site with weak acceptor character.

The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that is not part of the aromatic sextet, so it can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a para-substituted benzene ring carrying two groups on opposite sides. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall arrangement has an approximate local symmetry axis running through the ring's para positions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with substituents at the 1 and 4 positions (para-disubstituted). The para arrangement gives the molecule an overall elongated shape with a mirror plane through the ring axis.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, forming a biphenyl scaffold with no fused ring systems. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold. The molecule is a substituted phenylboronic acid built on a single benzene ring. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached to one ring carbon, with a methyl group on the adjacent carbon and a methoxy group on the ring carbon further around, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The two B–OH groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the oxygen atoms of the boronic acid and the methoxy ether can accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no symmetry elements beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring in its planar conformation.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, the methoxy oxygen and the amine nitrogen can accept them, and the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and trifluoromethyl groups add only limited conformational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4-pattern. A carboxylic acid group sits at one position, opposite to it a methoxy group is present, and a trifluoromethyl group occupies the position between the carboxylic acid and methoxy substituents' neighboring carbon, adjacent to the methoxy group. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern: a carboxylic acid group, a methoxy group, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the nitro and methoxy oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two phenyl rings that are not fused to each other. The carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the other is an aminomethyl group, a CH2 linker bearing a primary amine. The para substitution pattern gives the molecule a degree of two-fold symmetry along its long axis, apart from the small flexibility of the two side chains. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the primary amine can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

This molecule is a fused polycyclic aromatic system built from three six-membered rings sharing edges, forming a phenanthroline-type scaffold in which two pyridine-like nitrogen atoms sit on the outer rings in a bay-facing arrangement. The two ring nitrogens each carry a lone pair oriented outward from the framework, so they can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall, the structure is asymmetric, planar, and chelation-capable through its nitrogen pair.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework, with three substituents attached. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group and a nitro group occupy two adjacent positions, so the hydroxyl and nitro groups are ortho to each other. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, with only limited rotational freedom around the bonds to the substituents. The phenolic OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, unbranched-backbone ketone with five carbons in its main chain, bearing a methyl group on the fourth carbon from one end. A single carbonyl group sits at the second carbon, flanked by a terminal methyl on one side and a methylene linker on the other, so the scaffold is a simple aliphatic chain with no ring systems or ring fusion. The branched terminus gives the molecule an asymmetric shape, lacking any internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis. Its only heteroatom is the oxygen of the carbonyl, which can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The chain's several rotatable single bonds make the molecule conformationally flexible.

This molecule is a 1H-imidazole ring bearing two substituents: a methyl group on one carbon of the five-membered ring and a phenyl group attached to the carbon between the two nitrogen atoms. The imidazole is an aromatic, planar, five-membered heterocycle with two nitrogens at the 1 and 3 positions, one of which carries an N-H. The phenyl ring is a simple unsubstituted benzene ring linked to the imidazole by a single bond, allowing relatively free rotation about that bond, so the molecule is only moderately flexible. The overall scaffold is a 2-arylimidazole with a 4-methyl group, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl and phenyl groups sit at different positions. The N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated imidazole nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4-pattern: a methyl group, a nitrile (cyano) group, and a trifluoromethyl group. The methyl and trifluoromethyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the nitrile is positioned para to the methyl group, so the ring is fully substituted on six sides only at three positions and otherwise carries aromatic hydrogens. The nitrile contributes a linear, rod-like carbon–nitrogen triple bond that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair. The trifluoromethyl group is a bulky, strongly electron-withdrawing fluorinated group with no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The molecule has no stereocenters, and its overall shape is essentially planar and rigid, with only the rotation of the trifluoromethyl group adding minor flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Three substituents are attached around the ring: an acetyl group (a ketone bearing a methyl group) at one position, a methyl group at a second position, and a nitro group at a third position adjacent to the methyl group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The acetyl and nitro groups are both electron-withdrawing, while the methyl group is a small, non-polar hydrocarbon substituent. Because the ring is planar and the substituent pattern is asymmetric, the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local plane. Its hydrogen-bond capability is acceptor-only: the carbonyl oxygen and the two oxygens of the nitro group can accept hydrogen bonds, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a primary carboxamide, and a nitro group. The carboxamide (C(=O)NH2) sits para to the methyl group, while the nitro group is ortho to the methyl and meta to the carboxamide, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is a single fused-free ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the rotation of the amide and nitro groups adding limited flexibility. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donors (the NH2) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the nitro group contributes two strong acceptor oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A methyl group sits at one ring position, a sulfonamide group (a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to an NH2 group) sits para to the methyl, and a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing a formal positive charge and two oxygens, one drawn as an anion) sits ortho to the methyl and meta to the sulfonamide. The ring is aromatic, planar, and rigid, with only the methyl rotation and the sulfonamide and nitro bonds providing limited flexibility. The sulfonamide NH2 acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while its two sulfonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern. One substituent is a methyl group, another is a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing two oxygens, one drawn as an N-oxide), and the third is an isocyanate group (a nitrogen double-bonded to a central carbon that is double-bonded to oxygen). The nitro group sits ortho to the methyl group, while the isocyanate is para to the methyl group. The core is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, and it lacks any symmetry. Its rotatable bonds are limited to the nitro and isocyanate attachments, so the scaffold is rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the nitro and isocyanate groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no additional fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons of the ring: a methyl group and a nitro group, the latter drawn as a charge-separated N-oxide-type nitro moiety bearing two oxygens. The methyl group is an electron-neutral alkyl substituent, while the nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and planar with the ring. Because the ring is flat and the substituents are small and rigid, the scaffold has little conformational flexibility and no internal symmetry, since the two substituents differ. The ring nitrogen and the two nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule offers no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to the ring is an acetyl group, a ketone in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a methyl group and to the ring, and a methyl group sits para to it, on the opposite side of the ring. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,4-disubstituted, which gives the molecule a two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring and the attached groups. The ring and carbonyl are largely planar and rigid, while the methyl groups add little conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methyl group and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2. The aromatic core is planar and fully conjugated, so the scaffold is rigid, with only the two substituents able to rotate about their bonds to the ring. The boron atom is trigonal planar and bonded to two hydroxyl groups, which together form the functional handle of the molecule. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and an acceptor through its lone pairs. The molecule has no stereocentres and an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the methyl carbon, the ring centroid, and the boron atom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no ring fusion, that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a methyl group attached directly to the ring, and the other is an aminomethyl group, a CH2 linker bearing a primary amine. Because the two substituents sit opposite each other, the ring has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the carbons bearing them. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the aminomethyl arm adds some rotational flexibility. The primary amine is both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, and the aromatic ring can take part in weaker pi-interactions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent hydroxyl groups and one methyl group, giving a catechol-type scaffold with a methyl substituent. The six-membered aromatic ring is a single, fully conjugated, planar unit with no additional ring fusion. The two hydroxyl groups sit on neighboring carbons, while the methyl group occupies a position meta to one hydroxyl and para to the other, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planar geometry. The core is rigid, with only the hydroxyl and methyl groups free to rotate. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the adjacent pair can cooperate in chelating or intramolecular interactions.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle with a single fused-free ring, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 separated by one carbon, which is the imidazole scaffold. One ring nitrogen bears a hydrogen atom and acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other nitrogen has a lone pair in the plane of the ring and serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. A methyl group is attached to a ring carbon adjacent to the non-protonated nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, making it rigid, and the only flexible element is the rotation of the methyl group.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one sulfur atom at positions that are separated by a two-carbon bridge on one side and a three-carbon bridge on the other, giving a 1,4-relationship across the ring. The nitrogen bears a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine with no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The sulfur is fully oxidized to a sulfone, carrying two double-bonded oxygen atoms, which creates a strongly polar, electron-withdrawing group. The sulfone oxygens and the nitrogen lone pair act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the ring is non-aromatic, flexible in a chair-like conformation, and lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the methyl group and the sulfone.

The molecule is a straight-chain carboxylic acid built on a six-carbon backbone with a methyl branch: the carbon skeleton ends in an isopropyl-type terminus, giving a 5-methylhexanoic acid framework. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and no ring fusion is present. The single functional group is a terminal carboxylic acid, which carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). Because the branch sits on the far end from the acid, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry, though its branched tail makes it somewhat bulkier than a plain linear chain. Its chain is flexible, with freely rotatable single bonds along the alkyl portion.

This molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, with two benzene rings joined by a single bond between their para positions. One ring carries a linear n-butyl chain at the para position, while the other carries a nitrile group, also at the para position, giving the structure a rod-like, elongated shape. Both rings are aromatic and planar, so the rigid core contrasts with the flexible alkyl tail. The molecule has an approximate two-fold axis of symmetry running through the long axis, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The nitrile nitrogen serves as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring bearing a linear ten-carbon alkyl chain on one side and a primary amino group on the other. The benzene core is a single aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the decyl chain is fully saturated and flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds. Because the substituents sit on opposite carbons of the ring, the arrangement has a rod-like, approximately linear shape with a two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the rest of the molecule is essentially nonpolar hydrocarbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a straight, unbranched twelve-carbon alkyl chain attached through an ether oxygen, giving a flexible, long hydrocarbon tail. The opposite side carries a carboxylic acid group directly bonded to the ring, so the aromatic core is flanked by a flexible chain and a planar, polar head. The para substitution gives the molecule an overall elongated, roughly linear shape with a two-fold axis of approximate symmetry through the ring. The ether oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with a seven-carbon straight alkyl chain (heptyl) on one side and a carboxylic acid group on the opposite side, giving it a linear, elongated shape. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, and it is not fused to any other ring system. The alkyl chain is flexible, with free rotation around its single bonds, while the aromatic core remains rigid. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry along its long axis, though the two ends differ chemically. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the rest of the molecule contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit para to each other across the ring: a linear seven-carbon alkyl chain attached through an ether oxygen, and a primary amino group. The alkyl chain is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, and the ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall shape is elongated and only approximately symmetric, since the two ends differ in chemical character.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. One substituent is an acetamide group, a carbonyl attached to a methyl and to an NH that links to the ring. A second is a nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, placed para to the amide nitrogen. The third is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon carrying three fluorine atoms, positioned ortho to the amide. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the substitution pattern is 1,2,4, so the molecule has no symmetry. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and separated positions. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) sits on one ring carbon, and a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) occupies the position para to it. A trifluoromethyl group (a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the nitrile, placing it ortho to that group and meta to the nitro group. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, flat and rigid, with the three substituents giving the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern and no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The nitrile nitrogen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, serving as a planar aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. A sulfonamide group, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and bonded to a primary amine (NH2), is attached at one carbon of the ring. A nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygen atoms with one formally charged, sits on the carbon directly opposite, giving a para substitution pattern. The arrangement is symmetric about the long axis of the ring and fairly rigid, with limited rotational freedom beyond the bonds to the substituents. The sulfonamide NH2 offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the sulfonyl and nitro oxygens serve as multiple hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on opposite positions of that ring, giving a para (1,4) substitution pattern. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) attached directly to the ring, and the other is a nitro group (–NO2) at the opposite position. The carboxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the molecule has a high degree of symmetry about its long axis, with the two substituents lying along a common line through the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a chlorine atom, and the other is a nitro group, with its nitrogen bearing two oxygen atoms in a formally charged arrangement. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, and it is rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core scaffold. The para substitution gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the two substituent positions. The carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework. Two substituents sit on the ring in a para (1,4) relationship: a nitro group, where a nitrogen bearing two oxygens is attached to the ring, and a hydroxymethyl group, a CH2 linked to an OH. The ring is planar and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl arm adds a small degree of rotational flexibility. The arrangement has a two-fold axis of symmetry through the two substituents, though the groups themselves are different. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with a nitro group (–NO2) on one side and an ether oxygen on the other. The ether oxygen links the ring to a methylene carbon that is bonded to a carbonyl, forming an aryloxyacetyl unit, and that carbonyl is part of a hydrazide group (–C(=O)NH–NH2) at the chain end. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the –O–CH2–C(=O)– linker gives the molecule some conformational flexibility. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing substituent, and the terminal hydrazide offers two N–H donors along with carbonyl and nitro oxygen acceptors. Overall the molecule has an elongated, roughly linear shape with a single mirror-symmetric axis through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit para to each other across the ring, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis through those two positions. One substituent is a nitro group, a nitrogen bearing two oxygens, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and can accept hydrogen bonds through its oxygen atoms. The other is an isothiocyanate group, a linear N=C=S unit attached to the ring through nitrogen, which is also electron-withdrawing and has a reactive central carbon. The aromatic ring and the linear isothiocyanate make the molecule rigid and flat, with little conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but its nitro oxygens and isothiocyanate nitrogen and sulfur can act as acceptors.

The molecule consists of two benzene rings joined through a single sulfur atom, forming a diaryl sulfide scaffold. One ring carries a nitro group at the position para to the sulfur linkage, giving a para-disubstituted pattern on that ring, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aromatic rings are planar, and the C–S–C bridge introduces moderate conformational flexibility around the sulfur, so the molecule is not fully rigid. It lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two rings differ in substitution.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, which is a strongly electron-withdrawing acceptor group. The other side carries an ester-type linkage to a sulfonyl group, where a sulfur bonded to two oxygens is attached to a trifluoromethyl carbon bearing three fluorine atoms. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ether-like oxygen and sulfonyl linkage allow some rotational freedom. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring, though the substituents differ. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the nitro and sulfonyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is an acetic acid side chain, consisting of a methylene group linked to a terminal carboxylic acid, and the other is a nitro group attached directly to the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker grants the carboxylic acid group some rotational freedom. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the ring axis, though the two substituents differ. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), whereas the nitro group contributes only hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused partners. Attached at one position is a vinyl group, a two-carbon chain with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, and at the position directly opposite (para) is a nitro group, where a nitrogen bears two oxygens, one doubly bonded and one carrying a formal negative charge. This para-disubstituted pattern gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry along its long axis. The ring and the vinyl unit are conjugated and largely planar, making the structure fairly rigid, with only the vinyl group offering limited rotation. The nitro group has no hydrogen-bond donors but its oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the rest of the framework contributes no donor capacity.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One position bears a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group), and the opposite position bears a sulfur atom linked to a nitro-type N-oxide fragment, giving a sulfur–nitrogen bond with two oxygens on the nitrogen. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the overall shape is rigid apart from rotation around the single bonds to the methoxy and sulfur groups. The substitution pattern is symmetric about the long axis of the ring, though the two substituents themselves are different. The methoxy oxygen and the nitro-type oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving it a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings. Two adjacent methoxy groups (–OCH3) occupy positions that are ortho to each other, and a nitro group (–NO2) sits on the ring at a position para to one of the methoxy groups, establishing a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The ring is flat and rigid, while the methoxy groups add minor conformational flexibility through rotation about their C–O bonds. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the two ether linkages and the nitro group provide several hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a straight-chain eight-carbon alkyl group, which gives the molecule a long, flexible, nonpolar tail. The opposite side carries a carboxylic acid group, a polar functional unit containing both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the two oxygen atoms). The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the alkyl chain can adopt many conformations. The para pattern gives the molecule an approximate linear, rod-like shape with a degree of symmetry along its long axis.

The molecule is a linear biphenyl-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single bond at their para positions, forming a rigid, rod-like core. One ring carries a straight-chain octyl group at the para position, while the other carries a nitrile (cyano) group, also at the para position, giving a highly symmetric, elongated structure with substituents at opposite ends. The aromatic rings are fully planar and conjugated, so the core is stiff, while the eight-carbon alkyl tail adds conformational flexibility at one end. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, with no ring fusion. A linear five-carbon n-pentyl chain is attached to one ring carbon, and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, sits on the carbon directly opposite it, giving a para (1,4) substitution pattern. The molecule therefore has an elongated, rod-like shape with a flexible alkyl tail and a rigid aromatic core. The boron atom bears two hydroxyl groups, which can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aromatic ring offers only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character. The overall arrangement has no internal symmetry axis beyond the two-fold symmetry of the ring itself, since the alkyl chain and the boronic acid group differ in shape and polarity.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring carrying two groups on opposite sides: a pentyloxy chain (an oxygen bonded to a five-carbon straight alkyl group) and a carboxylic acid. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, which is planar and rigid, while the linear pentyl tail adds conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is symmetric about the long axis of the ring, giving the molecule an elongated, rod-like shape. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a diaryl ether scaffold, with two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom. One ring carries an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) attached directly to the ring, positioned para to the ether linkage, which gives a clean 1,4-disubstitution pattern on that ring. The other ring is unsubstituted phenyl. There are no fused ring systems, and the molecule has only one carbonyl oxygen as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, with no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aromatic rings can rotate about the C–O–C ether bonds, so the molecule is moderately flexible, though the aromatic planes keep it fairly extended and rigid in local regions.

The molecule is built on a diaryl ether scaffold, in which two benzene rings are joined through a single oxygen atom. One ring carries a primary amino group (-NH2) at the position para to the ether oxygen, while the other ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric across the two aromatic units. Neither ring is fused to another, and the molecule contains no stereocenters. The ether linkage provides rotational flexibility around the C-O bonds, allowing the two rings to adopt a range of relative orientations, though the aromatic rings themselves are planar and rigid. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the ether oxygen serves as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from a straight four-carbon chain attached through an ether oxygen to a benzene ring, giving a phenoxy group at one end and a carboxylic acid at the other. The benzene ring is a single unsubstituted six-membered aromatic ring, so there is no ring fusion and no additional substituents on the ring carbons, which yields a simple monosubstituted pattern. The terminal carboxylic acid group contains a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and a hydroxyl hydrogen that can donate one, and the ether oxygen provides an additional acceptor site. The three methylene units in the chain make the molecule fairly flexible, with several rotatable bonds connecting the rigid aromatic ring to the polar acid terminus. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the aromatic ring.

The molecule is built on a diaryl ether scaffold, with two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen bridge. One ring carries a free hydroxyl group on the carbon para to the ether linkage, giving a para-substituted phenol unit, while the other ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group. Both aromatic rings are planar and rigid, but the ether oxygen allows rotation about the two C–O bonds, so the overall shape is moderately flexible. The molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric pattern across the whole structure because the hydroxyl makes the two rings chemically distinct. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a central thiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing both sulfur and nitrogen. One carbon of this thiazole carries a phenyl ring, and the carbon flanked by sulfur and nitrogen carries a pyridin-2-yl ring, so the two outer rings sit at non-adjacent positions. There are no sp3 carbons, no rotatable linkers beyond the two single bonds joining the rings, and no polar functional groups such as hydroxyls or amines. The pyridine nitrogen and the thiazole nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the scaffold is largely planar and fully aromatic, with modest conformational flexibility limited to rotation about the two inter-ring bonds.

The molecule is built on a 1,3-thiazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. At the carbon between the sulfur and nitrogen (position 2) sits a meta-tolyl group, meaning a benzene ring bearing a methyl group at the position one removed from the attachment point. Position 4 of the thiazole carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the molecule is a 2,4-diarylthiazole with no ring fusion. It contains no classical hydrogen-bond donors, while the thiazole ring nitrogen can serve as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The biaryl linkages allow some rotation, and the fully aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid.

This molecule is a thiosemicarbazide in which a hydrazine unit is attached to a thiocarbonyl carbon that is bonded to an anilino nitrogen. The scaffold is an acyclic thiourea-type backbone, with a terminal NH2 group on one nitrogen and a phenyl ring on the other. The phenyl ring is a single benzene ring with no fusion and is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion carries no additional functional groups. The thiocarbonyl group (C=S) and the adjacent NH groups form a thioamide-like unit that can act as both hydrogen-bond donors through its N–H bonds and acceptors through the sulfur atom. The chain is flexible about its single bonds, though the thioamide portion has partial double-bond character that limits rotation.

The molecule is built on a diphenylamine-azobenzene scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a central N=N azo linkage, with the second ring also bearing an NH bridge to a third phenyl ring. Each of the three benzene rings is a fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The azo group and the secondary amine nitrogen are the principal functional groups, and the para-disubstituted central ring carries both linkages on opposite sides. The structure is largely planar and conjugated across the chain, which makes it fairly rigid, though rotation about the single bonds to the amine and the rings remains possible. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the azo nitrogens and the amine nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an azobenzene derivative: two phenyl rings joined by a nitrogen–nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) configuration, giving a largely planar, rigid scaffold. The first ring carries a hydroxyl group at the position para to the azo linkage, while the second ring is unsubstituted. The two rings are not symmetrically equivalent because only one bears the hydroxyl substituent. The azo nitrogens each have a lone pair and can accept hydrogen bonds, and the phenolic oxygen is also an acceptor, while the hydroxyl hydrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond donor.

This molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a diazo bridge (–N=N–), giving an azobenzene-type scaffold in which the two aromatic rings sit on opposite ends of a linear, conjugated linker. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries an isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S) at the position para to the azo link, so the substitution pattern is simple and asymmetric. The molecule is largely planar and rigid because of the aromatic rings and the conjugated azo unit, with only limited rotational freedom about the single bonds connecting the rings to the linker. It has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two azo nitrogens and the nitrogen and sulfur atoms of the isothiocyanate group.

This molecule consists of a single benzene ring bearing a four-carbon chain at one position, so it is a monosubstituted aromatic compound with no ring fusion. The side chain is a straight, flexible series of three methylene groups that terminates in a carboxylic acid, which is the sole functional group present. The carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the aromatic ring contributes no hydrogen-bond capability of its own. The phenyl ring is planar and rigid, whereas the alkyl linker gives the overall structure conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the ring and the terminal acid group.

The molecule is built on a cinnamic acid-type skeleton: a carboxylic acid group joined to a carbon-carbon double bond that is attached to a benzene ring, with the alkene held in the trans (E) geometry. The aromatic ring carries a second phenyl ring at the position opposite the side chain, giving a linear biphenyl unit fused to nothing, so the two benzene rings are connected by a single bond and can rotate relative to each other. Overall the structure is extended and fairly rigid along its length, with the conjugated alkene-acid system adding planarity, while the biphenyl linkage retains some torsional freedom. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The aromatic rings and alkene contribute only weak, non-classical interactions, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local two-fold symmetry of each phenyl ring.

This molecule is a biaryl-type structure made of two rings joined by a single bond: a benzene ring and a five-membered aromatic heterocycle. The five-membered ring is an imidazole, containing two nitrogen atoms separated by one carbon, with one nitrogen bearing a hydrogen. The phenyl group is attached at a carbon position of the imidazole ring, so the two rings are connected but not fused. The molecule is largely planar and fully aromatic, which gives it a rigid scaffold with limited conformational flexibility, apart from rotation about the single bond linking the rings. The N–H group of the imidazole can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The phenyl ring contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a five-membered 1,2,4-triazolidine-3,5-dione core, a saturated-looking ring bearing two carbonyl groups at positions adjacent to the ring nitrogens. The ring contains three nitrogen atoms, two of which carry hydrogens and one of which is bonded directly to a phenyl ring, so the phenyl group is attached at a single ring nitrogen with no additional fusion. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors while the two N–H groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, giving the core a strongly polar, donor-and-acceptor-rich character. The unsubstituted phenyl ring is a flat aromatic system that rotates about its single bond to the ring nitrogen, providing modest conformational flexibility. Overall the scaffold lacks any internal symmetry because the phenyl substituent breaks the symmetry of the heterocyclic core.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. A hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached to the ring carbon at the 4-position, which is para to the nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is symmetric across the ring. The piperidine nitrogen is a secondary amine, bearing one hydrogen, and it can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the primary alcohol oxygen can likewise donate and accept. The ring is fully saturated and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, with the hydroxymethyl substituent able to occupy an equatorial position.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. A two-carbon side chain is attached at the 4-position, placing the substituent para to the ring nitrogen. That side chain ends in a primary amide, a carbonyl group bonded to an NH2 group, connected to the ring through a single methylene linker. The ring itself is flat and fully conjugated, while the linker gives the side chain some rotational freedom. The amide nitrogen and carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the pyridine nitrogen provides an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site.

This molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with a tert-butyl group on one side and a chloroacetyl group on the other. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, fully saturated quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, which gives the molecule a rigid aromatic core with a compact, sterically demanding substituent. The ketone carbonyl is directly attached to the ring, and its alpha carbon carries a chlorine atom, so the side chain is a short, flexible two-carbon unit. The molecule has an approximate local symmetry axis running through the ring, though the chloromethyl end breaks full symmetry. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fusion to any other ring. One ring carbon carries a tert-butyl group, a central quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups, which adds a bulky, nonpolar, three-dimensional region. The ring carbon directly opposite it, at the para position, bears a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, where boron is bonded to two hydroxyl groups. The two substituents sit symmetrically across the ring, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold axis through the ring. The aromatic core and the boron center are rigid and planar, while the tert-butyl group is rigid but bulky. The boronic acid's two hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and also accept one through their oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a tert-butyl group, a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups, which adds bulk and a compact, roughly spherical hydrophobic region. The other substituent is a carbohydrazide group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to an amide nitrogen that carries a free terminal amino group, giving a planar amide linkage followed by a flexible N–N single bond. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the tert-butyl group is rotationally symmetric around its attachment point, and the hydrazide tail has some rotational freedom. The amide N–H and the terminal NH2 act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pairs serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a tert-butyl group, a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups, which is bulky and nonpolar. The other is a carboxylic acid group attached directly to the ring, giving the molecule its only polar functional group. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The para arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry about its long axis, and the rigid aromatic ring limits conformational flexibility, though the tert-butyl and carboxyl groups can rotate. The carboxylic acid offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the rest of the structure contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving it a planar, rigid aromatic core with a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. One substituent is a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3), a strongly electron-withdrawing group attached directly to the ring. The other is a benzylic methylene linker (-CH2-) bonded to a sulfonyl chloride group (-SO2Cl), whose sulfur carries two double-bonded oxygen atoms and a chlorine. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The chain between the ring and the sulfonyl group provides some rotational flexibility, whereas the aromatic core and the trifluoromethyl group remain fixed in shape.

The molecule is a 5-aryl-1H-tetrazole, in which a tetrazole ring is attached directly to a benzene ring. The five-membered tetrazole contains four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, and it carries a single N-H on one of its nitrogens, which makes it an acidic, hydrogen-bond donor site. The benzene ring bears two chlorine substituents, one ortho to the tetrazole attachment and the other at the meta position relative to it, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern on the aromatic core. The two rings are joined by a single bond and are not fused, so the molecule has a relatively rigid, planar-leaning biaryl-type framework. The nitrogen-rich tetrazole provides several hydrogen-bond acceptor positions, while the chlorines add lipophilic bulk without contributing hydrogen-bonding ability.

The molecule consists of a 1H-tetrazole ring bonded directly to a benzene ring that carries two chlorine atoms at the positions flanking the biaryl bond, giving a 2,6-dichlorophenyl group. The five-membered tetrazole ring contains four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, with the carbon bearing the bond to the phenyl ring and the remaining ring nitrogen carrying a hydrogen. Because the two chlorines sit on both sides of the linking bond, the phenyl and tetrazole rings are forced out of coplanarity, producing a twisted, fairly rigid biaryl arrangement. The overall framework has an approximate mirror plane through the biaryl axis, so the two chlorines are equivalent. The acidic N–H on the tetrazole serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule consists of a benzene ring bearing a chlorine atom at the para position relative to a single bond to a second ring. That second ring is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, which is a 1H-tetrazole with the ring attached through its carbon. The two rings are joined directly by a single bond, giving a biaryl-type scaffold with no fused ring system. The phenyl ring is planar and carries only the chlorine as a substituent, so its substitution pattern is para-disubstituted. The tetrazole ring bears an acidic N-H that serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while its several nitrogen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rotatable bond between the two rings allows limited conformational flexibility, and the overall shape is largely planar and elongated.

The molecule is built around a planar 5-membered rhodanine-type ring: a thiazolidine ring bearing a thiocarbonyl (C=S) and a lactam carbonyl (C=O), with an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond at the 5-position. This exocyclic alkene links the heterocycle to a para-substituted benzene ring carrying a dimethylamino group (N(CH3)2) at the opposite end, giving a largely conjugated, extended scaffold with a rigid, nearly flat geometry. The benzene ring's substitution pattern is para (1,4), which imparts a two-fold pseudo-symmetry along the long molecular axis. The ring NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, thiocarbonyl sulfur, and dimethylamino nitrogen act as acceptors.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined directly by a single bond, with no linker atoms between them. One ring is a benzene ring carrying a single fluorine atom at the position para to the connection point, so the substitution pattern is simple and para-disubstituted. The other ring is a five-membered isoxazole, a heteroaromatic ring containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, attached through a carbon next to the oxygen. The bond between the two rings allows rotation, so the overall shape is largely planar but with some conformational flexibility. The fluorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a biaryl-type compound built from a para-substituted anisole ring linked directly to a tetrazole ring. The benzene core carries a methoxy group (an aryl ether, O-CH3) on one carbon and the tetrazole on the carbon opposite it, giving a para substitution pattern with a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. The five-membered tetrazole is a fully nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic ring with four nitrogens and one carbon, attached to the benzene through its carbon atom. The N-H on the tetrazole ring makes it a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogens and the ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is largely planar and rigid, with only the methoxy group offering limited conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a nitro group, a hydroxyl group, and a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen. The nitro group and the hydroxyl sit on adjacent carbons, so the hydroxyl is ortho to the nitro group, while the morpholine nitrogen sits para to the nitro group on the opposite side of the ring. The morpholine is a saturated six-membered ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen, adopting a chair-like conformation that adds some three-dimensional bulk relative to the flat aromatic core. The phenolic hydroxyl can donate a hydrogen bond, while the nitro oxygens, the morpholine oxygen, and the morpholine nitrogen can all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the molecule is largely planar in its aromatic portion with a flexible, non-aromatic appendage.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a bromine atom on one carbon and a tetrazole ring on another, placing the two substituents in a meta relationship across the ring. The bromine is a halogen substituent that makes the pyridine ring electron-poor, while the tetrazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, attached to the pyridine through a single carbon-carbon bond. This biaryl-type linkage permits some rotation about the bond joining the two rings, giving moderate rather than complete rigidity. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a planar arrangement of its aromatic rings, and the lack of a mirror plane between the two rings makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The tetrazole's N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine nitrogen and the several tetrazole nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a biaryl built from two pyridine rings joined by a single bond between carbon atoms adjacent to the ring nitrogens, giving a 2,2'-bipyridine-type scaffold. Each pyridine carries one methyl substituent on the ring carbon meta to the linking position, so the two methyl groups sit on the same side relative to the central bond and the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoint of the inter-ring bond. The two aromatic rings are fully planar and fused to nothing else, and the rigid, conjugated framework allows little conformational flexibility apart from rotation about the central bond. The two ring nitrogens are positioned to face each other across that bond, making them hydrogen-bond acceptors with no hydrogen-bond donors present, and they can also serve as a chelating pair for metal coordination.

The molecule is built on a five-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms and three carbons in the ring, with the ring carbons bearing the cyclic core. One carbon of this ring is quaternary and carries two methyl substituents, giving a gem-dimethyl pattern on that position. The ring is fused to nothing else and is otherwise saturated apart from two carbonyl groups, one of which forms a cyclic urea-type unit with the two ring nitrogens and the other a ketone-like carbonyl adjacent to a carbon bonded to a nitrogen. The scaffold is compact and rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond the rotation of the two methyl groups.
