Hydrogen-bond capability is present: the two ring N–H groups act as donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as acceptors.

This molecule is a hydantoin ring, a five-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms and two carbonyl groups, with the carbonyl at the 2-position flanked by an NH and the carbonyl at the 4-position flanked by an NH. The carbon at the 5-position is quaternary and carries two phenyl rings, so the scaffold is a single saturated heterocycle with two pendant benzene rings attached at one sp3 carbon. Because the two phenyl groups share that carbon, they are arranged in a gem-diaryl pattern and are not fused to the central ring. The two imide-type N–H groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The core ring is fairly rigid, though the phenyl rings can rotate about their single bonds to the central carbon.

The molecule is a flavone-type scaffold: a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core carrying a phenyl ring attached at the 2-position of the pyranone ring. The chromone is a fused bicyclic system in which a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring shares an edge with a benzene ring, giving a flat, largely rigid aromatic framework with the pendant phenyl ring able to rotate about a single bond. On the fused benzo ring, three adjacent hydroxyl groups sit side by side, creating a vicinal polyphenol substitution pattern, while the unsubstituted phenyl ring contributes no polar groups. The carbonyl oxygen of the pyranone and the ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the three hydroxyl groups provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites. The molecule has no overall mirror or rotational symmetry because of the asymmetric hydroxylation pattern on one ring.

This molecule is a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 relationship, fused to nothing else, making it a single monocyclic ring. The ring is a pyrimidinedione-type scaffold: one carbonyl sits between the two nitrogens as a cyclic urea unit, and a second carbonyl sits adjacent to one of those nitrogens as a cyclic amide, so the ring carries two ketone-like C=O groups in total. A methyl group is attached to the ring carbon next to one nitrogen, giving a single substitution on an otherwise unsubstituted ring. The ring is partially saturated with one sp3 methylene carbon, so it adopts a non-planar, somewhat puckered conformation with limited flexibility. Both ring NH groups are hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because of the asymmetric methyl placement.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that contains two nitrogen atoms. The fused bicyclic core is fully aromatic and essentially planar, which makes the framework rigid with little conformational flexibility. Two methyl groups sit on adjacent carbons of the benzene portion, giving a 5,6-dimethyl substitution pattern. The imidazole ring carries one pyrrole-type N–H, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other, pyridine-type nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks symmetry beyond the planar framework itself, since the two methyl groups and the N–H position break any mirror-type equivalence within the ring system.

The molecule is built on a coumarin-type scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a six-membered α-pyrone (2H-chromen-2-one) ring that contains a lactone carbonyl and a ring oxygen. The bicyclic core is planar and largely rigid, with the fused rings sharing a bond. A methyl group sits on the pyrone ring at the carbon adjacent to the fusion, and two hydroxyl groups are attached to the benzenoid ring at meta positions relative to each other, one on each side of the ring oxygen's attachment. The two phenolic OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the lactone carbonyl oxygen and the ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the substituents are placed asymmetrically on the two sides of the fused system.

This molecule is built on an indoline-2,3-dione (isatin) scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring that carries two adjacent carbonyl groups. The benzene ring bears two methyl substituents, placed meta to each other, which breaks any mirror symmetry in the aromatic portion. The fused bicyclic core is essentially planar and rigid, with the 1,2-dicarbonyl unit and the amide-type nitrogen lying in the same plane as the aromatic ring. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a 2,3-dihydrobenzofuran scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered oxygen-containing ring that is partly saturated, with a CH2–CH2 unit linking the aromatic carbon to the ether oxygen. An acetyl group, a methyl ketone, is attached to the benzene ring at a position para to the ring oxygen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the aromatic plane. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, while the acetyl group retains some rotational freedom about its single bond to the ring. The ketone carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen provides a second, weaker acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone), a hydroxyl group, and a primary carboxamide. The hydroxyl and carboxamide groups sit on adjacent carbons, so they are ortho to each other, while the acetyl group sits meta to the carboxamide and para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the acetyl and carboxamide groups can rotate only modestly about their single bonds to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The phenol oxygen and the amide NH2 can both donate hydrogen bonds, while the ketone oxygen, the amide carbonyl oxygen, and the phenol oxygen can each accept them. The ortho arrangement of the hydroxyl and amide allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between them.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents. Two groups sit on adjacent ring carbons: a carboxylic acid and a hydroxyl group, forming an ortho-hydroxybenzoic acid arrangement. The third substituent, an acetyl group (a methyl ketone), sits on the ring at a position para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxyl and acetyl groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygens of the carbonyl and hydroxyl groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the planar ring, since the three substituents are distinct.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on the ring: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) on one carbon adjacent to the sulfur, and a nitrile group (C≡N) on the carbon at the opposite alpha position. This 2,5-disubstitution pattern places the two electron-withdrawing groups on opposite ends of the ring, giving the molecule an approximately linear, elongated shape with a single flat, rigid framework and only limited rotational freedom in the acetyl group. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, but the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no additional fused rings. An amino group (–NH2) is attached to one carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen's neighboring position, and a bromine atom is attached to the carbon directly next to the ring nitrogen on the opposite side, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pattern relative to the nitrogen. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the amino group's two N–H bonds make it a hydrogen-bond donor. The aromatic framework is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry that would make its two substituents equivalent.

This molecule is a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom in the ring. Two substituents sit on that ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a primary amino group on the carbon meta to the nitrogen, in the 5-position relative to the methoxy group. The substitution pattern is therefore 2,5-disubstituted, with the two groups placed on opposite sides of the ring. The scaffold is small, rigid, and planar, with few rotatable bonds beyond the methoxy group. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the ring nitrogen and the methoxy oxygen can accept them.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries an N-H group at the ring junction. The amino group (NH2) is attached to the benzene portion at a position that places it on the carbon remote from the fused ring junction, giving a single substitution on the six-membered ring. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the amine. The indole N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aromatic nitrogen lone pair and the primary amine nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the single amino substituent breaks the symmetry of the bicyclic core.

This molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated five-carbon chain, with no rings or fused ring systems, so its scaffold is simply a linear aliphatic backbone. At one terminus sits a primary amine (-NH2) attached to a methylene carbon, and at the other terminus is a carboxylic acid (-COOH), giving it a bifunctional, end-to-end substitution pattern. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror plane of the extended chain, and its many single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility. The amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carboxyl group offers both donor and acceptor capability through its hydroxyl hydrogen and carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. A carboxylic acid group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position of the pyrrole portion. On the benzene portion, a benzyloxy group (an oxygen linked to a CH2 bridge that leads to a second, separate phenyl ring) sits at the position para to the ring nitrogen's attachment point across the fused system. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the benzyloxy side chain adds some conformational flexibility. The NH of the indole and the carboxylic acid OH serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carboxyl oxygens, the ether oxygen, and the pyrrole-type nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, with the molecule lacking any symmetry.

The molecule is a substituted 2-pyridone, a six-membered aromatic-type ring containing one nitrogen atom with a carbonyl group adjacent to that nitrogen. The nitrogen carries a methyl substituent, so the ring nitrogen is tertiary and cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor. A methyl group sits on the carbon next to the carbonyl, and a bromine atom is attached to the ring carbon meta to the nitrogen, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only flexibility comes from the rotation of the two methyl groups. The lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen makes it the sole hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a pyrimidine core, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions. A tert-butoxy group, bearing a central oxygen bonded to a carbon that carries three methyl groups, is attached at the carbon between the two ring nitrogens. A bromine atom sits on the ring carbon at the 5-position, which lies across from that substituent. The ring is fully planar and aromatic, while the bulky tert-butyl group provides a compact, three-fold symmetric region. The ether oxygen and the two ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two pyridine rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond. One ring carries a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, placing the halogen at the 2-position relative to that nitrogen and next to the linking bond. The second pyridine ring carries a bromine atom at the 5-position, para-like to the linking carbon across the ring. Both rings are fully aromatic and planar, and the bond between them is rotatable, so the overall shape is only modestly flexible. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors because it has no N-H or O-H groups. The two pyridine nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two rings bear different substituents in different positions.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. One carbon carries a trifluoromethyl group, which is a single carbon bonded to three fluorine atoms and attached directly to the ring. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon next to the trifluoromethyl-bearing carbon, and a bromine atom is located on the ring carbon meta to the trifluoromethyl group and para to the chlorine. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with only the trifluoromethyl group rotating about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond a rough mirror plane through the ring, since the three substituents are all different. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the halogen atoms and fluorines can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions, forming a substituted phenol scaffold. Going around the ring, a hydroxyl group sits on one carbon, a bromine atom is placed meta to it, and a chlorine atom occupies the position para to the bromine and ortho to the hydroxyl, giving an asymmetric 1,2,4-type substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core, and the halogens lie in the ring plane. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine and bromine atoms serve only as weak halogen-bond acceptors. The compound has no fused ring systems and only one ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat aromatic scaffold with no fused ring systems. Three substituents sit on that ring: an ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain) on one carbon, a bromine atom on the carbon para to it, and a formyl group (a carbonyl bearing a hydrogen) on the carbon ortho to the ethoxy group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a loose overall symmetry, with the ethyl tail adding some conformational flexibility while the ring stays rigid. The aldehyde oxygen and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a planar, rigid scaffold with no ring fusion and no saturated portions. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a fluorine atom, placed on carbons adjacent to and across from the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the planar framework. The pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only hydrogens are on the methyl group and the ring carbons. The halogens and methyl group are attached directly to the aromatic ring with little conformational freedom, so the overall structure is compact and largely inflexible.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions: a nitrile (cyano) group, a fluorine atom, and a bromine atom. The nitrile carbon is attached directly to the aromatic ring and is linear, while the fluorine sits ortho to it and the bromine sits meta to the nitrile and para to the fluorine, giving an unsymmetrical, non-fused scaffold. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the substituents add no rotatable bonds, so the structure is essentially inflexible. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all ring positions not bearing substituents carry only aromatic C–H bonds.

This molecule is a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings or extra side chains beyond the two halogen substituents. A bromine atom sits on one ring carbon and an iodine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the two halogens are placed on opposite sides of the ring, giving a 2,5-disubstituted substitution pattern. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and it has no symmetry because the two substituents differ. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall, it is a small, flat, halogenated aromatic heterocycle.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned meta to each other within the ring. Bromine is attached to one carbon of the ring and iodine to another carbon flanked by the two nitrogens, so the two halogen substituents sit at non-adjacent positions and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the halogen attachments. Because the nitrogens lack attached hydrogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the two ring nitrogens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The halogens are weak acceptors and contribute to the overall electron-poor character of the aromatic core.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a single six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, placing it at the 2-position, and a bromine atom is attached to the ring carbon three positions away from the methyl-bearing carbon, at the 5-position, giving a 2,5-disubstitution pattern. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents sit on different positions. The pyridine nitrogen provides a hydrogen-bond acceptor site through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The methyl group and the bromine together make the scaffold asymmetric and contribute bulk on opposite sides of the ring.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two six-membered aromatic rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond. One ring is a pyridine, a nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic ring, and the other is an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the scaffold is a 2-phenylpyridine core. A bromine atom sits on the pyridine ring at the position meta to the nitrogen, on the carbon farther from the phenyl attachment, while the phenyl ring carries no substituents. The molecule has no stereocenters and only one rotatable bond linking the two rings, so it is largely planar and rigid, with limited conformational freedom. The pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: an aldehyde group, a hydroxyl group, a bromine atom, and a trifluoromethoxy group. The aldehyde carbon is directly attached to the ring, and the hydroxyl sits ortho to it, so the two groups are adjacent and can engage in an intramolecular interaction. The bromine and trifluoromethoxy groups are placed meta to each other on the opposite side of the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the trifluoromethoxy group adds some conformational freedom around its ether bond. The phenolic hydroxyl and the aldehyde oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, respectively.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Its substituents sit at positions around the ring: a hydroxyl group and an adjacent methoxy group form an ortho pair, a bromine atom sits meta to the aldehyde, and a formyl (aldehyde) group provides a carbonyl. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the methoxy oxygen, the aldehyde oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid apart from rotation of the methoxy and formyl groups, and it lacks any symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A carboxylic acid group is attached at the 3-position of the ring, relative to the nitrogen. Two halogen substituents are present on the ring: a chlorine atom adjacent to the nitrogen at the 2-position and a bromine atom at the 4-position, so the two halogens sit on adjacent carbons. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system, and the molecule has no symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on an indoline (2,3-dihydroindole) scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered saturated nitrogen-containing ring. The fused bicycle is largely planar on the aromatic side, while the CH2–CH2 bridge of the five-membered ring adds some conformational flexibility. A nitro group sits on the benzene ring adjacent to the ring-fusion nitrogen-bearing carbon, and a bromine atom is placed on the aromatic ring at a meta position relative to the nitro group. The secondary amine nitrogen (NH) in the five-membered ring acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and can also accept a hydrogen bond through its lone pair. The nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the nitro and bromo substituents break the symmetry of the aromatic ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents. A primary carboxamide group and a hydroxyl group sit on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho relationship, while a bromoacetyl group, a ketone bearing a CH2Br unit, sits on the ring meta to the amide. The hydroxyl is ortho to the amide, which allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between them. The ring itself is planar and aromatic, and the only notable flexibility comes from the rotatable bonds linking the carbonyl groups to the ring and from the CH2Br arm. The amide NH2 and the phenolic OH both act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and ketone carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the trivial one.

The molecule is a benzothiophene, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiophene ring sharing one carbon-carbon bond. The sulfur atom sits in the five-membered ring, and the two carbons of the thiophene ring not involved in fusion form a C=C double bond that together with the benzene ring makes the system fully aromatic and planar. A single bromine atom is attached to the benzene portion, placed on the ring carbon meta to the fusion-adjacent carbon on the same side as the thiophene ring's remote C-H positions. The fused framework is rigid and flat, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric arrangement because of the asymmetric bromine placement. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the thiophene sulfur provides only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries an N-H group. A bromine atom is attached to the benzene portion at the position meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen-adjacent side, giving a single halogen substituent on the six-membered ring. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the overall planar framework. The pyrrole N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen lone pair, being part of the aromatic sextet, is a weak acceptor. The bromine adds a lipophilic, electron-withdrawing substituent that is capable of weak halogen-bond interactions.

This molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. A carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and a bromine atom sits on a carbon positioned meta to that amide, with the ring nitrogen between them. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the framework is rigid and the molecule has only minimal conformational flexibility, mostly around the amide bond. The amide group supplies two hydrogen-bond donors (the NH2 hydrogens) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the pyridine nitrogen provides an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. Attached to this ring is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a chlorine atom, which is the most reactive functional group present. A bromine atom sits on the ring at the position meta to the carbonyl group and on the opposite side of the nitrogen, giving a 3,5-disubstituted pattern. The arrangement has an approximate mirror plane running through the nitrogen, the carbonyl carbon, and the midpoint of the ring. The ring is rigid and planar, with only the carbonyl bond offering rotational freedom. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O bonded to hydrogen) is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position. A bromine atom is bonded to a ring carbon at the 5-position, positioned meta-like to the nitrogen across the ring, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen acting as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no additional ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position. A bromine atom sits on the ring at the 5-position, meaning it is meta to the nitrogen across the ring and para to the carboxylic acid-bearing carbon. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the carboxylic acid's C–O bonds providing rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: an aldehyde group, a phenolic hydroxyl group on the carbon next to it, and a bromine atom positioned meta to the aldehyde and para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds other than the aldehyde carbon's attachment to the ring. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenolic hydroxyl hydrogen serves as a single hydrogen-bond donor. The ortho relationship between the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups allows an intramolecular hydrogen-bonding arrangement, and the overall substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a tricyclic aromatic system built from two fused pyridine-type rings and a central benzene-type ring, forming a phenanthroline-like angular scaffold. Its three rings are fully aromatic and fused in a rigid, planar arrangement, with the two ring nitrogens positioned on the outer rings so that they lie close together across the molecule's concave face. A single chlorine atom is attached to the central ring, giving a simple monosubstitution pattern on an otherwise unsubstituted framework. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, approximate planar symmetry, and its lack of rotatable bonds makes it highly rigid. Its two aromatic nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents, with one aromatic hydrogen remaining on the ring. Starting from the fluorine-bearing carbon, the ring carries a fluorine atom, two bromine atoms on adjacent carbons, and a chlorine atom positioned meta to one of the bromines. Because all substituents are halogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and only weak, halogen-based acceptor capacity, with no hydroxyl, amine, or carbonyl groups present. The aromatic core is fully rigid and planar, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered carbocyclic ring containing a ketone, forming an indanone (2,3-dihydro-1H-inden-1-one) core. The aromatic ring carries a single chlorine substituent positioned meta to the saturated ring fusion carbon bearing the CH2 group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the saturated CH2–CH2 linker in the five-membered ring retains some limited puckering flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all remaining hydrogens sit on carbon atoms.

The molecule is a diaryl ether built from two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen bridge. The first ring carries a hydroxyl group ortho to the ether linkage and a chlorine atom meta to the hydroxyl, giving a phenol-type unit. The second ring bears chlorine atoms at the positions para and ortho to the ether oxygen, so the two halogens sit on the same side of the bridge. Because the two rings are connected only through the central oxygen, the scaffold is fairly flexible, with the rings able to rotate about the C–O–C axis. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen is a weaker acceptor, and the molecule has no overall symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a sulfonamide group (-SO2NH2), a chlorine atom, and a fluorine atom. The sulfonamide sits on one ring carbon, with the fluorine on the adjacent carbon and the chlorine on a carbon farther around the ring, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the sulfonamide carbon-sulfur bond offers limited rotational freedom. The sulfonamide group contributes two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens and two hydrogen-bond donor N-H groups, whereas the halogens serve only as weak acceptors. The molecule therefore presents a compact, polar edge formed by the sulfonamide alongside a more hydrophobic halogenated face of the ring.

The molecule is a substituted aniline built on a single benzene ring, with six aromatic carbons forming a flat, fully conjugated scaffold. An amino group (–NH2) sits on one ring carbon and acts as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the nitrogen lone pair can also accept hydrogen bonds. Adjacent to the amine is a methoxy group (–OCH3), whose ether oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. A chlorine atom occupies the position para to the methoxy group, relative to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ, and its rigidity comes from the aromatic ring, with only the methoxy group showing rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern: a methoxy group, a chlorine atom, and an isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S). The methoxy oxygen sits ortho to the isothiocyanate nitrogen, while the chlorine is para to the methoxy group and meta to the isothiocyanate, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis beyond the ring plane. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the linear N=C=S unit adds a short, nearly straight extension, so the molecule has only limited conformational flexibility, mainly from rotation of the methyl group of the ether. The methoxy oxygen and the isothiocyanate sulfur and nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to one ring carbon is an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen), and on the adjacent carbon sits a hydroxyl group, so the aldehyde and phenol are ortho to each other. A chlorine atom occupies a position meta to the aldehyde and para to the hydroxyl, giving a trisubstituted ring with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups are small, rotatable-free substituents with limited conformational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that contains two nitrogen atoms. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with an extended aromatic system spanning both rings. A thiol group (-SH) sits on the carbon between the two nitrogens at the 2-position of the imidazole ring, and an ethoxy group (-OCH2CH3) is attached to the benzene ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The ethoxy tail adds some conformational flexibility, while the core remains fixed. The N-H of the imidazole ring and the thiol can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogen, the ether oxygen, and the sulfur can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two alkyl substituents. An ethyl group is attached at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen's neighboring position on one side of the ring, and a methyl group sits at the carbon directly next to the nitrogen on the opposite side, so the two substituents are placed in a 2,5-relationship relative to each other across the ring. The ring is flat and fully aromatic, with no fused rings, and the molecule is small, rigid at the core, and only modestly flexible through the rotation of the ethyl group. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the lone pair on the ring nitrogen, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The overall shape lacks any rotational symmetry beyond the trivial planar mirror plane of the aromatic ring.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused ring systems. A hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 attached to an OH) sits on one ring carbon, a fluorine atom is on another, and a trifluoromethyl group (a carbon carrying three fluorines) is on the carbon adjacent to the hydroxymethyl-bearing carbon, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern around the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the three substituents differ. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl group adds a single rotatable bond. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine and trifluoromethyl groups serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxyl group, a fluorine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group. Its six-membered aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and flat, with no fused rings. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, a fluorine is placed meta to it on the opposite side, and the trifluoromethyl group sits ortho to the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a single mirror plane through the ring. The rigid aromatic core limits flexibility, though the trifluoromethyl and hydroxyl groups can rotate. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned meta to each other across the ring. It carries three halogen substituents: a chlorine atom on the carbon between the two nitrogens, a second chlorine on an adjacent ring carbon, and a fluorine atom on the carbon flanking the remaining ring position. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all ring positions not bearing halogens are occupied by aromatic CH groups or are substituted.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an acetyl group (a carbonyl attached to a methyl), a hydroxyl group, and a fluorine atom. The acetyl and hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the fluorine is positioned meta to the acetyl group and para to the hydroxyl group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the acetyl group has a single rotatable bond that allows modest flexibility. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and it can also form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent carbonyl oxygen. The carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine atom serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: a primary amine group (-NH2), a fluorine atom, and an iodine atom, arranged on adjacent and meta-related positions around the ring. The amine nitrogen is the only hydrogen-bond donor, offering two N-H bonds, while the nitrogen lone pair and the fluorine atom can act as weak acceptors. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different. Its only notable flexibility is the rotation of the amine group about the carbon-nitrogen bond.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a fluorine atom, and a primary amine. The amine and methyl sit on adjacent ring carbons, with the fluorine located para to the methyl group and meta to the amine, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl and amino groups, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. The amino group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby carbons: a carboxylic acid group, a nitro group positioned ortho to it, and a fluorine atom located meta to the carboxylic acid and para to the nitro group. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the overall scaffold is rigid apart from rotation of the carboxylic acid and nitro groups. Substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis or mirror plane. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the nitro and fluorine groups act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents on adjacent and near positions: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing two oxygens, one formally charged), and a fluorine atom. The nitrile and nitro groups sit on neighboring carbons, forming an ortho arrangement, while the fluorine occupies a position meta to the nitrile and para to the nitro group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system, and the substituents are essentially coplanar with it. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the three different substituents break any mirror or rotational axis. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the nitrogen of the nitrile and the oxygens of the nitro group can act as acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen), a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. The aldehyde and nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the hydroxyl group sits on the carbon meta to the aldehyde and para to the nitro group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Only the aldehyde carbon-hydrogen bond and bond rotations at the single bonds to the ring offer limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring joined along one edge to a five-membered carbocycle, giving an indane-type skeleton. The aromatic ring carries a single hydroxyl group attached directly to one of its carbons, so the substitution pattern is a monosubstituted benzene ring fused at two adjacent positions. The saturated five-membered ring contains two sp3 methylene units bridging the fused carbons, which makes that portion conformationally flexible while the aromatic component remains planar and rigid. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, and the molecule has no internal symmetry other than the approximate planarity of its aromatic framework.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent carbons on one side of the ring, and a single iodine atom sits on the carbon directly across from them, giving a 1,2,3,5-type substitution pattern on the benzene core. The ring has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all oxygen atoms are ether oxygens carrying methyl groups; the three oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the three methoxy groups add some conformational flexibility through rotation about their C–O bonds. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric overall.

This molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains an NH group. The iodine atom sits on the benzene portion of the fused system, at a position on the six-membered ring that is meta to the carbon bearing the ring-fusion junction, giving a single halogen substitution. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so the molecule can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aromatic nitrogen's lone pair is part of the delocalized π system and offers only weak acceptor character. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of its rings.

This molecule is a six-membered heteroaromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, with carbonyl groups on the carbons flanking one nitrogen pair, forming a pyrimidinedione scaffold. The ring is fully conjugated and essentially planar, giving it a rigid, flat geometry with no rotatable bonds. A single iodine atom sits on the carbon between the two carbonyl carbons, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric about the ring but the core retains an approximate mirror-like arrangement. Both ring nitrogens carry hydrogen atoms, so the structure can act as two hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen atom. Attached to one carbon of this ring is an isopropyl group, a branched alkyl substituent that adds some bulk and lipophilic character. A carboxylic acid group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen that lacks a hydrogen, so the two substituents occupy positions that are not symmetrically equivalent. The pyrazole core is planar and rigid, with only the isopropyl and carboxyl groups providing rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid contributes both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the ring N-H acts as an additional donor and the unprotonated ring nitrogen serves as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The benzene portion carries a single methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) positioned on the carbocyclic ring, while the thiazole carbon between sulfur and nitrogen bears a methyl substituent. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the methoxy and methyl groups lying in the same plane and the molecule lacking any meaningful symmetry because the two substituents sit at different positions. The ether oxygen and the thiazole nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure is aromatic, compact and essentially inflexible apart from rotation of the methoxy group.

The molecule is a flavone-type scaffold: a benzopyranone core in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring bearing a carbonyl group. A second, unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached directly to the pyranone at the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, giving an extended, largely planar aromatic framework. A single methoxy group sits on the fused benzene ring at the position next to the carbonyl-bearing carbon, which breaks any symmetry in that ring. The carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ring oxygen and methoxy oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused and biaryl-linked rings make the structure rigid, with only the methoxy group offering rotational flexibility.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains an NH group. A methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) is attached to the benzene ring at a position para-like to the ring fusion, giving the molecule an electron-donating substituent on the carbocyclic portion. On the five-membered ring, a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with a hydrogen) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the NH-bearing ring carbon. The fused aromatic framework is essentially flat and rigid, with only the methoxy and aldehyde groups providing limited rotational freedom. The pyrrole NH acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aldehyde oxygen and methoxy oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a fully aromatic, flat tricyclic system built from three fused six-membered rings, with two nitrogen atoms placed in the outer rings. Its scaffold is a phenanthroline-type framework, in which two pyridine-like rings are joined through a central benzene-like ring. Each nitrogen sits adjacent to a ring fusion carbon, so the two nitrogens lie on the same side of the molecule and face one another across the central region. A single methyl group is attached to the central ring, providing the only substitution. The molecule has an approximately planar, rigid geometry with no rotatable bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, but its two ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing both oxygen and nitrogen, giving a benzoxazole-type scaffold. The five-membered ring bears a thiocarbonyl (C=S) group at the carbon between the oxygen and the nitrogen, and the nitrogen carries an N–H, so the ring is a cyclic thiocarbamate-like unit. A single methyl group sits on the benzene ring, placed meta to the ring-fusion nitrogen-bearing carbon, which breaks any symmetry of the fused framework. The fused, planar aromatic core is essentially rigid, with almost no rotatable bonds. The N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur and ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, which makes it a pyrimidine-type scaffold. The ring carries a carbonyl group (C=O) and a thiocarbonyl group (C=S) on adjacent or flanking carbons, and a methyl group attached to one ring carbon, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. Both ring nitrogens bear hydrogen atoms, so the molecule has two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the oxygen and sulfur atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The single fused-free ring is fully conjugated and essentially planar, which limits conformational flexibility, with the methyl group being the only substituent that can rotate freely.

The molecule is built on a benzothiophene scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiophene ring containing one sulfur atom. The two rings share an edge, making the fused framework fully aromatic and essentially planar, which gives it a rigid, flat shape. A single methyl group is attached to the benzene portion of the bicyclic core, creating a simple substitution pattern with no other functional groups. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H bonds, and its sulfur atom offers only weak acceptor character. Its overall structure has no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group and no internal symmetry that would be preserved by the methyl placement.

The molecule is built on a benzofuroxan-type bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing one oxygen and two nitrogens in a 1,2,5-oxadiazole arrangement. The fused system is planar and rigid, with the two rings sharing an edge along the aromatic framework. A methyl group sits on the benzene ring at a position that breaks the symmetry of the carbocyclic portion, so the molecule has no mirror symmetry overall. The nitrogen at the fusion-adjacent position carries an N-oxide, giving a formally charged N-oxide group whose oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since all ring and substituent hydrogens are attached to carbon and the N-oxide oxygen only accepts.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A propylamino group (–NH–CH2CH2CH3) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position. A nitro group (–NO2) sits on the ring carbon at the 5-position, roughly opposite the amine across the ring. Because the ring is aromatic and the two substituents are fixed in place, the core is essentially planar and rigid, while the flexible propyl chain adds conformational freedom. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic furan ring, with no fused rings present. Attached to one ring carbon is an aldehyde group, a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen and double-bonded to oxygen. On the carbon at the opposite side of the ring, a nitro group is attached, with nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one of them formally charged, and the molecule is 2,5-disubstituted in that pattern. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the bonds to the substituents able to rotate. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents differ. Its hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no OH or NH groups, while the aldehyde oxygen, the nitro oxygens, and the furan ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic furan ring, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Attached at the 2-position is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to both an oxygen and a chlorine atom. At the 5-position, opposite that carbonyl group, sits a nitro group, which carries a formally charged nitrogen bonded to two oxygens. The substitution pattern is therefore a 2,5-disubstituted furan with two electron-withdrawing groups on opposite sides of the ring. The structure is essentially planar and rigid, with little conformational flexibility, and it lacks any symmetry beyond the ring's approximate local arrangement. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its oxygen atoms in the nitro and carbonyl groups and the ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to an imidazole ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The five-membered ring contains two nitrogen atoms: one bears a hydrogen atom and acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other is a pyridine-like nitrogen that serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. A nitro group, consisting of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with formal charges, is attached to the benzene ring at a single position, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the nitro group. The nitro substituent is strongly electron-withdrawing and adds additional hydrogen-bond acceptor sites through its oxygen atoms.

The molecule is built on an indoline scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, which gives a bicyclic framework. The saturated portion of that five-membered ring contains two adjacent sp3 carbons, so the ring is partly flexible while the fused aromatic system remains planar and rigid. A nitro group is attached to the benzene ring at a position para to the nitrogen-bearing ring-fusion carbon, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The secondary amine nitrogen carries one hydrogen, allowing it to act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro group's oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, and a nitro group is attached as well. The substituents sit at positions 1, 3, and 5 around the ring, so they are arranged in a symmetric meta pattern. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing functional group, with its nitrogen bearing formal positive charge and its two oxygens carrying negative charge. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the methyl and nitro groups able to rotate. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no OH or NH groups, but the oxygens of the nitro group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework bearing four substituents. The molecule is an acyclic saturated alcohol built on a straight-chain carbon skeleton, with no rings and no multiple bonds. A single hydroxyl group sits on a secondary carbon that is roughly central along the chain, so the structure is a branched-looking but still aliphatic framework with one oxygen-bearing carbon. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O bonded to a hydrogen) sits at the 3-position relative to the ring nitrogen, while a piperidine ring is attached at the 6-position through its nitrogen atom, making that ring nitrogen a tertiary amine-type substituent. The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidine ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, giving a planar purine-type core with nine ring atoms and four nitrogens. The six-membered ring contains two nitrogens in a 1,3-relationship, while the five-membered ring carries one NH group, which acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, alongside the aromatic nitrogens that serve as acceptors. A single methylthio group (–S–CH3) is attached to the carbon of the pyrimidine ring that sits between two nitrogens, providing the only substituent and the only sp3-hybridized carbon. The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic compound with no rings, built from a six-carbon backbone bearing two functional groups at opposite ends. One terminus carries an acetamide group, where a methyl-substituted carbonyl is bonded to a nitrogen atom, and the other terminus carries a terminal carboxylic acid. The molecule is built on a tetralin scaffold, meaning a benzene ring fused to a saturated cyclohexane ring that shares two adjacent carbons with it. The aromatic ring is fused to a partially saturated six-membered carbocycle, which contributes some conformational flexibility through its CH2 groups. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks any N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a benzoxazinone scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered heterocycle containing an oxygen and a nitrogen, which in turn bears a lactam carbonyl. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone) is attached to the benzene ring, giving a single substituent at a position that breaks the ring's symmetry. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the lactam carbonyl, the ketone oxygen, and the ring ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzofuranone (phthalide-type) scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered lactone ring that contains an ester oxygen and a carbonyl group. An aromatic primary amine (–NH2) sits on the benzene ring at a position that is meta to the ring fusion carbon bearing the carbonyl-adjacent carbon, giving a single, asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with only the lactone ring carrying limited conformational freedom. Hydrogen-bond capability is present on both sides: the amino group can act as a donor through its two N–H bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring ester oxygen, and amine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system built from two fused six-membered rings, a quinoline-type scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring. The nitrogen sits in the pyridine ring and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, with no hydrogen-bond donors present. A methyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to that nitrogen, while a bromine atom is attached to the benzene ring on the opposite side of the fused system, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with only the methyl group contributing any rotational freedom.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic carboxylic acid with no rings, so its scaffold is a linear six-carbon backbone, with the carboxyl carbon counted as one of the chain atoms. The carboxylic acid group sits at one terminus, consisting of a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl group, while a bromine atom occupies the opposite terminal carbon, giving a monosubstituted, end-to-end pattern with no branching or stereocenters. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a rough mirror relationship between its two ends, which differ in their functional groups. The hydroxyl hydrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a substituted uracil-type pyrimidinedione, a six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions with two carbonyl groups. Both ring nitrogens carry methyl substituents, and a chlorine atom sits on one of the ring carbons, leaving a single C-H on the remaining sp2 carbon. The ring is planar and largely rigid, with conjugation running through the carbonyls and the C=C bond. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors because all nitrogens are methylated, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, a planar, fully unsaturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 relationship. It carries three substituents: two methoxy groups (–OCH3) and one chlorine atom, placed on the ring carbons flanking the nitrogens and at the remaining position, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful internal symmetry. The methoxy oxygens and the two ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the ring is rigid and the substituents are small and attached directly to it, the overall structure is compact and largely inflexible, with only the methyl groups of the methoxy substituents able to rotate.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, so there is no ring fusion, with five substituents arranged around it. Reading around the ring, a methyl group sits on one carbon, a chlorine on the carbon two positions away, a nitrile (cyano) group on the carbon adjacent to the chlorine, and a fluorine on the carbon next to the methyl group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and only the methyl rotor adds minor conformational freedom. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a single benzene ring, a fully aromatic six-membered carbon scaffold with no fused or additional rings. Its substituents are arranged around the ring in a contiguous pattern: a methyl group, a fluorine atom, a hydroxymethyl group, and a chlorine atom occupy adjacent and nearby positions. The hydroxymethyl group is the only functional group present, consisting of a primary alcohol with its hydroxyl oxygen available as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The fluorine and chlorine halogens contribute only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry, and the aromatic core is rigid while the hydroxymethyl group retains some rotational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. A chlorine atom sits on the ring carbon adjacent to that nitrogen, placing the halogen at the 2-position relative to the nitrogen, while a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid) is attached at the 5-position. This arrangement gives the molecule a 2,5-disubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry, because the two substituents sit on different sides of the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the CH2 linker and the carboxylic acid provide a small degree of rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a bicyclic scaffold in which a six-membered saturated oxygen-containing ring is fused to a benzene ring, giving a chromanone (dihydrochromen-4-one) core. The heterocyclic ring contains a ring oxygen attached directly to the aromatic system, a two-carbon CH2 chain, and a ketone carbonyl at the position adjacent to the fused benzene ring. A single chlorine atom sits on the benzene ring, para to the ring oxygen and meta to the carbonyl-bearing carbon, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused system is largely planar and rigid, though the saturated portion of the heterocycle retains some conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen and ring ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. An acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to chlorine, is attached at the 3-position relative to the nitrogen. A chlorine atom sits directly on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 6-position. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy different positions. The carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, which serves as the central scaffold. A boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl substituents, is attached to one ring carbon at the meta position relative to the nitrogen, while a chlorine atom occupies the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen on the opposite side of the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, and the substituents impart a rigid, flat geometry with only limited rotational freedom about the carbon-boron bond. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the two substituents are placed asymmetrically. The two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogen along with the oxygen atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a carboxylic acid group is attached to the ring carbon positioned para to the nitrile-bearing carbon, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pattern. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only limited conformational flexibility, mainly rotation of the carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the pyridine nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three substituents on adjacent positions. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen) sits at one ring carbon, a hydroxyl group sits on the immediately neighboring carbon, and a fluorine atom occupies the carbon on the other side of the aldehyde. This ortho-ortho substitution pattern leaves the ring with three adjacent hydrogen-bearing carbons and creates a crowded, asymmetric arrangement with no internal symmetry axis. The rigid aromatic core constrains the molecule, while the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups provide limited rotational freedom. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the carbonyl oxygen and fluorine serve as acceptors, and the aldehyde can form an intramolecular interaction with the adjacent hydroxyl.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with no rings, aromatic groups, or heteroatoms other than the single oxygen. A straight, unbranched carbon chain runs through the structure, with a carbonyl group (C=O) located internally, so that one side of the carbonyl carries a long alkyl segment and the other side carries a shorter one. The chain is entirely saturated and carries no substitution, giving the molecule no stereocenters and no symmetry beyond an approximate mirror-like balance of chain lengths about the carbonyl. Because all bonds are single except the carbonyl, the molecule is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small monocyclic heteroaromatic compound built on a six-membered pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned meta to each other. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, one on a carbon adjacent to a nitrogen and one on the other ring carbon, while a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon between the two nitrogens. Because the hydroxyl can tautomerize to a ring carbonyl form, the structure can be viewed as a pyrimidinone. The ring is flat and fully conjugated, giving the molecule a rigid, planar scaffold with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl groups. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indanone scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that contains a ketone. The aromatic ring carries a single methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) attached at a position para to one ring-fusion carbon and meta to the other, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The five-membered ring is largely planar and fairly rigid, with the two saturated CH2 groups adjacent to the carbonyl providing a little flexibility. The ketone oxygen and the methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle, forming a tetralone-type framework. The aromatic ring carries a single methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) positioned meta to one ring-fusion carbon and para to the other, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The saturated ring contains three methylene units and a ketone carbonyl adjacent to the aromatic ring, so the carbonyl is conjugated with the benzene system. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the three CH2 groups allow some conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused six-membered aromatic rings sharing one edge, so it is fully planar and rigid. A methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) is attached to one ring, and an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, with a hydrogen) is attached to the other ring, placing the two substituents on opposite rings of the fused system. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group offers a second, weaker acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens sit on carbon. Its overall shape is elongated and essentially asymmetric because the two substituents are placed at different positions on the naphthalene core.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic amine built from a benzene ring fused to a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring, giving a tetrahydroquinoline scaffold. The aromatic ring bears a single methyl substituent on the carbon meta to the ring-fusion carbon that carries the nitrogen-attached side, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The nitrogen is a secondary amine within the saturated ring, bonded to one aromatic carbon and one saturated carbon, so it is non-planar and can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and an acceptor through its lone pair. The fused saturated ring adds some conformational flexibility, while the benzene portion remains rigid and planar. Overall, the structure combines a rigid aromatic region with a more flexible saturated heterocycle.

The molecule is built on an indanone scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocyclic ring that contains a ketone. The aromatic ring carries a single methyl substituent positioned meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the carbonyl side, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, with only the saturated two-carbon bridge of the five-membered ring offering slight flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a simple monosubstituted pyridine, built on a single six-membered aromatic nitrogen-containing ring with no fused rings. A methyl group sits on one carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a hydroxymethyl group sits on the other carbon adjacent to that nitrogen, giving a 2,6-disubstituted pattern with a mirror plane through the nitrogen and the ring carbon opposite it. The hydroxymethyl arm contributes a primary alcohol functional group, which can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond. The pyridine nitrogen lone pair serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl group retains some rotational flexibility around its single bonds.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared edge. The nitrogen sits in the pyridine ring, adjacent to the fusion carbon, giving the bicycle a planar, aromatic, and rigid character. A methyl group occupies one position on the benzene-type ring, while a nitro group is attached at a carbon adjacent to the other fusion carbon, placing the two substituents on neighboring positions of the carbocyclic ring. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and offers two oxygen atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the ring nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is built on a chromone scaffold, a benzopyran-4-one in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyranone ring that contains the ring oxygen and a ketone carbonyl. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid. A methyl group sits on the benzene ring, and a nitrile (cyano) group is attached to the pyranone carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the methyl and nitrile substituents are placed asymmetrically on the fused system. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the carbonyl oxygen, the ring ether oxygen, and the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. A formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O attached to carbon) is bonded to the pyrrole ring at the position adjacent to the nitrogen-bearing carbon, which makes it a substituted indole-3-carbaldehyde type arrangement. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with the aldehyde group able to rotate only slightly out of the ring plane. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl and formyl substituents break the symmetry of the bicyclic core.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, so it has no fused rings and a planar, rigid scaffold. The aromatic nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, and the aldehyde oxygen is an additional acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A methyl group sits on the carbon directly adjacent to that nitrogen, while a carboxylic acid group is attached to the other carbon flanking the nitrogen, giving a 2,6-disubstituted pattern that is symmetric about the nitrogen-carbon axis in terms of substituent placement. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The methyl group is a small nonpolar substituent that adds steric bulk near the ring nitrogen without introducing any donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a quinoline scaffold. The nitrogen atom sits in the six-membered ring that is fused to the carbocycle, and the fused rings are planar and fully conjugated, giving the molecule a rigid, flat shape with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any mirror-plane symmetry because the methyl group breaks the symmetry of the fused system. The molecule is a bicyclic fused system: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered heterocycle containing both oxygen and nitrogen, specifically a benzoxazolone core, in which the five-membered ring carries a carbonyl group flanked by an NH and an oxygen.
