The fused framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the nitro group sits on one side of the fused system.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The fused bicyclic system is flat and fully aromatic, making the core rigid with no rotatable bonds. A single nitro group is attached to the benzene portion of the bicycle, at a position that breaks the molecule's symmetry. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The thiazole nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. The nitro group, a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent bearing two oxygen atoms, is attached to the benzene portion of the fused system at the position meta to the ring-fusion carbon on one side. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so the molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor site, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rigid, planar framework has no rotatable bonds within the core and lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the nitro group.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic fused scaffold: a five-membered pyrrole-type ring fused to a six-membered pyrimidine-2,4-dione ring, giving a pyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidine core. The pyrimidinedione portion carries two N-methyl groups and two carbonyl oxygens, while the five-membered ring bears a carboxylic acid group on one carbon and a 3-methoxypropyl chain on the ring nitrogen. Because the fused core is planar and aromatic-like, the molecule is fairly rigid, with flexibility confined mainly to the propyl ether side chain. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl) and acceptors (its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the carbonyl oxygens of the dione and the ether oxygen provide further acceptor sites. The substitution pattern is asymmetric overall, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry.

This molecule is a quinoline, a bicyclic aromatic scaffold made of a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring that shares two carbon atoms and forms a planar, fully conjugated system. A trifluoromethyl group (-CF3) is attached to the carbon on the benzo ring, positioned meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen-adjacent carbon, which breaks any mirror symmetry of the bicyclic framework. The pyridine nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The three fluorine atoms of the CF3 group are weak acceptors, and the group adds strong electron-withdrawing character to the aromatic system.

The molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated chain of seven carbon atoms with no rings, ending in a primary amine group at one terminus and a carboxylic acid group at the other. The amine nitrogen is attached to the first carbon of the chain, and the carboxyl carbon forms the terminal end, giving the molecule a linear, symmetric-free shape. The amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carboxylic acid contributes both donor (via its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (via its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens) capability.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic aromatic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, forming an indole-type bicyclic system with the nitrogen on the fused pyrrole side. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aromatic nitrogen's lone pair is part of the ring and gives limited acceptor capability. A primary amino group is attached to the benzene ring at the position adjacent to the ring fusion, which places it next to the fused carbon that bears the pyrrole nitrogen. The amino group provides two additional hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone-pair acceptor site. The fused framework is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the amino substituent breaks the symmetry of the bicyclic system.

The molecule is built on a tetrahydroisoquinoline scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The aromatic ring carries a single bromine atom at one position, giving a simple, non-symmetric substitution pattern on the benzene portion. The saturated ring contains a secondary amine, which serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The fused bicyclic framework is fairly rigid, though the saturated ring can adopt puckered conformations. Overall, the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a seven-membered 1,5-dioxepine-type ring containing two oxygen atoms, giving a benzodioxepine scaffold. The aromatic ring is substituted at one position with a bromoacetyl group, meaning a carbonyl carbon bearing a CH2Br unit directly attached to the ring. The ketone oxygen and the two ether oxygens of the fused ring can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The saturated three-carbon bridge of the seven-membered ring gives it some conformational flexibility, whereas the fused aromatic portion remains planar and rigid. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a quinoline-type scaffold with the nitrogen atom in the heteroaromatic ring. A hydroxyl group is attached to the carbon at position 4 of the fused system, placing it on the pyridine-side ring adjacent to the ring fusion. A chlorine atom is bonded to the benzenoid ring at a position meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen-adjacent carbon, giving a substitution pattern on one side of the fused framework. The fully aromatic, planar, rigid core has no rotatable bonds beyond the hydroxyl. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a coumarin-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered α-pyrone (2H-chromen-2-one) ring that contains a lactone carbonyl and a ring oxygen. A methyl group sits on the pyrone ring at the carbon adjacent to the fused junction, and an ethoxy group is attached to the benzene ring at a position para-like to the ring oxygen. The bicyclic fused system is essentially planar and rigid, with only the ethyl chain of the ether substituent showing conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks rotational symmetry, since the methyl and ethoxy substituents break any mirror or rotational pattern. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the lactone carbonyl oxygen, the lactone ring oxygen, and the ether oxygen each serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains an NH group. A single fluorine atom is attached to the benzene portion at the carbon adjacent to the ring-fusion atom, placing it at the 7-position of the indole core. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the fluorine sits on one side of the fusion. The pyrrole N–H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the fluorine provides only weak acceptor character and the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic system.

The molecule is a polycyclic aromatic ketone built from fused benzene-type rings. A central carbonyl carbon sits in a six-membered ring that is fused to a benzene ring on one side and to a naphthalene-like unit on the other, creating a rigid, nearly planar framework. Its skeleton is a fully conjugated carbon scaffold with no sp3 centers, so it is highly rigid with essentially no conformational flexibility. The only functional group is a single ketone, and the carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor with no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is unsubstituted apart from the ring fusion, so the molecule is achiral and has a roughly planar, low-symmetry outline.

This molecule is a bicyclic fused heteroaromatic system built on a benzopyranone (coumarin-type) scaffold, in which a six-membered lactone-containing pyranone ring is fused to a benzene ring. The lactone carbonyl sits on the pyranone ring, adjacent to the ring oxygen, and a single phenolic hydroxyl group is attached to the benzenoid ring at a position remote from the fusion, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with little conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, forming an indane skeleton. The aromatic ring carries two substituents, a methyl group and a hydroxyl group, placed on adjacent carbons with the hydroxyl flanked by the ring fusion. The saturated five-membered ring contributes two methylene units, giving it a modest degree of puckering while the fused aromatic portion remains planar and rigid. Because the substituents break the symmetry of the benzene ring, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local ring geometry. The phenolic hydroxyl acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the rest of the framework is hydrocarbon in character with no additional polar groups.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. A methyl group sits on the benzene portion adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, placing it at the position next to the fused junction. A formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an attached hydrogen) is attached to the pyrrole ring at the carbon beside the fusion, which gives an electron-withdrawing carbonyl acceptor. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, making it an N–H hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with only the aldehyde and methyl groups able to rotate, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic compound built on an indazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrazole ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The pyrazole portion contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen, giving an N-H group that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other nitrogen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. A nitro group is attached to the benzene ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, which places it near the N-H region. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the nitro substituent sits on one side of the ring system.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with a linear, unbranched carbon skeleton of seventeen carbons in total, containing no rings, fused systems, or aromatic groups. The single functional group is a ketone, where a carbonyl carbon is bonded to two straight alkyl chains, one of eight carbons and one of six carbons, so the substitution pattern is simply a central carbonyl flanked by two n-alkyl arms. The molecule has no symmetry, since the two chains differ in length, and it is highly flexible because the many single C–C bonds allow free rotation along the chains. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor through the carbonyl oxygen, as it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic heterocycle built on a quinoline scaffold, consisting of a pyridine ring fused to a benzene ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen in the pyridine-type ring, while a chlorine atom is attached to the benzenoid ring at the position next to the fusion carbon that also bears the nitrogen-adjacent environment, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fully aromatic, planar fused system is rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl and chloro substituents. The ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, since its lone pair lies in the plane of the ring, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a tricyclic fused-ring system built around a nitrogen atom that bridges two of the rings. A benzene ring carries a hydroxyl group on one carbon, and this aromatic ring is fused to a saturated six-membered ring containing the nitrogen, which in turn is linked through a three-carbon chain to a second saturated ring. The nitrogen is a tertiary amine with no hydrogen on it, so it can accept a hydrogen bond but cannot donate one. The phenolic hydroxyl is the sole hydrogen-bond donor and can also act as an acceptor. The fused framework is largely rigid, with the aromatic ring and nitrogen-containing ring locked together, while the saturated aliphatic chain offers some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the hydroxyl sits on only one side of the scaffold.

The molecule is built on a tetralin-type scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle. The aromatic ring carries a single methoxy group (an aryl ether, with the oxygen able to accept a hydrogen bond) on the position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted on the benzene ring. The saturated ring bears a carboxylic acid group on a carbon one position away from the aromatic fusion, which contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites. The fused framework is fairly rigid, though the non-aromatic ring can adopt different puckered conformations. The molecule has no internal symmetry, so it is chiral at the carbon bearing the carboxyl group.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene-type bicyclic scaffold, consisting of two fused six-membered aromatic rings sharing one edge. One of the rings contains a nitrogen atom at a position adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, making it a fused pyridine-benzene system. A methyl group is attached to the carbon immediately beside that fusion point, on the carbocyclic ring, which breaks any mirror symmetry of the framework. The fully aromatic, planar structure is rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The ring nitrogen possesses a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule consists of a straight, unbranched seven-carbon saturated chain that links a terminal carboxylic acid group to a monosubstituted benzene ring at the opposite end. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fusion and no further substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the ring carries no symmetry-breaking features beyond the attachment point. The carboxylic acid group contains a carbonyl oxygen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and a hydroxyl group that can act as both a donor and an acceptor. The long methylene chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, while the phenyl ring and the carboxyl group are comparatively rigid and planar.

The molecule is built on an anthracene core, three fused benzene rings in a linear arrangement, with a fully aromatic, flat, rigid scaffold. The 9 and 10 positions of the central ring each carry an ethynyl linker (a carbon-carbon triple bond) that connects to a terminal phenyl ring, so the two substituents are placed symmetrically across the central ring. The overall framework is highly conjugated and largely rigid, with the alkyne linkers imposing linear geometry and the molecule possessing an approximate two-fold symmetry. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, since it is composed solely of carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is 9-(hydroxymethyl)anthracene, built on a linear, fully aromatic three-ring anthracene scaffold in which three benzene-type rings are fused in a straight line. A hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 bearing an OH) is attached to the central ring at the 9-position, which is the reactive meso carbon, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule loses the mirror symmetry of bare anthracene. The fused tricyclic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2–OH arm adds a small degree of conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic framework contributes only weak interactions.

The molecule is built on a 9-bromo-9-phenylfluorene scaffold: a fluorene core in which the C9 sp3 carbon bears both a bromine atom and a phenyl ring. The fluorene unit is a rigid, planar tricyclic system made of two benzene rings fused to a central five-membered ring, and the C9 carbon is a quaternary center that places the phenyl group and bromine above and below that plane. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H groups, and its only heteroatom is the bromine, which provides weak acceptor character. The scaffold is largely rigid, with limited flexibility restricted to rotation of the pendant phenyl ring around the C9–phenyl bond.

The molecule is built on a phenanthrene scaffold, a three-ring fused aromatic system in which two benzene rings are angularly fused to a central ring. A single bromine atom is attached to one of the outer rings at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only heteroatom is the bromine, which is a weak halogen acceptor. The fully fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds.

The molecule is built on a linear three-ring fused aromatic scaffold, an anthracene-type skeleton, with a chlorine atom attached to the central ring at a position adjacent to one of the ring fusions. Its carbon framework is fully aromatic and planar, so the ring system is rigid with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine is only a weak acceptor, while the pi-electron-rich rings provide a diffuse, nonpolar surface for weak interactions. Apart from the single chlorine substituent, the remaining positions carry only hydrogens, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any significant symmetry element beyond the mirror plane of the flat aromatic framework.

The molecule is a tricyclic aromatic ketone built on a fluorenone scaffold: two benzene rings are joined by a direct carbon-carbon bond and bridged by a five-membered ring containing a carbonyl carbon. The central five-membered ring is fused to both benzene rings, giving a fully planar, rigid, and conjugated framework. The carbonyl group sits at the bridging position, making it the only functional group present, and the four benzo hydrogens are unsubstituted, so the molecule has no substituent variation. Its overall structure is highly symmetric, with a mirror plane passing through the carbonyl carbon and the midpoint of the biaryl bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a carbonate diester linking a 9H-fluoren-9-ylmethyl group to a pentafluorophenyl ring through a central C(=O)O unit. The fluorene portion is a rigid, planar tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central five-membered ring, and the CH2 linker attaches at the sp3 carbon (position 9) of that five-membered ring. The pentafluorophenyl ring carries five fluorine substituents, one at each ring position other than the oxygen-bearing carbon, which makes the aryl portion strongly electron-poor and gives it no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The carbonate carbonyl and the ether-type oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is largely rigid and aromatic, with flexibility confined mainly to the single bonds of the CH2–O–C(=O) linkage.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, so its scaffold is entirely acyclic. The chain carries a carbon-carbon triple bond (an alkyne) located near the middle of the backbone, flanked by long saturated segments on both sides. At one terminus sits a carboxylic acid group, which is the only polar functional group present. The skeleton is linear and highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, though the alkyne imposes local rigidity and linearity at its position. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the triple bond is not centered along the chain. The carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the remainder of the structure offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic aromatic scaffold made of four six-membered rings, with the central rings arranged in an angular rather than linear fashion. A vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond attached to the ring system) projects from one of the central positions, serving as the only substituent and the only non-aromatic unsaturation. The skeleton is fully planar and rigid, with the vinyl group the sole source of conformational flexibility. The molecule contains no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its substitution pattern lacks any meaningful symmetry.

The molecule is an acyclic acetal built around a single tetrahedral carbon bearing a methyl group and two methoxy groups, with the carbon also attached to a methyl and an additional methoxy on the other side. Specifically, it is a central sp3 carbon connected to two oxygen atoms, each bonded to a methyl group, and to a second methyl group, giving a compact, branched, unfused skeleton with no rings. It contains two ether oxygen atoms as functional groups, and the molecule has no aromatic or unsaturated centers. The structure is highly flexible, since all bonds are single and freely rotatable, and it possesses no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks O–H or N–H bonds, while its two oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small acyclic amide built on a two-carbon skeleton: a methyl group bonded to a carbonyl carbon that is in turn bonded to a primary amino group. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so its scaffold is simply the amide functional group itself. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the two N-H bonds of the amino group can each act as hydrogen-bond donors. Because the molecule has only a few atoms and a single planar amide linkage, it is structurally rigid at the amide core, with only the methyl group free to rotate.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to one ring carbon is an acetamide group, an acetyl unit (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group) joined through a nitrogen atom that bridges to the ring, making it a secondary amide. The substitution pattern is monosubstituted, so the five remaining ring positions are unsubstituted C–H sites, and the molecule has a mirror plane through the ring and the amide linkage, giving it high local symmetry. The amide group is conformationally fairly rigid because of partial double-bond character across the C–N bond, while the aryl–nitrogen bond allows modest rotation. The N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

Acetonitrile is a very small linear molecule built from just two carbon atoms and one nitrogen atom, with no ring systems or ring fusion. One carbon carries three hydrogen atoms in a methyl group, which is bonded to a second carbon that forms a carbon-nitrogen triple bond. The nitrile functional group is the sole feature of the structure, and the nitrogen's lone pair gives it hydrogen-bond acceptor capability while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The triple bond makes the nitrile axis rigid and perfectly linear, while the methyl group offers only minimal conformational freedom. The molecule has a high degree of local symmetry around its long axis, reflecting its simple, unsubstituted scaffold.

The molecule is a small, acyclic amide built on a three-carbon skeleton, with no rings present. It contains a terminal vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond at one end) directly attached to a carboxamide carbon, which bears a primary amide nitrogen carrying two hydrogens. The conjugation between the alkene and the carbonyl makes the arrangement planar and fairly rigid around that unit, though the molecule overall is small and has limited conformational flexibility. It has no symmetry elements of note, since the two ends are chemically distinct. The primary amide group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is built on an adamantane cage, a rigid, highly symmetric tricyclic hydrocarbon scaffold made of three fused cyclohexane-type rings. A carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached directly to one of the bridgehead carbons of the cage. The cage itself contributes no heteroatoms or unsaturation, so the only polar functionality is the primary amide. That amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites on its nitrogen and one hydrogen-bond acceptor site on its carbonyl oxygen. Because the scaffold is locked into a fixed three-dimensional geometry, the molecule is conformationally rigid, and the substituent sits on a single bridgehead position with no competing sites.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic dicarboxylic acid built on a linear six-carbon backbone, with a carboxyl group capping each end. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom substituents beyond the two terminal carboxylic acid groups, so the substitution pattern is simply symmetric, with both acid groups at opposite termini. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the middle of the carbon chain, and the central methylene units are chemically equivalent in pairs. The chain is highly flexible, since its sigma bonds allow free rotation and many accessible conformations. Each carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), giving the molecule strong hydrogen-bonding capability at both ends.

This molecule is an acyclic six-carbon polyol, with a straight chain of carbons bearing a hydroxyl group on each carbon except the two terminal ones, which each carry a primary hydroxymethyl group. There are no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic character, and the skeleton is entirely saturated and sp3-hybridized. The four internal stereocenters give the chain a defined three-dimensional arrangement, and the molecule as a whole has no internal mirror plane of symmetry because the stereochemical pattern differs along its length. Because the chain is flexible and rotates freely about its single bonds, it can adopt many conformations, and its hydroxyl groups give it six hydrogen-bond donor sites and six hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to an imidazole ring through two adjacent carbons. A propylthio group (a three-carbon chain attached through a sulfur atom) sits on the benzene ring at a position that breaks the symmetry of the fused core. At the 2-position of the imidazole ring, a carbamate group is attached through its nitrogen, carrying a methyl ester. The imidazole N-H and the carbamate N-H can each act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the imidazole nitrogen, the carbamate carbonyl oxygen, and the ester oxygens serve as acceptors. The fused aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the propyl chain and methyl ester contribute conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a small, acyclic-chain ether built around a three-membered epoxide (oxirane) ring. A flexible two-carbon linker, a CH2-O-CH2 unit, connects an allyl group (a terminal vinyl group attached through a CH2) to the epoxide ring at one of its ring carbons. The structure contains a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, an ether oxygen, and a strained three-membered cyclic ether, and it has no fused rings or aromatic systems. Because the molecule carries no stereocenter specified in the SMILES, it is not symmetric, and its chain segments are rotationally flexible apart from the rigid epoxide. The ether and epoxide oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a short carbon chain, with no ring systems present. It contains an allyl group, a terminal vinyl unit attached to an oxygen, which is bonded to a carbonyl carbon forming the ester linkage. The acyl portion is a methacrylate-type fragment, with a second terminal double bond on the alpha carbon adjacent to the carbonyl, and a methyl substituent on that same carbon. The structure is flexible, since it has several rotatable single bonds along its chain, and it has no internal symmetry of note. Regarding hydrogen bonding, it has no donor groups, and its two ester oxygens serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single alpha-substituted acetonitrile, in which one carbon bears both a nitrile group (a carbon-nitrogen triple bond) and a phenyl ring, with a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen atom. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, carrying no additional groups on its six carbons, so it is a simple benzene ring. The morpholine is a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen separated by two carbons on each side, so it is non-aromatic and adopts a chair-like conformation. The central sp3 carbon is a stereocenter, but the molecule is drawn without stereochemistry, and there is no overall symmetry beyond local features. The nitrile nitrogen and the morpholine oxygen and nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a two-carbon-backbone carboxylic acid bearing two aromatic rings on the same alpha carbon. The central sp3 carbon carries a free carboxylic acid group, a phenyl ring attached directly, and a sulfur atom linking to a second phenyl ring, giving a thioether bridge. Both benzene rings are unsubstituted, so the aromatic portions are simple monosubstituted phenyl groups with no additional ring fusion. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites, while the thioether sulfur offers a weak acceptor. The molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric plane because the alpha carbon is a stereocenter, and it has moderate flexibility from rotation around the single bonds linking the rings to the central carbon.

This molecule is a bicyclic sugar derivative built on a fused bis-acetal scaffold, with a five-membered furanose-type ring fused to a second five-membered 1,3-dioxolane ring. The fused system is cis-configured at the ring junction, giving it a rigid, compact bowl-like shape. A free secondary hydroxyl sits on the ring, and an exocyclic side chain carries a further hydroxyl-bearing carbon and a terminal primary hydroxymethyl group. The other substituent is a trichloromethyl group attached to an acetal carbon, which adds a bulky, electron-poor region. The molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry because its stereocenters and substituents differ on each side. Its several oxygen atoms and hydroxyl groups give it multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a single sp3-hybridized carbon that bears three substituents: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), a phenyl ring, and a cyclohexyl ring. The phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, and the cyclohexyl ring is a saturated six-membered carbocycle with no fused partners. Neither ring is fused to the other, so the scaffold consists of two separate rings joined through the central carbon. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry beyond local ring symmetry, and its linear nitrile and two rigid rings make the core fairly rigid, while the cyclohexyl ring can adopt chair conformations. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acrylic acid derivative built on a three-carbon α,β-unsaturated backbone, with a carboxylic acid group at one end and a benzyl-type styryl unit at the other. Two phenyl rings are attached: one on the α-carbon and one on the terminal β-carbon of the alkene, giving a diarylacrylic acid scaffold. The central C=C double bond is trisubstituted and carries a defined geometry, which restricts rotation and makes the core fairly rigid, while the two aromatic rings are unfused and can twist relative to the alkene plane. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the two phenyl rings are nonpolar and offer no hydrogen-bonding capability. The molecule lacks a plane of symmetry because the two phenyl groups occupy different positions on the alkene.

The molecule is a benzylsulfonamide: a single benzene ring carries a CH2 group that links it to a sulfonamide unit, with the sulfur bearing two double-bonded oxygens and a terminal NH2 group. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, so it is a simple monosubstituted phenyl with no ring fusion and no additional heteroatoms. The sulfonamide group is the only polar functional group, and its two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors while the NH2 offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites. The methylene linker gives the molecule some rotational freedom, though the aromatic ring and the tetrahedral sulfur keep the overall structure fairly compact. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local rotational symmetry of the phenyl ring.

The molecule is built from a linear, fully aromatic fused polycyclic skeleton made of four six-membered rings joined edge-to-edge in a straight row, with no substituents attached to the carbon framework. Each ring shares one bond with its neighbor, creating an extended planar ring system in which all carbon atoms are sp2-hybridized and part of a continuous conjugated pi-electron network. The structure has no functional groups, so there are no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and the molecule is hydrocarbon-only. Its symmetry is high: the scaffold is essentially mirror-symmetric across its long axis, and its rigid, flat geometry leaves little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a fused tricyclic aromatic system built on a phenanthroline-type scaffold, containing two nitrogen atoms positioned in the outer rings so that they sit close together in a chelating arrangement. Two of its rings are pyridine-like and the central ring is a benzene-like carbocycle, with the fused rings sharing edges to make the framework largely planar and rigid. Two phenyl rings are attached as substituents at separate positions on the core, and two methyl groups sit adjacent to the ring nitrogens. The molecule has an approximate twofold symmetry axis through the central ring, and its two basic ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule consists of a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing one substituent. That substituent is a sulfonic acid group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and single-bonded to a hydroxyl group and to the ring carbon. The ring itself is fully unsaturated and planar, while the sulfur center adopts a tetrahedral-like geometry that gives the overall structure a rigid, largely flat aromatic core with limited conformational freedom. Because only one position on the ring is substituted, the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local mirror plane through the ring and the sulfonyl group. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single sp3 carbon bearing two phenyl rings, so it has a diphenylmethyl (benzhydryl) scaffold with no fused ring system. That central carbon also carries an isothiocyanate group, a nitrogen double-bonded to a carbon that is in turn double-bonded to sulfur, in a linear, rod-like arrangement. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted, and the two rings sit symmetrically on either side of the stereocenter, giving the molecule a propeller-like shape with a single chiral carbon that is not a true stereogenic center here because the two phenyl groups are identical. The overall framework is moderately flexible about the single bonds linking the rings to the central carbon. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen and sulfur of the isothiocyanate can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzo-fused sulfur heterocycle built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing a sulfonyl group. The sulfur atom carries two double-bonded oxygen atoms, forming a sulfone, and it is connected to a cis-configured carbon-carbon double bond that is also part of the fused ring system. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so its six carbons each carry a single hydrogen. The fused bicycle is largely planar and rigid, with little conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the sulfone and the alkene sit on one side of the fusion. The sulfonyl oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a benzothiophene scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiophene ring containing one sulfur atom, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the sulfur in the five-membered ring, so the substitution is at the 2-position of the thiophene portion. The fused system and the amide carbonyl make the framework rigid, with only the amide C–N bond offering limited rotation. The amide provides two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 group and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the sulfur and the aromatic ring contribute weaker acceptor character. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the carboxamide breaks the symmetry of the fused ring system.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic aromatic scaffold in which a five-membered thiophene ring is fused to a benzene ring, forming a benzothiophene core. A carboxylic acid group (-COOH) is attached directly to the thiophene ring at the carbon adjacent to the sulfur atom, which defines a single substitution site on an otherwise unsubstituted fused system. The fused rings are planar and rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom, apart from the carboxyl group's rotation about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the two oxygens), while the sulfur atom of the thiophene ring can act only as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzothiophene scaffold, in which a five-membered thiophene ring is fused to a benzene ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat bicyclic aromatic core. A cyanomethyl group (a methylene bridge bearing a nitrile) is attached to the carbon at the 3-position of the thiophene ring, adding a linear, polar C≡N unit. The fused ring system is essentially rigid and planar, with only the single CH2–CN side chain providing rotational freedom. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and the sulfur atom in the thiophene ring can contribute weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a small fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen atom in an N-O arrangement. The nitrogen in the five-membered ring carries a formal positive charge and an attached oxygen bearing a negative charge, giving an N-oxide-type zwitterionic group. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, with four adjacent aromatic C-H positions and no additional functional groups, so the substitution pattern is simply the fused framework itself. The fused bicycle is planar and rigid, and it has only the local symmetry of the benzo-fused ring, with no stereocenters or rotatable bonds. The N-oxide oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it lacks N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic aromatic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing an N-oxide-bearing nitrogen and an oxygen, forming a benzofuroxan-type benzoxadiazole core. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached to the benzene ring, giving a single substitution on the fused system. The fused bicyclic framework is planar and rigid, with the extensive aromatic conjugation locking the atoms into a flat geometry and offering little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the carboxyl group. The molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry because the single carboxylic acid substituent breaks the symmetry of the fused ring system. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the N-oxide oxygen and ring heteroatoms serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

This molecule is a hydrobenzoin-type vicinal diol built on a two-carbon ethane backbone, with each of the two central carbons bearing a hydroxyl group and two phenyl rings, giving four phenyl substituents in total. Each carbon is quaternary, bonded to two phenyl groups, one hydroxyl oxygen, and the other central carbon. The four benzene rings are unfused, each being a simple monocyclic aromatic ring attached through a single bond. The molecule possesses a two-fold rotational symmetry axis running through the central carbon-carbon bond, so the two halves are structurally equivalent. Because the central bond can rotate and the phenyl groups are bulky, the framework is fairly congested yet still conformationally flexible. The two hydroxyl groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aromatic rings offer only weak pi-based interactions.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring that contains both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom. The fused bicyclic core is fully aromatic and planar, which makes the framework rigid, with no rotatable bonds. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the benzene portion at the position meta-related to the ring-fusion carbon, giving a single substituent on that six-membered ring. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the nitrile sits off-centre on the benzo ring. The thiazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen provides a second, weaker acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is benzoyl fluoride, built on a single benzene ring bearing one acyl fluoride group attached directly to the ring. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion and no substituents other than the carbonyl carbon, so its substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The acyl fluoride group, a carbonyl bonded to a fluorine atom, is the only functional group, and the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is compact and largely rigid, with a single rotatable bond between the ring and the carbonyl, and it has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and the C=O axis.

The molecule is built around a ketone linking two aromatic rings through a single methylene bridge. One side carries a plain phenyl ring attached to the CH2 group, while the carbonyl carbon is bonded directly to a second benzene ring. That second ring bears a bromine atom located para to the carbonyl, giving a symmetric 1,4-disubstitution pattern on that ring. Both benzene rings are flat and aromatic, but the sp3-hybridized methylene linker adds some rotational flexibility between them. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a pyridine-based ester. A six-membered aromatic pyridine ring carries a carboxylate ester at the 3-position, and a hydroxyl group sits at the 6-position, adjacent to the ring nitrogen; this hydroxyl exists in tautomeric equilibrium with the corresponding pyridone form. The ester oxygen is bonded to a benzyl group, a phenyl ring attached through a flexible methylene linker, so the molecule has two separate aromatic systems that are not fused. The overall shape is largely planar within each ring, with rotational freedom about the ester and benzyl linkages. The hydroxyl (or pyridone N-H) provides a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and the carbonyl and ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single tetrahedral alpha carbon that bears a nitrile group, a benzyl ester, and an aryl ring, so the scaffold is a branched, non-planar core. The aryl ring is a benzene ring carrying a nitro group ortho to the attachment point and a trifluoromethyl group meta to it, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern without any internal symmetry. The benzyl ester contributes a second, unfused phenyl ring linked through a flexible CH2 and ester oxygen, which adds rotational freedom. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the nitrile, ester carbonyl and ether oxygen, and nitro oxygens serve as acceptors. Overall the molecule has no fused ring systems and is moderately flexible around its sp3 center and ester linkage.

This molecule is a benzyl methyl ether, built on a single benzene ring that serves as its scaffold. The benzene ring is a fully aromatic, planar six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, and it carries one substituent, a methoxymethyl group (–CH2–O–CH3), attached at one ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The molecule has no stereocenters and, apart from the local rotation of the flexible ether linkage, has no symmetry beyond the mirror-plane approximation of the aromatic ring. Its ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it contains no O–H or N–H bonds.

This molecule is an ester built from two benzene rings joined through a central carboxylate linkage. One aromatic ring bears a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl, placing the phenol ortho to the ester. The other ring is attached through a flexible methylene (CH2) bridge to the ester oxygen, so it is a benzyl group. Both rings are unfused and monosubstituted or disubstituted, with no stereocenters. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic hydroxyl act as hydrogen-bond acceptors and donors respectively, while the rotatable ester and benzylic bonds give the molecule moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a tertiary phosphine built around a central phosphorus atom bearing three substituents. Two of these are unsubstituted phenyl rings directly bonded to phosphorus, and the third is a benzyl group, meaning a phenyl ring attached through a single methylene (CH2) linker. Because the benzyl linker contains a rotatable sp3 carbon and the P–C bonds can rotate, the structure is fairly flexible with no fused ring systems. The molecule has no stereocenters and no halogens or other substituents on the rings, and the three aromatic rings give it an approximate propeller-like arrangement around phosphorus. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the lone pair on phosphorus gives it a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

This molecule is a benzylidenemalononitrile, consisting of a benzene ring attached through a single carbon-carbon double bond to a central carbon bearing two nitrile groups. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion has no substitution pattern to distinguish positions and is effectively symmetric about the axis running through the ring and the exocyclic double bond. The two cyano groups are linear and strongly electron-withdrawing, and the conjugated system from the ring through the alkene to the nitriles is largely planar and rigid. The nitrogen atoms of the nitrile groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since all its hydrogens are attached to carbon.

This molecule is an acyclic phosphonate-based amino acid derivative with no fused ring systems; its only ring is a single benzene ring, a phenyl group attached to a CH2 linker. The central carbon bears three substituents: a methyl ester group (COOCH3), a carbamate nitrogen (NH-C(=O)-O-), and a dimethyl phosphonate group (P(=O)(OCH3)2), giving it a tetrahedral, stereogenic alpha-carbon. The carbamate is a benzyl-protected amine, with the carbonyl and ether oxygens flanking the nitrogen. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is limited to the single N-H, while the ester carbonyl, carbamate carbonyl, and phosphoryl oxygen provide several acceptor sites. The molecule is flexible, with many rotatable single bonds, and lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single bond. One ring carries a carboxylic acid group at the position para to the biaryl linkage, so the substitution pattern is 1,4 on that ring, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. Both rings are aromatic and planar, and the connecting bond allows some rotation, giving the overall framework moderate rigidity. The molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that spans both rings, since only one ring is functionalized.

The molecule is a simple acyclic ether built from a two-carbon unit and a three-carbon unit joined through a single oxygen atom, giving a flexible, unbranched chain with no rings or fused systems. Each terminal carbon carries one chlorine atom, so the two halogen substituents sit at the ends of the chain in a symmetric arrangement. The central oxygen is the only heteroatom besides the halogens, and it acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs while offering no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The absence of any N-H or O-H groups means the molecule cannot donate hydrogen bonds. Its many rotatable single bonds make the backbone highly flexible, and the overall shape lacks any rigid or planar features.

This molecule is a symmetric disulfide, built from two identical para-chlorophenyl rings joined through a central sulfur–sulfur bond. Each benzene ring is a fully aromatic, planar six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and each carries one chlorine atom at the position opposite the sulfur attachment, giving a para substitution pattern. The two aryl halves are mirror-related across the S–S axis, so the overall framework is highly symmetric. The S–S linkage gives the molecule some rotational flexibility about the bond, while the aromatic rings remain rigid and flat. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and only weak acceptor character from the sulfur and chlorine atoms.

The molecule is a triarylphosphine, with a single trivalent phosphorus atom bonded to three separate benzene rings. Two of the rings are para-methoxy substituted, each carrying an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl group at the position opposite the phosphorus attachment, while the third ring is unsubstituted. The three aryl groups are not fused to one another, so the scaffold is built from three independent six-membered aromatic rings radiating from the central phosphorus. The phosphorus center is pyramidal and gives the molecule a propeller-like, three-bladed shape with a rotatable, moderately flexible arrangement around the P–C bonds. The phosphorus lone pair and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule has a linear four-atom carbon-carbon triple bond (an alkyne unit) bridging two phosphorus centers, with each phosphorus bearing two phenyl rings, so it is a bis(diphenylphosphino)acetylene framework. There are no fused ring systems; the only rings are two pairs of separate, unsubstituted benzene rings, one pair on each phosphorus. The phosphorus atoms are trivalent with lone pairs, making them potential coordination sites, while the molecule has no classical hydrogen-bond donors and only weak acceptor character at phosphorus. The alkyne unit is rigid and linear, and the two diphenylphosphino ends are related by a near two-fold symmetry about the central triple bond, though the phenyl rings can rotate about their P–C bonds, giving the overall structure moderate conformational flexibility at its outer edges.

This molecule is 1,2-bis(diphenylphosphino)ethane: a two-carbon ethylene bridge connects two tricoordinate phosphorus centers, each bearing two phenyl rings. The phosphorus atoms are trivalent and carry lone pairs, making them the key donor sites, while the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its phenyl rings are aromatic and planar. The structure has approximate two-fold symmetry about the midpoint of the central C–C bond, and the four phenyl groups are arranged around the two phosphorus centers. The ethylene linker gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility, whereas the phenyl rings are rigid and bulky.

This molecule is a symmetric, linear alkyne built around a central carbon-carbon triple bond. Each end of the triple bond is bonded to a silicon atom, and each silicon carries three methyl groups, giving two trimethylsilyl units joined by an acetylenic linker. There are no rings, ring fusions, or heteroatoms other than silicon and carbon. The structure is highly symmetric, with the two trimethylsilyl groups mirror-related across the alkyne axis, and the overall geometry is rigid and rod-like because the triple bond enforces linearity. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it has no N, O, or H atoms bonded to electronegative atoms.

This molecule is an oxime carbonate: a tert-butyl carbonate ester whose oxygen is bonded to the nitrogen of an oxime derived from a benzylic ketone bearing a nitrile. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, purely aliphatic unit that adds steric shielding around the carbonate linkage. A benzene ring is attached directly to the oxime carbon, and the C=N double bond carries defined geometry, so the scaffold is largely planar and rigid. The nitrile group sits on the same carbon as the oxime, giving a linear, electron-poor substituent. The molecule has no stereocenters and only modest overall symmetry, with the phenyl ring as its most symmetric region. The carbonyl and nitrile nitrogen and the oxime nitrogen and oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a short, acyclic two-carbon chain, with no rings and therefore no ring fusion. Its skeleton is a single methylene group linking a terminal carboxylic acid to a bromine atom, so the bromine sits on the carbon alpha to the carbonyl. The carboxylic acid group carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the carbon-bromine bond adds a polarizable halogen site. The structure is small and conformationally flexible about its single bonds, and it lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no fused or bridged rings and no double bonds. Its only substituent is one bromine atom attached to a ring carbon, so it is a monosubstituted cyclohexane with no stereocenters that would create multiple distinct isomers from this description alone. The ring carries a single halogen functional group and no other heteroatoms, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability beyond the weak halogen contribution. The cyclohexane ring can interconvert between chair conformations, making the core moderately flexible, while the molecule as a whole has only limited symmetry because the bromine breaks the ring's otherwise uniform substitution pattern.

The molecule is a small acyclic haloalkane built on a single carbon atom, so it has no ring systems and no ring fusion. That central carbon carries one hydrogen and three halogen substituents: two chlorines and one bromine, arranged as a dihalomethyl group bearing a bromine. Because the sole carbon is tetrahedral and the substituents are chemically distinct, the scaffold is not symmetric in the sense of a mirror plane with identical halogen pairs, though the two chlorines are equivalent. The structure is very rigid at the central carbon and has no rotatable bonds to speak of. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only hydrogen is bonded to carbon, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors beyond the weakly electronegative halogens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Five of the six ring carbons carry fluorine atoms and the remaining one carries a bromine atom, so the ring is fully substituted with no free hydrogens. The substitution pattern is a pentafluoro-bromo arrangement, with the bromine sitting opposite the fluorine-bearing carbon that is bonded to the other ring positions in a repeating sequence. The molecule has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and the aromatic ring is fully rigid and planar, with the halogen substituents lying in the ring plane. Its structure has an approximate local symmetry, with the halogens arranged around the ring in a nearly mirror-symmetric pattern. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, and its only potential acceptors are the fluorine and bromine atoms, which are weak.

The molecule is a short, unbranched aliphatic chain of four carbons ending in a primary amide group, so it has no ring systems and no ring fusion. The terminal carbon of the chain is a carbonyl carbon bonded to an amino group, giving a C(=O)NH2 functional group. The carbonyl oxygen and the two amide hydrogens together give the molecule a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, with two N-H donors and one carbonyl oxygen acceptor. The chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the simple linear arrangement of its atoms.

This molecule is a simple, acyclic aliphatic nitrile: a straight, unbranched chain of four carbon atoms terminated by a cyano group, with the nitrile carbon forming a carbon-nitrogen triple bond. It contains no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no substituents along the chain, so the substitution pattern is entirely linear. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the trivial linear arrangement of its heavy atoms, and the saturated alkyl segment provides some conformational flexibility around its single bonds, while the triple-bonded nitrile group is rigid and linear. The nitrogen atom of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a xanthine-type scaffold: a pyrimidine-2,6-dione ring fused to an imidazole ring to form a planar bicyclic purine-based system. The six-membered ring carries two carbonyl groups and three N-methyl substituents, one on each of the two ring nitrogens flanking the carbonyls and one on the imidazole nitrogen. The imidazole ring contains a single unsubstituted aromatic nitrogen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while all carbonyl oxygens also serve as acceptors. Because every ring nitrogen bears a methyl group, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The fused system is rigid and essentially flat, with only the methyl groups providing minor rotational freedom.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpene-type ketone built on a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane skeleton, with a gem-dimethyl group on one bridge and an angular methyl group at a bridgehead carbon. The single carbonyl sits in a six-membered ring adjacent to the quaternary bridgehead, giving a ketone functional group. The scaffold is compact, rigid, and cage-like, with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is camphorquinone, a bicyclic terpenoid built on a bornane skeleton. It contains a rigid bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane framework in which two fused five-membered rings share a bridging carbon arrangement, and a gem-dimethyl group sits on one bridge carbon while an angular methyl group occupies a bridgehead position. The defining feature is an adjacent pair of ketone carbonyls, forming a 1,2-diketone, on the two-carbon bridge of the bicycle. Because the cage is conformationally locked, the molecule is essentially inflexible, and it lacks any hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its overall framework is chiral, with no internal mirror plane.

The molecule is a fully aromatic tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, giving a planar carbazole-type scaffold. Its three rings are linearly fused, so the framework is rigid and flat with essentially no rotatable bonds. The only substituent positions are the unsubstituted carbons around the two benzo rings, so there is no functional group or substitution pattern beyond the parent ring system. The molecule has a mirror plane through the nitrogen, giving it a high degree of symmetry. The ring nitrogen bears one hydrogen, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while its lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic system and it is a poor acceptor.

This molecule is an acyclic anhydride built from two identical chloroacetyl units joined through a single oxygen bridge, giving it a symmetric, linear skeleton with no ring systems. Each half carries a carbonyl group bonded to a methylene carbon that bears a chlorine atom, so the substitution pattern is a terminal chlorine on each two-carbon arm. The central C–O–C linkage is the defining reactive feature, and the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its flexibility comes from the rotatable single bonds in the chain, though the carbonyl groups keep each arm fairly planar.

This molecule is a small acyclic ketone built on a three-carbon chain. A methyl group is attached to a carbonyl carbon, which is in turn bonded to a methylene group carrying a chlorine atom on the terminal carbon, so the chlorine sits alpha to the ketone's neighboring carbon, one position removed from the carbonyl. The structure contains no rings and no ring fusion, and the single C=O group is the only polar functional group apart from the carbon-chlorine bond. The chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the chlorine is positioned on only one end. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since it carries no O-H or N-H groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds and no fused partners. One hydrogen on this ring is replaced by a chlorine atom, so it is a monosubstituted benzene and there is no other functional group present. The structure is planar and fully rigid, with the ring and the C–Cl bond lying in one plane and no rotatable bonds to add conformational flexibility. The molecule has a local mirror plane through the C–Cl axis, giving it higher symmetry than an arbitrary substitution pattern would. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks O–H or N–H groups, and its only acceptor-like site is the weakly polar chlorine atom.

The molecule is an organosilicon compound built around a single silicon center bearing four substituents. One substituent is a straight, unbranched chain of eighteen carbon atoms, giving it a long, flexible alkyl tail with no rings or fused systems. The other three substituents on silicon are two methyl groups and one chloro group, so the silicon is tetrahedral and the molecule has a distinct polar head at one end and a nonpolar hydrocarbon tail at the other. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only heteroatom capable of acting as a weak acceptor is the chlorine. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond local rotational freedom around the chain, and its conformational flexibility arises mainly from rotation about the many carbon-carbon single bonds.

The molecule is chloroform-type structure built on a single carbon atom, with no ring systems and no fused rings. The central carbon is sp3-hybridized and bonded to three chlorine atoms and one hydrogen atom, giving it a simple tetrahedral-like scaffold. There are no additional functional groups beyond the three carbon-chlorine bonds, and the substitution pattern is a trisubstituted methane. The molecule has three-fold local symmetry around the C-H axis, and because it has no rotatable bonds it is essentially rigid. It carries no hydrogen-bond donor on heteroatoms, since the only hydrogen is attached to carbon, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings, with a cholestane-like skeleton: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring arranged in the classic tetracyclic pattern. A carbon-carbon double bond sits within one of the six-membered rings, and two angular methyl groups project from the ring junctions. A long, branched aliphatic side chain extends from the five-membered ring, and the fused system is largely rigid, with the side chain providing flexibility. At one position on the six-membered ring, a secondary ester oxygen links the scaffold to a benzoate unit bearing two chlorine substituents on its aromatic ring. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ester ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydroxyl or amine groups to serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The overall molecule is asymmetric because of the unsymmetrical side chain and the off-center ester substitution.

This molecule is a steroid built on the cholestane-type four-ring fused scaffold, with a cyclohexene ring A bearing a C5–C6 double bond typical of cholesterol-like frameworks. A linear nonanoyl ester (an eight-carbon-chain acyl group attached through an ester oxygen) is attached at the C3 position of the A ring. The side chain at C17 is a branched alkyl chain terminating in an isopropyl-type end, and two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions. The fused rings make the core largely rigid, while the side chain and the long acyl ester tail are highly flexible. The only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two ester oxygens, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a dibenzylideneacetone-type linear conjugated dienone: a central carbonyl flanked by a phenyl ring on one side and, through a two-carbon-two-double-bond chain (a 1,3-butadiene unit), a styryl group ending in a second phenyl ring on the other side. The two benzene rings are unfused and each carries no substituents, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted on both aromatic rings. The extended conjugation runs through the entire chain from one ring to the other, giving a largely planar, rigid backbone with restricted rotation about the double bonds. The ketone oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring, bearing two carboxylic acid groups on adjacent carbons, which places it in the 1,2-disubstituted cyclohexane family. Both substituents are carboxyl groups, each consisting of a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl oxygen, so the molecule contains two carbonyl acceptors and two hydroxyl donors. The stereochemical notation at the two ring carbons specifies a defined relative configuration, and the molecule is considered chiral. The cyclohexane ring is non-aromatic and adopts chair-like conformations, giving moderate conformational flexibility, while the two carboxylic acid groups can rotate about their attachment bonds. The molecule has no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry that maps the two halves onto each other.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 4, which makes it a piperazine scaffold. Two methyl groups are attached to the carbon atoms adjacent to the same nitrogen on one side, so the substitution pattern is a 2,5-dimethyl arrangement on the ring, with the two stereocenters specified in the SMILES. The ring is fully saturated with no double bonds or fused rings, so it adopts a relatively rigid chair-like conformation with limited flexibility. Both nitrogens are secondary amines, each able to act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The molecule lacks a mirror plane of symmetry because of its chiral centers.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring containing a single cis-configured double bond, giving a cyclohexene scaffold. Two carboxylic acid groups are attached to adjacent (1,2) ring carbons, and the stereochemistry at both substituted carbons is specified, indicating a defined relative arrangement of the two groups. The ring is only partially rigid: the alkene fixes one segment in place while the remaining saturated carbons allow some conformational flexibility. Each carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, so the molecule offers four acceptor sites and two donor sites in total.

This molecule is a single eight-membered carbocyclic ring with no fused or bridged rings and no heteroatoms, so its scaffold is simply a cyclooctene framework. Its only unsaturation is one carbon-carbon double bond, located between two adjacent ring carbons, and there are no other functional groups or substituents. The ring is fully symmetric in its unsubstituted form, lacking any stereocentres. Because the ring is medium-sized and contains a double bond, it is conformationally flexible yet less mobile than an open chain. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is a small five-membered unsaturated ring containing a single ring oxygen, forming a lactone-type scaffold with two carbonyl groups. One carbonyl is part of the ring and sits adjacent to the ring oxygen, while the other is a ring carbon bearing a double bond to a neighboring carbon. A methyl group is attached to the alkene carbon, giving a simple, asymmetric substitution pattern. The ring is essentially planar and rigid, with little conformational flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

Cyanogen bromide, written here as N#CBr, is a very small linear molecule with no ring systems at all. Its skeleton is a single carbon atom triple-bonded to nitrogen on one end and single-bonded to a bromine atom on the other, so the whole framework lies along one straight axis. The nitrile group (C≡N) is the only functional group present, and the bromine is attached directly to the carbon of that nitrile. Because the molecule is linear and has no substituent positions to vary, it has high symmetry about its long axis and essentially no conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen lone pair can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane skeleton, a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring with no fused or bridged rings and no heteroatoms in the ring. A single aldehyde group, a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bearing a hydrogen, is attached directly to one ring carbon, so there is no substitution elsewhere on the ring and no stereocenter-driven symmetry beyond that of the monosubstituted ring. The ring itself is conformationally flexible, able to interconvert between chair forms, while the planar aldehyde group adds only limited rigidity. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring hydrogens are on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold, with no fused or bridged ring systems and no heteroatoms in the ring itself. The only functional group is a thiol (sulfhydryl, -SH) attached to one ring carbon, so there is no substitution pattern beyond this single monosubstitution. The ring is conformationally flexible, able to interconvert between chair and other conformers, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local symmetry of the cyclohexyl unit. The sulfur-bearing hydrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom can serve only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the overall hydrogen-bonding capacity is limited.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no fused or bridged rings and no unsaturation. One ring carbon bears a hydroxyl group, making the compound a secondary alcohol, and the remaining positions are plain methylene carbons. Because only one substituent is present, the molecule has no substitution pattern to speak of beyond that single attachment, and its overall shape lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry in the way the hydroxyl sits relative to the ring. The cyclohexane ring is conformationally flexible, able to interconvert between chair forms, while the hydroxyl can adopt axial or equatorial orientations. The hydroxyl oxygen-bound hydrogen is a hydrogen-bond donor and the oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the rest of the framework is nonpolar.

The molecule is a ketone in which a carbonyl group bridges a phenyl ring and a cyclohexyl ring. The aromatic benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple monosubstitution at a single carbon. The cyclohexane ring is fully saturated, attaches to the carbonyl carbon at one position, and can adopt flexible chair conformations, while the planar aromatic ring is rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry axis beyond the free rotation about the single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a saturated carbocycle: a single nine-membered ring with no double bonds, no ring fusion, and no additional rings. Its only functional group is one primary amine (-NH2) attached to a ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted, with no other atoms or branches on the ring. The ring carbons are sp3-hybridized, giving a flexible, conformationally mobile framework rather than a rigid one, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial identity because the amine breaks the symmetry of the ring. The amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its two N-H bonds) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (through its lone pair).

The molecule is built from a simple saturated carbocycle bearing a two-carbon side chain. A cyclopentane ring, with no ring fusion or heteroatoms in the ring, is attached through a single methylene linker to a carboxylic acid group, so the molecule is a cyclopentylacetic acid scaffold. The ring is monosubstituted, and its flexible puckered conformations give the molecule moderate conformational freedom, with the rotatable CH2-COOH arm adding further flexibility. The carboxyl group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl O-H) and two acceptor oxygens (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), making it the only polar region in an otherwise nonpolar hydrocarbon framework. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local mirror-like arrangement of the ring, and no stereocenters are specified.

The molecule is built on a single three-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopropane, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. A primary carboxamide group, consisting of a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to an NH2 group, is attached directly to one ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The cyclopropane ring is strained and rigid, while the amide bond itself is planar and partially restricted in rotation. Because the carboxamide carries two N-H donors and one carbonyl oxygen acceptor, the molecule can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The overall structure is small and lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local threefold character of the ring.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing one edge. A dimethylamino group, N(CH3)2, is attached to one ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, while a primary sulfonamide group, SO2NH2, sits on the other ring, also next to the fusion. The two substituents therefore lie on opposite rings and are arranged asymmetrically, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The fused aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the sulfonamide and dimethylamino groups have some rotational freedom. The sulfonamide's NH2 group can donate hydrogen bonds and its sulfonyl oxygens can accept them, whereas the tertiary amine nitrogen lacks an N-H and can only act as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing an edge. One ring carries a dimethylamino group, a tertiary amine attached to the aromatic carbon, and the other ring bears a sulfonyl chloride group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to chlorine. These substituents sit on different rings, on opposite sides of the fused core, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused aromatic framework is rigid and planar, while the dimethylamino and sulfonyl chloride groups can rotate about their single bonds to the ring. The sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the amine nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl carbon bonded directly to two identical aromatic rings. Each ring is a benzene ring carrying five fluorine substituents, so every ring position except the one attached to the carbonyl bears a fluorine atom. The two pentafluorophenyl groups are chemically equivalent and arranged symmetrically about the C=O axis, giving the molecule a high degree of symmetry.
