The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The scaffold is fairly rigid, though rotation about the two aryl–carbonyl single bonds is still possible.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single bond between their first carbons, so it has a central biphenyl scaffold. Each ring is fully substituted with fluorine atoms: the first ring bears four fluorines and the second bears five, so the molecule carries nine fluorine substituents in total and no hydrogen atoms on either ring. The two aromatic rings are fully fluorinated and planar, and the single linking bond allows some rotation between them, though steric crowding from the ortho fluorines restricts it. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the fluorine atoms, which are weak. Overall it is not symmetric because the two rings carry different fluorine counts.

This molecule is a cyclic siloxane built on a twelve-membered ring that alternates silicon and oxygen atoms, with six silicon centers and six oxygen bridges. Every silicon atom carries two methyl groups, so the scaffold is fully substituted with no hydrogen-bearing ring positions and no functional groups beyond the Si–O backbone and the methyls. The ring is fully saturated, flexible, and lacks any fused or bridged ring systems, though the Si–O bonds give it considerable conformational freedom. Its symmetry is high, with the methyl-bearing silicon centers arranged in a repeating pattern around the ring. Because the oxygen atoms have no attached hydrogens and the methyl groups are nonpolar, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and only weak acceptor capability at the ring oxygens.

The molecule is an unbranched, saturated carbon chain of ten carbons with no rings, double bonds, or substituents along the backbone. Its one functional group is a carboxylic acid located at the terminal carbon, where a carbonyl carbon bears both a double-bonded oxygen and a hydroxyl group. The structure is linear and symmetric about its long axis, apart from the polar head group at one end. The long methylene chain is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds that allow numerous conformations. The hydroxyl hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two oxygen atoms of the carboxyl group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, unbranched aliphatic chain of ten carbon atoms with a nitrile group at one terminus. The carbon skeleton is entirely saturated apart from the carbon-nitrogen triple bond, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents along the chain. The nitrile carbon is linear, giving the terminal end a rod-like geometry, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond its constitutional arrangement. The chain is highly flexible because of free rotation about its many single bonds, while the nitrile end is rigid. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a six-membered 2H-pyran-2,4(3H)-dione-type ring, a lactone with an endocyclic carbonyl and an enol-ether oxygen within the same ring. Its carbonyl carbons sit at ring positions adjacent to the oxygen and at a position next to a carbon bearing a sp3 carbon. A ring double bond sits between the carbon bearing a methyl group and the adjacent carbon, so the ring is partly unsaturated and largely planar. At the sp3 carbon between two carbonyls, an acetyl group (a methyl ketone) is attached, giving an additional carbonyl outside the ring. The scaffold has no internal symmetry, since the methyl and acetyl substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The ring is fairly rigid, while the acetyl side chain can rotate freely. Oxygen atoms in the carbonyls and the ring ether can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a six-membered lactone, a cyclic ester built on a saturated oxane-type ring containing one ring oxygen and a carbonyl carbon adjacent to that oxygen. The ring is fully saturated apart from the exocyclic-to-ring carbonyl double bond, so it has a single ring system with no fusion or aromatic components. A linear n-butyl chain is attached to the ring carbon next to the ring oxygen, creating a single substitution point with no stereochemical symmetry across the scaffold. The ring offers moderate conformational flexibility, with the saturated carbons able to adopt chair-like arrangements while the ester group stays comparatively planar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the carbonyl oxygen and the ring ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a deoxybenzoin-type scaffold: a ketone carbonyl bridging two aromatic rings through a single methylene carbon. One ring is a plain phenyl group attached directly to the carbonyl carbon, while the other is a benzyl group, with the methylene linker sitting between the carbonyl and a second unsubstituted phenyl ring. Both aromatic rings are unsubstituted benzene rings, so the substitution pattern is simple and there is no additional heteroatom functionality beyond the ketone. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane arrangement through the carbonyl and methylene carbons, and the two phenyl rings can rotate about their single bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a fully saturated five-membered cyclic ether, a tetrahydrofuran-type ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbon atoms, with no double bonds or aromatic character. Four of the ring carbons each carry an oxygen-bearing substituent: two bear hydroxyl groups, one of which is an anomeric carbon also bonded to the ring oxygen and a hydroxymethyl group, and another ring carbon bears a hydroxymethyl arm. Two additional hydroxymethyl side chains project from the ring, giving a polyhydroxylated scaffold with several stereocenters. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. Its many hydroxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring itself is fairly rigid with limited conformational freedom.

Di(thiophen-2-yl)methanone is built around a single central carbonyl carbon bonded to two aromatic five-membered rings. Each ring is a thiophene, a planar heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, and both are attached through their 2-position carbons, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the carbonyl. The two rings are conjugated with the ketone, giving a largely planar, relatively rigid scaffold, although rotation about the two bonds linking the carbonyl to the rings remains possible. The molecule has an approximate twofold symmetry axis running through the carbonyl oxygen and carbon. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic thioether built from two allyl groups joined through a single sulfur atom, giving a simple dialkyl sulfide scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. Each terminal allyl unit contains a carbon-carbon double bond at its end, so the molecule carries two terminal alkene functional groups in an otherwise saturated framework. The two allyl arms are chemically equivalent, so the structure has a mirror-type symmetry through the sulfur atom. Its chain segments are flexible and free to rotate about single bonds, which gives the molecule considerable conformational freedom. The sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a tricyclic scaffold in which two benzene rings are fused to a central seven-membered ring containing one sulfur atom and one ketone carbonyl. The carbonyl carbon sits between one benzene ring and the sulfur-bearing ring, while a methylene (CH2) group links the other benzene ring to the sulfur, giving a dibenzothiepinone-type framework. The two aromatic rings are unsubstituted, so the structure carries no additional substituents on the benzene rings. The central ring is non-planar and somewhat flexible, though the two fused aromatic systems constrain its overall shape. The molecule has no strict symmetry because the carbonyl and the CH2 group occupy different positions. The ketone oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is dibenzofuran, a rigid, planar, tricyclic aromatic system in which two benzene rings are fused on either side of a central five-membered furan ring containing one oxygen atom. The three rings share edges to form a fully conjugated, flat scaffold with no rotatable bonds and no sp3 carbons. Its structure has two-fold symmetry about an axis running through the furan oxygen and the midpoint of the C–C bond joining the two benzene rings. The molecule carries no substituents, so every ring position is an unsubstituted C–H. The furan oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is dibenzyl carbonate, built around a central carbonate group in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to two oxygen atoms, each of which connects to a benzyl group. Each benzyl unit consists of a methylene linker attached to a monosubstituted benzene ring, so the two aromatic rings are unfused and are separated from the central carbonate by flexible CH2–O bonds. The structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the carbonyl carbon, with the two benzyl arms related to each other. Functionally, the molecule contains two phenyl rings and one carbonate ester, with no hydrogen-bond donors and three oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rotatable C–O and CH2–C bonds make the molecule fairly flexible overall.

This molecule is dibenzyl disulfide, built from two benzene rings each attached through a methylene (CH2) linker to a central sulfur-sulfur (disulfide) bridge. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted, carrying only hydrogen atoms, so the substitution pattern is simple and identical on both sides. The two halves are related by a twofold symmetry axis through the S–S bond, giving the molecule an overall C2-like arrangement. The disulfide linkage and the two CH2 groups provide rotational flexibility, while the aromatic rings are rigid planar units. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors beyond the sulfur atoms, which are weak acceptors at most.

The molecule is built on a short, acyclic three-carbon backbone with no ring systems and no ring fusion. Its central carbon is a quaternary sp3 carbon bearing two bromine atoms, flanked on both sides by carboxamide groups, so the scaffold is a malonamide core with the central methylene replaced by a geminal dibromide. The two primary amide groups, each containing a carbonyl oxygen and an NH2 nitrogen, are the only functional groups present. The arrangement is symmetric about the central carbon, with the two bromines on opposite faces of that carbon, and the molecule has relatively few rotatable bonds, giving it moderate flexibility. Each amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N-H bonds and an acceptor site at its carbonyl oxygen, so the molecule has four donor and two acceptor capabilities in total.

This molecule is a small tetrahedral organosilicon compound built around a single silicon center. The silicon atom carries two methyl groups and two chlorine atoms, giving it a symmetric substitution pattern in which the two methyls are equivalent and the two chlorines are equivalent. It contains no rings, no fused systems, and no multiple bonds, so the structure is acyclic and conformationally simple. The silicon-chlorine bonds are the most reactive functional features, while the molecule offers no hydrogen-bond donor sites and only weak, non-classical acceptor character from the chlorine atoms.

This molecule is a small organophosphorus compound built on a single benzene ring attached directly to a phosphorus atom. The phosphorus is trivalent and carries two chlorine substituents, making it a dichlorophosphino group bonded to one aromatic carbon of the phenyl ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted apart from this one attachment, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the ring has a planar, six-membered aromatic scaffold. The phosphorus center is pyramidal and the P–C and P–Cl bonds give limited rigidity beyond the aromatic ring, with the overall molecule lacking any internal symmetry axis beyond the local mirror plane through the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor character is weak, arising from the phosphorus lone pair.

This molecule is a macrocyclic polyether built from two fused cyclohexane rings, each bridged into a larger ring through a chain of ether oxygens and two-carbon linkers. The two cyclohexane units share a fused junction with the polyether ring, giving a rigid, cup-like bicyclic framework at each end of the macrocycle. The ring contains repeating –O–CH2–CH2– units, so the oxygens are spaced regularly around the cavity and act as hydrogen-bond acceptors while offering no hydrogen-bond donors. There are no carbonyls, amines, or other polar functional groups, and the molecule is largely symmetric, with its two halves mirrored across the central ring. Its many sp3 carbons and ether linkages give it considerable conformational flexibility within the macrocyclic loop.

The molecule is a small, flexible acyclic amine built on a two-carbon-unit backbone. Its skeleton is a linear chain in which a central secondary nitrogen is flanked on both sides by two-carbon segments, each terminating in a hydroxyl group, so it contains no ring systems and no ring fusion. The two terminal alcohol groups and the central secondary amine make up its only functional groups, and the arrangement is symmetric about the nitrogen. Because all bonds are single and the chain is unconstrained, the structure is highly rotatable and conformationally flexible. The two hydroxyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the two hydroxyl groups and the secondary amine N-H can each donate them.

The molecule is a diethyl ester of a 2-(benzotriazol-1-yl-imino) malonic acid: an open-chain malonate core whose central carbon is double-bonded to a nitrogen that is part of a benzotriazole ring system. The benzotriazole is a bicyclic scaffold in which a five-membered triazole ring is fused to a benzene ring, and the attachment to the imine nitrogen occurs at a ring nitrogen of the triazole. Two ethyl ester groups flank the central carbon, providing carbonyl oxygens as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused aromatic system is rigid and planar, whereas the two ethyl ester arms are flexible. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the imine links the two ester groups asymmetrically to the aromatic heterocycle.

Diethyl acetylenedicarboxylate is a small, linear, and highly rigid molecule built around a central carbon-carbon triple bond. Each end of this alkyne is attached directly to a carbonyl carbon, forming two ester groups, and each ester is capped by an ethyl group through its oxygen atom. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the midpoint of the triple bond, so the two halves are mirror images of one another. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the sp-hybridized alkyne keeps the backbone essentially straight. The carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an acyclic malonate diester, built on a central quaternary carbon bearing two ethyl ester groups. That central carbon also carries two identical 2-cyanoethyl chains, each ending in a nitrile group. Because the central carbon is tetrasubstituted and the two ester arms and two nitrile arms are arranged around it, the molecule has a high degree of symmetry about that center. It contains no rings and has many rotatable single bonds, so it is quite flexible. The two ester carbonyl oxygens and the two nitrile nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from a simple, acyclic two-carbon-ethyl skeleton joined through a single ether oxygen, giving a symmetric arrangement in which each ethyl group is attached to the central oxygen. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or multiple bonds, so its structure is entirely saturated and sp3-hybridized. The only functional group is the ether linkage, and there are no substituents beyond the two terminal methyl groups. The molecule is highly flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon and carbon-oxygen single bond. The oxygen atom can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites because it carries no hydrogen directly bonded to oxygen or nitrogen.

This molecule is a small acyclic diester built on a four-carbon chain, with two ethyl ester groups at the chain ends. The two central carbons each carry a secondary hydroxyl group, giving a vicinal diol flanked by the ester carbonyls. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and fairly flexible, with free rotation about the single bonds. The two stereocenters are arranged in a configuration that gives the molecule a two-fold rotational symmetry, since the two halves are mirror-like copies of each other. Each hydroxyl oxygen and each ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the two hydroxyl groups also serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a single tetrahedral acetal-type carbon that bears two ethoxy groups and one aryloxy group, so it is an orthoester-like framework. The aromatic portion is a plain benzene ring with no fused rings and no substituents other than the single oxygen link, making the phenyl group monosubstituted. Two ethyl chains extend from the central carbon through ether oxygens, adding conformational flexibility, while the phenyl ring stays rigid and planar. The molecule has no stereocenters and only local symmetry: the two ethoxy groups are chemically equivalent. It has three ether-type oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, and no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single tetrahedral carbon that carries two ethyl ester groups and one phenyl ring, making it a diethyl phenylmalonate-type scaffold. Each ester consists of a carbonyl group bonded to an oxygen that is in turn attached to an ethyl chain, so the two ester functionalities are symmetric about the central carbon. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, a simple six-membered aromatic system fused to nothing else. The central carbon bears one hydrogen, so it is a stereocenter only in the sense that its two ester groups are identical, which removes chirality. The molecule is fairly flexible because of the rotatable single bonds in the ethyl chains and the central linkage, and it has two carbonyl oxygens and two ester oxygens as hydrogen-bond acceptors while lacking any hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small acyclic organophosphorus compound built around a single central phosphorus atom. Each of the two ethoxy groups, consisting of an ethyl chain bonded through an oxygen, is attached directly to phosphorus, giving a symmetric pattern with two identical substituents. The phosphorus also carries a hydroxyl group, so the structure has a P–OH unit that behaves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule contains no ring systems, so it is highly flexible with freely rotating single bonds.

Diethyl sulfide is an acyclic thioether with no rings, so its scaffold is simply a central sulfur atom bonded to two ethyl groups, each a two-carbon saturated chain. The molecule has no stereocenters and no functional groups beyond the thioether linkage itself. Its structure is highly flexible, since rotation about the single C–S and C–C bonds allows many conformations, and it possesses approximate two-fold symmetry through the sulfur atom. Sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites because it contains no N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is a simple acyclic sulfone, with a central sulfur atom bearing two oxygen atoms in a doubly bonded arrangement and flanked on either side by an ethyl group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and consists of a single hexavalent sulfur center linked to two two-carbon alkyl chains. The two ethyl groups are identical, giving the molecule a mirror-symmetric structure about the sulfonyl core. The skeleton is highly flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-sulfur and carbon-carbon bond. The sulfonyl oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because all attached hydrogens are on saturated carbon atoms.

The molecule has a simple acyclic scaffold: two ethyl groups joined through a single nitrogen atom, giving a dialkylamine rather than any ring or fused system. Each ethyl group is a two-carbon saturated chain, so the skeleton is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the nitrogen, so its two arms are structurally equivalent. The nitrogen carries one hydrogen, making it a secondary amine, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through that N–H and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. No other functional groups or substituents are present.

The molecule is a flexible, open-chain polyether-alcohol built from a two-carbon-unit backbone: two terminal primary hydroxyl groups are joined through a central ether oxygen. Its scaffold contains no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic or alkene units, so it is entirely saturated and sp3-hybridized. The molecule is symmetric about the central oxygen, with each arm identical, and it has many rotatable single bonds that give it considerable conformational flexibility. Both terminal hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the central ether oxygen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is a flexible, acyclic chain built from a two-carbon ethyl group, two ether oxygens, and a terminal primary alcohol, giving it a simple linear scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. Its backbone consists of ethylene units separated by ether linkages, so the chain has many rotatable bonds and can adopt a wide range of conformations. There are no aromatic groups, stereocenters, or other substituents, so the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond the local arrangement of its repeating units. The terminal hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated ether-alcohol with a linear chain skeleton of carbon and oxygen atoms, containing no rings or ring fusion. Starting from one end, a four-carbon n-butyl group is bonded to an ether oxygen, followed by a two-carbon ethylene unit, a second ether oxygen, another two-carbon unit, and finally a terminal hydroxyl group. There are two ether oxygens, each acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and one terminal hydroxyl that can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The chain has no branching or stereocenters, so it is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds and no symmetry beyond an approximate mirror arrangement along its length.

The molecule is built around a single silicon atom, which forms the central scaffold, rather than any ring or carbon chain. Silicon is bonded to two methoxy groups, each consisting of an oxygen atom attached to a methyl group, and to two additional methyl groups directly on the silicon. Because there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no multiple bonds, the structure is small, acyclic, and highly flexible, with free rotation around each Si–O and Si–C bond. The arrangement is tetrahedral around silicon and carries a degree of symmetry, since the two methoxy groups and the two methyl groups are pairwise equivalent. The oxygen atoms are the only hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a linear aliphatic diester with no rings, aromatic systems, or stereocenters. Its backbone is a straight chain of twelve carbons, with a methyl ester group at each end, so the two terminal carbonyl carbons each bear a methoxy group. The structure is fully symmetric about the midpoint of the chain, and the central methylene segment is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds. Each ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because no N–H or O–H groups are present.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring, which carries an N–H group that can donate a hydrogen bond. Two adjacent carbons on the ring each bear a methyl ester group, one next to the nitrogen and one further along, while the remaining two adjacent ring carbons each carry a hydroxyl group. The compound has no fused rings, and its substitution pattern is unsymmetrical because the two ester groups sit in different environments. The ring is rigid and planar, though the ester and hydroxyl substituents can rotate. The two hydroxyl groups and the N–H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl and ether oxygens of the esters act as acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, five-carbon chain with carbonyl groups at both ends and a central ketone. Each terminal carbon is part of a methyl ester, so the structure is a symmetric dimethyl ester built around a ketone. The skeleton is fully acyclic, with no ring systems or fusion. It has two ester carbonyl oxygens and one ketone oxygen as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The central methylene groups between the carbonyls are flexible and can adopt many conformations, and the molecule has a mirror-plane symmetry through the central ketone carbon.

This molecule is a short, acyclic diester built on a four-carbon backbone. Its central feature is a carbon-carbon triple bond flanked on each side by an ester group, so the two carbonyl carbons sit directly attached to the alkyne. Each terminal ester is a methyl ester, with a methoxy oxygen bonded to a carbonyl oxygen, giving two carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bond acceptors and two ether-type oxygen acceptors. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no ring systems. The structure is linear and rigid because of the alkyne unit, and it possesses a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the midpoint of the triple bond.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single bond between their para positions. Each ring carries a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that bears a methyl group) at the position opposite the biaryl linkage, so the two ester substituents sit at the termini of a linear, rod-like framework. The structure is highly symmetric, with the two halves related by a center of inversion. The aromatic rings are rigid and planar, while the ester groups have limited rotational freedom about their single bonds. The carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is dimethyl disulfide, a small acyclic compound with no rings. Its scaffold is a two-atom sulfur-sulfur bond flanked on each side by a methyl group, giving a simple linear chain of the form CH3-S-S-CH3. It contains no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no functional groups beyond the disulfide linkage itself. The molecule is highly symmetric, with the two methyl groups related by a two-fold axis through the S-S bond, and the S-S bond allows torsional flexibility around its axis. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

Dimethyl fumarate (or its isomer, dimethyl maleate) is the structure here; this SMILES has a trans/cis-unspecified C=C, so I'll describe the skeleton without naming it. The molecule is a short, linear four-carbon chain built around a central carbon-carbon double bond, with a methyl ester group at each terminus. Each ester carries a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since no N-H or O-H groups are present. There are no ring systems or fused rings, so the scaffold is acyclic and fairly rigid around the double bond, but the ester C-O single bonds and methyl groups allow rotational flexibility. The two ester groups are arranged symmetrically across the double bond, giving the molecule a balanced, mirror-related substitution pattern.

The molecule is an acyclic, non-ring structure built around a short carbon backbone bearing three carbonyl-containing ester groups. A methoxy group (CH3-O-) is attached to one end of a carbon-carbon double bond, and the other alkene carbon carries two methyl ester groups (-C(=O)OCH3). The two methyl esters on the same carbon make the arrangement roughly symmetric about that central carbon, while the methoxyvinyl unit sits off to one side. Because the double bond and the ester linkages are the main rigid elements, the molecule is fairly flexible overall, with free rotation about the single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no O-H or N-H groups are present, but its three ether and carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene core, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge. Two methyl ester groups, each a carbonyl bearing an oxygen-linked methyl, are attached to the ring carbons, one on each ring, placed on opposite sides of the fused system (a 2,6-disubstitution pattern). The structure is planar and largely rigid, because the aromatic framework constrains the geometry, with only the ester groups able to rotate. The molecule is highly symmetric, possessing an inversion-like arrangement in which the two ester substituents are related by the center of the fused ring system. The carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a simple acyclic diester built on an oxalate skeleton: two carbonyl carbons joined directly by a carbon-carbon single bond, with each carbonyl bearing a methoxy group. Its structure is entirely open-chain, containing no rings, no fused ring systems, and no stereogenic centers. Each ester unit consists of a C=O double bond and an ether-type oxygen linked to a terminal methyl group, giving the molecule two equivalent ester functionalities arranged symmetrically about the central C–C bond. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoint of that central bond, and its flexibility comes mainly from rotation about the single bonds. Ester carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because no N–H or O–H groups are present.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methyl ester groups on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic diester. Each substituent is a carbonyl carbon bonded to an oxygen that carries a methyl group, so the core scaffold is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no fused rings. The two ester groups are neighboring, which creates a fixed substitution pattern and a moderately rigid framework, though the methoxy groups can rotate about their single bonds. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the two ester arms are chemically equivalent but sit next to each other on the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the four oxygen atoms of the two carbonyl and ether linkages can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a pyridine ring bearing two methyl ester groups, one attached directly to the ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (position 2) and the other on the carbon at position 6, so the two substituents flank the nitrogen symmetrically. The aromatic six-membered heterocycle is planar and rigid, with the nitrogen contributing a lone pair that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Each ester carbonyl oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all its hydrogens are bound to carbon. The methoxy groups give the esters some conformational flexibility, and the overall structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis passing through the nitrogen and the para carbon.

This molecule is dimethyl terephthalate, built on a single benzene ring carrying two methyl ester groups at the 1 and 4 positions, which are directly opposite each other. Each ester consists of a carbonyl carbon bonded to an oxygen that is in turn bonded to a methyl group, so the molecule contains no fused ring systems and only one aromatic ring. The para substitution pattern gives the structure a centrosymmetric, linear, and largely planar shape, with the two ester groups symmetrically related across the ring. Its scaffold is conformationally rigid, with limited flexibility beyond rotation of the methyl ester groups. The carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all its hydrogens are on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single silicon center bearing two methyl groups, a hydrogen atom, and one phenyl ring, making it a dimethylphenylsilane scaffold. The phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, so there is no substitution pattern on the aromatic portion and no ring fusion. The molecule has no heteroatom functional groups beyond the silicon–hydrogen bond, and its silicon–hydrogen bond is a reactive site rather than a polar donor. Because the silicon is tetrahedral with two identical methyl groups, the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the Si–H and Si–phenyl bonds. It contains no classical hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its single rotatable bond to the phenyl ring gives it only modest flexibility.

This molecule is an acyclic phosphate triester-type structure built around a central phosphorus atom bearing one double-bonded oxygen, one free hydroxyl group, and two identical n-butoxy chains attached through oxygen linkages. The scaffold therefore contains no rings and no ring fusion, and its only heteroatoms are the phosphorus and the four oxygens. Two unbranched four-carbon alkyl tails flank the phosphorus center, so the molecule is symmetric about the P atom, apart from the difference between the P=O and P–OH oxygens. The flexible saturated chains give it considerable conformational freedom, while the tetrahedral phosphorus center stays rigid. The free P–OH group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxygen atoms, particularly the P=O, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a linear diester built from a ten-carbon dicarboxylic acid backbone, with a straight saturated chain of methylene units running between two ester carbonyl groups. Each end is capped by an unbranched n-butyl group attached through an ester oxygen, so the molecule is fully symmetric about its center. It contains no rings, no aromatic systems, and no stereocenters, making it highly flexible with many accessible rotational conformations. Each ester group offers two oxygen atoms, with the carbonyl oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an acyclic dialkyl thioether, built from two straight unbranched chains joined through a single sulfur atom. Each side is a four-carbon n-butyl group, so the overall skeleton is a linear, symmetric chain with the sulfur at its center. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no other functional groups or substituents beyond the central thioether linkage. The molecule is highly flexible, since rotation about its many single C–C and C–S bonds gives it many conformations. Sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

This molecule is an acyclic dialkyl thioether, with two straight-chain nonyl groups joined through a single sulfur atom, giving a symmetric skeleton of nine carbons on each side of the central divalent sulfur. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents beyond the terminal methyl ends, so its substitution pattern is simply linear and mirror-symmetric about the sulfur. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon and carbon-sulfur single bond, allowing many conformations. The sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

This molecule is a diester built on a benzene core. The central scaffold is a benzene ring bearing two ester groups on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho substitution pattern. Each ester carbonyl is bonded to an oxygen that carries a straight, unbranched eight-carbon alkyl chain, so the two chains are identical and the molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the ring. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the two long octyl tails are highly flexible and conformationally mobile. The ester oxygens and carbonyl oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic secondary amine built from two straight, unbranched eight-carbon alkyl chains joined through a single nitrogen atom, giving a symmetric dioctylamine-type skeleton. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems. The only functional group is the central secondary amine, which bears one hydrogen on nitrogen, so it can act as a single hydrogen-bond donor and as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The molecule is highly flexible because of the many freely rotating carbon-carbon single bonds, and its mirror-symmetric arrangement about the nitrogen gives it a long, linear, amphiphilic-like shape with a polar head and two nonpolar tails.

This molecule is diphenyl ether, consisting of two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom, giving a C–O–C bridge between two aromatic scaffolds. Each ring is an unsubstituted six-membered aromatic ring, so there are no additional functional groups or substituents beyond the central ether linkage. The two phenyl rings are related by a symmetric arrangement about the oxygen, which gives the molecule a pseudo-symmetric, twisted shape rather than a fully planar one. The ether oxygen is flexible around its two C–O bonds, allowing the rings to rotate relative to each other. The oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds through its lone pairs, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a phosphoramidate built around a central phosphorus atom bearing one double-bonded oxygen (a phosphoryl group), one free amino group (NH2), and two phenoxy substituents. Each phenoxy unit is a simple benzene ring attached through an oxygen atom, so the scaffold is a tetrahedral phosphorus center flanked by two aromatic rings with no ring fusion. The two phenyl rings are unsubstituted and symmetrically related, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold relationship across the P center. The P=O oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The P–O–aryl linkages add rotational flexibility, though the aromatic rings themselves remain rigid and planar.

This molecule is a diester built on a benzene-1,2-dicarboxylate (phthalate) core, in which two carbonyl carbons sit on adjacent positions of a central benzene ring. Each carbonyl is bonded through an ester oxygen to a separate phenyl ring, so the structure contains three aromatic six-membered rings in total. The two ester groups are ortho to each other, giving a twisted, non-planar arrangement and a substitution pattern that is not symmetric about the central ring. The ester carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Rotation about the ester and aryl-oxygen bonds makes the scaffold moderately flexible.

The molecule is diphenyl sulfoxide, built around a single tetravalent-looking sulfur atom that is bonded to one oxygen atom (as an S=O group) and to two separate benzene rings. Each benzene ring is an unsubstituted six-membered aromatic ring, with no fusion between the rings and no additional substituents, so the two rings are attached only through the central sulfur. The molecule has an approximately twofold symmetry through the S=O axis, and the rotation about each sulfur-to-ring bond gives moderate conformational flexibility. The sulfinyl oxygen is a good hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring carrying two ester groups in a para (1,4) arrangement. Each ester links the ring carbonyl carbon to an oxygen that is bonded to a separate, unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the scaffold is symmetric about the central ring. The core is a fully aromatic, extended, rod-like framework with three benzene rings joined through rigid ester linkages. Each ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its aromatic rings and planar ester units give limited conformational flexibility, mainly from rotation about the ester C–O bonds.

The molecule is a tertiary phosphine built around a central phosphorus atom bonded to three aryl groups. Two of these are unsubstituted phenyl rings, while the third is an ortho-tolyl ring, meaning a benzene ring carrying a methyl group directly adjacent to the phosphorus attachment point. The three aromatic rings are monocyclic and not fused to one another, so no bridged or fused ring system is present. The phosphorus center is trivalent with a lone pair, giving a pyramidal geometry that makes the molecule conformationally flexible around the P–C bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups, and its phosphorus lone pair gives it only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character.

The molecule is built around a single sp3 carbon bearing a carboxylic acid group and two phenyl rings, giving a diphenylacetic acid scaffold. Each benzene ring is unsubstituted, so both aromatic rings carry no additional functional groups, and the two rings are attached symmetrically to the central carbon. The methine carbon is a stereocenter only in the sense that it carries two identical phenyl groups, so the molecule is achiral and possesses a mirror plane through the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid functions as both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the phenyl rings contribute only aromatic surface without hydrogen-bonding capability. The sp3 linkage gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility around the single bonds, though the bulky aryl groups restrict rotation.

This molecule is a diphenylphosphine oxide, built around a single tetrahedral-like phosphorus center bearing a P=O group and one P-H bond. Two unsubstituted phenyl rings are attached directly to the phosphorus atom, so the scaffold is a simple, non-fused aromatic arrangement with no additional ring fusion. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted and can rotate about the P-C bonds, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility. The phosphoryl oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the P-H group offers only weak donor character, and the molecule is largely free of other polar functionality.

This molecule is di-tert-butyl azodicarboxylate, built around a central nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in a trans (E) configuration. Each nitrogen carries a carbonyl group forming a carbamate-type ester, and each ester oxygen is bonded to a tert-butyl group. The molecule has no rings, so its scaffold is a short, acyclic chain with a rigid planar core. It shows approximate two-fold symmetry across the N=N bond, with the two tert-butyl ester arms mirroring each other. The carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a malonate diester built around a single three-carbon chain: a central methylene (CH2) flanked by two carbonyl carbons. Each carbonyl is esterified with a tert-butyl group, so the two ends are bulky, identical, and symmetric about the central carbon. There are no rings and no fused systems, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. Its two ester carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens sit on carbon. The central CH2 is flexible, but the bulky tert-butyl groups restrict rotation around the adjacent ester linkages.

The molecule is an open-chain six-carbon sugar with no rings, so its scaffold is a flexible linear chain of carbons. The terminal carbon at one end is an aldehyde group, and the other end is a primary alcohol, with four secondary hydroxyl groups sitting on the four internal stereogenic carbons. Because every carbon in the backbone is a stereocenter, the chain is chiral and has no internal symmetry. The many hydroxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen adds further acceptor capacity.

The molecule is built on a five-membered saturated lactone ring, a gamma-butyrolactone-type scaffold containing one ring oxygen and one carbonyl carbon adjacent to that oxygen. The ring carries two methyl groups on the same carbon, creating a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern, and a hydroxyl group on the carbon directly next to the carbonyl. Because the ring is fused to nothing and bears no further rings, the framework is compact and only modestly flexible, with the ring puckering as its main conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry element, since the gem-dimethyl carbon and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon break any mirror plane through the ring. The hydroxyl group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic six-carbon polyol, with a straight chain of carbons each bearing a hydroxyl group at every interior position and primary hydroxyl groups at both terminal carbons. There are no rings, so the scaffold is a flexible open-chain backbone. The four stereocentres along the chain are all specified, giving a defined three-dimensional arrangement of the hydroxyls. Because the terminal carbons carry identical substituents, the molecule has a degree of mirror-like symmetry about its centre, though the stereochemistry of the interior centres limits this. Every oxygen is a hydroxyl, so the molecule offers six hydrogen-bond donors and six acceptors, making it highly capable of forming hydrogen-bond networks.

The molecule is a bicyclic imide built on a norbornene-type bridged framework: a cyclohexene-derived ring bridged by a two-carbon unit, with the remaining core fused to a five-membered cyclic imide. The imide ring carries a carbonyl on each side flanking a nitrogen that bears a hydroxyl group, giving an N-hydroxy imide with both hydrogen-bond donor (the N–OH) and acceptor (the two carbonyl oxygens) capability. A carbon-carbon double bond sits within the bridged bicyclic core, providing a site of unsaturation. The fused and bridged ring system is conformationally rigid, and the cis-fused ring junctions give the scaffold a compact, three-dimensional shape with limited flexibility.

CCS is ethanethiol, a two-carbon acyclic molecule with no rings, so there is no ring fusion or scaffold beyond a simple linear chain. The skeleton consists of an ethyl group bonded to a terminal sulfur atom, which carries one hydrogen and forms a thiol functional group. The molecule has no substitution pattern to speak of, and its only stereochemical feature is the absence of any stereocenter. Its flexibility is high, since rotation about the carbon-carbon and carbon-sulfur single bonds is essentially unrestricted. The thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S-H bond, while the sulfur atom is only a poor hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an acyclic, open-chain compound built on a short carbon backbone with no rings. Its central feature is a trisubstituted alkene (a carbon-carbon double bond) bearing an ethyl ester group and a nitrile group on one carbon, and a methyl group and an ethoxy group on the other. The ester carbonyl and the nitrile nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the double bond fixes the geometry of the substituents, the structure is fairly rigid at that center, although the two ethyl chains remain flexible. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two ends of the alkene carry different groups.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring bearing three substituents. At one ring nitrogen sits a para-nitrophenyl group, a benzene ring carrying a nitro group opposite the point of attachment. The adjacent carbon bears a trifluoromethyl group, while the carbon across the ring carries an ethyl ester. The pyrazole and phenyl rings are linked by a single bond, so they can rotate relative to each other, giving the scaffold moderate flexibility around that bond while the rings themselves remain rigid. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since its only acidic positions are substituted, but it has several acceptors at the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen, the nitro oxygens, and the pyrazole nitrogen.

This molecule is a small aromatic heterocycle built on a five-membered pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms. An ethyl ester group is attached to one carbon of the ring, so the structure has a carbonyl oxygen and an ether-type oxygen in the ethoxycarbonyl unit. The ring carries an N-H group on one of its nitrogen atoms, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated ring nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is essentially planar in its aromatic core, with only the ethyl chain providing conformational flexibility. It lacks any internal symmetry because the substituent sits on a single carbon position of an unsymmetrically substituted ring.

The molecule is built around a five-membered thiazole ring, a heteroaromatic system containing both sulfur and nitrogen. An ethyl ester group, bearing a carbonyl and an ethoxy oxygen, is attached to one carbon of the thiazole, while a methyl group sits on the adjacent carbon. At the other ring carbon, a phenyl ring is connected directly, and that phenyl carries a primary amino group at the meta position relative to the thiazole linkage. The fully aromatic, conjugated framework of two linked rings makes the scaffold largely planar and fairly rigid, with only the ethyl ester chain showing rotational freedom. The primary amine offers hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the ester oxygens and the thiazole nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond an approximate planar arrangement, because the substituents are placed asymmetrically on each ring.

This molecule is a 2-aminothiophene built around a five-membered sulfur-containing aromatic ring. The thiophene carries an ethyl ester on one carbon adjacent to the sulfur-bearing carbon that also bears a free amino group, and a 3,4-dimethylphenyl ring attached to the neighboring carbon at the ring's other side. The biaryl linkage between the thiophene and the benzene ring allows some rotational freedom, while the fused aromatic framework itself is rigid. The primary amine and the ester carbonyl oxygen provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the two methyl groups on the phenyl ring add lipophilic bulk without introducing any symmetry across the molecule.

The molecule is built on a thiophene five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. Carrying an ethyl ester group (CH3CH2-O-C(=O)-) on one ring carbon and a free primary amine on the carbon adjacent to the sulfur, the scaffold is substituted at two positions. A para-tolyl group, which is a benzene ring bearing a methyl substituent opposite the point of attachment, is connected to the adjacent carbon of the thiophene. The ring system is aromatic and fairly rigid, though the biaryl linkage and the ethyl ester allow some rotational flexibility. The amine and ester carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, respectively, while the molecule has no overall symmetry.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries four substituents. An ethyl ester group (–C(=O)OCH2CH3) sits on one ring carbon, and an amino group (–NH2) sits on the carbon directly beside it, so the two form an ortho pair. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) occupy the remaining positions in a 1,2-relationship that is meta to the ester on one side and para to the amine. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ethyl and methoxy tails add some conformational freedom. The amino group and the ester carbonyl oxygen can both take part in hydrogen bonding, with the NH2 acting as a donor and the carbonyl and ether oxygens acting as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic thiazole ring, containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. At one carbon of the ring sits an ethyl ester group, a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries an ethyl chain, while the adjacent position bears a primary amino group. A methyl group occupies the remaining ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is fully defined and the ring is unsymmetrical. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the ethyl ester chain offering rotational flexibility. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the ester carbonyl and ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, which contains one sulfur atom. The ring carries three substituents: an amino group on the carbon next to sulfur, a methyl group on the adjacent carbon, and an ethyl ester (ethoxycarbonyl) group on the carbon at the other side of the methyl. Because it has no ring fusion, the scaffold is compact and largely planar, with only the ethyl ester tail offering rotational flexibility. The primary amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen, together with the amine nitrogen, can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry because its three substituents differ from one another.

This molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an oxazole ring, bearing two substituents. The ring contains one oxygen and one nitrogen separated by a carbon, with a carbon-hydrogen position on the remaining carbon. At one ring carbon sits an ethyl ester group, a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries an ethyl chain, providing a hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen and the ester oxygen. At the other carbon adjacent to both heteroatoms sits a primary amino group, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the ethyl ester chain offering rotational flexibility, and the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ester, built on a short straight-chain scaffold with no ring systems or ring fusion. An ethyl group is attached through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon, which forms the ester functional group. The alpha carbon adjacent to the carbonyl carries a bromine substituent and is also bonded to an ethyl group, so the substitution is concentrated at a single stereogenic-capable center with no internal symmetry. The chain is flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds. The ester oxygens and carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

Ethyl 2-methyl-1,4-diphenylpyrrole-3-carboxylate is not what the SMILES encodes; let me describe only the structure. The core is a five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring bearing nitrogen at position 1, with no ring fusion. The nitrogen carries a phenyl substituent, and a second phenyl ring is attached directly to a carbon on the pyrrole ring, giving a biaryl-like linkage. Adjacent to the nitrogen sits a methyl group, and the remaining ring carbon bears an ethyl ester, whose carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogen and oxygen atoms are fully substituted, and it is relatively rigid across the aromatic core, with some rotational freedom in the ethyl ester and the two phenyl rings.

The molecule is built on a benzofuran scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a furan ring that shares two carbons with it, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. Attached to the five-membered furan ring are an ethyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries an ethyl chain) at one position and a primary amino group on the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents sit side by side. The benzene portion is unsubstituted. The molecule has no stereocenters and little internal symmetry, and its rigid fused core limits flexibility to rotation of the ethyl ester chain. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds, while the ester carbonyl oxygen, the ester ether oxygen, and the furan oxygen can each accept them.

This molecule is an acyclic, open-chain ester built from a short carbon backbone with no ring systems or fused scaffolds. Its central feature is an α,β-unsaturated ester: an ethyl ester group (CCOC(=O)-) attached to a carbon–carbon double bond, which bears a methyl substituent on one carbon and an ethoxy group (-OCH2CH3) on the other. The ethoxy ether oxygen and the ester carbonyl oxygen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it lacks O–H or N–H groups. The double bond makes the framework rigid around that segment, whereas the two terminal ethyl groups provide considerable conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry.

The molecule is an acyclic, open-chain diester built on a three-carbon propanoate backbone. One ester carbonyl carries an ethyl group on its alkoxy oxygen, while the other ester oxygen is attached to an ethoxy-ethyl chain that terminates in a second ethyl ether linkage. The structure contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic character. Two ester groups and one ether oxygen supply hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The chain is highly flexible with many freely rotating single bonds, and the lack of symmetry gives it no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is built on a 1,4-benzothiazine scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered heterocycle containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The heterocyclic ring is partially unsaturated, with a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to an ethyl ester group, and it carries a methyl substituent on the alkene carbon adjacent to the nitrogen. The ring is non-planar, giving the scaffold a somewhat folded, flexible character, while the benzo portion remains rigid and planar. The ethyl ester contributes two additional carbon-oxygen bonds and a rotatable chain, adding conformational freedom. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ester oxygen can serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears an ethyl ester group, with the carbonyl attached directly to the ring and the ethoxy oxygen on the far side. The other side carries a benzyloxy group, an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 that connects to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. The molecule therefore contains two aromatic rings joined through a flexible ether-methylene linker, giving it a generally elongated, extended shape. The ester and ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, open-chain ester with no rings, so it is fully flexible about its single bonds. It has a two-carbon ethyl group bonded through an oxygen to a carbonyl, which forms an ester linkage. From that ester carbonyl, a methylene carbon connects to a second carbonyl, making a ketone, and that ketone carries a terminal chloromethyl group, so the chlorine sits on the carbon farthest from the ester. The molecule has no symmetry and no stereocenters. Its ester and ketone oxygens can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving it a symmetric, flat, rigid aromatic core. One side bears a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), a linear, strongly electron-withdrawing unit whose nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The other side carries a CH2 linker attached to an ethyl ester, where the carbonyl oxygen and ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors while no hydrogen-bond donors are present. The flexible ethyl ester chain contrasts with the rigid ring system, so the overall framework is largely planar with one rotatable terminal segment.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a trans-acrylate ester chain, a hydroxyl group, and a methoxy group. The ester is an ethyl ester of an α,β-unsaturated acid, with the carbonyl conjugated through a C=C double bond to the aromatic ring, which gives the chain a rigid, planar, extended shape. The phenyl ring carries the hydroxyl group para to the acrylate linkage and the methoxy group ortho to that hydroxyl, a 1,2,4-substitution pattern that makes the ring asymmetric. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ester carbonyl and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall, the structure is largely flat and conjugated, with only the terminal ethyl group and the methoxy methyl providing conformational flexibility.

This molecule is an ethyl ester of a para-substituted phenylacetic acid. A benzene ring forms the central scaffold, bearing a CH2 linker that connects to an ethoxycarbonyl group (an ester with an ethyl chain) at one position and a hydroxyl group at the position directly opposite on the ring. The ring is a single aromatic system with no fused rings, and the 1,4 (para) substitution pattern gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker and the ethyl ester chain add conformational flexibility. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a 1,2,3-thiadiazole ring containing one sulfur and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. Bromine sits on one ring carbon, and an ethyl ester group (a carbonyl bearing an ethoxy substituent) is attached to the adjacent carbon, giving a 4,5-disubstituted pattern with no symmetry across the ring. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, while the ethyl ester side chain adds some conformational flexibility around its single bonds. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic isoxazole ring, a heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms. Attached to the nitrogen-adjacent carbon is an ethyl ester group, a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries an ethyl chain. A methyl group sits on the ring carbon next to the oxygen, giving the ring a 3,5-type substitution pattern with no symmetry across the ring. The ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester tail adds some conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, and the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen can also act as acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzofuran scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered furan ring that shares an edge with it. A methoxy group sits on the benzene portion, at a position adjacent to the ring fusion carbon bonded to the furan oxygen, while an ethyl ester group is attached to the furan ring at the carbon next to the oxygen. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the ester and methoxy substituents extending from it in a fixed pattern that gives the molecule no internal symmetry. The ethyl ester chain is the main source of conformational flexibility. The furan oxygen and the ester carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

Ethyl 2-(9H-fluoren-9-ylidene)acetate: the scaffold is a fluorene-type tricyclic system, with two benzene rings fused to a central five-membered carbocycle. The exocyclic carbon at position 9 is double-bonded to a CH carbon that carries an ethyl ester group, so the molecule contains a conjugated α,β-unsaturated ester extending from the fused aromatic framework. The two benzo rings are unsubstituted, giving a symmetric arrangement across the central ring. The fused polycyclic core is essentially planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester tail adds some conformational flexibility. The ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small, acyclic ester-ketone built on a four-carbon chain with no rings and no aromatic systems. An ethyl group is attached through an oxygen to a carbonyl that forms an ester, and a methylene carbon links this ester carbonyl to a second carbonyl that bears a methyl group, giving a ketone at the far end. The two carbonyl groups are separated by a single methylene unit, so they are not conjugated with each other. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks symmetry, since the two ends carry different groups. Its flexible single bonds allow considerable conformational freedom. Both carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

Ethyl butanoate is an open-chain ester with no rings, so its skeleton is a simple linear four-carbon acyl chain attached through a carbonyl carbon to a two-carbon ethyl group. The only functional group is the ester linkage, consisting of a carbonyl (C=O) flanked by a single-bonded oxygen that connects to the ethyl terminus. The molecule has no aromatic or fused ring systems and no stereocenters, and its substitution pattern is entirely unbranched. Its chain can rotate freely about its many single bonds, making it highly flexible. Regarding hydrogen bonding, it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two oxygen atoms of the ester group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

Ethyl chloroacetate is an acyclic molecule built on a short two-carbon backbone with no ring systems or ring fusion. Its central feature is an ester group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a double-bonded oxygen and to a single oxygen that links onward to an ethyl group. The ethyl portion is a simple saturated two-carbon chain, while the carbon directly attached to the carbonyl carbon bears a chlorine substituent, making the substitution pattern a monohalogenated methylene adjacent to the ester. The molecule is flexible, since its single bonds allow free rotation along the chain, and it has no meaningful internal symmetry. Regarding hydrogen bonding, it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl and ester oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a short acyclic chloroformate ester, built from a two-carbon ethyl group attached through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon that carries a chlorine atom. There are no rings, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule is small and flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The central functional group is the carbonyl (C=O), flanked by an ester-type oxygen and a directly bonded chlorine, which makes the carbonyl carbon electron-poor. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local free rotation of the ethyl group. It can accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and ether oxygens but has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated carbon chain: a ten-carbon acyl unit (decanoyl) joined through an ester linkage to a two-carbon ethyl group. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system to consider. The only functional group is the ester, a carbonyl carbon bearing a double-bonded oxygen and a single-bonded oxygen that connects to the ethyl chain. Because the chain is linear with no substituents, the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a simple extended form, and its long methylene backbone is highly flexible with many accessible rotational conformations. The ester oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since it carries no N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a straight, unbranched chain with no rings and no aromatic systems. It contains a seven-carbon acyl unit, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a C=O group, that is joined through a single ester oxygen to a two-carbon ethyl group. The carbon framework is fully saturated apart from the carbonyl, so the backbone is linear and highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds. Symmetry is low because the two ends of the molecule differ, with a long alkyl chain on one side and a short ethyl group on the other. The ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

Ethyl indole-3-acetate is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that shares a bond with it. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a free N-H, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. A CH2 linker at the 3-position of the five-membered ring attaches an ethyl ester group, a carbonyl oxygen that serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor alongside the ester's ether oxygen. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester side chain adds conformational flexibility. Because the substitution is confined to one position, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule is an acyclic ethyl ester built on a short carbon chain. The central carbon carries an ethoxycarbonyl group, a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), and a C=N double bond whose nitrogen bears a hydroxyl group, making it an oxime. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and flexible, with several rotatable single bonds along the ethyl and ester portions. The molecule is essentially unsymmetrical, since the ester, nitrile, and oxime groups are all distinct and attached to one carbon. The oxime hydroxyl acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester carbonyl oxygen, ester ether oxygen, nitrile nitrogen, and oxime nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

Ethyl thioglycolate is an acyclic molecule built on a short carbon chain with no rings or fused ring systems. Its backbone consists of an ethyl group attached through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which is bonded to a methylene group that terminates in a thiol (sulfhydryl) group. The principal functional groups are an ester, with its carbonyl oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and a terminal thiol, whose sulfur can both donate and weakly accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial, and its several rotatable single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. Overall, its hydrogen-bond donor capacity is limited to the single thiol hydrogen.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons of that ring, making it an ortho-disubstituted benzene. One substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, and the other is an ethyl ester, in which a carbonyl carbon bonded to an ethoxy group is attached to the ring. The molecule is essentially planar and fairly rigid, with only the ethyl tail of the ester free to rotate. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen of the ester can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an ethyl ester of a straight-chain saturated fatty acid: a fourteen-carbon acyl chain (CCCCCCCCCCCCCC, with the carbonyl carbon included) attached through a single ester linkage to an ethyl group. It has no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a single unbranched aliphatic chain. The only functional group is the ester, which contains one carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and one ether-type oxygen that is a weaker acceptor; there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule is essentially unsubstituted apart from that ester at the chain terminus, and it has no stereocenters or symmetry beyond the chain's extended form. The long methylene segment gives it considerable conformational flexibility, with the chain able to adopt many rotameric arrangements, while the planar ester group remains comparatively rigid.

This molecule is an ethyl ester built from a straight, unbranched saturated carbon chain. The acyl portion is an eleven-carbon chain whose terminal carbon forms a carbonyl group, which is bonded through a single ester oxygen to a two-carbon ethyl group. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing substituents beyond the ester linkage. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, so the molecule can adopt many conformations. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor, through the carbonyl oxygen and the ester oxygen, since it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small, acyclic, unbranched ether built from a two-carbon vinyl group and a two-carbon ethyl group joined through a single oxygen atom. It contains no rings and no ring fusion, so its scaffold is simply a linear C–O–C chain with one terminal carbon-carbon double bond. The vinyl end provides a reactive alkene functional group, while the ethyl end is a saturated alkyl group. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry, and its flexibility is high because all bonds are freely rotatable. The oxygen atom can accept a hydrogen bond but carries no hydrogen, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is an acyclic dicarboxylic acid built on a short carbon chain: an ethyl group is attached to the alpha carbon of a propanedioic (malonic-type) unit, giving a three-carbon backbone with two terminal carboxyl groups. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely flexible and open-chain. Each carboxylic acid carbon bears a C=O carbonyl and an OH group, meaning the molecule has two hydrogen-bond donors (the two O-H groups) and four hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens. The substitution pattern is asymmetric about the central carbon, which carries one hydrogen, the ethyl group, and the two carboxyl groups, so the two acid arms are attached to the same carbon and the molecule has a single stereogenic center. Overall it is a small, conformationally flexible diacid with substantial polar character concentrated at its two ends.

This molecule is a flavone, built on a 4H-chromen-4-one (chromone) scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring. A second, unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached at the 2-position of the pyranone, directly adjacent to the ring oxygen. The fused bicyclic core and the attached phenyl ring are largely planar and conjugated, giving the molecule a rigid, flat framework with little conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen on the pyranone ring is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because all ring positions carry only aromatic hydrogens or substituents.

This molecule is built on a diarylamine scaffold, with two benzene rings joined through a single secondary amine nitrogen. One ring carries a carboxylic acid group directly on the carbon adjacent to the amine, giving an ortho-substituted pattern. The other ring bears a trifluoromethyl group at the meta position relative to the nitrogen. Both aromatic rings are planar and conjugated with the central N–H, while the C–N bonds allow rotation, so the molecule is moderately flexible. It has no internal symmetry because the two rings carry different substituents. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (O–H) and acceptor (C=O), and the amine N–H serves as an additional donor, while the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a spiro-fused polycyclic system in which a phthalide-type lactone ring shares a single tetrahedral carbon with a xanthene-type framework. The xanthene portion consists of two hydroxylated benzene rings bridged by a central pyran-like ring containing one oxygen atom, so the two aryl rings are fused and nearly coplanar. The lactone carbonyl sits on a fused benzo-five-membered ring, which is attached at the spiro center perpendicular to the xanthene plane, giving a rigid, three-dimensional, non-symmetric architecture. Two phenolic hydroxyl groups provide hydrogen-bond donor capacity, while the carbonyl oxygen, the lactone ring oxygen, the ether oxygen of the central ring, and the phenolic oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an aromatic amide built from a single benzene ring bearing one substituent, with no additional fused or appended ring systems. A formamide group (a formyl carbon bonded to nitrogen) is attached directly to one carbon of the benzene ring through its nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the aromatic ring has no other substituents. The molecule is fairly compact and largely planar, since the aromatic ring and the amide linkage can conjugate, although rotation about the aryl–nitrogen bond gives it some flexibility. It has a degree of local symmetry about the ring, but the overall structure is not symmetric because the formyl group breaks the ring's symmetry. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a four-carbon linear chain with a carbon-carbon double bond at its center, flanked on each end by a carbon-nitrogen triple bond. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or ring system to describe. Its only functional groups are the two nitrile groups at the termini, and the molecule has a symmetric substitution pattern, with the two nitriles mirroring each other across the central alkene. The structure is rigid and planar because of the conjugated double and triple bonds, with essentially no rotational flexibility along the backbone. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while each nitrogen of the nitrile groups can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a triacetylated glycerol, built on a three-carbon propane backbone. Each of the three hydroxyl positions of the glycerol skeleton carries an acetyl ester group, so the structure consists of a central methine carbon bonded to an acetoxy oxygen and two methylene carbons, each bearing its own acetoxy group. There are no ring systems or ring fusions; the molecule is fully acyclic.
