The substitution pattern is symmetric, with the two terminal ester groups identical and the central one differing only by its position. The chain is flexible, with several rotatable bonds along the backbone and ester linkages. The molecule has three carbonyl oxygens that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydroxyl groups are capped as esters.

The molecule is built around a methacrylate ester: a short acyclic skeleton with a terminal alkene (a methylene group and a methyl group on one carbon) bonded to a carbonyl that is part of an ester linkage. The ester oxygen connects to a methylene carbon that is attached to an epoxide ring, a strained three-membered ring containing one oxygen and two carbons. The molecule is unsymmetrical, with no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry, and it is fairly flexible because of the rotatable single bonds linking the alkene, ester, and epoxide units, though the epoxide ring itself is rigid. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ester and epoxide oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing one ether substituent, making it a phenyl ether scaffold. The ether oxygen links the aromatic ring to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a three-membered oxirane (epoxide) ring, so the molecule contains one aromatic ring and one strained, fused-free saturated heterocycle connected by a flexible methylene linker. The substitution pattern on the benzene is monosubstituted with no other groups, giving the aromatic portion a high degree of local symmetry. The overall structure is moderately flexible because of the rotatable C–O and C–C bonds in the linker, while the epoxide ring is rigid. The ether oxygen and epoxide oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single nitrogen atom bonded to two silicon centers, forming a silicon-nitrogen-silicon linkage in an open, acyclic chain with no rings or fused systems. Each silicon carries three methyl groups, so the two trimethylsilyl units are identical and the overall framework is symmetric about the central nitrogen. The nitrogen bears one hydrogen atom, making it a secondary amine-type site that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while its lone pair gives it weak acceptor capability. The Si-N-Si bond angle and the rotation about the Si-N bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility, and the bulky, non-polar methyl groups shield the central nitrogen, sterically hindering its reactivity.

The molecule is built on a single saturated seven-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom, which makes it an azepane scaffold. Every ring atom is sp3-hybridized and there are no fused rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. The only heteroatom is the secondary amine nitrogen, which carries one hydrogen and therefore has one hydrogen-bond donor and one lone pair acting as an acceptor. Apart from that nitrogen, the ring is an unsubstituted methylene chain, so the substitution pattern is minimal and the molecule has no stereocenters. The ring is conformationally flexible, able to interconvert among several puckered forms.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain aliphatic aldehyde with six carbons, so it has no ring systems, fused rings, or aromatic character. Its scaffold is a simple unbranched hexyl chain, with the terminal carbon of the chain bearing a formyl group (CHO) at one end. The molecule has no substituents along the chain and no stereocenters, and its only functional group is the aldehyde carbonyl. Because it is a flexible chain of single bonds, it can adopt many conformations and shows little rigidity. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the aldehyde C–H is not a meaningful donor.

This molecule is a straight-chain saturated carboxylic acid with six carbons in total, so it has no rings and no fused ring systems. Its skeleton is a linear, unbranched alkyl chain of five methylene and methyl carbons attached to a terminal carboxyl group. The only functional group is that carboxylic acid, which carries both a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and a hydroxyl group that can donate one. The chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the trivial end-to-end arrangement.

The molecule is a bicyclic lactone built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring containing an ester linkage. The benzene ring is ortho-disubstituted, sharing two adjacent carbons with the heterocycle, so the fused system is planar and fairly rigid. The heterocyclic ring contains a cyclic ester (a lactone) with a carbonyl carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, and a methylene group sits between the aromatic ring and the lactone carbonyl. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-symmetric outline, with no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ring ester oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a five-membered saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms and three carbon atoms, with ring atoms arranged so that the ring is a hydantoin-type imidazolidine skeleton. It carries two carbonyl groups: one is a ketone-like carbonyl on a ring carbon, and the other is a urea-type carbonyl flanked by both ring nitrogens. Only one nitrogen bears a hydrogen, and the other ring nitrogen is joined to the urea carbonyl with its hydrogen also present, so there are two N-H groups available as hydrogen-bond donors. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is small, planar-leaning, and rigid with no rotatable bonds, and it has no substituents beyond the ring atoms, so it is essentially unsubstituted and lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered carbocycle, giving an indane skeleton. The aromatic six-membered ring is fully unsaturated and planar, while the fused cyclopentane ring contains two saturated methylene units that sit in the same plane as the benzene ring, resulting in a largely flat, rigid framework. No heteroatoms or functional groups are present, and the aromatic ring is unsubstituted, so the structure is a simple hydrocarbon with no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The arrangement has a degree of symmetry about the mirror plane through the fused edge and the methylene carbons, though the saturated ring is slightly puckered and gives it some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries an N-H group. Attached at the 3-position of the five-membered ring is a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid group. The indole core is planar and aromatic and therefore rigid, while the saturated two-carbon linker gives the side chain some rotational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the fused rings. The indole N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carboxylic acid provides both donor and acceptor capability through its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygen atoms.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains an N-H group. A formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O bonded to a hydrogen) is attached to the benzene portion of the fused system, placing it on the carbon that sits meta to the ring-fusion atom on the six-membered ring. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the aldehyde carbon's single bond to the ring. The pyrrole N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aldehyde oxygen and the pyrrole nitrogen's lone pair can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule given by this SMILES is a single carbon atom bonded to three iodine atoms and one hydrogen atom, so its skeleton is one tetrahedral sp3 carbon with no chain or ring structure. There are no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no functional groups beyond the carbon-iodine bonds themselves. The substitution pattern is a trisubstituted methane, with iodine occupying three of the four tetrahedral positions. The molecule has local threefold symmetry around the central carbon, and because it has no rotatable bonds it is essentially rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor sites are the lone pairs on the iodine atoms.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built on a short branched carbon chain. An acetyl group (a two-carbon unit bearing a carbonyl) is bonded through an oxygen atom to a CH2 group, which connects to a central CH carrying a methyl branch, giving an isobutyl-type fragment at the alkyl end. There are no ring systems or ring fusion, and the structure is fully saturated apart from the ester carbonyl C=O. Its flexibility comes from several freely rotating single bonds, so it has no fixed three-dimensional rigidity and no meaningful symmetry. The ester oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built on a short linear carbon chain, with no ring systems and no fused scaffold. Its principal functional group is an acrylate: a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond terminating the chain) directly attached to the carbonyl carbon of an ester. The ester oxygen links the carbonyl to a branched alkyl group, an isobutyl-type arrangement in which a methyl-bearing carbon sits at the chain end. The structure lacks any stereocenters and has no internal symmetry beyond the two methyl groups on the terminal carbon. Because the chain has several single bonds and no rings, the molecule is fairly flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the two oxygen atoms of the ester group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small acyclic aldehyde built on a three-carbon chain: a central carbon bearing two methyl groups (an isopropyl unit) bonded to a terminal formyl carbon. Its scaffold is entirely saturated apart from the carbonyl, so there are no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no aromatic substitution pattern to describe. The single functional group is the aldehyde, a carbon-oxygen double bond at the chain end, which makes the molecule a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the oxygen lone pairs but gives it no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The two terminal methyl groups are equivalent, giving the molecule a local mirror-plane symmetry, and the chain is small and flexible with only modest rotational freedom about its single bonds.

This molecule is an acyclic anhydride formed from two identical isobutyryl units joined through a central oxygen atom, giving a symmetric C(=O)–O–C(=O) backbone. Each end carries a branched isopropyl group attached to the carbonyl carbon, so the structure contains no rings and no ring fusion. The only functional groups are the two carbonyl oxygens and the bridging ether-type oxygen, which together make up an anhydride. Because the two halves are mirror images of each other, the molecule has a clear two-fold symmetry about the central oxygen. The chain is fairly flexible around its single bonds, although the bulky methyl branches limit rotation somewhat. Neither the molecule nor its carbonyl groups have any hydrogen-bond donors, and the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a straight-chain butanoyl (four-carbon acyl) skeleton joined through its ester oxygen to a branched five-carbon alkyl chain bearing a methyl group at the third carbon from the oxygen. It contains no rings and therefore no ring fusion. The central functional group is a single ester linkage, a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to an ether-type oxygen that connects the two alkyl portions. Because the chains are flexible and unsaturated bonds are absent apart from the carbonyl, the molecule has many rotatable bonds and considerable conformational freedom. It carries no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two oxygen atoms of the ester group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system built from a fused benzene ring and pyridine ring, forming an isoquinoline-type scaffold. The two six-membered rings share an edge, making the framework planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core. A formyl group (an aldehyde, –CHO) is attached to the carbocyclic ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substituent sits in a peri-like arrangement relative to the nitrogen-containing ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the aldehyde breaks the symmetry of the fused system. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the aldehyde oxygen is an additional acceptor and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small, acyclic, saturated amide with no rings, so it is entirely flexible. Its backbone is a straight-chain carbon skeleton in which a terminal primary amide group sits at one end, attached to a CH2 linked to a branched isopropyl unit (a CH bearing two methyl groups). The primary carboxamide, consisting of a carbonyl bonded to an NH2 group, is the only functional group present. Because the branching is asymmetric relative to the amide, the molecule has no symmetry element beyond a local rotational freedom around the methyl groups. The amide's NH2 provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a six-membered saturated ring containing one oxygen atom, a pyranose-type scaffold with no fused or additional rings. Five ring carbons each carry a hydroxyl group, and the ring carbon adjacent to the oxygen bears a methyl group, so the substitution pattern is fully decorated around the ring. Two of the hydroxyls sit on carbons flanking the ring oxygen, one of which is an anomeric hemiacetal position, while the rest are secondary alcohols. The stereocenters are all specified, giving a rigid chair-like framework with substituents in defined orientations and no internal symmetry. Every hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ring oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain of 18 carbons ending in a single carboxylic acid group at one terminus, so its scaffold is a linear fatty acid skeleton with no ring systems and no ring fusion. Two carbon-carbon double bonds sit along the chain, separated by a methylene unit, and both are positioned toward the methyl end of the molecule, giving a polyunsaturated pattern. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, and the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid head contains one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the long hydrocarbon tail contributes only nonpolar, non-hydrogen-bonding character.

This molecule is a small, acyclic, chiral amino alcohol built on a four-carbon chain. It carries a primary amine on the stereogenic carbon and a primary hydroxyl group on the terminal carbon, giving a 1,2-amino alcohol motif. A methylthioether (a sulfur atom bearing a methyl group) sits at the far end of the chain, linked through a two-carbon segment. Because there are no rings, the scaffold is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The amine and hydroxyl groups each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the thioether sulfur is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is a saturated bicyclic amine built from two fused six-membered rings that share a nitrogen atom and one carbon, forming a quinolizidine-type scaffold. One ring carries a hydroxymethyl group (a primary alcohol, –CH2OH) attached to a stereogenic carbon adjacent to the ring fusion. The tertiary nitrogen at the fusion point is the only heteroatom besides the oxygen, and it is non-aromatic and fully substituted. The molecule is conformationally flexible, since both rings can adopt chair-like arrangements, and it has no internal symmetry because of the single substituent and defined stereocenters. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary amine nitrogen can serve only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a five-membered cyclic anhydride built from a single lactone-type ring containing one oxygen atom flanked by two carbonyl groups, which places it in the class of unsaturated cyclic dicarboxylic anhydrides. The ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond between the two carbons that are not part of the anhydride linkage, so the core is planar and rigid with no sp3 stereocenters. Each carbonyl carbon is directly bonded to the central ring oxygen, giving an electrophilic anhydride scaffold that is reactive toward nucleophiles and ring-opens readily. The structure has a mirror plane through the ring oxygen and the midpoint of the double bond, giving it high symmetry. Both carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is malononitrile, a three-carbon chain in which the two terminal carbons each bear a nitrile group. Its scaffold is a simple, acyclic, unbranched propane-type backbone with no ring systems or ring fusion. Both nitrile functional groups are linear carbon-nitrogen triple bonds, and the central methylene carbon sits between them, making it an activated, flexible sp3 center. The molecule has a mirror plane through the central carbon, giving it high symmetry, and its hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, while the two nitrogen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small acyclic hydrazide built around a single benzene ring. A phenyl group is attached to a two-carbon chain whose first carbon carries a hydroxyl group and whose second carbon is a carbonyl bearing a terminal hydrazide (–C(=O)NHNH₂) unit. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion has no positional pattern to describe, and the molecule as a whole lacks any symmetry element beyond the local ring symmetry. The α-hydroxy carbon is a stereocenter, and the chain offers several rotatable bonds, giving the structure moderate flexibility. Hydrogen-bonding capacity is high: the hydroxyl, the amide-type N–H, and the terminal NH₂ act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic dicarboxylic acid built on a four-carbon chain, with a carboxylic acid group at each terminal end. A thiol (sulfanyl) group sits on the second carbon of the backbone, between the two carboxyl-bearing positions, so the molecule has one stereocenter and no ring systems. The chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds, and it has no internal symmetry because the thiol-bearing carbon makes the two carboxyl ends chemically distinct. Each carboxyl group contributes an oxygen-bearing hydroxyl that can donate a hydrogen bond and a carbonyl oxygen that can accept one, and the thiol adds a weaker hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no ring fusion, and carries three methyl groups plus one aldehyde (formyl) group attached at different positions around that ring. The aldehyde carbon is directly bonded to the aromatic ring, and the two methyl groups flanking it sit at the adjacent ortho positions, which creates steric crowding around the carbonyl. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make all sides identical. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups and aldehyde are small and rotate freely. The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, bearing four substituents. Three of these are methyl groups, placed at positions that give the ring a 2,4,6-trimethyl pattern, while the fourth is a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile). The aromatic ring is fully conjugated and planar, and the nitrile carbon-nitrogen triple bond is linear, so the molecule is rigid apart from rotation about the single bond joining the CH2 to the ring. Its substitution pattern is asymmetric overall, though the ring carries a local two-fold symmetry axis through the cyanomethyl-bearing carbon. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks any N-H or O-H groups. The nitrogen of the nitrile group can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the aromatic pi system offers a weak secondary site for interactions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Three methyl groups are attached to the ring, one on each of three carbons arranged in a 1,3,5 pattern, so the substitution is symmetric about an axis through the ring. There are no heteroatoms and no polar functional groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The benzene core is rigid and planar, while the three methyl substituents are small, freely rotating groups that add only minor conformational flexibility.

The molecule is methacrylamide, a small acyclic amide built from a three-carbon chain. It has no ring systems or ring fusion, so its scaffold is a simple open chain. The structure contains a terminal vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond to a CH2 unit) bearing a methyl substituent on the internal carbon, which is directly attached to a primary carboxamide group. The molecule is small and has little conformational freedom beyond rotation about its single bonds, and it has no internal symmetry element apart from the local planarity of the conjugated C=C–C=O arrangement. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites on the nitrogen and one hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is methanesulfonic anhydride, built around a central oxygen atom bridging two sulfur centers. Each sulfur is bonded to two oxygen atoms and one methyl carbon, forming a symmetric, acyclic, two-fold arrangement with no ring systems or fused rings. The two sulfonyl groups are identical, so the molecule has a mirror-like symmetry through the central oxygen. The structure is essentially flexible around the single S–O–S linkage, with only a few rotatable bonds. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since no hydrogens sit on heteroatoms, and its oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring, which is fully substituted with four groups: two methyl groups sit on the ring nitrogen and on one adjacent carbon, a second methyl group is on another ring carbon, and a methyl ester (a carbonyl group bonded to an oxygen bearing a methyl) is attached to the remaining ring carbon. The compound has no fused rings and no stereocenters, so its skeleton is compact and essentially planar, with only the ester's methyl rotation adding flexibility. The ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ester's ether-type oxygen can accept as well, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor because the nitrogen is capped by a methyl group. The arrangement of substituents is asymmetric, lacking any rotational or mirror symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl ester group (a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to an oxygen that carries a methyl group) and two hydroxyl groups. The ester sits at one ring position, and the two phenolic hydroxyls sit at positions that are meta and para relative to it, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the ring has no internal symmetry axis aside from the trivial planar layout. There are no fused or additional ring systems, so the scaffold is a simple, planar, rigid aromatic core with only the ester's C–O bonds and the hydroxyl O–H bonds providing modest flexibility. The two hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl and ester oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, giving the molecule several sites for intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring, which carries an N-H group at one position that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The ring bears two methyl substituents on adjacent carbons near the nitrogen and a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen-linked methyl) on a third ring carbon. The ester's carbonyl oxygen and ether-type oxygen can both accept hydrogen bonds. The scaffold is a single, fully planar, unfused ring with no stereocenters, so it is essentially rigid apart from rotation about the bond joining the ester to the ring.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a three-carbon backbone with no rings, so its scaffold is entirely open-chain and flexible. A terminal vinyl group (C=C) is attached to a central carbon that carries an acetamido group (an N-acetyl nitrogen bonded to a methyl-substituted carbonyl) and a methyl ester (a carbonyl bearing an O-methyl group). The alpha-carbon is therefore a fully substituted sp2 center, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of its conjugated amide and ester groups. Hydrogen-bond capacity is modest: the amide N-H serves as a donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen act as acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, forming a methyl ester of a substituted benzoic acid. The ester group (a carbonyl bonded to a methoxy oxygen) is attached directly to one ring carbon, with a bromine atom on the adjacent carbon, placing the two groups in an ortho relationship. A nitro group sits meta to the ester on the opposite side of the ring, creating a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl ester adds limited rotational freedom. The nitro and carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small fused-free bicyclic-free monocyclic aromatic-type heterocycle: a six-membered pyranone ring containing one ring oxygen and a carbonyl, i.e., a 2-pyrone (2H-pyran-2-one) scaffold. A methyl ester group, bearing a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries a methyl group, is attached to the ring carbon at the 3-position, next to the lactone carbonyl. The ring is largely planar and conjugated, with a lactone carbonyl and an ester carbonyl both contributing to the electron-poor character of the system. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom about the single bond linking the ester to the ring, so it is fairly rigid. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while its three oxygen atoms in the two carbonyl groups and the ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. It carries two substituents placed meta to each other: a methyl ester group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to an oxygen that bears a methyl group, and a bromomethyl group, a CH2 unit bearing a bromine atom. The ester contributes a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The scaffold is largely rigid because of the aromatic ring, though the ester and bromomethyl side chains each have rotatable single bonds. The substitution pattern lacks the mirror or rotational symmetry of a para-disubstituted ring, and the molecule is achiral.

Methyl 3-(thiophen-2-yl)acrylate-type structure: the molecule has a methyl ester group attached to a carbon-carbon double bond that is in the trans (E) configuration, with the other end of the alkene bonded directly to a thiophene ring. The thiophene is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, and it is attached at its 2-position, leaving the remaining ring carbons unsubstituted. The overall scaffold is essentially linear and planar, since the conjugated system of the ester, alkene, and aromatic ring tends to lie in one plane, which makes the molecule fairly rigid with only the methyl ester rotating freely. The ester carbonyl oxygen and ether-type oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond local planarity.

The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, whereas the propyl tail of the amide chain and the acetyl group contribute some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents occupy distinct positions. Hydrogen-bond capability is notable: the amide N–H and the phenolic O–H act as donors, while the amide carbonyl oxygen, the acetyl carbonyl oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imide ring containing a nitrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups. The fused aromatic-imide core is planar and rigid. The nitrogen carries a three-carbon saturated chain that terminates in a primary hydroxyl group, adding a flexible tail to the otherwise rigid bicyclic system. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror plane through the imide ring, giving it approximate symmetry in the core. The two imide carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the terminal hydroxyl can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One side bears a primary amino group, and the other bears a carboxamide linked through an ethyl-type chain to a terminal carboxylic acid. Because the ring is fully aromatic and unfused, the scaffold is planar and rigid, while the three-carbon chain on the amide side adds conformational flexibility. The structure carries an aromatic amine, a secondary amide, and a carboxylic acid, giving it several hydrogen-bond donors (the amine N–H, the amide N–H, and the acid O–H) and multiple acceptors (the amide carbonyl and the acid carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The para arrangement lends a roughly linear, elongated overall shape.

The molecule is built around a five-membered maleimide ring, a cyclic imide containing two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen, with a carbon-carbon double bond between the two remaining ring carbons. The nitrogen is bonded to a phenyl ring, which carries a bromine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, giving a para-substitution pattern. The phenyl and imide rings are connected through a single N-C bond, so the two ring systems are not fused but can rotate relative to one another, while the planar maleimide ring itself is rigid. The structure has no internal rotational symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through the molecule's long axis. The two imide carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since the nitrogen is fully substituted.

This molecule is a maleamic acid-type compound built on a four-carbon backbone bearing a carboxylic acid at one end and an amide at the other, joined by a cis or trans carbon-carbon double bond depending on stereochemistry as written (the SMILES omits stereo marks). The amide nitrogen is attached to a benzene ring, which carries a single fluorine atom at the position para to the nitrogen, giving a 1,4-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the conjugated enone-like linker adds limited flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is substantial: the carboxylic acid provides both a donor and acceptor, the amide N–H serves as a donor, and the carbonyl oxygens act as acceptors, with the fluorine offering only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring containing two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen carries a para-hydroxyphenyl substituent, so the molecule has a planar aromatic core linked to a second benzene ring through a single C–N bond. The bicyclic imide core is rigid and flat, while rotation about the N–aryl bond gives limited conformational flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the phenolic hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only approximate local symmetry across the phthalimide ring.

The molecule is built from a biphenyl core, with one ring carrying a methoxy group at the para position and the other bearing a sulfonamide at the para position. The sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to the alpha-carbon of a phenylalanine-like unit, which carries a benzyl side chain and a terminal carboxylic acid. The structure contains three aromatic rings in total, linked by a single biaryl bond and a flexible sulfonamide and amino-acid tail that gives it considerable conformational freedom. The sulfonamide NH and the carboxylic acid OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl oxygens, the carboxyl oxygens, and the methoxy oxygen serve as acceptors. The stereocenter at the alpha-carbon is not specified in the SMILES, so the configuration is left undefined.

The molecule is an N-benzylidene aniline, often called a Schiff base or imine, built from two benzene rings joined by a C=N linkage. One ring carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) at the position para to the imine carbon, giving a para-disubstituted pattern on that ring. The other ring is an unsubstituted phenyl attached directly to the imine nitrogen. The central C=N unit is planar and conjugates the two aromatic rings, so the scaffold is fairly rigid with an extended, flat conformation, though the rings can twist somewhat about their single bonds. The imine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the methoxy oxygen provides a second weak acceptor site; the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local symmetry of each ring.

The molecule is an N-substituted phthalimide, built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring that contains a nitrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups. The nitrogen carries a flexible, unbranched five-carbon chain ending in a terminal alkyne, giving a rigid planar aromatic-imide core with a floppy tail. The fused bicyclic core is flat and has no stereocenters, and the benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the scaffold itself has mirror-plane symmetry while the alkyl tail breaks that symmetry. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the imide nitrogen is fully substituted.

The molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered cyclic imide, so the two carbonyl groups flank a nitrogen atom that sits within the ring. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the benzo ring fused across the C–C bond shared with the imide ring. The imide nitrogen carries a single substituent, a bromomethyl group (–CH2Br), which is the only flexible portion of the structure and gives the molecule a reactive alkyl halide site. Overall the molecule has approximate mirror symmetry through the imide ring and no stereocenters. Its hydrogen-bond capability is limited: it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic glycine-derived ester bearing a tert-butyl ester group, attached through a CH2 linker to an imine nitrogen. The imine carbon is substituted by two phenyl rings, giving a diaryl ketimine (benzophenone-imine) motif, and each phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The molecule contains no fused or bridged ring systems, and the two aryl groups are rotationally flexible about their bonds to the central imine carbon. The tert-butyl group provides a bulky, symmetric, three-fold-symmetric terminus. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ester carbonyl oxygen and the imine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a phthalimide-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring, where the nitrogen is flanked by two carbonyl carbons. The nitrogen also carries an N-linked ethyl carbamate (ethoxycarbonyl) group, so the core is an N-acylated phthalimide. The fused aromatic ring is unsubstituted, giving a planar, rigid bicyclic framework, while the ethoxy tail adds a small degree of conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, mirror-type symmetry through the imide plane. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, but the three carbonyl oxygens (two imide, one carbamate) and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small, acyclic amide built on a two-carbon backbone. An acetyl group (a methyl attached to a carbonyl carbon) is bonded to a nitrogen atom, which in turn carries a hydroxymethyl substituent (a CH2 group bearing an OH). There are no ring systems, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and flexible, with rotation possible about several single bonds. The amide C–N bond has partial double-bond character, which constrains rotation about that bond and gives the molecule a degree of planarity around the amide unit. The molecule has no symmetry elements of note because its two ends carry different groups. The amide N–H and the terminal hydroxyl O–H both act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold, meaning a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring that contains two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen atom. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the aromatic ring sharing an edge with the imide ring. The nitrogen carries a hydroxymethyl substituent, a CH2 group bearing a terminal hydroxyl, which adds a small flexible arm to the otherwise rigid framework. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the imide nitrogen and the hydroxymethyl group. Two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl group can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

This molecule is N,N-dibenzylaniline: a central tertiary amine nitrogen bonded to three aryl groups, one phenyl ring directly and two benzyl groups through methylene linkers. There are no fused ring systems; the three benzene rings are separate and each is unsubstituted. The nitrogen is trisubstituted and sp2-like in character, so its lone pair is delocalized into the attached phenyl ring. The structure has approximate three-fold arrangement around the nitrogen but the two benzyl groups are conformationally flexible through their CH2 linkers. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the nitrogen is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is an N,N-dibenzylhydroxylamine: a central nitrogen bearing a hydroxyl group and two benzyl substituents. Each benzyl group consists of a methylene linker attached to an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the scaffold is built from two independent phenyl rings joined through flexible CH2–N bonds. There are no fused ring systems, and the two aromatic rings are not bridged. The nitrogen-bonded oxygen forms an N–OH group, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through the O–H and an acceptor through the oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry about the N–O axis, and the rotatable benzyl arms make it conformationally flexible.

This molecule is a symmetric urea, N,N'-dicyclohexylurea, built around a central carbonyl group flanked by two nitrogen atoms. Each nitrogen bears a saturated cyclohexane ring attached at one of its carbon atoms, so the two rings are identical and related by a mirror-like symmetry through the urea core. The cyclohexyl rings are non-aromatic and adopt flexible chair-like conformations, while the urea linkage itself is relatively planar and somewhat rigid. Each N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the molecule a compact, polar core flanked by bulky aliphatic hydrocarbon rings.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic amine built on a linear three-carbon chain with no rings, aromatic systems, or fused scaffolds. One end carries a tertiary amine bearing two ethyl groups on a single nitrogen, and the other end carries a primary amine, giving a diamine with the two nitrogens separated by a flexible propylene linker. The molecule has no stereocenters and no true symmetry axis, though the two ethyl groups on the tertiary nitrogen are equivalent. Its many rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible. The primary amine provides two N–H hydrogen-bond donors and a lone pair acceptor, while the tertiary nitrogen contributes only an acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a diethylamino group, in which a nitrogen atom is bonded to the ring and to two ethyl chains, giving the nitrogen a tertiary, non-planar-leaning environment that is conjugated with the aromatic system. The other substituent is a nitroso group (a nitrogen double-bonded to oxygen) attached directly to the ring at the position opposite the amine. The ethyl groups are flexible, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The arrangement has an approximate pseudo-symmetry through the long axis of the ring, but the two different substituents break full symmetry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen carries no hydrogen, while the oxygen of the nitroso group and the tertiary amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic thiourea, built on a central thiocarbonyl carbon double-bonded to sulfur and flanked by two nitrogen atoms. Each nitrogen carries an ethyl group, so the scaffold is symmetric about the C=S axis, with no rings or fused systems present. The thiocarbonyl group serves as the principal functional unit, and each N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor while the sulfur atom acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule is small and fairly flexible, since rotation about the C–N and C–C single bonds is essentially unrestricted apart from partial double-bond character along the N–C(=S) linkage.

The molecule is a symmetric acyclic urea, built around a single carbonyl carbon bonded to two nitrogen atoms, each of which carries an ethyl group on one side and an N-linked methylene-ethyl chain on the other, so the skeleton is an N,N'-diethyl-substituted urea with no ring systems or ring fusion. The central C=O group is the only heteroatom-bearing functional group besides the two secondary amide-type NH centers, and the substitution pattern is fully symmetric about that carbonyl. The two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The chain is flexible, with freely rotating C–C and C–N single bonds, though the planar urea core itself is relatively rigid.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic diamine built on a straight three-carbon propyl chain. One terminus carries a primary amine group (–NH2), while the other terminus bears a tertiary amine in which the nitrogen is bonded to two methyl groups. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or multiple-bond features, so the scaffold is fully saturated and flexible, with free rotation about its single C–C and C–N bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two nitrogen ends differ in substitution. The primary amine offers two N–H hydrogen-bond donors and a lone pair acceptor, while the tertiary amine contributes only a lone-pair acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold. Two substituents sit on the ring at a meta relationship to each other: a dimethylamino group, where the nitrogen carries two methyl groups, and a nitro group, where the nitrogen is bonded to two oxygen atoms with one formally charged. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the substituents are attached through single bonds with limited rotational freedom. The molecule has no fused rings and no stereocenters, and it possesses only an approximate mirror plane through the ring. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen of the dimethylamino group is fully substituted. The nitro oxygens and the tertiary amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic tertiary amine built on a straight, unbranched saturated carbon chain of twelve carbons. The nitrogen sits at one end of the chain and carries two methyl groups, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. Its only functional group is the tertiary amine, which has a lone pair on nitrogen, making it a hydrogen-bond acceptor but giving it no hydrogen-bond donor capability since no N–H or O–H bonds are present. The molecule has no stereocenters and a single, unbranched hydrocarbon tail, so its overall shape is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds. The long alkyl chain is largely nonpolar in character, while the amine nitrogen is the only polar feature of the structure.

This molecule is N,N-dimethylformamide-type scaffold: a single, acyclic, unbranched core consisting of one carbonyl carbon bonded to a hydrogen atom and to a nitrogen atom that carries two methyl groups. There are no rings and no ring fusion, so the structure is small, open-chain, and flexible about its single bonds. The defining functional group is a tertiary amide, in which the carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor while the molecule has no N–H or O–H groups and therefore no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The two N-methyl substituents are identical, giving the molecule a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the C–N–C plane. Because of partial double-bond character across the C–N bond, the amide portion is planar and comparatively rigid, while the methyl groups can rotate freely.

The molecule is an acyclic thiourea, with a central thiocarbonyl carbon double-bonded to sulfur and single-bonded to two nitrogen atoms. Each nitrogen carries an unbranched n-butyl chain, so the scaffold is a symmetric N,N'-dibutyl arrangement with no rings and no ring fusion. The thiocarbonyl group (C=S) and the two N-H groups make it capable of acting as a hydrogen-bond donor through each NH and as a weak acceptor through the sulfur. The flexible butyl chains give the molecule considerable conformational freedom, while the thiourea core is comparatively planar and rigid. Overall the structure is linear and highly symmetric about the central C=S unit.

The molecule is a symmetrical urea, built from a single central carbonyl carbon bonded to two nitrogen atoms, each of which carries a straight-chain n-butyl group. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and the molecule is structurally simple. The only functional group is the urea unit, which contains an amide-type C=O with two N–H groups flanking it. Because the two butyl chains are identical and attached symmetrically, the molecule has a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the central carbonyl. The flexible alkyl chains give it conformational freedom, while the urea core is planar and can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H groups and an acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is a short, flexible, acyclic chain built from a three-carbon backbone with no rings. At one end, an acetyl group is attached to a nitrogen atom, forming a secondary amide (an acetamido group). At the other end, the chain terminates in a carboxylic acid group. The two polar functional groups are separated by a two-carbon linker, giving the molecule an unbranched, linear substitution pattern with no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry. The amide N–H and the carboxylic acid O–H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and acid carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, so the molecule can engage in multiple hydrogen-bonding interactions.

This molecule is an N-acetylated amino acid built on a three-carbon backbone bearing a carboxylic acid at one end and an acetamido group on the alpha carbon. A benzyl side chain extends from the alpha carbon, and its phenyl ring carries a single fluorine atom at the para position relative to the methylene linker, giving a simple para-disubstituted aromatic system. The stereocenter at the alpha carbon makes the scaffold chiral, and the flexible CH2 and C-C bonds allow moderate conformational freedom, while the aromatic ring remains planar and rigid. Hydrogen-bond capability is provided by the amide N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H as donors, with the amide carbonyl, the carboxyl oxygens, and the fluorine serving as acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring is fused to a benzene ring along a shared carbon-carbon bond. The indole nitrogen carries an acetyl group, an N-acyl substituent that removes the N-H hydrogen-bond donor and leaves the carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor. A formyl group, an aldehyde, sits at the C3 position of the five-membered ring, adding a second carbonyl acceptor. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, while the acetyl and formyl groups add limited conformational freedom through rotation about their single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis or mirror plane because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically on the ring system.

This molecule is an N-acetylated derivative of the five-carbon amino dicarboxylic acid skeleton, with a single stereogenic center at the alpha carbon. The backbone is a linear, flexible chain of four carbons bearing a terminal carboxylic acid on each end, with an acetamido group attached to the carbon adjacent to one of them. There are no rings, so the structure is entirely acyclic and free of ring fusion, and it lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution at the alpha position. The two carboxylic acid groups and the secondary amide N–H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of the amide and both carboxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The chain's many rotatable single bonds give the molecule considerable conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a naphthalene core, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, bearing two cyano (nitrile) groups. One nitrile is attached to a carbon on one ring and the other to the carbon directly across on the same ring, placing them in a 1,4 relationship across that ring. The fused system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Each nitrile carbon is linear and sp-hybridized, and the nitrogen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement retains a two-fold axis of symmetry through the midpoint of the fused bond, reflecting the positions of the substituents.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge, making it a flat, rigid aromatic system. A sulfonyl chloride group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to a chlorine, is attached to one carbon of the naphthalene ring adjacent to the ring fusion, which places the substituent at the alpha position. The sulfonyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, though its oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the substituted ring, and the sulfonyl group is the only polar feature, with the remaining structure being entirely hydrocarbon in character.

The molecule is an N-benzyl acrylamide: a three-carbon acrylamide unit whose terminal vinyl group is conjugated to a secondary amide carbonyl, with the amide nitrogen bearing a benzyl group. The benzyl substituent consists of a single unfused benzene ring attached through a flexible methylene linker, so there is no fused ring system and the phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited internal symmetry, since the phenyl ring's six-fold symmetry is broken by the attachment point. Its flexibility is concentrated at the CH2 linker and the amide-to-vinyl bonds, while the amide C–N bond is partly rigid because of resonance. The secondary amide N–H serves as one hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as one hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzamide, consisting of a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group in which the amide nitrogen carries a benzyl substituent (a CH2 linker attached to a second phenyl ring). The scaffold therefore contains two separate, unfused benzene rings joined through a flexible amide-containing linker, with no fused or bridged ring systems. The amide C(=O)–NH unit is the sole functional group, providing one hydrogen-bond donor (the N–H) and one hydrogen-bond acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two aromatic rings occupy different positions relative to the amide. The amide bond gives partial rigidity, while the methylene linker and the rotatable bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused ring systems. Attached to the ring is a one-carbon methylene linker, and that linker bears a tertiary amine nitrogen carrying two methyl groups, so the overall framework is a benzyl group joined to a dimethylamino unit. The nitrogen is trivalent and has no hydrogen atoms, so it can accept a hydrogen bond but cannot donate one, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker and the N-methyl groups give the chain some rotational flexibility. The structure has a local mirror-type symmetry through the nitrogen and the benzylic carbon, but no stereocenters are present.

This molecule is built around a five-membered cyclic imide, a maleimide ring, which contains a carbon-carbon double bond flanked by two carbonyl groups and a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen is substituted with a benzyl group, meaning a methylene linker attached to a benzene ring, so the phenyl ring is connected to the imide through a single flexible CH2 bridge. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the imide nitrogen carries no hydrogen and therefore offers no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The planar, conjugated maleimide core is rigid, whereas the benzyl group can rotate about its single bonds, giving the overall structure moderate flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two halves differ in ring type.

The molecule is an N-protected alpha-amino acid built on a linear four-carbon (butyl-derived) side chain attached to a single stereogenic alpha carbon bearing a free carboxylic acid. The nitrogen is acylated by a carbamate linkage (N-C(=O)-O) whose oxygen is bonded to a benzyl group, so an unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached through a flexible CH2 spacer. The phenyl ring is the only ring system, with no ring fusion and no further substitution on the aromatic core. Overall the structure is moderately flexible because of its several rotatable single bonds, with a defined chiral center at the alpha position. It has two hydrogen-bond donors (the carbamate N-H and the carboxylic O-H) and four acceptor sites across the carbonyl and ether-type oxygens.

This molecule is an acyclic, open-chain amino acid derivative built on a four-carbon backbone bearing a secondary alcohol at one end and a carboxylic acid at the other. The nitrogen is protected as a benzyl carbamate, which links a phenyl ring through a CH2 group to an O-C(=O)-NH unit attached to the alpha carbon. The single benzene ring is unsubstituted, and the stereocenters at the alpha and beta carbons give the chain defined three-dimensional handedness. Because the backbone is flexible, with many rotatable single bonds, the molecule can adopt numerous conformations. Its functional groups include a hydroxyl, a carbamate NH, two carbonyl oxygens, and a carboxylic acid OH, so it can donate several hydrogen bonds and accept several more.

The molecule is a linear, acyclic chain of five carbons bearing two carboxylic acid groups, one at each terminus, which makes it a dicarboxylic acid derivative. A single stereogenic carbon sits along the chain and carries a carbamate nitrogen, so its backbone is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds. The nitrogen is capped by a benzyloxycarbonyl group, an ester-type carbamate attached to a monosubstituted phenyl ring, which is the only aromatic ring present. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two acid ends are differently positioned relative to the stereocenter. Both carboxylic acids and the carbamate N–H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of the acids and carbamate serve as acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic amino acid derivative built around a single stereogenic alpha carbon that carries a short 2-(methylthio)ethyl side chain, a carboxylic acid group, and a nitrogen atom. That nitrogen is acylated by a benzyloxycarbonyl carbamate, which links it to a monosubstituted benzene ring through a flexible CH2 spacer. The scaffold contains one aromatic ring with no fused rings, and the thioether sulfur sits at the end of the side chain. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the carbamate N–H and the carboxylic acid O–H, while acceptor sites include the carbonyl oxygens, the ester-type oxygen, and the sulfur atom. The molecule has no internal symmetry and is moderately flexible due to several rotatable single bonds.

The molecule is a carbamate built from a benzyl ester of a carbamic acid, with the nitrogen bearing a chiral carbon that carries a hydroxymethyl group and a benzyl substituent. Two unfused phenyl rings are present, one attached through a methylene linker to the ester oxygen and the other to the stereocenter via a CH2 bridge, so the scaffold is an open-chain amino alcohol derivative rather than a fused polycycle. The carbamate C=O and the ester-type oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the carbamate N-H and the primary alcohol O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the single stereocenter, and its several rotatable single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility, with the two aromatic rings providing localized rigidity.

This molecule is a carbamate-protected amino acid built on a serine-like backbone. A benzyl group is attached through an oxygen to a carbonyl, which in turn is bonded to a nitrogen that carries the alpha carbon of the chain. The alpha carbon bears a hydroxymethyl side chain and a terminal carboxylic acid, giving a single stereogenic center with defined configuration. The only ring system is a monosubstituted benzene ring attached to a flexible CH2 linker, so the molecule lacks any fused rings and has no internal symmetry. Its several rotatable bonds make it fairly flexible. Hydrogen-bond capability is substantial: the carbamate NH, the hydroxyl OH, and the carboxylic acid OH act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and the ether-type oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a tyrosine derivative whose alpha-amine is protected as a benzyl carbamate. The core is a para-hydroxyphenyl ring linked through a CH2 to a chiral alpha-carbon bearing a free carboxylic acid, giving an L-amino-acid-like backbone. The carbamate nitrogen is attached to a benzyloxycarbonyl group, which contributes a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring connected through a flexible CH2–O linkage. The phenolic hydroxyl, carbamate N–H and carbonyl oxygen, and carboxylic acid provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its several single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility, with the two aromatic rings providing limited rigidity.

The molecule is an alpha,alpha-disubstituted amino acid derivative in which the alpha carbon is a quaternary stereocenter bearing a methyl group, a free carboxylic acid, and a naphthalen-2-yl ring. The amine nitrogen is protected as a tert-butyl carbamate, with a tert-butyl group attached through an oxygen to the carbonyl. The bicyclic naphthalene system is fused and planar, contributing rigidity, while the tert-butyl and methyl groups add bulk around the stereocenter. The carbamate NH and carboxylic acid OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygens and ether oxygen act as acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic carbamate, built from a central carbonyl carbon bonded to one nitrogen and one oxygen, giving a C(=O)(N)(O) core. The nitrogen carries a single ethyl group, so it is a secondary amide-type nitrogen with one N–H. The ester-like oxygen is bonded to a tertiary carbon that bears three methyl groups, creating a compact, bulky tert-butyl-type substituent. The molecule contains no rings, aromatic systems, or stereocenters, and its linear chain segments give it considerable conformational flexibility around the single bonds. The N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ether-type oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic carbamate-type structure built on a single carbonyl carbon. A tert-butyl group, bearing three methyl groups around a central quaternary carbon, is bonded through an ester-type oxygen to the carbonyl, which in turn is bonded to an NH that carries a hydroxyl group on nitrogen, giving an N-hydroxy carbamate arrangement. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is flexible, with rotation possible about the single bonds, though the planar carbamate unit imposes some local rigidity. The bulky tert-butyl group provides steric shielding, and the molecule has no true symmetry beyond the local threefold arrangement of the methyl groups. The NH and N–OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a Boc-protected amino alcohol built on a three-carbon chain with a stereocenter at the carbon bearing the nitrogen. The nitrogen is part of a carbamate, where it is bonded to a carbonyl that is also linked to a bulky tert-butyl group through an oxygen. A primary hydroxymethyl group extends from the stereocenter, providing one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor, while the carbamate contributes an additional donor (N-H) and acceptor (C=O). A benzyl group, a phenyl ring attached through a methylene linker, is attached to the other side of the stereocenter. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted and unfused, and the overall scaffold is moderately flexible due to several rotatable single bonds.

This molecule is an N-protected derivative of tyrosine, built around a single chiral alpha carbon that carries a methyl ester on one side and a carbamate-protected amine on the other. The side chain is a benzyl group bearing a para-hydroxyl substituent on an aromatic ring, which is the only ring system present and is planar and fully unsaturated. The amine is capped by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, giving a carbamate linkage with a bulky, branched tert-butyl unit that provides steric shielding. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the phenolic hydroxyl and the carbamate N-H, while hydrogen-bond acceptors include the ester and carbamate carbonyl oxygens, the ester and carbamate ether oxygens, and the phenolic oxygen. The molecule is fairly flexible overall because of several rotatable single bonds along the backbone, though the aromatic ring and carbamate and ester planes are comparatively rigid.

The molecule is an N-bromo lactam built on a seven-membered ring, a caprolactam skeleton in which the nitrogen is bonded to a bromine atom. The ring is fully saturated apart from the carbonyl carbon, which is a planar sp2 center adjacent to the nitrogen, giving an amide-type C=O and an N–Br bond at the same position. There are no additional substituents or stereocenters, so the structure is achiral and has a simple, unbranched arrangement around the ring. The seven-membered ring is conformationally flexible, though the amide linkage is planar and restricts rotation locally. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because the nitrogen carries the bromine rather than a hydrogen.

The molecule is a para-substituted benzene ring bearing two groups on opposite positions. One substituent is a butyl ester: a four-carbon straight alkyl chain attached through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon that is bonded directly to the ring. The other substituent is a hydroxyl group sitting para to the ester on the same aromatic ring. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring with no additional fused systems. The para arrangement gives the ring a high degree of symmetry along its long axis, while the flexible butyl chain adds conformational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic ether built from a straight-chain butyl group bonded through a single oxygen atom to an ethyl group, giving a simple dialkyl ether scaffold with no rings or fused ring systems. The oxygen atom is the only functional group, and it sits between two saturated carbon chains with no additional substituents or branching. Because the chains are flexible single bonds, the molecule can adopt many conformations and has no fixed rigid shape. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the trivial, since the two alkyl chains differ in length. Its oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites because it lacks any O–H or N–H groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, linear chain built around a four-carbon backbone with no rings and no ring fusion. At one end sits a urea-type unit, a carbonyl flanked by two nitrogens, and at the other end a terminal carboxylic acid. Between them lies a rigid, planar carbon-carbon double bond connecting two carbonyl carbons, which is typically trans and limits conformational flexibility. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two termini carry different functional groups. Its hydrogen-bond capability is strong: the urea nitrogens and the carboxylic acid hydroxyl act as donors, while the three carbonyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

Decane is an acyclic straight-chain alkane made of ten carbon atoms, each bonded to its neighbors through single bonds and saturated with hydrogen. The molecule has no rings, no ring fusion, and no functional groups, so there is no substitution pattern to speak of. Its skeleton is a single unbranched chain with a mirror-image arrangement along its length, giving it a high degree of conformational flexibility because rotation about each carbon-carbon bond is essentially free. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it has no heteroatoms or polar bonds.

This molecule is a straight-chain saturated hydrocarbon, an alkane built from a single unbranched backbone of carbon atoms linked by single bonds. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups of any kind. Every carbon is sp3-hybridized and bears only hydrogen atoms besides its chain neighbors, so there is no substitution pattern to speak of. The chain is conformationally flexible, able to adopt many rotational arrangements about its single bonds, and the molecule is essentially symmetric about its midpoint. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a simple acyclic alkane skeleton: a central quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups and a two-carbon chain ending in a chlorine atom. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom ring systems. The only functional group is a primary alkyl chloride, with the chlorine attached to a terminal CH2 that is bonded to the bulky tert-butyl-type carbon. The three methyl groups around the quaternary carbon give the molecule a high degree of local symmetry, with a threefold axis running through the C–C bonds of the tert-butyl unit. The structure is fairly flexible through rotation about its single bonds, though the bulky quaternary center restricts some conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atom is only a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small acyclic amide built on a two-carbon acetyl backbone, with no rings and no fused systems. Its skeleton consists of an ethyl group attached to a nitrogen, which is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that also carries a methyl group. The central functional group is a secondary amide, in which the carbonyl oxygen and the amide nitrogen define the polar core. Because the amide bond has partial double-bond character, the local geometry around it is planar and comparatively rigid, while the terminal ethyl and methyl groups retain some rotational freedom. The nitrogen bears one hydrogen, so the molecule can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an N-protected cysteine derivative built around a chiral alpha-carbon bearing a free carboxylic acid and a carbamate nitrogen. The nitrogen is capped by a 9-fluorenylmethoxycarbonyl group, whose fused three-ring aromatic fluorene system is largely planar and rigid. The sulfur side chain carries a trityl group, a central sp3 carbon bonded to three phenyl rings arranged in a propeller-like, bulky arrangement. Hydrogen-bond donors are the carbamate N–H and the carboxylic acid O–H, while the carbonyl oxygens of the carbamate and acid, along with the ester-type oxygen, serve as acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its stereocenter and differing substituents, and its flexibility is concentrated in the CH2–S and CH–CH2 linkages between the rigid aromatic blocks.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a urea-like backbone, with a central nitrogen-carbon-nitrogen linkage flanked by an amide-type carbonyl on one side and a formyl group on the other. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system, and its scaffold is essentially a short, unbranched chain. Its functional groups are two amide-type carbonyls and three nitrogen atoms, with one terminal primary amide and one N-formyl unit, and the arrangement lacks any substitution pattern beyond these groups. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two ends carry different substituents. Its chain is flexible, with rotation available about its single bonds, though the planar amide character of the carbonyl-nitrogen bonds restricts that freedom somewhat. Several N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a straight-chain saturated alkane with seven carbon atoms linked in a single unbranched backbone, so it has no rings, no fused ring systems, and no heteroatoms. Its only functional features are carbon-hydrogen bonds, with no hydroxyl, carbonyl, amine, or other polar groups present. Because there are no branches or substituents, the substitution pattern is simply uniform along the chain. The molecule is highly flexible, since rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond allows many conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, as neither a hydrogen bonded to an electronegative atom nor a lone-pair-bearing heteroatom is present.

This molecule is a fully saturated, unbranched aliphatic chain of sixteen carbon atoms with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms. Its scaffold is a single linear alkyl backbone terminated at both ends by methyl groups, so it has no functional groups and no substitution pattern to speak of. The structure is highly symmetrical about its midpoint, with the two halves being mirror images of one another. Because every bond is a freely rotating single bond, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, as all bonding is carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built from a short unsaturated acid and a straight six-carbon alcohol chain. The acyl portion is an acrylate unit, consisting of a terminal vinyl group conjugated to a carbonyl carbon. Joined through the ester oxygen is an unbranched hexyl chain of six sp3 carbons, so the structure contains no rings and no ring fusion. The molecule is flexible, since the long saturated tail can rotate freely about its single bonds, and it has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry. It has one carbonyl oxygen and one ester ether oxygen that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built from a methacrylic acid unit linked to a straight six-carbon alkyl chain. The acyl portion carries a terminal carbon-carbon double bond with a methyl group on the same carbon, giving a 2-methyl-substituted alkene directly conjugated to the carbonyl. The ester oxygen connects this unit to an unbranched hexyl chain, so there are no ring systems or fused rings. The ester group provides one hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen and one at the ether-type oxygen, with no hydrogen-bond donors present. The hexyl tail is highly flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds, while the acrylate-type end is comparatively rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a single substituent at the 3-position relative to that nitrogen. That substituent is a carbohydrazide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydrazine unit (an N–N bond with a terminal NH2). The scaffold is planar and rigid at the ring, while the hydrazide side chain has rotational freedom about its single bonds. The pyridine nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two NH groups of the hydrazide act as hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local ring geometry, since the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons (an ortho arrangement). One substituent is a methylamino group, a nitrogen carrying one methyl group and one hydrogen attached directly to the ring, making it a secondary aryl amine. The other is a nitro group, with a formally charged nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, which is strongly electron-withdrawing. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, while the methyl group offers only minor conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents differ. The amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro oxygens and the amine nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a methylamino group (-NHCH3), a secondary amine attached directly to the aromatic ring. The other is a nitro group (-NO2) on the opposite side of the ring, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and drawn as a charge-separated N+ with an O- and a double-bonded O. The ring is flat and fully aromatic, with no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid apart from rotation of the methyl and nitro groups. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through both substituents, though the methyl group breaks it slightly. The amine NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro oxygens and the nitrogen lone pair serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold, with no fused or additional rings and no aromatic or unsaturated bonds. A methylamino group (–NH–CH3) is attached to one ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the molecule carries no stereochemical symmetry beyond the ring's conformational flexibility. The secondary amine nitrogen bears one hydrogen, allowing it to act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and its lone pair allows it to act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Apart from the nitrogen, the structure consists only of sp3-hybridized carbon and hydrogen, so the ring can adopt chair and other conformations and the overall molecule is moderately flexible.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated carbon chain of seven carbons with no rings or aromatic systems, bearing a terminal N-methylamino group on one end and a primary alcohol on the other. Along the chain, four hydroxyl groups are attached to consecutive stereogenic carbons, giving a polyol pattern with a defined stereochemical arrangement. The nitrogen is a secondary amine, able to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while each hydroxyl contributes donor and acceptor capability. Because the backbone is linear and carries numerous single bonds, the structure is quite flexible, though the multiple hydroxyl groups make it capable of extensive intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the substituent pattern is not mirrored along the chain.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A nitrogen atom is attached directly to one ring carbon, and that nitrogen carries both a methyl group and a formyl group, so it forms a tertiary amide (N-methyl-N-phenylformamide). The substitution pattern is monosubstituted, with the remaining five ring positions bearing hydrogen. The amide C=O oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitrogen has no N–H and therefore no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The amide linkage gives the molecule partial rigidity, and the N–aryl bond allows some rotation, so the scaffold is moderately flexible rather than fully rigid. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the ring and the substituent, given the planar aromatic ring.

The molecule is built on a five-membered imide ring fused to a benzene ring, forming a planar bicyclic scaffold. The nitrogen in the five-membered ring carries a methyl group, and both carbonyl carbons flanking that nitrogen are part of the imide functionality. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion has no additional substituents beyond the fused connection. The fused framework is rigid and largely flat, with the N-methyl group as the only sp3-hybridized substituent. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen is fully substituted.

This molecule is an acyclic secondary amide built on a straight, unbranched five-carbon acyl chain. The carbonyl carbon is bonded to a linear n-butyl group on one side and to a nitrogen atom that carries a single methyl substituent on the other, so the scaffold has no rings and no ring fusion.
