The only functional group is the amide, whose N–H can donate a hydrogen bond while the carbonyl oxygen can accept one. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond the local planarity of the amide unit. Its rigidity is limited to the partial double-bond character of the C–N amide bond, with the alkyl chain otherwise free to rotate and flex.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three adjacent hydroxyl groups on one side and an ester at the opposite position. The ester carbonyl is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and its oxygen links to a straight, unbranched eight-carbon alkyl chain, giving a long, flexible tail. Three phenolic OH groups sit on consecutive ring carbons, creating a catechol-like pyrogallol arrangement, with the remaining two aromatic positions bearing hydrogens, so the ring substitution is asymmetric. The phenolic hydroxyls act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the alkyl ester chain is highly flexible.

The molecule is built from a single benzene ring bearing one linear eight-carbon alkyl chain, so it is a monosubstituted aromatic hydrocarbon with no other functional groups. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, consisting of six sp2 carbons in a conjugated cycle, and it has no ring fusion. The octyl side chain is saturated and unbranched, giving the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, since the chain can adopt many rotameric arrangements. The overall structure has only partial symmetry, with a local mirror-like plane through the ring and the chain axis, but it lacks any higher symmetry. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, as it has only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

The molecule is an N-phenyl benzamidine, built around a central amidine carbon bonded to three nitrogen-containing groups. One terminal nitrogen is an unsubstituted imine (=NH), while the other is an amine (–NH–) attached to a phenyl ring, and the carbon itself carries a second phenyl ring directly. Both aromatic rings are unfused benzene rings, each with an unsubstituted, monosubstituted pattern, giving the molecule two separate rings joined through the amidine core. The amidine unit is conjugated and largely planar, which lends the scaffold moderate rigidity, although the single bonds to the phenyl rings permit some rotation. Overall the molecule has no rotational symmetry. The imine and amine nitrogens together can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the two aromatic rings offer hydrophobic and π-stacking surfaces.

This molecule is an ester built around a two-carbon ethyl group attached to a carboxylate, with a single methylene linking the carbonyl carbon to a secondary amine. The amine nitrogen is bonded directly to a benzene ring, so the scaffold is an N-aryl glycine ester: an unsubstituted phenyl ring connected through an NH bridge to an acyclic ester chain. The aromatic ring is monosubstituted and carries no other groups, which gives it a symmetric, flat profile about its axis. The ester carbonyl and the aniline-type nitrogen provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the N–H group serves as a single hydrogen-bond donor. Apart from the rigid phenyl ring, the chain has several rotatable single bonds, so the molecule is moderately flexible.

The molecule is built around two benzene rings joined by a secondary amine (–NH–) bridge, forming a diarylamine scaffold. One ring carries a primary amino group (–NH2) positioned para to the bridging nitrogen, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern on that ring, while the other ring is unsubstituted. Neither ring is fused, and the two aromatic rings are connected through a single flexible C–N–C linkage that allows rotation about its bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two rings bear different substitution. Its hydrogen-bond capability is notable: the two amine nitrogens each carry N–H bonds that can act as donors, and their lone pairs can act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold, meaning a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring that contains a nitrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid. The imide nitrogen carries a propargyl substituent, a three-carbon chain ending in a terminal alkyne (carbon-carbon triple bond). The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen is fully substituted and there are no N-H or O-H groups. The terminal alkyne adds a linear, rod-like segment that extends away from the otherwise compact aromatic core.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a propyl ester group, in which a three-carbon straight chain is attached through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon that is bonded to the ring. The opposite side carries a phenolic hydroxyl group directly attached to the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the propyl chain adds some conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ester carbonyl and ether-type oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the ring, since the substituents lie on opposite sides.

This molecule is a simple acyclic ester built on a linear three-carbon propyl chain attached through an oxygen atom to a formyl group. Its skeleton is entirely unbranched and contains no ring systems or ring fusion, so there is no rigid scaffold and the chain can adopt many conformations. The defining functional group is the ester linkage, a carbonyl carbon bonded to both a single-bonded oxygen (joined to the propyl group) and a hydrogen, which makes it a formate ester. There is no substitution pattern to speak of beyond this terminal ester, and the molecule lacks any elements of symmetry apart from local rotational freedom along the chain. Regarding hydrogen bonding, it has no donor groups, since all hydrogens are attached to carbon, while the two oxygen atoms of the ester can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an N-tert-butyl nitrone, built from a tert-butyl group bonded to a nitrogen atom that carries an N-oxide oxygen and forms a C=N double bond to a benzylic carbon. The central motif is a conjugated C=N(+)–O(-) unit linking the quaternary tert-butyl carbon to a phenyl ring, giving a planar, rigid core around the nitrone group. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the benzene ring carries no additional functional groups and the pattern is monosubstituted. The bulky tert-butyl group sterically shields the nitrogen side of the nitrone. The molecule has no stereocenters, and the C=N double bond fixes the geometry, so the arrangement is essentially rigid apart from rotation about single bonds. The oxygen atom of the N-oxide acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an N-substituted benzamide built on a single benzene ring with no fused or additional ring systems. A benzene ring carries a carboxamide group directly attached to one ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted with no positional isomerism to consider. The amide nitrogen is bonded to a tert-butyl group, a bulky, highly branched, and sterically demanding alkyl substituent. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the amide linkage is fairly rigid, leaving the overall molecule with limited conformational flexibility, though the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk.

This molecule is a straight, fully saturated hydrocarbon chain: a single unbranched backbone of carbon atoms, each bearing hydrogens, with no rings, no double or triple bonds, and no heteroatoms. Because there are no functional groups, substituents, or stereocenters, the molecule has no branching points and its only symmetry is the mirror-like equivalence of the two ends of the chain. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds allowing it to adopt many conformations, though extended zigzag arrangements are favored. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an ethyl ester of an amino acid: a glycine-type unit whose nitrogen is bonded to a trityl-type carbon bearing three phenyl rings. The ethyl ester group (CCOC(=O)) is attached through a methylene to a secondary amine nitrogen, which in turn connects to a quaternary carbon carrying three unsubstituted benzene rings arranged in a propeller-like, sterically crowded geometry. The three phenyl rings are each monosubstituted-free aromatic rings with no additional substituents, giving a threefold pattern around the central sp3 carbon. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The bulky triaryl core makes the scaffold rigid, while the ethyl ester chain adds some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is N-vinylphthalimide. It consists of a phthalimide scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered cyclic imide ring containing a nitrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups. The nitrogen carries a vinyl substituent (a CH=CH2 group) attached directly to the ring nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the vinyl group adds a small degree of conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen is fully substituted, but the two imide carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic compound made of a benzene ring fused to a five-membered heterocycle containing a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom. The five-membered ring is a saturated lactam-type ring in which a carbonyl group is bonded to an NH that sits next to a sulfonyl group (SO2), and the sulfonyl sulfur is attached to the benzene ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted apart from this fusion, so the aromatic portion carries no additional groups. The overall framework is planar and rigid, with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local mirror plane through the fused system. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Five of the six ring positions carry fluorine atoms, while the remaining position bears a trifluoromethyl group, so the scaffold is a fully fluorinated, substituted benzene. The substitution pattern is asymmetric in its arrangement relative to the CF3 group, with fluorines filling every other available carbon. The ring is rigid and planar, and the trifluoromethyl group rotates only slightly about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, so it has no fused or aromatic systems. It contains a single terminal primary alcohol (hydroxyl group) at one end and one internal carbon-carbon double bond, located near the middle of the chain with a cis or trans geometry not specified in the SMILES. The chain is long and flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, and it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the double bond sits off-center. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the skeleton is nonpolar and contributes only van der Waals interactions.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with no fused ring system. Each ring carries an amino group (–NH2) and a methyl group (–CH3) placed ortho to each other, so the substitution pattern is the same on both sides and the molecule is roughly symmetric about the central bond. The two aromatic rings are planar and conjugated, but the biaryl bond allows some rotation, giving moderate rigidity. Each amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor through its lone pair, while the methyl groups contribute only nonpolar bulk.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, which makes it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a methyl group attached directly to the ring, and the other is a formyl group, an aldehyde consisting of a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to a hydrogen. The aromatic ring is fully conjugated and planar, and the aldehyde carbonyl is conjugated with it, which gives the framework considerable rigidity. The only rotatable bond is the one linking the formyl group to the ring, so the molecule is otherwise quite compact. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons: a methyl group and a sulfonyl chloride group, making it an ortho-substituted toluene derivative. The sulfonyl group, consisting of a central sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom, is attached directly to the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is a single, planar six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the substitution pattern breaks any mirror symmetry the ring would otherwise possess. The sulfonyl chloride unit is strongly polarized and the two sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid aromatic ring contrasts with the freely rotating sulfur-carbon and sulfur-chlorine bonds, giving the molecule only modest conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which is a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A methyl group and a hydroxyl group are attached to the ring at positions para to each other, so the substitution pattern is 1,4 and the molecule has a two-fold axis of symmetry through both substituents. The hydroxyl group is a phenolic OH that can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the methyl group is a nonpolar alkyl substituent that adds only steric bulk. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the only notable flexibility coming from rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogen.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic dicarboxylic acid built from a linear, unbranched carbon backbone with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms other than the two terminal carboxyl groups. Each end of the chain carries a carboxylic acid functional group, consisting of a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl oxygen attached to a single terminal carbon. The chain is fully saturated, with only single carbon-carbon bonds, so it is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations through free rotation about its bonds. Because the two acid groups sit at opposite ends of the molecule, the structure is symmetric about its midpoint. Each carboxyl group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites in total.

This molecule is a single saturated macrocyclic lactone: a 16-membered ring containing one ester linkage, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a ring oxygen. The remaining fifteen ring atoms are all methylene carbons joined in an unbranched chain, so there are no fused rings, aromatic systems, or extra substituents. The ring is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations, with no stereocenters and an overall mirror-symmetric, unbranched arrangement. The only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two oxygens of the ester group, the carbonyl oxygen and the ring oxygen, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, fully substituted with one cyano group and five fluorine atoms, so no ring hydrogens remain. The cyano group is a linear nitrile, with a carbon-nitrogen triple bond attached directly to the aromatic ring. Each of the five fluorines sits on a ring carbon adjacent to the next, giving a densely halogenated, pentafluorinated pattern that places the nitrile at one position and the fluorines at all others. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and its substitution pattern lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile and the fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic saturated hydrocarbon built on a straight five-carbon chain, with no rings, no fused systems, and no heteroatoms. Every carbon is sp3-hybridized and bears only hydrogens and neighboring carbons, so there are no functional groups and no substitution pattern to speak of. The skeleton is linear and symmetric about its central carbon, with the two terminal methyl groups mirror-equivalent. Because the chain has many freely rotating single bonds, it is highly flexible and can adopt a range of conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

This molecule is a single central iodine atom bonded to four oxygen atoms, with no carbon framework, so it has no carbocyclic or heterocyclic ring systems and no ring fusion. The iodine center carries a formal positive charge in a higher-valent state, while three of its oxygens bear formal negative charges and the fourth is a neutral hydroxyl group. The arrangement is tetrahedral around iodine, and the three equivalent oxygens are symmetric in connectivity, giving the molecule near three-fold local symmetry. Because the structure is small and compact with rigid geometry and no rotatable bonds, it is conformationally constrained. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the three charged oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a phenothiazine scaffold: two benzene rings joined to a central six-membered ring containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom, positioned across from each other. This tricyclic system is fused and therefore largely planar, though the central ring is folded along the sulfur-nitrogen axis, giving it a characteristic butterfly-like shape. The unsubstituted aromatic rings carry no additional functional groups, so the structure is symmetric about the axis running through the two heteroatoms. The secondary amine N-H is the only hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen lone pair and the sulfur atom can each act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rigid fused framework limits conformational flexibility to the modest ring puckering of the central ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A phenoxy oxygen is attached to one ring carbon, and that oxygen links to a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid group, so the aryl ether and the acid form the flexible side chain. The carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptor (the C=O) capability, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring is monosubstituted, so the molecule has no substitution isomerism on the aromatic core, and the side chain gives it moderate conformational flexibility around the ether and methylene bonds.

This molecule is a vinyl sulfone, consisting of a benzene ring bonded directly to a sulfonyl group, which in turn is attached to a terminal vinyl (ethenyl) group. The sulfur is in its fully oxidized form, bearing two S=O double bonds that act as strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion is symmetric about the C–S axis, and the sulfonyl-vinyl unit is electron-withdrawing and conjugated with the terminal alkene. The structure is compact and largely rigid, with the aromatic ring and the planar vinyl sulfone unit restricting conformational freedom, while rotation about the aryl–sulfur bond remains possible.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolidine-3,5-dione ring, a saturated heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and two carbonyl groups flanking one carbon. The ring carries a linear n-butyl chain on the carbon between the two carbonyls, which is the only sp3 carbon bearing a substituent other than the ring nitrogens. Each of the two ring nitrogens is bonded to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the scaffold is symmetric about the N–N axis and the two aromatic rings are attached at equivalent positions. The imide-like carbonyl groups and the tertiary nitrogens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ring is relatively rigid, with the flexibility coming mainly from the butyl chain and rotation around the nitrogen–phenyl bonds.

This molecule is an alpha-keto acid built from a phenyl ring attached directly to a two-carbon unit that carries a ketone and a carboxylic acid. The benzene ring is a single unsubstituted six-membered aromatic ring, so its substitution pattern is simple and it has a planar, rigid scaffold. The carbonyl carbon bonded to the ring is flanked by the acid group, and the chain between the ring and the acid is short, which limits conformational freedom. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptors (the two oxygens), while the ketone oxygen adds one further acceptor site. Overall the structure is compact, largely planar, and has no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the ring.

The molecule is a substituted malonic-type ester built around a single sp3 carbon that bears two carbonyl-derived groups and a phenyl ring. One end carries a free carboxylic acid, which is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the other end carries a benzyl ester, giving a second carbonyl acceptor and an extra aromatic ring. The central carbon is a stereogenic center, and its phenyl substituent sits beside the two carbonyl arms. Both aromatic rings are unfused benzene rings, so the scaffold is flexible, with several rotatable bonds linking the rings to the central carbon. Overall the molecule has no internal symmetry, and it offers two acceptor carbonyl oxygens plus one acidic hydroxyl donor.

This molecule consists of a single silicon atom bonded to three chlorine atoms and one phenyl ring, giving a tetrahedral silicon center with an aromatic substituent. The benzene ring is a simple monocyclic six-membered aromatic system with no ring fusion and no additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The overall structure is rigid around the aromatic ring, while rotation about the silicon–carbon bond provides some conformational freedom. Because all hydrogen atoms are bonded to carbon, and the silicon and chlorine atoms carry no hydrogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. It also lacks any polar heteroatom with lone pairs suited for hydrogen-bond acceptance beyond the weakly accepting chlorine atoms.

This molecule is trimethoxy(phenyl)silane, built on a tetrahedral silicon center bearing one phenyl ring and three methoxy groups. The phenyl group is a simple, unfused benzene ring with no substituents on the ring, so it is a monosubstituted aromatic system. Each Si–O–CH3 unit is a flexible linkage, giving the molecule considerable conformational freedom around the silicon atom, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The three methoxy oxygens each carry lone pairs and can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H bonds. The arrangement around silicon is approximately threefold symmetric with respect to the three methoxy groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) carbohydrazide substituents, each consisting of a carbonyl group attached to the ring and a terminal hydrazine nitrogen-nitrogen bond. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbon ring with no fused rings, and the two side chains are arranged in a 1,2-substitution pattern. The molecule has approximate local two-fold symmetry across the ring axis, though the terminal NH2 groups make the ends chemically equivalent. Each hydrazide unit contains both N-H donors and carbonyl and amide-type oxygen and nitrogen acceptors, giving the molecule multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the C-C(=O) and C-N bonds of the side chains allow moderate rotational flexibility.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic dicarboxylic acid built on a linear six-carbon backbone with no rings, branches, or substituents along the chain. Each end of the chain terminates in a carboxylic acid group, so the two functional groups are located symmetrically at opposite termini of the molecule. The overall structure is therefore symmetric, with both carboxyl groups identical in environment. Because the chain consists solely of single bonds between sp3-hybridized carbons, the molecule is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. Each carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites in total.

This molecule is a single saturated six-membered heterocycle containing four sp3 carbon atoms and two nitrogen atoms placed at opposite positions in the ring, giving a 1,4-diazinane scaffold. There are no fused rings, double bonds, or exocyclic substituents, so the structure is fully unsubstituted apart from the hydrogens on the nitrogens and carbons. The two secondary amine nitrogens are symmetrically positioned, giving the ring a high degree of symmetry. The ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation that can interconvert between conformers. Each nitrogen carries one N-H that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and each nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a six-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle, joined through its nitrogen to an amide carbonyl. The carbonyl is attached to a conjugated dienyl chain of two carbon-carbon double bonds, both with E geometry, which connects to a benzene ring fused to a five-membered methylenedioxy (1,3-benzodioxole) ring. The aromatic ring carries its substituent at one position, leaving the fused dioxole system as the other part of the scaffold. The chain is largely planar and conjugated, giving rigidity, while the piperidine ring can adopt flexible chair conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the amide nitrogen is fully substituted, but the carbonyl oxygen and the two dioxole oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a five-membered 1,3-dioxole ring, which is a methylenedioxy-bridged aromatic scaffold. The two oxygen atoms of the dioxole ring are bonded to adjacent carbons of the benzene ring, and the CH2 unit links them, so the fused system is essentially planar and rigid. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the benzene ring at a position meta to one of the ring oxygens, making the substitution pattern asymmetric. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two ether oxygens of the dioxole ring can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused ring systems. Two substituents sit para to each other on that ring: an ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain) on one side and a primary amino group on the other. The ether oxygen and the nitrogen of the amine can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two N–H bonds of the amine serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the ethyl chain of the ethoxy group is flexible and can rotate freely. The para arrangement gives the molecule a degree of linear symmetry along its long axis.

This molecule is a three-carbon chain with a terminal alkyne group at one end and a primary alcohol at the other. The carbon-carbon triple bond sits between the first two carbons, making that end linear and rigid, while the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group is an sp3 center that adds a small degree of conformational flexibility. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution pattern beyond the two terminal functional groups. The structure has no meaningful symmetry because the alkyne and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon are chemically distinct. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkyne offers only a weak, π-electron-rich acceptor site.

This molecule is a three-carbon chain built on a propiolic acid scaffold, with no rings present. A terminal alkyne (carbon-carbon triple bond) sits at one end of the chain, directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon of a carboxylic acid group at the other end. The carboxylic acid contributes a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and a hydroxyl group that can both donate and accept them. The molecule is small and essentially linear around the alkyne and carboxyl unit, giving it little conformational flexibility, and it has no internal symmetry beyond the local linear geometry of the triple bond.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement: a methyl group and a sulfonamide group. The sulfonamide consists of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and bonded to an NH2 group, so it is a primary sulfonamide. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar with no ring fusion, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring. Its only rotatable bonds are the ring-to-sulfur and sulfur-to-nitrogen bonds, so it is fairly rigid. The NH2 group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methyl group on one carbon and a nitrile group on the carbon directly opposite. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the overall framework is planar and rigid, with the nitrile's linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond extending the shape along the ring axis. The molecule has a high degree of symmetry along the axis joining the two substituents. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The methyl group is a small, non-polar alkyl substituent.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a ketone-linked side chain in a para arrangement, giving it a simple, symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion. Attached to the ring is a carbonyl group that bears a methylene linker ending in a nitrile, so the side chain contains both a ketone and a cyano functional group. The aryl ring and carbonyl are planar and conjugated, while the CH2 linker and nitrile give some local flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, but the carbonyl oxygen and nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is pyrazine, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms positioned at the 1 and 4 positions of the ring, so they sit directly opposite one another. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, with all carbon atoms bearing a single hydrogen and no substituents, giving the structure a high degree of symmetry with two-fold axes passing through the nitrogen atoms and through the midpoints of opposite carbon-carbon bonds. Because the ring is rigid and lacks any rotatable bonds, its conformation is fixed. Each nitrogen's lone pair lies in the plane of the ring and can accept hydrogen bonds, so the molecule functions as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at both nitrogen sites and has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is pyridazine, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 2 of the ring, with four carbon atoms completing the ring. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, giving a rigid scaffold with no rotatable bonds and no stereocenters. It carries no substituents, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted and the molecule has high ring symmetry with a two-fold axis through the midpoint of the N–N bond and the midpoint of the opposite C4–C5 bond. Because the nitrogen lone pairs lie in the plane of the ring and are not part of the aromatic sextet, both nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the ring carbons offer no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is built from two pyridine rings, each bearing a carboxylic acid group at the 3-position and a carbonyl group at the 2-position, and the two carbonyl carbons are joined through a shared anhydride oxygen. Each pyridine ring is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom, so the scaffold is a symmetric bis-pyridyl anhydride with a free carboxylic acid on each side. The ring nitrogens and the carboxylic acid oxygens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while each free carboxylic acid OH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The aromatic rings are planar and rigid, but the anhydride linkage gives the overall structure some conformational flexibility around the central C–O–C bridge.

The molecule is a pyridine ring bearing a thioamide group at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so it is a 2-substituted pyridine with a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle and no fused rings. The thioamide unit consists of a carbon double-bonded to sulfur and single-bonded to an NH2 group, which together give the substituent both hydrogen-bond donor capacity from the two N–H bonds and acceptor capacity from the sulfur and the ring nitrogen. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, since the thioamide sits on one side of the nitrogen and the remaining ring positions are unsubstituted. Apart from rotation about the bond linking the ring to the thioamide carbon, the structure is largely planar and rigid, with few other flexible segments.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional rings. A nitrogen atom occupies one position of the ring, and an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, with one hydrogen) is attached to a ring carbon at the meta position relative to the nitrogen. The rest of the ring carries hydrogen atoms only, so the substitution pattern is minimal. The structure is flat and rigid, with the aldehyde group capable of rotating only slightly around its bond to the ring. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the aldehyde oxygen is also an acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the simple flat geometry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three hydroxyl groups are attached to three adjacent carbons, so the substitution pattern is contiguous: two hydroxyls flank a central one, and the remaining three ring positions carry hydrogens. Because the three oxygen-bearing carbons sit together on one side of the ring, the molecule has a single mirror plane through the central hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon, giving it a simple planar, rigid skeleton. Each hydroxyl group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept one through its oxygen lone pairs, and the adjacent placement allows intramolecular hydrogen bonding between neighboring hydroxyls. Overall the structure is compact and largely inflexible, with rotation limited mainly to the O–H bonds.

The molecule is a short, acyclic three-carbon chain: a methyl group bonded to a ketone carbonyl, which is directly attached to a carboxylic acid carbon. The two adjacent carbonyl groups make it an alpha-keto acid, with the ketone and the carboxyl sharing a single bond and no rings present. Because the skeleton contains only single C–C bonds and no ring or branching points, it is flexible, with free rotation about the central carbon–carbon bond. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a trivial one, since the methyl end and the carboxylic acid end are chemically distinct. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat, fully aromatic, rigid framework. A boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached to the carbocyclic ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, which places it peri to the pyridine-side ring atoms and yields an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no symmetry elements. The two hydroxyl groups on boron can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms and the pyridine-type ring nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Because the bicyclic core is planar and the boronic acid is the only freely rotating substituent, the molecule is largely rigid with limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The nitrogen sits in the pyridine ring, adjacent to the fusion carbon, making the aromatic bicycle fully planar and rigid. A carboxylic acid group is attached to the benzenoid ring at a position remote from the nitrogen, giving the molecule a single, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor capability (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on a cyclohexene ring bearing gem-dimethyl and methyl substituents, which together form a bulky, lipophilic end group. The ring is attached through a conjugated polyene chain of alternating double bonds, with several methyl branches along the chain, giving a long, extended and fairly rigid backbone. The chain terminates in a carboxylic acid group, which is the only polar functional group present. The carboxylic acid can both donate a hydrogen bond from its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, while the hydrocarbon portion contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability. Overall, the molecule is elongated and largely nonpolar, with one polar end.

The molecule is a small five-membered heterocycle containing a ring nitrogen, a ring carbonyl carbon, a ring methylene, and a ring carbon bearing a thiocarbonyl group, so its core scaffold is a thiazolidine-type ring with two sulfur-containing and one nitrogen-containing heteroatom arrangement. The ring is non-fused and carries no substituents beyond its own atoms, so there is no ring fusion and no substitution pattern to describe. Its functional groups are an amide-type carbonyl within the ring, a thiocarbonyl (C=S) group, and a ring sulfur, with the nitrogen bearing a hydrogen. The compact, nearly planar ring gives the molecule a rigid framework with little conformational flexibility and no meaningful internal symmetry. The N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and thiocarbonyl sulfur can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship, giving it a flat, aromatic, rigid core with a two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring. One substituent is a methyl group, which is a small, non-polar hydrocarbon feature. The other is a sulfonyl group (SO2) bonded directly to the ring, which is attached to a nitrogen that is linked to a second sulfur atom. This sulfur carries two methyl groups and a further sulfoxide-type oxygen, forming a sulfoximine-like unit. The N-S linkage and sulfonyl group are polar, with oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the nitrogen carries no hydrogen and so offers no hydrogen-bond donor site.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, ortho to each other: a formyl group (an aldehyde, with a carbonyl carbon bonded to one hydrogen) and a hydroxyl group bonded directly to the ring. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, and the phenolic hydroxyl can also donate one. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with only the rotation of the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups giving minor conformational freedom. It has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring and its two substituents.

This molecule is an aryl imine built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-nitrogen double bond, with the imine carbon bearing one hydrogen. One ring carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, so the two substituents sit in an ortho relationship on that first ring, while the second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached directly to the imine nitrogen. The scaffold is essentially planar and conjugated across the C=N linkage, giving it limited rotational freedom about the bonds connecting the rings to the imine. The ortho hydroxyl and the imine nitrogen can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, and the hydroxyl oxygen and imine nitrogen also serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the molecule has no rings fused to one another and no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of each phenyl ring.

The molecule is built on a six-membered saturated heterocycle, a piperazine-type ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. Both ring nitrogens are tertiary, each carrying a methyl substituent, and the ring also contains two carbonyl groups, making it a cyclic diamide with one amide on each side of the ring. The two carbonyls sit in positions that give the scaffold an approximately symmetric arrangement about the ring's central axis, so the two halves are closely related. The ring is non-aromatic and somewhat flexible, though the amide linkages add partial planarity and restrict rotation around the C–N bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are fully substituted, but the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexene scaffold with no fused or bridged rings. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to one ring carbon that is part of a carbon-carbon double bond, so the acid is conjugated with the alkene. Three secondary hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent and nearby ring carbons, forming a contiguous pattern of stereocenters that gives the ring a defined three-dimensional arrangement. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its ring and substituents restrict conformational freedom, so it is fairly rigid. Overall it presents four hydrogen-bond donors (the acid and three alcohols) and four acceptor oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered 1,3-dioxolane ring, a saturated heterocycle containing two oxygen atoms separated by one carbon. The ring carbon between the oxygens carries two methyl groups, making it a geminal dimethyl acetal-type center, while the adjacent ring carbon bears a hydroxymethyl side chain. There are no ring fusions, aromatic rings, or double bonds, so the scaffold is fully saturated and sp3-hybridized. The two ring oxygens function only as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the terminal primary hydroxyl group can act as both a donor and an acceptor. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the hydroxymethyl substituent breaks the mirror relationship of the ring. Its ring is conformationally somewhat flexible, and the side chain can rotate freely about its single bonds.

This molecule is a sorbitan-type ester built on a five-membered oxolane (tetrahydrofuran) ring fused to nothing else, bearing two hydroxyl groups on the ring carbons. A linear eighteen-carbon saturated acyl chain is attached through an ester linkage to a primary carbon of an acyclic side chain that carries a secondary hydroxyl group. The ring oxygen and the remaining free hydroxyls on the ring and side chain make the molecule a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The long saturated tail is highly flexible, while the polyhydroxylated head is conformationally more constrained by the single ring and the stereocentres, giving the molecule an amphiphilic, asymmetric character with no internal symmetry.

This molecule is an acyclic polyamine with a linear carbon skeleton built from a four-carbon chain and a three-carbon chain joined through a secondary amine nitrogen. Both ends terminate in primary amine groups, so the structure contains three nitrogen atoms in total, with the central nitrogen bearing one hydrogen and flanked by two methylene segments. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or substituted branching, which gives the molecule a simple, unbranched arrangement. The chain is highly flexible, since all single bonds are freely rotatable and no conformational constraints are present. Each primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and a lone pair acceptor, while the central secondary amine contributes one donor and one acceptor, giving the molecule several hydrogen-bonding capabilities distributed along its length.

This molecule is an acyclic polyene built on a long, unbranched carbon chain bearing several methyl branches, with no rings anywhere in its skeleton. It contains a terminal isopropylidene unit and four additional internal trisubstituted carbon-carbon double bonds, each with its methyl group, spaced out along the backbone by methylene segments. Because all of these double bonds are trisubstituted and separated by flexible sp3 linkers, the molecule has no true mirror or rotational symmetry and is highly flexible. It contains no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic dicarboxylic acid with a four-carbon backbone, built from two terminal carboxyl groups joined by a two-carbon methylene bridge. It contains no rings, so it is fully acyclic and flexible, able to adopt many rotameric conformations about its single C–C bonds. Each end carries a carboxylic acid group, which is a hydroxyl attached to a carbonyl carbon, and this pair of functional groups is arranged symmetrically across the center of the chain. Each carboxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, giving the molecule four acceptor sites and two donor sites in total.

The molecule is a five-membered cyclic anhydride, built from a saturated ring of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom in the ring. Two carbonyl groups sit at positions flanking the ring oxygen, so the ring oxygen links the two carbonyl carbons in a single ester-like bridge. The two methylene carbons between the carbonyls are unsubstituted, giving the scaffold a simple, symmetrical pattern with a mirror plane through the ring oxygen and the midpoint of the CH2–CH2 bond. The ring is fairly rigid and planar-leaning, with little conformational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a non-reducing disaccharide built from two six-membered sugar rings, one of which is a pyranose and the other a furanose, linked through a single glycosidic oxygen bridge. The pyranose unit is a fully hydroxylated ring whose carbon bearing the anomeric oxygen is attached to the bridge and to a hydroxymethyl group. The furanose ring is a five-membered oxygen heterocycle carrying several hydroxyl groups and a hydroxymethyl substituent at the anomeric carbon, which is acetal-linked to the other sugar. Its skeleton is rich in stereocenters, giving a rigid, compact three-dimensional framework with limited conformational freedom at the ring junctions. Numerous hydroxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, with the ring oxygens serving as additional acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship, giving it an elongated, roughly linear shape with a mirror-plane symmetry along the long axis. One substituent is a primary aromatic amine (an aniline-type NH2 group), which can donate hydrogen bonds and acts as a weak electron donor to the ring. The other is a sulfonyl group bonded to a nitrogen that is in turn acylated by an acetyl group, forming an N-acyl sulfonamide. This sulfonamide unit contains an NH donor and several oxygen acceptors, and the S=O oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the structure is fairly rigid through the aromatic core, with limited flexibility only around the single bonds of the sulfonamide and acetyl linkage.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit para to each other across the ring: an amino group (-NH2) and a sulfonic acid group (-SO3H), which is attached through sulfur. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor and the sulfonic acid contributes both donor and strongly polar acceptor oxygens. The ring is rigid and planar, while the substituents have limited rotational freedom about their single bonds. The para arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring's long axis.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Two cyano groups, each a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, are attached directly to the ring at positions one and four, placing them on opposite sides so the substitution pattern is para. This arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with a central axis and an inversion center running through the ring. The scaffold is rigid and planar, since the aromatic ring and the linear cyano groups allow no conformational flexibility. The nitrogen atoms of the nitrile groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built on a four-carbon chain, with no rings present. It contains a ketone carbonyl at the second carbon position and an ester linkage whose oxygen is bonded to a tert-butyl group, which is a quaternary carbon carrying three methyl substituents. The structure is flexible, since the chain has several rotatable single bonds, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond local rotation of the methyl groups. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent because there are no O–H or N–H groups. The two carbonyl oxygens and the ether-type ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule has a single central carbon atom bonded to three methyl groups and one hydroxyl group, giving it a branched, tetrahedral skeleton with no rings or ring fusion. Its only functional group is a secondary-free, tertiary alcohol, meaning the hydroxyl oxygen sits on a carbon that is itself bonded to three other carbons. The three methyl groups are equivalent, so the molecule has high local threefold rotational symmetry about the C–O axis. Its structure is compact and rigid in its carbon framework, with only the O–H bond free to rotate. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs.

The molecule is a small acyclic ether built on a quaternary carbon center. A central tertiary carbon bears three methyl groups and is bonded to a single oxygen atom, which in turn connects to one terminal methyl group, so the structure is essentially a methyl ether of a tert-butyl group. It contains no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic or other functional groups beyond the ether linkage. The molecule is highly symmetric around the C–O axis, with the three methyl groups on the tertiary carbon equivalent to one another, and it is conformationally flexible about its single bonds, though the bulky tert-butyl group restricts rotation somewhat. The oxygen atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule has a single tertiary carbon bearing three methyl groups, with that carbon bonded to a primary amine nitrogen, so the skeleton is a compact, acyclic scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. Its only functional group is a primary amine (–NH2), which sits on one end of the tree-like carbon framework. The substitution pattern is a symmetric quaternary-type carbon: the three methyl groups are chemically equivalent, giving the molecule local threefold symmetry around the central carbon-nitrogen axis. Because all bonds are single and there are no rings or double bonds, the structure is quite compact, with limited conformational variation confined to rotation about the C–C and C–N bonds. The amine nitrogen carries two hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and its lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is tetracyanoethylene, built from a single two-carbon ethylene backbone whose central carbon-carbon double bond is the only skeletal feature. Each of the two sp2 carbons carries two cyano groups, giving four nitrile substituents arranged symmetrically around the double bond. There are no rings, so the structure is compact and planar with essentially no conformational flexibility. The molecule has high symmetry, with the four cyano groups related by a twofold or higher axis through the double bond. Each nitrogen of the four nitrile groups can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated acyclic chain built from repeating ethylene-oxide units, with an ether oxygen between each pair of two-carbon segments. Both ends are capped by methyl groups, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or other substituents along the backbone. The only functional groups are the ether linkages, which repeat in a regular, symmetric pattern about the central oxygen. The chain is highly flexible because each C–C and C–O bond can rotate freely. Each ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no O–H or N–H groups.

This molecule is a symmetric disulfide built from two identical halves joined by an S–S bond. Each half is a thiocarbonyl group (C=S) attached to a diethylamino nitrogen, so the scaffold is a dithiocarbamate motif on either side of a central disulfide linkage. There are no rings and no fused ring systems, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis passing through the S–S bond. Its structure is fairly flexible because of the many single bonds and the freely rotating ethyl groups. The thiocarbonyl sulfur atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all nitrogen and sulfur positions are fully substituted with carbon.

The molecule is a single saturated five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbon atoms, which is the scaffold of oxolane (tetrahydrofuran). It has no fused rings, no substituents, and no functional groups beyond the ether oxygen, which sits within the ring as the sole heteroatom. The ring is fully saturated with sp3-hybridized carbons, so it adopts a non-planar, flexible puckered conformation that interconverts between envelope and twist forms. The molecule possesses no stereocenters and has a high degree of local symmetry through the ring. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, but it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability because no hydrogen is bonded to a heteroatom.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle built from five methylene carbons and one oxygen atom, forming a single closed ring with no fused or bridged systems. The ring contains no double bonds, so the scaffold is fully sp3 and carries no conjugated or aromatic character. Every carbon is unsubstituted, bearing only hydrogens, so there are no pendant functional groups or substitution pattern to describe. The ring can adopt a flexible chair-like conformation, and the oxygen atom gives it a symmetrical outline about that heteroatom. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

This molecule is a tetrahedral silicon center bearing four identical methoxy groups, so it is tetramethyl orthosilicate, which is a common and benign reagent; describing its structure is routine. The core scaffold is a single silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms, each of which connects to a terminal methyl group, giving a highly symmetric arrangement with no rings and no ring fusion. The four Si–O–CH3 arms are the only functional units, and they are all equivalent, so the substitution pattern is simply uniform, with each oxygen linking silicon to a methyl. Each arm can rotate freely about its single bonds, so the molecule is flexible rather than rigid, and its overall shape approximates tetrahedral symmetry around the central silicon. The oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all hydrogens are on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single central carbonyl carbon bonded to two nitrogen atoms, forming a urea-type scaffold. Each nitrogen carries two methyl substituents, so the structure is fully N,N,N',N'-tetramethylated with no N-H bonds. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no stereocenters. The molecule is highly symmetric, with the two dimethylamino halves related by a mirror plane through the carbonyl. Its only functional group is the amide-type C=O, which can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The carbon-nitrogen bonds have partial double-bond character, which limits rotation about them and gives the core moderate conformational rigidity.

The molecule is built around a central phosphorus atom that is double-bonded to a nitrogen, forming an iminophosphorane. Three phenyl rings are attached to the phosphorus, and a fourth phenyl ring is attached to the nitrogen, so the scaffold is entirely aromatic carbocyclic rings with no ring fusion. The phosphorus center is tetrahedral-like and gives a propeller-shaped arrangement of the three P-bound rings, while the rotatable P-N and P-C bonds add some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no strong hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. Its only potential hydrogen-bond acceptor is the nitrogen lone pair of the P=N unit, which is also a site of basicity.

The molecule is built on a central five-membered thiophene ring, an aromatic sulfur heterocycle with one ring sulfur and four carbons. Four phenyl rings are attached to the thiophene, one at each of the two alpha positions (flanking the sulfur) and one at each of the two beta positions, so the core is fully substituted with no ring hydrogens remaining. The structure contains no heteroatom functional groups beyond the ring sulfur, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors and no acceptor sites beyond the weakly basic sulfur lone pairs. The molecule is highly aromatic and conjugated, with the bulky phenyl groups crowded around the thiophene core, which restricts rotation and gives it a largely rigid, propeller-like shape. It has no true mirror symmetry beyond an approximate two-fold relationship between the alpha and beta substituent pairs.

This molecule is built from two five-membered sulfur-containing rings joined by a central double bond, forming a symmetric bis(1,3-dithiole)-type scaffold. Each ring contains two sulfur atoms positioned in a 1,3-relationship, with a carbon-carbon double bond within each ring, so both rings are unsaturated and essentially planar. The two rings are connected through an exocyclic double bond at a shared carbon, creating an extended conjugated pi-system across the whole framework. The arrangement is highly symmetric, with the two halves mirror-related, and the rigid fused-like conjugated core leaves little conformational flexibility. There are no classical hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom separated by a carbon, which is the thiazole scaffold. The ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no fused rings, pendant substituents, or functional groups attached to it. Because the ring carries no substitution, the molecule has high symmetry about an axis running through the sulfur and the opposite carbon, and it is completely rigid. The ring nitrogen has a lone pair that is not part of the aromatic sextet, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ring offers no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system built from two five-membered rings fused along a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat, fully conjugated scaffold. One ring is a thiophene, and the second is also a thiophene, so the structure contains two sulfur atoms, each placed at the outer edge of its respective ring. Neither ring carries any substituents, so the hydrogen atoms are the only peripheral groups and no functional groups are present. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the fused bond, and its rigid planar framework leaves essentially no conformational flexibility. Because the sulfur atoms have lone pairs but no attached hydrogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character at the sulfur positions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a single substituent: a thiocarboxylic acid group (–C(=O)SH) attached directly to one ring carbon. The aromatic ring is a simple, fully unsaturated six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, and the substitution pattern is monosubstituted, so the ring carbons are not all equivalent but the molecule has an effective mirror plane through the ring and the carbonyl. The thioacid group is planar and conjugated with the aromatic π-system, which gives the framework substantial rigidity, with only rotation about the ring-to-carbonyl bond and the C–S bond contributing flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the sulfur-bound hydrogen acts as a weak hydrogen-bond donor.

This molecule is a small aromatic aldoxime built on a thiophene scaffold. A five-membered, sulfur-containing aromatic ring carries a single substituent at the 2-position, which is an aldoxime group: a carbon bearing a hydrogen, double-bonded to a nitrogen that is in turn bonded to a hydroxyl group. The C=N double bond introduces geometric isomerism, and the oxime nitrogen and hydroxyl oxygen together provide one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor sites (the nitrogen and the oxygen). The ring sulfur contributes weak acceptor character, and the molecule is otherwise planar and largely rigid, with only limited rotational freedom about the bond linking the ring to the oxime carbon.

The molecule is a small acyclic hydrazide built around a single aromatic thiophene ring. A two-atom hydrazide unit, NH-NH2 attached to a carbonyl group, is connected through a methylene linker to the carbon at the 3-position of a five-membered, sulfur-containing aromatic ring. The thiophene ring is unsubstituted apart from this attachment, so the substitution pattern is simple and the scaffold has no ring fusion. The molecule has no stereocenters and little symmetry beyond the ring's local planarity. Its flexibility comes mainly from the rotatable CH2 linker, while the aromatic ring and the amide-like carbonyl remain rigid and planar. The terminal hydrazide NH2 and the adjacent NH act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and terminal nitrogen act as acceptors.

The molecule is an aldoxime built from a thiophene scaffold: a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. The oxime group, consisting of a carbon double-bonded to nitrogen with a hydroxyl on the nitrogen, is attached to the ring through a single carbon bridge, with the methine carbon bonded directly to the ring at the 3-position relative to sulfur. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, with no fused rings or additional substituents, so the molecule is small and largely rigid, though the C–C bond linking the oxime to the ring allows rotation. The oxime hydroxyl acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and the oxime nitrogen as an acceptor, while the thiophene sulfur is a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to a sulfur atom that carries a hydrogen, giving a thioacid group. The other is a hydroxyl group directly attached to the ring, so the two groups sit in an ortho arrangement. The ring is planar and rigid, while the thioacid and hydroxyl groups have limited rotational freedom about their bonds to the ring. Because the two substituents differ, the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a possible planar arrangement. The hydroxyl oxygen and the thioacid sulfur can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen can accept one.

This molecule is an unsaturated carboxylic acid built on a short, four-carbon acyclic chain, with no ring systems or ring fusion. The carbon-carbon double bond sits between the second and third carbons, and each end of it carries a methyl group, so the alkene is tetrasubstituted and the two methyl groups are arranged across it in a defined geometry. The terminal carboxylic acid group is the dominant functional group, featuring a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl group. Because the chain is small and contains only one rigid double bond, the molecule is quite compact and has limited conformational flexibility. The carboxyl group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygen atoms.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no double bonds or heteroatoms in the ring itself. Two carboxylic acid groups, each a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl, are attached to adjacent carbons, so the substitution pattern is 1,2 on the ring. Both stereocenters are specified, which fixes the relative spatial arrangement of the two acid groups. The ring adopts a flexible chair-type conformation, with the acids able to sit in either axial or equatorial positions. Each carboxylic acid offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites in total.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, with no aromatic or unsaturated centers and no fused rings. Two hydroxyl groups are attached to adjacent carbons of the ring, making it a vicinal diol with a 1,2-substitution pattern. The two stereocenters at those carbons define a specific relative configuration, so the ring is chiral and not superimposable on its mirror image. The cyclohexane framework is conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair-like forms, though the bulky adjacent hydroxyls bias its preferred arrangement. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the rest of the ring is purely hydrocarbon in character.

This molecule is a cinnamic acid derivative built on a benzene ring bearing two chlorine substituents at the 2 and 4 positions relative to the side chain. The side chain is an acrylic acid unit, a carboxylic acid group attached to an alkene carbon with a trans (E) double bond linking it to the ring, giving the molecule a largely planar, rigid extended geometry. The aromatic ring is unfused and carries no ring-fusion features, and the only other rotatable bond is the single bond between the vinyl group and the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the chlorine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors and contribute to an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a cinnamic acid scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a methoxy group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, connected through a carbon-carbon double bond to a carboxylic acid. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered ring with the methoxy substituent in the ortho position, and the alkene linker has a trans (E) geometry that keeps the aryl ring and the acid group on opposite sides. The carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group serves as an additional acceptor. The conjugated aryl-alkene-carbonyl arrangement makes the core fairly rigid and planar, with the methoxy and acid groups as the main points of conformational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond what its planar framework allows.

This molecule is a cinnamic-acid-type structure: a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon acrylic acid side chain attached through a trans (E) carbon-carbon double bond. The aromatic ring is monosubstituted with a fluorine atom at the meta position relative to the vinyl linkage, giving an unfused, planar benzene core. The terminal carboxylic acid group is conjugated with the alkene and the aromatic ring, which keeps the entire backbone largely flat and rigid, with only the carboxyl OH free to rotate. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the fluorine is a weak acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of its ring.

The molecule is an open-chain alkene with six carbon atoms, containing no rings and no heteroatoms. Its backbone is a straight, unbranched chain, with a single carbon-carbon double bond located between the third and fourth carbons counting from one end. The double bond has a trans (E) geometry, meaning the two chain segments flanking it lie on opposite sides, which gives the chain an extended, nearly linear shape. The molecule has no functional groups beyond the alkene itself, and it lacks any hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen. Its flexibility comes from the freely rotating single bonds in the saturated segments, while the double bond restricts rotation locally.

The molecule is a substituted cinnamic acid built on a single benzene ring. The ring carries a hydroxyl group and a methoxy group on adjacent carbons, giving a guaiacol-type pattern, with the carbon at the para position relative to the hydroxyl bearing the side chain. That side chain is an α,β-unsaturated carboxylic acid: a carbon-carbon double bond with trans geometry connecting the ring to a terminal carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring and the conjugated alkene form a largely planar, rigid framework, with the methoxy group the main source of conformational freedom. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms of the methoxy, hydroxyl, and carbonyl groups act as acceptors.

The molecule is a cinnamic acid derivative built on a benzene ring carrying a methoxy group at the para position relative to the side chain. A single aromatic ring forms the core scaffold, with no ring fusion or additional ring systems present. The side chain is an acrylic acid unit: a carbon-carbon double bond with a defined trans geometry linked to a terminal carboxylic acid group. Because the aromatic ring, the double bond, and the carboxyl group are conjugated, the framework is largely planar and fairly rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the methoxy group. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through its long axis, giving it a roughly symmetric outline. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the methoxy oxygen provides an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methoxy group, an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group, attached directly to the ring. The other is a propenyl chain, a three-carbon unit with a carbon-carbon double bond whose geometry is trans (E) about that double bond, linking the chain to the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is compact and planar, while the trans alkene and the single bond to the ether oxygen add some conformational freedom. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the ring centre and the two substituent positions. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a simple two-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring, forming a cinnamyl-type skeleton. The benzene ring is a single unfused six-membered aromatic ring with no substituents on it, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The side chain contains a trans (E) carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with the aromatic ring and terminated by an aldehyde group, which is a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen. The conjugated system makes the chain largely planar and fairly rigid, with limited rotation about the double bond. Overall the molecule has a mirror plane through its extended chain, giving it an approximately symmetric shape. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single phosphorus atom bearing three substituents, one of which is a naphthalene unit directly attached to a central naphthalene ring system, while the other two substituents are each 1-naphthyl groups. The core is therefore a tri(1-naphthyl)phosphine-type scaffold, with three fused bicyclic aromatic ring systems radiating from the phosphorus center. Each naphthalene unit is attached through its alpha (1-) position, giving a non-symmetric arrangement of ring fusions that is roughly three-fold around the phosphorus. The structure is rigid and bulky, with extensive planar aromatic surfaces, and it contains no hydroxyl, amine, or carbonyl groups, so it offers no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The phosphorus lone pair can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is tri-p-tolylphosphine, built around a single trivalent phosphorus atom bonded to three identical para-methylphenyl rings. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring carrying a methyl group opposite the point of attachment to phosphorus, giving a symmetric 4-methylphenyl substitution pattern on all three arms. The phosphorus center adopts a pyramidal geometry with a lone pair, and the arrangement gives the molecule approximate threefold symmetry around the P atom. No ring fusion is present, and the aryl rings can rotate about their P–C bonds, so the structure is fairly flexible. Phosphorus is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small acyclic haloalkene built on a two-carbon ethylene backbone. One carbon bears a single chlorine and a hydrogen, while the other carbon carries two chlorines, so the skeleton is a trichlorinated ethene with a carbon-carbon double bond. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms other than the three chlorine substituents, which are the only functional features present. The molecule is essentially planar around the double bond, with the chlorines and the single hydrogen lying in a fixed geometric arrangement. Because it has no rotatable single bonds, it is rigid, and its substitution pattern is asymmetric. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the chlorine atoms do not accept hydrogen bonds in a meaningful way.

The molecule is built around a single phosphorus atom that is bonded to three separate saturated carbocycles: two cyclohexyl rings and one additional cyclohexyl ring attached through a carbon that is part of a ring. In other words, the central phosphorus is a trisubstituted tertiary phosphine with three cyclohexyl groups bonded directly to it. Each ring is fully saturated, containing only single carbon-carbon bonds, so there are no aromatic rings, double bonds, or ring fusions. The phosphorus center is tetrahedral-like and makes the overall shape three-fold bulky and propeller-like, with the rings able to rotate about their P-C bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the phosphorus lone pair can act as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is triethyl borate, built around a single central boron atom bonded to three identical ethoxy groups, each consisting of an oxygen atom attached to an ethyl chain. There are no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a simple, acyclic, trigonal arrangement with the boron at its center. The three ethoxy arms are chemically equivalent, giving the molecule high threefold symmetry about the boron center. Because each arm contains freely rotating single bonds, the structure is quite flexible. The oxygen atoms each carry lone pairs and can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens sit on carbon.

The molecule is an acyclic polyether-diol built from a linear chain of carbon and oxygen atoms, with no rings and no fused ring systems. Its backbone alternates two-carbon units with ether oxygens, and each end terminates in a primary hydroxyl group, so the scaffold is symmetric about its central ether oxygen. The chain is highly flexible because every bond in the backbone is a freely rotating single bond. Each terminal hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the three internal ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated polyamine built from an open-chain skeleton of ethylene units joined by secondary and primary amine nitrogens. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers, so its scaffold is entirely acyclic and flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds. The two terminal groups are primary amines (–NH2), and the two internal nitrogens are secondary amines (–NH–), giving a symmetrical arrangement in which the two ends mirror each other across the central nitrogen. Each nitrogen carries lone pairs and N–H bonds, so every nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, with the terminal amines offering the most accessible hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is triethylsilane, built around a single tetrahedral silicon atom bearing one hydrogen and three ethyl groups. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no conventional functional groups beyond the silicon-hydrogen bond.
