The three ethyl chains are identical, giving the molecule approximate threefold rotational symmetry around the Si–H axis. Because all the bonds are single and the chains can freely rotate, the structure is highly flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, since the Si–H hydrogen is not an acidic donor, and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, since there are no lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms.

The molecule is built around a single sulfur atom that is bonded to an amino group, two oxygen atoms in sulfonyl (S=O) double bonds, and a trifluoromethyl group, making it a primary sulfonamide. There are no rings, so the scaffold is acyclic and essentially a compact tetrahedral-like arrangement centered on sulfur. The three fluorine atoms on the carbon attached to sulfur create a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent, and the molecule is small and conformationally rigid, with free rotation only about the S–C and S–N bonds. The NH2 group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and possesses a local three-fold symmetry around the C–S axis from the CF3 group.

The molecule is a symmetric acid anhydride built around a central oxygen atom bridging two sulfonyl groups, with no rings present, so the skeleton is entirely acyclic and flexible about its S–O bonds. Each sulfur atom is tetrahedrally coordinated to two terminal oxygen atoms and a trifluoromethyl group, which places the three fluorine-bearing carbons at the ends of the chain. The two halves are mirror-related through the central oxygen, giving the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis passing through that bridging oxygen. Because the sulfonyl oxygens carry no hydrogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but its four terminal sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the fluorine atoms provide weak additional acceptor character.

The molecule is built around a single central boron atom bonded to three oxygen atoms, each of which connects to an isopropyl group, giving a trialkyl borate-type scaffold. There are no rings and no fused ring systems, so the framework is entirely acyclic. The functional groups are three borate ester linkages (B–O–C), each carrying a branched two-carbon-terminated isopropyl unit, and the three arms are identical, giving the molecule a threefold symmetric arrangement about the boron center. The chain segments are flexible, allowing free rotation about the C–O and O–C bonds, while the trigonal boron center keeps the core planar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since it contains no O–H or N–H groups, but its three oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents. Two of them are methyl ester groups (–C(=O)OCH3) and one further ester group is also a methyl ester, so the molecule is a trimethyl ester of a benzene tricarboxylic acid, with the three ester carbonyls attached at ring positions 1, 2, and 4 (a 1,2,4-substitution pattern). There are no fused rings, and the aromatic core is a single six-membered ring. The arrangement of substituents is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry across the whole structure. The ester linkages allow some rotational freedom, but the aromatic ring keeps the core fairly rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on carbon, and it has six oxygen atoms in the carbonyl and ether positions that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is trimethyl borate, built around a single central boron atom bonded to three oxygen atoms, each of which is in turn bonded to a methyl group. There are no rings and no fused ring systems, so the scaffold is a compact, acyclic, trigonal arrangement with the boron at the center. The functional groups are three borate ester linkages, B–O–C, arranged symmetrically around the boron, giving the molecule approximate threefold symmetry about the central atom. Its three C–O–B linkages and the single-bond connections allow rotation about the bonds, so the molecule is fairly flexible. Because the oxygen atoms carry lone pairs but no hydrogen is bonded to any heteroatom, the molecule can accept hydrogen bonds at its oxygens but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is built around a single central phosphorus atom and has no rings, so it is acyclic and entirely flexible. The phosphorus is bonded to three oxygen atoms, and each of those oxygens carries a methyl group, giving a trimethyl phosphite-type scaffold with a trivalent phosphorus center and three identical ester-like P–O–CH3 arms. Because the three arms are equivalent, the molecule has high local symmetry around the phosphorus, and its conformations can interconvert freely about the P–O and O–C bonds. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks any N–H or O–H groups, but its three oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short acyclic chain built on a pivaloyl-type scaffold: a tert-butyl group, with three methyl groups attached to one quaternary carbon, is bonded to a carbonyl carbon. That ketone is followed by a methylene unit bearing a terminal nitrile group. The structure contains no rings and no ring fusion, so it is entirely flexible apart from the rotation about its single bonds. The tert-butyl group gives local three-fold symmetry, while the carbonyl and nitrile functions break overall symmetry. The ketone oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen provides a second acceptor site, with no hydrogen-bond donor groups present.

The molecule is built on a single saturated five-membered ring containing four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, which places it in the oxolane (tetrahydrofuran) family. There are no additional rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents on the carbon framework, so the scaffold is the bare ring itself. The ring oxygen is an ether linkage, which can accept hydrogen bonds but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the molecule contains no other functional groups. Because the ring is fully saturated, it adopts a puckered, flexible conformation, and the unsubstituted skeleton possesses a high degree of symmetry about the oxygen atom.

The molecule has a single phosphorus atom at its center, bonded to three carbon-containing groups: two methyl groups and a tert-butyl-like arrangement is not present here, so the scaffold is a simple tetrahedral-type phosphorus core bearing two methyl substituents and a third carbon substituent through a phosphorus-carbon bond. A phosphoryl-type double bond to oxygen sits on the phosphorus, making it a P=O functional group that acts as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor at the oxygen. The molecule contains no ring systems, so it is acyclic and small, with rotation possible around the single bonds to the methyl groups. Its overall arrangement is fairly compact and lacks any hydrogen-bond donor sites, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The structure has approximate three-fold local symmetry around the phosphorus center, with the two methyl groups arranged in a similar way.

This molecule is a trialkyl phosphate ester: a central phosphorus atom doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to three oxygen atoms, each of which connects to an unbranched four-carbon n-butyl chain. The phosphorus center is tetrahedral in its bonding pattern, and the three butyl arms radiate from it, giving a flexible, acyclic scaffold with no ring systems or fused rings. The P=O oxygen is the sole strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ester oxygens provide weaker acceptor capability and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the three identical arms are attached at one center, the molecule has approximate threefold symmetry around the P–O axis, and the many rotatable single bonds make it conformationally flexible.

This molecule is built around a single phosphorus atom bonded to three identical n-butoxy chains, giving it a central P–O scaffold with no rings. Each arm is an unbranched four-carbon alkyl chain attached through an oxygen atom, so the structure is fully acyclic and possesses no ring fusion. The phosphorus center carries one hydrogen and is formally a P(III) species with three ether-type oxygens, and the molecule contains no carbonyl or other polar functional groups beyond these phosphite-type linkages. The three butyl arms are arranged symmetrically around the phosphorus, so the molecule has approximate threefold symmetry at the core. Its flexible alkyl chains allow considerable conformational freedom, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites on heteroatoms, with only the oxygen atoms able to act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a fully aromatic polycyclic hydrocarbon built from five fused benzene-type rings arranged around a central core. Each ring shares an edge with its neighbors, producing a compact, planar, rigid framework with no sp3 carbons and no rotatable bonds. The skeleton contains only carbon and hydrogen, so it carries no functional groups, heteroatoms, or substituents beyond the ring hydrogens. Its fused arrangement gives it a degree of symmetry, with the two outer benzo rings related by an approximate mirror-like pattern across the central ring system. Because it has no N–H or O–H groups and no lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a central sp3-hybridized carbon bearing three phenyl rings, giving a triphenylmethyl (trityl) scaffold with one additional hydrogen on that central carbon. Each of the three benzene rings is an unsubstituted six-membered aromatic ring, and no ring fusion is present, so the rings are attached independently to the single shared carbon. The structure has no heteroatoms or functional groups such as hydroxyl, carbonyl, or amine groups. Because the central carbon is tetrahedral, the three rings are arranged propeller-fashion around it, which gives an overall three-fold-like pseudo-symmetry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since its only C–H bonds are non-polar, and its propeller-shaped framework is relatively rigid around the central carbon while the phenyl rings can rotate.

This molecule is triphenylphosphine sulfide, built around a single tetrahedral phosphorus center bonded to three phenyl rings and one sulfur atom joined by a double bond. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to phosphorus through one carbon, with no additional functional groups on the aromatic rings. The three rings are arranged around the phosphorus in a propeller-like fashion, giving the molecule approximate threefold symmetry about the P=S axis. The P=S group is the only polar functional unit, with sulfur serving as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and no hydrogen-bond donor sites present. The structure is fairly rigid at the core, though the phenyl rings can rotate about their P–C bonds.

The molecule is a triarylphosphine: a single phosphorus atom bonded to three separate benzene rings, each carrying one fluorine atom at the meta position relative to the phosphorus. The aromatic rings are not fused to one another; they are connected only through the central trivalent phosphorus, which gives the structure a propeller-like, three-bladed shape. Each ring is substituted in a 1,3 pattern, so the fluorines sit symmetrically on the outer edges of their rings. The overall framework has approximate threefold symmetry around the phosphorus center. The phosphorus lone pair is the only site capable of accepting a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement is moderately flexible about the P–C bonds but is otherwise rigid within each aromatic ring.

The molecule is built on a single phosphorus atom that is bonded to three separate para-chlorophenyl rings, giving a triarylphosphine scaffold. Each benzene ring is fused to nothing else and carries one chlorine atom at the position opposite the phosphorus attachment, so the substitution pattern is identical on all three arms. The three aryl groups are arranged around the central phosphorus in a propeller-like geometry, and the molecule has an approximate threefold symmetry axis through the phosphorus. The phosphorus center has a lone pair and no hydrogen atoms, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor sites are the lone pair on phosphorus and the chlorine atoms, which are weak.

This molecule is built around a single phosphorus atom bonded to three identical tert-butyl groups, each consisting of a central quaternary carbon carrying three methyl substituents. The phosphorus center is trivalent, carrying a lone pair in addition to its three carbon bonds, and there are no rings or ring fusions in the structure. The overall framework is a compact, highly branched aliphatic scaffold with no aromatic character and no heteroatoms besides the phosphorus. Its three-fold symmetry about the P–C axis gives it a fairly rigid, bulky, cone-like shape, with the methyl groups sterically crowding the phosphorus. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor site is the phosphorus lone pair.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic tropane-type scaffold: a seven-membered-plus-bridge framework in which a nitrogen atom bridges two carbons of a cyclohexane-like ring, creating a rigid, bridged bicyclic system. The nitrogen carries a methyl substituent, making it a tertiary amine that can accept a hydrogen bond but cannot donate one. A ketone group sits on one of the ring carbons adjacent to the bridgehead, serving as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Two stereogenic bridgehead carbons define a fixed three-dimensional geometry, so the framework is conformationally constrained with little flexibility. Overall, the molecule has limited symmetry because the ketone breaks the mirror relationship of the bridged core.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic aldehyde, with no rings, aromatic systems, or ring fusion present. Its skeleton is an unbranched chain of eleven carbon atoms, with the terminal carbon bearing a carbonyl group, so the aldehyde functional group sits at one end of the chain and no substitution occurs elsewhere along it. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the trivial one, since the aldehyde end differs chemically from the alkyl end. The long saturated chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through rotation about its single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability because it contains no O-H or N-H groups.

The molecule is built on a fused four-ring steroid scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, arranged in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene pattern with all rings saturated and fused in a rigid, mostly trans configuration. A carboxylic acid is attached through a short saturated chain at the end of one side group, providing a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor pair. Two secondary hydroxyl groups sit on the ring framework, each able to both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and two angular methyl groups project from the ring junctions. The overall shape is rigid and lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, because the substituents are placed asymmetrically around the stereogenic centers.

This molecule is a simple straight-chain aliphatic nitrile, consisting of a five-carbon saturated alkyl chain terminated by a cyano group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no branching, so the scaffold is a linear, fully flexible carbon backbone. The only functional group is the carbon-nitrogen triple bond at one terminus, which makes the nitrogen a hydrogen-bond acceptor while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is unsymmetrical because the alkyl end differs from the nitrile end, and its rotatable single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility along the chain.

This molecule is a simple aryl ketone built from a benzene ring bearing a single acyl substituent. The aromatic ring is a monosubstituted six-membered carbon ring with delocalized pi electrons and no fused rings. Attached to one ring carbon is a carbonyl group whose other side carries an unbranched five-carbon chain, giving a flexible alkyl tail with several rotatable single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall structure lacks symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the phenyl ring, and it combines a rigid aromatic region with a flexible aliphatic chain.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its aromatic scaffold, with no fused ring systems. The ring carries three substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl group) and a hydroxyl group that sit adjacent to each other, along with an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, with one hydrogen) positioned across the ring from the hydroxyl. Because the aldehyde and hydroxyl are para to one another, the substitution pattern is 1,2,4, and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and aldehyde groups have limited rotational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the oxygen atoms of the methoxy and carbonyl groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a short, unbranched four-carbon chain built on a carboxylic acid scaffold, with no rings present. A terminal carbon-carbon double bond sits at one end of the chain, giving the molecule an alkenyl group, while the other end is a carboxylic acid functional group (-COOH). The carboxyl group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry, and its chain is fairly flexible, with rotation possible around its single bonds.

The molecule is built around a diaryl sulfone core, with two benzene rings joined through a central sulfur atom bearing two oxygen atoms. Each ring is para-substituted, so the two substituents on each ring sit on opposite sides, giving the molecule an approximately mirror-symmetric, linear shape. One ring carries a free primary amino group, while the other carries a secondary amine linked to a glycine-type chain ending in a carboxylic acid. The sulfone and the carboxylic acid are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two nitrogen-bound hydrogens plus the acid hydrogen act as hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic rings make the framework fairly rigid, while the CH2-C(=O)OH tail adds some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is an acyclic amino acid derivative built on a short linear carbon chain with no rings. The alpha carbon bears an acetamido group (an N-acetyl amide attached to the nitrogen), a carboxylic acid group at one end, and a side chain that terminates in a primary carboxamide. Because the molecule contains several amide and acid functionalities arranged along a flexible, freely rotating backbone, it has no ring fusion and no meaningful internal symmetry. The acid, the two amide N-H groups, and the primary amide NH2 provide multiple hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of the acid and amides serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The indole nitrogen carries a 4-chlorobenzoyl group, an aryl ketone attached through a carbonyl, and the benzo portion bears a methoxy group para to the fused ring junction on one side. The C3 position of the indole carries a methyl group and the C2 position is bonded to an acetic acid ester linkage, forming a glycolic-acid-derived ester terminating in a free carboxylic acid. The aromatic systems and the amide-like N-acyl linkage make the core fairly rigid, while the ester side chain adds flexibility. The carboxylic acid OH and ester carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the methoxy oxygen and the aryl chloride offer weaker acceptor or lipophilic character. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its unsymmetrical substitution pattern.

This molecule is acyclovir, but I must describe only its structure without naming it. It is built on a fused bicyclic purine-type scaffold, with a six-membered pyrimidinone ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring. The six-membered ring carries an amino group at one position and a carbonyl with an adjacent ring NH, giving a lactam-like arrangement. The five-membered ring bears a flexible acyclic side chain attached through a nitrogen, consisting of a CH2–O–CH2–CH2–OH unit that adds rotational freedom. The fused aromatic core is essentially planar and rigid, whereas the side chain is flexible. Overall the molecule offers several hydrogen-bond donors (the amino group, the ring NH, and the terminal hydroxyl) and multiple acceptors (ring nitrogens, the carbonyl oxygen, and the ether and hydroxyl oxygens). It lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on an imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine bicyclic scaffold, a fused five-membered imidazole ring sharing an edge with a six-membered pyridine ring. A para-chlorophenyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the bridgehead nitrogen of the imidazole, and a chlorine atom sits on the pyridine portion of the fused core. The fused aromatic system is largely planar and rigid, while the attached methylene linker to a tertiary amide gives the molecule some conformational flexibility. That amide bears two symmetric n-propyl chains on its nitrogen, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as the main hydrogen-bond acceptor, since the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a uracil-type pyrimidine-2,4-dione core, a six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms and two carbonyl groups. One ring nitrogen carries a methyl group and the other carries a 2-methylallyl substituent, which contains a terminal carbon-carbon double bond. The ring also bears a primary amino group on the carbon adjacent to one of the nitrogens, giving it an amino substitution pattern. The fused-free, single heterocyclic ring makes the scaffold fairly rigid, while the alkenyl side chain adds some flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens and the amino group provide hydrogen-bond acceptor and donor capability, respectively.

The molecule is built on a purine-type bicyclic scaffold: a pyrimidine ring fused to an imidazole ring, with an amino group on the six-membered ring. The amino substituent sits at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogens, making it a classic adenine-like arrangement. The imidazole nitrogen is alkylated by a benzyl group, which carries a chlorine atom and a fluorine atom on adjacent positions of the phenyl ring, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the benzyl linker provides some rotational flexibility. The amino group and the unsubstituted ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the halogens contribute only weak polar character.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring. One side carries an aryl ether linked through a three-carbon chain bearing a secondary alcohol and an isopropylamino group, which together form an amino-alcohol side chain. The other side carries a acetamide unit, a CH2 attached to a primary carboxamide, giving the ring a symmetrical 1,4 substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the saturated chain between the ether oxygen and the secondary amine provides rotational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donors include the hydroxyl group, the secondary amine N-H, and the two primary amide N-H protons. Acceptors include the ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, the amide carbonyl oxygen, and the basic nitrogen.

This molecule is built on a bicyclic tropane scaffold, a nitrogen-bridged bicycle in which a piperidine-type ring and a pyrrolidine-type ring share a carbon-nitrogen bridge, giving a rigid, cage-like framework. The bridgehead nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but not a donor. A secondary alcohol on the six-membered ring forms an ester with a 2-hydroxymethyl-2-phenylacetic acid unit, so the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen serve as acceptors. The free primary hydroxyl group is the molecule's only hydrogen-bond donor site. The phenyl ring is attached at a single stereocenter, which breaks overall symmetry, while the rigid bicyclic core limits conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen, which carries an n-butyl chain on that nitrogen. Attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen is a carboxamide group, where the carbonyl is bonded to an aniline-type nitrogen. That aromatic ring is a benzene bearing two methyl groups on the positions flanking the amide attachment, creating a 2,6-dimethyl substitution pattern. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the piperidine stereocenter and the N-butyl chain break any mirror plane. The amide bond is conformationally restricted, while the butyl chain and the piperidine ring remain flexible. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and the tertiary piperidine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, two benzene rings fused along a shared edge, which makes it a flat, rigid aromatic system. A carbamate group, with a nitrogen bearing one methyl substituent and a carbonyl bonded to an ether oxygen, is attached at the 1-position of the naphthalene ring, giving a monosubstituted pattern with no symmetry axis. The carbamate contributes one N-H hydrogen-bond donor and two oxygen acceptors, the carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygen. The aromatic core is largely hydrophobic and offers no additional donors, while the carbamate linker provides a modest degree of rotational flexibility around its C-O and C-N bonds.

This molecule is an acyclic, achiral diester-like structure built around a quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group, a propyl chain, and two CH2 arms. Each arm terminates in a carbamate group: one is a primary carbamate (O-C(=O)-NH2) and the other is an N-isopropyl carbamate (O-C(=O)-NH-CH(CH3)2). There are no rings, so the scaffold is fully flexible, with many rotatable bonds along the alkyl chain and the carbamate linkers. The two carbamate units supply hydrogen-bond donors through their N-H groups and hydrogen-bond acceptors through their carbonyl and ether oxygens. The substitution pattern is asymmetric because the two carbamate termini differ in their nitrogen substituents, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry element.

This molecule is built on a benzoxazinone scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered heterocycle containing both a nitrogen and an oxygen atom. The heterocycle includes a cyclic carbamate, where a carbonyl sits between the ring oxygen and the nitrogen, and the nitrogen also carries a CH2 bridge connected to the benzene ring. Attached to the ring nitrogen is an exocyclic acetamide side chain, a CH2 linked to a primary amide group. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, while the acetamide side chain adds rotational flexibility. The primary amide offers both hydrogen-bond donor sites from its NH2 group and acceptor capability from its carbonyl oxygen, and the ring carbonyl and ring oxygen provide further acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a single sp3 carbon bearing a tertiary alcohol, two aryl groups, and a 2-(dimethylamino)ethyl side chain, so it is a flexible, non-fused scaffold rather than a fused polycycle. One phenyl ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries a chlorine atom at the position ortho to the attachment point, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aliphatic chain contains a tertiary amine with two N-methyl groups, which acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but cannot donate. The hydroxyl group on the quaternary carbon serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Overall, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis and has considerable conformational freedom along its rotatable bonds.

The molecule is built on a quinolone scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridone ring that carries a ketone at one position and a carboxylic acid on the adjacent carbon of the five-membered-side pyridine ring. The nitrogen of that pyridone ring bears a cyclopropyl group, and the benzene portion carries a fluorine atom and a piperazine ring attached through a nitrogen. The piperazine contributes a secondary amine that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carboxylic acid and ketone oxygens serve as additional acceptors and the acid as a donor. The fused aromatic core is essentially planar and rigid, whereas the piperazine ring and cyclopropyl group add modest conformational flexibility or steric bulk. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are distributed asymmetrically around the bicyclic framework.

This molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing a methoxy group, a primary amino group, and a chlorine atom, with a carboxamide linking it to a piperidine ring. The amide nitrogen is attached to the piperidine at the 4-position, and the piperidine nitrogen carries a benzyl group, so the molecule has two separate aromatic rings joined through a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle. The substitution pattern on the first benzene ring is crowded, with the amide, amino, chloro, and methoxy groups arranged around it in a non-symmetric fashion. The piperidine and amide linkage provide some conformational flexibility, while the two aromatic rings remain rigid. The amide N-H and the primary amino group act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide carbonyl oxygen, the methoxy oxygen, and the tertiary piperidine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring. A methoxy group sits on the benzenoid ring, and a 4-chlorobenzoyl ketone is attached at the adjacent carbon of the pyrrole ring, with a methyl group on the neighboring position. The indole nitrogen carries an N-linked acetic acid side chain, which terminates in a carboxylic acid. The fused aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the side chains give some conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, and the ketone carbonyl and methoxy oxygen act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon propanolamine backbone, with a secondary amine bearing a tert-butyl group on one end and an aryl ether on the other. A hydroxyl group sits on the central carbon of the chain, making it a β-amino alcohol. The aromatic ring is a benzene ring linked through its oxygen, and it carries two chlorine atoms at the 2 and 5 positions relative to the ether oxygen, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The aryl ring is planar and rigid, while the aliphatic chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the two chlorines are inequivalent and the chiral center bearing the hydroxyl group is unbalanced. The hydroxyl and secondary amine groups each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ether oxygen serves only as an acceptor.

This molecule is built from a 2,3-dimethylphenyl ring linked through a methylene bridge to the 4-position of an imidazole ring. The benzene ring carries two adjacent methyl groups, which together with the single attachment point give it a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The imidazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogens, one of which bears a hydrogen and can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited internal flexibility, since the methylene linker is the sole rotatable connection between two otherwise planar aromatic rings. The overall shape is largely asymmetric because the methyl groups sit on one side of the benzene ring.

This molecule is built around a 2,4-diaminopyrimidine core, a six-membered aromatic ring with two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship and amino groups on the carbons flanking one of them. A single methylene carbon links the pyrimidine ring at its 5-position to a 3,4-dimethoxyphenyl ring, so the two aromatic systems are not fused but joined by a flexible one-atom bridge. The benzene ring carries two adjacent methoxy ether groups, which add oxygen acceptors and conformational freedom around the aryl-oxygen bonds. The overall shape is largely planar within each ring, with some rotational flexibility at the methylene linker. Hydrogen-bond donation comes from the two primary amino groups on the pyrimidine, while the ring nitrogens and methoxy oxygens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is an amide built from a phenylacetic acid unit linked to a 2-aminopyridine. A para-biphenyl group, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single bond, sits at one end, connected through a CH2 spacer to the carbonyl carbon. The amide nitrogen bears a pyridine ring attached at its 2-position, which places the ring nitrogen adjacent to the amide linkage. The molecule is largely planar and aromatic, with the single CH2 and amide bonds providing modest rotational flexibility. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene core that carries three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern: a methoxyacetamide group, a phenylthio (diaryl sulfide) group, and a nitrogen-linked carbamoyl guanidine unit. The phenylthio group attaches a second unmonosubstituted benzene ring through a flexible sulfur bridge, so the molecule has no internal symmetry and lacks a fused ring system. The central guanidine-type carbon bears two methyl carbamate (N-C(=O)OCH3) arms, and the amide and carbamate carbonyls provide several hydrogen-bond acceptors. The amide and guanidine N-H groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur-linked rotatable bonds give the overall structure considerable conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a para-substituted benzene ring bearing a methylsulfonyl group, which is a sulfone attached to a methyl group and two oxygens. The opposite side of the ring carries a side chain containing a secondary alcohol, a carbon bearing a fluoromethyl group, and an amide nitrogen connected to a dichloroacetyl group. The amide carbonyl and the sulfone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl and amide N–H groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has two stereocenters in the side chain and is otherwise flexible along its acyclic linker, with only the benzene ring contributing rigidity.

This molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The ring bears three substituents: an ethyl carbamate group (an NH linked to a C=O bearing an O-ethyl ester) on one carbon, a primary amino group on the adjacent carbon, and a secondary amine on the carbon across from the ring nitrogen. That secondary amine carries a 4-fluorobenzyl group, a benzene ring with a fluorine atom para to the CH2 linker. The scaffold is therefore a fused-free, linear-to-branched chain of aromatic rings connected by flexible single bonds, giving moderate conformational freedom around the benzylic and carbamate linkages. Several hydrogen-bond donors are present (the carbamate NH, the amino NH2, and the secondary amine NH), while the carbonyl oxygen, ester oxygen, pyridine nitrogen, and fluorine atom serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one core, a seven-membered diazepine ring fused to a benzene ring. The diazepine contains a lactam carbonyl, an imine (C=N) nitrogen, and a tertiary amide-type nitrogen bearing a cyclopropylmethyl substituent. The fused benzene ring carries a chlorine atom, and the pendant phenyl ring attached to the imine carbon carries a single fluorine atom at the ortho position. The seven-membered ring is non-planar and fairly flexible, while the fused aromatic systems are rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogens are fully substituted or doubly bonded, but the carbonyl oxygen and the imine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a 5-methylisoxazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, which carries a carboxamide at the 3-position. This amide links through a flexible two-carbon ethylene chain to a para-disubstituted benzene ring, giving a linear, elongated arrangement. The benzene ring bears a sulfonylurea group, in which a sulfonyl bridge connects to a urea unit whose terminal nitrogen is part of a saturated azepane (seven-membered nitrogen ring). The aromatic rings and the amide and sulfonylurea linkages are relatively rigid, while the ethylene linker and the azepane ring add conformational flexibility. Several N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl and sulfonyl oxygens and the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a six-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle that bears an N-methyl group on the ring nitrogen. The fourth carbon of this ring is quaternary, carrying both a phenyl group and a propanoyl (ethyl ketone) substituent, so the ring is not fused to any other ring system. The aromatic ring is a benzene bearing a single hydroxyl group at the meta position relative to the point of attachment, making it a phenolic moiety. The ketone carbonyl provides a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the phenolic OH acts as both a donor and an acceptor, and the tertiary amine nitrogen serves as a basic hydrogen-bond acceptor. The scaffold is largely sp3-rich and somewhat flexible, with the ethyl ketone chain and the piperidine ring able to adopt multiple conformations, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the meta-substituted phenol.

The molecule is built around a saturated five-membered thiazolidine ring, which contains one sulfur and one nitrogen atom, bearing a carboxylic acid on the carbon next to nitrogen. A two-carbon chain attached at the adjacent ring carbon links through a thioether sulfur to an ethyl ester of acetic acid. The ring nitrogen is a secondary amine that can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carboxylic acid contributes a donor and two acceptor oxygens. The ester carbonyl adds further acceptor capacity, and the thioether sulfur offers weak acceptor character. The molecule has no symmetry, is fairly flexible owing to its acyclic chains, and has only one ring system.

This molecule is built around a central sp3 carbon bearing a hydrogen, two para-cyanophenyl rings, and a 1,2,4-triazol-1-yl group, giving a diarylmethyl-type scaffold. Each benzene ring is substituted at the para position with a nitrile (C≡N) group, which acts as a strong electron-withdrawing feature and a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The 1,2,4-triazole is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle whose ring nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds, and it is attached through a single nitrogen to the central carbon. The two aryl groups are related by a near mirror symmetry through the central carbon, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its rotatable bonds around the central carbon give it moderate conformational flexibility, with the aromatic rings relatively rigid.

This molecule is a steroid-type polycyclic framework built from four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene arrangement. Its ring system is largely fused and rigid, with several quaternary and tertiary stereocenters locking the three-dimensional shape. The rings carry an exocyclic methylene group, a ring alkene conjugated with a cross-ring enone (a cyclohexenone with a carbonyl), a methyl-substituted double bond, and two angular methyl groups. A ketone-bearing acetyl side chain and an acetate ester are attached at a quaternary carbon. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its carbonyl and ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The overall scaffold is asymmetric because of its substitution pattern.

The molecule is built around a two-carbon chain: a primary carboxamide (NC(=O)) bonded to a methylene that connects to a sulfoxide sulfur. That sulfur is attached to a single tetrahedral carbon bearing two phenyl rings, giving a benzhydryl group. The two benzene rings are separate, unfused, and carry no ring substituents, so the molecule has no ring fusion and a relatively open, flexible framework. The sulfoxide oxygen and the amide carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amide NH2 provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites. The benzhydryl carbon is a stereocenter, so the molecule is chiral, and the two phenyl groups are not symmetry-equivalent in a rigid arrangement.

This molecule is a benzodiazepine-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a seven-membered diazepine ring containing two nitrogen atoms. The fused benzene ring carries a chlorine substituent at a position para to the ring-fusion nitrogen, and the imine carbon bears an unsubstituted phenyl group. The seven-membered ring contains an amide-type carbonyl adjacent to an NH, and a hydroxyl-bearing sp3 carbon sits between that amide and the imine nitrogen, making the ring partially saturated and non-planar. Hydrogen-bond donors include the amide NH and the hydroxyl OH, while the carbonyl oxygen, the imine nitrogen, and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built around a phenothiazine tricycle, in which two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom, and the chlorine sits on one of the benzo rings at a position para to the sulfur-bearing carbon. The ring nitrogen of this tricycle bears a three-carbon propyl linker that connects to a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring with two nitrogens opposite each other. The distal piperazine nitrogen carries a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group. The fused tricyclic core is largely planar and rigid, whereas the propyl linker and hydroxyethyl arm are flexible. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric chloro substitution. The terminal hydroxyl is the only hydrogen-bond donor, while the two piperazine nitrogens, the phenothiazine nitrogen, the sulfur, and the hydroxyl oxygen can act as acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing one ring nitrogen, forming a piperidine-2,4-dione-type scaffold. The ring carbon at position 3 bears two ethyl groups, making it a quaternary carbon that is the only stereocenter-free point of substitution on the ring, so the two ethyl substituents are equivalent. The ring carries two carbonyl groups, one ketone and one amide (lactam) carbonyl, with the amide carbonyl adjacent to the NH nitrogen. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two oxygen atoms of the carbonyls act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is non-aromatic and fairly flexible, with the two ethyl chains providing additional conformational freedom.

This molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that bears two phenyl rings, a benzyl-type CH2 linking to a third phenyl ring, an isopropyl-like branch, and an ester oxygen connected to a propanoyl group. Its skeleton is therefore acyclic apart from the three separate, unfused benzene rings, which sit on the same central carbon and give the molecule a bulky, propeller-like shape. The ester carbonyl and ether-type oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the tertiary amine on the terminal dimethylamino group can also accept a hydrogen bond and is the only basic centre. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, since every heteroatom is fully substituted. The chain between the central carbon and the amine offers considerable rotational flexibility, whereas the three aromatic rings restrict overall conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned at the 1 and 4 locations, making it a pyrazine scaffold. A carboxamide group (a carbonyl bonded to an amino group) is attached to one of the ring carbons, adjacent to a ring nitrogen. The ring is fully planar and aromatic, and the molecule has no stereocenters and little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the amide group. The amide NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and both ring nitrogens can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the single substituent breaks the symmetry of the otherwise symmetric ring.

This molecule is built around an imidazole ring attached through a flexible two-carbon linker to a central tertiary carbon that bears an ether oxygen. That carbon connects to a 2,4-dichlorophenyl ring on one side and, through a CH2-O bridge, to a benzothiophene unit on the other. The benzothiophene is a fused bicyclic system of a thiophene ring joined to a benzene ring, carrying a chlorine on the benzo portion. The two chlorinated aromatic rings each carry chlorine substituents at ortho and para positions, giving the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern. The ether oxygen and the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered 1,3-oxazol-2-one-type heterocycle, specifically a 4,5-dihydrooxazole ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen. The ring carries a dimethylamino group on the carbon bearing the double bond to nitrogen, giving an amidine-like, electron-rich carbon. Adjacent to the ring oxygen sits a carbonyl (lactone-type) carbon, and the saturated carbon next to it bears a phenyl ring, creating a stereogenic center at that position. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and attached in a monosubstituted pattern, so the overall arrangement lacks any internal symmetry. The fused-free, compact scaffold is fairly rigid apart from rotation about the bond to the phenyl group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring oxygen, and ring nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built around a valsartan-like acyl-amino acid scaffold: a valine-derived core with a pentanoyl group on the nitrogen and an isopropyl side chain. The nitrogen is tertiary, bearing an N-benzyl group in which a para-substituted phenyl ring is linked by a single bond to a second ortho-disubstituted benzene ring, forming a biphenyl unit. A 1H-tetrazole ring, attached at the ortho position of the distal phenyl, is an acidic, aromatic five-membered heterocycle with an N-H donor and multiple nitrogen acceptors. The carboxylic acid terminus adds a further hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor oxygens. Overall the molecule has no internal symmetry, a flexible aliphatic chain, and several rotatable bonds linking its rigid aromatic blocks.

The molecule is built on a six-membered pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione (barbiturate-type) ring, a saturated heterocycle containing two ring nitrogens flanked by three carbonyl groups. The single quaternary carbon at position 5 carries two alkyl substituents, a vinyl (ethenyl) group and a sec-butyl chain, so the ring is not symmetric. The two ring NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the three carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is essentially rigid, with the quaternary center fixing the substituent geometry, while the alkyl and vinyl side chains retain conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a methoxy-substituted benzene ring linked through an amide to a sulfonyl group, which connects to an ortho-methyl-substituted phenyl ring. A second aromatic unit is an N-methylindole, joined to the first benzene through a methylene bridge, giving a flexible, fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system. The indole carries a carbamate substituent on its benzo ring, formed from a cyclopentyl ester. The amide N-H and the sulfonamide N-H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl and sulfonyl oxygens, the methoxy oxygen, and the carbamate oxygens act as acceptors. This molecule is built on a thiazole ring bearing a methyl group at one carbon and an azo linkage at an adjacent carbon, with the thiazole's other carbon carrying a vinyl unit. The molecule is built around a thiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing sulfur and nitrogen, which carries a methyl group on one carbon. The molecule is built around a benzothiazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. Attached at the 2-position of this thiazole is an acrylamide-type unit: a carbon bearing a primary carboxamide group, which is linked through a carbon-carbon double bond to a para-fluorophenyl ring. The molecule is built around a benzothiazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing sulfur and nitrogen. This molecule is built around a five-membered pyrazolone ring, a heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl group. This molecule is built from a para-tolyl ring (a benzene ring bearing a methyl group) connected through a hydrazone-type linkage (NH–N=C) to a five-membered pyrazolone-like heterocycle. The heterocycle contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, a ring carbonyl, and a carbon carrying a trifluoromethyl group, which is attached to the ring through a single bond. The substitution on the benzene ring is para, so the aromatic portion has a plane of symmetry through the methyl and the attachment point. Conjugation across the aryl ring, the hydrazone linkage, and the heterocycle gives the scaffold a largely planar, rigid character with few rotatable bonds. The NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolone-type ring containing two adjacent nitrogens, with a carbonyl carbon adjacent to one nitrogen. A trifluoromethyl group is attached to the ring carbon that is double-bonded to the other nitrogen, giving a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. At the remaining ring carbon, an exocyclic hydrazone linkage (C=N–NH) connects the heterocycle to a para-chlorophenyl ring, which is planar and aromatic. The conjugated system spanning the ring, hydrazone bridge, and benzene ring makes the molecule largely planar and comparatively rigid, with only limited rotational freedom about the single bonds. The NH groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a rough local planarity, since the trifluoromethyl group and the chlorophenyl ring sit at different ends of the scaffold.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a partially saturated six-membered ring is joined to an aromatic five-membered triazole-type ring through a shared nitrogen-carbon edge, giving a triazolopyrimidine-like scaffold. A nitrile group and a primary amino group are attached to adjacent carbons of the unsaturated portion of the six-membered ring, forming an enamine-type arrangement. A trifluoromethyl group sits on the carbon of the aromatic triazole ring, while a 2,6-dichlorophenyl ring hangs from the sp3 carbon at the ring junction, making the substitution pattern asymmetric. The sp3 center and the attached aryl group add three-dimensional bulk, but the fused ring system itself is fairly rigid. The amino group and the ring NH provide hydrogen-bond donor capacity, while the nitrile nitrogen and the ring nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a hydrazone built from a 2,5-dimethylphenyl ring linked through an NH-N=C unit to a five-membered pyrazolone-type ring. The aryl ring is a benzene core bearing two methyl groups para to each other on one side and the hydrazine nitrogen on the adjacent carbon, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern. The heterocycle contains a ring carbonyl (C=O) flanked by an NH and an N=C, and its carbon bearing the exocyclic double bond carries a trifluoromethyl group. The aryl-NH-N=C linkage is conjugated across the two ring systems, which keeps the framework largely planar and conformationally restricted. The molecule has one N-H donor on the hydrazine and one on the ring lactam, and several acceptor sites at the carbonyl oxygen and the imine-type nitrogens.

This molecule is built around a five-membered pyrazolone-type ring containing two adjacent nitrogens, one of which carries a carbonyl group, forming a cyclic hydrazide. The ring carries a trifluoromethyl substituent on one carbon, and an exocyclic azo-type linkage (C=N–NH) connects the adjacent ring carbon to a para-bromophenyl group, giving a hydrazone-like extended conjugated system. The benzene ring is para-disubstituted, so it has a mirror-plane symmetry axis through the bromine and the attachment point. The planar, conjugated arrangement makes the core fairly rigid, with limited rotation about the linking bonds. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the ring N–H and the hydrazone N–H, while the carbonyl oxygen and the imine-type nitrogens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a linear, two-ring aromatic framework joined by an imine (C=N) linker, giving an extended, rod-like scaffold. One end carries a ten-carbon saturated alkyl chain attached through an ether oxygen to a para-substituted benzene ring, which provides a flexible, lipophilic tail. The other end bears an ethyl ester of an acrylic acid unit (a C=C–C(=O)O–ethyl group), also at the para position of a second benzene ring. The two aryl rings are conjugated through the central imine, so the core is largely planar and rigid, while the long alkyl chain adds considerable conformational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate two-fold, pseudo-linear symmetry about its long axis. The ether and ester oxygens and the imine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built from a linear, conjugated chain of aromatic and unsaturated units. A para-tolyl ring (a benzene bearing a methyl group) is attached to a furan ring, which is in turn linked through a vinyl bridge to a ketone that connects to a second furan. The carbonyl is an enone, conjugated with both the alkene and the terminal furan, giving a flat, extended framework with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two furan oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen, while it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered cyclohexanone ring that carries a methyl group on one ring carbon and a ketone on another. Two exocyclic carbon-carbon double bonds, each linking to a para-nitrophenyl group, flank the carbonyl, creating a cross-conjugated dienone system. The two nitro groups sit at the far ends of the aryl rings, making the structure largely planar across the conjugated core. Because the scaffold is rigid with limited rotational freedom about the alkene bonds, the overall shape is relatively extended and asymmetric owing to the single methyl substituent. The ketone oxygen and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a central alkene carbon that bears two aryl groups, giving a stilbene-like, 1,1-diarylethene core. One aryl ring is a benzene ring carrying a methyl ester (a methoxycarbonyl group) ortho to the attachment point, while the other is a para-nitrophenyl ring. The alkene is further substituted by a methyl ester on the same carbon, so the scaffold has two ester groups and one nitro group. The two benzene rings are not fused and are connected only through the sp2 alkene, leaving a conjugated but fairly flexible framework. Ester carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a cyclohexene ring bearing an exocyclic-to-ring alkene linkage: a cyclohexane carbon is part of a C=C double bond that connects to a CH2 group, which in turn is attached to a phenyl ring. A carboxamide group (C(=O)NH) is attached to the adjacent ring carbon, and its nitrogen carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving an anilide. The molecule contains three separate aromatic or partly unsaturated rings joined by flexible linkers, so it is fairly conformationally flexible. Its only hydrogen-bond donor is the amide N-H, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as the hydrogen-bond acceptor, with no stereocenters or symmetry elements of note.

The molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type skeleton built around a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane core carrying gem-dimethyl and angular methyl groups. A ketone sits on the cyclohexane-derived ring, and an adjacent 1,2-dicarbonyl unit (alpha-keto ketone) is conjugated through an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond to an aromatic ring. That benzene ring bears a nitro group at the ortho position relative to the vinyl linkage, giving a non-symmetric substitution pattern. The bridged core is rigid, while the exocyclic alkene and nitro group add limited conformational freedom. Carbonyl oxygens and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a symmetric acid anhydride built from two identical α-methyl-substituted dienoyl units, each carrying a terminal phenyl ring. Each half consists of a carbonyl group bonded to a branched carbon that participates in a conjugated carbon-carbon double bond, followed by a second double bond and an unsubstituted benzene ring, giving an extended conjugated polyene system. The two acyl halves are joined through a central anhydride linkage, C(=O)–O–C(=O), which contains two carbonyl oxygen acceptors and a bridging ether-type oxygen acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its many sp2 centers and conjugated double bonds make it fairly rigid and planar along the chain, while the anhydride oxygens provide the only polar acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a tertiary dimethylaniline unit, whose para position is attached to a carbon bearing a phenyl ring and a conjugated side chain. That side chain connects to a partially saturated fused bicyclic core: a dihydroquinoline-type system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The nitrogen of that ring carries an N-nitroso group, which is the main polar, electron-withdrawing feature. The molecule has no formal symmetry, and its extended conjugated backbone and fused rings make it fairly rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the dimethylamino nitrogen, the nitroso oxygen, and the nitroso nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolone ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, with a ketone carbonyl at one ring position and an exocyclic hydrazone linkage (C=N-NH) connecting to a phenyl group. A second phenyl ring is attached directly to the N-1 nitrogen, while a para-nitrophenyl group, bearing an electron-withdrawing nitro substituent, is attached to a ring carbon. The scaffold is fully conjugated across the rings, which limits rotation and gives the structure considerable rigidity, though the N-aryl bonds remain somewhat twisted. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two phenyl groups and the nitro-substituted ring differ in their attachments. The hydrazone N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the nitro oxygens, and several ring and imine nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a propyl chain, an ethyl ester group, and two identical exocyclic alkylidene links, each leading into a camphor-derived bicyclo[2.2.1]heptan-2-one scaffold. Each bicyclic unit is a rigid, bridged system bearing a ketone and gem-dimethyl groups, and the two halves are related by symmetry, giving the molecule a near-mirror-symmetric arrangement about the central carbon. The alkene linkages conjugate with the ring ketones, forming enone units that are planar and add rigidity around the attachment points. The ester is the only oxygen-containing group besides the two carbonyls of the ketones, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic terpenoid-like skeleton containing a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane-type) unit fused to a second bridged bicyclic system, with four quaternary carbons each bearing methyl groups. It contains two ketone (C=O) groups, one on each of two cyclic systems, and a conjugated exocyclic/endocyclic double bond linking them through a short diene segment. The substitution pattern is highly branched and asymmetric, with gem-dimethyl groups and angular methyls that create a rigid, compact three-dimensional framework. The rings are largely locked in place, giving the molecule little conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two acetamido groups (N-acetyl amide linkages) at meta positions relative to each other, with additional substituents at the remaining ring positions. Its planar aromatic and vinyl segments are rigid, while the rotatable single bonds to the amide and styryl groups add some conformational flexibility. The two amide N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide carbonyl oxygens and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring bearing an acetamide group (an N-acetyl amide, CH3C(=O)NH-) on one position, with two nitro groups and two styryl (trans-CH=CH-phenyl) arms attached at the remaining positions. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents at positions para to each other relative to a shared axis, each being an ethyl acrylate-type unit: a C=C double bond conjugated to an ethyl ester carbonyl. A free primary amino group sits on the ring adjacent to one of the vinyl arms, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern on the aromatic core. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid across the central ring and its conjugated side chains, while the two terminal ethyl ester groups provide some rotational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is mixed: the amine offers two N–H donor sites, while the two ester carbonyl oxygens and the ester ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: two identical-looking α,β-unsaturated methyl ester arms (each a –CH=CH–C(=O)OCH3 group) and one primary amino group. Hydrogen-bond capability is moderate: the amino group can act as a donor through its two N–H bonds, while the two ester carbonyl oxygens and the two ester ether oxygens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring that carries two styryl-type arms joined through carbon-carbon double bonds, making a stilbene-like, extended conjugated framework. One terminal ring is a benzene bearing a primary amino group ortho to the vinyl linkage, while the other terminal end is an unsubstituted phenyl ring attached through a second vinyl bridge. The amino group provides hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring carrying three substituents. This molecule is built on a tetrahydroquinoline scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring, with the nitrogen bearing a hydrogen. Overall, it has three aromatic rings and two N–H groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen atoms serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring carrying two identical arms attached at the meta positions (1,3-substitution). The molecule is built around a central alkene, a C=C double bond, that links two aromatic rings. One side carries a benzene ring bearing a nitro group (-NO2) on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, so the substitution is ortho. The molecule has no fused ring systems and only a modest degree of symmetry, while the conjugated alkene and two aromatic rings make it fairly rigid. The nitro group and pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a meta (1,3) pattern. One substituent is an acrylic acid unit, a carboxylic acid group joined to the ring through a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond. Each carboxylic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and the two bromine atoms add halogen substituents to the vinyl portion. Overall the structure is largely flat and rigid, with limited flexibility apart from rotation around the single bonds connecting the side chains to the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents at the 1, 3, and 5 positions, giving a meta-disubstituted pattern with a third group placed symmetrically relative to them. Two of those substituents are unsaturated carboxylic acid chains: one is a propiolic (alkyne-linked) acid and the other is an acrylic (alkene-linked) acid, each ending in a carboxyl group. The remaining position bears a bromine atom on the aromatic ring. The rigid triple bond and aromatic core limit conformational freedom, while the two terminal carboxylic acid groups each provide both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered lactam ring containing an amide nitrogen and carbonyl, forming a 3,4-dihydroquinolin-2(1H)-one-type core. On the benzene ring, two side chains sit adjacent to one another: an acrylic acid group bearing a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to the ring, and an acetic acid group attached through a methylene linker. The structure contains two carboxylic acid groups and one secondary amide, so it has multiple hydrogen-bond donors (the acid hydroxyls and the amide N-H) and several acceptors (the carbonyl oxygens). The fused lactam ring is partly saturated and the acrylic side chain is conjugated, giving a moderately rigid core with some rotational freedom in the acetic acid arm.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring carrying two identical side chains at the 1 and 3 positions, a meta-disubstituted pattern. Each side chain is a vinyl group bearing a methyl ester, so the structure contains two α,β-unsaturated ester units joined to the aromatic core. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the ring, and its ester carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule offers no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring carrying two substituents at the meta positions (1,3-substitution). Each substituent is a three-carbon acrylate unit: a C=C double bond conjugated to an ester carbonyl, which is terminated by an ethyl ester group (–CH=CH–C(=O)–O–CH2CH3). The two arms are identical, giving the molecule a mirror-plane or C2-type symmetry through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the unsaturated ester arms add some conformational flexibility through their single bonds. The carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a 3-nitrophenyl ring attached directly to a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic core: a 1,2,4-triazole ring fused to a partially saturated 1,3,4-thiadiazine-type ring containing sulfur and an sp3 carbon bearing a styryl (trans-CH=CH-phenyl) side chain. The fused system is largely planar and rigid, while the styryl arm adds conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond acceptor sites include the nitro oxygens and the triazole nitrogens, and there is one N-H that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built from a three-atom backbone that links an acetyl-derived carbon to a semicarbazone unit on one end and an anilide on the other. A terminal phenyl ring, an unfused benzene with no substituents, is attached through an amide nitrogen, giving a simple monosubstituted aromatic end. The central chain contains a C=N hydrazone double bond whose geometry is locked, so the scaffold is fairly rigid, with rotation possible mainly around the single bonds to the phenyl ring and the terminal urea. Functional groups present are an amide, a hydrazone, and a urea-type carbamoyl group. The NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the imine nitrogen serve as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis.

This molecule is a flavonol built on a benzopyranone (chromone) core, with a benzene ring fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring. A phenyl ring is attached at the 2-position of the pyranone ring and carries a benzyloxy ether substituent alongside a free hydroxyl group. The benzo-fused ring carries a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group, and the pyranone carbonyl sits adjacent to a hydroxyl group on the central ring. Several hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring oxygen, and ether oxygens serve as acceptors. The fused ring system is largely planar and rigid, although the benzyl ether linkage provides some conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry.

The molecule is asymmetric, with several sp3 stereocentres and a fairly rigid ring-rich core combined with some rotational freedom at the alkenyl linker.

This molecule is a barbiturate-like pyrimidinetrione scaffold, specifically a 2-thiobarbituric acid core in which the C5 position carries an exocyclic hydrazone linkage. The six-membered heterocycle contains two ring NH groups, two carbonyl oxygens, and a thiocarbonyl sulfur at C2, giving it a dense pattern of hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The C5 carbon is double-bonded to an exocyclic nitrogen, which connects through an N–H to a phenyl ring bearing a nitro group at the meta position relative to the hydrazone attachment. The aromatic ring and the conjugated hydrazone-pyrimidine system are largely planar, which limits conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the two sides of the heterocycle are chemically distinct.

This molecule is an ethyl ester of a 2-cyano-2-(arylhydrazono)acetic acid. A linear ethyl ester group sits on one end, attached to a central carbon that carries a nitrile group and is double-bonded to a hydrazone nitrogen. The hydrazone links through an N-H bridge to a para-chlorophenyl ring, a six-membered aromatic ring bearing a single chlorine atom at the position opposite the hydrazone attachment, giving a symmetric para substitution pattern on the benzene ring. The conjugated system spanning the hydrazone, nitrile, and ester groups makes the core fairly planar and rigid, with only the ethyl tail flexible. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester carbonyl oxygen, the nitrile nitrogen, and the other hydrazone nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a chalcone-type scaffold: two aromatic rings joined by a three-carbon unit containing an α,β-unsaturated ketone. One ring is a para-hydroxyphenyl group attached to the carbonyl, bearing a hydroxyl substituent at the position opposite the ketone.
