The aromatic rings are planar and the amide linkage gives moderate conformational restriction, but the molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by an amide linker. One ring is a benzene bearing a methyl group ortho to the nitrogen attachment, so the aniline portion is a simple 2-methylphenyl unit. The amide carbonyl connects this ring to a pyrazine, a six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 arrangement, which carries a bulky tert-butyl group on the carbon across from the carboxamide attachment point. The amide N-H can donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygen and the two pyrazine nitrogens can accept them. The two aromatic systems are conjugated through the planar amide, giving a fairly rigid scaffold with limited rotational freedom apart from the bonds around the tert-butyl group and the methyl.

The molecule is built from a tetrachlorinated benzene ring fused to a dibenzofuran-like core, where a central oxygen-containing ring links the aromatic system to a second fused framework. Four chlorine atoms sit on the first benzene ring, arranged in a contiguous pattern that leaves the substitution asymmetric overall. A saturated five-membered carbocycle is fused to an unsubstituted benzene ring, and the bridging ether oxygen connects the chlorinated and non-chlorinated portions into a rigid, largely planar polycyclic scaffold. Aryl ether linkages and an alkyl ether oxygen provide hydrogen-bond acceptor capability, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused ring system confers substantial rigidity, with limited conformational flexibility beyond the saturated ring.

The molecule is a benzodioxole-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered 1,3-dioxole ring, with the two oxygens bridging across the aromatic carbons. The benzene ring carries four chlorine substituents at every remaining position, so it is fully halogenated and lacks any aromatic C–H. The acetal carbon of the dioxole ring, which sits between the two oxygens, bears a phenyl group, giving the molecule a second aromatic ring attached through a single bond. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the phenyl ring can rotate about its bond to the acetal carbon. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two ether oxygens serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, flexible chain built around a central phosphorus atom bearing a formal positive charge and an oxido group, with a methoxy substituent and a 1-aminoethyl arm attached to it. One nitrogen of this phosphorus-containing unit links to a glutamic acid-like diester backbone, where both carboxylic acids are present as ethyl esters. A hexanoyl-type linker connects the amide carbonyl to a phthalimide ring system, which is a fused benzene and five-membered dicarbonyl imide unit. The phthalimide contributes the only aromatic ring and is largely planar and rigid, while the remainder of the molecule is highly flexible. Hydrogen-bond donors are limited to the secondary amide and amine N–H groups, and acceptors are numerous, including the ester, imide, amide, and phosphoryl oxygens.

The molecule is built around an adamantane cage, a rigid tricyclic saturated hydrocarbon scaffold, to which a carboxamide is attached at a bridgehead carbon. The amide nitrogen carries a short two-carbon ethylene linker connected through an ether oxygen to a methylene and then a terminal carboxylic acid group. The adamantane core is highly rigid and bulky, while the ethylene ether chain adds conformational flexibility at the far end. The amide N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide carbonyl oxygen, ether oxygen, and carboxyl oxygens serve as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the substituent is attached at a single bridgehead position.

The molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered cyclic imide containing two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen atom. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, so the benzene portion carries no additional groups and the fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid. The imide nitrogen bears a flexible side chain made of an ether oxygen linking two two-carbon units, ending in a terminal primary alcohol. The molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric pattern along the side chain, since the chain is asymmetric with a hydroxyl at one end. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the terminal hydroxyl group can act as both a donor and an acceptor, while the two imide carbonyls and the ether oxygen serve as acceptors only.

This molecule is an ethyl ester of a cyanoacrylate-type acid, in which the alpha carbon bears both a nitrile group and an exocyclic double bond to a ring carbon. That ring carbon is part of a saturated five-membered 1,3-dithiolane ring containing two sulfur atoms separated by a two-carbon bridge, so the ring is not fused to any other system. The ester and nitrile groups are conjugated with the exocyclic alkene, which keeps the framework largely planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester tail adds some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its oxygen, nitrogen, and sulfur atoms can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central ethylene unit (a C=C double bond) that carries two nitrile-free substituents on the same carbon: one carbon bears a cyano group (C≡N) and an amide carbonyl, while the other carbon of the alkene is flanked by two thioether linkages. The amide nitrogen is part of a saturated six-membered morpholine ring, which is a flexible, chair-capable heterocycle containing both nitrogen and oxygen. Two benzyl groups are attached through sulfur atoms, each consisting of a phenyl ring connected to a CH2 unit, giving the scaffold considerable conformational flexibility. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because the two benzylthio arms are attached to different alkene carbons. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the nitrile nitrogen, amide carbonyl oxygen, and morpholine oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a fused tricyclic core: a partially saturated bicyclic ring containing a quaternary methyl-bearing carbon, a nitrogen, and a cyclohexadiene-like ring, joined to an indane-1,3-dione unit through an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond. The indanedione portion contributes a fused benzene ring and two carbonyl groups flanking the exocyclic alkene, forming a vinylogous amide-type conjugated system with the adjacent nitrogen. The ring system is largely planar in its conjugated regions while the quaternary carbon introduces a local three-dimensional kink, giving moderate rigidity overall. There is no internal symmetry. The secondary amine-type NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic system built on an oxygen-containing bridged skeleton, with a five-membered ring containing a single oxygen atom fused across a second carbocyclic ring that shares two bridgehead carbons. One ring carries a carbon-carbon double bond bearing a methyl substituent, while the other ring holds a ketone carbonyl flanked by two geminal dichloro-substituted carbons on each side. The four chlorine atoms are arranged in two gem-dichloro pairs, which sterically crowd the carbonyl and lock the framework into a rigid, cage-like shape with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the methyl-bearing alkene and the carbonyl sit on different sides of the framework. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ether oxygen and the ketone oxygen can act as acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a five-membered pyrazole ring bearing a methyl group on one carbon and a hydroxymethyl group on another, with the ring's second nitrogen attached directly to a pyridine ring at its 2-position. The pyrazole and pyridine are joined by a single N–C bond, so there is no ring fusion, and the two aromatic rings can rotate relative to each other, giving moderate flexibility at that linkage. The hydroxymethyl group is the main polar feature, offering both a hydrogen-bond donor through its OH and an acceptor at oxygen. The pyridine nitrogen and the unsubstituted pyrazole nitrogen can each serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no other donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is an aryl thioester built from two benzene rings joined through a sulfur-carbonyl linkage. One ring is an aniline-type benzene carrying a primary amino group at the position ortho to the sulfur attachment, while the other is an unsubstituted phenyl ring attached directly to the carbonyl carbon. The thioester group (S–C=O) links the two aromatic systems, giving a flexible connection that allows the rings to rotate relative to one another. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the sulfur atom contributes only weak acceptor character. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the two rings differ in substitution.

The molecule is a bridged bicyclic system built around a seven-membered oxygen-containing framework, in which a central oxygen atom links two carbon bridges to form a rigid cage-like scaffold. One of the bridges carries a ketone group, a carbonyl carbon sitting within the ring system, which serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Within the skeleton there is a single carbon-carbon double bond, a cyclic alkene that adds a point of unsaturation and some rigidity to the structure. The compound contains no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since there are no hydroxyl or amine substituents, and the oxygen atoms can only act as acceptors. Overall the framework is highly constrained, with limited conformational flexibility due to its fused and bridged ring junctions.

This molecule is built on a fused tricyclic framework: a methoxy-substituted benzene ring is fused to a five-membered carbocycle, and that five-membered ring shares a spiro-type quaternary carbon with a cyclohexane ring. The aromatic ring carries a single methoxy ether group, and the five-membered ring bears a secondary hydroxyl group adjacent to the benzylic position. A second, tertiary hydroxyl sits on the cyclohexane ring, which also carries a para-tert-butylphenyl substituent on the same carbon. Taken together, the molecule has two hydroxyl groups that can act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ether oxygen serves only as an acceptor. The fused and spiro ring junctions give the scaffold considerable rigidity, with the bulky tert-butyl group adding steric bulk at one end.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic core in which a central five-membered pyrazole-type ring, bearing an N-acetyl group on one nitrogen and a carbonyl on the adjacent carbon, is fused to a five-membered oxazole-type ring and then to a benzo-fused ring through a naphthalene-like arrangement. The acetyl group attached to a ring nitrogen introduces an amide-like carbonyl, while the ring carbonyl adds a further C=O acceptor site. Because the fused rings are largely planar and aromatic, the scaffold is rigid, with only the acetyl side chain offering conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are substituted, but the oxygen atoms and the ring nitrogen provide several hydrogen-bond acceptor positions. Overall, the substitution pattern is asymmetric, with the acetyl group and carbonyl placed on one edge of the fused system.

This molecule is built around a five-membered 1,3,4-thiadiazole-type ring fused to a triazole, giving a bicyclic heteroaromatic core in which a triazole nitrogen-bearing ring is linked through a sulfur atom to a hypervalent phosphorus center. That phosphorus carries a para-methoxyphenyl group and a sulfido substituent, creating a P=S-type polar unit. A trifluoromethyl group sits on the triazole carbon, adding a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. The scaffold is largely planar and rigid, with the aryl ring attached through a single bond to phosphorus. The methoxy oxygen and the sulfido sulfur can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the ring N–H is a possible hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built from two linked five-membered rings. One is a succinimide ring, a saturated pyrrolidine-2,5-dione bearing two carbonyl groups flanking the nitrogen. The other is a 1,3,4-thiadiazole, an aromatic ring containing one sulfur and two nitrogen atoms, which is attached through a single bond at its carbon to the imide nitrogen, so the two rings are not fused. A trifluoromethyl group sits on the opposite carbon of the thiadiazole, giving the aromatic ring a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. The succinimide carbonyl oxygens and the thiadiazole nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is fairly rigid, with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation about the single bond joining the two rings.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is joined to a five-membered, nitrogen-containing ring, giving a benzimidazoline-type core. The two nitrogen atoms sit on the five-membered ring, flanking a single spiro-linked carbon. That quaternary carbon also belongs to a cyclopentane ring, so the molecule is spirocyclic and three rings meet at one atom. Both nitrogens are secondary amine (N–H) groups, so the scaffold can act as both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, and the overall structure is relatively rigid, with the saturated spiro-cyclopentane adding some three-dimensional bulk.

The molecule is a spiro-fused polycyclic system in which a 2-amino-4H-chromene-type pyran ring is joined through a single quaternary spiro carbon to an oxindole-like unit, with a cyclohexene ring fused onto the pyran. The pyran ring carries a nitrile group on one alkene carbon and a primary amino group on the carbon bearing the ring oxygen, giving an enamine-nitrile arrangement. The lactam ring of the oxindole contains an amide carbonyl and an N-H, and it is fused to a benzene ring. Because the spiro junction holds the rings in roughly perpendicular orientations, the structure is rigid and lacks a plane of symmetry. The amino and amide N-H groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrile nitrogen, ring oxygen, amide carbonyl, and amino nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a tricyclic fused scaffold: a benzene ring joined to a pyranone (coumarin-type lactone) ring and a pyridine ring, forming a planar, largely rigid aromatic core. An ethyl ester group is attached to the pyridine portion, and a methylamino group (NH-CH3) sits on the adjacent carbon, giving the substitution pattern on one side of the ring system. The fused framework has no internal symmetry, and only the ester ethyl chain and the methyl group offer any conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is modest: the secondary amine NH acts as a donor, while the ester and lactone carbonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a coumarin scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a six-membered lactone (2-pyranone) ring, giving a planar bicyclic aromatic core. The lactone carbonyl sits on the pyranone ring, and the ring oxygen is part of the ester linkage that closes the fused system. At the 4-position of the pyranone ring, a butylamino group (a secondary amine bearing a linear four-carbon chain) is attached, so the ring is substituted on one side only. The fused aromatic framework is largely rigid and flat, while the n-butyl tail adds conformational flexibility. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a coumarin scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a six-membered α-pyrone (2H-chromen-2-one) lactone ring that contains an ene-lactone carbonyl. The bicyclic core is fully aromatic and planar, giving it a rigid framework. On the pyranone ring, a primary amino group sits adjacent to the ring fusion, and a diethylaminomethyl side chain is attached at the neighboring carbon, adding a flexible, tertiary-amine-bearing arm. The compound lacks any molecular symmetry because the two substituents are at different positions and the side chain is unsymmetrical. Hydrogen-bond capability is mixed: the primary amine provides two donor hydrogens, while the lactone carbonyl oxygen, the ring ether oxygen, and the tertiary amine nitrogen act as acceptors.

The molecule is a thieno[2,3-b]thiophene core, a fused bicyclic system of two five-membered sulfur-containing rings sharing an edge and making it flat and rigid. Two amino groups sit on the central carbons of the fused system, one on each ring, and each is flanked by a phenyl ester. Each ester carries a carbonyl attached to the thiophene carbon and an oxygen bonded to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the two arms are related by a pseudo-symmetric arrangement across the core. The amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl and ester oxygens, together with the ring sulfur atoms, serve as acceptors. The two phenyl rings can rotate about their ester linkages, adding some conformational flexibility to an otherwise planar core.

This molecule is built on a thieno[2,3-b]thiophene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system made of two five-membered sulfur-containing rings sharing a carbon-carbon bond. Each of the two thiophene rings carries an ethyl ester group, and each also bears a primary amino group on the carbon adjacent to the ester, giving a symmetric 2,5-bis(ester)-3,6-diamino substitution pattern across the fused core. The aromatic fused framework is essentially planar and rigid, with the ester and amino substituents lying close to the ring plane. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of the ester groups and the ring sulfur atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a coumarin-type scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing heterocycle, forming a flat, rigid bicyclic core. The pyranone-like ring carries a thiocarbonyl group (C=S) in place of the usual lactone carbonyl, adjacent to the ring oxygen, and an ethyl ester group sits on the carbon next to it. The ester contributes a flexible ethoxy tail attached to a planar carbonyl, while the fused aromatic system remains essentially unsubstituted on the benzene side. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, but the ester oxygens, ring oxygen, and sulfur can all act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall, the structure has little internal symmetry and is largely planar apart from the rotatable ethyl group.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl linking two benzene rings. One ring is a 1,2-dimethoxy-4-nitrophenyl unit, carrying two adjacent methoxy ether groups and a nitro group positioned ortho to the ketone on the same ring. The other ring is a meta-bromophenyl group, with a bromine atom at the 3-position relative to the carbonyl. The two aromatic rings are not fused, and the ketone bridge allows some rotational flexibility about its two single bonds, so the molecule is not fully rigid. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two rings bear different substituents. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the carbonyl, the nitro group, and the two methoxy groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl linked to two separate benzene rings, with no ring fusion present. The first ring carries two adjacent methoxy groups and, on the carbon next to the carbonyl-bearing position, a nitro group, giving a crowded, electron-rich and electron-poor substitution pattern. The second ring is a simple para-chlorophenyl group, so the overall molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The two aryl rings can rotate around the single bonds to the carbonyl, so the scaffold is moderately flexible rather than fully rigid. The carbonyl oxygen, the nitro oxygens and the two methoxy oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group linking two benzene rings. The first ring carries two adjacent methoxy groups (a 3,4-dimethoxyphenyl unit), while the second ring bears a single methyl group at the meta position relative to the carbonyl attachment. Neither ring is fused to another, so the scaffold consists of two separate aromatic rings joined through one sp2 carbonyl carbon. The rings can rotate about the two single bonds to the carbonyl, giving moderate conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two rings carry different substituents. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a 3-carbon chain bearing two acetyl (methyl ketone) groups on a central carbon that is doubly bonded to a hydrazone nitrogen. That hydrazone nitrogen is linked through a second NH to a benzene ring, which carries a single bromine atom at the position para to the hydrazine attachment, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern. The benzene ring is the only ring system, so the scaffold is a simple aryl hydrazone with no ring fusion. The two carbonyl oxygens and the hydrazone nitrogen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the N-H is a hydrogen-bond donor. The conjugated C=N and aromatic system make the core fairly rigid, though the acetyl arms retain some rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two acetyl groups are inequivalent relative to the aryl hydrazone arm.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione ring, a cyclic malonate-type diester bearing a gem-dimethyl group on the carbon between the two ring oxygens. Its C5 position carries an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond linking to a furan ring, which is substituted at the 5-position by a para-chlorophenyl group, giving a largely conjugated, extended aromatic system. The ring carbonyls act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The conjugated framework is rigid and planar, with the gem-dimethyl group providing a small amount of steric bulk above the dioxanedione ring. The chlorine atom is a single halogen substituent positioned at the far end of the pendant phenyl ring.

The molecule is built on a six-membered cyclohexane-1,3-dione-type ring bearing a gem-dimethyl group on one carbon, which gives the scaffold a non-planar, puckered character. Two carbonyl groups sit on the ring, and the carbon between them carries an exocyclic hydrazone linkage (C=N-NH) that connects to a benzene ring. That benzene ring carries a nitro group on the position adjacent to the hydrazine nitrogen, an ortho substitution pattern. Overall the structure is conjugated across the hydrazone, aryl ring, and nitro group, while the saturated ring remains somewhat flexible. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens, the nitro oxygens, and the imine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,3-dioxin-4-one ring, a cyclic acylal-type lactone bearing two methyl groups on the same sp3 carbon, which makes that position a quaternary center. Adjacent to the lactone carbonyl sits an exocyclic hydrazone linkage (C=N-NH), connecting the ring to a para-hydroxyphenyl group. The phenol ring has a single hydroxyl substituent positioned opposite the hydrazine attachment, giving a 1,4-disubstitution pattern. The core is largely planar and conjugated across the hydrazone and aryl system, with the gem-dimethyl group adding some steric bulk. Hydrogen-bond capability is present: the phenolic OH and the N-H can act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygens, ring oxygens and imine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione ring, a cyclic diester in which a gem-dimethyl group sits on the carbon between the two oxygens. At the carbon between the two carbonyls, the ring bears an exocyclic hydrazone linkage (C=N-NH) that connects to a phenyl ring. That phenyl ring carries a nitro group at the meta position relative to the hydrazine nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is 1,3 on the benzene ring. The compound has an extended conjugated system, with the aromatic ring, the hydrazone, and the dione carbonyls in near planarity, which makes the core fairly rigid, while the two methyl groups are the only flexible-looking features. The N-H of the hydrazone can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens, the ring oxygen, and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built from an alpha-amino acid backbone: a three-carbon chain bearing a carboxylic acid at one end, with the nitrogen on the central carbon capped as an acetamide. A benzyl-type CH2 links that backbone to a benzene ring that is fused to a five-membered 1,3-dioxole ring, through two adjacent aromatic carbons bearing an O-CH2-O bridge. The substitution pattern on the benzene ring is 1,3,4, with the methylenedioxy group occupying two adjacent positions. Because the chiral center and the flexible side chain allow rotation, the molecule is moderately flexible, while the fused aromatic-dioxole system is rigid and planar. Hydrogen-bond capability includes the amide N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H as donors, and the amide and carboxyl carbonyl oxygens along with the ring oxygens as acceptors.

The molecule is a tricyclic fused scaffold built from a central lactone ring flanked by a dihydro-naphthalene-like carbocycle and an aromatic benzene ring. The benzene ring carries a single methoxy substituent positioned para to the ring-fusion oxygen, giving it an asymmetric substitution pattern. A six-membered unsaturated lactone (a coumarin-type pyranone fused to the aromatic ring) contains an ester linkage, with its carbonyl oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring system carries a propyl chain and a gem-dimethyl group on the lactone carbon adjacent to the carbonyl, adding steric bulk. The fused framework is largely rigid, while the propyl side chain provides some conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core in which a 4H-pyran ring is fused to a pyridone-type ring, with a phenyl-substituted sp3 carbon bridging the two. The pyran-type ring carries a methyl ester on one alkene carbon and a primary enamine-type amino group on the adjacent alkene carbon, forming a push-pull arrangement. The pyridone ring bears a methyl group and an N-linked phenethyl chain, and its carbonyl is conjugated with the fused system. A para-methoxyphenyl group hangs off the central sp3 carbon, and the phenyl of the phenethyl chain adds a second aromatic ring. The amino group and carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the rigid fused core limits conformational freedom apart from the flexible ethylene linker.

This molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The ring carries an ethyl ester group (an ethoxycarbonyl substituent) at one carbon position, a methyl group on a second ring carbon, and a hydroxymethyl group attached to one of the ring nitrogens. Because the ring is aromatic and planar, the core is rigid, while the ethyl ester and hydroxymethyl side chains add some conformational flexibility. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen with no substituent can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl group of the hydroxymethyl substituent can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since each ring position bears a distinct substituent.

The molecule is built around a central aminal carbon (a CH bearing two nitrogen atoms) that links two benzamide units, with one of the nitrogens also attached to a phenyl ring carrying an ortho benzyloxy group. Each of the three phenyl rings is unfused and monosubstituted at the ring positions involved, so there are no fused ring systems. The compound contains two secondary amide groups, each with an N-H donor and a C=O acceptor, and a benzyl ether oxygen that serves only as a weak acceptor. A chlorine atom sits on the terminal benzyl ring at the ortho position relative to the ether linkage. The structure is rather flexible because of several rotatable single bonds around the aminal carbon and the ether linkage, and it lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is a para-substituted toluene ring bearing a thioamide group. The benzene ring carries a methyl group at one position and a thiocarbonyl carbon at the opposite position, giving a symmetric, rod-like aromatic core. The thiocarbonyl carbon is bonded to the nitrogen of a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, which adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The C=S bond acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites because the nitrogen is fully substituted and there are no N-H or O-H groups.

Parsing the SMILES: a thiophene-2-carbonyl group is attached to a bicyclic fused system. The core is a 5-membered isoxazoline ring (C=N–O) fused to a 5-membered succinimide-type ring (a pyrrolidine-2,5-dione), giving a bicyclic [3.3.0]-type scaffold with a cis-fused ring junction. The imide nitrogen carries an ortho-chlorophenyl substituent, and a thiophene ring is linked through a ketone to the isoxazoline C=N carbon. The molecule has no symmetry, and the fused bicycle is rigid while the aryl and thienyl groups can rotate. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N–H or O–H groups, while the two imide carbonyls, the ketone oxygen, and the ring oxygen and nitrogen act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a five-membered isoxazoline ring (containing N–O) fused to a five-membered succinimide-type lactam ring, giving a bicyclic scaffold with a bridgehead-like cis ring fusion at two adjacent sp3 carbons. A benzoyl ketone is attached to the C=N carbon of the isoxazoline, and the imide nitrogen carries a para-hydroxyphenyl substituent. The molecule has two carbonyls in the imide and one ketone, plus an oxime-like ether oxygen and a phenolic hydroxyl, giving hydrogen-bond donor capability through the phenol OH and acceptor capability through the multiple oxygen and nitrogen atoms. The fused core is fairly rigid, while the benzoyl and hydroxyphenyl groups add some rotational freedom.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a six-membered 1,2,3-triazine-type ring is fused to a five-membered isoxazole ring, giving a planar, fully aromatic core. A methyl group sits on the triazine carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, and a second methyl group is attached to the carbon of the isoxazole ring next to its oxygen. A phenyl ring is bonded to the triazine carbon opposite the methyl substituent, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the two methyl groups are not equivalent. Apart from the rotation of the phenyl ring, the scaffold is rigid. The ring nitrogens and the ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a five-membered pyrazoline ring fused to a succinimide-type five-membered ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a rigid, partly saturated scaffold. The pyrazoline nitrogen bears an unsubstituted phenyl ring, and the imide nitrogen carries a meta-nitrophenyl group, which contributes a strongly electron-withdrawing nitro substituent. A para-tolyl ketone is attached to the pyrazoline carbon adjacent to the C=N double bond. Two carbonyl oxygens of the imide and one ketone oxygen, together with the nitro oxygens, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The three aryl rings give the molecule an overall asymmetric, elongated shape with limited conformational flexibility around the fused core.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a pyrrolo[3,4-c]pyrazole-type framework in which a five-membered pyrazoline ring is fused to a five-membered succinimide (cyclic imide) ring. The imide nitrogen carries a para-substituted phenyl ring bearing a carboxylic acid, which gives a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site. The pyrazoline nitrogen is substituted with an unsubstituted phenyl ring, and a para-chlorobenzoyl ketone is attached to the pyrazoline carbon. Multiple carbonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fused core and the attached aromatic rings make the molecule fairly rigid, though the single bonds linking the aryl groups allow some rotation.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a five-membered pyrazoline-type ring (containing two adjacent nitrogens, one of them double-bonded to carbon) fused to a five-membered succinimide-type ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. A phenyl ring sits on the pyrazoline nitrogen, and a para-bromophenyl group sits on the imide nitrogen. A para-chlorobenzoyl ketone is attached to the carbon of the C=N unit. The two imide carbonyls and the ketone carbonyl are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one carbon-carbon bond. It carries four substituents: two methyl groups and two chloromethyl groups, one on each ring at positions adjacent to the fusion. The substitution pattern is arranged so that the two chloromethyl groups sit on opposite halves of the bicyclic core, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold relationship across its long axis. The aromatic framework is rigid and planar, while the chloromethyl groups provide some rotational freedom around their single bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatoms are the two chlorine atoms, which can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, a 3H-pyrazole-type scaffold with two adjacent nitrogens, one of which is double-bonded to a carbon in the ring. Two phenyl rings are attached: an unsubstituted phenyl group on the ring carbon that carries the C=N double bond, and an ortho-tolyl group (a benzene ring bearing a methyl substituent next to the attachment point) on the saturated sp3 carbon. The core therefore combines an aromatic-like framework with a partially saturated carbon, giving the scaffold moderate rigidity around the ring while the aryl groups can rotate about their single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two aryl substituents differ. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, and the two ring nitrogens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that bears a phenyl substituent. The fused bicyclic core is largely planar in its aromatic portion, while the saturated five-membered ring adds some puckering and conformational flexibility. A methyl ester group is attached to the saturated ring at a carbon adjacent to the fused benzene ring, and a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached at the position next to the ester-bearing carbon. The molecule has two aromatic rings and one carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, with no hydrogen-bond donor groups present. It has no internal symmetry, since the two substituents sit at different positions on the ring system, and it contains a stereocenter at the carbon bearing the ester.

The molecule is an amide built from two pieces: a phenyl ring attached to the nitrogen of an anilide, and a bicyclic indane unit on the carbonyl side. The indane core consists of a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, and the carbonyl carbon is bonded to the sp3 carbon at position 1 of that cyclopentane ring, which makes the scaffold a substituted indane-1-carboxamide. The amide linkage (C(=O)NH) is a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and an acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry beyond the local ring geometry, and the fused bicyclic core is comparatively rigid, while the single bonds to the anilide and the amide linkage allow some rotational flexibility.

The molecule is built on an indane-type scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle through a shared edge, giving a bicyclic framework with a single benzylic sp3 carbon carrying a substituent. The aromatic ring bears one methoxy group (an ether linkage, O-CH3) positioned meta to the ring-fusion carbon that attaches to the cyclopentane-type ring. At the non-aromatic position of the five-membered ring sits a carboxylic acid group, which is the dominant functional group. The fused system is largely rigid, with only modest flexibility from the carboxyl group's rotation. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methoxy and acid substituents break the mirror plane of the parent framework. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the methoxy oxygen serves as an additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle. The aromatic ring carries a methoxy group and an isopropyl group on adjacent carbons, which gives it an ortho substitution pattern. The five-membered ring is saturated apart from the fused aromatic bond, and a carboxylic acid group is attached at the carbon that sits between the ring fusion and the methylene bridge. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, while the isopropyl and carboxylic acid groups retain some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen of the methoxy group serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on an indane-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, with the saturated ring carrying a nitrile group on the carbon that bridges the aromatic ring and the methylene carbon. The benzene ring bears two adjacent substituents, a methoxy group and a methyl group, placed ortho to one another and meta to the ring-fusion carbons. The aromatic system and the fused cyclopentane together make the core fairly rigid, while the nitrile is linear and the methoxy and methyl groups can rotate freely. The molecule has no symmetry elements beyond the trivial one, because the substitution pattern on the benzene ring is unsymmetrical. Functionally, the nitrile nitrogen and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that bears a cyclopropane-like bridging pattern. Parsing the SMILES, the aromatic ring carries a methoxy group and an adjacent methyl group, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern on the benzene portion. The fused five-membered ring is saturated apart from the shared aromatic bond, and a carboxylic acid group is attached at the ring carbon adjacent to the fusion. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the methoxy oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, though the carboxylic acid substituent retains rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of its substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on adjacent and nearby positions, making it a substituted benzoic acid. A carboxylic acid group sits on one ring carbon, flanked on one side by a hydroxyl group and on the other by a methyl group, while a bromine atom occupies a position on the far side of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the carboxyl and hydroxyl groups able to engage in intramolecular hydrogen bonding with each other. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and several oxygen acceptors, while the bromine and methyl groups add steric bulk and lipophilic character.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring bearing four groups: a carboxylic acid, a methoxy group, a bromine atom, and a methyl group. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and the methoxy group sits on the carbon immediately adjacent to it, so the acid is flanked by an ortho substituent. The bromine occupies a position next to the methoxy group on the far side, while the methyl group sits para to the bromine across the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the carboxyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygen able to act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The carboxylic acid also provides a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl group. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the four substituents are all different.

The molecule is a carbamate, built from a central carbonyl bonded to an anilide nitrogen on one side and a benzylic oxygen on the other. The N-attached ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group, while the benzylic ring carries two nitro groups on adjacent-to-the-CH2 and opposite-side positions (2,6-dinitro substitution relative to the CH2 linkage), giving a non-symmetric pattern. Both aromatic rings are planar, but the carbamate and methylene linkers add rotational flexibility between them. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the carbamate ether oxygen, and the four nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three nitro groups and one bromomethyl group, giving a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The nitro groups sit at positions 1, 3 and 5 relative to one another, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis passing through the bromomethyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The three nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing, and the bromomethyl group adds a flexible CH2 linker to a bromine atom. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2Br arm can rotate. The nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic aromatic system built around a central five-membered ring that bridges a dimethyl-substituted benzene ring and a quinoxaline unit. The benzene ring carries two methyl groups positioned para to each other on one side of the fusion, while the pyrazine ring of the quinoxaline contributes two nitrogen atoms that can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The overall framework is planar and rigid, with extended conjugation across all fused rings and little rotational freedom. The two methyl groups are the only saturated substituents and are the only sp3 carbons present. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its arrangement is asymmetric because the methyl groups sit on only one side of the fused core.

The molecule is built on a quinoline-type bicyclic scaffold, in which a pyridine ring is fused to a benzene ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat, fully aromatic system. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a phenyl ring is attached at the carbon on the opposite side of the nitrogen, at the fusion-adjacent position of the pyridine ring. The two substituents are not symmetrically placed, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry in its overall shape. The fused core is rigid, but the bond linking the phenyl ring can rotate, adding modest conformational flexibility. The pyridine-type nitrogen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a spiro compound in which two benzene rings are joined through a five-membered lactone ring and a shared quaternary carbon. One aromatic ring is fused to the lactone, giving a benzofuranone-type bicyclic core, while the second benzene ring is fused onto an indane-like framework that shares the spiro center. The lactone carbonyl, an ester oxygen embedded in the ring, and the spiro carbon make up the principal functional groups. Each benzene ring carries an unsubstituted, symmetrical pattern of hydrogens, and the spiro junction imposes a rigid, three-dimensional geometry with the two halves oriented roughly perpendicular to each other. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks N-H or O-H groups, but the carbonyl oxygen and ring ester oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a fused polycyclic aromatic core in which a benzene ring is bridged to a five-membered carbocycle, giving an indane-type fused system with an additional aromatic ring fused into it. Two methyl ester groups (–C(=O)OCH3) are attached to the outer aromatic ring at adjacent positions, producing an ortho substitution pattern. The arrangement is largely planar and rigid across the fused aromatic framework, while the two ester side chains retain some rotational freedom. The molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry through its central axis. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, but the four carbonyl and ether oxygens of the esters can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a fused polycyclic scaffold containing a central six-membered ring fused to a benzene ring and a cyclobutane-like bridge, forming a rigid framework with a fused tricyclic core. Two methyl ester groups are attached to adjacent carbons of a carbon-carbon double bond within the central ring, giving a conjugated, electron-poor alkene flanked by two carbonyls. The aromatic ring carries substitution only at the fusion positions, so the arrangement is largely planar and rigid, with the methylene linkers adding limited flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the four ester oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a cyclobutene-type ring through two shared carbons, giving a benzocyclobutene core. The six-membered aromatic ring carries four methyl substituents, placed on consecutive positions around the ring, so the substitution pattern is dense and contiguous, with no hydrogens left on the aromatic carbons. The four-membered ring contains two saturated methylene groups, which add strain and rigidity to the framework. The molecule is largely planar and conformationally rigid, with only minimal flexibility from the small methylene ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms and no heteroatoms or polar functional groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two methyl groups and two trifluoroacetate ester substituents. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with the methyl and ester groups arranged in a para-related pattern across the ring, giving the molecule a centrosymmetric, two-fold symmetric scaffold. Each ester oxygen links the ring to a carbonyl bearing a trifluoromethyl group, so the trifluoromethyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing. The ester carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid, with only the ester linkages providing some conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on an indane (benzo-fused cyclopentane) scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered saturated carbocycle. The five-membered ring carries a tertiary alcohol: a methyl group and a hydroxyl group sit on the same sp3 carbon, which is adjacent to the aromatic ring fusion carbon. A chlorine atom is attached to the benzene ring at a position ortho to the fusion carbon bearing the quaternary center, giving a specific substitution pattern on the arene. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, while the saturated ring retains some puckering flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the chlorine and the aromatic system contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a five-membered lactone ring, a fully unsaturated butenolide-type scaffold containing one ring oxygen and a carbonyl carbon adjacent to it. The ring carries a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with the carbonyl, and two methyl groups sit on the alkene carbons, giving a tetrasubstituted, planar core. A hydroxyl group is attached to the carbon next to the ring oxygen, forming a hemiacetal-like arrangement. The ring is essentially rigid and flat, with no stereocenters that would introduce conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, respectively, while the ring oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge. Attached to the naphthalene core at one position is a phenyl ring, linked directly through a single bond, giving a biaryl-type arrangement. The ester functional group, an acetate group bonded through an oxygen atom, is attached to the naphthalene ring adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical. The aromatic rings are planar and rigid, though the bond between the naphthalene and phenyl rings allows some rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ester oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a saturated six-membered oxygen-containing heterocycle, which is a chroman-type (isochroman-like) framework. The heterocycle carries an acetal-like hemiacetal carbon bearing a hydroxyl group, adjacent to the ring oxygen, and a second carbon that bears a para-methoxyphenyl substituent. The aryl ring is a benzene with a methoxy ether group at the para position relative to the point of attachment, giving a simple 1,4-disubstitution pattern. Because the core contains sp3 centers and a single aryl linkage, the structure is moderately rigid overall, with some conformational freedom in the saturated ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring oxygen and methoxy oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a flexible acyclic carbon chain bearing four benzoyl groups, namely a central chain with two ketone-containing arms on each end. Parsing the SMILES, a chain of four carbons (CH2, CH, CH, CH2) is capped at each end by a ketone linked to a phenyl ring, and each internal CH carries a benzoyl (phenyl ketone) substituent, giving a tetraketone with four unfused monocyclic benzene rings. The phenyl rings are unsubstituted and each is a separate, non-fused aromatic ring, while the carbonyl groups are the only functional groups present. The chain is conformationally flexible owing to its sp3 centers and single bonds, though the aromatic rings and carbonyls add bulk and some rigidity locally. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no O-H or N-H groups, but its four carbonyl oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single sulfur atom bridging two benzylic carbons, forming a thioether (sulfide) linkage between two aromatic rings. Each aryl ring is a benzene ring carrying three methyl substituents, and the two rings are identical in substitution pattern, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry about the central sulfur. The aromatic rings are fused to nothing, so the scaffold consists of two separate monocyclic arenes linked through a flexible CH2–S–CH2 chain. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only heteroatom, the sulfur, offers weak acceptor character. The molecule is largely hydrophobic and rotationally flexible around the methylene-sulfur bonds.

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic hydrocarbon scaffold of three six-membered rings joined linearly, with the two outer rings each carrying a conjugated double bond and the central ring sharing its edges with both. It bears four methyl ester groups, two on each of the outer carbocycles, arranged in a symmetric pattern across the fused core. The molecule has an approximate two-fold or mirror symmetry through the central ring. Its fused ring system is largely planar and rigid, while the methylene linkers and the ester groups add some conformational flexibility. Carbonyl oxygens of the esters can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a tricyclic fused heteroaromatic system built around a central nitrogen that bridges two rings. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to that nitrogen on one ring, giving a simple, non-symmetric substitution pattern. The core consists of a benzene ring fused to a pyridine-like ring, which in turn is fused to a second benzene ring that carries a ring carbonyl (C=O) adjacent to the nitrogen, forming a lactam-type amide within the aromatic framework. The fused, largely planar ring system is rigid, with the methyl group as the only freely rotating feature. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic system built around a central nitrogen-containing core. A benzene ring is fused to a five-membered lactam ring that carries a carbonyl group directly bonded to the nitrogen, giving an amide-type functionality. A second benzene ring is fused to a partially saturated six-membered ring that contains a cis-configured carbon-carbon double bond, and the two halves are joined through a shared bridgehead carbon attached to the nitrogen. The overall framework is rigid and largely planar in its aromatic regions, with limited conformational freedom imposed by the multiple fused rings. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local arrangement of its aromatic rings. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because the nitrogen is fully substituted within the ring system.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic scaffold: a benzene ring is fused to a pyridone-type six-membered ring containing an amide-like carbonyl and a nitrogen, which in turn is fused to a saturated third ring bridging the nitrogen and an aromatic carbon. The benzene ring carries a single methoxy group (an aryl ether, OCH3) at one position, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern on the aromatic portion. The lactam carbonyl and the tertiary ring nitrogen are conjugated with the aromatic system, while the saturated ring adds conformational flexibility to an otherwise largely planar, rigid core. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen and another at the ether oxygen, and no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring bearing four methyl groups is joined to a partially saturated nitrogen-containing ring system. A saturated CH2 links the aromatic ring to a bridging carbon that belongs to a dihydropyridine-type ring with two conjugated C=C double bonds, and the nitrogen of that ring is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that closes a lactam-like ring onto the benzene. The four methyl substituents occupy adjacent positions on the aromatic ring, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful internal symmetry. The fused ring system is largely rigid, though the saturated CH2 provides some local flexibility. The amide carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen is tertiary.

This molecule is a fused tricyclic system built around a central six-membered ring that carries a ketone. One outer ring is a benzene-type aromatic ring bearing two methyl substituents in a meta-like arrangement, and it is fused to a second six-membered ring containing a methylene bridge. That second ring is fused to a pyridinium-type ring in which the nitrogen carries a positive charge and is directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon, which makes the ketone an acyl-substituted cationic nitrogen. The scaffold is largely planar and rigid because of the extensive aromatic fusion, with only the methylene bridge providing minor conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, but the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. It has no internal symmetry element beyond the approximate mirror plane of the planar core, because the two methyl groups are placed asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic core in which a five-membered cyclopentanone ring is fused to a benzene ring, giving an indanone-type scaffold. The aromatic ring carries two methyl ester groups (methoxycarbonyl substituents) and two methyl groups, arranged on alternating positions around the ring, which gives it a symmetric substitution pattern. The fused five-membered ring contains a ketone carbonyl and two saturated CH2 units, so it is fairly rigid while the ester side chains retain some rotational freedom. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent because there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the three carbonyl oxygens (two ester and one ketone) and two ether-type oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic carbon framework, with a benzene-like aromatic ring bearing two methyl substituents and two carbonyl groups attached to fused five-membered rings. Parsing the SMILES, the central six-membered ring is fused on opposite edges to two cyclopentanone-type rings, one bearing a ketone carbonyl in each. The aromatic core carries two methyl groups in adjacent positions, which breaks any mirror symmetry along the main axis. The ring system is largely rigid because of the fusion, with only limited flexibility. Both ketone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built from a fused polycyclic core in which a benzene ring is bridged by two additional five-membered rings. One five-membered ring is a cyclic ketone (a cyclopentanone-type ring containing a carbonyl and a methylene group), and the other is a second cyclic ketone fused across the aromatic ring, so the structure contains two carbonyl groups and a flat, rigid aromatic framework. The two rings share the benzene core in a linearly fused arrangement, giving the molecule a largely planar, rigid shape with limited conformational flexibility. Both carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The overall structure is fairly symmetric about the central aromatic ring.

This molecule is built on an indanone scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that carries a ketone. The benzene ring bears two methoxy groups (–OCH3) placed at positions that flank the ring fusion on the opposite side, giving a 1,4-dimethoxy pattern across the aromatic ring. The five-membered ring is fused to the benzene ring at two adjacent carbons, creating a rigid, nearly planar bicyclic framework. The ketone sits on the saturated carbon of the five-membered ring, adjacent to the CH2 group. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single mirror-type plane of approximate symmetry through the ketone and the ring. The carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an indanone scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocyclic ring that carries a ketone. The aromatic ring bears a methoxy group and a methyl group in a meta relationship to each other, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, with only the methylene carbon of the five-membered ring offering limited flexibility. The ketone carbonyl and the ether oxygen of the methoxy group can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small bicyclic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, forming an indanone-type scaffold. A methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) is attached to the aromatic ring, placing it on a carbon adjacent to the ring fusion and giving the benzene ring a single substitution pattern with no symmetry across the whole framework. The five-membered ring contains a ketone (carbonyl) group, which is conjugated with the fused aromatic system and makes the framework largely rigid and planar. The methoxy oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered carbocyclic ring containing a ketone, making it an indanone-type framework. The benzene ring carries a single methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) attached to a carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry. The five-membered ring is nearly planar and fully conjugated with the aromatic system, giving the bicyclic core a fairly rigid, flat geometry with little conformational flexibility. The ketone carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all its hydrogens sit on carbon atoms. The ether oxygen of the methoxy group provides a second, weaker acceptor site.

The molecule is built on an indanone scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that contains a ketone. The aromatic ring carries a single methyl substituent positioned on the benzene ring, which breaks any symmetry of the bicyclic framework. The fused five-membered ring is largely rigid and planar, with the carbonyl carbon sitting at the junction between the saturated CH2 unit and the aromatic system. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a six-membered lactone ring is fused to a benzene ring, giving a benzo-fused dihydroisochromanone (isochroman-1-one type) core. The benzene ring carries a single methoxy substituent, placed para to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the lactone carbonyl. The saturated carbon at the 3-position of the lactone ring is quaternary, bearing two methyl ester groups, so the scaffold is substituted at one stereocenter-like carbon with two identical-type ester arms. Its overall shape is largely rigid because of the fused aromatic and lactone rings, though the ester groups add some conformational freedom. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no hydrogen atoms bonded to nitrogen or oxygen. Hydrogen-bond acceptor capability is present at the carbonyl oxygens of the lactone and the two ester groups, and at the ether oxygens of the methoxy group and the lactone ring oxygen.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered lactone (cyclic ester) ring containing a ring oxygen and a carbonyl group. The quaternary carbon at the lactone's alpha position carries two methyl ester groups, giving a geminal diester arrangement. A methoxy group sits on the aromatic ring, para to the ring fusion, which breaks any symmetry in the aromatic portion. The fused ring system is fairly rigid, while the ester side chains retain some rotational freedom. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, but the three ester and lactone carbonyl oxygens and the ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a spiro-fused scaffold in which a tetramethyl-substituted benzene ring is joined through a quaternary carbon to an indane-1,3-dione unit, with the second benzene ring of the dione fused to a five-membered ring. A γ-lactone (a fused five-membered ring containing an ester oxygen and a carbonyl) bridges the aromatic ring and the spiro carbon, so the aromatic core is tetrasubstituted with four methyl groups. Two ketone carbonyls flank the spiro center on the indanedione side, and the lactone carbonyl adds a further ester functionality. The rigid, fused polycyclic framework has little conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while its three carbonyl oxygens and the ring ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic lactone built on a fused ring system: a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing heterocycle, giving an isochromanone-type scaffold. The lactone carbonyl sits on the carbon adjacent to the aromatic ring, and the ring oxygen bonds to a carbon bearing a methyl ester group. That ester, written as a methoxycarbonyl substituent, is attached at the ring carbon next to the lactone oxygen, so the substitution pattern is fixed rather than symmetric. The fused framework is fairly rigid because of the aromatic ring and the planar ester and lactone units, although the saturated CH2 and CH carbons allow some ring puckering. The molecule has no internal symmetry. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: it has no donor groups, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the two ring or ether oxygens act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzopyranone (coumarin-type) scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered lactone ring, with the saturated carbon of the lactone bearing a para-nitrophenyl group. The fused bicyclic core is largely planar and rigid, while the nitrophenyl substituent can rotate about its single bond to the lactone ring. A methoxy group sits on the benzo portion of the fused system, and the nitro group on the pendant phenyl ring is strongly electron-withdrawing. The lactone carbonyl and the ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are placed asymmetrically on the two aromatic rings.

The molecule is a bicyclic lactone built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring containing an ester group. The fused system is a 3,4-dihydroisocoumarin-type scaffold, in which the lactone carbonyl is attached directly to the aromatic ring and the ring oxygen sits adjacent to a carbon bearing a saturated cyclohexyl substituent. The aromatic ring is ortho-fused to the lactone ring and carries no further substituents, while the cyclohexyl group is attached as a non-planar, saturated appendage. The lactone and the fused ring system give the core moderate rigidity, while the cyclohexyl ring and the single methylene linker add conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two oxygen atoms of the ester group, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic lactone: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered unsaturated lactone ring, forming a 3,4-dihydroisocoumarin-type scaffold. The lactone carbonyl is conjugated with the fused aromatic ring, and the ring oxygen links the carbonyl to a sp3 carbon bearing the aryl substituent. That pendant phenyl ring carries a nitro group at the para position, giving a single, asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused core is largely rigid and planar, while the bond to the pendant aryl group permits some rotation. The nitro and lactone carbonyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a para-substituted benzene ring carrying a nitroso group (N=O) on one side and an ester on the other. The ester links that ring to a bicyclic indane-type unit: a five-membered carbocycle fused to a second benzene ring, with the ester oxygen attached at the saturated carbon of the five-membered ring. The fused bicyclic system is largely rigid, while the ester linkage gives the molecule some rotational freedom. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups. The carbonyl oxygen, ester oxygen, and nitroso oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ends differ in substitution.

The nitrogen carries an N-phenyl substituent, and a neighboring carbon of the ring carries a second, C-linked phenyl group, so the two benzene rings are attached at adjacent positions. The core ring is aromatic-like and planar, while each phenyl ring is a flat six-membered carbon ring with no fusion to the heterocycle. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. Overall the structure is rigid and largely planar, with limited conformational flexibility beyond rotation around the single bonds joining the phenyl rings to the core.

The molecule is built on a saturated cyclohexane ring bearing a methyl group and an isopropyl group, giving it a menthol-type monoterpene framework. The ring carries an ester oxygen at the carbon adjacent to the isopropyl substituent, so the substitution pattern is contiguous and the ring is substantially non-planar and conformationally flexible. The ester links this ring to a 2,3-diphenylpropanoic acid unit, where two phenyl rings sit on the alpha and beta carbons. The ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall structure lacks any clear mirror or rotational symmetry because of its several stereocenters and asymmetric substitution.

The molecule is built on an acyclic carbon backbone that carries two ester groups and two ketone groups, with the central carbon bearing an alkyl branch. One terminal ester is an ethyl ester, while the other is attached to a cyclohexane ring that is substituted with a methyl group and an isopropyl group. The cyclohexane ring is a single saturated ring with no fusion, and its substituents are arranged in a fixed relative geometry that makes the ring fairly rigid. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two ester arms differ and the ring substitution is asymmetric. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every heteroatom is a carbonyl or ether oxygen, but the four oxygen atoms in the ester and ketone groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring carrying a methyl group and an isopropyl group on adjacent-to-one-another positions, with the ring carbon bearing the isopropyl also adjacent to the carbon that bears the ester oxygen. The only functional group is an ester: an oxygen linking the ring to a cyanoacetyl unit, in which a methylene sits between the carbonyl and a terminal nitrile. The substitution pattern is therefore a trisubstituted cyclohexane with no ring unsaturation or fusion, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The ring is conformationally flexible and can interconvert between chair forms, while the acyclic ester-nitrile chain adds rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen together with the nitrile nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a bornane (1,7,7-trimethylbicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) skeleton, a rigid, cage-like bicyclic framework bearing gem-dimethyl and angular methyl groups. Attached to this bicycle are a carboxylic acid group and a 2-hydroxy-2-phenylethyl side chain, which carries a secondary alcohol and an unsubstituted benzene ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the carboxylic acid and the hydroxyethyl-phenyl arm sit on different carbons of the cage. The carboxylic acid and the secondary alcohol can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the phenyl ring contributes only aromatic, nonpolar character.

The molecule is built on a saturated cyclopentane ring that carries three methyl groups, with one quaternary carbon bearing both a methyl and a short side chain, giving a compact, sterically crowded aliphatic framework. The side chain is a ketone (C=O) linked through a two-carbon ethylene spacer to an O-thiocarbamate unit, where a thiocarbonyl (C=S) is flanked by an ester-type oxygen and a nitrogen bearing a phenyl ring. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion is a simple monosubstituted benzene. The aliphatic core is conformationally flexible, while the thiocarbamate-anilide region adds some polar character. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen, ether-type oxygen, and sulfur can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a saturated cyclohexane ring carrying several methyl groups: one methyl on a ring carbon adjacent to a quaternary carbon, and a gem-dimethyl pattern on the carbon next to it, giving a densely substituted, sterically crowded aliphatic core. A single quaternary ring carbon bears one methyl and a side chain consisting of a CH2 linker attached to an aniline nitrogen. That nitrogen is a secondary amine bonded directly to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the molecule contains one aromatic ring fused to nothing, with no other heteroatoms present. The secondary aryl amine offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the N–H) and one weak acceptor (the nitrogen lone pair, delocalized into the ring), while the hydrocarbon framework is otherwise nonpolar. The bulky, branched aliphatic portion restricts rotation, making the overall shape moderately rigid, with the flexible CH2–NH linkage being the main point of conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a saturated cyclopentane ring fused to nothing else, carrying methyl groups at several positions, including a gem-dimethyl pair on one carbon and a quaternary carbon bearing a methylene linker. That linker connects through an ester oxygen to a para-nitrobenzoyl group, a benzene ring with a nitro substituent directly opposite the carbonyl. The aliphatic bicyclic-like framework is rigid and bulky, while the aromatic ring is planar and conjugated with the ester carbonyl and the electron-withdrawing nitro group. The ester oxygens and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure lacks any internal symmetry axis because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a single saturated five-membered carbocycle, a cyclopentane ring bearing four methyl groups in a gem-dimethyl and two additional methyl substitutions, which gives a compact, sterically crowded all-carbon scaffold with no ring fusion. Attached at one quaternary ring carbon is a two-carbon chain containing a ketone carbonyl followed by an ether-type oxygen linked to an ester. The ester carbonyl connects to a benzene ring, so the aromatic portion is a simple monosubstituted phenyl group with no further ring substitution. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane of note due to the asymmetric placement of methyl groups, and it contains several rotatable bonds in the ketone-ester side chain, while the cyclopentane core remains rigid. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its three oxygen atoms (ketone and ester carbonyls plus the ester ether oxygen) act as acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-like scaffold built from a camphor-type bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane skeleton, with two geminal methyl groups on one bridge carbon and an angular methyl on a bridgehead. A cyclopentanone-type ketone sits in the five-membered ring, and the adjacent exocyclic carbon bears an enaminone unit (C=C–NH) linked to an anthranilic acid fragment. That aromatic ring is a benzene bearing an ortho carboxylic acid, creating a substitution pattern on adjacent positions. The bicyclic core is conformationally rigid, while the aryl-amino arm offers some rotational freedom. The molecule has an overall asymmetric shape. It presents hydrogen-bond donors at the enamine N–H and the carboxylic acid O–H, and several acceptors at the ketone, the carboxyl oxygens, and the amine nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a cyclopentane ring that carries three methyl groups, with one ring carbon bearing both a methyl group and a carboxylic acid, and the adjacent quaternary carbon bearing two methyls. A side chain on a neighboring ring carbon consists of a two-carbon unit in which each carbon carries one bromine atom, and the far carbon is bonded to a phenyl ring, giving a vicinal dibromide attached to an aromatic group. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and planar, while the cyclopentane is saturated and sterically crowded by its geminal and vicinal methyl groups. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites, whereas the bromine atoms are only weak acceptors and the rest of the framework offers no additional hydrogen-bonding capability. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because its substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is built around a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane-type) scaffold, a rigid, bridged cage of seven carbons bearing gem-dimethyl groups on one bridge and a methyl group at a bridgehead. Adjacent to the cage is a secondary hydroxyl group, and the ring carbon bearing the amine is also flanked by this alcohol, giving a vicinal amino-alcohol arrangement. The nitrogen is a secondary amine linked through a CH2 group to a quaternary carbon carrying both a hydroxyl group and an ethyl chain, so the molecule contains two hydroxyl groups and one N-H amine. Overall the structure is conformationally constrained in its core but has a flexible side chain, and it is asymmetric because the substituents are not arranged in a symmetric pattern. The two oxygen atoms and the nitrogen together provide three hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is built on a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) scaffold carrying a gem-dimethyl bridge and an angular methyl group, which together make the core rigid and compact. Two adjacent carbons on the bicyclic framework each bear an amide nitrogen, and each amide is linked to a para-nitrophenyl ring, so the two arms are substituted in a 2,3-trans-like arrangement across the saturated core. The structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry relating the two benzamide halves, although the stereocenters break perfect mirror symmetry. Each amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the molecule is conformationally constrained at the core but has flexibility at the two aryl amide arms.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered oxygen-containing ring (a tetrahydropyran), with no aromatic rings and no ring fusion. The ring carries a quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group and an adjacent carbon bearing two methyl groups, which together create a bulky, sterically crowded substitution pattern.
