A carboxylic acid group sits on the ring, and a secondary alcohol is attached through a branched isopropyl-substituted side chain. The molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry because the substituents are distinct, and its ring and side chain provide moderate conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ring oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built around a saturated six-membered oxane ring that bears gem-dimethyl and methyl substituents on the same carbon framework, with a carboxylic acid group attached to one ring carbon. A single quaternary carbon, which is also attached to the ring oxygen-adjacent position, carries both a hydroxyl group and two 1-naphthyl ring systems, giving a bulky, sterically crowded center. Each naphthalene is a fused bicyclic aromatic unit, and because the two naphthyl groups are attached to the same carbon, the molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry. The oxane ring is conformationally constrained, while the bulky aryl groups restrict rotation around their attachment points. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the hydroxyl and carboxylic acid OH groups, and acceptor capability comes from the ring ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is built on a saturated six-membered oxygen-containing ring (a tetrahydropyran) bearing two methyl groups on one carbon and one methyl group on the adjacent quaternary carbon next to the ring oxygen. Attached to that quaternary carbon is a carbinol carbon that carries a hydroxyl group and two unsubstituted phenyl rings, giving a diphenyl-substituted tertiary alcohol side chain. A carboxylic acid group sits on the ring carbon adjacent to the gem-dimethyl carbon, so the substitution pattern is dense and asymmetric. The ring is conformationally constrained by its quaternary centers, while the two phenyl groups provide rotational freedom around their attachment bonds. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring ether oxygen together with the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two para-aminophenyl rings joined through a single methylene carbon that bears a ketone, so the scaffold is a diaryl ketone with a CH2 spacer, giving a deoxybenzoin-type skeleton. Each benzene ring is a simple unfused six-membered aromatic ring with no fused ring systems. Each ring carries a primary amine (NH2) para to its point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the central carbonyl-methylene axis. The two aromatic rings are rigid and planar, while the CH2 linker and the carbonyl group add some conformational flexibility. The two primary amines can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a symmetric, rod-like diarylalkyne in which a central carbon-carbon triple bond joins two para-substituted benzene rings. Each terminal ring carries a benzamide group attached through an amide nitrogen, so the structure has an overall linear, extended scaffold built from three aromatic rings and one alkyne linker, with no saturated ring systems or ring fusion. The two amide groups, each bearing an N-H donor and a C=O acceptor, sit at opposite ends of the molecule, and each terminal phenyl ring is unsubstituted apart from that amide. The arrangement is highly rigid because of the linear alkyne and planar aromatic rings, with the amide linkages providing some conformational freedom at their ends. The molecule can therefore accept hydrogen bonds at the carbonyl oxygens and donate them from the two N-H groups.

This molecule is a benzaldehyde core, meaning a benzene ring carrying a formyl group (CHO) on one carbon. The ring is bearing two chlorine atoms at meta positions relative to the aldehyde, and a nitro group sits on the carbon immediately adjacent to the aldehyde, so the three substituents occupy three consecutive ring positions. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and only the aldehyde and nitro groups can rotate slightly out of plane. The molecule lacks any symmetry element that would make its two chlorines equivalent, since the nitro group breaks the mirror relationship. In terms of hydrogen bonding, it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygens of the aldehyde and nitro groups act as acceptors, and the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors.

This molecule is built on a menthane-type skeleton: a cyclohexane ring bearing a methyl group and an isopropyl group in a 1,2,4 relationship, with the carbinol carbon attached to the ring adjacent to the isopropyl-bearing carbon. The six-membered carbocycle is fully saturated, so there are no ring fusions or aromatic rings within this core. The ring oxygen-free ester linkage at that carbinol carbon connects to a 2,3-diphenylpropanoyl acyl group, which contributes two separate, unfused phenyl rings. The molecule has several stereocenters and no internal symmetry, so it is conformationally flexible yet bulky. It has one carbonyl oxygen and one ester oxygen as hydrogen-bond acceptors and no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a saturated six-membered carbocycle (a cyclohexane ring) bearing three substituents: a methyl group, an isopropyl group, and an ester oxygen, arranged in a 1,2,5-pattern around the ring. The ester links the ring to a diphenylacetyl unit, in which a single sp3 carbon carries two phenyl rings, giving the acyl portion a bulky, propeller-like shape. The ring is fully saturated and conformationally flexible, while the two phenyl groups add rotational freedom. The molecule has one stereogenic-rich framework with no internal symmetry. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two oxygens of the ester group, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a short aliphatic chain: a methyl-bearing carbon attached to a carboxylic acid group, which connects to a quaternary-type carbon that carries a hydroxyl group and two phenyl rings. Those two benzene rings are unfused, each a simple six-membered aromatic ring hanging off the same central carbon, giving the molecule a propeller-like arrangement. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary hydroxyl adds another donor and acceptor site. The two phenyl groups are attached to the same carbon, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about that center, although the adjacent stereocenter breaks overall symmetry. Several rotatable single bonds make the scaffold moderately flexible.

The molecule is built on an indanone scaffold: a five-membered ring fused to a benzene ring, with the carbonyl carbon sitting in the five-membered ring adjacent to the fused aromatic system. The five-membered ring carries a methyl group on one alkene carbon and a phenyl group on the other, giving a substituted indenone-type core with a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to the ketone. The fused bicyclic framework is largely planar and rigid, while the pendant phenyl ring can rotate about its single bond to the core. The molecule lacks any molecular symmetry because the methyl and phenyl substituents sit on different carbons. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the ketone oxygen serves as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring, a heteroaromatic scaffold containing three nitrogen atoms and two carbons. A phenyl ring is attached directly to one of the ring nitrogens, giving an N-aryl substitution that adds a flat, rigid aromatic group to the core. The triazole carries a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a carboxylic acid group on the other, so the two carbon positions are substituted and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. Both the hydroxyl and the carboxylic acid can donate hydrogen bonds, while the ring nitrogens and the carbonyl oxygen can accept them. The fused-free arrangement of two separate aromatic rings linked by a single nitrogen–carbon bond gives the molecule a rigid, largely planar framework with limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a five-membered 1,2,4-triazol-3-one ring, with a carbonyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogens. One ring nitrogen carries a carboxamide group (a urea-like C(=O)NH2 unit), while the other nitrogen bears a phenyl ring, giving an N-aryl substitution. The carbon at position 5 of the triazolone core carries a saturated cyclohexyl ring attached directly to it. The phenyl and cyclohexyl groups are bulky, non-fused appendages, so the scaffold consists of one fused-free heterocycle with two separate carbocyclic substituents. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its rotatable bonds to the phenyl and carboxamide groups give moderate flexibility around a fairly rigid central ring. The primary amide NH2 and the ring carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, respectively, while the remaining ring nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing a common edge. A bromine atom sits on one ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, which breaks the symmetry of the naphthalene core. At the other ring, a vinyl-linked hydrazone group extends outward, connecting the naphthalene to an unsubstituted phenyl ring through an N-H bridge. The hydrazone nitrogen bearing the hydrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the imine nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond. The fully aromatic framework is largely planar and conjugated, giving it a rigid character, with only the single bonds around the hydrazone linker allowing limited rotation.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing one edge. A nitrile group (C≡N) sits on one ring at a position adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, while a benzamide-type substituent is attached to the other ring at the peri position across from it, forming an amide linkage (–NH–C(=O)–) to an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The aromatic rings are fully planar and conjugated, giving the core considerable rigidity, while the amide bond allows some rotational freedom around the aryl–N and N–C(=O) connections. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents are on different rings at non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is built around a five-membered pyrazolone-type ring, a heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a carbonyl group, giving a lactam-like amide linkage within the ring. One nitrogen bears an unsubstituted phenyl ring, while the carbon at the other side of the ring is attached through a double bond to a para-aminophenyl group, so the two aryl rings sit at opposite ends of the core. The primary amine on the aniline ring is a hydrogen-bond donor and the ring carbonyl oxygen and imine-type nitrogen serve as acceptors. The core is largely planar and conjugated, with the aromatic rings limiting conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two aryl substituents differ.

This molecule is built from two pyrazolone rings joined through a methylene bridge at their C4 positions, giving a symmetric, bis-heterocyclic scaffold. Each five-membered ring contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a phenyl substituent, and a ring carbonyl adjacent to the CH bridge. Each ring also bears an ethyl ester group on the carbon-nitrogen double bond, so the two halves are mirror images of one another. The phenyl rings are attached as pendant aromatic groups rather than fused systems, and the central methylene linker gives the molecule moderate flexibility. The carbonyl oxygens and ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around two 5-membered pyrazolone-type rings, each bearing a methyl group on a carbon adjacent to a C=N bond and an N-phenyl group on the ring nitrogen. The rings are joined through an sp2 exocyclic C=C linkage in one half and a single sp3 carbon bridge in the other, so the scaffold is not planar overall and has limited rigidity. Each ring carries a C=O (lactam-type carbonyl) and a C=N imine, providing hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the two N-phenyl rings are unsubstituted and extend the aromatic surface. A bromine atom sits on the vinylic carbon of the exocyclic double bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and because the two halves differ in their linkage and bromine placement, it lacks any apparent symmetry.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolone ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring attached directly to the nitrogen. The ring has a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the imine-type nitrogen and a carbonyl group at the position next to the N-phenyl nitrogen. The carbon between the methyl-bearing carbon and the carbonyl is sp3 and bears a benzyl-type substituent, where a methylene links the core to a second phenyl ring that carries a hydroxyl group on the ortho position. The molecule therefore contains three ring systems, two of them benzene rings, with no ring fusion, and it is asymmetric because the two aryl groups differ. Rotation about the single bonds linking the aryl groups gives moderate flexibility. The phenolic hydroxyl and the ring carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ring nitrogens provide additional acceptor sites.

This molecule is a fused polycyclic system built around a three-membered aziridine-like ring containing an oxygen and nitrogen, in which a strained N–O bond bridges a bicyclic core. The structure is fused to a benzene ring through the nitrogen, forming a benzo-fused heterocycle with a ketone carbonyl adjacent to the benzene ring. A methyl ester group is attached to the same quaternary bridgehead carbon that bears the ring oxygen. Because the rings are fused and bridged, the scaffold is rigid and largely planar in its aromatic portion, with little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, ester oxygens, and ring heteroatoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a flexible two-carbon-linked diamine chain, with an ethylene bridge on each side connecting two ortho-substituted benzene rings. Each benzene ring carries an acetamido group (an N-acetyl amide, NH-C(=O)CH3) at the position adjacent to the ethyl linker, so the two rings are mirror-related and the molecule as a whole is close to C2-symmetric. The central secondary amine (NH) sits between the two phenethyl arms and is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Each amide contributes one N-H donor and one carbonyl oxygen acceptor, giving the molecule two additional donors and two additional acceptors. The aromatic rings are rigid planar units, while the CH2-CH2 linkers and the secondary amine allow considerable conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a cyclohexane ring carrying a methyl group and an isopropyl group on adjacent carbons, which together form a menthane-type scaffold. A single ester linkage connects that ring through an oxygen atom to a separate, fully saturated cyclopentane ring bearing three methyl substituents, including a quaternary carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. The molecule contains no aromatic rings, no double bonds apart from the carbonyl, and no heteroatoms other than the two ester oxygens. It has several stereocenters and no internal symmetry, so it is conformationally flexible yet bulky and compact. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two ester oxygens, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a compact, bridged tricyclic cage in which a cyclopropane-fused bicyclic framework (a pinane-like carbon skeleton bearing gem-dimethyl groups) is joined to a quaternary carbon that carries a 4-methoxyphenyl ring. An exocyclic alkene is attached to the cage, and that alkene is substituted with two phenyl rings, so the molecule contains three separate benzene rings in total. The methoxy group (an aryl ether) sits para on one ring, which gives that ring a single-position substitution pattern and a mild electron-donating character. The only hydrogen-bond capability comes from the ether oxygen, which can act as a weak acceptor, since the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid cage and conjugated aromatic substituents make the structure largely fixed in shape, with relatively little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring carrying three substituents at alternating positions around the ring: two acetamido groups (NHC(=O)CH3) and one ethyl chain bearing a benzamide terminus, with the arrangement placing one acetamido group adjacent to a 2-(benzamido)ethyl side chain. Each of the three side chains is a flexible two-carbon linker ending in an amide-linked phenyl ring, so the structure contains four benzene rings in total, with the central ring fully substituted and the three peripheral phenyl rings unfused. The molecule lacks any symmetry that would make all three arms equivalent, and its many rotatable bonds make it conformationally flexible. Each of the three secondary amide groups supplies one N-H hydrogen-bond donor and one C=O hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving six donor and acceptor sites in total.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring bearing substituents at positions 1, 3, and 5 (meta-relationship between the two nitro groups, with the ethyl-linked chains positioned to flank a nitro group). Two nitro groups (–NO2) sit on the ring, each strongly electron-withdrawing. Two 2-(benzamido)ethyl side chains extend from the ring, each containing a secondary amide linking an ethylene spacer to a terminal phenyl ring, so the molecule has three benzene rings in total. The side chains are flexible with rotatable bonds, while the central ring and terminal phenyls are rigid and planar. The molecule lacks a clear symmetry plane because the substitution pattern is asymmetric around the central ring. Each amide N–H can donate a hydrogen bond, and the amide carbonyl oxygens and nitro oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring carrying four substituents at positions 1, 2, 4 and 5 (the ring is substituted on alternating positions, with two protons remaining). Two of these substituents are acetamido groups (–NH–C(=O)CH3), and the other two are 2-carbon ethyl linkers that each terminate in a benzamide unit (–CH2CH2–NH–C(=O)–phenyl). The arrangement is therefore approximately centrosymmetric, with the two arms mirror-related across the ring. The scaffold has several rotatable single bonds in the ethyl linkers and amide-to-aryl bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility, while the aromatic rings and amide planes remain rigid. Each of the two amide N–H groups and the two acetamido N–H groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the four carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring carrying three substituents: an acetamide group (an N-acetyl amide) and two two-carbon ethyl linkers, each terminating in a benzamide group. The aromatic ring is substituted at three positions in a 1,2,4-pattern, so the two ethyl-benzamide arms are adjacent and the acetamido group sits meta to one arm. Overall the structure contains three amide linkages and three phenyl rings, making it a fairly extended, flexible molecule. Each amide N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and each carbonyl oxygen can act as an acceptor, giving it multiple hydrogen-bonding sites. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the substitution pattern on the central ring is asymmetric.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type scaffold built on a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) framework, bearing three methyl groups, one of which sits at a bridgehead position and two of which form a gem-dimethyl unit on the one-carbon bridge. A ketone is located on the ring adjacent to a quaternary bridgehead, and a side chain on the adjacent carbon carries a formate ester, with the ester oxygen linked through a CH2 group. The rigid, cage-like skeleton limits conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the ketone and the formate side chain. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the ketone and ester oxygens, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-like ketone built on a fused and bridged carbon skeleton, with two bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane-type cages linked through a short saturated chain. Each cage carries gem-dimethyl and angular methyl substituents, giving the framework a compact, highly branched, and sterically crowded character. There are two ketone carbonyl groups, each flanked by quaternary carbons, which are the only heteroatom-bearing functionalities present. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two carbonyl oxygens serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rigid polycyclic cages make the structure largely inflexible, with limited rotational freedom apart from the central linking chain.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-like scaffold built on a bornane (camphor-type) framework, with two fused five- and six-membered carbocyclic rings sharing a bridged bond. It carries a ketone on the bridge-adjacent ring carbon and a three-carbon side chain ending in a primary amide, bearing a methylene linker and a carbonyl-bearing carbon that connects the ring to the amide. Three methyl groups sit on the bridgehead and bridge carbons, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no obvious mirror or rotational symmetry in the side chain. The rigid bicyclic core limits conformational flexibility, while the side chain retains some rotational freedom. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site, and the ketone adds a further hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a symmetric bis-semicarbazone built on a central benzene ring. Two identical acetyl-derived arms sit at the 1 and 3 positions (meta-substituted), each consisting of a C=N hydrazone linkage bonded to a urea-like semicarbazide terminus with a free NH2 group. The central aromatic ring is planar and the molecule has approximately two-fold symmetry through the ring. Each arm contains a conjugated C=N–NH–C(=O)–NH2 unit, which gives the molecule considerable rigidity along the conjugated framework while the N–N and C–N bonds allow some rotational freedom. Multiple N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and imine nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methyl ester, with a carbonyl group bonded to the ring and an oxygen bridging to a methyl group. The other substituent is a three-nitrogen unit, a triazirine-type ring, in which one nitrogen is bonded to the aromatic carbon and the remaining two nitrogens close a strained three-membered ring. Because the benzene ring is fully aromatic and the para pattern is symmetric about its axis, the aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ester and the small nitrogen ring are relatively compact. The ester carbonyl oxygen and ester ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the nitrogens of the three-membered ring can also accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane skeleton, a rigid bridged framework that resembles a camphor-type scaffold. It carries a ketone on one bridge-adjacent carbon, which sits conjugated with an enaminone unit: a carbon-carbon double bond linking to an NH group that is attached to a phenyl ring. Three methyl groups are placed on the quaternary bridgehead and bridge carbons, giving the core a bulky, sterically crowded profile. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as an acceptor, and the phenyl ring adds an aromatic, flat region. The compact cage limits conformational flexibility, though the N-aryl enamine arm retains some rotational freedom.

The molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-like scaffold built on a bornane-type framework, with a gem-dimethyl bridge and an angular methyl group giving it a compact, rigid, three-dimensional shape. Fused to the cyclohexanone portion is a ketone adjacent to an exocyclic enaminone-type alkene that carries an N-hydroxy-N-phenyl amine substituent, so the phenyl ring is attached through nitrogen and conjugated with the enone system. The ring system is saturated apart from this conjugated unit, and the bicyclic core is conformationally constrained, with little rotational freedom. The hydroxylamine oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen can both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the N–OH group provides a hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution pattern on the enone side.

The molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-like framework built on a bornane-type skeleton, with two methyl groups on a bridgehead-adjacent carbon and one more on the other bridgehead. A cyclohexanone-type ring is fused through a bridged arrangement to a cyclopentane, giving a rigid, compact cage with limited conformational flexibility. A ketone sits adjacent to the bicyclic core, and a second carbonyl links to a naphthalene ring system attached through its 1-position, so the molecule contains an extended fused aromatic unit. Molecular symmetry is low because the naphthoyl group breaks the symmetry of the cage. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a central azo group (N=N) that links two identical benzene rings, giving a symmetric, roughly linear, conjugated scaffold. Each phenyl ring carries an acetyl ester substituent (–O–C(=O)CH3) at the meta position relative to the azo linkage, so the two substituents sit on opposite sides in a mirror-related pattern. The aromatic rings are fully unfused and rigid, while the ester groups add some conformational flexibility through their single bonds. The ester carbonyl oxygens and the azo nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all N–H and O–H positions are absent.

This molecule is a symmetric azobenzene scaffold, with two phenyl rings joined through a central N=N double bond. Each ring carries an acetamido group (–NHC(=O)CH3) attached at the meta position relative to the azo linkage, giving a 3,3'-disubstituted pattern across the two rings. The two aryl rings are unfused, and the azo bridge makes the core largely planar and conjugated, though the rings can rotate about their bonds to the nitrogen. Each acetamide group offers one N–H hydrogen-bond donor and a carbonyl oxygen acceptor, and the azo nitrogens provide additional weak acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring carrying two identical arms, each formed by a benzylidene-aniline unit: a carbon–nitrogen double bond (an imine) links the ring to a phenyl group. The two imine-bearing substituents sit on the central ring in a para-type arrangement relative to one another, with a nitro group (–NO2) on the same ring, placed meta to one imine and ortho to the other. The two outer phenyl rings are unsubstituted and freely rotate around their single bonds, so the framework is largely planar and conjugated but has some flexibility at the imine linkages. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, and each imine nitrogen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall, the structure lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the nitro group.

This molecule is built on an indole-fused framework: a pyrrole ring fused to a benzene ring, with a second pyrrole-type ring fused across the benzene to create a tricyclic system. Its core is a nitrogen-containing fused aromatic scaffold, and the saturated ring contributes a partly flexible, non-planar region. An N-acetyl amide group sits on one ring nitrogen, and a methyl group is attached to the carbon of the aromatic pyrrole ring, with an additional methyl group on the saturated ring carbon. The free aromatic N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any obvious symmetry because the substituents are placed unevenly across the fused ring system.

The molecule is a symmetric bis-imine built on a meta-disubstituted benzene core, with two identical arms attached at the 1 and 3 positions. Each arm consists of a benzylidene-type carbon-nitrogen double bond (C=N) linked to a two-carbon chain that terminates in an acetal carbon bearing two ethoxy groups, so the molecule carries four ethoxy substituents in total. The central benzene ring is aromatic and rigid, while the flexible aliphatic chains and ethoxy groups add considerable conformational freedom. The imine nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the ether oxygens of the acetal groups are additional acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents placed meta to each other (1,3-disubstitution). Each substituent is a carbonyl group bonded directly to the ring, and each carbonyl carries a chloromethyl group, so the structure is a symmetric aryl diketone with two alpha-chloroketone arms. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, while the attached acyl chains have rotational freedom around their single bonds. The molecule has a mirror-type symmetry through the ring, with the two side chains related by that symmetry. The carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a four-carbon ketone chain: a carbonyl flanked by a benzyl group (a phenyl ring attached through a CH2) on one side and a CH2 leading to a branch carbon on the other. That branch carbon carries a furan ring, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen, and a piperidine nitrogen, making it a tertiary amine within a saturated six-membered ring. The phenyl and furan rings are separate, unfused aromatics, and the piperidine ring is fully saturated, so the structure has no fused ring systems. Its flexible, multi-bonded chain gives it considerable conformational freedom. The ketone oxygen and furan oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the piperidine nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a ketone carbonyl bridging two substituents: on one side a benzyl group (a CH2 linked to a phenyl ring), and on the other an alpha-carbon bearing both a phenyl ring and a piperidine nitrogen. The two phenyl rings are simple unfused benzene rings, and the piperidine is a saturated six-membered ring containing one tertiary amine nitrogen attached to the alpha-carbon. The substitution pattern is unsubstituted on each aromatic ring, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two sides differ. The chain between the rings is flexible, while the aromatic rings and the piperidine ring are comparatively rigid. The ketone oxygen and the tertiary nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups present.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four chlorine atoms and two dichloromethyl groups, giving a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no heteroatoms other than halogens. The two dichloromethyl groups, each a CHCl2 unit, are attached at positions para to one another, while two aromatic chlorine atoms occupy the remaining ring positions, producing a symmetric substitution pattern with a center of inversion. The ring is rigid and planar, and the carbon-chlorine bonds give the surface a lipophilic, electron-poor character. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen sits on carbon, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two adjacent (ortho) substituents: a 2-aminoethyl chain and an acetamido group. The ethyl linker ends in a carbamate, a nitrogen bonded to a carbonyl that is also bonded to a methoxy oxygen, so the carbamate sits at the terminus of the side chain. The acetamide is a secondary amide formed from the ring nitrogen and an acetyl group. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule has no stereocenters or internal symmetry. The two side chains give moderate conformational flexibility around the ethyl linker, while the aromatic ring and amide planes are rigid. Both the carbamate and acetamide N-H groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and their carbonyl oxygens, along with the methoxy oxygen, serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, with two benzene rings joined by a single bond at the para positions of each ring. One ring carries an acetamido group (an N-acetyl amide, NH-C(=O)CH3) at the para position, while the other ring bears a para-substituted nitrogen that is part of a hydrazine unit: one nitrogen is acylated with an acetyl group and the other is bonded to a phenyl ring. The molecule is essentially symmetric in its central biphenyl core, though the two ends differ in substitution. Its aromatic rings are rigid and planar, with the biaryl bond allowing some rotation between the rings. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the two amide-type N-H groups, and acceptor capability from the two carbonyl oxygens.

The molecule is built around a central biphenyl unit, with one ring carrying a para-substituted phenylazo group (an N=N linkage bridging to a second phenyl ring). The opposite ring of the biphenyl bears a nitrogen substituent that is an N-acetyl hydrazine: an acetamide nitrogen bonded to a second nitrogen that connects to an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The molecule is extended and largely planar through its conjugated aromatic and azo segments, though the hydrazine linker introduces some rotational flexibility. It contains no stereocentres and has no internal symmetry beyond the local para-disubstituted patterns. The amide carbonyl and azo nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the single N-H of the hydrazine provides one hydrogen-bond donor site.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, giving a quinoline-like or indole-like framework with an exocyclic-type arrangement of double bonds around the fused system. An acetate ester group, an acetyl group bonded to an oxygen, is attached at one carbon of the five-membered ring. At the adjacent sp3 carbon sits a pyridin-2-yl substituent, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen. The overall substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, lacking any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The fused ring system is largely planar and rigid, while the bond linking the pyridine ring to the scaffold allows some rotational flexibility. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule contains no strong hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by a short two-carbon linker. One ring is a nitro-substituted benzene, with the nitro group (-NO2) attached at the position ortho to the linker, so the substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted. The other ring is a pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, attached to the linker through a carbon adjacent to that nitrogen. The two-carbon bridge carries a chlorine atom on each carbon, creating two adjacent stereocenters and adding conformational flexibility around the single bonds. The nitro group and the pyridine nitrogen are both hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring systems are chemically distinct.

This molecule is built on an acenaphthene-type tricyclic core, where a naphthalene unit is fused to a five-membered saturated ring bridging two peri positions, giving a rigid, nearly planar polycyclic framework. Attached to the aromatic core is a ketone carbonyl, which is bonded to a carbon bearing a bromine atom and a phenyl ring, so the alpha carbon is a stereogenic center. The aromatic rings are fully conjugated and largely flat, while the two-carbon bridge of the five-membered ring contributes limited flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the acyl group and the phenyl-bearing side chain break the symmetry of the fused core. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a symmetric, roughly linear scaffold built around a central bond-linked para-phenylene core flanked by two identical 1,2-dichloroethyl-bridged aryl arms. Each terminal ring is a benzene bearing a nitrile group para to the linking carbon and a nitro group ortho to it, so the substitution pattern is identical on both ends. The four sp3 carbons each carry a chlorine atom, which makes the central chain flexible in the sense of free rotation about its C–C bonds, while the aromatic rings stay rigid. The nitrile and nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two methylene-linked side arms at positions that are meta to each other across the ring. Each arm is a quaternary carbon carrying one chlorine atom and two ethyl ester groups, so the scaffold is a symmetric, flexible diaryl-type framework with a single aromatic core. The benzene ring carries two nitro groups, which are positioned adjacent to each other and sit in a pattern that makes the ring electron-poor. The four ester carbonyl oxygens and the two nitro groups supply multiple hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rotatable C–C bonds of the side arms give the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, whereas the benzene core remains rigid and planar.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two identical side chains at the 1 and 3 positions, giving it a meta substitution pattern and an approximately mirror-symmetric overall shape. Each side chain is a two-carbon unit in which each carbon carries a bromine atom, and the far end terminates in a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is in turn bonded to a methyl). Because the two chains are attached to the same ring, the molecule has two stereogenic carbon centers on each side. The benzene ring is rigid and planar, while the saturated carbon-carbon linkers allow considerable rotational flexibility. The two ester carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a fused tricyclic scaffold: a benzene ring is fused on one side to a six-membered lactam ring and on the other to a second six-membered lactam ring, giving a linear-style bis-lactam core. Both lactam rings contain an amide carbonyl bonded to a ring nitrogen bearing an N–H. Two ethyl ester groups are attached to saturated carbons adjacent to the carbonyls, one on each lactam ring, so the molecule has two identical ester arms. The arrangement is approximately symmetric across the central aromatic ring, though the saturated portions show some conformational flexibility. Each N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and each amide and ester carbonyl oxygen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from two identical barbiturate-type rings, each a six-membered pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione (a cyclic urea fused to a dicarbonyl system), joined through a methylene linker to a central benzene ring. The central ring is a meta-disubstituted benzene, with the two CH2 bridges attached at positions 1 and 3, giving the molecule a roughly mirror-symmetric, C2-like overall shape. Each heterocycle carries three carbonyl groups and two N-H groups, so each unit is rich in hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The molecule is largely rigid in its aromatic and heterocyclic cores but retains rotational freedom about the two benzylic methylene linkers.

This molecule is a fused tricyclic system built from two saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing rings flanking a central benzene ring, so the skeleton resembles a bis-fused tetrahydroquinoline-type scaffold. The aromatic core is a benzene ring carrying two ring fusions, one on each side of the benzene, and each fused ring contains one secondary amine nitrogen in a saturated, non-aromatic position. The two nitrogens sit on the benzene ring in a meta-like relationship to each other, and the saturated CH2 chains give the framework some conformational flexibility, though the fused rings limit overall motion. Each secondary amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The molecule is not symmetric, because the two fused rings differ in the length of their saturated chains.

This molecule is a symmetric bis-azoxy compound built on a linear, extended scaffold: a central para-phenylene ring bearing an azo (N=N) link on each side, with each azo group further connected to a second para-phenylene ring and then to a terminal phenyl ring through an azoxy (N-oxide) unit. The structure is therefore composed of five benzene rings joined in a chain, with the aromatic rings all unfused and each linked at the para positions, giving a rod-like, rigid, and highly conjugated framework. Two azo and two azoxy N=N bridges provide the chain connectivity, and the N-oxide oxygens are the principal hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The molecule possesses an approximate two-fold symmetry about a central axis through the middle benzene ring, and its nearly planar, elongated shape results from the extended conjugation across the azo and azoxy linkages.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with two identical acyl groups on opposite positions of the aromatic core. Each substituent is a carbonyl (ketone) carbon bonded to the ring on one side and to a dichloromethyl group on the other, so the scaffold is a symmetric, linear, essentially planar diaryl-type diketone. The two terminal carbons each bear two chlorine atoms, giving a CHCl2 unit next to each carbonyl. The structure has a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring centre and is fairly rigid because of the aromatic core, though the C–C bonds to the carbonyls allow some rotation. The carbonyl oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two acetamido groups (N-acetyl amide linkages) and one methyl group, giving a trisubstituted core. The ring bears an azo linkage (–N=N–) that connects it to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the overall scaffold is a diaryl azo system with extended conjugation across both aromatic rings. The two acetamide groups each offer an N–H donor and a carbonyl oxygen acceptor, while the azo nitrogens serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Substitution is arranged so the two amide groups sit in a meta-like relationship on the central ring, and the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The planar aromatic rings and azo bridge limit flexibility, though the amide and aryl–nitrogen bonds allow some rotation.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring bearing a methyl group, an isopropyl group, and two azo bridges (–N=N–), one linking to a phenyl ring on each side of the core. Both azo linkages are fully conjugated with the aromatic rings, so the overall scaffold is planar and largely rigid, with the three aromatic rings held in an extended, nearly linear arrangement. The substitution pattern on the central ring is asymmetric: the two azo groups sit meta to each other, while the methyl and isopropyl groups occupy the remaining positions, so the molecule lacks any clear mirror or rotational symmetry. The structure has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H groups, but the two azo nitrogens can each act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built around a central azo-type linkage connecting two aromatic systems, with each side carrying a benzene ring. One side is a simple unsubstituted phenyl ring attached through an N=N double bond, while the other side is a substituted benzene ring bearing a methyl group ortho to the azo nitrogen. The second aryl ring also carries an unusual N-oxide-type nitrogen group, drawn here as a charge-separated N(+)–O(−) arrangement with an additional N=N double bond to a phenyl ring. The molecule has no fused ring systems, and its aromatic rings are joined by linear, planar linkers, giving a largely rigid, extended framework with limited conformational flexibility. Overall symmetry is low because the two ends differ in substitution. The oxygen atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the azo nitrogens provide additional weak acceptor sites, while the molecule has no strong hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a methyl group, an isopropyl group, and two arylazo-type substituents, giving it a crowded, highly substituted aromatic core. One azo linkage (N=N) connects the central ring to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, while the other nitrogen is part of an azoxy unit (N-oxide form) joining the ring to a second phenyl group. The two terminal phenyl rings are unsubstituted and rotate relatively freely about their single bonds, so the molecule is fairly flexible overall, though the extended conjugated system keeps it largely planar. It lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are placed asymmetrically around the central ring. The azoxy oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the azo nitrogens offer additional weak acceptor sites, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings that share an edge, so the framework is flat and rigid. An aldehyde group (a formyl, C=O with an attached hydrogen) sits on one ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, while a bromine atom and a nitro group (–NO2) are attached to the other ring, placed on opposite sides of the fused junction. Because the three substituents occupy unlike positions and differ in kind, the molecule has no internal symmetry. The nitro group and the aldehyde oxygen are good hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only hydrogens are aromatic C–H or the aldehydic C–H.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene core, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing an edge. Two benzoyl units are attached: one through an amide linkage (C(=O)NH) to the naphthalene at one position, and one through an ester linkage (O–C(=O)) at another position on the same naphthalene ring, giving a 2,6- or 2,7-type disubstitution pattern that is not symmetric. Both benzene rings are unsubstituted phenyl groups, and the amide NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor while the carbonyl oxygens of the amide and ester act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, while the ester and amide bonds allow some rotational freedom at the linking positions.

The molecule is built on a tetrahydroquinoline scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that carries a methyl group on the saturated carbon adjacent to nitrogen. The nitrogen is acylated by a 4-nitrobenzoyl group, forming a tertiary amide, while the fused benzo ring bears a nitro group and a 3-oxobutyl side chain, each attached at adjacent positions. The molecule contains two nitro groups and a ketone, which together make it a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, with no hydrogen-bond donors present. The saturated portion of the bicyclic core provides some conformational flexibility, whereas the aromatic rings and the planar amide linkage are rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are distributed asymmetrically across the rings.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic core: a pyridine ring is fused to a benzene ring, which is in turn fused to a partially saturated six-membered ring containing a nitrogen atom, giving a benzo-quinoline-type skeleton. The pyridine nitrogen sits in an aromatic ring, while the second nitrogen is a tertiary amide-type nitrogen bonded to a benzoyl group, so the molecule carries a carbonyl and a phenyl ring as pendant substituents. A methyl group is attached to the pyridine ring adjacent to its nitrogen, and a second methyl group sits on the saturated ring. The fused framework is largely rigid, while the saturated ring and the benzoyl linkage add some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since no N–H or O–H groups are present, but the pyridine nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a fused tetracyclic bis-amide built around a central tricyclic core in which two saturated five-membered nitrogen-containing rings are fused to a central benzene ring, forming a symmetric indoline-type framework. Each indoline-like nitrogen is acylated by a benzoyl group, so the two phenyl rings hang off the core as pendant aromatic substituents. The two carbonyl groups are amide functionalities, and the molecule has no free N–H or O–H groups, so it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor. Its two amide oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fused polycyclic core is rigid, while the N-benzoyl groups retain some rotational freedom around the C–N amide bonds and the bonds linking them to the rings.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring carrying four substituents: two nitro groups and two ethyl linkers, each ending in a benzoate ester. Its two nitro groups sit on adjacent ring positions, and the two ester-bearing ethyl chains occupy the remaining positions, giving a symmetric arrangement about the ring's center. The two benzoyl ester units each contribute a phenyl ring, so the molecule contains three aromatic rings in total, connected by flexible two-carbon chains. The ester carbonyl oxygens and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The flexible ethyl linkers allow considerable conformational freedom, contrasting with the rigid aromatic cores.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds, and carries no fused rings. Two identical 2-chloroethyl side chains, each a two-carbon chain ending in a chlorine atom, are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 4, which makes the substitution pattern para. Because the two substituents are identical and opposite each other, the molecule has high symmetry, with a central axis passing through the ring. The only functional groups are the aryl carbon-chlorine bonds at the chain ends, which are alkyl chlorides rather than aryl chlorides. The ethyl linkers give the side chains some conformational freedom, while the aromatic core stays rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring bearing two identical side chains at opposite positions. Each side chain consists of a two-carbon ethylene linker attached to the ring, terminating in an ester oxygen that is bonded to an acetyl group, so the structure is a symmetric bis-ester built on a central aromatic core. The benzene ring is planar and aromatic, and the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the centers of the ring's C–H bonds. Each ester carries a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ethylene linkers and ester bonds provide some conformational flexibility, whereas the central ring remains rigid.

The molecule is built on a quinoxaline core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrazine ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship. Two benzyl groups, each a phenyl ring attached through a single methylene linker, are bonded to the two carbon atoms of the pyrazine ring that sit between the nitrogens, giving a symmetric 2,3-disubstitution pattern. The fused aromatic system is fully planar and rigid, while the two benzyl arms add rotational flexibility around their CH2 linkers. The pyrazine nitrogens are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic 1,2-diketone bearing two phenyl rings, with one carbonyl flanked by a benzyl (phenylmethyl) group and the other bonded to a benzylic carbon. That benzylic carbon carries a bromine atom and a second phenyl ring, so the bromine sits on the carbon directly next to the adjacent carbonyl. Both aromatic rings are unsubstituted benzene rings, giving a simple substitution pattern with no additional ring fusion. The chain has several rotatable single bonds, so the structure is fairly flexible, though the two carbonyl oxygens and the bulky aryl groups limit its conformational freedom. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. There is no internal symmetry, since the two ends of the molecule differ in their attachments.

The molecule is built from a linear, extended chain of aromatic rings joined by an amide linkage. A 4-methoxybenzoyl group is attached through a secondary amide to a para-substituted phenyl ring, which is bonded directly to a fused bicyclic benzotriazole system carrying an N-phenyl substituent on one of its triazole nitrogens. The fused benzotriazole unit consists of a benzene ring fused to a five-membered triazole ring, and the substitution pattern on the benzo ring is meta-like relative to the biaryl bond. Overall the scaffold is rigid and largely planar, with the amide being the main point of conformational flexibility. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the methoxy oxygen, and the triazole nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from three benzene rings joined through a central hydrazine-like nitrogen framework and an azo linkage. One phenyl ring carries a diazenyl (N=N) bridge connecting it to a second phenyl ring, giving an extended, conjugated arrangement with a flat, rigid aromatic portion. The central nitrogen atoms are bonded to an acetyl group (a carbonyl attached to a methyl) and to a third phenyl ring, which forms an N-acylated, N-aryl hydrazine unit. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three rings are attached at different positions. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the amide-type carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen atoms act as acceptors, while there are no strong N-H or O-H donors.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge. A carboxylic acid group sits on one ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, and a methoxy group sits on the same ring, ortho to the carboxylic acid. A nitro group is attached to the other ring, positioned on the opposite side of the fused system. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the carboxylic acid and methoxy substituents can rotate about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the nitro group and methoxy oxygen act as acceptors, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the substituents are placed asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on a 1,2-diphenylethane-1,2-diol backbone: two benzene rings are attached to adjacent carbons that each carry a hydroxyl group. One of the phenyl rings bears a nitro group at the position ortho to the point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical. The two aromatic rings are simple monocyclic benzene systems with no fused rings. The two secondary alcohol groups are free to form hydrogen bonds as donors and acceptors, while the nitro group contributes oxygen acceptor sites. The central two-carbon linker with its single bonds allows considerable conformational flexibility.

This molecule is an indole core, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, bearing three acetoxy (acetate ester) groups and one phenyl substituent. The indole nitrogen carries an N-acetoxy group, while the C3 position of the pyrrole ring bears an O-acetyl group and the C2 position carries a phenyl ring. A third acetoxy group sits on the benzenoid ring at the carbon adjacent to the fusion, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern across the bicyclic framework. The fused aromatic system is rigid and planar, with the phenyl ring and acetate arms providing some rotational flexibility. The molecule has no N–H or O–H groups, so it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor, but the multiple carbonyl oxygens of the ester groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a central isoxazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms. Three substituents are attached to this core: a phenyl group on one carbon, another phenyl group on the adjacent carbon, and a 2-aminophenyl group on the remaining carbon. The aniline-bearing ring carries a primary amino group ortho to the bond linking it to the isoxazole, which creates a sterically crowded arrangement that twists the rings out of plane. The overall scaffold is largely aromatic but not fully rigid, since the biaryl bonds allow rotation. The primary amine provides hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries an amino group, two bromine atoms, and a benzyl substituent. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The primary amine is attached to one ring carbon, flanked by a bromine on one side, and the benzyl group sits on the adjacent carbon, giving a 2,4-dibromo-6-benzyl aniline-type substitution pattern. A second, unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached through a flexible methylene bridge, so the molecule has rotatable bonds and is not rigid overall. The amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl group bridges two benzene rings. One ring is a 2-aminobenzoyl unit carrying two bromine atoms at positions meta to each other, flanking the ring so that it is substituted at three positions in addition to the carbonyl attachment. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached directly to the carbonyl carbon. The two aromatic rings are not fused to each other, but they are connected through the sp2 carbonyl, which gives the scaffold a modest degree of conformational flexibility around the single bonds. The primary amine on the substituted ring can donate hydrogen bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pair can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two rings are differently substituted.

The molecule is built on a diarylmethanol scaffold, with a central sp3 carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and bridging a phenyl ring to a substituted aniline ring. The aniline ring carries a primary amine and two bromine atoms at positions meta and para relative to each other, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern that breaks any overall mirror symmetry. The unsubstituted phenyl ring is a plain benzene ring with no fusion to other rings. Because the central carbon is a stereocentre, the molecule can exist in enantiomeric forms. The two aromatic rings give the structure considerable rigidity, while the single bonds around the central carbon allow moderate conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl and primary amine groups each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the bromine atoms contribute to halogen-based interactions.

This molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. At the 3-position of the indole sits a benzoyl ketone group, and the 2-position carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving a twisted, bulky arrangement around the pyrrole. The indole nitrogen is acylated by a second benzoyl group, and the benzo portion of the indole bears a nitro group, which is a strong electron-withdrawing substituent. The molecule contains five aromatic rings in total, so it is largely planar and rigid in its core, though the phenyl and benzoyl substituents can rotate. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen is fully substituted, but it offers several acceptors through its two carbonyl oxygens and the nitro group oxygens.

The molecule is a benzanilide-type structure built from two benzene rings joined through an amide linkage, with the nitrogen attached to one ring and a carbonyl attached to the other. The first ring carries a carboxylic acid group ortho to the amide nitrogen and a nitro group positioned meta to the amide and para to the carboxylic acid, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached directly to the carbonyl carbon. The amide and the aromatic systems provide substantial rigidity, while the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. The amide N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide carbonyl, carboxyl oxygens, and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic system where a benzene ring is fused to a pyrrole ring that carries an N–H group. A second ring, containing a carbonyl and a nitrone-type C=N⁺–O⁻ unit, is fused onto the benzene portion, giving an extended, largely planar tricyclic framework. Two phenyl rings are attached as substituents: one on the pyrrole carbon adjacent to nitrogen and one on the carbon bearing the imine. An acetate ester (O–C(=O)CH₃) is attached to the aromatic ring on the carbon next to the ring fusion. The scaffold lacks any internal symmetry, and its rigid fused core restricts conformational flexibility to rotation of the two phenyl groups. The N–H group and the ester carbonyl oxygen provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the ketone and N–O⁻ oxygen add further acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: an ethyl ester, a nitro group, and a benzamide-type amide linkage. The ethyl ester (CCOC(=O)) is attached at one ring position, and the nitro group sits para to it, giving the ring an electron-poor, strongly polarized character. Ortho to the ester, an amide nitrogen bridges to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring through a carbonyl, so the molecule contains two aromatic rings linked by an amide. The nitro and carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amide N–H provides one hydrogen-bond donor. Overall the scaffold is largely planar and rigid, with only the ethyl ester chain adding conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on an indolin-3-one (indoxyl-type) bicyclic scaffold, in which a five-membered ring containing a ketone and an imine nitrogen is fused to a benzene ring. A phenyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the imine, giving a conjugated, largely planar framework. A nitro group sits on the fused benzene ring, placed meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen, which makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The C=O and C=N double bonds are rigid and conjugated with the aromatic rings, so the core is inflexible. The ketone oxygen, the imine nitrogen, and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an anthraquinone-type tricyclic scaffold: two outer benzene rings fused to a central para-quinone ring that carries two carbonyl groups. One outer ring bears a methyl group and a nitro group on adjacent positions, while the other outer ring is fully substituted with four chlorine atoms, giving a clearly asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with the nitro and carbonyl groups conjugated into it. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, but the two carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two nitro groups, which sit ortho to each other on the ring. Two arms extend from the ring through ether oxygens and two-carbon ethylene linkers, and each arm terminates in a benzoate ester, so the two phenyl rings are attached to the ends of the flexible chains. The overall framework is linear and symmetric about the central ring, which carries two aryloxy substituents at the positions opposite each other. The nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, while the ester carbonyls and ether oxygens provide additional acceptor sites, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The four ethylene and ether segments make the molecule considerably flexible compared with its rigid aromatic core.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents on a single aromatic core, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so it is essentially planar and symmetric about the ring. Two nitro groups sit on the ring, in a para-like arrangement relative to each other, and two ether-linked side chains are attached through oxygen atoms. Each side chain is a two-carbon ethoxy linker terminated by an acetate ester, so the two chains are identical and the molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry. The structure has many hydrogen-bond acceptors from the nitro oxygens, ether oxygens, and ester carbonyls, but no hydrogen-bond donors. The ethoxy linkers and ester groups give the side chains considerable conformational flexibility, while the aromatic core remains rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents in a 1,2,4,5-tetrasubstituted pattern, with two ortho-related nitro groups and two secondary amine linkages. Each amine nitrogen attaches to the ring and to a CH2 group that is part of an ethyl ester chain (–CH2–C(=O)–O–CH2CH3), so the two side arms are chemically equivalent and arranged across the ring roughly symmetrically. The nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons flanked by the amine substituents, making the core a nitro-aniline type scaffold. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the ethyl ester side chains provide conformational flexibility. The two NH groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ester carbonyls and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two nitro groups at positions that flank one substituent pattern, with two identical arms attached. Each arm consists of an acetyl group (CH3-C(=O)-) bonded to an imine carbon, where the imine nitrogen carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so each side contains a ketone, a C=N double bond, and a terminal aromatic ring. The overall arrangement is roughly symmetric, with the two arms related to each other across the central ring, though the nitro groups break perfect mirror symmetry. The central core and phenyl rings are rigid and planar, while the single bonds linking the arms allow some conformational flexibility. The molecule contains no strong hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, but the ketone oxygens, nitro oxygens, and imine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central sp3 carbon bearing an acetyl group and a benzoyl group, which together form a 1,3-dicarbonyl (β-diketone) unit. Attached to that central carbon is a benzene ring carrying two nitro groups and one chlorine atom, placing the nitro groups ortho and para to the point of attachment and the chlorine meta to it. The unsubstituted phenyl ring of the benzoyl group is a separate aromatic system linked through a carbonyl. Overall the structure contains three aromatic rings-based features, multiple carbonyl oxygens and nitro oxygens that serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and no hydrogen-bond donors. Rotation about several single bonds gives the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, while the aromatic rings remain planar and rigid.

The molecule is built around a central sp3 carbon that bears a phenyl ketone (benzoyl) group and a second phenyl ring, so it is a 1,2-diaryl ketone skeleton. The central carbon carries one hydrogen and is a stereogenic center, with no symmetry relating its two aryl substituents. The third aromatic ring is a benzene bearing a chlorine atom and two nitro groups on the same ring, creating a strongly electron-poor, substituted scaffold. The ketone carbonyl and the two nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is fairly flexible around the sp3 linkage but contains three rigid aromatic rings.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing an amide substituent on one carbon, with a fluorine and a chlorine atom on adjacent ring positions, giving a 1,2,4-type trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The amide nitrogen is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and its carbonyl carbon is bonded to a quaternary carbon that carries a methyl group and two trifluoromethyl groups, making that portion of the scaffold bulky and highly fluorinated. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the fully substituted aliphatic carbon restricts rotation and contributes a compact, three-dimensional region. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the ring substitution is unsymmetrical. It has one hydrogen-bond donor, the amide N–H, and hydrogen-bond acceptor sites at the carbonyl oxygen and, more weakly, at the fluorine and chlorine atoms.

The molecule is an anilide built from a benzene ring bearing an amide nitrogen attached to one carbon, with two nitro groups on the ring at the positions ortho and para to that nitrogen-bearing carbon, giving a 2,4-dinitrophenyl substitution pattern. The amide carbonyl connects to a quaternary carbon that carries three trifluoromethyl groups, forming a bulky, highly fluorinated acyl unit with no rotational flexibility at that center. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the molecule as a whole has only limited symmetry because the nitro groups break the ring's symmetry. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and the two nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears an acetyl group, a carbonyl attached directly to the ring and to a methyl group, which acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The other side bears an amide linkage, where an NH group is attached to the ring and a carbonyl points away from it, giving one hydrogen-bond donor and one further acceptor. The amide carbonyl is bonded to a quaternary carbon that carries three trifluoromethyl groups, creating a bulky, highly fluorinated, roughly tripod-shaped terminus. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the bond rotations around the amide and acetyl linkages add some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry overall, though the three CF3 groups are equivalent to one another.

The molecule is an anilide built on a benzene ring carrying a single methyl group and a secondary amide linkage, placing the two substituents in a meta relationship on the aromatic ring. The amide nitrogen bears one hydrogen, making it a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as an acceptor. The acyl portion is a quaternary carbon bearing three trifluoromethyl groups, giving a sterically bulky, highly fluorinated, and rigid tert-alkyl unit. The aromatic ring is planar and unfused, whereas the rotatable amide bond and the C–N linkage introduce limited conformational flexibility. Overall the molecule lacks any symmetry axis due to the asymmetric meta-substitution on the ring.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a methyl group on one carbon and an amide-linked nitrogen on the adjacent carbon next to the ring nitrogen. The amide carbonyl connects to a long perfluorinated alkyl chain of eight carbons, each fully fluorinated except the terminal carbon, which carries three fluorines. The ring has no fusion and only two substituents, so its substitution pattern is ortho-like. The fluorinated chain is highly flexible and rod-like, whereas the aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the molecule lacks symmetry. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an anilide built from a benzene ring bearing two nitro groups, one at the position para to the amide nitrogen and one ortho to it, giving a 2,4-dinitrophenyl substitution pattern. The amide nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens serve as acceptors. The acyl side is a fully fluorinated eight-carbon perfluoroalkyl chain attached to the carbonyl, which makes it long, linear, and conformationally flexible, in contrast to the rigid aromatic ring. The aromatic core is planar and asymmetric because the two nitro groups occupy different positions.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with an ethoxy group on one side and an amide nitrogen on the other. The amide links the aromatic ring to a long, fully fluorinated carbon chain, a perfluorinated alkyl segment of eight carbons ending in a trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the perfluorinated tail is extended and stiff, though the ethoxy group adds a small degree of conformational freedom. Along the chain, the carbon-fluorine bonds are strongly electron-withdrawing, and the sequence of carbons near the amide carbonyl is fully substituted with fluorine. The secondary amide N-H is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an anilide built from a benzene ring bearing an amide nitrogen on one carbon and a nitro group on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The amide carbonyl is attached to a fully fluorinated eight-carbon perfluoroalkyl chain, a saturated and highly rigid-to-moderately-flexible tail with no ring fusion or stereocenters. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the long perfluoroalkyl chain adopts an extended conformation with considerable rotational freedom about its carbon-carbon bonds. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the two ends differ fundamentally. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an amide built from a pyridine ring and a fully fluorinated carbon chain. A 2-aminopyridine unit is linked through its exocyclic nitrogen to a carbonyl carbon, which is attached to a linear perfluorinated chain of eight carbons ending in a trifluoromethyl group. The pyridine ring is a single aromatic six-membered ring bearing one nitrogen atom, with substitution at the 2-position only, giving no symmetry across the whole molecule. The perfluoroalkyl segment is highly flexible along its carbon backbone but has a sterically bulky, electron-withdrawing character. The amide N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an amide built from a fully fluorinated eight-carbon perfluoroalkyl acyl chain linked through a secondary amide nitrogen to a 1-phenylethyl group. The perfluorinated chain is a long, linear, highly flexible segment whose carbon-fluorine bonds are fully substituted, while the terminal phenyl ring is a single unfused aromatic ring attached to a stereogenic carbon bearing a methyl group. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and the carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ends differ markedly in structure.

The molecule is an N-methyl amide built from a perfluorinated acyl chain and a cyclohexyl group. The carbonyl carbon is attached to a fully fluorinated eight-carbon chain, so the acyl portion is a linear, saturated, all-fluorinated tail ending in a trifluoromethyl group. The nitrogen carries a methyl group and a cyclohexyl ring, which is a saturated, non-aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fusion or substitution beyond the single attachment point. The amide C=O is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there is no N-H, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The fluorinated chain is highly flexible in principle but is sterically bulky, while the cyclohexyl ring adopts a chair-like conformation, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two ends differ.

This molecule is an anilide built around a central amide linkage, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to a carbon bearing two trifluoromethyl groups, giving a branched, highly fluorinated acyl portion. The nitrogen is attached to a benzene ring carrying a bromine atom on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, so the aromatic ring is ortho-disubstituted. The benzene ring is planar and rigid, while the aliphatic carbon framework and the two CF3 groups add some bulk and rotational freedom around single bonds. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the bromine breaks the symmetry of the aromatic ring.

This molecule is built around a central amide linkage connecting a carbonyl carbon to an aniline-type nitrogen. The aromatic portion is a single benzene ring bearing two chlorine atoms on adjacent positions flanking the nitrogen attachment point, giving a 2,6-dichlorophenyl substitution pattern. The acyl side carries a carbon bearing two trifluoromethyl groups, each a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky substituent, creating a compact, highly fluorinated branch. The aromatic ring and amide plane are conjugated and fairly rigid, while the bis(trifluoromethyl) branch adds steric bulk with limited flexibility. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and the carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor, and the fluorine atoms offer only weak acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, with two benzene rings joined by a single bond. One ring carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) and an amide nitrogen on the adjacent carbon, forming an anilide.
