The amide is acylated by a carbon bearing two trifluoromethyl groups, so the acyl portion is a CH bearing two CF3 substituents. The phenyl ring on the other side of the biaryl bond is unsubstituted. The aromatic framework is rigid and planar, while the biaryl bond allows some rotation and the bulky CF3 groups add steric demand. The amide N-H is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen and methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methyl groups, giving a 3,4-dimethyl substitution pattern. Attached at the position para to one methyl is an amide nitrogen, so the aromatic ring is linked through an N-H amide to a carbonyl carbon. The acyl portion carries a central carbon bearing two trifluoromethyl groups, which makes that end of the molecule bulky and highly fluorinated. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the amide linkage and the bond to the fluorinated carbon allow some conformational flexibility. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor; the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituent ends differ.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three methyl groups, arranged so that two sit meta to each other and the third lies ortho to the amide nitrogen, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is fused to nothing else and is fully planar and rigid. Attached to the ring through a nitrogen is an amide group, whose carbonyl carbon bears a carbon that carries two trifluoromethyl groups, making that portion highly fluorinated and bulky. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The alkyl branch and amide linkage provide some conformational flexibility around the single bonds.

The molecule is an acyclic tertiary amide built on a short carbon chain with no rings. The nitrogen carries two identical unbranched hexyl chains, making it a dihexyl-substituted amide nitrogen, and it is bonded directly to a carbonyl carbon. The alpha carbon next to the carbonyl bears two trifluoromethyl groups, which together form a compact, strongly electron-withdrawing substitution pattern. The two hexyl chains give the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, while the amide linkage adds some rigidity around the nitrogen-carbonyl bond. The amide oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor because the nitrogen is fully substituted.

The molecule is an N-butyl amide built on a short acyclic chain, with no rings present. Its backbone is a three-carbon unit: a carbonyl carbon bearing the amide nitrogen, which connects to an n-butyl group, and an alpha carbon that carries two trifluoromethyl groups, giving a branched, sterically crowded center. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The six fluorine atoms are concentrated on one end of the molecule, producing a strongly electron-withdrawing region, and the molecule is flexible overall because of its many single bonds, apart from the partially rigid amide linkage. It has no internal symmetry beyond the local equivalence of the two CF3 groups.

This molecule is a dihydropyrimidinone built on a six-membered ring containing two nitrogens and a cyclic urea-type amide carbonyl, fused to nothing but carrying two appended aromatic rings. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon adjacent to an ester, and the ester is a benzyl ester whose phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The third ring carbon bears a catechol group, a benzene ring with two adjacent hydroxyl substituents. The ring contains one stereogenic carbon, linking the ring to the catechol, so the scaffold is non-planar and only partly flexible. Hydrogen-bond donors include the ring N–H groups and the two phenolic O–H groups, while acceptors include the carbonyl oxygens and the phenolic oxygens.

The molecule is a dihydropyrimidinone-type scaffold: a six-membered ring containing two nitrogens and a urea-like carbonyl, bearing a methyl group and an amyl ester on adjacent ring carbons. The sp3 carbon at the ring junction carries a fused benzodioxole group, a bicyclic aromatic system made of a benzene ring joined to a five-membered methylenedioxy ring. The ester and cyclic urea carbonyls, along with the two ring N–H groups, provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the dioxole oxygens act as acceptors. The pentyl chain is flexible, whereas the fused ring systems are largely rigid, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the core.

This molecule is a dihydropyrimidinone built on a six-membered ring containing two nitrogens and a urea-type carbonyl, bearing a methyl group on one ring carbon and a propyl ester on another. The fourth ring carbon, which is sp3-hybridized, carries a 1,3-benzodioxole group, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered dioxole ring through an O-CH2-O bridge. The pyrimidinone ring is not fully planar, giving the core moderate rigidity, while the propyl chain adds conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two ring systems and substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the central ring. Two N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens, the ester carbonyl, and the ring oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a dihydropyrimidinone built on a six-membered partially saturated pyrimidine ring, with a cyclic urea unit (an NH–C(=O)–NH arrangement) embedded in the ring. A carbon–carbon double bond conjugates with the ring nitrogen and the adjacent ester, creating a planar enamine-like region, while the sp3 carbon bearing the phenyl group sits at the ring junction and gives the scaffold a puckered, moderately rigid shape. A monosubstituted phenyl ring is attached to that sp3 carbon, and a methyl group sits on the double bond. The propyl ester carries a carbonyl oxygen and an ether oxygen as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two ring NH groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the phenyl and ester substituents occupy distinct positions.

This molecule is a 3,4-dihydropyrimidine-2(1H)-thione, a six-membered partially saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms and a thiocarbonyl group in place of a ring carbonyl. The ring carbons bear a methyl group and a benzyl ester substituent on one alkene carbon, and a phenyl ring on the sp3 carbon between the ring nitrogen and the alkene carbon, so the scaffold is non-planar at that position. Two unsubstituted phenyl rings are present, one attached directly to the ring and one linked through a CH2 to the ester oxygen, giving the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The thiocarbonyl and ester carbonyl act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two ring N–H groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The benzyl ester and pendant phenyl groups add rotational flexibility, whereas the fused-looking core remains comparatively rigid.

This molecule is a dihydropyrimidine-2-thione built around a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms, a cyclic thiourea unit, and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with the ester. A propyl ester group is attached to one ring carbon, and a methyl group sits on the adjacent alkene carbon. The ring carbon bearing the phenyl group is sp3-hybridized, so the scaffold is partly puckered rather than fully planar, with a pendant unsubstituted phenyl ring as the only other ring system. The thiourea N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the thiocarbonyl sulfur and the ester carbonyl oxygen serve as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its flexibility comes mainly from rotation about the propyl chain and the phenyl bond.

This molecule is a 1,4-dihydropyridine built on a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that carries an NH group, two methyl substituents, and two isopropyl ester groups at the 3- and 5-positions. The C4 carbon of the dihydropyridine ring is sp3-hybridized and bears a phenyl ring substituted with a hydroxyl group ortho to the attachment point and a methoxy group meta to it. The two ester groups are symmetric about the ring, giving the dihydropyridine core a near-mirror-symmetric arrangement, although the substituted aryl group breaks overall symmetry. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygens, the ester oxygens, the methoxy oxygen, and the phenolic hydroxyl act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the phenol also contributes a donor site. The dihydropyridine ring is partially rigid, while the ester and aryl substituents add rotational flexibility.

The molecule is a 1,4-dihydropyridine built around a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that is non-aromatic and partially saturated, with the sp3-hybridized carbon at position 4 giving the ring a boat-like, non-planar shape. Two propyl ester groups are attached to the ring at positions 3 and 5, making the two ester substituents chemically equivalent in their placement. A methyl group sits at each of positions 2 and 6, flanking the ring nitrogen. The fourth position carries an aryl substituent: a benzene ring bearing a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons. The ring NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygens of the ester groups, the ring nitrogen, and the methoxy and hydroxyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a dihydropyridine built on a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that is non-aromatic, with one sp3 carbon bearing a phenyl substituent. The ring carries two methyl groups and two ester groups, each a propyl ester, positioned on opposite sides of the ring in a symmetric pattern. The phenyl ring is attached at the sp3 carbon, so it sits out of the plane of the heterocycle. Its nitrogen bears a hydrogen, which makes it a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens of the esters act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is partly rigid, but the propyl ester chains are flexible.

The molecule is a disubstituted malonic acid: a single quaternary carbon carries two carboxylic acid groups, a methyl group, and a benzyl group (a CH2 linked to a phenyl ring). The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and fused to nothing, so the only ring system is this simple aromatic benzene ring attached through a flexible methylene linker. The quaternary center is not symmetric, because the methyl and benzyl groups differ, giving the molecule no internal mirror or rotational symmetry; the central carbon is also a stereocenter in principle, though the SMILES specifies no configuration. Because of the sp3 center and rotatable single bonds, the framework is fairly flexible apart from the rigid phenyl ring. Each carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), for a total of two donors and four acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings in the classic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene arrangement: three six-membered rings fused to a five-membered ring. The ring fusion is largely saturated, with a single ring-internal carbon-carbon double bond in the first six-membered ring and an exocyclic ethylidene group attached to the five-membered ring. A secondary acetate ester is attached to one carbon of the first ring, and two angular methyl groups sit at ring junctions. The only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two oxygens of the ester, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid fused framework contrasts with the flexible ethylidene side chain and the rotatable acetate group.

This molecule is built on a steroid-type scaffold of four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, with the five-membered ring fused at the far end. The skeleton has a methyl group at each of two angular ring-junction positions, which gives the core a rigid, compact shape. A carbon side chain projects from the five-membered ring and terminates in a carboxylic acid, an acid group that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. Two secondary hydroxyl groups sit at separate positions on the ring framework, each able to donate and accept hydrogen bonds. One ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond, adding some planarity to that region. The molecule lacks any symmetry, because its substituents are placed asymmetrically around the fused ring system.

This molecule is built on a steroid scaffold: four fused rings in the classic cyclopentanohydrophenanthrene arrangement, three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, with all ring-fusion junctions bearing angular methyl groups. At one end of the five-membered ring sits an acetate ester, an oxygen-linked acetyl group, while on the opposite side of the framework a two-carbon acetyl ketone is attached to a six-membered ring. Two angular methyl groups project from the ring junctions, adding steric bulk. The fused ring system is largely rigid, though the saturated rings can adopt chair-like conformations and the side chains retain some rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond limited local symmetry. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the oxygens of the ester and ketone groups, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic skeleton built from four rings, three six-membered and one five-membered, joined in a linear-angular arrangement typical of the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene core. It contains one isolated ring-fusion alkene in the five-membered ring and a second conjugated double bond in the ring A system, which is accompanied by a ketone (enone) group. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-fusion carbons, adding steric bulk and rigidity to the framework. Overall the scaffold is largely rigid, with limited rotational freedom, and it has only a single hydrogen-bond acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen) and no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a steroid-type fused polycyclic scaffold of four rings, three six-membered and one five-membered, with angular methyl groups at two ring-junction carbons. The five-membered ring carries a ring double bond and an alkyne linker bearing a phenyl group, which projects outward from the framework. A formate ester (an O-formyl group) sits on one carbon of the six-membered ring. Overall the skeleton is rigid and fused, while the phenylethynyl and formate substituents add some flexibility. The ester oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its asymmetry arises from the substitution pattern.

This molecule is a steroid-type tetracyclic scaffold: three fused six-membered rings followed by a fused five-membered ring, with two angular methyl groups at the ring junctions. The A ring carries a hydroxyl group on a saturated carbon and is conjugated through an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone, which sits in the central B ring region. A ketone also appears on the terminal five-membered D ring, so the molecule has two carbonyl acceptors and one hydroxyl that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The fused, largely rigid polycyclic framework has limited conformational flexibility, and the lack of any internal symmetry means the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

This molecule is a steroid built on a fused four-ring scaffold of three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring, with angular methyl groups at two ring-fusion positions. Two acetate esters are present: one on the A-ring hydroxyl position and one on the D-ring carbon, which also bears a phenylethynyl substituent. Because the rings are fused together, the framework is conformationally rigid, with only the side chains and ester groups free to rotate. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the two ends carry different substituents. Its only hydrogen-bond capability comes from the four carbonyl oxygens of the acetate groups, which can act as acceptors, while no donor groups are present.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic scaffold built from four rings: three saturated six-membered carbocycles fused linearly with a five-membered ring, the usual cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene framework. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-junction carbons, and the ring system is largely rigid, with a phenethyl chain attached to one of the five-membered ring carbons. A secondary hydroxyl is on the first ring and a tertiary hydroxyl is on the five-membered ring, both able to donate and accept hydrogen bonds. A terminal phenyl ring is attached through a two-carbon linker, adding flexibility to that side portion, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused tetracyclic framework with three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, built from the fused cyclohexane and cyclopentane units typical of a cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton. The A-ring carries a secondary acetate ester, an acyloxy group attached to a ring carbon, which provides a carbonyl oxygen acceptor and an ester oxygen acceptor but no hydrogen-bond donors. One ring carbon bears a cyclic 1,3-dioxolane ketal, formed from a ketone protected with ethylene glycol, which adds two ether-type oxygen acceptors. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-fusion positions, contributing rigid steric bulk. The fused ring system is largely saturated and conformationally constrained, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a tetracyclic steroid-type scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, in the classic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene arrangement. It carries two ketone groups, one on a six-membered ring and one on the five-membered ring, along with a single ester group in which an acetyl unit is bonded to an oxygen on the first ring. The two angular methyl groups sit at ring-fusion carbons, and the ring fusions give the core a largely rigid, fused character with limited conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no hydroxyl or amine groups, but its two ketone oxygens and two ester oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall, the structure is asymmetric, with the substituents placed unevenly across the polycyclic framework.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, all fused together in a rigid, largely saturated framework. The ring system is fully carbocyclic with no heteroatoms in the core, and angular methyl groups project from the ring junctions. A propylidene-type double bond sits exocyclic to the five-membered ring, adding a short unsaturated side chain. The only heteroatom-bearing group is an ester on one of the six-membered rings, formed by an oxygen linked to a carbonyl carbon carrying a methyl group, which contributes a hydrogen-bond acceptor site. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries two identical 3,5-dimethyl-4-hydroxyphenyl rings and two ethyl ester arms, one of which is a CH2 linked to a second CH2 bearing the ester on the other side, giving a 3,3-diaryl pentanedioate skeleton. Each aryl ring is a benzene ring with two ortho methyl groups flanking a phenolic hydroxyl at the para position, so the ring systems are monocyclic with no ring fusion. The two phenol OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the two ester carbonyl oxygens and the ester ether oxygens serve as acceptors. The molecule shows approximate twofold symmetry through the central quaternary carbon, and its sp3 centers and rotatable ester chains make it fairly flexible.

This molecule is a fused, fully aromatic polycyclic system built around a central six-membered ring that contains two oxygen atoms. Its skeleton is a planar, rigid scaffold of four linearly or angularly fused six-membered rings: two benzene rings flank a central pyrazine-type ring, and a dioxin-type ring bridges them through two ether oxygens. The two nitrogen atoms sit in the pyrazine ring, one on each side of the fused system. The molecule has no stereocenters and no flexible side chains, so it is essentially flat and conformationally locked. Because the nitrogens lack attached hydrogens, they can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two ether oxygens offer additional weak acceptor sites and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four identical substituents, so its scaffold is a tetrasubstituted aromatic core. Each substituent is a –CH2–O–CH2–C≡C–H chain, meaning a benzylic methylene linked through an ether oxygen to a propargyl group carrying a terminal alkyne. The ring carries no fused rings, and the four arms are placed at alternating positions, giving a symmetric pattern with two pairs of ortho-related arms. Because each arm is attached through several rotatable single bonds, the molecule is quite flexible, while the rigid benzene core and linear alkyne ends limit some conformational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are carbon-bound, but the four ether oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a tetrahydronaphthalene (tetralin) scaffold, in which a saturated six-membered carbocycle is fused to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring carries two methyl substituents at positions that leave the remaining aromatic carbons unsubstituted on one side, giving a 1,4-dimethyl-type pattern relative to the ring fusion. The saturated ring bears an acetate ester, an O-acyl group in which an acetyl carbonyl is bonded through oxygen to a carbon on the non-aromatic ring. The ester carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining N-H and O-H positions are absent. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid, while the ester side chain offers some rotational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane ring, a saturated six-membered carbocycle with no fused or bridged rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons of this ring, giving it a 1,2-disubstitution pattern. One substituent is a free carboxylic acid group, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The other is an ester linked to a 2-hydroxyethyl group, which contributes a carbonyl acceptor along with a terminal hydroxyl that acts as both a donor and an acceptor. The ring itself is flexible and can adopt chair conformations, while the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a six-membered 1,3,5-thiadiazine-type ring containing a nitrogen and a sulfur atom is fused to a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring, with the two rings sharing a nitrogen-carbon bond. An isopropyl group sits on the saturated nitrogen of the six-membered ring, and a pyridin-3-yl group is attached to the carbon of the triazole ring. The aromatic pyridine nitrogen and the triazole nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused core is largely rigid and planar, with the isopropyl group providing a small, flexible branch, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a 1,2,4-triazole ring fused to a six-membered thiadiazine ring that contains sulfur and a nitrogen bearing an aryl substituent. A 3-nitrophenyl group is attached directly to the triazole carbon, placing the nitro group meta to the point of connection. The second substituent, a 2-nitrophenyl group, hangs off the nitrogen in the six-membered ring, with its nitro group ortho to that attachment. Both nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and contribute oxygen acceptor sites, while the fused heterocycle offers additional nitrogen acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are fully substituted and no N–H or O–H groups are present. The fused ring system is largely planar and rigid, with the two aryl rings giving the molecule a relatively extended, asymmetric shape.

This molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring fused to a six-membered 1,3,5-thiadiazine ring, sharing an N–C bond. Attached to the triazole carbon is a meta-nitrophenyl group, with the nitro group (a strongly electron-withdrawing, hydrogen-bond-accepting substituent) positioned at the meta carbon of that benzene ring. The opposite side of the bicyclic system carries an ortho-tolyl group, a benzene ring bearing an adjacent methyl substituent, attached through a ring nitrogen. The triazole nitrogens and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused core and two aromatic rings make the structure fairly rigid, though the N-aryl bond and the biaryl linkage allow some rotation.

This molecule is built from a benzoic acid core: a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with a chlorine atom on the ring positioned para to the azo linkage and meta to the acid. An azo group (N=N) links that benzene ring to a five-membered thiazolidine-type heterocycle, which contains a sulfur atom, a thiocarbonyl (C=S), and a ring carbonyl (C=O) adjacent to the azo-bearing carbon. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, while the thiazolidinone ring is partly saturated and the azo bridge lends the overall framework a degree of conjugation and rigidity, though the bond to the heterocycle allows some rotation. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the two ring systems and their substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The carboxylic acid OH and the ring N-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens, the thiocarbonyl sulfur, and the azo nitrogens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic core: a five-membered triazole ring fused to a five-membered thiadiazole ring, both containing multiple nitrogen atoms and a sulfur atom. Two aryl rings are attached to this core at different positions, creating a largely planar, extended conjugated framework. One aryl ring is a para-substituted benzene bearing a linear n-butoxy ether chain, which adds a flexible tail. The other is a benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom and a nitro group on adjacent carbons, giving an electron-poor, asymmetric substitution pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because of these differing substituents. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the nitrogen atoms of the heterocycles, the ether oxygen, and the nitro oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a five-membered thiazolidinone ring, specifically a rhodanine-type scaffold with a ring carbonyl adjacent to an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond and a thiocarbonyl group. That exocyclic alkene links the heterocycle to a para-substituted benzene ring, giving an extended conjugated system with a rigid, largely planar core. The benzene ring carries a bis(2-chloroethyl)amino group at the position opposite the linkage, and the ring nitrogen of the thiazolidinone bears a second bis(2-chloroethyl)aminomethyl arm, adding two flexible side chains. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the two substituent arms differ in attachment. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the carbonyl oxygen, thiocarbonyl sulfur, and tertiary nitrogen atoms can act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered rhodanine-type ring, a thiazolidinone bearing a thiocarbonyl group at C2 and a carbonyl at C4, with an exocyclic C=C double bond at C5 linking it to a substituted phenyl ring. That phenyl ring carries a hydroxyl group and a methoxy group in an ortho relationship, giving a guaiacol-like pattern. The nitrogen of the thiazolidinone ring bears a CH2-NH linker that connects to a second benzene ring, which is substituted with a nitro group in the meta position relative to the amine. The arrangement is largely planar and conjugated across the exocyclic alkene, which limits rotation, while the CH2 linker adds some flexibility. The hydroxyl and amine NH serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl, thiocarbonyl, nitro, and methoxy oxygens act as acceptors.

This molecule is a 5-benzylidene rhodanine-type scaffold: a five-membered thiazolidine ring bearing a thiocarbonyl at C2 and a carbonyl at C4, with an exocyclic C=C linking the ring to a substituted phenyl group. The phenyl ring carries a methoxy group ortho to a hydroxyl group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted benzene pattern. The ring nitrogen is substituted with a CH2 linker leading to an NH-bridged para-nitrophenyl group, which is strongly electron-withdrawing. The conjugated arylidene system makes the core largely planar and fairly rigid, while the N-CH2-NH linker adds some flexibility. The phenol OH and the NH serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl, thiocarbonyl, nitro, methoxy, and ring oxygen and nitrogen atoms act as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a 1,2,4-triazole ring is joined to a 1,3,4-thiadiazine-type six-membered ring that contains a sulfur atom, a saturated sp3 carbon bearing a hydrogen, and an N-H. Attached to the triazole is a para-ethoxyphenyl group, and attached to the saturated carbon is a para-methoxyphenyl group, so the two aryl rings sit at opposite ends of the scaffold. Both aromatic rings carry electron-donating alkoxy substituents at the para position, each with an oxygen acceptor. The molecule has an overall elongated, roughly linear shape with a flexible ethyl and methyl ether tail on either end, while the fused core is comparatively rigid. The ring N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the triazole nitrogens and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a six-membered thiadiazine-type ring (containing a sulfur atom and an sp3 carbon) is fused to a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring. A para-dimethylaminophenyl group hangs off the saturated carbon of the six-membered ring, giving a strongly electron-rich, donor-substituted aromatic end. On the triazole ring sits a meta-nitrophenyl group, which introduces a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent that contrasts with the dimethylamino group across the molecule. The scaffold is largely rigid because of the fused heteroaromatic system, while the two aryl substituents can rotate about their single bonds. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the two aryl groups sit on different rings and have different substitution patterns. The triazole nitrogens and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the single N–H on the saturated ring can serve as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a five-membered triazole ring is fused to a five-membered thiadiazine-type ring containing a sulfur atom and a saturated carbon bearing a 4-methoxyphenyl group, with an NH linking into the triazole nitrogen. The triazole carries a 4-nitrophenyl substituent at a ring carbon, giving a para-substitution pattern on both benzene rings. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing feature, while the methoxy group is an electron-donating ether. Overall the scaffold is largely rigid and planar in its aromatic portions, with the sp3 carbon adding some three-dimensional character. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the triazole nitrogens, the nitro oxygens, and the methoxy oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring is joined to a five-membered thiadiazine-type ring containing sulfur, forming a rigid triazolothiadiazoline scaffold. A meta-nitrophenyl group is attached directly to one carbon of the triazole ring, and the nitro substituent sits on the benzene ring at the meta position relative to that attachment point. A para-chlorophenyl group is bonded to the saturated carbon of the thiadiazine ring, giving the molecule two aromatic rings, one on each side of the fused core. The nitro group acts as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the ring nitrogens provide additional acceptor sites and the NH group offers a single hydrogen-bond donor. Overall the molecule is largely planar and conformationally restricted, with limited symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the substituents.

The molecule consists of a meta-substituted nitrophenyl ring attached directly to a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system. The nitro group sits on one side of the benzene ring, and the other carbon atom at the meta position bonds to a triazole ring, which is fused to a partially saturated five-membered thiadiazine-type ring. A phenyl group hangs off the saturated portion, creating a sp3-bearing carbon within the fused system. The nitro group contributes strong electron-withdrawing character and oxygen acceptor sites, while the ring nitrogen atoms serve as additional acceptors; the single NH within the fused ring can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The fused core and aromatic rings are largely planar and rigid, though the phenyl substituent gives some conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry axis due to its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a 1,2,4-triazole ring is joined to a 1,3,4-thiadiazine-type six-membered ring that contains both a sulfur atom and an NH nitrogen, forming a rigid, partially saturated scaffold. Two 2-methoxyphenyl groups are attached: one directly to the triazole carbon, and one to the sp3 carbon that bridges the sulfur and the NH nitrogen. Each methoxy group is an aryl ether, and the ortho placement of both methoxy substituents creates a fairly crowded, twisted arrangement around the core. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the two aryl groups sit on chemically different parts of the scaffold. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the triazole and ether oxygens and nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a 1,2,4-triazole ring joined to a five-membered thiadiazoline ring that contains sulfur, creating a triazolothiadiazole scaffold. A 2-methoxyphenyl group is attached directly to the triazole carbon, and a phenyl group sits on the saturated carbon of the thiadiazoline ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused heteroaromatic core is largely planar and rigid, while the two pendant aryl rings can rotate about their single bonds. The methoxy oxygen and the ring nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds, and the ring NH group can donate one.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core: a 1,2,4-triazole ring fused to a 1,3,4-thiadiazine-type ring containing a sulfur atom and an N-H. A para-methoxyphenyl group is attached directly to the triazole carbon, giving an aryl substituent with an ether oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds. A furan-2-yl ring hangs off the sp3 carbon that bridges the nitrogen and sulfur, and this substitution introduces a stereocenter. The aromatic rings are largely planar, while the partially saturated six-membered ring adds some conformational flexibility. The single N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and several nitrogen atoms along with the ether and furan oxygens act as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core in which a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring is joined to a five-membered thiazolidine-type ring sharing one bond, giving a rigid, nearly planar fused scaffold. The triazole carries a pyridin-3-yl group on one carbon, adding an aromatic nitrogen-containing substituent. The saturated carbon linking the sulfur and the ring nitrogen bears a 2-methoxyphenyl group, with the methoxy ether oriented ortho to the attachment point. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its rotatable bonds are limited to the biaryl-type connections to the methoxyphenyl and pyridyl rings. Its hydrogen-bond capacity comes from the pyridine and triazole nitrogens, which can accept hydrogen bonds, the ether oxygen as an additional acceptor, and the ring N–H as a single donor.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one ring nitrogen. Attached at the 2-position is a hydrazine group, a nitrogen-nitrogen chain whose terminal NH2 is free and whose adjacent NH links it to the ring. At the 5-position sits an N-hydroxy nitro-type group, a nitrogen bearing both an oxide and a hydroxyl, which is attached to the ring carbon through nitrogen. The substitution is therefore non-symmetric, with the two substituents placed on opposite sides of the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydrazine and the oxygenated nitrogen group provide some rotational freedom. The hydrazine NH groups and the hydroxyl can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogen, the oxygen atoms, and the hydrazine nitrogens can act as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a six-membered oxygen-containing ring, a dihydropyran-type scaffold with one carbon-carbon double bond within the ring. The ring carries three hydroxyl groups on adjacent sp3 carbons, one of which bears a hydroxymethyl arm. A methyl imidate group, an O-methyl ester analog with an exocyclic C=NH, is attached to the ring carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, giving the ring an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The lack of symmetry and the cis or trans relationships among the hydroxyls make the framework fairly rigid, though the hydroxymethyl arm adds some flexibility. The hydroxyl groups and the imine nitrogen provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the ring oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygens, and the imine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic ethyl ester built around a single ketene dithioacetal-type alkene. The carbon backbone is a short chain: an ethyl group bonded through an ester oxygen to a carbonyl carbon, which is attached to a tetrasubstituted C=C double bond. One alkene carbon carries a nitrile (C≡N) group, while the other carries two methylthio (–SCH3) substituents, giving an electron-rich, sulfur-substituted terminus opposite the electron-poor cyano-ester end. There are no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is flexible, with free rotation about the single bonds of the ethyl and methylthio groups. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond a local, approximate two-fold relationship between the two methylthio groups. The ester carbonyl oxygen and nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built from an isoquinoline core, a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, and this core carries a hydroxy group and a methoxy group on its benzenoid portion. Through a single methylene linker at the isoquinoline's carbon-1 position, it connects to a second aromatic ring, a phenol bearing a methoxy group ortho to the hydroxyl. The two aromatic halves are attached by a flexible CH2 bridge, so the molecule has some rotational freedom while the fused and substituted rings remain planar and rigid. Its hydrogen-bond capacity comes from the two phenolic hydroxyl groups, which can act as donors, and from the nitrogen of the isoquinoline ring and the oxygens of the methoxy groups, which can act as acceptors. The overall arrangement is asymmetric, since the two aryl halves carry different substitution patterns.

The molecule is a fused tetracyclic system built around a central pyrazolone-type core: a five-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogens, one of which carries an N-methyl group and the other an N-phenyl group, with the adjacent ring carbon bearing a carbonyl oxygen. This heterocycle is fused to an aromatic ring that carries a methylthio (S-methyl) substituent, and that ring is further bridged to a dihydro-fused bicyclic unit containing a CH2-CH2 linkage and a second benzene ring, creating a largely planar, rigid polycyclic framework. Although the phenyl ring on the nitrogen can rotate, the fused core is essentially fixed and lacks any meaningful symmetry. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all nitrogens are substituted and no N-H or O-H bonds are present.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring that carries a phenyl ring at one position, giving a biphenyl-type scaffold with no ring fusion. The central ring bears two pyrrolidine substituents, each attached through its nitrogen, placed at the meta positions relative to the phenyl link, so the pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the biaryl bond. Both pyrrolidine rings are saturated five-membered amines, and the tertiary nitrogens are fully substituted, so they carry no N-H donors. The aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, while the pyrrolidines add some conformational flexibility. The nitrogens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a dihydropyrimidine-2-thione built on a six-membered partially saturated ring containing two nitrogen atoms, with a thiocarbonyl group (C=S) at the carbon between them. The ring carries a methyl group on one alkene carbon and a methyl ester on the adjacent carbon, forming a conjugated enamine-ester arrangement. A phenyl ring is attached to the sp3 carbon at the ring's far side, giving a single benzene substituent with no other substitution on it. The molecule is largely planar in its conjugated core while the saturated ring carbon introduces a modest out-of-plane twist. The two N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur and ester carbonyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a single acyclic backbone with no ring systems, so it is a flexible, open-chain structure. The central carbon-carbon double bond bears a dithio-type substituent on one end: a nitrogen atom carrying two allyl groups (each a three-carbon chain with a terminal alkene), and on the other end a methylthio group attached to the same carbon. The adjacent carbon carries a nitrile group, and the far end of that alkene carbon bears a primary carboxamide. The two terminal alkenes and the thioether sulfur add further conformational freedom, so the molecule lacks any rigid or symmetric core. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated in the primary amide, which can both donate hydrogen bonds through its NH2 group and accept them at the carbonyl oxygen, while the nitrile nitrogen and the tertiary amine nitrogen act only as weaker acceptors.

This molecule is a six-membered 2-pyridone (pyridin-2(1H)-one) ring bearing an N-amino group on the ring nitrogen. The ring carries a nitrile substituent adjacent to the carbonyl, a trifluoromethyl group on the neighboring carbon, and a thiophene ring attached at the position opposite the nitrile-bearing carbon. The thiophene is a separate five-membered aromatic ring linked by a single bond, so the molecule has no fused ring system and a largely planar, conjugated aromatic framework with limited flexibility beyond rotation about the biaryl bond. Hydrogen-bond donation is limited to the exocyclic N–H of the amino group, while the carbonyl oxygen, nitrile nitrogen, and fluorine atoms serve as acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry element.

The molecule is built around a benzothiazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. Attached at the 2-position of this heteroaromatic unit is a carbon that carries a nitrile group and is double-bonded to a cyclopentylidene ring, so the exocyclic alkene links the aromatic scaffold to a non-aromatic carbocycle. The fused benzothiazole is planar and rigid, while the cyclopentylidene portion adds a small, puckered, non-aromatic ring. The molecule has no stereocenters and no obvious internal symmetry, since the aromatic and aliphatic halves differ. The nitrile nitrogen and the thiazole nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built from a central furan ring bearing, at its 2-position, an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond that links to a 3-acetylbutan-2-one-type fragment, so two acetyl groups flank the alkene carbon. The furan's 5-position carries a phenyl ring, which is itself substituted at the meta position with a nitro group, giving a biaryl-type arrangement. The conjugated system spans the furan, the vinylic linker, and the attached aryl ring, producing an extended, largely planar framework with limited rotational freedom about the single bonds that join the rings. The two carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement is asymmetric because the two acetyl groups sit on the same carbon but the nitro group occupies only one side of the biaryl system.

The molecule is built around a three-atom acrylamide-type backbone: a nitrile carbon and a primary carboxamide carbon flank a central alkene carbon. A para-chlorophenyl ring is attached to the alkene through a single carbon-carbon bond, so the aromatic ring is a simple six-membered benzene system with one substituent at the position opposite the point of attachment. The nitrile group (a carbon-nitrogen triple bond) and the primary amide (a carbonyl bearing an NH2 group) are both electron-withdrawing and conjugated with the double bond. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with restricted rotation about the alkene and limited flexibility overall. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site, while the nitrile nitrogen and carbonyl oxygen serve as additional acceptors.

This molecule is an unbranched, conjugated carboxylic acid built around a six-carbon chain bearing a methyl group at the alpha position. The carbon backbone contains two consecutive carbon-carbon double bonds that extend conjugation out to a monosubstituted benzene ring attached at the terminal end, giving a planar, extended scaffold. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so it carries no additional functional groups and has no substitution pattern to speak of. The terminal carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens. Because the double bonds are rigid, the molecule is relatively stiff along its length, with limited rotational freedom compared with a saturated chain, and it has no internal symmetry axis beyond what the planar conjugated system imposes.

This molecule is an ethyl ester of a cyanoacrylic acid, with the alpha carbon carrying a nitrile group and a beta carbon double-bonded to a furan ring. The furan is substituted at its 5-position by a biphenyl-like unit: a second benzene ring bearing an ortho methoxy group. The scaffold is largely planar and conjugated across the acrylate, furan, and aryl rings, which makes the core fairly rigid, while the ethyl ester and methoxy groups add some rotational freedom. There is no internal symmetry. The molecule has two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites in the ester and one each in the nitrile, furan oxygen, and methoxy oxygen, but no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a flat bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. At the 2-position of the thiazole sits a hexylthio chain, a flexible six-carbon alkyl group attached through a sulfur atom. The benzene ring carries an amide linkage, where an NH group is bonded to a carbonyl that connects to a methylene and an aryl ether oxygen. That terminal aryl ring is a 2,4-dichlorophenyl group, with chlorines at the ortho and para positions relative to the ether oxygen. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, and its rigid aromatic core contrasts with the flexible alkyl chain and ether linker. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen, the ether oxygen, and the thiazole nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a coumarin scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a six-membered α-pyrone (2H-chromen-2-one) lactone ring, giving a flat bicyclic aromatic core. The lactone carbonyl sits on the pyranone ring, and the nitrogen of a propylamino group is attached at the 4-position of that ring, so the substituent is a secondary amine NH bearing an n-propyl chain. The fused system is essentially rigid and planar, while the propyl tail adds a small degree of conformational flexibility. The amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two styryl arms placed at the 1 and 3 positions, a meta substitution pattern. Each arm consists of a carbon-carbon double bond linking the central ring to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the overall skeleton is a symmetric, extended conjugated system with two phenyl termini. The two C=C double bonds carry the connectivity of the arms, and the planarity of the conjugated framework makes the molecule fairly rigid, with little flexibility beyond rotation about the single bonds. It contains no heteroatoms, no hydroxyl, amine, or carbonyl groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a five-membered oxazolone (azlactone) ring, a heterocycle containing one oxygen and one nitrogen, with a methyl group on the carbon between them. The ring carries an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond at the position adjacent to the nitrogen, which links it to a para-methylphenyl group, so the two ring systems are conjugated through a planar, extended pi system. A carbonyl group sits on the ring carbon next to the ring oxygen, making this an ester-type lactone. Overall the framework is largely flat and rigid, with little conformational freedom beyond the methyl rotation. The carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered 1,3-oxazol-5(4H)-one ring, a heterocycle containing an oxygen and a nitrogen with a lactone-type carbonyl adjacent to the ring oxygen. At the 2-position of this ring sits a phenyl group, which is attached through a single bond and is free to rotate. At the 4-position, an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond links the ring to a thiophene ring bearing its attachment at the 2-position, giving the molecule an extended conjugated, largely planar framework. Overall the structure is rigid and conjugated, with three aromatic or unsaturated ring systems in a fused-like arrangement across the ring junctions. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the sulfur and ring oxygen contribute weaker acceptor character.

The molecule is built around a central pyran-type ring that is fused on both sides to saturated carbocycles: one fused cyclohexane on each flanking edge, giving a tricyclic, largely rigid scaffold with a planar conjugated core. An exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond links this core to a para-methoxyphenyl group, so the methoxy ether oxygen sits at the far end of an extended conjugated system. The only oxygen-containing functions are the aryl methyl ether and the ring ether oxygen within the central heterocycle, which can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Apart from the flexible methylene units in the saturated rings, the framework is fairly rigid, and the substitution pattern on the benzene ring gives it a roughly mirror-symmetric, elongated shape.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The nitrogen at position 1 carries a methyl group, so it is an N-alkylated indole with no free N-H. A methyl group sits at position 3 of the five-membered ring, and a phenyl ring is attached at position 2, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pattern. The fused bicyclic framework is largely planar and rigid, with the phenyl ring able to rotate about its single bond to the indole. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only N-H position is capped by methyl. The aromatic nitrogen's lone pair is part of the aromatic system, so it is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a barbiturate-type pyrimidinetrione ring: a six-membered ring containing two amide-like NH groups flanked by three carbonyl carbons, with the central carbon bearing an exocyclic double bond. That alkylidene carbon links to a furan ring, which is substituted at its 5-position by a para-bromophenyl group, giving a biaryl-like extension. The conjugated chain of furan, phenyl, and the trione ring makes the framework largely planar and rigid, with few rotatable bonds beyond the biaryl linkage. The two ring NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the three carbonyl oxygens and the furan oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The bromine on the terminal phenyl ring gives the molecule a single, unsymmetrical substitution pattern.

The molecule is a fused tricyclic system built around a central pyranone (a six-membered oxygen-containing heterocycle bearing a carbonyl group). A fully saturated carbocyclic ring is fused to each side of this pyranone core, so the scaffold is a linear arrangement of three six-membered rings sharing edges. The aromatic-like pyranone ring carries a ketone-type carbonyl and an ether-type ring oxygen, both of which can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two outer cyclohexane-type rings are conformationally flexible and aliphatic, in contrast to the flatter, more rigid central heterocycle. The overall framework is largely unsubstituted beyond the fused ring positions, giving it a compact, roughly planar core with a mildly asymmetric shape.

The molecule is built on a six-membered cyclohexane-1,3-dione-type ring bearing a gem-dimethyl group on one carbon, giving a non-planar, somewhat rigid aliphatic scaffold. Two carbonyl groups sit on the ring, and the carbon between them carries an exocyclic hydrazone linkage (C=N–NH) that connects to a para-bromophenyl ring. The aromatic ring is disubstituted at opposite positions, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about its long axis, while the gem-dimethyl groups add a local steric bulk to the otherwise planar conjugated hydrazone system. The NH group of the hydrazone can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the two ring carbonyl oxygens and the imine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the molecule has a fairly extended, partially conjugated framework with limited conformational flexibility around the aryl–hydrazone junction.

The molecule is built from three connected aromatic and unsaturated units: a para-tolyl ring (a benzene carrying a methyl group) bonded directly to a furan ring, which in turn is linked through an exocyclic vinylic carbon to a five-membered unsaturated lactone (a butenolide-type ring). The furan and the lactone are joined by a C=C double bond, giving an extended conjugated, largely planar scaffold. The lactone carbonyl oxygen and the furan and ring oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The isobutyl side chain on the lactone ring is the only sp3-rich, flexible portion, and the methyl group on the tolyl ring adds a small, non-symmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule has a five-membered pyrazolidine-3,5-dione ring, a saturated-looking heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms with a carbonyl on each side of the ring. One nitrogen carries a phenyl substituent, while the other bears an N-H group. The carbon between the two carbonyls is joined through an exocyclic double bond to a benzylidene unit, giving an extended conjugated system that links the heterocycle to a second phenyl ring. The two phenyl rings are unfused and attached at different points, so the overall scaffold is fairly planar and rigid. Hydrogen-bond capability is set by the N-H as a donor and the two carbonyl oxygens as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a furan ring, a five-membered aromatic oxygen heterocycle, which is bonded at its 2-position to a phenyl ring carrying a nitro group on the carbon adjacent to the biaryl bond. The furan's 5-position connects through a vinylic CH=C linkage to a carbon bearing two acetyl groups, giving a 1,3-diketone unit with the alkene conjugated across the full framework. The nitro substituent is ortho to the furan-phenyl bond, which twists the two aromatic rings out of coplanarity and introduces some steric crowding. The conjugated, largely planar backbone is rigid in its core but has rotatable single bonds at the biaryl and acetyl positions, giving moderate flexibility. There is no molecular symmetry of note because the two ends of the molecule are chemically distinct. The carbonyl oxygens and nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a thioamide built around a central thiocarbonyl carbon that links two aromatic rings. One ring is a para-methoxyphenyl group, with the methoxy ether oxygen sitting opposite the point of attachment to the thiocarbonyl carbon. The other side is an N-phenyl group, so the thioamide nitrogen bears a plain unsubstituted benzene ring. The C=S and N–H groups together form a thioamide unit, where the NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and the sulfur and methoxy oxygen can act as acceptors. The two benzene rings are not fused, and the thioamide linker gives the molecule a moderate degree of conformational flexibility around its single bonds.

The molecule is built on a coumarin-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered α-pyrone (2H-chromen-2-one) ring, giving a flat, rigid bicyclic framework. The pyranone ring carries a lactone carbonyl within the ring, and a formyl (aldehyde) group sits on one carbon of the pyranone, while an amino group is attached to the adjacent carbon. These substituents are placed on adjacent positions of the heterocyclic ring, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry. Because the fused system is essentially planar with few rotatable bonds, the structure is conformationally rigid. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the carbonyl oxygens of the lactone and aldehyde and the ring oxygen can accept them.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. Substituents are arranged around the ring: an ethyl group on one carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, a primary amino group on the carbon between the two nitrogens, a chlorine atom on the carbon on the other side of the second nitrogen, and a methyl group on the remaining ring carbon. Because the ring is fully aromatic and carries no fused partners, the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the ethyl group contributing conformational flexibility. The amino group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, with two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, so there is no fused ring system. Three substituents decorate the ring: an ethyl group on one carbon, a methyl group on the adjacent carbon, and an amino group and a hydroxyl group flanking the second nitrogen-bearing carbon. The ring nitrogens and the exocyclic amino and hydroxyl groups together give the scaffold several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry, and its rigid planar core contrasts with the freely rotating ethyl group.

This molecule is built on a benzofuran core, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered furan ring that shares an oxygen-containing edge. The benzene ring carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) at a position para to the furan oxygen's attachment point, giving a single, asymmetric substitution pattern. At the furan carbon adjacent to the oxygen sits a three-carbon chain ending in a ketone, which adds rotational flexibility. At the neighboring furan carbon is a 5-methylfuran ring attached directly by a single bond, so the molecule is largely planar and aromatic across its fused and biaryl-like portions. The ketone oxygen and the ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries two adjacent methoxy groups, placing them in a 3,4-dimethoxy pattern relative to the carbonyl attachment, while the other ring bears a single chlorine atom at the position para to the carbonyl. Neither benzene ring is fused to another ring, so the scaffold consists of two separate aromatic rings joined through a single sp2 carbon. The molecule is largely planar and rigid around the ketone, though the methoxy groups and the twist between the two rings allow some conformational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen and the two methoxy oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a 4-(dimethylamino)phenyl ring linked through a vinylic carbon to a five-membered oxazolone (azlactone) heterocycle, which carries a phenyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. The exocyclic C=C double bond conjugates the aminophenyl ring with the oxazolone carbonyl, giving an extended, largely planar framework. The dimethylamino group is a tertiary amine that can only accept hydrogen bonds, while the lactone carbonyl and ring nitrogen serve as acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its rigid, conjugated core limits conformational flexibility to the rotation of the phenyl substituent.

The molecule is built around a furan ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, which carries two substituents at positions 2 and 5. At one end, an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond links the furan to an ethyl ester group and a nitrile (cyano) group, giving an electron-poor, conjugated acrylate-type unit. At the other end, the furan is joined directly to a para-nitrophenyl ring, so the molecule is essentially a linear, extended conjugated system with a nitro group on the terminal benzene. Its planar, rigid backbone limits rotation apart from the ethyl ester chain. Hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are abundant, from the carbonyl oxygen, nitrile nitrogen, nitro oxygens, and furan oxygen, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing a common edge. A carboxamide group is attached to one ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, and that amide nitrogen bears a phenyl ring, giving an anilide-type linkage. A bromine atom sits on the other ring of the naphthalene core, on the carbon next to the fusion atom, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and the carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor. The aromatic rings make the core largely planar and rigid, with only the C–N amide bond and the bond to the phenyl ring allowing rotation.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine scaffold, a planar aromatic system in which a five-membered pyrazole ring shares an edge with a six-membered pyrimidine ring. A para-methoxyphenyl group is attached to the pyrazole carbon, extending the conjugated framework. The pyrimidine ring carries a methyl group and a trifluoromethyl group, which sit on opposite sides of the fused core. The fused aromatic system is rigid, with the methoxyphenyl ring able to rotate only about a single bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen atoms and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered heteroaromatic ring containing one oxygen atom and a thiocarbonyl-type sulfur substituent, forming a pyran-4-thione core. Two phenyl rings are attached to the carbons flanking the ring oxygen, giving a 2,6-diaryl substitution pattern. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, and the two phenyl groups are rotationally fixed relative to it, so the scaffold is fairly rigid with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry through the axis running through the oxygen and the opposite carbon. The sulfur atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a central amide linkage connecting two aromatic systems. On one side sits a benzoyl group, a plain benzene ring bearing no substituents, attached directly to the carbonyl carbon. On the other side the nitrogen of the amide is bonded to the 2-position of a five-membered 1,3-thiazole ring, which carries a phenyl group at the 4-position, so the scaffold is a 4-phenylthiazol-2-yl amide. The molecule is largely planar and conjugated across the amide and the three aromatic rings, which limits rotational freedom to a few single bonds. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the thiazole ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a Meldrum's acid derivative: a six-membered 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione ring bearing a gem-dimethyl group on the carbon between the two ring oxygens, making it a cyclic diester of a dicarboxylic acid. The ring carbon at position 5 is sp2 and carries an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond linking it to a furan ring, which is substituted at its 5-position with a phenyl group, giving a biaryl-like extended conjugated system. The two carbonyl groups are lactone-type esters, and the exocyclic alkene is conjugated with both of them, making the arrangement largely planar and fairly rigid, with the gem-dimethyl groups providing the only notable three-dimensional bulk. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its four oxygen atoms in the ring and furan can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a furan ring bearing a para-tolyl group at one alpha position, so the two aromatic rings are joined directly into a biaryl-like arrangement. At the other alpha position of the furan, a vinyl linker connects to a cyclic 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione (Meldrum's acid-type) ring, which carries a gem-dimethyl group on the acetal carbon. The exocyclic C=C is conjugated with both the furan and the two ring carbonyls, making the overall scaffold largely planar and rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the tolyl linkage. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while its two lactone-type carbonyl oxygens and the ring oxygens of the furan and dioxanedione serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolidine-3,5-dione ring, a saturated ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and two carbonyl groups flanking the central carbon. One nitrogen carries a phenyl ring attached directly through a single bond, which makes the scaffold a 1-aryl derivative with no ring fusion. The exocyclic carbon at position 4 bears an isopropylidene group, giving a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with the adjacent carbonyl. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom around the phenyl and isopropylidene bonds, so it is fairly rigid. It has one N-H donor and two carbonyl oxygen acceptors, along with the nitrogen lone pairs in the ring.

This molecule is built on a five-membered oxazolone (azlactone) ring, a heterocycle containing an oxygen and a nitrogen atom alongside a carbonyl group. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the carbon between the ring oxygen and nitrogen, while the other ring carbon bears an exocyclic double bond leading to a benzylidene group, a second phenyl ring. The conjugated arrangement of two aromatic rings, the C=N and exocyclic C=C bonds, and the lactone carbonyl makes the scaffold largely planar and rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters, and the overall framework has an approximately two-fold pseudo-symmetry around its central axis. The carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione (Meldrum's acid-type) ring bearing a gem-dimethyl group at the carbon between the two ring oxygens, which gives the core a rigid, puckered shape. An exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond links this ring to a furan, which is substituted at the 5-position by a biphenyl-type unit: a phenyl ring attached to a second, nitro-bearing phenyl ring at the meta position. The nitro group, a strong electron-withdrawing substituent, sits on the outer ring at the meta position relative to the furan linkage. The conjugated system is largely planar and rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the bond joining the two phenyl rings. The lactone carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a 2,2-dimethyl-1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione (a Meldrum's acid-type) six-membered ring that bears two carbonyl groups flanking a gem-dimethyl ketal carbon. At the C5 position of this ring sits an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond linked to a 5-methylfuran ring, a five-membered aromatic oxygen heterocycle carrying a methyl group at the position adjacent to the ring oxygen. The conjugated arrangement of the furan, the exocyclic alkene, and the two ester-type carbonyls makes the framework largely planar and fairly rigid, with the gem-dimethyl group projecting out of that plane. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis of note because the furan and the dioxanedione ring are attached asymmetrically. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the two ring oxygens provide several hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a central ethylene unit, with one carbon bearing two nitrile groups (C#N) and the other carbon bearing two benzylthio groups, giving a fully substituted C=C double bond. Each sulfur atom links the alkene carbon to a CH2 that is attached to a phenyl ring, so the two benzyl groups are unfused, unsubstituted benzene rings. The two nitrile groups are linear and strongly electron-withdrawing, while the thioether sulfur atoms are flexible linkers. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry about the central double bond, though the benzyl arms can rotate freely, making the overall shape moderately flexible. The nitrogen atoms of the nitriles can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a furan-based acrylic acid: a five-membered aromatic furan ring bearing a single oxygen heteroatom, attached at its 2-position to a short two-carbon chain. That chain is an alpha,beta-unsaturated carboxylic acid, with a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated directly to the ring and terminated by a free carboxyl group. The conjugation between the furan ring, the alkene, and the carbonyl makes the scaffold largely planar and rigid, with restricted rotation about the linking bonds and no stereocenters. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a simple planar arrangement. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the furan oxygen acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring, forming an isoindole-1,3-dione (phthalimide-type) core. The benzene ring carries two methyl groups on adjacent-to-fusion positions in a 1,4-relationship, which gives the aromatic portion a symmetric substitution pattern across its long axis. The five-membered ring contains two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen that bears an N-methyl substituent, so the nitrogen is fully substituted and has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the fused framework is largely planar and rigid, with only the two methyl groups providing minor rotational freedom.

This molecule is a fused tetracyclic steroid-type scaffold: three cyclohexane-like six-membered rings fused linearly to a five-membered ring, with two angular methyl groups at ring-junction carbons. It contains three ketone (carbonyl) groups, located on the five-membered ring and on two of the six-membered rings, with no hydroxyl or amine groups present. The ring fusions are saturated and largely rigid, giving the framework limited conformational flexibility, while the carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the carbonyls are placed asymmetrically around the fused rings.

The molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic framework made of four rings, three six-membered and one five-membered, joined in a rigid, mostly trans-fused arrangement. A carboxylic acid group sits at the end of a flexible side chain attached to the five-membered ring, and the core carries two ketone (carbonyl) groups on separate rings. Two angular methyl groups project from ring junctions, adding steric bulk and limiting conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any clear mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are placed asymmetrically around the fused core. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes only from the carboxylic acid hydroxyl, while the two ketone oxygens and the acid carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a fused polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from three linearly or angularly fused benzene rings, specifically an anthracene-type framework extended with an additional fused ring, giving a planar, rigid, fully conjugated scaffold. Two chlorine atoms are attached as substituents, one on each of the two outer terminal rings, each positioned adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon, which makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it contains no N-H or O-H groups, and it offers no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor sites since the only heteroatoms are the halogens, which are weak acceptors. The structure is essentially flat and has very limited conformational flexibility, with the only motion arising from minor ring-plane distortions.

This molecule is an acyclic amide built on a simple chain: a tert-butyl group is bonded to the nitrogen of a secondary amide, whose carbonyl carbon is attached to a central carbon bearing two trifluoromethyl groups. The structure contains no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is entirely flexible and open-chained. Its only functional group is the secondary amide, which provides one hydrogen-bond donor at the N–H and one acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen. The tert-butyl group is bulky and symmetric, while the two CF3 groups on the alpha carbon give the molecule a local, though not overall, symmetric arrangement. Because it has several rotatable single bonds and no rigid elements, it can adopt multiple conformations.

This molecule is a dihydropyrimidinone built around a six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms and a urea-type carbonyl, with a ring carbon bearing an ethyl ester group and a methyl group on the adjacent alkene carbon. The partially saturated ring is non-aromatic and somewhat puckered, and the sp3 carbon linking the ring to a furan substituent introduces a stereocenter. The furan is an attached five-membered aromatic oxygen heterocycle, joined through a single bond at its 2-position. The lactam-like urea unit provides two N–H hydrogen-bond donors and a carbonyl oxygen acceptor, while the ester carbonyl and furan oxygen serve as additional acceptors. Overall the scaffold is moderately rigid with limited symmetry.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, arranged in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene framework. The fusion is fully saturated, with no double bonds or aromatic rings, so the core is rigid and largely planar-angular in shape. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-junction carbons, and a side chain on the five-membered ring ends in a primary hydroxyl group, which is the only polar functional group present. That hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the remaining carbon framework is purely hydrocarbon and offers no hydrogen-bonding capability. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond local ring-fusion features, owing to its asymmetric side chain and multiple stereocenters.

The molecule is built on an indene-type scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle through a shared edge. The fused bicyclic core contains a non-aromatic sp3 carbon that bears a phenyl ring as a pendant substituent, while the five-membered ring carries a methyl group on the double-bonded carbon adjacent to the fusion. The structure is composed entirely of carbon and hydrogen, with no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. The molecule is largely planar and rigid within the fused framework, though the phenyl group can rotate about its single bond to the core. It lacks any symmetry element, since the methyl and phenyl substituents break the potential symmetry of the bicyclic system.

The molecule is built on an indene scaffold, a five-membered carbocyclic ring fused to a benzene ring, with the fused bicyclic core being planar and rigid. The five-membered ring carries a methyl group on one sp2 carbon and a phenyl substituent on the adjacent sp2 carbon of the carbon-carbon double bond, so the substitution pattern is contiguous across that ring. The methylene carbon at the other end of the five-membered ring is sp3 and provides the only point of local flexibility, while the benzene ring and the attached phenyl ring are otherwise planar and aromatic. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, and its overall symmetry is low because the methyl and phenyl groups are not equivalent.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Four of its six ring positions carry methyl groups, and the remaining two positions each carry a chloromethyl group, so the substitution pattern is fully substituted around the ring. The two chloromethyl groups sit in a 1,4 (para) relationship across the ring, which gives the molecule a centrosymmetric arrangement. The ring has no fused partners, and its substituents are small and attached by single bonds, so the core is rigid while the methyl and chloromethyl groups can rotate. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, since its only heteroatoms are the two chlorine atoms, which are poor acceptors.
