The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing a common edge. An acetamido group (an N-acetyl amide, –NH–C(=O)–CH3) is attached to one ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, while a nitro group (–NO2) sits on the other ring, also adjacent to the fusion, giving a 1,5-type disubstitution pattern across the bicyclic core. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and its carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor, and the nitro oxygens act as additional acceptors. The aromatic framework is fully planar and rigid, with only the acetyl methyl and the bond to the amide nitrogen offering rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents sit on different rings in an asymmetric arrangement.

This molecule is a dihydropyrimidinone built on a six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms and a urea-like carbonyl, with the ring carbon adjacent to the amide carbonyl carrying an ethyl ester group. The ring is partially saturated, with one sp3 carbon bearing a para-nitrophenyl substituent, which gives the molecule a non-planar, somewhat puckered core attached to a rigid aromatic ring. The nitro group on the phenyl ring is a strong electron-withdrawing feature, and the ring fusion is absent since the two ring systems are only linked by a single bond. Hydrogen-bond donation comes from the two ring N–H groups, while the ester and the two carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens serve as acceptors. The molecule lacks overall symmetry because the aryl group and the ester sit on different parts of the ring.

This molecule is an indole core, a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole-type ring sharing one edge. The nitrogen of the five-membered ring carries a methyl group, so it is N-substituted and contributes no N–H donor. At the 3-position of the indole, a ring carbon bears an acetyl group, a ketone with a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with only the small methyl and acetyl substituents providing limited conformational freedom. Overall the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and one acceptor site, and it lacks any symmetry beyond the local planarity of its ring system.

This molecule is built around a single, acyclic carbon backbone with no ring systems, so its scaffold is open-chained and flexible. The central feature is a carbon-carbon double bond bearing two nitrile groups, which are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors but cannot act as donors. One carbon of that alkene is also attached to an allylamine-type nitrogen bearing a hydrogen, giving a secondary amine that can serve as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the same carbon carries a methylthio group. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two nitrile groups are equivalent but the amino and methylthio substituents are distinct, and the terminal vinyl group adds further conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, with two fused benzene rings forming a planar, rigid bicyclic aromatic core. An amide group links the naphthalene at its 1-position through a nitrogen atom to a carbonyl carbon. That carbonyl is attached to a carbon bearing two trifluoromethyl groups, each a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and the carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor, while the fluorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor capacity. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis and is only moderately flexible, with rotation possible about the amide and single bonds linking the substituents.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazole ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries an N-H hydrogen. Two methyl groups sit on the carbons flanking the ring's nitrogen atoms, and a benzyl group, a benzene ring connected through a single methylene bridge, is attached to the remaining carbon of the pyrazole. The pyrazole ring is fully aromatic and planar, while the benzyl linker gives the molecule a degree of rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The pyrazole N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the unprotonated pyridine-like nitrogen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the benzyl group occupies a position that breaks the symmetry of the substitution pattern.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. Each of those substituents is an ester linkage in which an oxygen atom from the central ring is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that also attaches to a second, unsubstituted benzene ring. The structure therefore contains three aromatic rings joined through two ester groups, with no fused ring systems. Its overall shape is nearly linear and symmetric about the central ring, with only the ester bonds providing some conformational flexibility. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a steroid-like tetracyclic framework built from four fused rings: two saturated six-membered rings and a five-membered ring in a trans-fused arrangement typical of the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene core. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, which adds bulk and rigidity to the scaffold. At one end, the D-ring carries a spiro-fused 1,3-dioxolane, an ethylene ketal in which two oxygen atoms flank a saturated two-carbon bridge; these oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors but not donors. The molecule contains no hydroxyl or amine groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The fused rings are largely rigid, with only the saturated ring bonds and the dioxolane offering conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a fused tetracyclic steroid-type scaffold, with three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring joined by shared edges. Along one ring, a ketone sits on the five-membered ring, and a tertiary alcohol bearing an ethyl group occupies a quaternary carbon on another ring. Two angular methyl groups extend from the ring-fusion carbons, which gives the framework a bulky, three-dimensional shape. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the ethyl and hydroxyl substituents add limited flexibility. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and one hydrogen-bond acceptor (the ketone oxygen), and it lacks any clear mirror-symmetry element because of its asymmetric substitution.

The molecule is an N'-phenyl hydrazide, built around a central acyl-hydrazine unit in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a nitrogen that is itself bonded to a second nitrogen. One end of this hydrazine linkage carries a plain benzene ring attached directly to the nitrogen, while the carbonyl carbon bears a saturated cyclohexane ring, giving a fully aliphatic carbocycle opposite the aromatic one. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, so its substitution pattern is simple, and the molecule as a whole lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two ring ends differ in character. The NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the aromatic-bound nitrogen serve as acceptors. The amide-like bond and the N–N linkage add moderate conformational flexibility, whereas both rings remain rigid.

This molecule has a four-ring steroid-type scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, arranged in the classic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene pattern. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, and a ketone carbonyl is located on the five-membered D ring, which is the only heteroatom-bearing functional group present. The ring fusions are all trans-type junctions that make the core fairly rigid and rod-like, with limited conformational flexibility beyond ring puckering. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the substituents are not matched across the frame. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the single carbonyl oxygen serves as the only hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzamide built from a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group at one position and two nitro groups at the meta positions relative to that carbonyl, giving a 3,5-dinitro substitution pattern. The amide nitrogen is linked through a two-carbon ethylene chain to a pyridine ring attached at its 2-position, so the molecule contains three aromatic rings in total: one benzene and one pyridine. The nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and the amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the pyridine nitrogen, and the nitro oxygens act as acceptors. The ethylene linker gives the molecule conformational flexibility, whereas the aromatic rings are planar and rigid. Overall the structure has no symmetry axis because the two aromatic halves differ.

The molecule has a linear, flexible aliphatic chain bearing a methyl branch, with a phenyl ring attached through a methylene linker at one end and a terminal carboxylic acid at the other. The benzene ring is unsubstituted and unfused, so the only ring system is a single aromatic six-membered ring, with no stereocentres in the ring itself. The carboxylic acid group (–COOH) provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two acceptor sites through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The overall framework is largely unsymmetrical and conformationally flexible, owing to the rotatable single bonds in the chain, and the molecule has a single chiral centre at the methyl-bearing carbon.

Let me parse the structure: two pyrazole rings are linked through a central nitrogen that bears a phenyl group. Each pyrazole carries a methyl group and a methyl ester. The pyrazole rings are attached via N1 to CH2 linkers, which connect to a tertiary aniline nitrogen. The two pyrazole units are arranged symmetrically around the central nitrogen. Neither pyrazole ring is fused to another ring, though the phenyl ring is a separate aromatic system. The molecule is fairly flexible because of the CH2–N linkages, and the ester carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from a 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione (Meldrum's acid-derived) ring, a six-membered cyclic diester with two carbonyl groups flanking a central sp2 carbon and a gem-dimethyl group on the oxygen-bearing carbon. An exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond links this ring to a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methoxy substituents at the 3- and 4-positions, giving a 3,4-dimethoxyphenyl group. The conjugated arylidene linkage makes the scaffold largely planar and fairly rigid, with the gem-dimethyl groups adding a small degree of steric bulk. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its four oxygen-containing carbonyl and ether sites serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indene scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, and it carries a phenyl group attached to the double bond of that five-membered ring. The fused bicyclic core is planar and aromatic on the benzo side, while the cyclopentene ring contributes a single sp3 CH2 that gives the framework a modest degree of puckering. A carbon-carbon double bond sits within the five-membered ring, conjugated with both the fused benzene and the pendant phenyl ring, which extends the pi system across the molecule. There are no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its overall shape is largely rigid and aromatic, with the phenyl substituent able to rotate about a single bond.

This molecule is a benzanilide-type structure built from two benzene rings joined through an amide linkage. One ring bears a methyl ester group (a methoxycarbonyl substituent) at the position ortho to the amide nitrogen, while the other ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached to the carbonyl carbon. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen and the ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. There are no fused ring systems, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two aromatic rings carry different substitution patterns. The amide and aryl–N bonds allow moderate conformational flexibility, though the planar aromatic rings and partial double-bond character of the amide keep the core fairly rigid.

This molecule is a Meldrum's acid derivative: a six-membered 1,3-dioxane-4,6-dione ring bearing a gem-dimethyl group on the carbon between the two ring oxygens. At the C5 position the ring carbon is joined by a double bond to an azo-type hydrazone nitrogen, which links through an N–H to a para-chlorophenyl ring. The 1,3-dioxane-dione core is fused to nothing else, so the scaffold is a single six-membered heterocycle with a pendant aryl group. The ring carbonyls and the ring oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydrazone N–H is the sole hydrogen-bond donor. The conjugated hydrazone and aryl system is largely planar and rigid, whereas the gem-dimethyl ring carbon adds a fixed, non-planar bulk to the otherwise flat framework.

The molecule is a thiocarbonate built around a single central carbon bonded to one sulfur atom by a double bond and to two oxygen atoms, each of which connects to a phenyl ring. Both phenyl rings are unsubstituted benzene rings, so the scaffold is symmetric about the central C=S carbon. There are no fused ring systems and no stereocenters. The thiocarbonyl sulfur acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two ether-type oxygens are weak acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its two aryl rings give it a fairly rigid, planar character, while the C–O single bonds allow some rotational flexibility around the central unit.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two identical substituents at the para positions, giving it a symmetric, linear arrangement. Each substituent is a ketone carbonyl attached directly to the ring, with a chloromethyl group (a CH2 bearing a chlorine atom) on the other side of the carbonyl. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, so the scaffold is compact and largely rigid, though the two side chains have some rotational freedom around their single bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H groups, but each of the two carbonyl oxygens can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall, the structure is a centrosymmetric bis-ketone with two reactive alpha-chloro groups.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond with no additional ring fusion. Each ring carries amino groups: one ring bears amines at three positions and the other at two, with the ortho positions adjacent to the biaryl bond bearing amines on both rings, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic rings are planar and conjugated, while rotation about the central biaryl bond introduces some conformational flexibility. Each primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, so the molecule has several hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic hydrocarbon scaffold with four six-membered rings arranged as two benzene rings joined through a central pair of saturated two-carbon bridges, giving a dibenzo-fused bicyclic core. Both aromatic rings are ortho-disubstituted through their fusion positions, and the two saturated ethylene bridges each connect the two aromatic units, producing a rigid, roughly planar-to-puckered framework. There are no heteroatoms, so no functional groups are present beyond the carbon-hydrogen framework. The molecule has a twofold or higher symmetry axis through its center, and its unsubstituted aromatic faces are essentially uniform, so the structure is largely symmetric and non-polar in its arrangement. With no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, it offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a bicyclic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring, forming an indanone-type scaffold. The aromatic ring carries two methyl substituents, located meta to each other and positioned on the same side of the fused system, which breaks any full mirror symmetry across the molecule. The five-membered ring contains a saturated methylene group and a ketone carbonyl adjacent to the ring junction, making it a conjugated aryl ketone. The fused framework is rigid and essentially planar, with little conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, with no fused rings and no heteroatoms in the ring itself. Going around the ring, there are two methoxy groups (–OCH3) and one bromine atom, along with three methyl groups (–CH3), so every ring carbon is substituted and no aromatic C–H remains. The two methoxy groups sit at positions that are separated from each other by a bromine, and the methyl groups fill the remaining positions, giving a densely crowded, highly substituted pattern. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no O–H or N–H groups. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, though the methoxy and methyl groups provide some rotational freedom, and the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a six-membered 2-pyridone ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle carrying a carbonyl group adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The nitrogen bears a benzyl substituent, a phenyl ring attached through a single methylene linker, which gives the molecule a flexible arm off an otherwise planar core. A nitro group sits at the 5-position of the pyridone ring, opposite the nitrogen across the ring, making it strongly electron-withdrawing. The pyridone carbonyl acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the ring nitrogen is substituted. The aromatic pyridone and phenyl rings are planar, while the benzylic CH2 linker permits rotation between them.

The molecule is a fused tricyclic-type steroid-like scaffold built from three six-membered rings, with two of them sharing a bridgehead quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group. The ring system contains an α,β-unsaturated ketone, where a carbonyl sits in one ring conjugated with a carbon-carbon double bond that links into the adjacent ring junction. A secondary alcohol is attached to the saturated ring at a carbon next to the ring fusion. Overall the structure is partly rigid because of the fused rings and the conjugated enone, while the remaining saturated ring carbons add some flexibility. The molecule has no clear mirror or rotational symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution. Its hydrogen-bond capability includes one donor from the hydroxyl group and two acceptors from the ketone oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen.

The molecule is built on an indane-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, with the fused cyclopentane carrying a nitrile-bearing carbon. The aromatic ring bears two methoxy groups on adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2-dimethoxy substitution pattern that makes the ring electron-rich and largely planar. The bicyclic core is fairly rigid, while the nitrile group projects from the saturated ring and the two ether oxygens are the only other polar features. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, whereas the nitrogen of the nitrile and the two methoxy oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond an approximate mirror relationship across the aromatic ring's long axis.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is ortho-fused to a seven-membered diazepine ring containing two imine nitrogens. Two methyl groups are attached to the carbon atoms of the heterocycle that flank the nitrogens, giving the ring a C=N double bond on each side of the benzo fusion. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is limited to these two methyl groups. The overall framework is largely planar and rigid across the fused aromatic and imine portions, with a modest degree of puckering expected in the seven-membered ring. Each imine nitrogen has a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that contains a CH2 group and a carbon bearing an acetoxy substituent. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, and the ester oxygen is attached directly to the saturated carbon of the five-membered ring at the position adjacent to the aromatic ring fusion. The acetate group consists of a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group, linked through an ester oxygen, giving the molecule one ester functional group. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the ester side chain retains some rotational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two ester oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. It is chiral at the carbon bearing the ester oxygen.

The molecule is built on an adenine-like purine scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a pyrimidine ring is fused to an imidazole ring and the amino group sits on the six-membered ring. The purine nitrogen at N9 carries a three-carbon linker that leads to a secondary amide. The amide connects to a benzene ring bearing two nitro groups in a meta (1,3) relationship on the aromatic ring. The fused heteroaromatic core and the benzene ring are both planar and rigid, while the propyl linker provides conformational flexibility. The primary amine and the amide N-H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogens, amide carbonyl, and nitro oxygens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic fused system: a pyrrole ring (five-membered aromatic ring bearing an N-methyl group on the nitrogen) is fused to a six-membered carbocyclic ring that contains a saturated CH2–C(CH3)2–CH2 segment and a ketone carbonyl. The pyrrole carbons on the fusion edge link the aromatic ring to the cyclohexanone-type ring, giving an indole-like, partially saturated scaffold. The gem-dimethyl group on the saturated ring breaks any symmetry, and the ring fusion makes the core fairly rigid, while the saturated portion adds some conformational flexibility. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor, since the nitrogen is N-methylated and no N–H or O–H groups are present.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic ketone built from a pyrrole ring fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle. The five-membered aromatic ring contains a nitrogen atom that carries a methyl substituent, so the nitrogen is N-alkylated and cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The fused cyclohexanone ring includes a carbonyl group adjacent to the ring junction, which serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and three methylene groups that give the saturated portion conformational flexibility. The overall framework is largely planar where it is aromatic and has limited symmetry because the substituents are not arranged to create a mirror or rotational axis. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a six-membered ring is fused to a second six-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms in an N=N arrangement, giving a pyridazine-like core fused to a pyridine-like ring. Two methyl groups sit on the carbon framework, one on each of the two rings, and a primary amino group is attached to the ring carbon adjacent to the azo-type nitrogen pair. The fused scaffold is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl and amino substituents. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl and amino substituents are placed asymmetrically across the two rings. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the ring nitrogen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a five-membered pyrazole ring is fused to a six-membered pyrimidine ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat, fully aromatic pyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidine scaffold. A methyl group sits on a carbon of the five-membered ring, and a second methyl group is attached to one of the ring nitrogens, which contributes to the rigidity and planarity of the framework. An amino group is attached to the six-membered ring, adjacent to a ring nitrogen. Because the fused core is rigid and has no rotatable bonds, the molecule is essentially planar and asymmetric. The amino group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the several ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring that carries a methyl group on one carbon and a nitro group on the adjacent carbon, with the other ring nitrogen bearing an aryl substituent. That aryl group is a benzene ring linked through a single bond to the triazole nitrogen, and it carries two nitro groups at positions meta and para to each other relative to the attachment point. The two aromatic rings are connected by a single bond with no fusion, so they are not planar-locked together and the link allows some rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents on each ring are distinct. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitro oxygens and the triazole nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a central seven-membered ring containing two ketone carbonyl groups, which sits between two fused benzene rings. Each benzene ring is ortho-fused to the central ring, so the scaffold is a tricyclic, dibenzo-fused cycloheptanedione framework. Both carbonyls are positioned on the central ring, separated from each other by methylene (CH2) units that connect them to the aromatic rings. The arrangement is symmetric: the two benzo rings and their attached carbonyl-methylene linkers mirror each other across the molecule. The central ring is non-aromatic and somewhat flexible, while the fused benzene rings are rigid and planar. The molecule has two carbonyl oxygens that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since there are no N-H or O-H bonds.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system made of two benzene rings sharing one edge. Methyl groups sit at two adjacent carbons on one ring, and bromine atoms occupy the two positions flanking them, so the substitution pattern alternates across the ring. The other ring is unsubstituted, giving the molecule an overall asymmetric but largely planar and rigid shape. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The bromine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors, and the aromatic pi system offers only limited acceptor character.

The molecule is built around a para-nitrophenyl ring linked through a hydrazone bridge (–NH–N=C–) to a central carbon that carries two unsubstituted phenyl rings, giving a benzophenone-derived scaffold. The nitro group (–NO2) sits on one terminal benzene ring at the position para to the hydrazine nitrogen, making that ring electron-poor while the other nitrogen-bearing substituent is electron-donating. There are no fused ring systems; the three aromatic rings are separate, attached around a single sp2 carbon. The C=N double bond and the N–N linkage make the core fairly planar but allow rotation about the single bonds to the phenyl rings, so the overall shape is moderately flexible. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro oxygens and the imine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a steroid-type scaffold: four fused rings in the classic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene arrangement, with three fused six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, all fully saturated. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring-fusion junctions, which adds bulk and rigidity to the core. A secondary alcohol is attached to one of the six-membered rings. At the five-membered ring, a quaternary carbon bears a methyl group and is part of a 1,3-dioxolane (cyclic ketal) ring, which contributes two ether oxygens. The alcohol provides one hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen acceptor sites, while the ketal oxygens serve as acceptors. Overall the framework is rigid and largely nonplanar, with little rotational freedom outside the side chain.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused ring systems. A methyl group sits on the ring carbon adjacent to the carbon bearing a CH2 linker, which leads to a secondary amide, an acetamide unit with a carbonyl oxygen and an N-H group. The pyridine nitrogen and the amide carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any overall symmetry axis or plane. Its rotatable bonds along the CH2 and amide linkages give it moderate conformational flexibility, while the aromatic ring remains rigid and planar.

The molecule is built on a 3H-indole-type core, specifically a 2,3-diphenyl-3H-indole in which the five-membered nitrogen-containing ring is fused to a benzene ring bearing a methoxy group. The indolenine ring contains a C=N imine double bond, making the nitrogen an acceptor site with no hydrogen-bond donor present. Two phenyl rings are attached as substituents at the carbons adjacent to the imine, one of them on the sp3-hybridized carbon, which breaks conjugation and gives the framework a partly three-dimensional shape. The methoxy group sits on the fused benzene ring at a position meta to the ring fusion, and its oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid, while the two phenyl groups can rotate about their single bonds.

The molecule is a diphenylacetamide, built around a central sp3 carbon that bears two unsubstituted phenyl rings and is bonded to a carbonyl group forming an amide. The amide nitrogen carries a third phenyl ring, so the structure contains three benzene rings in total, none of them fused to one another. The two phenyl groups on the alpha carbon are related by a local symmetry, while the N-phenyl ring breaks that symmetry and adds conformational freedom around the C–N and C–C bonds. The secondary amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as an acceptor. Overall the molecule is aromatic-rich and fairly flexible, with a single amide linkage connecting three otherwise unsubstituted aryl groups.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole-2-thione scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The C2 position carries an exocyclic thiocarbonyl group (C=S), which makes it a thione rather than a simple thiazole. The ring nitrogen bears a CH2 linker connected to a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing one tertiary amine nitrogen. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the piperidine ring is flexible and adopts chair-like conformations. The thione sulfur can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the piperidine nitrogen is a basic acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, here present as a pyridine N-oxide, in which the ring nitrogen carries a positively charged, oxygen-bearing substituent. Relative to that nitrogen, the ring is substituted at two adjacent carbons: a methyl group on one side and a carboxamide group (a primary amide, C(=O)NH2) on the other, giving an ortho-disubstituted pattern. There is no fused ring system and no internal symmetry, since the two substituents differ. The carboxamide is attached through a single bond, so it can rotate, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The N-oxide oxygen and the amide carbonyl oxygen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two amide hydrogens serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered pyridine-type aromatic ring that contains one nitrogen atom, which carries a formal positive charge and is bonded to an oxygen bearing a negative charge, making it an N-oxide. The ring is substituted at two adjacent carbon positions: a methyl group on one carbon and a nitrile (cyano) group on the neighboring carbon, with the remaining ring positions bearing hydrogen. Because the ring is fully aromatic and fused to nothing else, the framework is rigid and planar, and the only conformational freedom lies in the rotation of the methyl group. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, but the N-oxide oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings in the classic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene arrangement: three six-membered rings fused linearly to a five-membered ring. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, one of them at a quaternary carbon shared by the five-membered ring. The five-membered ring carries a ketone at the position furthest from the fused junction, giving the molecule its only polar functional group. A single carbon-carbon double bond occurs in one of the six-membered rings, introducing a small degree of rigidity there. The fused ring framework is largely rigid, with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is a symmetric diaryl urea, with a central carbonyl group bonded to two NH groups, each attached to a separate phenyl ring. Each phenyl ring is a simple benzene ring with no fusion, and each carries a nitro group at the meta position relative to the urea nitrogen. The two halves are mirror-related, giving the molecule overall symmetry across the central C=O axis. The urea linkage makes the structure moderately rigid around the carbonyl, while the two N-aryl bonds allow some rotation. The two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a ketone in which a benzyl group (a phenyl ring joined through a CH2) is attached to the carbonyl carbon, and the other side of the carbonyl bears a fused polycyclic aromatic system. That system is a naphthalene-based scaffold with an additional saturated five-membered ring fused across the peri positions, giving a rigid, mostly planar tricyclic core. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, while the polycyclic core carries the ketone at a single position, so there is no molecular symmetry. The CH2 linker gives the molecule some rotational flexibility at the benzyl side. The carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a methoxy group, a 2-amidoethyl chain, and a benzyloxy group, arranged so the methoxy and benzyloxy groups sit on adjacent carbons. The two-carbon chain ends in a secondary amide, where the nitrogen is attached to a 3-methylbutanoyl group with its branched isobutyl tail. A second, unsubstituted phenyl ring is connected through a single oxygen-linked methylene to the central ring. The structure contains only aromatic and sp3 carbons, with no fused ring systems. Its methoxy oxygen and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and the amide carbonyl as an acceptor. The chain linkers give it moderate conformational flexibility around the amide and the two ether linkages.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring bearing two amide groups on adjacent (ortho) carbons. Each amide nitrogen is bonded to the central ring, and each carbonyl carbon connects to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the structure is symmetric about the central ring's axis. Overall it is a 1,2-phenylenebis(benzamide)-type scaffold with three benzene rings and no fused ring systems. Each N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor and each C=O oxygen is an acceptor, giving two of each. The aryl–nitrogen and aryl–carbonyl bonds allow some rotation, but the amide groups and aromatic rings make the molecule fairly rigid overall.

The molecule is built from a phenyl ring attached through a single methylene carbon to a hydrazone-type chain. The unsubstituted benzene ring is a planar aromatic system with no ring fusion and no substituents on the ring itself, so the pattern is monosubstituted. The chain bears a urea-like semicarbazone unit, with a carbonyl flanked by two nitrogens on one end and a C=N double bond with an enolic hydroxyl on the other. Several groups can donate hydrogen bonds (the NH groups and the enol OH), while the carbonyl oxygen and the imine nitrogen can accept them. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of its aromatic ring, and the single CH2 linker plus several rotatable bonds make it fairly flexible overall.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing five substituents: a carboxylic acid group, an acetoxy (acetate ester) group, and two methoxy groups. The carboxylic acid sits at position 1, with the acetoxy group at position 3 and the two adjacent methoxy groups at positions 4 and 5, giving a crowded, contiguous substitution pattern on one side of the ring. Overall there is no ring fusion, and the scaffold is a planar, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with only modest conformational freedom from the rotatable ester and ether bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ester carbonyl and the ether oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are not arranged in a mirror-symmetric pattern.

The molecule is built around a five-membered heterocycle containing a ring of carbon atoms and two adjacent nitrogen atoms in a pyrazoline-type arrangement, with one carbon–carbon double bond and one N=N double bond present in the ring. A methyl group sits on a saturated ring carbon adjacent to the azo-type nitrogen, while an ethyl ester group (–C(=O)OCH2CH3) is attached to an sp2 ring carbon. The ring is fully unsaturated apart from that single sp3 carbon, giving it a largely planar, rigid core, with only the ethyl ester tail offering rotational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ester carbonyl oxygen and ester oxygen, together with the ring nitrogens, act as acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated sugar-derived chain with no rings. The carbon backbone carries a diethyl dithioacetal group at one terminus, where a single carbon bears two ethylthio substituents, so the sulfur atoms form thioether linkages. The remaining carbons each bear an acetate ester (acetoxy) group, which together make up the substitution pattern along the chain. Four of these ester oxygens sit on successive carbons, with a fifth ester at the terminal primary carbon. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry and is flexible, since its single bonds allow free rotation. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, because every oxygen and sulfur is capped with an alkyl or acyl group. The ester carbonyl oxygens and thioether sulfurs can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic core in which a six-membered pyrimidine ring is joined edge-to-edge with a five-membered pyrazole ring, creating a flat, fully conjugated scaffold. An amino group sits on the pyrimidine carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, and the pyrazole nitrogen that forms part of the fusion carries a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group. The core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxyethyl side chain adds a small degree of rotational freedom. Several ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the primary amine supplies hydrogen-bond donor capacity, and the terminal alcohol offers both donor and acceptor sites. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents are placed asymmetrically on the bicyclic framework.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a five-membered pyrazole ring is fused to a six-membered pyrimidine ring, giving a planar, rigid, fully aromatic scaffold. The pyrazole nitrogen bears a methyl group, and the carbon adjacent to the fusion carries a second methyl group, while an amino group sits on the pyrimidine ring. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the methyl groups and amino group occupy distinct positions on the fused framework. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the exocyclic amino group provides hydrogen-bond donor capability through its N–H bonds.

This molecule is a bicyclic fused heteroaromatic system: a five-membered pyrazole-type ring fused to a six-membered pyrimidine ring, giving a planar pyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidine scaffold. The nitrogen on the five-membered ring carries a methyl group, which sits at the N1 position and breaks any symmetry across the fused core. A hydrazinyl group (–NH–NH2) is attached at the carbon adjacent to the pyrimidine nitrogens, providing a flexible side chain at an otherwise rigid aromatic framework. The fused rings are fully conjugated and essentially flat, with the hydrazine chain offering the main rotational freedom. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydrazine NH groups can serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a 1,4-dihydropyridine built on a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that bears an N-H group, two methyl substituents, and two ethyl ester groups on the ring double bonds. The ring carries a furan (five-membered oxygen heterocycle) attached at the sp3 carbon position opposite the nitrogen, so the core scaffold is a non-planar, partially saturated ring fused to nothing else. The two ester carbonyls are conjugated with the ring alkenes, while the furan ring is a separate aromatic system linked by a single bond. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, since the furan sits on one side of the ring while the two esters are different in placement only by symmetry, giving a near-symmetric arrangement. The molecule has moderate rotational flexibility from the ethyl ester chains and single bonds to the furan, and one hydrogen-bond donor (the ring N-H) and several acceptors (the carbonyl oxygens, the ring oxygen, and the ring nitrogen).

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic core in which a six-membered pyrimidinone-type ring shares an edge with a five-membered pyrazole-type ring, giving a planar, rigid scaffold. The six-membered ring carries a carbonyl group adjacent to a ring nitrogen, and the ring-fusion nitrogen contributes to the aromatic system. A phenylthio substituent (a sulfur bridge to a benzene ring) is attached to the five-membered ring, while the adjacent carbon bears a 2,6-dichlorophenyl group, whose two ortho chlorine atoms are positioned symmetrically on one side of the biaryl bond. The aromatic carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure is largely rigid, with the sterically crowded biaryl linkage allowing only limited rotation.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic aromatic system built from a naphthalene-type unit bridged to a pyrazine ring. Three rings are fused together to form a rigid, planar scaffold, with a central six-membered ring sharing edges with both a benzo-fused unit and a five-membered ring. The pyrazine ring contributes two nitrogen atoms at para positions, which act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no explicit functional groups. The fully aromatic framework is essentially flat and conformationally locked, and it has no substituents beyond the ring atoms, so its substitution pattern is unsubstituted and its symmetry is limited to the planar arrangement of the fused rings.

The molecule is a phenyl ketone: a benzoyl group, with a carbonyl carbon bridging an unsubstituted phenyl ring and a fused polycyclic aromatic core. That core is an acenaphthene-type system, in which a naphthalene unit is fused to a five-membered saturated ring through a two-carbon ethylene bridge (the CH2–CH2 linkage). The carbonyl is attached to a naphthalene position, so the substitution pattern is 1-acyl with the phenyl ring unsubstituted. The molecule has no stereocenters and is largely planar and rigid across its aromatic framework, with only the ethylene bridge and the ketone-to-phenyl bond allowing limited flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a secondary alcohol built on a three-carbon chain that links two separate benzene rings. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon directly bonded to one phenyl ring, and the chain continues through three methylene units to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring at the far end. Both aromatic rings are simple monosubstituted benzenes, each planar and free of further substituents, so the overall framework is symmetric only in the sense of its two phenyl ends, not as a whole. The flexible, unbranched alkyl linker gives the molecule considerable conformational freedom, while the aromatic rings remain rigid. The single hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is built on an indane-type scaffold, consisting of a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle. The five-membered ring contains a ketone carbonyl at the carbon adjacent to the aromatic ring and a methylene (CH2) group between the carbonyl and the fused benzene carbon, so it is a 1-indanone. The fused bicyclic framework is largely planar and rigid, with the aromatic ring fully unsubstituted and no stereocenters present. The molecule has a mirror plane through the ketone and methylene carbons, giving it a degree of symmetry about that axis. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a five-membered, partially unsaturated ring containing one nitrogen atom, which places it in the pyrroline family. The ring carries a double bond between a carbon and the nitrogen (a cyclic imine), and a second double bond sits between two ring carbons, so the ring is conjugated across much of its framework. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, one on a carbon adjacent to the imine and one on the carbon next to the ring methylene. An ethyl ester group is attached directly to a ring carbon, contributing a carbonyl oxygen and an ether oxygen. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since the ring nitrogen is substituted into the imine and the ester has no N–H or O–H. It has several acceptors, namely the imine nitrogen and the two ester oxygens. The ring is largely planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester tail adds some conformational flexibility, and there is no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, and two nitro groups (-NO2) are attached to adjacent carbons, with one nitro group directly beside the amine, so the three substituents occupy consecutive positions around the ring. The ring carries no fused partners, and its planar geometry is rigid, with the nitro groups able to rotate slightly out of the ring plane. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically.

The molecule is built around a bicyclic core in which a saturated five-membered nitrogen-containing ring is fused to a benzene ring, forming an indoline (2,3-dihydroindole) scaffold. A second, unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached directly to the saturated carbon that sits adjacent to the nitrogen, placing it at the 2-position of the indoline. The only substitution is this single phenyl group, so the arrangement has no mirror plane through the full structure and the stereocenter at that carbon makes it chiral. The fused bicyclic portion is fairly rigid, while the bond linking the phenyl ring gives some rotational freedom. The secondary amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and an acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle built around one ring oxygen, with a sulfur atom doubly bonded to a ring carbon at the position opposite the oxygen, giving a thiopyrylium-type scaffold drawn as a 4-thioxo-pyran. Two methyl groups sit on the carbons flanking the ring oxygen, one on each side, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis running through the oxygen and the thiocarbonyl carbon. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two methyl groups. The exocyclic C=S group is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated chain of four carbons, with no rings or fused ring systems. The carbon at one end bears two ethylthio groups, both attached to the same carbon, which together form a dithioacetal arrangement. Three consecutive carbons in the chain each carry a hydroxyl group, giving a polyol segment, and the terminal carbon is a primary alcohol. Because the backbone is open-chained and contains many single bonds, the molecule is highly flexible and lacks any internal symmetry. Its three hydroxyl groups can act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the sulfur atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic polyol acetal-type structure with no rings at all. Its backbone is a linear chain of six carbons, with the first carbon bearing two ethylthio groups (–S–CH2CH3) on the same carbon, so it is a dithioacetal, and the remaining five carbons each carry a hydroxyl group. Because it contains no ring systems or fused rings, its conformational freedom comes entirely from rotation about single bonds, making it quite flexible. The two sulfur atoms are thioether acceptors, while the five hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The chain lacks any element of molecular symmetry, since the two ethylthio groups are the only identical substituents and they sit at one end of an otherwise unsymmetrical polyhydroxylated framework.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which places it in the pyrazole family. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group on one carbon next to the ring nitrogen, a second methyl group on the carbon at the other side of the same ring-nitrogen pairing, and a primary amino group on the remaining ring carbon. Because the ring is fully aromatic and planar with no fused rings, the scaffold is rigid, while the methyl and amino groups rotate freely. The ring nitrogen bearing a hydrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, the unprotonated ring nitrogen and the amino nitrogen act as acceptors and donors respectively, giving the molecule several hydrogen-bonding sites. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring is ortho-fused to a six-membered saturated carbocycle, giving a tetrahydrobenzothiophene core. The thiophene ring carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a primary amino group on one carbon adjacent to the sulfur atom, and an ethyl ester (ethoxycarbonyl) group on the neighboring carbon. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ester ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The cyclohexane portion is flexible, adopting non-planar conformations, whereas the fused thiophene-ester system is largely planar and rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are placed asymmetrically across the fused rings.

The molecule is a bicyclic lactone built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing ring, giving a 3,4-dihydroisocoumarin-type scaffold. The benzene ring is ortho-fused to the saturated heterocycle, so the two ring systems share a single carbon-carbon bond. The heterocycle contains a cyclic ester: a carbonyl carbon bonded to a ring oxygen, with a methylene group next to the carbonyl and another methylene attached to the aromatic ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the molecule has no substitution pattern beyond the fusion itself. Its framework is largely planar in the aromatic portion and fairly rigid overall, with limited conformational freedom in the fused ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring bearing two groups on opposite positions. One substituent is a straight four-carbon n-butyl chain attached directly to the aromatic carbon, giving a flexible alkyl tail. The other is an acetamido group, in which an amide nitrogen bonded to the ring carries an acetyl carbonyl. The arrangement is linear and roughly symmetric along the long axis of the ring, with the flexible butyl chain as the main source of conformational freedom. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as an acceptor.

The molecule is a carbamate-protected amino acid built on a serine-type backbone: a three-carbon chain bearing a free carboxylic acid at one end and a primary hydroxymethyl group on the alpha carbon. The nitrogen is acylated by a benzyloxycarbonyl group, which links through a carbamate C=O to a benzyl ether-type CH2 attached to an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The molecule contains one stereogenic center at the alpha carbon, and its flexible acyclic chain contrasts with the rigid, planar aromatic ring. Hydrogen-bond capability is substantial: the carboxylic acid, the hydroxyl, and the carbamate N–H act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of the acid and carbamate, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the carbamate ether oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core: a pyrrolidine-like five-membered ring containing one secondary amine nitrogen is fused to a larger ring that is part of a quinoline-type aromatic system, giving a rigid, largely planar tricyclic scaffold. The aromatic-looking portion contains a ring nitrogen double-bonded within the fused framework, while a partially saturated ring carries an NH group. A carboxylic acid group is attached to a carbon adjacent to that amine, and a methyl group sits on the carbon next to the ring junction, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, and the secondary amine NH adds an additional donor, while the ring nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic compound built on a benzene ring that is ortho-fused to a five-membered cyclic anhydride. The anhydride ring contains two carbonyl carbons joined through a shared oxygen, with the ring fusion occurring at two adjacent aromatic carbons. Two chlorine atoms sit on the benzene ring at adjacent positions, in a 4,5-disubstituted pattern relative to the anhydride carbonyls, which gives the aromatic core a mirror-symmetric arrangement across its central axis. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a symmetric diester built around a four-carbon saturated chain, with the central two carbons bearing carbonyl groups at both ends. Each carbonyl is bonded to an oxygen that links to a separate phenyl ring, so the structure contains two monosubstituted benzene rings connected through ester linkages. The two aromatic halves are mirror images of each other, giving the molecule overall two-fold symmetry about its central axis. Its flexible methylene linker allows considerable conformational freedom, while the aromatic rings remain planar and rigid. Each ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a symmetric diarylurea: a central carbonyl-bearing N–C(=O)–N unit links two identical para-tolyl rings. Each aromatic ring is a simple benzene ring carrying a methyl group para to the urea nitrogen, so the two halves mirror each other across the central C=O. The urea core is planar and conjugated with both rings, which limits rotation and makes the overall framework fairly rigid. Each N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the molecule a donor-acceptor pair capable of forming directional intermolecular contacts.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two naphthalene units joined by a single bond between their carbon atoms, giving a 1,1'-binaphthyl skeleton with each naphthalene carrying a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the linking carbon. Each naphthalene is a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing an edge, and the two units are connected at their 1- and 1'-type positions in a way that places each hydroxyl flanking the biaryl bond. The two naphthyl rings are twisted out of plane relative to one another because of steric crowding around the connecting bond, so the framework is rigid and nonplanar rather than fully flat. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry relating the two halves, and each phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a β-carboline-type tricyclic scaffold, in which a pyridine ring is fused to a central pyrrole that is in turn fused to a benzene ring, giving a largely planar, fully aromatic fused system. A secondary indole-type N–H sits on the pyrrole nitrogen, providing a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an acceptor. On the pyridine portion, a methoxymethyl group and an isopropyl ester carbonyl are attached, adding ether and ester oxygens that can accept hydrogen bonds. The benzene ring carries a benzyloxy substituent, an ether linkage to a pendant phenyl ring that adds a flexible, nonplanar tail to the otherwise rigid core. The overall framework lacks any symmetry because the substituents are placed unevenly across the three fused rings.

This molecule is a biphenyl-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with each ring carrying a hydroxyl group ortho to that linking bond. Each ring bears two bromine substituents, placed meta to each other and positioned so that the pattern is mirrored across the central bond, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry. The two hydroxyl groups can each act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and their ortho placement allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond to form. The aromatic rings are planar and conjugated, while the single inter-ring bond permits some rotation, so the molecule is moderately rigid overall.

This molecule is built on an indoline scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, with the nitrogen bearing an N-nitroso group (an N–N=O unit). The fused bicyclic framework is largely rigid, with only the saturated two-carbon bridge in the five-membered ring providing limited flexibility. The aromatic ring carries no additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the overall shape is not symmetric because the nitroso group sits on one side of the fused system. The nitroso oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two methyl groups in a para-like arrangement relative to each other, with the remaining ring positions fused to a five-membered anhydride ring. The anhydride ring contains two carbonyl carbons bridged by a ring oxygen, so the fused system is a rigid, planar bicyclic framework. Its substitution pattern is asymmetric about the individual rings but retains an overall two-fold symmetry axis through the anhydride oxygen and the midpoint of the aromatic ring. The molecule has no rotatable bonds within the core, making it highly rigid. It carries no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on an indane (benzocyclopentene) scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered carbocycle, and the fused system is entirely hydrocarbon. The saturated five-membered ring carries two methyl groups on one carbon and a methyl plus a phenyl group on the carbon adjacent to the fused benzene ring, giving a fully alkyl, sp3-rich substitution pattern with a bulky, unsymmetrical arrangement. The compound contains two aromatic rings, one fused and one pendant phenyl, and no heteroatoms or functional groups. The quaternary carbons restrict conformational freedom, so the molecule is fairly rigid overall. It has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para arrangement, giving it a flat, rigid aromatic core. One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl bonded to a methyl, which acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at the oxygen. The other is a sulfonylurea-type unit in which a sulfur bearing two oxygens connects to an NH, then to a urea carbonyl, and then to a second NH attached to a saturated cyclohexane ring. This linkage contributes several hydrogen-bond donors (two N–H groups) and multiple acceptors (the sulfonyl oxygens and the carbonyl oxygens). The cyclohexane ring adopts a non-planar, flexible chair-like conformation, contrasting with the planar aromatic portion.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic aromatic quinone built on a four-ring linear-angular scaffold: a central 1,4-benzoquinone-type ring bearing two carbonyl groups is fused on one side to a plain benzene ring and on the other to a naphthalene unit. The two carbonyl carbons sit on opposite positions of the central six-membered ring, giving a para-quinone arrangement with no substituents beyond the ring fusions. Because the rings are fully aromatic or conjugated and joined by shared edges, the framework is planar and rigid, with essentially no rotatable bonds. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the two carbonyls, and the only hydrogen-bond capability comes from the two carbonyl oxygens, which act as acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four chlorine atoms and two methyl groups, so its core scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings. The substituents alternate around the ring as methyl, chlorine, chlorine, methyl, chlorine, chlorine, giving a symmetric 2,3,5,6-tetrachloro-1,4-dimethyl pattern. Because the ring is fully substituted with no free hydrogens on carbon, the only remaining ring positions carry no hydrogens and the substitution pattern is highly regular. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H groups, and it has no hydrogen-bond acceptors beyond the weak halogen contributions. The rigid planar aromatic ring is conformationally restricted, with only the methyl groups able to rotate.

The molecule is a benzene-based scaffold, a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings. Three substituents sit around the ring: an amino group (-NH2), a chlorine atom, and a thiol group (-SH). The amino and thiol groups are on adjacent carbons, while the chlorine is positioned meta to the amine and para to the thiol. The planar aromatic core is rigid, with only the small substituents able to rotate. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds and act as an acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair, the thiol can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, and the chlorine is a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a fully saturated four-ring steroid scaffold: three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, the classic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene arrangement. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring-fusion carbons, one at each end of the framework. There are two hydroxyl groups, one on the five-membered D ring at a secondary position and one on the A ring at a secondary position, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. All ring junctions are sp3 and largely trans-fused, which makes the core rigid and compact, with only modest flexibility in the hydroxyl groups. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the remaining carbon framework is entirely nonpolar.

The molecule is a small, fully linear, acyclic compound built around a central carbon-carbon triple bond. Each end of that alkyne is capped by a carboxamide group, with one primary amide (C(=O)NH2) attached to each alkyne carbon, so the two amide units are arranged symmetrically across the molecule. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no branching or additional substituents. The alkyne linker enforces a rigid, rod-like geometry that holds the two amide groups at a fixed, opposite orientation. Each primary amide offers two N-H hydrogen-bond donors and a carbonyl oxygen acceptor, giving the molecule four donor sites and two acceptor sites in total.

This molecule is a substituted urea, with a carbonyl group flanked by two nitrogens, one of which is a terminal NH2 and the other an NH bonded to an aromatic ring. The aryl group is a single benzene ring bearing a chlorine atom at the position para to the urea nitrogen, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern with an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. The urea linkage is fairly planar and conjugated with the ring, which limits rotation and gives the molecule modest rigidity. The NH groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the chlorine contributes a weakly polar, lipophilic substituent on the aromatic ring.

This molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, with a methoxy group on the benzene ring. At the 2-position of the imidazole sits a sulfinyl group (S bonded to an oxygen and linked by a methylene bridge) that connects to a pyridine ring. The pyridine ring is substituted with a methyl group, a methoxy group, and a second methyl group, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. The sulfur stereocenter makes the molecule chiral, and the two aromatic ring systems joined by a single flexible CH2 linker give it moderate conformational flexibility. The imidazole N-H and the sulfinyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the pyridine and imidazole nitrogens and the methoxy oxygens provide additional acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a single sulfur atom that carries a sulfoxide oxygen and is bonded to a carbon chain leading to a primary amide. That amide (-C(=O)NH2) is attached through a methylene to the sulfinyl group, and the sulfur's other substituent is a methine carbon bearing two phenyl rings, giving a diphenylmethyl unit. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene, so the two aromatic groups are identical and the overall pattern is symmetric about the central carbon, though the sulfur stereocenter breaks full mirror symmetry. The sulfoxide oxygen and the amide oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two amide N-H groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The phenyl groups provide flexibility at the tetrahedral central carbon but no fused ring system is present.

This molecule is a saturated tetracyclic steroid-type skeleton of the cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene family, built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring. The rings are fused in a trans-anti arrangement, giving a rigid, fairly planar-folded framework with two angular methyl groups at the ring junctions. Two ketone groups sit on the periphery: one on the six-membered ring A at a carbon two positions from the junction, and one on the five-membered ring D. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall structure is largely aliphatic and lacks any stereochemical or positional symmetry.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, with the rings fused together in a rigid, roughly planar framework. It carries two angular methyl groups at the ring junctions, one of which sits on the ring-fusion carbon of the five-membered ring. A branched eight-carbon side chain with a methyl-substituted tail hangs from the five-membered ring, adding flexibility at that end. A single hydroxyl group is attached to one of the six-membered rings, which serves as the only hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site. A carbon-carbon double bond sits within one ring, introducing local planarity, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry.

This molecule is built on a fully saturated four-ring steroid scaffold, with three six-membered rings fused linearly to a five-membered ring at the far end. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, one of which is on the carbon bridging the five-membered ring. The five-membered D-ring carries a ketone (C=O) at the position distal to the fusion. A single secondary hydroxyl group sits on the A-ring, adding one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor, while the ketone contributes one acceptor. Apart from these two polar groups, the framework is entirely hydrocarbon and the rings are conformationally rigid, with only limited flexibility in the saturated six-membered rings.

This molecule is a fully saturated tetracyclic steroid scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene framework. The rings are fused trans-anti in the ring junctions typical of the androstane core, giving a rigid, compact three-dimensional shape with two angular methyl groups projecting from the ring junctions. One ring carries a ketone (a carbonyl group at a ring position), and the five-membered ring carries a secondary hydroxyl group. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the carbonyl and hydroxyl are placed asymmetrically. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ketone oxygen acts only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The SMILES CNC corresponds to a single nitrogen atom bonded to two carbon atoms, one of them a methyl group, which together make up a small acyclic amine skeleton. There are no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is fully open-chain. The nitrogen is a secondary amine, carrying one hydrogen and two alkyl substituents, and the molecule has no other functional groups or substitution pattern to describe. Its structure is highly flexible, with free rotation about the carbon-nitrogen bonds. The nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is a linear five-carbon hydrocarbon chain with two carbon-carbon double bonds, specifically a 1,4-diene arrangement. Its scaffold is acyclic, so there are no ring systems or ring fusion to consider. The only functional groups are the two terminal and internal alkene units, and the molecule has no heteroatoms or substituents along the chain. Because the chain is unbranched and lacks any polar groups, it carries no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. Its backbone is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds, while the double bonds impose local rigidity at their positions.

This molecule is an acyclic five-carbon hydrocarbon, a straight chain built from carbon atoms joined by single and double bonds, with no rings, fused systems, or heteroatoms present. Its skeleton is unbranched, and it contains two carbon-carbon double bonds positioned at the first and third bond locations, creating a conjugated diene arrangement. The molecule has no functional groups beyond these alkene units and therefore carries no substituents that would break its simple linear pattern. Its geometry is largely flexible because rotation is possible around the single bond between the two double bonds, although the conjugated system tends to favor a planar arrangement. Because it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule has a five-carbon acyclic skeleton, with a terminal vinyl (ethenyl) group attached to a branched carbon that carries a methyl substituent and a second methyl, giving an isopentyl-type scaffold with a 3-methylbut-1-ene arrangement. It contains no rings and no heteroatoms, so there are no ring fusions or heteroatom functional groups beyond the single carbon-carbon double bond. The only functional feature is that terminal alkene, and the substitution pattern places the branching at the allylic position. The molecule is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. It lacks a plane or axis of symmetry beyond local features, because the branched carbon bears two different alkyl groups.

The molecule is a simple, unbranched four-carbon chain with a terminal alkene, which makes it 1-butene. Its scaffold is entirely acyclic, so there are no ring systems or ring fusion to consider. The only functional group is the carbon-carbon double bond at the chain's end, which is a site of unsaturation rather than a polar group. The molecule is hydrocarbon-only, with no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. Its linear chain gives it considerable conformational flexibility through rotation about its single bonds, and it lacks any meaningful molecular symmetry beyond the trivial one.

The molecule has a three-membered cyclopropane ring bearing a single ethyl group attached to one of its carbon atoms, so it is an alkyl-substituted cyclopropane built from saturated carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen bonds only. The ring is highly strained because its bond angles are forced far below the ideal tetrahedral angle, which makes the small ring rigid, while the two-carbon ethyl side chain is flexible and can rotate freely about its single bonds. The structure contains no heteroatoms and no functional groups, and there is no fused ring system. The substitution pattern is monosubstituted, and the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis that would make it highly symmetric. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, since it consists entirely of nonpolar hydrocarbon bonds.

The molecule is built on a single three-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopropane, with no fused rings or heteroatoms present. Two methyl groups sit on the same ring carbon, and a third methyl group is attached to an adjacent ring carbon, giving a trimethyl substitution pattern on the cyclopropane. The ring carbons are unsaturated only by hydrogen, so the structure is fully saturated and contains no functional groups such as alcohols, carbonyls, or amines. The strained, compact ring makes the framework rigid, while the methyl groups are free to rotate. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror-like arrangement around the gem-dimethyl carbon.

This molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built from a straight chain of six carbon atoms, with a single carbon-carbon double bond located between the third and fourth carbons.
