It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic character. The only functional group is a secondary carbon-bromine bond, and the substitution pattern places the halogen symmetrically between two ethyl arms, so the molecule has a plane of symmetry through the C–Br bond. Its chain is flexible, with free rotation about the single C–C bonds allowing many conformers. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents at positions 1 and 4 (para to each other): one is an acetate ester, in which an acetyl group is bonded through an oxygen atom to the ring, and the other is a free phenolic hydroxyl group. The para arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring centre, and the flat aromatic core combined with the rigid ester linkage makes it fairly rigid, with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation about the ester bonds. The phenolic OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ester carbonyl oxygen and the ester ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid built on a bornane-type skeleton, with a fused bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane core carrying three methyl groups on the bridging carbons. The two carbons bearing methyls are bridgeheads and the single bridge carbon adjacent to one of them is part of a rigid, cage-like framework. A secondary alcohol sits on one carbon of the six-membered ring of the cage, making it the sole functional group and a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its hydroxyl oxygen. The scaffold is conformationally rigid with a defined stereochemistry at its stereocenters, and it lacks any overall symmetry because the hydroxyl breaks the mirror-like symmetry of the parent hydrocarbon.

This molecule is an unbranched primary amine built on a straight aliphatic chain of ten carbon atoms, with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. The only functional group is a terminal amino group attached to one end of the chain, which makes the molecule a simple linear alkylamine with no substitution pattern beyond that single position. Its skeleton is fully saturated and highly flexible, since rotation about the many single carbon-carbon bonds allows the chain to adopt many conformations. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the amino group sits at one end, making the two ends chemically distinct. The nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the hydrocarbon chain contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group (–OCH3), a primary amine (–NH2), and a chlorine atom. Its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion and the core is planar and rigid, with only the methoxy group offering rotational flexibility. The substitution pattern is 1,2,4-trisubstituted: the methoxy and chloro groups sit on adjacent carbons, and the amine is para to the methoxy group. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, so its three substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the oxygen of the methoxy group and the nitrogen of the amine serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl thiol, with a nine-carbon saturated chain terminated at one end by a sulfhydryl group. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution pattern beyond the single terminal group, so its scaffold is simply an unbranched aliphatic chain. The molecule is flexible, since rotation about its many carbon-carbon single bonds gives it considerable conformational freedom, and it has no internal symmetry other than the local mirror-like arrangement along the chain. The thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S-H bond, while sulfur offers only a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is an unbranched saturated hydrocarbon chain of ten carbon atoms with a chlorine atom attached to one terminal carbon, making it a primary alkyl halide. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-chlorine bond. The skeleton is linear and fully flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond, so the molecule can adopt many conformations. It has no internal symmetry apart from the approximate mirror relation of the two ends, and the chlorine occupies a single unique position. The chlorine atom can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is an ester built from a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon acrylate chain attached at one ring carbon, with the rest of the benzene ring left unsubstituted. The benzene ring is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no fused partners, and it is connected through a carbon-carbon double bond to a methyl ester group. The alkene between the ring and the carbonyl has an E (trans) geometry, which keeps the phenyl ring and the ester group on opposite sides and makes the framework fairly planar and rigid. The methyl ester contributes one carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and one ether-type oxygen that can also weakly accept them, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall structure is essentially unsymmetrical apart from the ring's local symmetry, and the single methoxy group gives a small degree of conformational flexibility at the ester end.

The molecule is an acyclic alkyl halide built on a six-carbon chain, with no rings or aromatic systems present. The carbon skeleton is branched: a central methine carbon carries two methyl groups at one end, while a second methine carbon sits along the chain and bears a bromine atom with an additional methyl group. The bromine is the sole functional group and is attached to a secondary carbon, which places it at a substitution pattern that is asymmetric, since the two ends of the chain are not equivalent. Because the molecule is entirely sp3-hybridized and contains several freely rotating single bonds, it is flexible and has no fixed geometry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents placed para to each other on that ring: a four-carbon n-butyl chain attached through an ether oxygen on one side, and a free hydroxyl group on the other. The ether linkage and the phenolic hydroxyl are the only heteroatom-bearing functional groups, and the flexible saturated alkyl tail contrasts with the rigid planar aromatic core. The para arrangement gives the molecule a roughly linear, elongated shape with a two-fold symmetry axis running through both substituents. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched-chain alkene built from a long saturated stretch and a single terminal double bond. The main chain carries a methyl group on the carbon that bears the double bond, so the terminal alkene is 1,1-disubstituted, with the two substituents on the same carbon. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond the carbon-carbon double bond. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry and is highly flexible, since its long chain can rotate freely about its many single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, because it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and an acetic acid side chain, giving a carboxylic acid functional group attached through a single methylene linker. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the substituents occupy three positions around it, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The two phenolic hydroxyls sit on ring carbons that are para to each other, while the carboxymethyl group is positioned meta to one of them and ortho to the other. The core is fairly rigid because of the planar aromatic ring, while the CH2-COOH arm adds some conformational flexibility. Overall the structure offers multiple hydrogen-bond donors from the three OH groups and the carboxylic acid, along with several oxygen acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic ketone built from two unbranched alkyl chains of five carbons each, joined through a single carbonyl carbon, giving a linear eleven-carbon skeleton. There are no rings and no fused ring systems, and the only functional group is the ketone, a carbon-oxygen double bond located at the central position of the chain. Because the carbonyl sits exactly in the middle, the two halves are identical, so the molecule has a mirror-symmetric, C2-like arrangement about the carbonyl carbon. The chains are highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, so the molecule can adopt numerous conformations. The oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

Ethyl 4-cyanobenzoate, a benzene ring bearing two substituents placed opposite one another (para) on the ring, forms the scaffold here. One substituent is an ethyl ester group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to an oxygen that carries a two-carbon ethyl chain. The other is a nitrile, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which projects linearly from the ring. The benzene core is a single aromatic ring with no ring fusion. The molecule has a flat, rigid aromatic core with a degree of conformational freedom only in the ethyl tail of the ester. Its symmetry is limited, since the two ends differ, though the para-disubstituted ring is itself symmetric about its long axis. The ester oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an open-chain, acyclic alkene with no rings, so its skeleton is a straight chain of eight carbons. Reading from the terminal end, it consists of a saturated five-carbon alkyl segment (an n-pentyl group) attached to a carbon-carbon double bond, which is bonded to a bromine atom on the terminal vinyl carbon. The double bond is a single trans-type disubstituted alkene with a halogen at one end, making the bromine the only heteroatom and the only functional group besides the C=C unit. The chain is flexible, with free rotation around its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond local planarity around the double bond. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine offers only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is an unbranched saturated hydrocarbon chain of eleven carbon atoms, with a single chlorine atom attached to the terminal carbon, so there is no ring system or ring fusion. Its scaffold is entirely aliphatic, built from sp3-hybridized carbons joined by single bonds. The only functional group is a primary alkyl chloride at one end, and the substitution pattern is simply a terminal halogen on a straight chain. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror relationship of the linear skeleton, and its many rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible. Its only polar feature is the carbon-chlorine bond, which can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is a small, acyclic, fully saturated haloalkane with a four-carbon-or-fewer chain, specifically a two-carbon skeleton built from an ethane-like backbone. The first carbon carries one methyl group and one chlorine atom, while the second carbon bears three chlorine atoms, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and clustered on the terminal end. There are no rings, no double bonds, and no aromatic systems, which leaves the molecule conformationally flexible about the central carbon-carbon single bond. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen is attached to carbon, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated-chain terminal alkyne: a straight carbon skeleton of twelve carbons with a carbon-carbon triple bond located at one end. The triple bond is linear and is the only unsaturated feature; the remainder of the chain consists of methylene units with single bonds. There are no rings, no ring fusion, no heteroatoms, and no other functional groups, so the substitution pattern is simply a single terminal alkyne with no branching or substituents. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the trivial, is highly flexible owing to free rotation about its many single bonds, and possesses no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone), a carboxylic acid, and a hydroxyl group sitting next to the carboxylic acid, so the acid and hydroxyl are ortho to each other on the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused systems, giving a flat, rigid scaffold with little conformational freedom beyond rotation of the acetyl and carboxyl groups. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl can each donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygens of the ketone and acid and the hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single saturated five-membered carbocycle, a cyclopentane ring, with no heteroatoms, no double bonds, and no aromatic character. Attached to one ring carbon is an unbranched eight-carbon alkyl chain, an n-octyl group, so the compound is a monosubstituted cyclopentane with no other substituents or stereocenters on the ring. There are no functional groups present, and the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The ring is fairly rigid while the long alkyl chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. Because the substitution is at one position only, the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the unsubstituted ring positions.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond with no fused ring system. One ring carries an ethyl group (–CH2CH3) at a meta position relative to the bond connecting it to the second ring, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The structure contains no heteroatoms and therefore no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Rotation about the central biaryl bond gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility, and the lack of symmetry arises from the single substituent on one ring.

This molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a single methylene bridge, giving a diarylmethane scaffold with no fused ring system. One ring carries a methyl group para to the bridging carbon, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The structure contains no functional groups beyond the aromatic rings and alkyl substituents, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The two aromatic rings can rotate about the sp3 carbon, which makes the framework moderately flexible rather than rigid. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two rings differ in substitution.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Two methoxy groups (O-CH3 ethers) sit on the ring at positions para to each other, giving the ring a symmetric 1,4-dioxygenated pattern. A nitro group (-NO2) is attached to the ring carbon adjacent to one of the methoxy substituents, so the ring carries three substituents in a 1,2,4 arrangement. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with the methoxy and nitro groups able to rotate only modestly about their bonds. The ether oxygens and nitro oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no ring fusion. Two substituents are attached to that ring at positions para to each other: an ethyl group (a two-carbon saturated chain) and a bromine atom. The ethyl group adds some conformational flexibility through its rotatable bond, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The molecule has no functional groups that act as hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it contains only carbon, hydrogen, and bromine. Its para-disubstituted pattern gives it a degree of local symmetry across the ring axis.

The molecule is a tertiary amine built around a single central nitrogen atom bearing three identical n-butyl chains, one attached to each of its three substituent positions. It has no rings and no ring fusion, so its scaffold is entirely acyclic and open-chain. The only functional group is the trialkylamine nitrogen, which carries a lone pair of electrons but no N-H bonds. Because of this, the molecule can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at nitrogen but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The three flexible saturated alkyl arms give it a high degree of conformational freedom, and its three-fold arrangement around the nitrogen gives it approximate local symmetry.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain saturated alcohol: a single unbranched carbon chain with a hydroxyl group on a secondary carbon near one end, giving it a methyl-terminated branch beside the alcohol carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the one hydroxyl. The substitution pattern is simple, with the oxygen-bearing carbon carrying one methyl group and the remaining long alkyl chain. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the hydroxyl sits off-center on the chain. The long saturated chain makes it highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the remainder of the structure is nonpolar hydrocarbon.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined directly by a single carbon-carbon bond, giving a biphenyl scaffold. One ring carries a chlorine atom at the position para to the connection to the second ring, so the substitution pattern is 1,4 on that ring, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The two aromatic rings are fused to nothing else, so there is no bridged or fused ring system, and the rings can rotate about the central bond, making the core moderately flexible. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the chlorine is a weak acceptor only. Its overall shape is elongated and roughly linear across the para axis.

This molecule is a straight-chain terminal alkyne, a 1-alkyne with a carbon-carbon triple bond at one end of an unbranched aliphatic chain. The scaffold is entirely acyclic, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms present. The only functional group is the terminal alkyne, where the sp-hybridized carbon bears a single hydrogen, and there are no branches or substituents along the chain to create a substitution pattern. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond its linear shape, and its many freely rotating single bonds make it highly flexible, though the triple bond itself is rigid and linear. It contains no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since the only polar-looking C–H is a weak, non-hydrogen-bonding terminal hydrogen.

This molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built on a long, unbranched chain of carbon atoms, with a single methyl branch located at the same carbon that carries a terminal alkene. The terminal double bond is a 1,1-disubstituted vinyl group, which is the only functional group present, and it contains no heteroatoms. There are no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no stereocenters, so the molecule has no symmetry beyond a rough mirror-plane arrangement of the chain. The long saturated segment is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through free rotation about its single bonds. Because it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

This molecule is 1,3-diphenylpropane: two benzene rings joined by a flexible three-carbon saturated chain. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so there are no functional groups, heteroatoms, or substitution patterns beyond the simple ring attachments. The overall shape is symmetric, with the two aromatic rings related by a mirror plane through the central methylene carbon. The three sp3 carbons in the linker give the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, while each benzene ring remains planar and rigid. Because the structure contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single saturated methylene bridge, with no fused ring system. One ring carries an ethyl group on the carbon adjacent to the bridge attachment point, giving an ortho-substituted, disubstituted benzene, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The skeleton is a diarylmethane framework, and its only functional groups are the aromatic rings and the alkyl chains, so there are no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The central CH2 linker gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility, allowing the two rings to rotate relative to one another, and the arrangement has no overall symmetry because the two rings differ in substitution.

The molecule is a biphenyl system in which one phenyl ring carries a carboxylic acid group at the meta position relative to the bond joining it to the second phenyl ring. The two aromatic rings are connected by a single C–C bond, giving an extended, fully conjugated scaffold built entirely from six-membered aromatic rings with no fused ring systems. The substitution pattern on the acid-bearing ring is 1,3 (meta), while the other ring is unsubstituted. The meta arrangement breaks any true mirror or rotational symmetry of the parent biphenyl, so the molecule has no internal symmetry axis through the carboxyl group. The biaryl bond allows some rotation between the rings, so the structure is moderately flexible, though conjugation favors a near-planar arrangement. The carboxylic acid group contains one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, making it the sole source of hydrogen-bonding capability in the molecule.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent-to-each-other positions relative to a meta arrangement: a nitro group (an N-oxide-type group with a positively charged nitrogen and a negatively charged oxygen, bonded to one ring carbon) and a bromine atom on a carbon separated from it by one ring carbon, giving a 1,3 (meta) substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no fused rings or additional stereocenters. The overall skeleton has only an approximate mirror plane through the nitro group, the bromine, and the ring axis, so it is nearly symmetric but not highly symmetric. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine offers only weak halogen-bonding acceptor character.

The molecule is built from a single benzene ring bearing one substituent, a straight nine-carbon saturated chain attached directly to one carbon of the aromatic ring. The benzene ring is planar, fully aromatic, and unfused, containing no heteroatoms and no additional functional groups. Because only one position is substituted, the molecule has no true symmetry element beyond the local symmetry of the ring and the chain's conformational freedom. The alkyl chain is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds, while the aromatic core is rigid. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it is made only of carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built on a linear twelve-carbon chain with a terminal alkene. Its skeleton is a straight-chain alkane-like backbone, except that the first carbon is a methylene (=CH2) double-bonded to a second carbon that also carries a methyl branch, so the unsaturation sits at the chain end. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or other functional groups beyond this single C=C. The substitution pattern is a 1,1-disubstituted alkene with a long unbranched alkyl tail. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond local conformational freedom, and its many rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is a saturated, fully aliphatic hydrocarbon with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms, so it contains no functional groups. Its skeleton is a straight chain of about twelve carbons with a single methyl branch located near one end of the main chain, creating an alkyl branch point at the carbon that bears the methyl group. The molecule has no symmetry, because the branch breaks any mirror or rotational equivalence along the chain. Its carbon-carbon single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility, with many rotatable bonds able to adopt different arrangements. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it has only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic aldehyde: a saturated, unbranched carbon backbone with a terminal formyl group (–CHO) at one end. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing ring systems, so the scaffold is purely acyclic. The aldehyde carbonyl is the only functional group, and it sits at the chain terminus, meaning there is no substitution pattern along the chain and the molecule has no internal branching. Its structure is essentially a long, flexible hydrocarbon tail capped by a polar carbonyl, so it has a single mirror-like axis of linear symmetry along the chain with no stereocenters. The chain is highly flexible due to free rotation about its many single bonds. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a biphenyl derivative in which one phenyl ring carries, at the ortho position relative to the biaryl bond, a carboxymethyl group (–CH2–COOH). Two benzene rings are joined by a single C–C bond, giving a flexible biaryl scaffold with no ring fusion, and the rings can rotate about that bond, though steric hindrance from the ortho substituent restricts this somewhat. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry axis that makes both rings equivalent, since only one ring is substituted. The carboxylic acid group is the sole polar functional group: its hydroxyl can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic rings contribute only π-system character and no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, which is a single six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings. An acetate ester group (a methyl ketone bonded through an oxygen to the ring) is attached at one position, and a bromine atom sits at the position directly opposite it, giving a para substitution pattern. The molecule has a flat, rigid framework, with only the acetyl and ester bonds able to rotate. The ester carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a diaryl alkane built from a five-carbon chain whose third carbon bears two separate phenyl rings, giving a 1,1-diphenylpentane skeleton. Both rings are simple, unfused benzene rings with no substituents on them, so the aromatic portion is unsubstituted and lacks any heteroatoms. The molecule contains no functional groups beyond the hydrocarbon framework, with only sp3 carbons linking the two aromatic rings to the alkyl tail. Because the central carbon carries two identical phenyl groups and a butyl chain, the structure has a plane of approximate symmetry through that carbon, and the flexible alkyl chain allows considerable conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, as it consists entirely of carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated hydrocarbon with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms, so it contains no functional groups. Its skeleton is a single unbranched chain of roughly seventeen carbons that carries one short two-carbon side branch (an ethyl group) on one internal carbon, which places the branch point well toward the middle of the chain. Because there are no rings or heteroatoms, the molecule has no symmetry beyond the trivial one and no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its many single bonds allow it to adopt a wide variety of conformations, making it highly flexible.

This molecule is an ester built on a biphenyl scaffold. A para-substituted benzene ring carries an ethyl ester group, CO2Et, whose carbonyl is attached directly to the aromatic ring. The opposite para position is bonded to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring through a single C–C bond, giving a linear, rod-like shape with two fused-free aromatic rings. The ester oxygen atoms are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid aromatic core limits flexibility, with some rotational freedom around the biaryl bond and the ethyl chain.

This molecule is a straight-chain, unbranched alkene: a terminal vinyl group (CH2=CH-) at one end of a saturated aliphatic chain. The scaffold is acyclic, with no rings or ring fusion present. Its only functional group is the single carbon-carbon double bond at the chain terminus, and there are no heteroatoms or substituents along the backbone. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the local arrangement of its methylene units, and its long, flexible chain can adopt many conformations due to free rotation about its single bonds. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it is composed entirely of carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is a saturated, acyclic hydrocarbon built on a single unbranched-then-branched carbon chain with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms. The longest chain runs through the main backbone, and one short ethyl-type branch is attached to a single interior carbon, creating a methyl side group near the middle of the chain. Because it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no functional groups, no aromatic or fused ring systems, and no sites that can act as hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The chain is highly flexible, with freely rotating carbon-carbon single bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond what the local chain conformations allow. Its overall shape is elongated and essentially nonpolar.

The molecule is a fully saturated, acyclic hydrocarbon built on a long, straight chain of carbon atoms with a single short branch. The main backbone runs through a continuous sequence of methylene units and ends in a terminal methyl group, while a methyl group and an ethyl-length arrangement sit at one carbon near the far end of the chain, creating an asymmetric branched alkane. The structure contains no rings, no fused ring systems, and no functional groups such as alcohols, carbonyls, or amines. Because all bonds are single and sp3-hybridized, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is an acetoxy group, an ester in which an acetyl carbonyl is bonded through an oxygen atom to the ring, and the other is an iodine atom attached directly to the aromatic carbon. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, while the ester linkage gives the molecule a small degree of conformational flexibility around the aryl C–O and O–C(=O) bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the ring that is broken by the differing substituents. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the two oxygen atoms of the ester group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic compound built on a single unbranched carbon backbone of twelve methylene units, with a terminal hydroxyl group on one end and a terminal bromine atom on the other. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing cyclic systems, so its scaffold is purely acyclic. The two functional groups sit at opposite ends of the chain, creating a linear, bifunctional arrangement with no substitution along the carbon framework and no internal stereocenters. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry along its length, but its overall shape is highly flexible due to free rotation about the many single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine atom serves only as a weak halogen acceptor.

This molecule is a short, fully saturated acyclic alkane built on a four-carbon chain, so it has no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic character. Three of its carbons carry bromine atoms: one secondary carbon bears a single bromine, while the central carbon carries two bromines and a methyl group, and the terminal carbon is part of a methyl group attached to the adjacent carbon. The bromine substitution is heavily concentrated near the middle of the chain, giving the molecule a markedly uneven, asymmetric distribution of its substituents. Because all bonds are single and the carbon framework is open-chain, the molecule is quite flexible and can adopt many conformations through rotation about its C–C bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atoms can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated three-carbon chain (a propane skeleton) bearing a bromine atom on each terminal carbon and one on the central carbon, giving a 1,2,3-tribromo substitution pattern. It contains no rings, no double bonds, and no other functional groups beyond the three carbon-bromine bonds. The central carbon carries a hydrogen and is attached to two of the bromomethyl arms, so the molecule has a mirror plane through that carbon and is achiral, with its two terminal CH2Br groups equivalent. Because all bonds are single and the backbone is unbranched beyond the central carbon, the chain is quite flexible and can adopt many rotational conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since the only heteroatoms are bromine atoms that are not strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a fully deuterated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from five fused six-membered aromatic rings in a compact, cata-condensed arrangement. Every peripheral position carries a deuterium atom in place of hydrogen, so the structure is a pure carbon-hydrogen framework with no heteroatoms or functional groups. The rings are fused in an angular, non-linear fashion, giving the scaffold a roughly bowl-shaped, partly curved outline rather than a flat linear strip. The molecule has no stereocenters and possesses only a limited symmetry element, with no strongly polar or rotatable groups, so it is essentially rigid and planar in its aromatic core. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since all exposed positions are carbon-deuterium bonds and no lone-pair-bearing atoms are present.

This molecule is a para-terphenyl scaffold: three benzene rings linked in a straight chain, with each bond between adjacent rings at the para positions of the central ring. Every ring carbon bears a deuterium atom in place of hydrogen, so the aromatic C–H positions are fully isotopically labeled. There are no functional groups, heteroatoms, or substituents beyond these deuterium atoms, so the molecule is a purely hydrocarbon aromatic system. The overall structure has a high degree of symmetry, with a two-fold axis running through the central ring and the chain. Overall, the structure is essentially planar and rigid, with the only conformational freedom coming from the methyl rotation.

The molecule is 2-methylpropene, a four-carbon acyclic alkene built on a short linear-branched skeleton. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or scaffold beyond the chain itself. The defining feature is a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, with the second alkene carbon carrying a methyl substituent, which makes the molecule a 1,1-disubstituted alkene. The structure is compact and quite rigid around the double bond, while the single bonds to the methyl groups allow only minor rotational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, so it cannot engage in hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is a fused tricyclic aromatic system built on a fluorene-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a central five-membered ring that contains one saturated CH2 carbon. The nitro group (-NO2) is attached to one of the outer benzene rings, para to the biaryl bond, so the substitution pattern breaks the symmetry of the framework. The CH2 bridge is the only sp3 carbon, which keeps the core largely planar and rigid, with little conformational flexibility. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework. It carries two primary amino groups, placed para to one another, and a nitro group sitting ortho to one of the amines, which gives the ring a 1,4-diamino-2-nitro substitution pattern. The arrangement is essentially planar, with the aromatic ring and its directly attached nitro and amino substituents lying in roughly the same plane, so the overall shape is rigid apart from rotation of the terminal groups. The two amino groups each supply hydrogen-bond donor capacity through their N–H bonds, while the nitro group offers oxygen atoms that act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond what its planar framework allows.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds, bearing a single substituent at one position. That substituent is a three-membered oxirane (epoxide) ring, a strained cyclic ether in which one oxygen atom is bonded to two adjacent carbons, and the epoxide carbons are directly attached to the phenyl ring. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the attached epoxide is also rigid but can rotate about the single bond connecting it to the benzene ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the phenyl ring and the epoxide, and the epoxide carbon bearing the phenyl group is a stereocentre. The oxygen atom of the epoxide can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a central 1,2,4-triazol-3-one ring bearing a sec-butyl group on one nitrogen, which is linked through an N-aryl bond to a para-phenylene unit. That phenylene carries a piperazine ring, whose opposite nitrogen attaches to a second para-phenylene. A dioxolane ring, a five-membered acetal with two oxygens and a defined stereocenter, is tethered to this aryl chain through a methylene ether linkage. Its quaternary acetal carbon bears a 2,4-dichlorophenyl group and a CH2-linked 1,2,4-triazole, which gives the substitution pattern a clear asymmetric, elongated profile. Overall the scaffold is rigid through its multiple fused and linked aromatic and heterocyclic rings, with the flexible ether and piperazine linkers allowing some conformational freedom. Nitrogen-containing heterocycles and ether oxygens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The other substituent is a chloroperoxy group, an oxygen-oxygen single bond connecting the ring to a terminal chlorine atom, which adds a flexible, weakly bonded linkage with two additional oxygen atoms that can act as acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with no ring fusion, while the peroxy side chain has rotational freedom around its bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents differ in identity and the chloroperoxy group is not symmetric about the ring.

This molecule is built around a cyclohexane-type six-membered carbocycle that is fused to a three-membered oxirane (epoxide) ring, creating a bicyclic framework in which the epoxide shares two adjacent carbons with the ring. A second, separate three-membered oxirane is attached directly to the carbocycle at a neighboring carbon, so the structure contains two epoxide rings in total. The epoxide oxygens are the only heteroatoms and act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused and strained three-membered rings make the framework fairly rigid, with limited conformational freedom, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric because the two epoxide units are attached differently to the carbocyclic core.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one hydroxyl group and three chlorine atoms, making it a trichlorophenol. The six-membered aromatic carbocycle forms a flat, rigid scaffold with no fused rings. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, while three chlorine substituents occupy adjacent positions on the opposite side of the ring, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror plane through the full set of substituents. The phenolic oxygen can donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H group and accept one through its lone pairs, whereas the chlorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the molecule is compact and has limited conformational flexibility, with the hydroxyl group being the only substituent capable of rotation.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons, forming a catechol unit. Two tert-butyl groups are attached to the ring at positions flanking the catechol pair on one side and at the meta position opposite, giving a 3,5-di-tert-butyl substitution relative to the hydroxyls. The ring itself is planar and aromatic, so the core scaffold is rigid, while the bulky tert-butyl groups are sterically demanding and rotate only about their attachment bonds. The molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry that would make its two sides identical, since the two hydroxyl groups and the two tert-butyl groups occupy different environments. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and an acceptor through its lone pairs, giving the molecule two donor and two acceptor sites overall.

The molecule is a diaryl ether urea built around a central urea linkage, with one nitrogen bearing two methyl groups (an N,N-dimethyl urea). The other urea nitrogen attaches to a para-substituted benzene ring, which is connected through an ether oxygen to a second benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom at the position para to the ether linkage. The two aromatic rings are joined by a flexible C–O–C bridge, giving the molecule moderate conformational freedom around the ether, while the aromatic rings and urea carbonyl remain largely planar. The structure has no overall symmetry because the dimethylamino end differs from the chlorinated aryl end. The N–H of the urea is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the ether oxygen, and the chlorine provide acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a saturated cyclohexane ring with no aromatic rings and no fused ring systems. Two carbons on the ring each carry an amino group, and one of them is a quaternary carbon bearing both a methyl group and an amino group, while the other bears a second quaternary carbon that carries two methyl groups and an amino group. The substituents are placed in a 1,4-relationship across the ring, giving a fairly symmetric but not strictly symmetric pattern. Because the ring is saturated and the bulky substituents are attached at quaternary centers, the scaffold is conformationally restricted, though the ring can still adopt chair-like forms. Both nitrogen atoms are primary amines, so each can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

This molecule is built on a benzo-fused cyclic sultone, a five-membered ring containing a sulfur atom bearing two oxo groups, a ring oxygen, and a quaternary carbon, which is fused to a benzene ring. That quaternary carbon carries two identical 3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxyphenyl substituents, so the two pendant aryl rings are related by a mirror-like symmetry through the central sp3 carbon. Each pendant ring bears two bromine atoms flanking a free phenolic hydroxyl group, giving the periphery a dense pattern of halogen and hydroxyl substitution. The phenolic OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The bulky, interlocked arrangement around the central carbon makes the framework fairly rigid.

This molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through an anhydride linkage, a C(=O)–O–C(=O) unit that bridges the two aromatic systems. Each benzene ring is a flat, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle, and each carries three carboxylic acid groups, giving six –COOH substituents in total. The substitution pattern on each ring places the carbonyl-bearing carbons in a 1,2,4 arrangement, so the two halves are not identical in their attachment positions relative to the anhydride. Each carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and the anhydride carbonyl oxygens act as additional acceptors. Overall the structure is rigid across its aromatic cores, with some rotational freedom only around the single bonds linking the rings to the anhydride.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, bearing a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and two hydroxymethyl groups as substituents. The ring nitrogen is adjacent to the carbon carrying the methyl group, and the remaining substituents occupy the other positions around the ring, giving a fully substituted pyridine with no unsubstituted ring carbons. Because the ring is aromatic and carries no further fused rings, the core is rigid and planar, while the two hydroxymethyl arms and the methyl group add some rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the substituents differ in identity and position. Its hydroxyl and hydroxymethyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a 1,3,5-triazine core, a six-membered aromatic ring containing three nitrogen atoms alternating with carbon atoms. Two of the three ring carbons each carry a chlorine substituent, while the third bears an arylamino group, giving an NH linker attached to a benzene ring. That benzene ring is ortho-substituted with a single chlorine atom adjacent to the point of attachment. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the aniline portion breaks the threefold symmetry of the triazine core. The fused-free, planar aromatic framework with a single rotatable C–N bond gives it moderate rigidity. The secondary amine NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the triazine ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) pattern. One side bears a four-carbon chain ending in a terminal carboxylic acid, giving a flexible tail with an acidic hydrogen-bond donor and two oxygen acceptors. The opposite side carries a tertiary aromatic amine whose nitrogen is bonded to two 2-chloroethyl arms, which are flexible and rotatable. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the alkyl chains add conformational freedom. The overall framework has an approximate two-fold relationship through the ring axis, though the substituents themselves are not symmetric.

The molecule is a triarylamine: a central nitrogen atom bonded to three separate phenyl rings, giving a propeller-like, non-planar arrangement around the nitrogen. Each of the three rings carries a single bromine atom at the position para to the nitrogen linkage, so the substitution pattern is identical on all three arms. This arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, approximately threefold about the central nitrogen. The aromatic rings are unfused and attached only through the nitrogen, so the structure has no fused ring systems. The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the attached rings and it is a poor hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rotatable bonds to the nitrogen give moderate conformational flexibility around the propeller shape.

The molecule is built around a sulfonylurea scaffold, in which a urea carbonyl bridges a propylamino group on one side and a sulfonyl group on the other. The sulfonyl group is attached to a benzene ring that carries a chlorine atom para to the sulfur attachment point, giving a 1,4-disubstituted aromatic system. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the propyl chain and the flexible urea-sulfonyl linker provide some conformational freedom. The molecule has no symmetry axis because the propyl chain and the chlorophenyl ring are structurally distinct. Its hydrogen-bond capability includes two N–H donors on the urea and sulfonamide nitrogens, and several acceptors from the carbonyl oxygen and the two sulfonyl oxygens.

This molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolone core, a heteroaromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl carbon. The ring carries a methyl group on one carbon, an isopropyl group on the adjacent carbon, and a second methyl group on the ring nitrogen that bears no hydrogen. The remaining ring nitrogen is substituted by an unsubstituted phenyl ring, which is a single flat aromatic six-membered ring attached through a single bond, so the structure has rotational freedom at that junction. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because all ring nitrogens are fully substituted. The overall architecture is asymmetric, with the bulky isopropyl group and the phenyl ring creating a non-uniform, moderately rigid scaffold.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring bearing four substituents: an amino group, a hydroxyl group, and two phenyl rings. Parsing the SMILES, the ring carries an NH2 group on one carbon, a phenyl ring on the adjacent-but-one carbon, a hydroxyl group flanked by two phenyl-substituted positions, and a second phenyl ring on the carbon next to it, giving a 1,3-diphenyl arrangement around a phenol-type core with the amine meta to the hydroxyl. The two outer phenyl rings are unfused, monocyclic aromatic systems attached by single bonds, so the scaffold is a terphenyl-like framework. The hydroxyl and amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and both heteroatoms can also accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry axis that maps the full structure onto itself, and its biaryl linkages allow some rotational freedom while the overall framework stays largely planar and rigid.

This molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazole ring bearing a nitrile group, a primary amino group, and a trifluoromethylsulfinyl group on adjacent carbons. The pyrazole nitrogen is substituted with a phenyl ring that carries two chlorine atoms flanking the attachment point and a trifluoromethyl group at the para position, giving a 2,6-dichloro-4-substituted aryl pattern. The two ring systems are linked by a single bond and are not fused, so the connection allows some rotation about the bond between them. The amino group and the sulfinyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the nitrile nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site. The molecule lacks any symmetry axis because of its asymmetric substitution.

This molecule is a salicylanilide, built from a benzene ring bearing an ortho hydroxyl group and a carboxamide linking it to a second benzene ring through an amide bond. The first aromatic ring carries a chlorine atom positioned meta to the amide carbonyl and para to the hydroxyl group. The second aromatic ring is an anilide that carries a chlorine atom ortho to the amide nitrogen and a nitro group para to the nitrogen. The amide NH and the phenolic OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, the phenolic oxygen, and the nitro oxygens serve as acceptors. The two aryl rings are connected by a relatively rigid amide linkage, giving the molecule limited conformational flexibility and no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a tricyclic scaffold in which two benzene rings are joined through a central six-membered ring containing a single oxygen atom and a methylene carbon, giving a fused, nearly planar, rigid framework. The oxygen bridges the two aromatic rings as an aryl ether, while the CH2 group links the other pair of ring carbons, so the central ring is fused on two opposite sides. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, with no functional groups beyond the ether oxygen and the methylene bridge. The skeleton has a degree of local symmetry about the central heterocycle but no substituents to break it further. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, and its only acceptor site is the lone pairs on the ether oxygen.

The molecule is built on a phenanthrene scaffold, consisting of three fused six-membered aromatic rings arranged in an angular rather than linear fashion. The ring system is fully aromatic and planar, so it is rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core. A single iodine atom is attached to one carbon of the central ring, giving a monosubstituted pattern with no symmetry element beyond the planar framework. The compound carries no hydrogen-bond donors, and the iodine offers only weak acceptor character through its lone pairs.

Ethyne, with the SMILES C#C, is the simplest alkyne: two carbon atoms joined by a carbon-carbon triple bond, each bearing a single hydrogen atom. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no functional groups beyond the triple bond itself. The molecule is perfectly linear and highly symmetric, belonging to the same symmetry class as a diatomic linear arrangement, with both terminal hydrogens lying along the same axis. Its skeleton is rigid, since the triple bond allows no rotation and fixes the geometry. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites in the conventional sense, because the only polar-looking groups are carbon-hydrogen bonds with little polarity, while the pi electron cloud of the triple bond offers only weak, nonclassical interactions.

This molecule is built on an acridine scaffold, a planar tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused on either side of a central pyridine ring. The amino group sits at the 9-position, the carbon in the middle ring that lies between the two fused benzene rings, and it is the only substituent, so the molecule has no other substitution pattern to consider. The fully aromatic, flat framework is rigid and has no rotatable bonds. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the exocyclic primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and can also accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule possesses a two-fold symmetry axis running through the ring nitrogen and the 9-position carbon.

This molecule is a small, acyclic amino acid built on a three-carbon backbone: a central alpha carbon bears a methyl group, a primary amine, a hydrogen atom, and a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid group sits at one end of the chain, giving the molecule a terminal C(=O)OH functionality. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is simply a flexible, open-chain skeleton. The alpha carbon is a stereocenter, so the molecule can exist in distinct handedness forms, although the SMILES as written does not specify one. Both the amine and the carboxylic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms of the carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the amine serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fully aromatic three-ring fused skeleton, a phenalene-like or anthracene-type tricyclic core. Three hydroxyl groups are attached directly to the aromatic ring carbons, positioned on the outer edges of the fused system, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric with respect to a single mirror plane. The fused ring framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable single bonds in the core. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its oxygen-bound hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. Several of the hydroxyls sit close enough to neighboring positions to allow possible intramolecular hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on an anthracene-type tricyclic skeleton, but with a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an attached hydrogen) on one of the central ring carbons, specifically at the meso position between two fused benzene-like rings. Three six-membered aromatic rings are fused linearly in an angular arrangement, giving a planar, fully conjugated, rigid framework. The only substituent is the aldehyde, so the substitution pattern is minimal and the molecule has no rotational flexibility beyond the carbonyl bond. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its overall symmetry is limited because the aldehyde breaks the mirror symmetry of the parent ring system.

This molecule is a long, symmetric polyene built from a central conjugated chain of alternating carbon-carbon double and single bonds, decorated with methyl groups along its length. At each end sits a six-membered cyclohexene ring bearing gem-dimethyl substitution and an exocyclic double bond linking it into the chain. The two terminal ring units are identical, giving the molecule an approximate mirror or two-fold symmetry about its midpoint. The extended conjugated framework makes the structure largely rigid and planar along its backbone, while the saturated ring ends and methyl groups add some local bulk. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, so its hydrogen-bonding capability is essentially nil.

This molecule is a diester built on a benzene ring with two substituents in the ortho positions, a 1,2-benzenedicarboxylate core. Each carboxyl group forms an ester with a long, branched, saturated alkyl chain: an isodecyl-type chain carrying a methyl branch near the terminus. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two long alkyl tails are highly flexible and free to rotate. The molecule has no symmetry-breaking stereocenters, but the two ester arms are chemically equivalent, giving an overall pseudo-symmetric shape. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and only the four oxygen atoms of the two ester groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

Vinyl chloride is a very small acyclic molecule built on a two-carbon backbone, with no ring systems or ring fusion. It contains a single carbon-carbon double bond, and one of the two terminal carbons carries a chlorine atom, which serves as the only functional group, a halogenated alkene. Because it has only two carbons and one chlorine, there is no meaningful substitution pattern beyond that one halogen, and the molecule is essentially planar with a rigid double bond that prevents rotation about the C=C axis. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no O-H or N-H groups, and its chlorine can act only as a very weak acceptor.

This molecule is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from five fused six-membered rings, each sharing an edge with its neighbor, forming a rigid, planar, fully conjugated scaffold. It contains no heteroatoms and no substituents, so there are no functional groups, and every ring atom is an aromatic carbon bearing a single hydrogen except at the fusion positions. The fused arrangement is angular rather than linear, producing a bent, somewhat curved outline with a bay-type inner edge. The framework has no true rotational symmetry in its fused pattern, though the outer rings are related by a mirror-like relationship. Because it lacks any N, O, or other polar atoms, the structure has neither hydrogen-bond donor nor hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

This molecule is a cage hydrocarbon built entirely from carbon atoms, with no heteroatoms and no functional groups. Its skeleton is a compact polycyclic framework in which every carbon is bonded to three other carbons in a fused, three-dimensional arrangement, giving a highly strained, rigid structure. The ring system is fused such that the cage closes on itself in several directions, leaving no free rotatable bonds and no flexible chains. The molecule is highly symmetric, with a repeating pattern of carbon positions around its core. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is a silicon-centered compound, a diphenylsilanediol, in which one tetrahedral silicon atom carries two hydroxyl groups and two phenyl rings. Each phenyl group is an unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to silicon, so the substitution pattern is simple and no additional functional groups are present. The two aromatic rings are not fused to each other, and the silicon center acts as a flexible hinge that allows them to rotate relative to one another. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis passing through the silicon atom, which relates the two phenyl groups. Each hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept one through its oxygen lone pairs, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is an acyclic peroxide built from two identical tert-butyl groups joined through an oxygen–oxygen single bond. Each tert-butyl unit is a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, so the skeleton is highly branched and symmetric about the central O–O axis. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems. The only functional group is the peroxide linkage, and the molecule is flexible about its single bonds, though the bulky tert-butyl groups restrict conformational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two oxygen atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain saturated primary alcohol: a single unbranched carbon backbone of twenty-two carbons terminating in a hydroxyl group on one end. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups or substituents along the chain, so the substitution pattern is simply a terminal hydroxyl with no branching. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the idealized mirror relationship of the chain's two ends, which differ because only one end carries the oxygen. The long alkyl chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, though it tends toward extended conformations. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the alkyl portion contributes only nonpolar, hydrophobic character.

This molecule is a small acyclic ester built on a three-carbon backbone. It contains no rings, so its scaffold is a flexible open chain. The central carbon bears a terminal methylene double bond (C=C) and a nitrile group (C#N), while a carbonyl (C=O) connected to an ethoxy group (OCH2CH3) forms the ester functionality. The alkene, nitrile, and ester groups are all directly attached to the same carbon, making the substitution pattern highly crowded and conjugated. The molecule lacks internal symmetry, and its rotatable single bonds in the ethyl ester give it considerable conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the nitrile nitrogen and the two carbonyl-type oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a hydroxyl group, an ethyl ester, and two para-chlorophenyl rings, giving a diaryl carbinol scaffold. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring with one chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, so the two rings are identical and related by a mirror-like symmetry through the central carbon. The ester carbonyl and the ether-type oxygen of the ethyl group are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the tertiary hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The central carbon is a stereogenic center, although the two aryl groups are identical, so no chirality arises at that position. The molecule has several rotatable single bonds, giving it moderate conformational flexibility, though the bulky diaryl arrangement restricts rotation around the central carbon.

The molecule is a short linear peptide-like chain built from two glycine-type units joined by an amide bond, giving the skeleton H2N-CH2-C(=O)-NH-CH2-C(=O)-OH. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system. The functional groups present are a primary amine at one terminus, a secondary amide linkage in the middle, and a terminal carboxylic acid at the other end. Because the chain is unbranched and carries no substituents on the carbon backbone, the substitution pattern is simple and the structure has no internal symmetry. The backbone contains several rotatable single bonds, so the molecule is quite flexible. Its amine and amide N-H groups and carboxylic acid O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and carboxyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen act as acceptors.

The molecule is a perfluorinated two-carbon chain, with a single carbon-carbon bond connecting two carbon atoms that each carry three fluorine atoms. Its scaffold is entirely saturated and acyclic, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. Every carbon bears only fluorine substituents, meaning the molecule contains no conventional functional groups such as alcohols, amines, or carbonyls. The structure has high local symmetry, with both carbons related by a threefold axis along the C–C bond, and rotation about that bond is essentially free. Because there are no hydrogen atoms bonded to electronegative atoms, it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and its fluorine atoms are weak, poorly polarizable acceptors only.

This molecule is methyl isocyanate, a very small acyclic structure with no rings and no stereocenters. Its skeleton consists of a single methyl group attached to a nitrogen atom that is connected by a double bond to a central carbon, which is in turn double-bonded to an oxygen atom, giving a linear N=C=O cumulene arrangement. The isocyanate group is the only functional group, and the molecule has no substitution pattern beyond the methyl group. Its heavy-atom framework is essentially linear and rigid, with only rotation about the bond to the methyl group. The oxygen atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

This molecule is an alpha-amino acid built on a three-carbon chain, with the alpha carbon bearing a primary amine and a carboxylic acid group. A benzyl side chain extends from the alpha carbon, and its phenyl ring carries a single hydroxyl group at the para position, giving a para-substituted aromatic ring with a phenolic OH. The stereocenter at the alpha carbon makes the molecule chiral, and the flexible CH2 linker lets the aromatic ring rotate relative to the backbone. Overall, the molecule offers several hydrogen-bond donors (the amine, the carboxylic OH, and the phenolic OH) and multiple acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the nitrogen).

CS is methanethiol, a single-carbon molecule in which a methyl group is bonded to a sulfur atom that carries a terminal hydrogen. The skeleton is acyclic and contains no rings, ring fusion, or aromatic systems. The only functional group is the thiol (sulfhydryl) group, which is the defining feature of the molecule. The structure has no substitution pattern to speak of, since the carbon bears only hydrogens and the sulfur bears only one hydrogen. The molecule is small and highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bond. The thiol hydrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a single central phosphorus atom, which forms a phosphoryl group, P=O, with an oxygen atom held by a double bond. Bonded to the phosphorus are one methyl group, a carbon atom bearing three hydrogens, and two chlorine atoms, giving a tetrahedral-like arrangement around the phosphorus centre. The structure contains no rings and no fused ring systems, so it is an acyclic, fully substituted scaffold. Its flexibility is limited to rotation about the single P–C bond, while the phosphoryl and dichloro units remain fixed in place. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local mirror relationship between the two chlorine atoms. The phosphoryl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites because it carries no N–H or O–H groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta arrangement, with no ring fusion. One substituent is an acetamido group, in which an acetyl carbonyl is bonded to an amide nitrogen attached directly to the ring, and the other is a methyl group on the ring. Because the aromatic ring is planar and rigid while the amide linkage can rotate about its bonds, the overall shape is mostly flat with limited flexibility. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and the carbonyl oxygen as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ring and methyl group contribute only hydrophobic character. The molecule has no symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through the ring and its substituents.

This molecule is N-hydroxy-N-acetyl aminofluorene, built on a fluorene scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a five-membered ring that contains a CH2 group, giving a rigid, nearly planar tricyclic system. The nitrogen sits on one of the outer aromatic rings, bearing both an acetyl group (a carbonyl attached to a methyl) and a hydroxyl group, so it is a hydroxamic acid-type functional group. The substitution is at a single position on one ring, leaving the molecule without any internal symmetry. The carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the hydroxyl hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor.

This molecule is an acyclic polyamine built on a two-carbon ethylene bridge connecting two tertiary nitrogen atoms, each of which is linked to a second ethylene unit joining two further tertiary nitrogens, giving a linear chain of four nitrogen centers. Each nitrogen carries two carboxymethyl arms, so the scaffold bears eight free carboxylic acid groups arranged in a symmetric pattern about the central backbone. Because there are no rings, the skeleton is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The carboxylic acid groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the tertiary amine nitrogens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an N,N-diethyl benzamide, built from a single benzene ring bearing one carboxamide group. The amide nitrogen carries two ethyl groups, making it a tertiary amide with no N-H bond. A methyl group sits on the aromatic ring at the meta position relative to the carbonyl, giving a 1,3-disubstituted benzene. The benzene ring is planar and aromatic, while the two ethyl chains are flexible and rotatable. The amide oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a symmetric 1,5-diphenylcarbohydrazide-type structure: a central carbonyl (C=O) flanked by two hydrazine-like nitrogen pairs, each connected to a phenyl ring. The core is a urea-like, or carbonyl-bridged, N–N linkage, with the carbonyl carbon as the central unit. Each terminal nitrogen is bonded to an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the two aromatic rings are attached through an N–N–C(=O)–N–N backbone. The two phenyl groups are equivalent, giving the molecule a near-mirror-symmetric arrangement about the carbonyl. The NH groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pairs act as acceptors. The aromatic rings are planar and fused to nothing, and the N–N bonds allow some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built from a linear hexamethylene chain (six CH2 units) flanked at each end by a biguanide unit, and each biguanide terminates in a para-chlorophenyl ring. The skeleton is therefore symmetric about the midpoint of the central alkyl chain, with the two halves mirror images of one another. There are two benzene rings, each carrying one chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, and no fused ring systems. The polyguanidine-type units contain multiple imine (C=NH) and amine (NH) groups that act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The central chain is highly flexible, while the biguanide and aryl regions are comparatively planar and conjugated.

This molecule is a linear, flexible aliphatic chain built around a central four-carbon (butyl) spacer that links two carbamate-protected amine ends. One terminus carries a tert-butyl carbamate (Boc-type) group attached to a straight CH2 chain, while the other end bears an alpha-carbon bearing a carboxylic acid and a nitrogen protected by a fluorenylmethyloxycarbonyl (Fmoc-type) group. The Fmoc unit contains a fused tricyclic aromatic system in which two benzene rings are joined to a central five-membered ring, which is largely planar and rigid. The molecule has a stereocenter at the alpha-carbon and no overall symmetry, since the two protected ends differ. Its hydrogen-bond capability comes from two carbamate N-H groups and a carboxylic acid O-H as donors, with multiple carbonyl and ether oxygens serving as acceptors.

This molecule is an ester built from a long linear eighteen-carbon alkyl chain attached through an oxygen to a propanoate carbonyl. The acyl end carries a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon linker to the carbonyl, and the ring is substituted at its 3 and 5 positions with two bulky tert-butyl groups flanking a central phenolic hydroxyl at position 4. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the long saturated chain and the ethylene linker are highly flexible. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the chain and ring are distinct, although the two tert-butyl groups are mirror-related about the ring. The phenol OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the ring is hindered by its flanking substituents.

The molecule is a single sulfur atom bonded to three oxygen atoms, with two of those bonds drawn as double bonds, giving a compact, non-ring structure with no carbon skeleton. Because there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents beyond the three oxygens, the substitution pattern is trivial. The central sulfur sits in a trigonal planar arrangement, so the molecule has high local symmetry. It is rigid, since there are no rotatable single bonds that would give conformational freedom. Each oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, as it contains no N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is a three-carbon chain containing a single carbon-carbon double bond at the terminal end, with no rings, no fused systems, and no heteroatoms. Its skeleton is a linear, unbranched propene-type scaffold, so there is no substitution pattern to speak of beyond the terminal alkene itself. The structure is essentially flat around the double bond and has a degree of flexibility from rotation about its single bond. Because the molecule contains only carbon and hydrogen and no polar functional groups, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is built on a linear polyene chain of conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds, with a terminal primary alcohol group (–CH2OH) at one end. At the other end, the chain is attached to a six-membered cyclohexene ring bearing a gem-dimethyl group on one carbon and a methyl group on the adjacent alkene carbon, so the ring is partially unsaturated and non-aromatic. The chain carries several methyl branches, which break its overall symmetry and make the molecule asymmetric. The extended conjugated system is largely rigid across its double bonds, while the single bonds and the saturated ring portion allow some flexibility. The single hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and there are no other polar heteroatoms.

The molecule is a single central sulfur atom bonded to four other atoms, with no carbon skeleton and no ring systems. Two of the sulfur's bonds are double bonds to oxygen atoms, and the remaining two substituents are a hydroxyl group (an oxygen bearing one hydrogen) and a fluorine atom, giving it a sulfonyl-type center with a tetrahedral-like arrangement. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the fluorine can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is very small and has no rotatable ring framework, so its shape is essentially rigid apart from rotation about the single bonds to the hydroxyl and fluorine substituents. Its substitution pattern is fully occupied around the central atom, leaving no sites for further substitution.

This molecule is a small, fully fluorinated two-carbon unit built around a single carbon-carbon double bond, with no rings present. Each of the two sp2 carbons carries two fluorine substituents, giving a symmetric, planar arrangement of atoms in which the carbon-carbon double bond forms the sole structural feature. The double bond restricts rotation, so the molecule is rigid rather than flexible. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the electronegative fluorine atoms, which interact weakly at best.

This molecule is a fully aromatic polycyclic hydrocarbon built from five fused six-membered rings arranged in a zigzag, angular pattern rather than a straight line. Its scaffold contains no heteroatoms and no functional groups, so the only substituents are hydrogen atoms on the ring carbons. The fused arrangement gives the framework a rigid, planar geometry with limited conformational flexibility. Because the structure has no polar groups, it offers no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. Its overall shape has only approximate symmetry, reflecting the asymmetric angular fusion of the rings.

This molecule is a single tetrahedral carbon atom with no ring system and no chain, so its scaffold is simply one central carbon bonded to four substituents. Three of those substituents are chlorine atoms, and the fourth is a deuterium atom, the heavy isotope of hydrogen, written as [2H].
