Because three identical chlorine atoms surround the carbon and one different substituent sits opposite them, the molecule has threefold rotational symmetry about the carbon-deuterium bond axis. It is entirely rigid, since no rotatable bonds or ring constraints create conformational flexibility. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single carbon atom that serves as the entire scaffold, with no ring systems or ring fusion present. That central carbon carries three chlorine substituents and one nitro group, which consists of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one drawn as a formal positive charge on nitrogen and one as a formal negative charge on oxygen. The three chlorines are identical, giving the molecule local threefold symmetry around the carbon axis, and the overall structure is compact and rigid with very little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability because it carries no hydrogen atoms bonded to electronegative atoms. Its two nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an unbranched, saturated carbon chain of thirteen carbons, with a carboxylic acid group at one terminus. The carbonyl carbon bears a double-bonded oxygen and a hydroxyl group, so the terminal end is a carboxylic acid functional group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents along the chain, so the scaffold is a simple linear alkane-derived framework. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror-like arrangement of an unbranched chain. Its long saturated chain gives considerable conformational flexibility. The carboxyl group provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is an acyclic organophosphate ester built around a single central phosphorus atom bearing one double-bonded oxygen (a phosphoryl group) and three singly bonded ethoxy substituents, each consisting of an oxygen attached to an ethyl chain. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and tetrahedral about phosphorus. The three ethoxy arms are chemically equivalent, giving the molecule a high degree of local symmetry around the phosphorus center. The phosphoryl oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ester oxygens are weaker acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ethyl groups provide considerable conformational flexibility through rotation about their C–C and C–O bonds.

The molecule is a small organosilicon compound built around a single central silicon atom. That silicon carries three methoxy groups, each consisting of an oxygen bonded to a methyl carbon, and a fourth substituent that is a hydrogen atom, so the silicon is tetrahedral with one Si–H bond. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the structure is entirely acyclic. Because the three alkoxy arms can rotate freely about their Si–O bonds, the molecule is flexible, though its overall arrangement around silicon retains approximate threefold local symmetry. The oxygen atoms can each accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since the only hydrogen is attached directly to silicon.

This molecule is a trialkyl phosphate ester, built around a single central phosphorus atom that is doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to three other oxygens. Each of those three oxygens links to a straight, unbranched eight-carbon alkyl chain, so the scaffold is flexible and essentially free of rings or fused systems. The phosphoryl (P=O) group is the principal functional group, and it is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ester oxygens can also accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no O–H or N–H groups. Its three identical octyl arms give it approximate threefold symmetry around the phosphorus center, with the flexible chains able to adopt many conformations.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built from a short linear skeleton with no ring systems and no fused rings. The vinyl ester group, C=C-O-C(=O), sits at one end, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to a branched alkyl carbon that carries an ethyl branch and a straight butyl chain. The alpha carbon is a stereogenic-capable tertiary center, and the chain is highly flexible because it contains only single C-C bonds apart from the terminal alkene and the carbonyl. The ester oxygens provide two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a vinyl ester built from a linear, unbranched chain. The acyl portion is a saturated straight-chain carbon backbone, while the other end carries a terminal vinyl group bonded through an oxygen atom. The ester functional group, a carbonyl joined to an ether-type oxygen, sits between the long alkyl chain and the small unsaturated end. There are no rings, fused systems, or aromatic groups, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond its simple linear form. Its long, flexible chain has many rotatable bonds, so it adopts many conformations. The only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two oxygen atoms of the ester, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from a cyclopropane ring, a three-membered all-carbon ring, bearing a phenyl group on one ring carbon and a primary amino group on an adjacent ring carbon, so the two substituents sit on vicinal positions of the strained ring. The phenyl ring is an unfused benzene ring with no additional substituents, giving a simple monosubstituted aromatic system. The amine nitrogen is the only heteroatom and functions as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair. The two stereogenic ring carbons define a specific relative and absolute configuration, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane. The rigid cyclopropane core restricts conformational freedom, while the phenyl ring can rotate about its single bond to the ring.

This molecule is built on a glycosylated aminocyclitol scaffold, where a central cyclohexane ring with several amino and hydroxyl substituents is linked through glycosidic oxygens to two saturated oxygen-containing rings, one of which is a tetrahydrofuran-type ring bearing a branched N-methylaminoethyl side chain. The fused-free arrangement of three separate rings joined by ether linkages gives a branched, three-dimensional framework. Multiple primary and secondary amine groups and several hydroxyl groups are distributed across the rings, creating a dense pattern of substitution with no internal symmetry. The many rotatable glycosidic bonds and ring junctions confer considerable conformational flexibility. Numerous nitrogen and oxygen atoms can each act as hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, giving the structure strong hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is built on a cyclopentanone scaffold, a five-membered carbocycle bearing a ketone at one ring position. The ring is substituted at adjacent carbons: one neighbor carries a hydroxyl group and a trans-configured alkene linked to a pentyl-containing secondary alcohol side chain, while the other carries a seven-carbon chain terminating in a carboxylic acid. The ring is saturated apart from its carbonyl, so it is non-fused and relatively compact, though the two long side chains add considerable conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is high: the hydroxyl groups and the terminal carboxylic acid can act as both donors and acceptors, while the ketone and the acid carbonyl serve as additional acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because its stereocenters and differing substituents break any mirror or rotational equivalence.

The molecule is built around a flexible open-chain backbone: a methoxy-terminated alkyl chain runs into a carbon bearing an oxime ether, where the C=N double bond connects to an O-linked two-carbon chain ending in a primary amine. A para-substituted benzene ring carries a trifluoromethyl group opposite the point of attachment to the oxime carbon, giving the aromatic portion a linear, unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. There are no fused or bridged ring systems; the only rigid element is the aromatic ring and the C=N unit, while the remaining chains are highly rotatable. Hydrogen-bond capability is present on the primary amine, which can donate hydrogen bonds, and the ether oxygens and oxime nitrogen can accept them. The trifluoromethyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor character of its own.

This molecule is a 1,4-dihydropyridine built on a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that is partially saturated, bearing a sp3 carbon at the 4-position. Two methyl groups sit at the 2- and 6-positions, and the ring carries two ester groups at the 3- and 5-positions, one a 2-methoxyethyl ester and the other an isopropyl ester, which makes the two sides of the ring electronically similar but not identical in shape. The 4-position is attached to a 3-nitrophenyl ring, with the nitro group at the meta position. The ring nitrogen bears a hydrogen, which acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester carbonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The overall framework is moderately flexible because of the rotatable ester and ether chains.

This molecule is an ester built around a central tertiary carbon that carries a hydroxyl group, a phenyl ring, and a cyclohexyl ring, all attached to a carbonyl carbon. The ester oxygen links this carbonyl to a flexible four-carbon chain containing a carbon-carbon triple bond, which is terminated by a diethylamino group. The two aromatic and saturated carbocycles are single unfused rings, and the phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The triple bond makes that section of the chain rigid and linear, while the remaining sp3 carbons provide considerable conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry element because the central carbon bears four different substituents. The hydroxyl group and the N-H-free tertiary amine offer hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen serve as additional acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core in which a five-membered saturated ring, bearing an ethylamino group on one carbon, is fused to a thiophene ring that carries a primary sulfonamide. The saturated ring contains a tertiary sulfonamide nitrogen, which is substituted with a flexible three-carbon chain ending in a methoxy group. Two sulfonyl groups are present, one on the ring nitrogen and one as a primary sulfonamide on the thiophene, giving the structure several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the N-alkyl and ethyl side chains add conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its single stereocenter at the amine-bearing carbon makes it chiral.

This molecule is built around a phenothiazine core, a tricyclic system in which a central six-membered ring containing both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom is fused to two benzene rings, giving a folded, butterfly-like scaffold. The ring nitrogen of this core carries a three-carbon propyl linker that terminates in a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring bearing two nitrogens, one of which is methylated. On the opposite benzene ring of the tricycle sits a sulfonamide group, where the sulfur is doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a dimethylamino nitrogen. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two sides of the tricycle differ in their substituents. The three-carbon chain and piperazine give considerable conformational flexibility, while the fused aromatic core is rigid. The sulfonamide oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all nitrogens are tertiary.

This molecule is built around a pyridinium scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom that carries a positive charge because it is methylated (an N-methylpyridinium cation). A dimethylcarbamate group, a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen and to a dimethylated nitrogen, is attached through the oxygen to the ring at the 3-position relative to the charged nitrogen, giving a meta substitution pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the carbamate linkage adds only limited conformational freedom through rotation about the ring-oxygen and oxygen-carbonyl bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond local two-fold equivalence of the two N-methyl groups on the carbamate nitrogen. The cationic ring nitrogen carries no hydrogen-bond donor capability because it is fully substituted, but the carbamate carbonyl oxygen and the ether-type oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single sp3 carbon bearing three substituents: an ortho-tolyl ring (a benzene carrying a methyl group next to the attachment point), an unsubstituted phenyl ring, and an ether oxygen. The ether oxygen links to a two-carbon chain ending in a tertiary dimethylamino group, so the scaffold is a diarylmethyl ether with a flexible aminoalkyl tail. Both aromatic rings are simple benzene rings with no fused systems, and the ortho methyl introduces asymmetry, so the molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry. The central carbon is a stereocenter, and the rotatable bonds in the ethoxy-amine chain make the molecule fairly flexible. The ether oxygen and tertiary amine nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a tetrahydrothieno[3,2-c]pyridine core, in which a thiophene ring is fused to a partially saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The nitrogen is tertiary, bonded to the fused bicyclic framework and to a single stereogenic carbon that carries both a methyl ester group and an ortho-chlorophenyl ring. The aryl ring is substituted at only one position, with a chlorine atom adjacent to the point of attachment. The fused thiophene-piperidine system is relatively rigid, while the single bond to the stereocenter allows conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry elements and contains one defined stereocenter. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its acceptor sites are the ester oxygens and the tertiary amine nitrogen.

This molecule is a 1,4-dihydropyridine built on a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that carries two methyl groups and two ester substituents, one ethyl ester and one methyl ester, placed on opposite sides of the ring's double bonds. The sp3-hybridized carbon at position 4 bears a meta-substituted phenyl ring, which itself carries a nitro group at the meta position relative to the attachment point. The dihydropyridine core is non-planar, giving the scaffold a somewhat puckered, moderately flexible shape, while the aryl ring rotates relative to it. The molecule lacks symmetry because the two ester groups differ. The secondary ring NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygens of the esters and the nitro group provide acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine core, a bicyclic fused system of a five-membered pyrazole ring sharing an edge with a six-membered pyrimidine ring, and it carries a nitrile group on the five-membered ring. Attached to the six-membered ring is a phenyl group, which bears at its meta position an N-ethyl acetamide substituent in which the nitrogen is tertiary, bonded to the ethyl group, the aryl ring, and the carbonyl carbon. The amide carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since every nitrogen is substituted. The biaryl linkage between the phenyl and fused heteroaromatic rings allows some rotational freedom, but the aromatic cores are rigid and planar. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond local ring planarity.

This molecule is a nucleoside analogue built on a pyrimidine-2,4-dione (uracil-type) base carrying a methyl group at the 5-position, linked through its N1 nitrogen to a five-membered oxygen-containing ring. The sugar-like ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond, making it an unsaturated dihydrofuran-type scaffold rather than a fully saturated sugar. A hydroxymethyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, providing a primary alcohol. The base contributes two carbonyl oxygens and one ring NH, so the molecule has several hydrogen-bond acceptor sites and at least one donor. The two stereocentres give it a defined three-dimensional arrangement, and the fused-looking connection between the rings is single-bonded, so the overall framework is moderately rigid with a flexible hydroxymethyl arm.

This molecule is a warfarin-type 4-hydroxycoumarin derivative built on a benzopyran-2-one (coumarin) scaffold, in which a fused benzene ring is joined to a six-membered lactone-containing ring. The coumarin core is largely planar and aromatic, and it carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, giving it enolic character. At the 3-position, a branched side chain bears a methyl ketone and a separate phenyl ring attached to a stereogenic carbon, which adds conformational flexibility and a chiral center. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the enolic hydroxyl, while the lactone and ketone oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from an imidazole ring attached through a CH2 linker to a two-carbon backbone bearing an ether oxygen, which connects two separate dichloro-substituted benzene rings. One aromatic ring carries chlorines at the 2 and 4 positions relative to its attachment point, and the other carries chlorines at the 2 and 4 positions as well, giving a 2,4-dichlorophenyl pattern on both sides. The central carbon bearing the ether oxygen is a stereogenic center, so the molecule is chiral and lacks any internal mirror symmetry. The ether linkage and single bonds between the rings and the flexible linker allow considerable conformational freedom, while the aromatic rings and the imidazole remain planar and rigid. The imidazole nitrogen that is not substituted can accept a hydrogen bond, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a nucleoside analog built from a six-membered cytosine-type pyrimidinone ring bearing an amino group at one position and a carbonyl at the adjacent position, with the ring nitrogen attached to a saturated five-membered oxathiolane ring. The oxathiolane contains one sulfur and one oxygen atom in a fused-free, single-ring arrangement connected to the pyrimidinone through an N-glycosidic-type bond. A hydroxymethyl group projects from the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, and two stereocenters define a fixed three-dimensional geometry. The pyrimidinone and oxathiolane are linked by a single bond, giving moderate conformational flexibility in the sugar-like ring. The amino group, carbonyl, ring nitrogens, and hydroxyl serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the molecule lacks any symmetry element.

This molecule is built on a purine-type bicyclic scaffold, a pyrimidine ring fused to an imidazole ring, with the imidazole nitrogen bearing a cyclopentene ring. The pyrimidine portion carries a primary amino group on one carbon and a cyclopropylamino group on the adjacent fused-ring carbon, giving the core a substitution pattern on both rings. The cyclopentene ring is attached through a stereogenic carbon and carries a hydroxymethyl group on a second stereocenter, with one ring C=C double bond providing rigidity within that five-membered ring. The fused bicyclic core is flat and aromatic, while the cyclopropyl and hydroxymethyl groups add limited, localized three-dimensional bulk. Multiple nitrogen atoms in the core and the amino group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the amino N-H groups and the terminal hydroxyl act as hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, a single nitrogen heterocycle with no fused or additional rings. The nitrogen carries an n-butyl chain, making it a tertiary amine. Three adjacent-to-nitrogen-region carbons bear secondary hydroxyl groups, and one carbon next to the nitrogen carries a hydroxymethyl group, giving a polyhydroxylated scaffold. The stereocentres are defined, so the hydroxyl groups sit in a fixed spatial arrangement that limits the ring's conformational freedom. The molecule is asymmetric because the substituents differ around the ring, and the flexible butyl chain adds rotational freedom. The four hydroxyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen give it several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

This molecule is a disaccharide-like structure built from two six-membered saturated oxygen-containing rings joined through a single glycosidic oxygen bridge. The first ring is a pyranose-type ring bearing a hydroxymethyl group, and the second is a furanose-type five-membered ring with a hydroxymethyl group and a hemiketal carbon bearing both a hydroxyl and a hydroxymethyl substituent. Multiple free hydroxyl groups are distributed around both rings, along with the primary alcohols on the exocyclic CH2OH groups, giving the molecule a dense, polar, highly oxygenated periphery. The numerous stereocenters create a defined three-dimensional arrangement, and the ring-linked ether oxygen gives the two rings a degree of conformational flexibility at the bridge. Collectively, the many hydroxyl groups make the molecule a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

This molecule is built on a three-carbon chain bearing a phenyl ring at one end and an aryloxy group at the other, with the central carbon also linked to the chain's terminal methylaminoethyl arm. The aryloxy portion is a para-substituted benzene ring carrying a trifluoromethyl group, which places a strongly electron-withdrawing, lipophilic substituent opposite the ether oxygen. The unsubstituted phenyl ring is a separate aromatic system, so the scaffold contains two non-fused benzene rings joined through a flexible, partly rotatable chain. The secondary amine is the only basic and hydrogen-bond donor site, while the ether oxygen and the nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The stereocenter at the central carbon gives the molecule chirality, though no specific configuration is encoded in the SMILES.

This molecule is a quaternary ammonium salt: a central nitrogen bears four carbon substituents, three of them ethyl groups and one a two-carbon chain leading to a tertiary alcohol carbon. That carbon carries both a phenyl ring and a cyclohexyl ring, creating a crowded, branched scaffold. The phenyl and cyclohexane rings are unfused and attached to the same carbon, so the aromatic ring is flat while the cyclohexane adopts a non-planar chair conformation. The tertiary hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the positively charged nitrogen has no hydrogen-bond capability. The molecule is flexible along its ethyl and ethylene linkers, with no internal symmetry beyond the local threefold arrangement of the ethyl groups.

The molecule is built around a single cyclobutane ring, one carbon of which is quaternary and bears both a 4-chlorophenyl group and a side chain. That side chain is a branched alkyl unit: the carbon next to the ring carries a dimethylamino group, and this is linked to an isobutyl-type fragment with a terminal pair of methyl groups. The para-chloro substitution on the benzene ring is the only aromatic feature, and the molecule contains exactly one aromatic ring. The only heteroatom functionality is the tertiary amine, which has no N-H, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and offers only the lone pair on nitrogen as an acceptor. The structure is largely saturated and flexible in its side chain, while the four-membered ring and the attached phenyl ring restrict conformational freedom around the quaternary centre. There is no element of symmetry across the whole molecule because the substituents on the quaternary carbon differ.

This molecule is built on a bicyclic core in which a five-membered thiazolidine ring is fused to a four-membered β-lactam ring, with a gem-dimethyl group on the sulfur-containing ring and a carboxylic acid on the carbon adjacent to the bridgehead nitrogen. A side chain attached through an amide linkage to the β-lactam ring carries a primary amine and a para-hydroxyphenyl group on the same carbon. The scaffold is rigid and fused, leaving only the side chain with rotational freedom. Several polar groups are present: the amide N–H, the carboxylic acid, the primary amine, and the phenolic hydroxyl act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens, the ring nitrogen, and the hydroxyl oxygen act as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because its stereocenters and substituents differ across the bicyclic core.

The molecule is built around a naphthalene core, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing an edge, with a single substituent attached at the 1-position. From that position extends a CH2 linker to a tertiary amine nitrogen bearing one methyl group, and the nitrogen's other arm is a flexible chain of an allylic CH2 followed by a trans-configured alkene and then an internal alkyne. The chain terminates in a tert-butyl-type group, a quaternary carbon bearing three methyls. The molecule has no symmetry because the naphthyl end and the branched aliphatic end differ fundamentally. Its aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the chain contributes considerable conformational flexibility. The tertiary amine is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a symmetric bis-quaternary ammonium compound built around a central oxamide (ethanediamide) linker, with a C(=O)–C(=O) unit flanked by two NH groups. Each terminal nitrogen is a fully substituted, positively charged quaternary ammonium center bearing two ethyl groups, a two-carbon ethylene bridge to the amide, and a 2-chlorobenzyl group. The two arms are identical, giving the molecule approximate two-fold symmetry about the central oxamide. Each 2-chlorobenzyl ring is a benzene ring with a chlorine atom ortho to the benzylic CH2 attachment, and the rings are not fused to any other ring system. The structure is highly flexible through its many single bonds, with the oxamide unit providing some conformational restriction. The two amide NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and the two amide carbonyl oxygens as acceptors, while the quaternary nitrogens carry no hydrogens and cannot donate them.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two methoxy groups on positions that are para to each other relative to a side chain, giving a 2,5-dimethoxy-substituted aromatic core. Attached at the remaining position is a two-carbon chain bearing a secondary alcohol on the carbon next to the ring, followed by a methylene linked to an amide nitrogen. That amide is acylated by a glycyl unit that ends in a free primary amine. The molecule has no stereodescriptors specified and is flexible through its acyclic chain, with the aromatic ring as the only rigid element. Hydrogen-bond donors include the hydroxyl, the amide N–H, and the terminal amine, while the two ether oxygens, the carbonyl oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a fused tricyclic system built around a bridged oxazolidine-type ring that is fused to a seven-membered diazepinone-like lactam. The core contains a saturated five-membered ring holding one nitrogen and one oxygen, and a carbon bearing both the ring junction and a 2-chlorophenyl substituent. A second benzene ring is fused to the lactam, carrying a single chlorine at a position para to the amide nitrogen. The amide carbonyl sits within the seven-membered ring, and the tertiary amine nitrogen is part of the saturated fused framework. The molecule is largely rigid because of its multiple ring fusions, with only the pendant chlorophenyl group free to rotate. It has no molecular symmetry, and the secondary amide N–H is its only hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring oxygen, and nitrogen atoms serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a sulfonylurea-type compound built around a central benzene ring bearing a para-substituted pattern: an ethyl linker from one side leads to a urea, while a sulfonyl group on the opposite side carries a second urea attached to a 4-methylcyclohexyl ring. The first urea connects to a five-membered unsaturated lactam (a 2-pyrrolinone) that carries an ethyl and a methyl substituent on its alkene carbons. The cyclohexane ring is saturated and flexible, while the benzene and pyrrolinone rings are rigid and planar. Several hydrogen-bond donors (the N-H groups of the two ureas and the sulfonylurea) and acceptors (the carbonyl oxygens and sulfonyl oxygens) are present. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because its substituents differ on each end.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a five-membered triazole-type ring with three adjacent nitrogens is fused to a six-membered pyrimidine-like ring that shares a bond with it, giving a flat, rigid scaffold. A carbonyl group sits on the triazole-side ring, and a carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) substituent is attached at a carbon of the fused framework. The N-methyl group is placed on a ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. The amide NH2 group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the ring nitrogens and both carbonyl oxygens can accept them.

The molecule is built on a dibenzocycloheptene scaffold, a central seven-membered ring fused on opposite sides to two benzene rings, giving a tricyclic, non-planar, butterfly-like core. One of the central ring carbons is sp2-hybridized and bears an exocyclic double bond linking to a three-carbon propyl chain that terminates in a secondary methylamino group. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, so the aromatic substitution pattern is simple, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the side chain sits on one side of the core. The secondary amine provides one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor site, while the flexible propyl linker contrasts with the rigid tricyclic framework.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4-pattern. A butoxy group sits on one ring carbon next to an amino group on the adjacent carbon, and the third substituent, para to the amine, is an ester. That ester links the ring carbonyl to a two-carbon chain ending in a diethylamino nitrogen, so the molecule combines an aromatic core with a flexible aliphatic tail. The aromatic ring and the ester carbonyl are planar and rigid, while the butyl chain and the diethylaminoethyl arm are flexible. The primary aromatic amine can donate hydrogen bonds, and the ether oxygen, ester oxygens, and tertiary amine nitrogen can all accept them. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

This molecule is a steroid-type tetracyclic scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, with a cross-conjugated dienone in ring A and a fully saturated, sterically crowded remainder. The A ring carries a ketone conjugated with two carbon-carbon double bonds, giving a rigid, planar region, while the B, C, and D rings are saturated and more three-dimensional. Substituents include two angular methyl groups, a chlorine on a quaternary carbon, a secondary alcohol, a tertiary alcohol, and a chloroacetyl side chain, which together create a dense, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. Hydroxyl groups and the ketone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the chlorine atoms contribute to polarity without offering hydrogen-bonding capacity.

This molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a six-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle, which is the central scaffold. At the carbon opposite the nitrogen sits a quaternary center bearing both an ethyl ester group and a phenyl ring. The piperidine nitrogen is tertiary, carrying a three-carbon chain that terminates in a nitrile group and a second quaternary carbon bearing two additional phenyl rings. The molecule contains three benzene rings in total, which are unfused and attached as pendant aromatic groups, along with the ester carbonyl and nitrile functionalities. Because the chain and ring junctions are largely sp3, the molecule is fairly flexible, and it lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, with the ester oxygens, the nitrile nitrogen, and the piperidine nitrogen serving only as acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic β-lactam antibiotic built on a fused four-membered β-lactam ring and a six-membered dihydrothiazine ring, which together form a rigid, bent core. A propenyl group sits on the alkene of the six-membered ring, and a carboxylic acid is attached to the adjacent alkene carbon. The β-lactam carbonyl is linked through an amide nitrogen to a side chain bearing a primary amine and a para-hydroxyphenyl ring, which gives the molecule a stereochemically defined, asymmetric shape. Several polar groups, including the carboxylic acid, the two amide carbonyls, the amine, and the phenolic hydroxyl, serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fused ring system limits conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a CH2 group linked to a methylhydrazine unit, giving an –CH2–NH–NH–CH3 chain with two adjacent nitrogens. The other side bears an amide, in which a carbonyl is bonded to an isopropyl-substituted nitrogen. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the hydrazine and amide tails add conformational flexibility. The amide N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and the hydrazine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the para-disubstituted ring.

This molecule is a symmetric stilbene-type scaffold built from a central carbon-carbon double bond bearing two ethyl-substituted alkene carbons, with each end linked to a para-hydroxyphenyl ring. Its skeleton is therefore a diaryl, conjugated 1,2-diethylstilbene framework with no fused ring systems; the two benzene rings are unfused and attached at symmetric positions. Each aromatic ring carries one phenolic hydroxyl group at the para position relative to the attachment point, giving two identical hydroxyl functional groups that can serve as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry through its central double bond. The conjugated alkene and aryl systems make the core fairly rigid, while the terminal ethyl groups add some conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents on adjacent positions, making it a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Going around the ring, an amino group sits next to a hydroxyl group, which sits next to a carboxylic acid group, with the remaining three ring positions bearing hydrogen. The carboxylic acid is the most polar feature, and its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens together with the amine nitrogen and phenolic oxygen give the molecule several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The ring itself is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate slightly around its bond to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents are different.

This molecule is a quaternary ammonium salt built on a quinuclidine (1-azabicyclo[2.2.2]octane) scaffold, in which the bridgehead nitrogen carries a methyl group and a formal positive charge. The bicyclic cage is rigid and three-dimensionally compact, with the ring nitrogen at one bridgehead and a carbon bearing an ester oxygen on the adjacent ring. The ester links this cage to a benzilic-type unit: a tertiary carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and two unsubstituted phenyl rings. The two phenyl rings are equivalent by a local mirror plane, giving the diaryl portion a symmetric arrangement, while the overall cationic framework has no net symmetry because of the chiral carbons. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and the ester carbonyl and ether-type oxygen as acceptors, whereas the quaternary nitrogen is fully substituted and cannot donate hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is a cardenolide glycoside built on a steroid scaffold of four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring. The five-membered ring carries an unsaturated butenolide (a lactone bearing a carbon-carbon double bond), and the steroid core has hydroxyl groups and angular methyl substituents, giving it a rigid, fused polycyclic framework. Attached to the core through an ether linkage is a chain of three sugar rings, each decorated with hydroxyl groups and methyl groups, which adds considerable conformational flexibility and polarity at the periphery. Overall it has no internal symmetry, and its many oxygen atoms make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, typical of a corticosteroid core. The A ring is a cross-conjugated dienone, containing a ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond system, while the rings to its side are saturated with several methyl branches and stereocenters. The five-membered D ring carries a thioester bearing a fluoromethyl group, and an ester of a propanoic acid sits on the same carbon. Two fluorine atoms and one free hydroxyl group are attached at different ring positions, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused ring system is rigid, with the ester and thioester side chains adding some flexibility. The ketone and ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the single hydroxyl group serves as both a donor and an acceptor.

The molecule is a tetraarylphosphonium cation: a single positively charged phosphorus atom bonded to four separate phenyl rings in a tetrahedral arrangement. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, with no additional functional groups or substituents on any of the six-membered rings. The phosphorus center carries the formal positive charge and makes the overall structure highly symmetrical, with the four aryl groups related by approximate threefold or higher symmetry about the P–C axes. The aryl rings are attached by single bonds that allow rotation, so the scaffold is moderately flexible, although the bulky groups around the central phosphorus restrict the range of conformations. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom is the phosphorus, which lacks a lone pair in this cationic form, so it offers essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

This molecule is built on a bicyclic fused scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidinone ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, forming a purine-type core. The six-membered ring carries an exocyclic amino group on one carbon and a carbonyl (C=O) group on the adjacent carbon, while the five-membered ring is substituted at a ring nitrogen with a flexible chain. That chain runs through two methylene units to a branching carbon bearing two hydroxymethyl groups, adding multiple hydroxyl functionalities. The fused aromatic core is largely planar and rigid, whereas the side chain is flexible and lacks symmetry. Together, the amino, carbonyl, ring nitrogens, and hydroxyl groups provide numerous hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

This molecule is a bis-coumarin-type structure: two benzopyranone units are joined through a single methylene bridge at their 3-positions. Each half is a fused bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing lactone-like ring, with a carbonyl on one ring and a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. The two halves are chemically identical and arranged symmetrically around the central CH2 linker, giving the molecule a mirror-symmetric overall shape. The fused aromatic rings are rigid and planar, while the methylene bridge allows some rotational flexibility between the two halves. Each unit offers two hydroxyl or carbonyl oxygen sites that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two hydroxyl groups can serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a beta-lactam antibiotic built on a bicyclic core in which a four-membered beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-membered dihydrothiazine ring, forming a rigid, fused scaffold. The fused lactam carries a carboxylic acid on the unsaturated ring, and a vinyl chloride sits on the double bond within that six-membered ring. A side chain attached to the lactam nitrogen-bearing carbon consists of an amide linked to a phenylglycyl unit, which contains a primary amine and a phenyl ring. The molecule lacks obvious symmetry, and its fused core is conformationally restricted while the side chain offers some flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donors include the primary amine, the amide N-H, and the carboxylic acid O-H, while the carbonyl oxygens of the lactam, amide, and acid provide acceptor sites.

The molecule is a bicyclic heterocycle built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring containing a sulfur dioxide unit (a sulfonyl group, S(=O)(=O)) and two nitrogen atoms, forming a 1,2,4-benzothiadiazine-type scaffold. The fused benzene ring carries a single chlorine substituent, placed para to one of the ring nitrogens and meta to the sulfonyl attachment, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. A methyl group sits on the carbon of the heterocycle between the two nitrogens, adding a small aliphatic branch. The sulfonyl group and the amidine-like C=N linkage are electron-withdrawing acceptors, while the ring NH is a hydrogen-bond donor and the sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fused, largely planar framework is rigid, with only the methyl rotation providing flexibility.

This molecule is built around a central acyclic chain bearing a secondary amide linked to a substituted benzene ring: a 2-methyl-3-hydroxyphenyl carbonyl group. The chain carries a phenylthio (phenyl sulfide) substituent and a secondary alcohol, and terminates in a nitrogen within a fused decahydroisoquinoline-type bicyclic ring system, where a saturated cyclohexane is fused to a piperidine. That piperidine nitrogen is tertiary and bears a carboxamide to a tert-butyl group. The molecule has several stereocenters, which together constrain its three-dimensional shape, and the bicyclic and aromatic regions are relatively rigid while the chain linkers remain flexible. Hydrogen-bond donors include the phenol, the two amide N–H groups, and the secondary alcohol, while the carbonyl oxygens, the hydroxyl oxygens, and the amine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a peptidomimetic scaffold with a fused decahydroisoquinoline core, a bicyclic saturated ring system in which a piperidine-type ring shares an edge with a cyclohexane ring. A tert-butyl amide hangs from this core, and the nitrogen of the bicycle is linked through a chain bearing a secondary hydroxyl group and a benzyl substituent. A linear sequence of amide linkages extends from there, including an asparagine-like side chain carrying a primary carboxamide, which terminates in an aromatic quinoline-2-carboxamide. The molecule lacks obvious symmetry because its stereocenters and substituents are distinct, and its many saturated rings and rotatable bonds make it fairly flexible overall, with the quinoline and phenyl rings providing rigid aromatic regions. Multiple amide N–H groups and the hydroxyl and primary amide N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and quinoline nitrogen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a tetracyclic anthraquinone-type scaffold, with four fused rings: two aromatic rings flanking a central quinone-like ring and a saturated cyclohexane ring fused to the aromatic system. The aromatic portion carries a methoxy group on one ring and two phenolic hydroxyl groups on the other, and the two carbonyls of the central ring sit between the aromatic rings. The saturated ring bears a tertiary hydroxyl and a hydroxyacetyl side chain, and it is linked through an oxygen to a sugar-like six-membered ring. That sugar ring carries an amino group, a hydroxyl, and a methyl group, giving it stereochemically defined centers. The molecule has no internal symmetry and is fairly rigid across its fused core, while the glycosidic linkage and side chain add some conformational flexibility. Multiple hydroxyl and amino groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl and ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a short, acyclic alpha-amino acid built on a linear carbon chain with no ring systems. The backbone is a four-carbon chain in which the carboxyl carbon is attached to the alpha carbon, which bears a primary amino group. The alpha carbon is bonded to a sec-butyl side chain, a branched group with a methyl and an ethyl arm, and this branching creates a second stereocenter. Functionally, the molecule contains one carboxylic acid group and one primary amine, both capable of acting as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. Because it has no ring and only single bonds along the chain, its conformational flexibility is high, and it lacks any internal symmetry due to the two distinct stereocenters.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents arranged around it: a primary sulfonamide, a carboxylic acid, and a secondary amine. The amine is linked through a CH2 group to a furan ring, an aromatic five-membered oxygen heterocycle, so the molecule contains two separate aromatic systems joined by a flexible methylene linker. A chlorine atom sits on the benzene ring adjacent to the sulfonamide, giving the core an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The sulfonamide NH2 and the carboxylic acid OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl and carbonyl oxygens, the amine nitrogen, and the furan oxygen serve as acceptors. Overall, the aromatic cores are rigid, but the benzylic-type linker gives the molecule a degree of conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle, bearing several functional groups around the ring. A methyl group sits at the 2-position adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a hydroxyl group occupies the 3-position and a formyl (aldehyde) group sits at the 4-position. At the 5-position, a CH2 linker connects the ring to a phosphate monoester, a phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded oxygen and two hydroxyl groups. The scaffold is a single aromatic ring with no fused rings, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry. The phosphate and hydroxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen, carbonyl oxygen, and phosphate oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Only the single rotatable CH2–O and C–C bonds to the ring and phosphate give it modest conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a short, acyclic amino diacid built on a four-carbon chain with no rings. The alpha carbon is a stereogenic center bearing a primary amine, and the chain terminates in two carboxylic acid groups, one directly on the alpha carbon and one at the end of a methylene linker. Because of this arrangement, the molecule has no internal symmetry and is conformationally flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. It carries multiple hydrogen-bond donors from the amine and the two hydroxyl groups, and several acceptors from the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens.

This molecule is a small, acyclic alpha-amino acid built on a linear carbon backbone with no ring systems or ring fusion. The skeleton carries a branched isobutyl-type side chain, in which a two-carbon methyl-bearing terminus is attached to a central methylene, and the alpha carbon bears both a primary amine and a carboxylic acid group. Its functional groups are therefore an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, with no further substitution or aromatic character. The molecule contains a stereocenter at the alpha carbon, and its flexible single bonds allow considerable conformational freedom. Both the amine and the carboxylic acid can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a fused tetracyclic carbon framework of four rings sharing edges, with the ring system being roughly linear-to-angular in arrangement. One terminal ring is an aromatic benzene ring bearing a phenolic hydroxyl group, while the other three rings are partially saturated, containing a ketone, an enol, and a carboxamide attached to a conjugated enol-ketone unit. A dimethylamino group sits on one saturated ring carbon, and several tertiary and secondary hydroxyl groups are distributed around the ring system, including a tertiary alcohol at a ring-fusion position. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically across the scaffold. It is fairly rigid through its fused ring core, though the dimethylamino and carboxamide groups provide some local conformational freedom. Its many hydroxyl, carboxamide, and carbonyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the dimethylamino nitrogen acts as an additional acceptor.

This molecule is a nucleotide built from a purine base linked to a ribose-type sugar bearing a phosphate group. The purine scaffold is a bicyclic fused system of a six-membered and a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, with an amino group on the six-membered ring. The sugar is a five-membered oxygen-containing ring attached to a ring nitrogen of the purine through its anomeric carbon. The sugar carries two hydroxyl groups and a CH2 linked through a phosphate ester, which is a phosphoryl group bearing two hydroxyl substituents. The molecule has several stereocenters, so it has no internal symmetry, and its fused aromatic core is rigid while the phosphate-bearing side chain is flexible. The amino group, hydroxyls, and phosphate oxygens act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogens, ring oxygen, and phosphoryl oxygens act as acceptors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic chiral amino acid built on a simple linear three-carbon backbone with no ring systems or ring fusion. The alpha carbon bears a primary amino group and carries a defined stereocenter, while the beta carbon carries a primary hydroxyl group, giving the side chain a polar alcohol. The terminus is a carboxylic acid group, so the molecule contains three functional groups: amine, alcohol, and carboxylic acid. Because the structure is flexible and lacks any ring or symmetry element, it can adopt many conformations. Its amino, hydroxyl, and carboxyl groups all act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen and nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a 1-hydroxy-2-(tert-butylamino)ethyl side chain at one position, a hydroxyl group para to it, and a hydroxymethyl group ortho to that hydroxyl. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, branched alkyl unit attached to a secondary amine, and the adjacent carbon bears a secondary alcohol, giving a flexible two-carbon linker between the aromatic ring and the nitrogen. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the side chain rotates freely about its single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the three ring substituents sit at distinct positions. It offers multiple hydrogen-bond donors from its hydroxyl and amine N–H groups and several acceptors from the oxygen and nitrogen atoms.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle, forming a tetralin-type core with a partially saturated ring. The saturated ring carries two adjacent secondary alcohol groups on stereogenic carbons, giving a defined relative configuration. An aryl ether links the aromatic ring to a three-carbon chain bearing a secondary alcohol and a secondary amine, which is capped by a bulky tert-butyl group. The aromatic ring is trisubstituted, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. The fused ring system is fairly rigid, while the flexible side chain adds conformational freedom. Overall there are several hydrogen-bond donors from the hydroxyl and amine groups and several acceptors from the oxygens and nitrogen.

This molecule is a biaryl built on a benzoic acid scaffold: a benzene ring carrying a carboxylic acid and an ortho-hydroxyl group, joined at the meta position to a second benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms at the 2 and 4 positions. The core is two six-membered aromatic rings connected by a single bond, giving a largely planar, rigid framework with limited conformational flexibility, though the biaryl bond permits some twisting. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl provide two hydrogen-bond donors and several acceptor sites on the oxygen atoms, while the fluorine substituents act as weak acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry element, since the two rings carry different substitution patterns.

This molecule is a small, acyclic organophosphorus compound built on a two-carbon chain. One end carries a carboxylic acid group, with a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl, and the other end carries a phosphonic acid group, which is a phosphorus atom double-bonded to oxygen and bearing two hydroxyl groups. The two acidic groups are joined through a single methylene carbon, giving a simple linear, unbranched scaffold with no rings and no stereocenters. Because the molecule has no ring systems and no symmetry element beyond a trivial one, it is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. It contains multiple hydrogen-bond donors from the four hydroxyl groups and several hydrogen-bond acceptors from the oxygen atoms on both the carbonyl and phosphoryl centers.

This molecule is built on a fused tetracyclic scaffold of four rings, three of them six-membered carbocycles and one bearing the aromatic benzene ring fused to a ketone-containing ring. The rings share edges, forming a rigid, angular framework with several stereocenters that limit conformational freedom. A dimethylamino group sits on one saturated ring carbon, and the core carries a primary carboxamide, a ketone, an enol, and several tertiary and secondary hydroxyl groups, with a phenolic hydroxyl on the aromatic ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry. Its many hydroxyl, amide, and ketone groups give it numerous hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

This molecule is a 1,4-benzodiazepine-type scaffold: a seven-membered diazepine ring fused to a benzene ring, with a second benzene ring attached as a pendant phenyl group at the imine carbon. The seven-membered ring contains an N-methyl amide (lactam) carbonyl, an alpha-hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to that carbonyl, and a C=N imine double bond linking to the phenyl substituent. A chlorine atom sits on the fused benzene ring, para to the ring nitrogen attachment. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, with the seven-membered ring adopting a non-planar, somewhat puckered conformation. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because of the asymmetric placement of the substituents. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and imine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with an acetamide group (an N-acetyl amide, CH3C(=O)NH-) on one side and an ether-linked chain on the opposite side. The chain is an oxygen-bridged three-carbon unit bearing a secondary alcohol on the middle carbon and terminating in a secondary amine carrying an isopropyl group. The single stereocenter at the carbinol carbon gives the molecule a defined chirality, while the para pattern lends it a roughly linear, elongated shape with partial flexibility from the saturated side chain. Functionally, the amide N-H and the hydroxyl and secondary amine N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, whereas the amide carbonyl, ether oxygen, hydroxyl oxygen, and amine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a 1,4-dihydropyridine scaffold, a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring with one sp3-hybridized carbon bearing the aryl substituent that breaks the ring's planarity. Two methyl groups sit on the ring's alkene carbons, and two ester groups are attached on either side: one methyl ester and one 2-(N-benzyl-N-methylamino)ethyl ester. A 3-nitrophenyl group is attached at the sp3 carbon, placing the nitro group on the meta position of that pendant benzene ring. Because the two ester groups differ and the aryl ring is unsymmetrical, the molecule has no internal symmetry. The dihydropyridine N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester carbonyls, nitro oxygens, and tertiary amine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving it a flat, rigid aromatic core with a degree of two-fold symmetry along its long axis. One substituent is a primary aromatic amine (an –NH2 group attached directly to the ring), which acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and a weak acceptor. The other substituent is a carboxamide linkage (–C(=O)NH–) connected to a flexible two-carbon chain ending in a terminal carboxylic acid (–CH2–COOH). The amide carbonyl oxygen and the acid's oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amide N–H and acid O–H serve as donors. The chain beyond the amide is conformationally flexible, contrasting with the planar, fused-free ring system.

This molecule is a fused tetracyclic system built around an imidazole ring that is bridged to a seven-membered lactam ring and a benzene ring. The imidazole carries an ethyl ester group on one carbon, and the benzene ring bears a single fluorine substituent positioned meta to the ring fusion. A tertiary amide (N-methyl lactam) is embedded in the central ring, providing a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused, largely planar aromatic framework makes the scaffold fairly rigid, with only the N-methyl and ethyl ester groups contributing conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are either tertiary or aromatic acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic heterocycle in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered ring containing two nitrogens and a sulfur bearing two oxygens, giving a benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide scaffold. The benzene ring carries a primary sulfonamide group and a trifluoromethyl group on adjacent positions, both electron-withdrawing. A benzyl substituent hangs from the saturated carbon of the heterocyclic ring, adding a pendant phenyl ring. The sulfonyl and sulfonamide groups provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the two N–H groups and the primary sulfonamide NH₂ serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The fused core is fairly rigid, while the benzyl arm adds conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule is a four-carbon, straight-chain amino acid backbone with no rings, so its scaffold is acyclic and fully saturated apart from the two carbonyl groups. A terminal carboxylic acid sits at one end and a primary carboxamide (a CONH2 group) sits at the other, with a primary amine attached to the stereogenic carbon adjacent to the acid. The single chiral center gives the molecule a defined handedness, but there is no internal symmetry, so the two ends are chemically distinct. The chain is highly flexible because all its bonds are single rotatable bonds. Several groups can serve as hydrogen-bond donors (the amine and the amide NH2 and the acid OH) and acceptors (the two carbonyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen).

The molecule is a steroid-like tetracyclic framework: three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, built on a fully saturated polycyclic carbon skeleton with two angular methyl groups. Ring A is replaced by a lactam, a six-membered cyclic amide containing one nitrogen and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to the carbonyl, which makes that ring partially unsaturated and planar in its immediate vicinity. A tert-butyl amide substituent hangs from the five-membered ring, contributing a bulky, branched alkyl group and a secondary amide linkage. The overall structure is rigid and cage-like, with defined stereocenters that fix the three-dimensional shape, and it lacks any obvious symmetry. Hydrogen-bond capability comes from two amide N–H groups acting as donors and two carbonyl oxygens acting as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a tetrahydroisoquinoline scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The nitrogen of that saturated ring carries a guanidine-type substituent, a carbon bearing two amino groups and a double bond to nitrogen. The aromatic benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the fused bicyclic core has no additional substitution pattern to consider. The guanidine group is highly polar and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the aromatic and saturated ring portions contribute little polarity. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the planar aromatic ring, and the fused ring system is fairly rigid with some flexibility in the saturated ring.

This molecule is a barbiturate-type scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring in which the 2-position carbonyl is replaced by a thiocarbonyl (C=S). The ring carries two carbonyls flanking the thiourea-like N-C(=S)-N unit, giving a cyclic imide arrangement. The fifth ring carbon is quaternary and bears two alkyl substituents, an allyl group (prop-2-enyl) and a branched sec-pentyl-type chain, which creates a tetrasubstituted, non-symmetric center. The ring has two N-H groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the sulfur atom serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The core ring is relatively rigid, whereas the appended alkyl and allyl chains are flexible.

This molecule is built around a five-membered ring containing a ketone carbonyl, fused on one side to a benzene ring, so the core is an indane-1,3-dione-type scaffold. The carbon between the two carbonyls (the C2 position) is sp3 and bears a single phenyl substituent, giving the molecule a stereogenic center that is not symmetric about that carbon. The fused benzo ring and the pendant phenyl ring are both unsubstituted aromatics, so the overall framework is largely planar and rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the bond connecting the phenyl group. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only acidic-type proton sits on the carbon flanked by the two carbonyls.

The molecule is built on a central five-membered pyrazole ring, which bears three substituents at distinct positions. One ring carbon carries a trifluoromethyl group, a second carbon is attached to a para-tolyl ring (a benzene ring with a methyl group opposite the attachment point), and the ring nitrogen is bonded to a para-substituted phenyl ring that carries a primary sulfonamide group. The molecule has no fused ring systems, but the three aromatic rings are linked by single bonds and can rotate relative to one another, giving moderate conformational flexibility around those connections. The sulfonamide group provides both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its NH2 and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its two sulfonyl oxygens, while the pyrazole nitrogen contributes an additional acceptor site.

This molecule is a fused, polycyclic morphinan-type scaffold with a rigid, three-dimensional cage built from four rings. A tertiary amine sits within a saturated nitrogen-containing ring, with an N-methyl group on the nitrogen. A benzene ring is fused to the remainder of the framework and carries a single phenolic hydroxyl group para to the ring fusion, so the aromatic portion has a simple one-substituent pattern. The fully saturated carbocyclic ring system contributes stereocenters, giving the framework little conformational flexibility. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the amine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a diarylamine built from two benzene rings joined through a nitrogen atom, with an NH group serving as the linker. One ring carries a carboxylic acid group at the position ortho to the nitrogen, giving a benzoic acid unit, while the other ring bears two adjacent methyl groups, one of which sits ortho to the NH linkage. The two aromatic rings are not fused to each other, but the connection through the nitrogen gives the scaffold moderate conformational flexibility, since the rings can twist relative to one another. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the OH) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the secondary amine NH provides an additional hydrogen-bond donor site. The molecule has no internal symmetry, because the substituents on the two rings are arranged asymmetrically.

This molecule is a steroid-type tetracyclic framework with four fused rings, comprising three six-membered rings and a fused five-membered acetonide ring that bridges the 16 and 17 positions. The A ring is a cross-conjugated dienone, with one carbonyl and two carbon-carbon double bonds, while the B and C rings are saturated. Two fluorine atoms sit on the framework, one on a ring carbon adjacent to the dienone and one on a quaternary carbon at a ring junction, and a hydroxyl group occupies a secondary position on the C ring. The side chain carries a ketone and a primary alcohol, and the acetonide contributes two ether oxygens. Overall, the rigid fused scaffold is largely non-planar yet compact, and the hydroxyl and ketone groups supply hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is built from two linked five- and six-membered heteroaromatic and saturated rings. One part is a pyrrolidine ring, a fully saturated five-membered ring containing a single nitrogen atom that carries a methyl group on that nitrogen, making it a tertiary amine. This pyrrolidine ring is attached through a carbon adjacent to the nitrogen to the second part, a pyridine ring, which is a flat six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. The attachment occurs at the pyridine's third ring position, so the two ring systems are joined by a single carbon-carbon bond rather than being fused. The molecule is largely rigid in its aromatic portion while the saturated ring adds some conformational flexibility, and it has no internal symmetry because the two rings differ. Its hydrogen-bond capacity is limited: the tertiary amine nitrogen and the pyridine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a 1,4-naphthoquinone core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered ring bearing two carbonyl groups in a para arrangement, and the benzo portion is unsubstituted. The quinone ring carries a methyl group and a long, branched, partly unsaturated hydrocarbon side chain attached at the adjacent carbon, which contains one trisubstituted C=C double bond and several stereocenters with defined configuration. The two ketone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bicyclic core is rigid and planar, whereas the saturated tail is highly flexible, and the overall molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric side chain.

This molecule is an acyclic urea-type scaffold: a central carbonyl carbon bonded to two nitrogens, one of which carries a nitroso group (N=O) and the other an N-H. The nitrogen bearing the nitroso group is also substituted by a 2-chloroethyl chain, while the N-H nitrogen carries a second 2-chloroethyl chain, so the two chloroethyl arms are placed on different nitrogens and the molecule is not symmetric. There are no ring systems, so the framework is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds along the chloroethyl chains and the urea linkage. Functional groups present are the N-nitroso group, the urea carbonyl, and two terminal alkyl chlorides. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and nitroso oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic secondary amine built around a central nitrogen atom that links two flexible chains. One side carries a benzyl group attached to a branched carbon bearing a methyl substituent, while the other side is a three-carbon chain ending in a carbon that bears two unsubstituted phenyl rings, giving a diphenylmethyl unit. The structure contains three separate benzene rings, each unfused and monosubstituted, so there is no fused ring system. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry overall and is conformationally flexible because of its multiple sp3 carbons. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and the nitrogen lone pair as an acceptor, while the aromatic rings offer only weak pi-based interactions.

This molecule is built on a piperazine core, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms placed opposite each other. One ring nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine, while the other is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that forms a urea linkage with a diethylamino group. The urea unit contributes a planar C=O group, but the piperazine ring itself is non-aromatic and can flip between chair conformations, so the overall structure is moderately flexible. The molecule lacks hydrogen-bond donors because it has no N–H or O–H bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen and the tertiary nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its substitution pattern is symmetric about the piperazine ring, with the two ethyl groups on the urea nitrogen giving local symmetry.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, a ketone carbonyl, and a pyridin-3-yl ring, with a second pyridin-3-yl ring attached to that same carbon. The carbonyl links the central carbon to one pyridine ring through its carbon atom, so the structure is a diaryl ketone-type scaffold in which the two pyridines are not fused to each other. Each pyridine is a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle attached at the meta position relative to the nitrogen, giving two basic ring nitrogens that serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The gem-dimethyl group creates steric bulk, and the molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. Its overall shape is non-planar and moderately flexible around the single bonds to the quaternary carbon.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic scaffold built from four rings: three saturated six-membered rings and one aromatic benzene ring fused at one edge, closed by a five-membered ring. The aromatic A-ring carries a cyclopentyl ether substituent (an oxygen linking the ring to a cyclopentane) at a position para-like to the fusion, giving it a single ring-level substitution pattern with no symmetry across the whole framework. At the junction of the D-ring, a quaternary carbon bears both a hydroxyl group and a terminal ethynyl group, along with an angular methyl group elsewhere on the scaffold. The hydroxyl oxygen and the ether oxygen provide hydrogen-bond acceptor capability, while the hydroxyl hydrogen provides one hydrogen-bond donor site. The fused ring system is largely rigid, with only the cyclopentyl ether substituent contributing conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a piperazine core, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. One nitrogen carries a benzhydryl-type group, a carbon bearing both a phenyl ring and a para-chlorophenyl ring, while the other nitrogen is linked through a two-carbon ethoxy chain to a terminal carboxylic acid. The two aromatic rings are unfused and attached to a single sp3 carbon, giving the bulky side of the molecule a three-dimensional, propeller-like arrangement. The chlorine sits at the para position of one phenyl ring, leaving the molecule without any internal mirror symmetry. The flexible ether-acid tail contrasts with the more rigid piperazine and aryl units, and the terminal carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen and tertiary amine nitrogens serve as additional acceptors.

This molecule is a large macrolide built around a 15-membered lactone ring containing a nitrogen atom within the ring, giving it an azalide-type scaffold. Two sugar-like rings, each a substituted saturated six-membered oxygen heterocycle, are attached to the macrocycle through glycosidic-type ether linkages. One of these sugars carries a dimethylamino group and the other a methoxy group, and both bear hydroxyl groups. The macrocycle also carries several hydroxyl groups, a tertiary amine within the ring, and multiple methyl and ethyl substituents, producing a stereochemically dense and highly branched framework. Its many hydroxyl and amine groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fused and bridged ring system limits conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a six-membered saturated ring containing one oxygen atom, a pyranose-type scaffold with all stereocenters defined. A hydroxymethyl group sits on one ring carbon adjacent to the oxygen, while three additional hydroxyl groups are attached to the other ring carbons, giving four hydroxyls in total. The anomeric carbon, the ring carbon between the oxygen and the sulfur, carries an isopropyl thioether substituent, which provides a single sulfur-containing side chain. The ring is fully saturated with no fused rings and no planar aromatic character, so it adopts a relatively rigid chair-like conformation. Its many hydroxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring oxygen and the sulfur atom serve as additional acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a pyridazine core, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, carrying a methyl group on one carbon and a phenyl ring attached at the opposite side of the diazine. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and is joined to the core by a single bond, giving a largely planar biaryl-type arrangement. The remaining ring position bears a secondary amine that links through a two-carbon ethylene chain to a morpholine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen in a chair-like conformation. The flexible ethylene linker and the saturated morpholine ring add conformational freedom compared with the rigid aromatic portion. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridazine nitrogens, the morpholine oxygen, and the morpholine nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a secosteroid built on a fused polycyclic framework, with three fused carbocycles in a steroid-like arrangement and a conjugated triene system linking two of the rings. The ring system contains one exocyclic methylene group on the A-ring and a carbon-carbon double bond that breaks the usual ring fusion, giving it a partially open, extended shape. A side chain attached at the D-ring terminates in a branched alkyl group with a stereocenter bearing a methyl substituent. Two secondary hydroxyl groups sit on the A-ring, each able to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The core is largely rigid because of its fused rings and conjugation, while the saturated side chain and the open region of the framework allow considerable conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built around a pyridine ring bearing two primary amino groups, one at the 2-position and one at the 6-position relative to the ring nitrogen, plus a fourth substituent at the 3-position that is an azo linkage. The azo group, a nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) geometry, connects the pyridine ring to a separate phenyl ring, giving an extended, largely planar, conjugated aromatic system with two rings joined through a rigid linker. The 2,6-diamino substitution pattern on the pyridine is asymmetric because the azo group sits off to one side, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the two halves identical. The amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N-H bonds, while the pyridine ring nitrogen and the azo nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the scaffold is rigid and flat, with only limited rotational freedom about the single bonds connecting the azo group to the rings.

This molecule is built on a six-membered glutarimide ring, a piperidine-2,6-dione, in which a nitrogen is flanked by two carbonyl groups. The quaternary carbon at position 3 of this ring carries both an ethyl group and a para-aminophenyl ring, so the substitution is geometrically crowded at a single sp3 center. The aromatic ring is a benzene bearing a primary aromatic amine para to the attachment point, which makes it a simple monosubstituted-pattern aniline. The imide N-H and the two carbonyl oxygens provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the aniline nitrogen adds one further donor and a weak acceptor. Because the quaternary center locks the ring substituents in place, the molecule has no internal symmetry plane and is fairly rigid overall, with flexibility limited mainly to the ethyl chain.

This molecule is a steroid-like tetracyclic framework: three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, with the aromatic A ring bearing a methoxy group. The first ring is a benzene ring fused to a saturated cyclohexane, and the aromatic ring carries a single methyl ether (O-CH3) substituent in a para-like position relative to the ring fusion. The five-membered D ring holds a quaternary carbon that bears an angular methyl group and an ethynyl (C#C) group, together with a tertiary hydroxyl. The fused, multi-ring core is rigid, with several defined stereocenters, while the methoxy and ethynyl groups are the main sources of conformational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a central pyrrole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle bearing an N-methyl group. One carbon of this pyrrole carries a ketone that links it to a para-tolyl ring, a benzene ring with a methyl group opposite the carbonyl attachment. The other side of the pyrrole carries a CH2 group that leads to a terminal carboxylic acid, providing a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor pair. The aryl ketone adds a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall the structure is an assembly of three planar aromatic and carbonyl-containing units joined by single bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility around the linkages.

This molecule is built on a tricyclic fused scaffold in which an imidazole ring is fused to a benzene ring and to a seven-membered diazepine ring.
