The imidazole carries a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to its nitrogen atoms, and the benzene ring bears a chlorine atom. A 2-fluorophenyl group is attached to the seven-membered ring at a carbon that forms a C=N imine double bond, which sits within that ring. The fused framework is largely planar and rigid, though the pendant fluorophenyl ring can rotate about its single bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the imine nitrogen and the imidazole nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a xanthine-type bicyclic scaffold, a purine-dione in which a six-membered pyrimidinedione ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring. Two N-methyl groups sit on the pyrimidinedione nitrogens, and the two carbonyl groups at the 2- and 6-positions are part of that ring. The imidazole nitrogen at the 7-position carries a 2,3-dihydroxypropyl side chain, which adds two flexible hydroxyl-bearing carbons. The fused core is largely planar and rigid, while the side chain gives some conformational flexibility. Two hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the carbonyl oxygens and imidazole nitrogen serve as additional acceptors.

This molecule is a nucleoside built from a uracil base linked to a sugar. The nitrogen-containing base is a pyrimidine-2,4-dione ring, with its ring nitrogen bonded to the anomeric carbon of a five-membered furanose ring. The sugar ring carries a hydroxymethyl group and two secondary hydroxyl groups, all with defined stereochemistry. Hydrogen-bond donors include the ring N-H of the pyrimidinedione and three hydroxyl groups, while the carbonyl oxygens and ring nitrogen act as acceptors. The molecule is chiral and fairly polar, with a rigid heteroaromatic base joined to a more flexible sugar ring.

This molecule is a morphinan-type polycyclic alkaloid built from a rigid, fused pentacyclic framework containing a phenanthrene-derived aromatic ring, a dihydrofuran bridge, and a piperidine ring bearing a tertiary N-methyl amine. The aromatic ring carries an acetate ester at one ring position, and a second acetate ester sits on a sp3 carbon of the cyclohexene ring, with a cis-alkene in the same ring. The cage-like fusion makes the scaffold highly three-dimensional and conformationally constrained, with no significant molecular symmetry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all heteroatoms are tertiary or ester-bound, but it offers several acceptors through the two ester carbonyl oxygens, the ester and ether oxygens, and the basic nitrogen.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core: a benzene ring joined to a five-membered imide-containing ring, specifically an isoindoline-1,3-dione scaffold with a gem-dimethyl group at the carbon between the two carbonyls. A methoxy group sits on the aromatic ring, adding an ether oxygen acceptor. The imide nitrogen carries a two-carbon linker that leads to a para-substituted phenyl ring bearing a sulfonylurea group, in which a cyclohexyl ring is attached to the terminal nitrogen. The sulfonylurea provides both hydrogen-bond donor NH groups and several acceptor oxygens, while the fused core and saturated cyclohexane contribute rigidity alongside the flexible ethylene linker. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is a para-substituted toluene bearing a sulfonylurea group, in which a benzene ring carrying a methyl group is attached to a sulfonyl (SO2) linker that connects to a urea-type N-C(=O)-N unit. The distal nitrogen of the urea is bonded to a saturated bicyclic amine: a pyrrolidine-type five-membered ring fused to a cyclopentane ring, forming a cis-fused bicyclic scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the sulfonylurea linker and the bicyclic portion contribute conformational flexibility. The NH groups of the sulfonylurea serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl oxygens, carbonyl oxygen, and tertiary amine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the two ring systems are differently substituted and oriented.

The molecule is a small, acyclic, open-chain compound built on a two-carbon backbone with no rings or ring fusion. An acetyl group (a methyl attached to a carbonyl) is bonded through an amide nitrogen to a CH2 unit, which in turn is attached to a terminal carboxylic acid carbon. Its functional groups are a secondary amide and a free carboxylic acid, both carbonyl-bearing, and the chain is unbranched and fairly flexible because of its single bonds. The amide N–H and the carboxylic acid O–H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the carboxyl hydroxyl oxygen act as acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry and no stereocenters.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic compound built from a benzene ring joined to a six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms... more precisely, one ring nitrogen and one ring sulfur, and the heterocycle is a 1,2,4-benzothiadiazine-type system in which the sulfur is oxidized to a sulfonyl (S,S-dioxide) group. The benzene ring carries a chlorine atom and a primary sulfonamide group, arranged so the sulfonamide sits para to the ring nitrogen-bearing carbon in the fused system. A flexible side chain on the saturated carbon of the heterocycle contains a thioether linkage and a terminal trifluoromethyl group. The sulfonyl and sulfonamide groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the sulfonamide NH2 and the ring NH provide hydrogen-bond donor capability. The molecule lacks any symmetry, and its fused ring core is fairly rigid while the side chain adds conformational flexibility.

This molecule is an acyclic urea-amide hybrid, built from a central carbonyl bearing a free amino group on one side and a secondary amide linkage on the other, with a CH2 spacer connecting to a benzene ring. The aromatic component is a single unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the ring carries no fused partners. The molecule is flexible, with several rotatable bonds along the CH2 linker and the acyclic urea-type chain. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the two N–H groups, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as acceptors. The structure lacks any stereocenters and has only partial symmetry, since the phenyl ring is the sole symmetric element.

This molecule is built around a seven-membered dibenzazepine ring: two benzene rings are fused to a central ring containing a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen carries a carboxamide group (a urea-type C(=O)NH2 substituent), and the central ring also contains a ketone carbonyl and a CH2 group, giving it a partly saturated, non-aromatic character. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is limited to the fused ring junctions. Because the central seven-membered ring is non-planar and the two aryl rings are not identical in their connectivity, the overall shape is somewhat bent and lacks any clear mirror or rotational symmetry. The primary amide NH2 can donate hydrogen bonds, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogen can accept them.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a seven-membered diazepinone ring is joined to a benzene ring, with a phenyl group attached at the imine carbon of the diazepine. The seven-membered ring contains a lactam carbonyl, a methylene carbon, an imine (C=N) double bond, and a secondary amide-type NH that closes back onto the fused benzene. A nitro group sits on the fused benzo ring, placed para to the ring nitrogen attachment, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The fused system is largely planar and conjugated, though the seven-membered ring confers some puckering and flexibility at the methylene position. The lactam NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, imine nitrogen, and nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a cinnamic acid-type scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon side chain that ends in a carboxylic acid joined through a carbon-carbon double bond. The double bond has E (trans) geometry, which keeps the chain extended and largely planar with the aromatic ring. The benzene ring carries two adjacent hydroxyl groups, forming a catechol unit, and these are located at the 3- and 4-positions relative to the side chain, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The molecule has limited conformational flexibility because of the conjugated system, while the carboxylic acid and both phenolic hydroxyls provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites and the oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an amino acid in which the side chain carries a 3-hydroxypyridin-4-one ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The nitrogen of that ring is substituted by a CH2 linker attached to a chiral alpha-carbon bearing a primary amine and a carboxylic acid group, giving a single defined stereocenter. The ring carries a ketone-type carbonyl at position 4 and an adjacent hydroxyl group at position 3, a vicinal arrangement that places a hydroxyl and a carbonyl oxygen in close proximity. The scaffold is largely planar and rigid in its ring portion, while the linker and amino acid unit provide rotational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor sites include the amine, the carboxylic acid OH, and the phenolic-type hydroxyl, and the acceptor sites include the carbonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a benzene core bearing four substituents: a butylamino group, a carboxylic acid, a primary sulfonamide, and a phenoxy group, arranged so that the carboxylic acid and sulfonamide sit meta to each other on one side of the ring while the phenoxy ether occupies the position flanked by the butylamino and sulfonamide groups. The phenoxy substituent contributes a second, unfused benzene ring joined through an ether oxygen, which gives the scaffold a diaryl ether character. There is no ring fusion, and the molecule as a whole is not symmetric, since the substituents differ in identity and placement. The aromatic core and diaryl ether linkage limit conformational freedom, while the n-butyl chain adds flexibility. The carboxylic acid and sulfonamide NH2 groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl and sulfonyl oxygens along with the ether and amine nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a saturated four-ring steroid-type scaffold, with three fused six-membered carbocycles and a fused five-membered ring. The ring system is fully aliphatic and rigid, with multiple fusion points that lock the core into a compact, non-planar shape. Embedded in one of the rings is a six-membered lactone, an ester in which the ring oxygen sits adjacent to a carbonyl, and the ring is fused to the adjacent carbocycle through a quaternary methyl-bearing carbon. A tertiary alcohol sits on the five-membered ring, and two angular methyl groups project from the ring-fusion carbons. The only hydrogen-bond donor is the hydroxyl group, while the two carbonyl and ether oxygens of the lactone act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a para-substituted benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid on one end and an anilide nitrogen on the other, linked through an amide to a central alpha-carbon. That alpha-carbon carries a benzyl-type side chain whose terminal phenyl ring is para-substituted with a hydroxyl group, and it also connects to a second amide that bears an unsubstituted benzoyl group. The three aromatic rings are not fused, so the scaffold is a flexible, chain-like arrangement of three benzene rings joined by two amide linkages and one stereogenic carbon. Overall the molecule has no internal symmetry because its two ends differ in substitution. Its hydrogen-bond capability is high: the carboxylic acid, phenol, and two amide N-H groups act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a pteridine scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a pyrimidine ring is fused to a pyrazine ring, and it carries a 2-amino group and a 4-oxo group on the pyrimidine portion. A methylene linker connects the pteridine core to a secondary aniline nitrogen, which is attached to a para-substituted benzene ring. That benzene ring bears an amide carbonyl leading to a glutamic acid unit, whose two carboxylic acid groups make the molecule polar and ionizable. The fused heteroaromatic core is planar and rigid, while the linker and the glutamate side chain add conformational flexibility. The structure has many hydrogen-bond donors (amino, NH, amide NH, and carboxylic OH groups) and many acceptors (ring nitrogens, carbonyl oxygens), and it lacks overall symmetry because the pteridine and glutamate halves differ.

This molecule is a geminal bisphosphonate, built around a single central carbon atom that carries two chlorine substituents and is bonded to two phosphorus atoms. Each phosphorus is part of a phosphonic acid group, bearing one terminal P=O double bond and two hydroxyl groups, so the scaffold has four acidic P–OH positions in total. The molecule contains no rings, so the skeleton is entirely acyclic and fairly flexible about its single bonds. Its symmetry is approximately two-fold through the central carbon, with the two chlorines and the two phosphonic acid arms related to one another. Each phosphonic acid unit provides both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl groups and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its phosphoryl oxygen.

This molecule is built on a five-membered 1,3,4-thiadiazole aromatic ring, which contains one sulfur and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The ring carries two substituents: at one carbon, an acetamido group (an acetyl group bonded through an NH to the ring), and at the other carbon, a primary sulfonamide group (SO2NH2). The molecule has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and its ring-substituent arrangement gives it only a rough, approximate symmetry. Its core is rigid and planar, while the acetamido and sulfonamide side chains add some rotational flexibility. The acetamido N–H and sulfonamide NH2 groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and sulfonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a fluoroquinolone-type scaffold built on a bicyclic quinolone core, in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridone ring. The nitrogen of the pyridone carries an N-ethyl group, and the ring carries a carboxylic acid at the 3-position adjacent to a ketone at the 4-position. A fluorine atom sits on the benzenoid ring, and a 4-methylpiperazin-1-yl group is attached at the neighboring carbon. The fused bicyclic system is largely planar and rigid, while the ethyl and N-methylpiperazine substituents add some conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group and the ketone oxygen provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, and the tertiary amines of the piperazine ring serve as additional acceptor sites.

This molecule is built on a quinazoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrimidine ring. The benzene portion carries two adjacent methoxy groups, giving it an electron-rich, symmetric-looking substitution pattern on the carbocyclic side. The pyrimidine ring bears a primary amino group, and the carbon at the 2-position is bonded to a piperazine ring that is in turn acylated by a tetrahydrofuran-2-carbonyl group, forming an amide. The overall framework is largely planar in its aromatic core but has flexibility from the saturated piperazine and tetrahydrofuran rings. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity comes mainly from the amino group, while the ring nitrogens, the amide carbonyl, the ether oxygens, and the furan oxygen act as acceptors.

This molecule is a flavin-type tricyclic scaffold, a dimethyl-substituted isoalloxazine core in which a benzene ring is fused to a central pyrazine ring that is in turn fused to a pyrimidinedione ring. The two methyl groups sit adjacent to each other on the outer benzene ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern across the otherwise flat, rigid, fully conjugated aromatic system. The nitrogen at the pyrazine-adjacent position bears a flexible four-carbon side chain carrying three stereodefined secondary hydroxyl groups and a terminal primary hydroxyl group. The pyrimidinedione ring contains two carbonyl oxygens and an N-H group, providing both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the polyol side chain adds further donor and acceptor capacity.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, which together form a substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused ring systems. An amino group and a hydroxyl group sit para to each other across the ring, while a carboxylic acid group sits on the carbon adjacent to the hydroxyl, creating an ortho relationship between the hydroxyl and the acid. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the three functional groups are relatively small and offer some rotational freedom at their attachment points. The amino, hydroxyl, and carboxylic acid groups each contain hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the oxygen and nitrogen atoms provide hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a linear, fully aromatic tricyclic scaffold in which three six-membered rings are fused edge-to-edge in a straight line, resembling an acridine-type framework with a nitrogen atom at the central ring position. Two primary amino groups are attached to the outer rings, one on each terminal ring, at positions that place them roughly opposite one another across the fused system. The structure is essentially planar and rigid, since every ring atom is sp2-hybridized and the fused aromatic system permits little conformational freedom, and the molecule possesses an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the central nitrogen. Each amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings and no heteroatoms in the ring. Every one of the six ring carbons carries a carboxylic acid group (–COOH), so the substitution pattern is hexasubstituted and each substituent sits directly on the aromatic core. The molecule has high local symmetry in its substitution, but because the acids are identical this arrangement is conformationally restricted, with the rigid planar ring limiting motion while the carboxyl groups can rotate about their single bonds. Each carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, giving the molecule six donor sites and twelve acceptor sites in total.

This molecule is built on a three-carbon backbone bearing a quaternary stereocenter that carries a methyl group, a primary amine, a benzylic CH2 linker, and a carboxylic acid. The benzylic linker connects to a benzene ring that is substituted with two adjacent hydroxyl groups on the ring, forming a catechol unit. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the aliphatic backbone provides some conformational flexibility around its single bonds. The amine and carboxylic acid groups are both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the two phenolic hydroxyls add further donor and acceptor capability. The molecule is chiral at its single stereocenter and lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system built from two fused six-membered rings, forming a pteridine-type scaffold containing four nitrogen atoms in the ring framework. One ring carries a single methyl substituent on a carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, which breaks the otherwise symmetric arrangement of the core. The fused aromatic rings are fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since every nitrogen lies within the aromatic system and the only carbon-bound hydrogens are on the ring and the methyl group.

The molecule is built on a dibenzo-fused seven-membered central ring, specifically a dibenzocycloheptene core in which two benzene rings are fused to the central ring on either side of a carbon-carbon double bond. Exocyclic to that central ring, one carbon is double-bonded to a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom. That nitrogen carries an N-methyl substituent, making it a tertiary amine. The nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond but cannot donate one, and the molecule has no hydroxyl or amide groups. The fused tricyclic system is largely rigid and planar, while the piperidine ring can flex between chair conformations.

This molecule is built on a tricyclic dibenzo-fused scaffold: two benzene rings are joined through a central seven-membered ring containing a nitrogen atom and a two-carbon bridge. The ring system is fused and largely planar in its aromatic portions, while the central ring adds some puckering and conformational flexibility. Attached to the central nitrogen is a three-carbon chain terminating in a secondary amine bearing a methyl group, which provides a flexible, basic side chain. The tertiary aryl-nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the secondary amine's N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the side chain breaks the otherwise symmetric arrangement of the tricycle.

The molecule is built on a quaternary carbon that carries a primary carboxamide, a phenyl ring, and a pyridin-2-yl ring, with a two-carbon chain leading to a tertiary amine. That amine bears two isopropyl groups, so the nitrogen is fully substituted and acts as a basic, non-donating center. The two aromatic rings, one benzene and one pyridine, are not fused; they are attached to the same central carbon and are free to rotate, which gives the molecule considerable conformational flexibility. The carboxamide offers two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 group and one acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the pyridine nitrogen adds a further acceptor. The overall structure lacks any symmetry because the three substituents on the central carbon are chemically distinct.

This molecule is a fenbuconazole-type structure built around a quaternary carbon bearing a nitrile group, a phenyl ring, a 1,2,4-triazol-1-ylmethyl arm, and a 2-(4-chlorophenyl)ethyl chain. The quaternary carbon makes the scaffold branched and three-dimensionally bulky rather than planar. The 4-chlorophenyl ring is para-substituted, giving it a simple mirror-symmetric pattern, while the unsubstituted phenyl ring has no fused ring systems. The central 1,2,4-triazole is an aromatic five-membered ring with nitrogen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, and the nitrile nitrogen is a further acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its several rotatable single bonds give it moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a 2-arylpropanoic acid skeleton, with a para-substituted phenyl ring bearing a fused bicyclic lactam on the opposite side. The lactam is an isoindolinone: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing a nitrogen and a carbonyl group, so the nitrogen sits directly on the phenyl ring as a tertiary amide. The alpha carbon of the propanoic acid chain is a stereocenter bearing a methyl group, and the terminal carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The amide carbonyl adds a further acceptor site, while the lactam nitrogen has no hydrogen to donate. The fused ring system is largely planar and rigid, while the propanoic acid side chain retains some rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because of the chiral center and the asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built around a piperazine ring whose one nitrogen is capped by an acetyl group, forming an amide, while the other nitrogen is bonded to a para-substituted phenyl ring. That phenyl ring carries an ether linkage leading to a chiral, five-membered 1,3-dioxolane ring, which bears a dichlorophenyl group and an imidazolylmethyl side chain on the same carbon. The dichlorophenyl ring is substituted at the 2 and 4 positions, and the imidazole is an aromatic five-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms. The structure contains several rings joined by flexible linkers, giving it a moderately elongated shape with one stereocenter. The acetamide carbonyl and the ether and imidazole nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered pyrimidine-type heterocycle: a ring containing two nitrogen atoms separated by a carbonyl carbon, with two additional carbonyl groups, so the core is a barbiturate-like 2,4,6-trioxo-hexahydropyrimidine scaffold. The carbon at the 5-position is quaternary, bearing two non-ring substituents: an allyl group (a three-carbon chain ending in a terminal alkene) and a branched sec-alkyl chain. Because this carbon is sp3 and carries two different substituents, the molecule has a stereocenter and lacks any internal mirror symmetry in its substituent arrangement, while the ring itself is relatively rigid and planar-leaning around its carbonyls. The two ring N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the three carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The alkyl and alkenyl side chains add conformational flexibility to an otherwise compact core.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core: a thiophene ring fused to a six-membered 1,2-thiazine ring that carries a sulfonyl group (S(=O)(=O)) and an N-methyl nitrogen. The sulfonyl sulfur and the adjacent nitrogen form part of the heterocyclic scaffold, making the ring system relatively rigid and planar. A hydroxyl group sits on a carbon of the enol-like double bond, and a carboxamide linker (C(=O)NH) extends from the ring to a pyridin-2-yl group. The amide and pyridine nitrogen create hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, with the hydroxyl and amide NH serving as donors and the carbonyl oxygen, sulfonyl oxygens, and pyridine nitrogen as acceptors. The molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry, and the bond between the carboxamide and pyridine ring allows some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a thiamphenicol-type scaffold built on a para-substituted benzene ring bearing a methylsulfonyl group (a sulfone attached directly to the ring). The aryl ring is linked to a three-carbon chain containing two adjacent stereogenic carbons, one bearing a secondary hydroxyl and the other a primary hydroxymethyl group, with the second carbon also carrying an amide nitrogen. That amide is acylated by a dichloroacetyl group, giving a terminal CHCl2 moiety. The molecule has no fused ring systems and only one aromatic ring, so it is fairly flexible through its acyclic chain and rotatable bonds. Its hydrogen-bond donors are the hydroxyl groups and the amide N–H, while the sulfone oxygens, the amide carbonyl, and the hydroxyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a phenothiazine scaffold: a tricyclic framework in which a central six-membered ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen is fused to two benzene rings, giving a folded, butterfly-like shape. One benzene ring carries a methylthio (S-CH3) substituent at a position para to the ring nitrogen, while the other is unsubstituted. The ring nitrogen bears a two-carbon linker ending in a piperidine ring, which is N-methylated, so the basic amine sits at the end of a flexible chain. The aromatic core is rigid, but the side chain adds conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution. The tertiary amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a steroid scaffold of four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, arranged in the classic cyclopentanophenanthrene fashion. The A ring is a cross-conjugated cyclohexadienone, containing two carbon-carbon double bonds and a ketone, which makes that ring largely flat and rigid. The D ring is a cyclopentane bearing a hydroxyl group and a two-carbon side chain that carries a ketone flanked by an ester of acetic acid. Additional substituents include a fluorine atom at a ring-fusion carbon, a free secondary alcohol, a second acetate ester, and two angular methyl groups. The fused framework is largely rigid, with the ester side chain adding some flexibility. Hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ketone and ester carbonyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a phenothiazine tricycle, in which two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom. The phenothiazine nitrogen carries a three-carbon propyl linker, and a trifluoromethyl group sits on one of the benzo rings, giving a single substituent on that aromatic system. At the far end of the linker is a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring with two nitrogens opposite one another, one of which bears an N-methyl group. The central tricyclic core is fairly rigid and folded along the sulfur-nitrogen axis, while the propyl-piperazine arm is flexible. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, but the two piperazine nitrogens and the phenothiazine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six substituents in a fully substituted pattern. Three of the ring positions carry iodine atoms, placed at alternating positions around the ring, while the other three carry two acetamido groups (each an acetyl group bonded through nitrogen to the ring) and one carboxylic acid group. Because the iodines and the amide and acid groups alternate around the ring, the arrangement has approximate threefold symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amide and acid side chains add some conformational flexibility. The two acetamido NH groups and the carboxylic acid OH serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygens of the amides and the acid act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a 4-oxo-4-(biphenyl-4-yl)butanoic acid, built from a biphenyl scaffold made of two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond. One ring carries a para-substituent consisting of a four-carbon chain: a ketone carbonyl attached directly to the aromatic ring, followed by two methylene groups ending in a terminal carboxylic acid. The other phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is strictly para on the first ring and absent on the second. The molecule is largely planar and rigid through its aromatic core, while the saturated chain adds rotational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated at the carboxylic acid, which can donate one hydrogen bond and accept two, and the ketone oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

This molecule is an organophosphorothioate ester built around a central phosphorus atom that is double-bonded to sulfur and bonded to two methoxy groups and one aryl ether oxygen. The aromatic portion is a benzene ring carrying three chlorine substituents at the 2, 4, and 5 positions relative to the ether linkage, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror plane. The ring is unfused and fully aromatic, so the core is rigid, while the P–O bonds and methoxy groups provide some rotational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens sit on carbon. Its acceptor sites are the phosphoryl sulfur, the ether and ester oxygens, and the chlorine atoms, which can weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a five-membered imidazolidine-2,4-dione (hydantoin-type) ring, a saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogens and two carbonyl carbons. The nitrogen at position 3 bears a 3,5-dichlorophenyl group, a benzene ring with chlorine atoms at the two meta positions, giving a symmetric substitution pattern. The other ring nitrogen carries an exocyclic carboxamide linked to an isopropyl group, which adds a branched alkyl terminus. The urea-like N-C(=O)-N unit and the ring carbonyls provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the secondary amide N-H serves as a single hydrogen-bond donor. The fused-looking but actually single-bonded aryl and amide substituents leave the core moderately rigid with limited conformational freedom.

This molecule is built on a phenothiazine scaffold: a tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom. The ring nitrogen of the phenothiazine core carries a three-carbon (propyl) linker that terminates in a six-membered piperazine ring. The piperazine bears a methyl group on its distal nitrogen, which makes the two piperazine nitrogens distinct, one tertiary and attached to the linker, the other tertiary and methylated. The overall framework is largely planar in its tricyclic portion, while the propyl-piperazine side chain adds conformational flexibility. The tertiary amine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present.

This molecule is a barbiturate-type pyrimidinetrione ring: a six-membered ring containing two amide-like NH groups flanked by three carbonyl carbons, giving a 2,4,6-trioxo-hexahydropyrimidine scaffold. The C5 carbon of this ring is quaternary, bearing both an ethyl group and a bicyclic substituent. That substituent is a bicyclo[2.2.2]octene-type cage with one C=C double bond attached directly to the ring junction, making it rigid and three-dimensional, with defined stereocenters. The two ring NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and the three carbonyl oxygens act as acceptors. Overall the molecule has little rotational symmetry because the bulky cage and the ethyl group sit on the same carbon, and the bicyclic portion is conformationally constrained while the ethyl chain remains flexible.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring bearing a biphenyl-type substitution: one ring is linked directly at the para position to a second phenyl ring, which in turn carries a terminal phenyl group, giving an extended, linear aromatic framework. At the opposite para position of the central ring sits a tetrahedral benzylic carbon that carries both a second unsubstituted phenyl ring and an imidazol-1-yl group attached through one of its nitrogen atoms. The imidazole ring is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle whose unsubstituted nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall structure is largely planar and rigid across the biaryl portion, with some conformational flexibility at the sp3 benzylic center, which introduces a three-dimensional twist.

This molecule is a tetracycline-type scaffold: four fused six-membered rings arranged linearly-angular, with the A ring carrying a dimethylamino group at one stereocenter and a carboxamide attached to an enol-bearing carbon. The B ring contains a ketone and several enol or hydroxyl groups, and the D ring is a substituted aromatic ring bearing a hydroxyl and a chlorine atom. The C ring is fused in a bridged, partly saturated arrangement with a tertiary carbinol carrying a methyl group. The molecule is asymmetric, with multiple defined stereocenters that make its three-dimensional shape rigid, while the dimethylamino and carboxamide groups add some conformational freedom. It has many hydrogen-bond donors from hydroxyl and amide groups and numerous acceptors from carbonyl and ring oxygens.

This molecule is a steroid built on a fused four-ring system: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, arranged in the classic cyclopenta-phenanthrene scaffold. The A ring is an enone, a cyclohexenone with a carbonyl conjugated to a carbon-carbon double bond, and the C ring carries a secondary hydroxyl group. The five-membered D ring bears a two-carbon side chain ending in a ketone adjacent to a primary alcohol, and two angular methyl groups sit at ring-fusion positions. The fused framework is conformationally rigid, while the side chain adds some flexibility. Overall the molecule has several hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, including two hydroxyl-type oxygens and two carbonyl oxygens.

The molecule is built around a central thiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing both sulfur and nitrogen, which is substituted at the 2-position by a guanidine group (a carbon bearing three nitrogen atoms with extensive C=N and N–H character). The 4-position of the thiazole carries a CH2 linker attached to a thioether sulfur, followed by a two-carbon chain ending in an amidine unit that is N-sulfamoylated, meaning a sulfonamide-type SO2NH2 group sits on the amidine nitrogen. The scaffold is therefore a flexible, chain-linked aromatic core with no ring fusion and no internal symmetry, since the two arms are chemically distinct. The guanidine, amidine, and sulfamoyl groups supply multiple hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H bonds and several acceptors through their nitrogen and oxygen atoms, while the thioether linkage adds conformational flexibility to the molecule.

This molecule is a substituted urea built from a 3,4-dichlorophenyl ring linked to an N-methoxy-N-methyl urea group. The central scaffold is a carbonyl flanked by a nitrogen bearing a methoxy and a methyl group on one side and an NH attached to the aromatic ring on the other. The benzene ring is a single unfused aromatic system carrying two adjacent chlorine atoms at the meta and para positions relative to the urea nitrogen. The urea carbonyl and the methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the single N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The aryl-to-urea bond and the N–N and N–O linkages give the molecule moderate conformational flexibility, with the aromatic ring remaining planar and rigid.

This molecule is built on a quinuclidine-type bicyclic amine scaffold, a saturated cage in which a nitrogen bridges two carbon framework paths. Attached to this cage is a vinyl group on one carbon and a secondary alcohol that links the cage to a 4-quinolyl ring system. The quinoline portion is a bicyclic aromatic unit, a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring, bearing a methoxy group on the carbocyclic ring. The molecule has one stereogenic carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and several additional stereocenters in the cage, so it lacks overall symmetry. The bicyclic framework is conformationally constrained, while the single bonds linking the alcohol to the quinoline allow some rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group and the basic tertiary amine can act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the quinoline nitrogen provides an additional acceptor.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core: a hydrindane-type system in which a six-membered ring is fused to a five-membered ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, with a conjugated diene running through the unsaturated portion. A 2,2-dimethylbutanoyl ester is attached to the ring at one position, forming a branched aliphatic acyl group. A second, separate fused lactone ring hangs from an ethyl linker off the core, containing a secondary alcohol and an internal cyclic ester. The substitution pattern includes several methyl groups and multiple stereocenters that give the molecule a non-symmetric, three-dimensionally crowded shape. Its rigid fused rings contrast with flexible saturated chains, and the hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ester and lactone carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a phenothiazine scaffold, a tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom. The central ring is folded along the sulfur-nitrogen axis, so the overall shape is butterfly-like rather than flat. The nitrogen at the ring junction carries a three-carbon chain ending in a dimethylamino group, which adds a flexible, basic side arm. One of the outer benzene rings bears a trifluoromethyl group at the position para to the sulfur, adding a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen and sulfur are substituted and no N-H or O-H groups are present, but the tertiary amine nitrogen and the ring nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a dibenzo-p-dioxin scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a central six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms opposite each other. One benzene ring is fully substituted with four chlorine atoms, while the other is unsubstituted. The fused tricyclic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has a near-symmetrical arrangement, with the chlorine atoms distributed across one side of the system. The two ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a single nitrogen atom that carries three substituents: a para-methoxyphenyl ring, a four-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, and a para-chlorobenzoyl group forming a tertiary amide. The two benzene rings are not fused; each is a separate six-membered aromatic ring, with the methoxy group on one and the chlorine on the other, both placed at the position opposite the point of attachment. The amide carbonyl and the terminal carboxylic acid provide the main hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the carboxylic acid OH is the only hydrogen-bond donor, and the ether oxygen adds one further weak acceptor. The aliphatic linker is flexible, whereas the amide and the aromatic rings add rigidity to the overall framework. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two aryl groups and the acid chain are chemically distinct.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is an ethylthiomethyl group (a CH2 linker bonded to a sulfur atom that carries an ethyl chain), which adds a flexible, lipophilic thioether arm. The other is a carbamate ester, an O-aryl linkage to a carbonyl bearing an N-methylamino group, which contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the N–H) and acceptor capability at the carbonyl and ester oxygens. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the side chains are conformationally flexible, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no double bonds and no fused or bridged rings. It carries two substituents on the ring at positions 1 and 4, so they sit across from each other: a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a chlorine atom on the carbon opposite it. Because both groups are on the same ring and sit at opposite positions, the molecule has a symmetric 1,4-disubstitution pattern, although the ring can adopt chair conformations that place each substituent axial or equatorial. The ring itself is largely flexible, while the hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the chlorine atom is a weak acceptor only.

The molecule is built on a norbornane (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) scaffold, a compact, rigid, cage-like framework in which two carbon bridges and a one-carbon bridge join two bridgehead carbons. A single chlorine atom sits on one of the two-carbon bridges, making it a monosubstituted chloro derivative with no other functional groups. The bicyclic core contains no heteroatoms or double bonds, so it is fully saturated. Its rigidity restricts conformational freedom, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane once the chlorine is placed on one side. The chlorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a single acyclic backbone with no ring systems, so it has no ring fusion and no aromatic core. Its central unit is a tertiary carbamate-type linkage, in which a methoxycarbonyl group and a methyl group are both attached to one nitrogen that also bears an acyl carbonyl, creating an imide-like arrangement. A methylene group bridges that carbonyl to a thioether sulfur, which connects to a tetravalent phosphorus center carrying two methyl groups, a methoxy group, and a phosphorus-bound sulfur. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, and the chain is highly flexible because of its many single bonds. Carbonyl oxygens and the ether and thiophosphoryl oxygens and sulfurs act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all its hydrogens sit on carbon or methyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a vinyl group (CH=CH2) and two chlorine atoms on adjacent or nearby carbons of the aromatic core. Taking the SMILES at face value, the vinyl group sits on one ring carbon with a chlorine on each of the two flanking positions, so the two chlorines are symmetric about the vinyl-bearing carbon, giving a 2,6-dichloro-substituted styrene-type pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the only other unsaturation is the terminal carbon-carbon double bond of the vinyl side chain. The chlorine atoms are halogen substituents that carry no hydrogen-bond donor capability and only weak acceptor character, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites at all. Overall the scaffold is fairly rigid apart from rotation of the vinyl group about its bond to the ring.

This molecule is a short fully saturated perhalogenated chain built on a three-carbon backbone. The first carbon carries three fluorine atoms, the middle carbon carries two fluorines, and the terminal carbon carries two fluorines and one iodine, so every carbon is fully substituted with halogens. There are no rings, no double bonds, and no heteroatoms other than the halogens, so no ring fusion or aromatic character is present. The chain is linear and has free rotation about its carbon-carbon bonds, giving it conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine and iodine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two ester groups on adjacent (ortho) carbons, making it a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic core. Each ester is a carbonyl carbon bonded to the ring on one side and to an oxygen on the other, which in turn connects to a long, branched alkyl chain of seven carbons ending in an isopropyl-type terminus. Because the two side chains are identical and attached symmetrically at the ortho positions, the overall structure has a mirror-type symmetry through the ring. The flexible alkyl tails contrast with the rigid aromatic core and the planar ester linkages. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks N-H or O-H groups, but its two carbonyl oxygens and two ether-type oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered barbiturate-type ring, a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione core in which the C5 carbon is quaternary and bears both an ethyl group and a phenyl ring. The two ring nitrogens each carry a methoxymethyl substituent, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric about the ring but the two N-side chains are identical. The phenyl ring is an unfused benzene attached through a single bond, giving a moderately flexible connection at the quaternary center. Three carbonyl groups are present, and the molecule has no N-H bonds, so it offers no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a 1,3,4-thiadiazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. At the 2-position sits an N-methyl urea unit, where a tertiary nitrogen bearing a methyl group is attached directly to the heteroaromatic ring and linked through a carbonyl to a secondary N-methyl amide nitrogen. The 5-position of the ring carries a trifluoromethyl group, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically compact. The scaffold is essentially planar and rigid through the aromatic core, while the urea linker and the methyl substituents add modest conformational flexibility. The urea NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen along with the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a six-membered partially saturated oxygen-containing heterocycle, a dihydropyran ring, bearing a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. A double bond sits within this ring, conjugated with a carboxamide group that links it to an unsubstituted phenyl ring through an amide nitrogen, so the anilide portion is planar and fairly rigid. The ring's remaining three carbons are sp3-hybridized and give the ring some conformational flexibility, while the aromatic and amide segments are constrained. The amide N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen together with the ring ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the aryl amide unit.

This molecule is a phosphate triester: a central phosphorus atom doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to three identical oxygen-linked branches. Each branch is a flexible three-carbon chain (a propyl unit) carrying a bromine on the middle carbon and another bromine on the terminal carbon, so there are six bromine substituents in total. The scaffold has no rings and no ring fusion, and it is highly flexible because of the many rotatable single bonds. The arrangement is threefold symmetric about the phosphorus center. The phosphoryl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the three ester oxygens are weaker acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small, acyclic haloalkane built on a two-carbon ethane skeleton, with no rings or ring fusion. One carbon is fully substituted by three fluorine atoms, forming a trifluoromethyl group, while the other carbon carries one fluorine and one bromine atom. The arrangement is an asymmetric substitution pattern on a flexible single-bonded backbone, with free rotation about the central carbon–carbon bond. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain saturated fatty amide: a single unbranched alkyl chain of eighteen carbon atoms terminated at one end by a primary carboxamide group, C(=O)NH2. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroaromatic systems, so the scaffold is purely acyclic. The carbonyl carbon bears a carbonyl oxygen and a terminal amino nitrogen, making the amide the sole functional group. The molecule has no stereocenters and no branching, and it possesses only a conformational mirror-like symmetry along its chain axis. Its alkyl portion is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds. The amide group offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites on the nitrogen and one hydrogen-bond acceptor site on the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is built from a fused polycyclic core containing two lactone rings, one of which is a fused bicyclic system bearing a cyclic anhydride-like ring and a separate unsaturated six-membered lactone (an α,β-unsaturated δ-lactone) attached as a pendant group. Several secondary hydroxyl groups are distributed around the scaffold, and a linear hexyl chain bearing a hydroxyl branches from one ring carbon, giving the molecule a substitution pattern that is asymmetric. The fused ring systems and the conjugated enone within the pendant lactone make much of the framework rigid, while the saturated hexyl chain and the single-bonded linkages add conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl groups and the carbonyl oxygens of the lactone and anhydride-type rings together provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle, giving a tetralin-type (1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene) framework. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, while the saturated ring carries two methyl groups on adjacent sp3 carbons, placed at the positions beta to the fused benzene junction. Because the two methyls sit on adjacent carbons of the saturated ring, the molecule has a substitution pattern that is roughly symmetric about the plane through the two methyl-bearing carbons. The saturated ring adopts a puckered, semi-flexible conformation, while the fused aromatic portion is rigid and planar. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor or donor capability.

The molecule is built on a six-membered 1,2,4-triazine ring, a fully unsaturated heteroaromatic scaffold containing three nitrogen atoms. The ring carries a carbonyl group at one position, which makes it a triazinone, and a methylthio group (a sulfur bearing a methyl) attached to the carbon between two nitrogens. A tert-butyl group, a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, sits on the adjacent ring carbon, providing bulk and steric shielding. An exocyclic primary amino group is bonded to a ring nitrogen, adding a hydrogen-bond donor. The ring is flat and rigid, with only the methyl and amino substituents able to rotate, and the carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, acyclic organosulfur compound built on a straight eight-carbon alkyl chain, with no rings and no branching. At one end, a sulfur atom links the chain to a nitrile-type carbon-nitrogen triple bond, giving a thiocyanate functional group (R–S–C≡N). The skeleton is highly flexible, since the saturated carbon chain can rotate freely about its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond the simple chain arrangement. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, because it carries no N–H or O–H bonds. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the nitrogen of the nitrile and, more weakly, the sulfur atom.

The molecule is a fully chlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxin, meaning two benzene rings are joined through a central six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms in a para (1,4) arrangement. Each benzene ring carries three chlorine substituents, placed at the lateral positions, so the molecule has six chlorine atoms in total. The tricyclic core is planar and rigid, with the two outer rings fused to the central dioxin ring, and the substitution pattern is nearly symmetric across the two halves. The ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and the aromatic C–H positions are limited to a single hydrogen on each ring.

This molecule is a triaryl phosphate built around a central phosphorus atom bearing one double-bonded oxygen and three aryloxy arms. Each aryl ring is a benzene ring carrying two methyl groups, with the oxygen attached at one position and the two methyls at the remaining positions, so the three rings share the same substitution pattern in an asymmetric arrangement. The central P=O unit acts as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ester-like P–O–aryl linkages allow considerable rotational freedom around the bonds to the phosphorus, giving the overall structure a moderately flexible, propeller-like three-dimensional shape.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. At the 2-position of the thiazole, the nitrogen-bearing carbon carries an N-methyl urea unit: a nitrogen bearing a methyl group that is bonded to a carbonyl, which in turn bears a second nitrogen with a methyl substituent. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the urea side chain adds some rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The urea carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the secondary N-H on the urea is a hydrogen-bond donor. The thiazole nitrogen can also act as an acceptor, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the substituents.

This molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a hydroxyl group, an isopropyl ester, and two para-bromophenyl rings, making it a diaryl-substituted α-hydroxy ester. The two benzene rings are unfused and each carries one bromine atom at the para position, so the aromatic substitution pattern is symmetric about the central carbon. The ester oxygen and carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the tertiary hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The central carbon is sp3-hybridized and the two aryl groups project outward, giving the framework a propeller-like, moderately flexible shape around that axis.

This molecule is an organophosphorothioate ester built around a central phosphorus atom that carries a thiophosphoryl (P=S) group, two methoxy groups, and an aryl ether oxygen. The aromatic portion is a single benzene ring bearing three halogen substituents: two chlorines and one iodine, arranged in a 2,4-dichloro-5-iodo pattern relative to the ether oxygen. There are no fused or additional ring systems, so the scaffold is a simple phenyl ring attached to a flexible phosphorus-centered core. The two methyl ester arms give the phosphorus center a near-tetrahedral geometry with limited symmetry, while the aromatic ring remains rigid and planar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its acceptor sites are the sulfur, the phosphoryl and ester oxygens, and the ether oxygen.

This molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by a secondary amine (NH) bridge, giving a diarylamine scaffold. One ring is a pyridine bearing a carboxylic acid group adjacent to the nitrogen-linked carbon, which places an acidic O–H donor and carbonyl acceptor next to the ring. The other ring is a benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a chlorine atom on the carbons flanking the NH attachment, creating an ortho-disubstituted, sterically crowded pattern. Because the two aryl rings are connected through a single NH linkage, the molecule has considerable conformational flexibility around that bridge, and it lacks any internal symmetry. Overall, it presents one N–H and one O–H as hydrogen-bond donors, while the pyridine nitrogen, the carbonyl oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated aliphatic chain with no rings, so its scaffold is a flexible linear skeleton. At one end sits a tert-butyl group, attached to a ketone carbonyl, followed by a methylene carbon and a second carbonyl. The other end carries a perfluorinated segment of three carbons bearing a total of seven fluorine atoms, terminating in a trifluoromethyl group. The molecule has a 1,3-diketone motif, with both carbonyl oxygens acting as hydrogen-bond acceptors and no hydrogen-bond donors present. Its overall shape is asymmetric, since the bulky tert-butyl end differs sharply from the fluorinated end.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: two methoxy groups and three chlorine atoms, arranged around the aromatic core. The two methoxy groups sit on adjacent carbons, and the three chlorines occupy three consecutive positions, leaving a single unsubstituted aromatic C–H. The scaffold is a single, fully aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and it is planar and rigid. The ether oxygens of the methoxy groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry in its substituent arrangement.

The molecule is a small aromatic carboxylic acid built around a four-carbon chain. A single benzene ring, unfused and unsubstituted on the ring itself, is attached to a branched carbon bearing a methyl group, so the chiral center sits on the chain next to the phenyl ring. From that branch point, the chain continues through two methylene units to a terminal carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the phenyl ring contributes only a flat, hydrophobic surface. The chain is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because of the stereogenic center.

The molecule is an acyclic carbamate-ester hybrid built around a central chiral carbon bearing a methyl group. One side carries an ethyl-substituted secondary amide, while the other side is an ester linked through an oxygen to a carbamate nitrogen that is attached to a phenyl ring, so the scaffold contains a phenyl ring with an unsubstituted, monosubstituted pattern. Two carbonyl groups are present, one amide and one carbamate, along with an ester-type oxygen linkage and two N–H groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors. The carbonyl oxygens and ether-type oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal ring besides the aromatic benzene ring, and it has several rotatable single bonds, giving it considerable conformational flexibility. It has no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the phenyl ring, since the stereogenic center breaks overall symmetry.

This molecule is a short, acyclic, chiral compound built on a three-carbon backbone with no ring systems. It carries an acetamide group (a methyl ketone-like carbonyl bonded to an NH) attached to the alpha carbon, which also bears a carboxylic acid group. The adjacent carbon is a quaternary center bearing two methyl groups and a thiol (sulfanyl) group, giving a bulky, branched substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The chain is fairly flexible, with several rotatable single bonds. The amide N-H and carboxylic O-H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and carboxyl carbonyl oxygens and the thiol sulfur act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short, fully saturated acyclic chain of four carbon atoms, forming a linear backbone with no rings and no double or triple bonds. Each of the four carbons carries chlorine substituents: the two terminal carbons each bear two chlorines, and the two central carbons each bear one, so the chlorines are distributed symmetrically along the chain. The structure contains no hydroxyl, amine, carbonyl, or other polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability beyond the weak halogen-type interactions of the chlorine atoms. The chain is flexible, since its single bonds allow free rotation about each carbon-carbon bond, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry about its central carbon-carbon bond.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a branched saturated carbon chain. Its backbone is a six-carbon chain bearing methyl branches: the carboxyl carbon sits at one end, the alpha carbon carries a methyl group, and the beta carbon carries an isopropyl group, giving a two-methyl-substituted pentanoic-type framework. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated units. The sole functional group is the terminal carboxylic acid, which can donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept two through its oxygen atoms. The molecule lacks any symmetry because its branches are placed asymmetrically along the chain, and its single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility.

This molecule consists of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, forming a biphenyl scaffold with no ring fusion. Every carbon on both rings carries a bromine atom, so the substitution is fully halogenated, with the ring-linking positions being the only carbons not bearing a bromine. The two rings are not coplanar in practice because the bulky bromine atoms flanking the bond sterically hinder free rotation, giving the structure a relatively rigid, twisted geometry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites in the usual sense, since the only heteroatoms are the bromines, which are weak halogen-bond donors rather than classical acceptors.

The molecule is a small, acyclic, non-aromatic compound built on a short two-carbon chain. A methyl group sits on a nitrogen atom that also bears an N-nitroso group (an N=O unit), so the nitrogen is a tertiary, nitrosated amine. The other carbon of the chain is a methylene that links to a terminal carboxylic acid, giving the molecule a free carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid OH is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the acid's other oxygen, and the nitroso oxygen all serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The structure has no ring systems, no stereocenters, and no internal symmetry, and its single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a single tetrahedral carbon bearing four different groups: a hydroxyl, a pyrimidin-5-yl ring, a cyclopropyl ring, and a para-methoxyphenyl ring. The methoxyphenyl is a benzene ring carrying a methyl ether at the position opposite the central carbon, which gives it a clear linear, substituted pattern. The pyrimidine is a six-membered aromatic ring with two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 arrangement, and it is attached through its carbon-5 position, leaving both nitrogens available as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The cyclopropyl group is a small saturated three-membered carbocycle that adds rigid, three-dimensional bulk. Overall, the molecule lacks internal symmetry because its substituents differ, the central carbon is a stereocenter, and the hydroxyl serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

This molecule is an azo dye built around two benzene rings joined by a central N=N linkage in the trans configuration. One ring carries a bromine atom flanked by two nitro groups, creating a strongly electron-poor, substituted aromatic system. The other ring is a more electron-rich benzene bearing an ethoxy group, an acetamido group, and a tertiary amine nitrogen that is substituted with two acetoxyethyl chains. The overall scaffold is largely planar and conjugated across the azo bridge, though the flexible ester-containing side chains add rotational freedom. Nitro oxygens and the ester and amide carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the acetamido N-H provides a single hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is boron trichloride, a small inorganic compound with a single central boron atom bonded to three chlorine atoms. It has no carbon skeleton and no ring systems or ring fusion. Its three B–Cl bonds are arranged around the boron in a trigonal planar geometry, giving the molecule three-fold symmetry about the central atom. The boron center is electron-deficient, lacking a full octet, and the chlorine atoms carry lone pairs but lack any hydrogen atoms. Consequently the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and its chlorine atoms can only weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic aromatic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a quinoline core. A single methyl group is attached to the carbocyclic ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry elements beyond the planar framework. The fully aromatic, rigid, planar system contains one ring nitrogen, which carries a lone pair that is not part of the aromatic sextet and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. There are no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the only hydrogens are aromatic C–H and the methyl C–H atoms. The methyl group is the sole non-ring substituent and adds only a small, non-polar, rotatable point to an otherwise rigid structure.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single bond between them. One ring carries a methyl group para to the linkage, and the other carries a methyl group meta to the linkage, so the two substituents sit on opposite rings in an unsymmetrical pattern. The scaffold is entirely aromatic and carbon-only, with no heteroatoms, no ring fusion, and no ionizable or polar functional groups. The inter-ring bond allows some rotation, though the aromatic framework remains largely planar and rigid overall. Because there are no N, O, or other heteroatoms bearing lone pairs or hydrogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is a small acyclic dinitrile built on a three-carbon chain, with a single quaternary carbon at its center bearing two methyl groups. Each of the two terminal carbons of the chain is part of a nitrile group, so the carbon skeleton consists of a central carbon flanked by two nitrile-bearing carbons, with a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern. The molecule has no ring systems and no stereocenters, and it carries a mirror-symmetric arrangement, with the two cyano groups related by a plane through the central carbon. The nitrile groups are linear and rigid, while the central sp3 carbon allows limited rotational freedom about the single bonds. Nitrogen atoms in the cyano groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a dibenzo-fused seven-membered ring framework: two benzene rings are joined through a central ring that also contains a two-carbon saturated bridge. The sp3 carbon bearing the carboxamide group sits between the two aromatic rings and is the only stereogenic-type center, so the scaffold is largely rigid around the aromatic portions while the central ring can adopt a non-planar, somewhat flexible conformation. A primary carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) is attached to that benzylic carbon, providing both a hydrogen-bond donor (the NH2 group) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, giving the molecule no additional polar groups and a fairly hydrophobic, aromatic character overall. The arrangement is not symmetric, because the carboxamide breaks the symmetry of the tricyclic core.

The molecule is a straight-chain fatty acid methyl ester, with a saturated, unbranched carbon chain of fifteen carbons ending in a methyl ester group. It contains no rings, no aromatic systems, and no stereocenters, so there is no ring fusion or substitution pattern to describe. The single ester functional group, C(=O)O–CH3, provides one carbonyl oxygen that can accept a hydrogen bond, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the carbon backbone is long and freely rotatable, the structure is highly flexible, and its overall shape is elongated and roughly linear, with the polar ester group confined to one terminus.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom, which is a piperidine scaffold with no additional ring fusion or fused systems. The ring nitrogen carries a nitro group, bonded through the nitrogen atom to form an N-nitro substituent, which is the only functional group present. The remaining five carbon atoms are unsubstituted CH2 units, so the substitution pattern is minimal and the ring is fully saturated. The ring adopts a chair-like conformation and is conformationally flexible, while the nitro group is polar and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated aliphatic compound built on a short carbon chain with no ring systems and no aromatic character. A single quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups sits at the center, flanked by a tertiary amine nitrogen carrying two N-methyl substituents on one side and a primary alcohol group (–CH2OH) on the other. The nitrogen is the only heteroatom besides the terminal oxygen, so the structure has one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the nitrogen lone pair and the oxygen). The molecule is flexible because all bonds are single and rotatable, and it lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond local methyl-group equivalence.

This molecule is a carbamate ester built on a benzene ring. A methylcarbamate group (N-methyl carbamoyl oxygen linkage) is attached to one carbon of the aromatic ring, and the adjacent ortho carbon bears a saturated 1,3-dioxolane ring, which is attached through its C2 carbon, making it an acetal. The benzene ring is ortho-disubstituted, and the dioxolane contributes two ether oxygens that can accept hydrogen bonds. The carbamate N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while its carbonyl and ester oxygens act as acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents differ, and the ring-to-ring bond allows moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a central azobenzene-type unit, with a para-phenylene ring bearing an N,N-dialkylamino group on one side and a trans N=N double bond linking it to a second benzene ring. That second ring carries a nitro group para to the azo linkage and a chlorine atom ortho to it, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern across the two aromatic rings. The tertiary amine nitrogen carries a 2-hydroxyethyl arm and a 2-cyanoethyl arm, both flexible chains that add rotatable bonds to an otherwise planar, rigid aromatic core. There are no ring fusions, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two ends differ in their substituents. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrile, nitro, and azo nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a cyclohexane ring that carries a morpholine ring attached through a nitrogen atom to one of the ring carbons, making it a 4-cyclohexylmorpholine-type scaffold. The cyclohexane is fully saturated and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the morpholine is a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one oxygen separated by two carbons on each side. The two rings are joined by a single C–N bond, with no ring fusion or additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and unbranched. The molecule lacks a plane or axis of symmetry beyond the local symmetry of each ring, and its single bond linkage allows rotation between the two ring systems. The tertiary amine nitrogen and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two ester groups at the para positions, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the ring's long axis. Each ester carbonyl links the aromatic ring to an oxygen that connects to a branched alkyl chain, where a two-carbon ethyl branch sits on a carbon adjacent to the chain. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two flexible branched chains extend outward and can rotate about many single bonds. Each ester contributes a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall arrangement is a linear, rod-like diester with an extended hydrophobic character.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents, and it contains no fused ring systems. Going around the ring, one position bears an oxyacetic acid side chain, an aryl ether linked to a carboxylic acid group (–O–CH2–COOH), while the adjacent position carries a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH), and a chlorine atom sits on the ring para to the ether oxygen. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, whereas the ether and methylene linkers give the side chains some conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the primary alcohol provides another donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen acts as an additional acceptor. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is an ester built from two straight, unbranched alkyl chains joined through a single carboxylate linkage, with no rings or fused ring systems present. The central C(=O)O unit is the only functional group: a carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ester oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. One side of the ester carries a five-carbon chain and the other carries a six-carbon chain, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and there is no meaningful molecular symmetry. Both chains are fully saturated and contain many freely rotating single bonds, making the molecule highly flexible rather than rigid.

The molecule is an azo compound built from two benzene rings joined by a nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) configuration. One ring carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) at the position adjacent to the azo linkage, giving an ortho substitution pattern, while the other ring is unsubstituted phenyl. The two aromatic rings are planar and conjugated through the azo bridge, which makes the skeleton fairly rigid, though the bonds around the methoxy group and the rings' attachments allow some rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, but the two azo nitrogens and the ether oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. It has no overall symmetry because the methoxy substituent makes the two halves different.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries two phenyl rings, a primary carboxamide group, and a chain leading to a branched carbon bearing a dimethylamino group, so its scaffold is a diphenyl-substituted, acyclic aliphatic backbone with no fused or bridged ring systems. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted and attached to the same carbon, creating a propeller-like, bulky arrangement that gives the molecule considerable steric hindrance around its core. A terminal primary amide (–C(=O)NH₂) and a tertiary dimethylamino nitrogen are the principal functional groups, with the amide offering both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability and the tertiary amine acting only as an acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two phenyl groups are equivalent but the chain carrying the amine and methyl branch is distinct. Its many rotatable single bonds make it fairly flexible overall, though the diphenyl quaternary center restricts some conformations.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic 1,3,5-triazine ring, with three nitrogen atoms alternating with three carbon atoms and no ring fusion. The ring carries three substituents at alternating positions: an isopropylamino group (an NH bonded to a branched isopropyl carbon), a primary amino group (NH2), and a chlorine atom. The amino groups contribute hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the ring nitrogens and the nitrogen atoms of the substituents serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rigid aromatic core and the lack of symmetry, since the three substituents differ, give the scaffold a fixed, planar shape with only modest flexibility in the isopropyl group.

This molecule is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from fused benzene-type rings, containing one methyl group attached to a terminal ring.
