Its skeleton is an angular, extended fused-ring system of five rings joined edge-to-edge, with the ring fusions creating a bent overall shape rather than a straight linear chain. No functional groups beyond the single methyl substituent are present, and the molecule consists only of carbon and hydrogen, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The fused framework is essentially planar and rigid, and the methyl group is the only feature that breaks the overall symmetry of the structure.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge, with an amino group and a carboxylic acid group attached to the same ring of the bicyclic system at adjacent positions. The carboxylic acid is a planar C(=O)OH unit that can donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen. The primary amino group contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone-pair acceptor site on the nitrogen. The fused aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and amino substituents have limited rotational freedom about their bonds to the ring. The substitution pattern lacks any internal symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric overall.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to an imidazole ring through a shared edge, giving a flat bicyclic aromatic system. The five-membered ring contains two nitrogen atoms: one bears an ethyl group on the ring nitrogen, while the other is a pyridine-like nitrogen with a lone pair that does not carry a substituent. A methyl group sits on the carbon between the two nitrogens, at the 2-position of the imidazole ring. The fused core has no stereocenters and shows no symmetry because the ethyl group breaks the mirror symmetry of the parent ring system. The aromatic core is rigid while the ethyl chain adds some conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen with the ethyl group has no hydrogen to donate, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the unsubstituted imine-type nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a single substituent at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen (the 2-position). That substituent is a dimethylamino group, in which a nitrogen atom is bonded to the ring carbon and to two methyl groups, so there is no ring fusion and the scaffold is a simple monosubstituted aromatic ring. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid across the ring, with the methyl groups giving only modest rotational freedom around the carbon–nitrogen bond. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the tertiary amine nitrogen is conjugated with the ring and has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors at all, and it lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local equivalence of the two methyl groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It bears one primary amino group (-NH2) on one ring carbon, and the remaining five ring positions carry fluorine atoms, with four of them adjacent to one another on one side of the ring, so the substitution pattern is highly fluorinated and asymmetric. The amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and because the only flexible part is the amino group, the molecule has very little conformational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with a hydroxyl group on one ring carbon and two sec-butyl groups (each a four-carbon branched alkyl chain attached through its second carbon) on the carbons flanking it at the meta-like 1,3 positions relative to each other, so the hydroxyl sits between the two alkyl groups. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no ring fusion, and the molecule has a mirror-type arrangement across the axis through the hydroxyl carbon, though the sec-butyl stereocenters break idealized symmetry. The two alkyl chains are flexible and can rotate, while the aromatic core is rigid. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the remaining atoms offer no additional hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built from a straight-chain seven-carbon acyl unit and a straight-chain four-carbon alkoxy unit, with no rings or fused ring systems. The central feature is a single ester group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to one oxygen double-bonded and another single-bonded to a linear butyl chain, flanked on the other side by a hexyl chain. Both alkyl arms are unbranched and unsubstituted, so the scaffold is a simple, symmetric-free aliphatic chain with no stereocenters. The molecule is highly flexible, since every single bond in the chains can rotate freely. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two ester oxygens, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a substituted cyclohexane built on a saturated six-membered carbon ring with no fused or additional ring systems. It carries three substituents on the ring: two methyl groups and one hydroxyl group, arranged so the ring carbons bearing the methyls sit in a 1,3-relationship to each other, with the hydroxyl-bearing carbon positioned between them on one side. Its only functional group is the secondary alcohol, which makes it a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through the oxygen-bound hydrogen and oxygen lone pairs. The ring is fully saturated and adopts a flexible chair-type conformation, so the substituents can shift between axial and equatorial orientations. The overall framework lacks a mirror-symmetric arrangement because the hydroxyl breaks the symmetry of the methyl pattern.

The molecule is a symmetric diketone-type skeleton built around a central carbonyl group, with two identical two-carbon chains (ethylene linkers) extending from it. Each chain terminates in an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the scaffold is a 1,5-diphenylpentan-3-one framework. The two benzene rings are not fused to each other or to anything else, and the ketone is the only functional group present. The molecule has approximately mirror symmetry through the carbonyl carbon. Its chain segments are flexible, while the aromatic rings are rigid and planar. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the ketone oxygen acts as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a small, acyclic carbamate ester built on a linear two-carbon chain. A carbamoyl group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to both an amino nitrogen and an oxygen, is attached through that oxygen to an ethyl unit that terminates in a free primary hydroxyl group. There are no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain. Substitution is limited to the unbranched backbone, and the molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond its overall flexibility. Because of the freely rotating single bonds along the chain, the structure is quite flexible rather than rigid. The amino group and the hydroxyl group each act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, ester-type oxygen, and hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic framework. An ethoxy group (-O-CH2-CH3) is attached to one of the ring carbons adjacent to the fusion point, which is a substitution pattern that breaks the symmetry of the parent ring system. The ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds but cannot donate them, and there are no other polar functional groups present. The fused rings are rigid while the terminal ethyl chain retains rotational flexibility around its single bonds.

This molecule is built on a six-membered oxathiine-type ring containing one oxygen and one sulfur atom, with the sulfur present as a sulfone bearing two oxygen atoms. The ring carries a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen and a carboxamide on the adjacent alkene carbon, which is conjugated with the ring double bond. The amide nitrogen is attached to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the anilide portion is a flat aromatic extension off the core. Overall the scaffold is only partly rigid: the sulfone-containing ring is fairly constrained, while the amide-linked phenyl ring can rotate about its single bonds. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen, the two sulfone oxygens, and the ring ether oxygen act as acceptors.

This molecule is an azobenzene-type dye built on a central N=N diazene linker joining two para-disubstituted benzene rings, with the trans (E) geometry shown by the slashes. One ring carries a nitro group para to the azo link, which is a strong electron-withdrawing acceptor. The other ring bears a chlorine atom ortho to the azo nitrogen and a tertiary amine para to the azo link, nitrogen substituted with two 2-hydroxyethyl arms. The two hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the nitro oxygens and the azo nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The extended, largely planar aromatic framework is rigid, with flexibility confined mainly to the two hydroxyethyl side chains, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two rings carry different substituents.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon scaffold with no fused rings. Four of the ring positions carry substituents: a hydroxyl group (phenol), a bromine atom, and two chlorine atoms, arranged so the bromine sits ortho to the hydroxyl and the chlorines occupy the remaining positions on either side of the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen able to rotate.

This molecule is an anthraquinone scaffold: three fused six-membered rings in a linear arrangement, with the central ring carrying two ketone (C=O) groups at opposite positions. The two outer benzene rings are unsubstituted, while the right-hand ring bears two secondary amine substituents at the positions flanking the ring fusion, each linked to a 2-hydroxyethyl chain. The arrangement is roughly symmetric about the long axis of the aromatic system, with the two side chains related by a mirror-like relationship. The fused aromatic core is essentially planar and rigid, whereas the two hydroxyethyl arms are flexible. The ketone oxygens and the amine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amine N-H and terminal hydroxyl O-H groups can serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule consists of two furan rings joined by a flexible disulfide linker, with each furan attached through a methylene group to one of the sulfur atoms. Each furan is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen atom, and both rings are substituted at the 2-position, so the substitution pattern is the same on each side. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the central S–S bond, and the CH2–S–S–CH2 linkage gives it considerable conformational flexibility compared with the rigid aromatic rings. The ring oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond with no ring fusion between them. One ring carries two adjacent methyl groups at the 3 and 4 positions relative to the biaryl bond, giving a 1,2-dimethyl substitution pattern on that ring, while the other ring is unsubstituted. There are no heteroatoms and no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, so the molecule is purely hydrocarbon in character. The two aromatic rings are free to rotate about the central bond, making the core moderately flexible, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element that makes the two halves identical.

The molecule is built from two identical five-membered unsaturated lactone rings, each a furan-2(5H)-one (butenolide) core, joined through a single acetal-type oxygen bridge at their C5 positions. Each ring carries two chlorine atoms on its carbon-carbon double bond, placed at the 3 and 4 positions, and the ring carbonyl sits adjacent to the ring oxygen. The two halves are related by a two-fold symmetry axis through the central oxygen, giving the molecule a symmetric, fairly rigid overall framework. Each lactone carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all carbon-bound positions are either substituted by chlorine or part of the ring system.

The molecule is built around an azobenzene core, two benzene rings joined by a central N=N double bond with the trans (E) geometry shown by the slashes. One ring carries a dimethylamino group at the position para to the azo linkage and a methyl group ortho to that amine, while the other ring bears a nitro group para to the azo bond. This creates a strongly push-pull arrangement, with the electron-donating amine on one side and the electron-withdrawing nitro on the other. Both aromatic rings are planar and fully conjugated through the azo bridge, giving the scaffold a largely rigid, flat shape, though the N,N-dimethyl group can rotate. The nitro oxygens and the azo nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic sulfoxide built on a simple open-chain skeleton, with no rings and no fused or aromatic systems. Two n-propyl groups, each three carbons long, are attached to a single tetravalent sulfur atom that also carries a sulfinyl oxygen double-bonded to it. Because the chain is flexible and unbranched, the molecule has considerable conformational freedom around its carbon-carbon and carbon-sulfur single bonds. The sulfur center is stereogenic in principle, but the two propyl substituents are identical, so the molecule is achiral and has a mirror plane through the S=O bond. The sulfinyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since every hydrogen sits on a saturated carbon.

This molecule is an acyclic dicarbamate built on a branched aliphatic backbone. Its central scaffold is a 2,2-disubstituted propane-1,3-diol-type unit whose quaternary carbon carries a methyl group and a linear propyl chain. Each of the two terminal oxygens is linked to a carbamate group: one is an N-butyl carbamate (a butylamine nitrogen bearing a hydrogen) and the other is a primary carbamate (an unsubstituted NH2 group). The molecule contains no rings, so its overall shape is flexible, with many rotatable single bonds along the alkyl chains and the O-C bonds. Each carbamate offers an N-H group that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and each carbonyl oxygen along with the ester-type oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic nitramine built around a single nitrogen-nitrogen bond. One nitrogen carries two methyl groups, making it a tertiary amine-type center, and it is bonded to a second nitrogen that bears both a formal positive charge and a nitro-type arrangement of two oxygens, one double-bonded and one carrying a negative charge. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic groups, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain. The two methyl groups are equivalent, giving the molecule a local mirror-type symmetry about the N–N axis. Because there are few rotatable bonds and no ring constraints, the structure is quite compact and flexible around the central N–N bond. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N–H or O–H groups are present, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro-type group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated hydrocarbon chain of ten carbons with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple straight-chain alkane backbone. Two bromine atoms are attached to the chain, one on the carbon at position 9 and one on the terminal carbon at position 10, so the substitution pattern is vicinal-like, with the two halogenated carbons adjacent to each other. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two bromines sit at different positions along the chain. Its many single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built on a six-carbon straight-chain skeleton, with no rings, heteroatoms, or functional groups beyond two carbon-carbon double bonds. One double bond is terminal, sitting at the end of the chain as a vinyl group, while the other is internal, placed on the fourth carbon as a 1,1-disubstituted alkene bearing a methyl group. The chain is highly flexible, since all single bonds are free to rotate and no ring constrains its conformation. The molecule has no symmetry elements of note because the two alkene ends are chemically distinct. It has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, as it consists solely of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is a small, tetrahedral phosphorus-centered species with no carbon framework and no ring systems. The central phosphorus atom is double-bonded to a sulfur atom and single-bonded to three chlorine atoms, giving it a thiophosphoryl-type, P=S functional arrangement. The substitution pattern is fully symmetric about the phosphorus center, with three equivalent chlorine substituents, so the molecule has high local symmetry and no stereocenters. Its geometry is rigid and compact, with no rotatable bonds. The sulfur atom can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic hydrocarbon built from a benzene ring joined to a saturated six-membered carbocycle, forming a tetralin-type (1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene) scaffold. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, and the only substituent is a single methyl group attached to the saturated ring at the carbon next to the benzylic CH2 position, so the substitution pattern is minimal and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial one. The saturated ring adopts a non-planar, half-chair-like conformation, giving it moderate flexibility, while the fused benzene ring remains rigid and planar. The compound contains no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so it has neither hydrogen-bond donor nor acceptor capability.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from five six-membered rings in an angular, bay-region arrangement. Its scaffold is an extended, fully aromatic system where the rings share edges to form a rigid, planar framework, with no sp3 linkers and essentially no rotatable bonds. A single methyl group sits on one of the outer rings, providing the only substitution and breaking the otherwise uniform carbon-hydrogen periphery. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it offers no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites either, and its overall shape lacks any significant symmetry because of the asymmetric fusion pattern and the placement of the methyl group.

This molecule is a phthalate diester built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent carboxylate ester groups in an ortho (1,2) substitution pattern. Each ester carbonyl is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and each ester oxygen connects to a straight, unbranched eleven-carbon alkyl chain. The two chains are identical, giving the molecule an approximate mirror symmetry through the central ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two long saturated tails are highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on carbon. Its four carbonyl and ether oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzo[b]thiophene scaffold, consisting of a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiophene ring that contains one sulfur atom, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A hydroxyl group is attached to the benzene ring at a position adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, so the substituent sits on the carbocyclic portion next to the thiophene junction. Because the ring system is rigid and planar and the only substituent is a single hydroxyl group, the molecule has no rotatable bonds and lacks any internal symmetry. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the thiophene sulfur is only a weak acceptor.

The molecule is an acyclic-chain malonic-type derivative built around a central carbon bearing a butyl chain, a free carboxylic acid, and a carbonyl that forms part of a hydrazide. The hydrazide nitrogen is fully substituted by a phenyl ring and is connected through a second nitrogen to another phenyl ring, giving two aromatic benzene rings attached to a flexible N–N linkage. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted and unfused, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two aryl groups sit on different nitrogens. Its flexible alkyl chain and rotatable bonds contrast with the rigid aromatic rings. The carboxylic acid OH acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygens and the carboxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the secondary aryl-amine N–H provides an additional donor site.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four substituents. Reading around the ring, there is a methyl group, then an amino group, then a nitro group, and finally a carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) group, with the methyl and carboxamide groups on adjacent carbons. This substitution pattern makes the ring fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings present. The nitro group and the carboxamide are electron-withdrawing, while the amino group is electron-donating, so the three functional groups are arranged in a push-pull fashion across the ring. The scaffold is conformationally rigid apart from rotation of the methyl, nitro, amino, and amide groups about their bonds to the ring. Overall the molecule has no symmetry, since its four substituents are all different. The amino and carboxamide groups can each act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide carbonyl and nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single sp3-hybridized carbon that bears a methyl group and two identical para-chlorophenyl rings, so the skeleton is a 1,1-diarylethane. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring with no fused partners, and each carries one chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, giving a symmetric para-disubstituted pattern. The two halves are related by a mirror relationship through the central carbon, although the central carbon is a stereogenic center bearing four different groups, so the molecule can exist in chiral forms. Apart from rotation about the single bonds to the rings, the framework is fairly rigid. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms are only weak acceptors, so its hydrogen-bonding capacity is minimal.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one amino group and four chlorine atoms, giving a tetrachloroaniline scaffold. The aromatic ring is fully substituted except for one position, which carries a hydrogen, so it has no ring fusion and no additional ring systems. The amino group sits adjacent to two chlorines, creating a sterically crowded arrangement around the nitrogen, while the remaining chlorines are distributed unevenly around the ring, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the amino group offering modest rotational freedom. The NH2 group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine substituents are weak halogen-bond participants and do not act as typical hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring in a para (1,4) arrangement: a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond attached directly to the ring) and an ethyl group. Because the two substituents are opposite each other, the molecule has a high degree of symmetry along the axis through the ring. The vinyl group contributes some conformational flexibility, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is a biaryl compound built from two aromatic rings joined by a single carbon–carbon bond. One ring is a benzene ring with no substituents, giving a plain phenyl group. The other is a six-membered pyrimidine ring, a diazine containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, attached to the phenyl group at the carbon between those nitrogens. Both rings are fully aromatic and planar, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no flexible chain, so its conformational freedom is limited mainly to rotation about the central bond. The ring nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its six ring positions are fully substituted in an alternating pattern: three amino groups (-NH2) and three nitro groups (-NO2) occupy adjacent positions around the ring, so each nitro group sits between two amino groups. The arrangement gives the molecule threefold symmetry, with the ring and its substituents lying essentially flat and the rotation of the nitro groups being the main source of flexibility. The amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an azo compound built from two aromatic rings joined by a central nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) configuration. One ring is a benzene bearing a dimethylamino group para to the azo linkage, making it an electron-rich, strongly donor-substituted aryl unit. The other ring is a benzene carrying a nitro group ortho to the azo bond, which makes it electron-poor. The overall scaffold is extended, planar, and rigid, with the two rings and the azo bridge lying largely in one plane. The dimethylamino nitrogen and the azo nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a straight-chain, saturated aliphatic compound built from a single unbranched carbon backbone with no rings and no fused ring systems. At one terminus sits a carboxylic acid group, which provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. At the opposite terminus, a bromine atom is attached to the final methylene carbon, giving a terminal primary alkyl halide. Because the chain is linear and carries no branching or stereocenters, the molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the trivial, and it is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds along its length.

This molecule is a small monocyclic pyrimidine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and an isopropyl group attached to the carbon between the two nitrogens. The hydroxyl on the ring can tautomerize toward the pyrimidinone form, so it may act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two ring nitrogens serve as additional acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy different positions. Its rigid aromatic core contrasts with the freely rotating isopropyl group.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, with no fused rings. Four positions carry bromine atoms and two carry methyl groups, arranged so that the two methyls sit adjacent to each other on the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl and bromo groups contribute only modest rotational freedom around their single bonds to the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror plane or rotational axis that would map the ring onto itself beyond the local arrangement of the two methyls. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites beyond the weakly polarizable halogen atoms.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring is ortho-fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle, giving a tetralin-type (1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene) framework. A single methyl group sits on the aromatic ring adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the fused cyclohexane portion is flexible and can adopt half-chair conformations. The molecule contains no heteroatoms or functional groups such as hydroxyls, amines, or carbonyls, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, so it has no ring systems, ring fusion, or aromatic character. Its skeleton consists of a continuous run of saturated carbon atoms, with a single terminal aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bearing one hydrogen) at one end. Because there are no branches or substituents along the chain, the molecule has no stereocenters and possesses only the mirror-plane-like symmetry inherent to a linear chain, with the aldehyde end distinguishing its two termini. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds allowing it to adopt numerous conformations. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an ethyl ester of a phenylacetic acid derivative, with a phenyl ring attached to the alpha carbon that also bears a thiophosphate-type sulfur substituent. The core scaffold is a single benzene ring bonded directly to a tetrahedral stereogenic carbon, which carries an ethoxycarbonyl group and a sulfur atom linked to a phosphorus center. The phosphorus is bonded to a double-bonded sulfur and two methoxy groups, giving a P(=S)(OMe)2 unit. The ring is unsubstituted, so there is no substitution pattern on the aromatic system. The molecule is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds along the ester and thioether linkages, and it has no ring fusion. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, while the carbonyl oxygen, ester oxygens, and phosphorus-bound oxygens and sulfur provide acceptor sites.

The molecule is sulfur hexafluoride, a single central sulfur atom bonded to six fluorine atoms with no carbon framework, ring systems, or fused rings. The sulfur sits at the center of a regular octahedral arrangement, and the six S–F bonds are identical, giving the molecule very high symmetry. It has no conformational flexibility, since all atoms are fixed relative to one another by the octahedral geometry. The structure contains no functional groups beyond the sulfur–fluorine bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The fluorine atoms can act only as weak acceptors, and none of them carries a hydrogen.

The molecule is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from four fused six-membered rings in an angular arrangement, with no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond a single methyl substituent on one of the central rings. The methyl group sits at a ring-fusion-adjacent position, breaking the molecule's symmetry so that it lacks any mirror or rotational axis of symmetry. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds apart from the methyl group. Because the structure contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its only interactions are through the delocalized pi-electron system.

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic aromatic scaffold of three six-membered rings, with two rings fused in an angular arrangement on a central ring, giving a phenanthrene-type core. A single methyl group is attached to one of the outer aromatic rings, creating a simple substitution pattern on an otherwise unsubstituted hydrocarbon framework. The structure is fully aromatic and planar, so it is rigid, with no rotatable bonds. It lacks any heteroatoms or hydrogen-bond donors, and it has no hydrogen-bond acceptors, so it has no capacity for hydrogen bonding. Overall, the molecule has low symmetry because the methyl group breaks the symmetry of the fused ring system.

The molecule is built on an azobenzene scaffold, with two benzene rings joined by a central nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) configuration. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries a diethylamino group at the position para to the azo linkage, which gives the molecule a push-pull arrangement across its extended conjugated system. The two aromatic rings are planar and the azo bridge keeps them largely coplanar, making the core rigid, though the two N-ethyl groups add some conformational flexibility at their ends. The molecule has no symmetry axis overall because the two rings differ in substitution, although each ring individually has local symmetry. The tertiary amine nitrogen has no hydrogen on it and can act only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the azo nitrogens can likewise accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated chain of fifteen carbon atoms, with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems, and a single chlorine atom attached to one terminal carbon. Its scaffold is therefore a long, flexible alkyl backbone, and the only functional group is the primary alkyl chloride at one end. Because there is only one substituent and no branching, the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror relationship along its length. The extended chain is highly flexible, with freely rotating carbon-carbon bonds that allow many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks O-H or N-H groups, and its only potential acceptor is the chlorine atom, which is a weak one.

This molecule is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from five fused six-membered rings arranged in a compact, angular fashion, with no heteroatoms and no functional groups beyond a single methyl substituent. The methyl group sits on a carbon of the central fused system, breaking the symmetry of the framework so that the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. Because every ring is fused and planar, the skeleton is rigid, with the only conformational freedom being rotation of the methyl group. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

This molecule is an acyclic tertiary amine built on a central nitrogen atom bearing three identical-looking two-carbon-chain arms, each carrying a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the methylene linked to nitrogen. Each arm is a substituted butyl-type chain: a CH2 bonded to the nitrogen, then a CH bearing an OH, then an ethyl group terminating the chain. There are no ring systems or fused rings, so the scaffold is fully flexible and open. The three secondary alcohol groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the central nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The structure has approximate threefold pseudo-symmetry around the nitrogen, with the three arms being constitutionally identical, and the conformational freedom of the many single bonds makes the overall shape highly flexible.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a single long alkyl substituent: a sixteen-carbon chain in which the attachment point sits on an internal carbon, so the chain branches into a fifteen-carbon linear arm and a four-carbon butyl arm from that same tertiary carbon. The phenyl ring is unfused and carries no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the aliphatic chains are highly flexible and free to rotate about their many single bonds. The molecule has no stereocenters that are specified and no meaningful symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the two branches. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it is composed only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

The molecule consists of a long, unbranched saturated alkyl chain of roughly eighteen carbons joined to a single benzene ring, with one additional short ethyl branch on the carbon that bears the aromatic ring. Its scaffold is therefore a simple monosubstituted benzene attached to an aliphatic tail, with no fused ring systems and no heteroatoms. The sole aromatic feature is the planar six-membered ring, which carries no other substituents and so displays no particular substitution pattern beyond monosubstitution. There are no functional groups such as hydroxyls, carbonyls, or amines. Because the molecule contains no polar atoms, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The long chain is highly flexible and lacks any internal symmetry, while the benzene ring remains rigid and planar.

This molecule is an ester built from two cyclohexane-based epoxide units joined through a central ester linkage. Each half is a six-membered carbocycle carrying a fused three-membered oxirane ring, so each ring system is a bicyclic epoxycyclohexane (cyclohexene oxide type) with the epoxide bridging two adjacent ring carbons. The carbonyl carbon of the ester connects one bicyclic unit directly at a ring carbon and the other through a methylene-linked CH2 group, giving the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern. Both epoxide rings are strained and rigid, while the ester and methylene linker provide rotational flexibility between the two halves. The molecule has a single ester carbonyl oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two epoxide oxygens also serve as acceptors, with no hydrogen-bond donor groups present.

The molecule is a fully aromatic polycyclic hydrocarbon built from fused six-membered rings, with a methyl group attached to one of the rings. The fused system contains five rings arranged in a compact, nearly planar, rigid framework, with several ring-fusion carbons shared between adjacent rings. The single methyl substituent breaks the symmetry of the otherwise extended aromatic core, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry in its substitution pattern. Because the skeleton is rigid and flat, there is essentially no conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it offers no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites either; its only interactions are through its extended pi-electron surface.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with one position carrying a butoxy group (a four-carbon straight alkyl chain attached through an ether oxygen) and the opposite position bearing an ester group. The ester carbonyl connects the ring to a two-carbon ethylene linker that leads to a tertiary amine, where the nitrogen carries two ethyl substituents. The ring is aromatic and planar, while the butyl and diethylaminoethyl chains are flexible and can adopt many conformations. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a rough two-fold pseudo-symmetry along the ring axis. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogen and oxygen atoms carry no hydrogens. It offers acceptor sites at the ether oxygen, the ester oxygens, and the tertiary amine nitrogen.

This molecule is an ester built on a benzene ring. A single phenyl ring, a fully aromatic six-membered system with no fusion, serves as the scaffold, and a propyl group is attached through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon that is bonded directly to the ring. The substitution pattern is monosubstituted, so the ring carries no other groups and has high local symmetry. The ester group contains a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic ring and the planar ester linkage make the core fairly rigid, whereas the flexible n-propyl chain adds conformational freedom at one end.

The molecule is a five-membered saturated lactam-imide ring, a succinimide scaffold in which the nitrogen carries an N-ethyl substituent. The ring contains two carbonyl groups flanking the nitrogen, with a two-carbon saturated CH2–CH2 bridge between them, so no ring fusion or additional ring systems are present. The only functional group is the cyclic imide, and the ethyl group on nitrogen is the sole substituent, so the substitution pattern is simple and unbranched. The ring is essentially planar with a small amount of flexibility from the ethyl chain, and the molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the nitrogen and the ring. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen is fully substituted.

The molecule is an anilide built from a branched aliphatic acyl chain and a substituted benzene ring linked through an amide bond. The acyl portion is a 2-methylpentanoyl group, with a stereogenic carbon bearing a methyl branch alongside a flexible n-propyl tail. The amide nitrogen attaches to the aromatic ring, which carries a methyl group and a chlorine atom on adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted benzene pattern relative to the nitrogen. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the alkyl chain adds conformational flexibility. The secondary amide provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the N–H) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the chlorine offers a weak, halogen-type contact site.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid aromatic framework. Two primary amino groups are attached to the same ring, one at the 1-position and one at the 4-position, so the substitution pattern is para across that ring, with the ring fusion carbon in between. Each amino group carries two N–H bonds, so both act as hydrogen-bond donors, and each nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond. The arrangement has a mirror plane running through the two substituted carbons and the fusion bond, giving the molecule approximate symmetry about that axis. Because the core is fully aromatic and the amines are directly bonded to it, there is little conformational flexibility beyond slight rotation of the N–H groups.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a simple straight-chain scaffold, with no rings and no ring fusion. A seven-carbon linear alkyl chain is attached through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which in turn bears a two-carbon ethyl group, so the ester functional group sits between the two alkyl segments. The structure has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the free rotation of its chains, making it highly flexible. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks any N–H or O–H groups.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold, bearing two methyl substituents on carbons that are separated by one ring carbon, giving a 1,3-disubstitution pattern. The two stereocenters are specified, so the two methyl groups are fixed in defined spatial orientations relative to the ring. There are no heteroatoms or functional groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The ring adopts a chair-like conformation with each methyl group able to occupy either an equatorial or axial position, though the equatorial arrangement is generally preferred. The molecule has no rotational symmetry of high order and is largely rigid, with flexibility limited to ring conformational interconversion.

The molecule is an anilide built from a methacrylic acid unit linked through an amide bond to a benzene ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, bearing the amide nitrogen at one position and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the nitrogen. The acyl portion carries a terminal alkene conjugated to the carbonyl, with a methyl group on the internal alkene carbon, so the acrylamide-type unit is planar and rigid. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and the carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two chlorines are inequivalent, but it is relatively flat and conformationally restricted around the amide linkage.

This molecule is built on a tetrahydroisoquinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The aromatic ring carries two adjacent methoxy groups, which are ether oxygens serving as hydrogen-bond acceptors. At the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen sits a two-carbon linker that connects to a second benzene ring bearing a single chlorine atom at the position opposite the linker. The tertiary amine nitrogen, which carries an N-methyl group, is a hydrogen-bond acceptor but has no donor hydrogen. The partially saturated core gives the scaffold moderate conformational flexibility, while the two aromatic rings add rigidity to their respective regions.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined directly by a single carbon-carbon bond with no fused or bridging ring. Each ring carries one methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group) attached at the position opposite the biaryl bond, giving a para-disubstituted pattern on both rings. The structure is symmetric, with the two methoxy-bearing rings mirror-related through the central bond, and it is largely planar and rigid, with restricted rotation about the biaryl axis. Each oxygen atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused together through a shared edge, forming a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. Four methyl groups are attached as the only substituents, distributed across both rings, so the core carries no heteroatoms or polar functional groups. The substitution pattern is asymmetric: one ring bears two methyl groups and the other bears two, placed at positions that break any mirror or rotational symmetry of the parent naphthalene. The rigid fused framework allows essentially no conformational flexibility, with only the methyl C–H bonds free to rotate. Because the molecule contains no N–H or O–H groups and no lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is an acetamide attached to a biphenyl scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond. The acetyl amide group (CH3C(=O)NH–) sits on the ortho position of one ring, relative to the bond linking it to the second ring, so the substitution pattern is 1,2 on the first ring and monosubstituted on the second. The two rings are not fused; they are connected through a single rotatable bond, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility, though the ortho substituent restricts free rotation about the biaryl axis. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two rings differ in substitution.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused six-membered aromatic rings sharing a common edge. Each ring carries a single chlorine atom attached directly to an aromatic carbon, so the molecule is a dichloro-substituted naphthalene. The chlorines sit on different rings at positions that are not mirror-related, which gives the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fully aromatic, planar fused system is rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no hydrogen-bond donors. Its only polar features are the carbon-chlorine bonds, so it can act at most as a weak acceptor, and it has no hydrogen-bond donating capability.

The molecule is an ester built from a short linear chain, with no rings present. Its backbone consists of an allyl group (a three-carbon unit bearing a terminal carbon-carbon double bond) joined through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which in turn bears a linear three-carbon propyl chain. The ester functional group, with its carbonyl oxygen and single-bonded ether-type oxygen, serves as the only polar center, and the molecule can accept hydrogen bonds at those two oxygens but has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The structure is entirely acyclic and largely flexible, with rotation possible about each single bond, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the two ends of the molecule differ in their substituents.

This molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond with no fused ring system. Each phenyl ring carries one chlorine atom attached at the para position, opposite the biaryl linkage, so the substitution pattern is symmetrical and the molecule as a whole has a centre of inversion. The only functional groups present are the aryl chlorides, and the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, since chlorine is a very weak acceptor. The two rings can rotate about the central bond, giving the scaffold some conformational freedom, though the aromatic rings remain planar and rigid individually.

This molecule is a linear aliphatic diester with no rings and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing ring systems. Its backbone is a straight chain of six methylene units flanked on each end by a carbonyl carbon, so the structure is a symmetrical dicarboxylate in which both terminal groups are identical ethyl esters. The two ester groups each contain a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no N-H or O-H groups. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, so it can adopt many conformations, and its mirror-symmetric substitution pattern gives it a C2-like symmetry about the midpoint of the chain.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving a trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. One ring position carries a methylcarbamate group, an O-aryl ester of N-methylcarbamic acid, which contains a carbonyl flanked by an NH and an ether-type oxygen. Two further ring positions carry methyl groups, and the third carries a methylthio (thioether) group, with the methyl groups and thioether arranged in a pattern that breaks the ring's symmetry. The core is largely rigid and planar, while the carbamate and thioether side chains add limited rotational flexibility. The carbamate N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl and ring-linked oxygen can act as acceptors, while the thioether sulfur offers weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A carbamate group, with a methylamino nitrogen attached to a carbonyl that is bonded through an oxygen to the ring, is attached at one position. A dimethylamino group sits at the para position relative to the carbamate oxygen, and a methyl group occupies the ring position adjacent to the dimethylamino group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic core. The carbamate contributes an N-H that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and carbonyl and ether oxygens that can act as acceptors, while the tertiary dimethylamine nitrogen is a further acceptor site. The molecule has no stereocenters and only modest overall symmetry, since the three substituents are distinct. Its rotatable bonds around the carbamate and the aryl-nitrogen linkages make it moderately flexible, while the planar aromatic ring stays rigid.

The molecule is built around a carbamate linkage connecting a branched propargylic alcohol unit to a meta-substituted aniline ring. On one side sits a terminal alkyne (C#C) attached to a chiral secondary carbon bearing a methyl group, which then bonds through an oxygen to the carbonyl of the carbamate. The carbamate nitrogen is attached to a benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the nitrogen, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the aliphatic chain and the carbamate C–O and C–N bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility. The N–H group of the carbamate serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the terminal alkyne C–H can weakly donate.

The molecule is built on a phenylalanine-like scaffold: a single benzene ring bearing a para-substituted aromatic core, with the ring carrying an amino-bearing side chain that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The side chain contains one stereogenic carbon bearing a primary amine, linked through a methylene to the carboxylic acid group. The para position of the benzene ring carries a tertiary nitrogen substituted with two 2-chloroethyl arms, which are flexible and terminate in carbon-chlorine bonds. The amine and carboxylic acid groups together provide hydrogen-bond donor capacity and several hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, while the tertiary nitrogen contributes an additional acceptor. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, whereas the side chains are highly flexible, giving the overall molecule an elongated, asymmetric shape without any internal symmetry.

This molecule is an aryl ether ester built on a benzene ring that carries three chlorine atoms. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion. An oxyacetate side chain is attached to one ring carbon through an ether oxygen, and the terminal carbonyl is esterified with an ethyl group. The three chlorines sit at the 2, 4, and 5 positions relative to the ether oxygen, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is rigid and planar, while the ester side chain is flexible through its rotatable C–O and C–C bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its ester carbonyl, ester oxygen, and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six substituents in a contiguous pattern: a dipropylamino group, two nitro groups, and a methyl group. The tertiary nitrogen carries two n-propyl chains and is attached directly to the aromatic ring, so it is a tertiary aryl amine. Two nitro groups sit on the ring, one ortho to the amine and one meta to it, with the methyl group positioned para to the amine across the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the two propyl chains provide conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since the amine nitrogen is fully substituted, but the oxygens of the nitro groups and the amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic 1,3,5-triazine ring, with three substituents placed symmetrically around it. One position carries a chlorine atom, another carries an ethylamino group (an NH bonded to an ethyl chain), and the third carries a diethylamino group (a nitrogen bearing two ethyl chains). The substitution pattern places the chlorine and the two amino groups at alternating ring positions, so the scaffold is fully substituted and carries no ring hydrogens. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the secondary NH is the only hydrogen-bond donor. The ethyl side chains give the molecule some conformational flexibility, but the aromatic core is rigid and planar.

The molecule is an anthraquinone-type tricyclic scaffold: two outer benzene rings fused to a central six-membered ring that carries two carbonyl groups at opposite positions. One outer ring bears two adjacent primary amino groups (a 1,2-diamine pattern) on the carbons flanking one of the fusion positions, so the substitution is concentrated on a single ring and the other ring is unsubstituted. The fused, planar aromatic framework is rigid, and the molecule has no rotatable bonds beyond the amino groups. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The overall skeleton lacks a mirror-symmetric substitution pattern because the amines are on only one side.

This molecule is a benzothiazole-based scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The thiazole portion carries an exocyclic imine (=NH) at the carbon between the heteroatoms, and the ring nitrogen bears a hydrogen, giving the core an amidine-like arrangement. A methoxy group (–OCH3) is attached to the benzene ring, placed meta to the ring-fusion carbon bonded to sulfur, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused bicyclic system is planar and rigid, with only the methoxy methyl group contributing conformational flexibility. The exocyclic NH and the ring NH can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the imine nitrogen, the ring nitrogen, and the ether oxygen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a linear aliphatic diester built from a single unbranched chain of eight carbons, with a methyl ester group at each terminus. Its scaffold is entirely saturated and acyclic, so there are no rings, ring fusions, or aromatic systems. The two functional groups are identical carboxylate esters, each consisting of a carbonyl oxygen double-bonded to the carbon and a methoxy oxygen attached to the terminal methyl, and they sit at symmetric positions on the chain. The molecule is therefore symmetric about its center, and the long methylene segment is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations. Each ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a straight-chain fatty acid methyl ester with no rings, aromatic systems, or branching. The skeleton is a long, unbranched saturated hydrocarbon chain of seventeen carbons, with the terminal carbon bearing a carboxylate group that is capped by a methyl group on the ester oxygen. The only functional group is the ester, which contains one carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ester oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen sits on carbon. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the simple linear arrangement, and its many rotatable single bonds give it a highly flexible, extended conformation.

The molecule is an aromatic ester built on a benzene ring. A linear octanoyl chain (eight carbons, the last being the carbonyl) is attached through an ester oxygen to the ring carbon at position 1. The ring carries bromine atoms at both positions ortho to that ester oxygen (2 and 6), and a nitrile group at the position para to it (4). This gives the ring a symmetric 2,6-dibromo-4-cyano substitution pattern. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The long saturated alkyl chain is flexible, whereas the substituted benzene ring is planar and rigid.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no double bonds and no heteroatoms. Three methyl substituents are attached to adjacent and nearby ring carbons, specifically on two neighboring carbons (positions 1 and 2) and one carbon two positions away (position 6 relative to the first), so the substitution pattern is clustered on one side of the ring. The molecule has no functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The ring is fully sp3-hybridized and can adopt chair-like conformations, but the three methyl groups create some steric crowding and reduce conformational freedom compared with unsubstituted cyclohexane. Overall the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the identity operation.

This molecule is built around a piperazine ring, a six-membered saturated ring with nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 4, which serves as the central scaffold. One nitrogen of the piperazine is attached through a three-carbon chain to a ketone, which in turn bears a para-fluorophenyl ring, giving a 4-fluorophenyl ketone. The other piperazine nitrogen carries a pyridin-2-yl group, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen. The molecule is flexible along its aliphatic propyl linker and piperazine ring, while the two aromatic rings are rigid and planar. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites include the carbonyl oxygen, the fluorine, and the pyridine nitrogen, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge, with a single n-butyl chain attached at one of the alpha positions adjacent to the ring junction. The fused bicyclic core is fully aromatic and planar, giving it a rigid framework, while the four-carbon alkyl tail adds conformational flexibility. There are no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so the molecule offers no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its substitution pattern is asymmetric because the butyl group sits at only one position on the fused system, so the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the aromatic rings. Overall, it is a hydrocarbon with a rigid aromatic core and a flexible saturated side chain.

The molecule is a small saturated five-membered heterocycle containing one ring carbon bearing a dimethylamino group, with the ring formed by a carbon-sulfur-sulfur-carbon linkage: specifically a 1,2-dithiolane ring, where two adjacent sulfur atoms form a disulfide bridge. The N,N-dimethylamino substituent is attached directly to the ring carbon that sits between a methylene and a disulfide-linked sulfur, so the substitution pattern is a single tertiary amine on one ring position with no other substituents. The ring is non-planar and relatively compact, giving limited conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the amine-bearing carbon breaks the ring symmetry. The tertiary nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but cannot donate a hydrogen bond, and the sulfur atoms offer only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a fully halogenated two-carbon acyclic chain, with no rings and no double bonds, built on a simple ethane skeleton. One carbon carries three fluorine atoms, and the adjacent carbon carries two chlorine atoms and a fluorine atom plus a chlorine on its other side; in total the two carbons carry a mix of fluorine and chlorine substituents with no hydrogens attached. Because the skeleton is saturated and free of stereocenters in the sense of a fixed ring, rotation about the central carbon-carbon bond gives it considerable conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the halogen atoms, which are weak. Overall, its substitution pattern is asymmetric, so it does not possess a high degree of molecular symmetry.

The molecule is a saturated five-membered heterocycle: a tetrahydrothiophene (thiolane) ring containing one sulfur atom and no double bonds. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring carbons on either side of the sulfur, one on each carbon adjacent to it, so the two substituents sit at the 2 and 5 positions. Because the ring is fully saturated and non-aromatic, it adopts a puckered envelope-like conformation and is flexible rather than rigid. The molecule has no stereocenter-independent mirror plane beyond the ring itself, and the two methyl-bearing carbons are stereogenic, so the arrangement can exist in several stereoisomeric forms. The sulfur is a thioether with two lone pairs, so it can accept a hydrogen bond, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule has a single carbon atom at its center, bonded to one oxygen atom through a double bond and to one fluorine atom through a single bond. It is a small, acyclic molecule with no rings, so there is no ring fusion or ring system to describe. The carbon bears a carbonyl group, which makes it an aldehyde-type functional group, while the fluorine sits directly on the carbonyl carbon as a halogen substituent. Because the structure is so compact and lacks any branching, it is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no internal flexibility. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry since the oxygen and fluorine are different atoms. The oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, carrying a phenolic hydroxyl group flanked by a bulky tert-butyl group on one ortho position, with the two nitro groups placed meta to each other on the opposite side of the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, giving a rigid scaffold with no ring fusion. The substitution pattern is asymmetric: the tert-butyl group and hydroxyl sit adjacent, while the nitro groups occupy the remaining positions in a 3,5-relationship relative to the hydroxyl, so the overall molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis through the ring. The tert-butyl group contributes a compact, three-methyl branched hydrocarbon bulk that is rotationally flexible but sterically hindering. The phenolic OH is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms.

This molecule is built on a chroman (benzopyran) scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated six-membered oxygen-containing heterocycle. The aromatic ring carries a free phenolic hydroxyl group together with two adjacent methyl substituents, giving a crowded, tri-substituted benzenoid core. The pyran ring bears a quaternary carbon at the ether position, which is attached to a long, branched, saturated hydrocarbon chain with several methyl branch points, making that portion of the molecule highly flexible. The only hydrogen-bond donor is the phenolic OH, while the ring oxygen and the phenol oxygen act as acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic alkaloid-type scaffold: a rigid, largely planar tetracyclic aromatic core in which two benzene-like rings are joined to a phenanthrene-type unit, further fused to a saturated bridged nitrogen-containing ring system. Four methoxy groups (C–O–CH3 ethers) decorate the aromatic rings, and they are the only oxygen-based functional groups present. The tertiary amine sits within the saturated fused ring and serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The methoxy substitution is asymmetric, so the overall structure lacks a clear mirror or rotational symmetry, and the saturated portion gives it some conformational constraint beyond the planar aromatic region.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two ester groups on adjacent (ortho) carbons, making it a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic core. Each ester carbonyl is attached directly to the ring and connects through an oxygen to a long saturated alkyl chain. One chain is a straight eight-carbon n-octyl group, while the other is a branched alkyl chain of similar length carrying a methyl branch near its terminus. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, whereas the two long alkyl tails are highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The two ester groups are not symmetric with each other because one tail is linear and the other branched, so the overall molecule lacks any internal symmetry. Each ester provides two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a salicylanilide-type structure: a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group, with the amide nitrogen attached to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. The first ring carries a hydroxyl group ortho to the amide carbonyl and a chlorine atom para to the hydroxyl, giving a 2-hydroxy-5-chloro substitution pattern. The intramolecular hydrogen bond between the phenolic OH and the carbonyl oxygen makes the amide region fairly planar and conformationally restricted. The molecule has two aromatic rings joined by a flexible-but-conjugated amide linker and has no internal symmetry. It offers one amide N-H and one phenolic O-H as hydrogen-bond donors, with the carbonyl oxygen and phenolic oxygen serving as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two adjacent carbons on that ring carry primary amino groups, and a third substituent, an ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain), sits meta to one of them and para to the other amine. The two neighboring amines form an ortho-diamine motif, giving the ring a substitution pattern that is asymmetric, since the ethoxy group breaks any mirror symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the ethoxy tail adds some conformational flexibility. Each amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its N–H bonds and accept them through its lone pair, and the ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type ketone built on a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) framework. Two methyl groups sit on the bridgehead and on a quaternary carbon adjacent to the ketone, giving a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern next to the carbonyl. The cyclohexane-like bridge carries a single carbonyl (C=O) that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, with no hydrogen-bond donors present. The rigid, cage-like skeleton is conformationally locked, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane because of the asymmetric placement of the methyl and carbonyl groups.

The molecule is a small six-membered carbocyclic ring containing one carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with a ketone, making it a cyclohexenone scaffold. The ring is monocyclic with no fused or bridged ring systems. A methyl group is attached to one of the alkene carbons, which sits adjacent to the carbonyl carbon, giving a substitution pattern on the enone unit. The ketone oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The ring is partially flexible due to its saturated methylene positions, but the conjugated enone portion is relatively planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the methyl group.

This molecule is a salicylanilide, built from a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons, with the amide nitrogen attached to a second benzene ring. The salicylic-acid-derived ring carries two chlorine substituents at positions meta and para to the carbonyl-bearing carbon, while the anilide ring carries chlorines at its 3 and 4 positions, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. Both aromatic rings are planar and conjugated through the central amide linkage, which imparts considerable rigidity to the overall framework. The phenolic hydroxyl is positioned ortho to the amide carbonyl, allowing an intramolecular hydrogen bond, and the N–H of the amide serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The carbonyl oxygen, the phenolic oxygen, and the chlorine atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors to varying degrees.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene core, two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with no heteroatoms in the ring system. A linear n-butyl chain is attached to one of the carbon atoms on the same ring as the fusion, placing the substituent at a beta-type position of the bicyclic framework. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, while the saturated butyl tail adds conformational flexibility. The molecule has no functional groups bearing lone pairs or acidic hydrogens, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. Its overall symmetry is reduced by the asymmetric placement of the single alkyl substituent.

The molecule is built on a four-membered cyclobutane ring, a saturated carbocycle with no fused or bridged ring systems. Two carboxylic acid groups, each a carbonyl bearing a hydroxyl, are attached to adjacent carbons of the ring, so the substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted. Because the two groups sit on neighboring positions, the molecule can adopt cis or trans arrangements across the ring, and the small ring imposes considerable rigidity while the carboxyl groups retain some rotational freedom. Each carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor capability (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites in total. The overall structure has limited symmetry, with the 1,2-substitution pattern producing a molecule with no mirror plane in its general form.

The molecule is built on a four-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclobutane core, with an exocyclic methylene group attached to one carbon of the ring. Its scaffold therefore contains no fused or bridged ring systems and no heteroatoms. The only functional group is the carbon-carbon double bond of the methylene unit, which is conjugated with nothing else and sits outside the ring. Because the ring carbons are otherwise unsubstituted, the molecule has a simple pattern with no positional isomers to distinguish. The structure is rigid at the ring but has a small degree of puckering flexibility, and it has a plane of symmetry through the sp2 carbon and the opposite ring carbon. It has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an open-chain, non-aromatic compound built on a five-carbon backbone that carries an ethyl ester at one terminus and a free carboxylic acid at the other. The alpha carbon bears a primary amino group, placing the amine adjacent to the acid, and the chain is entirely saturated and unbranched apart from these substituents. There are no rings or fused systems, so the scaffold is flexible, with several freely rotating single bonds along the carbon chain. The functional groups present are an ester, a carboxylic acid, and a primary amine. The amine and the acid's hydroxyl can each donate hydrogen bonds, while the carbonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen act as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry and no stereochemical center is specified in the given SMILES.

This molecule is a simple acyclic organoborane: a single boron atom sits at the center and is bonded to three identical n-propyl chains, so the structure is a tripropylborane skeleton with no rings or fused systems. Each propyl group is a straight three-carbon alkyl chain, and the boron carries no other substituents, making the molecule highly symmetric with approximately threefold symmetry about the boron center. The structure is flexible because the propyl chains can rotate freely around their single bonds. Functionally it contains only carbon-carbon and carbon-boron single bonds, with no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms capable of accepting hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is an acyclic organophosphorus compound built around a short flexible chain. It contains a secondary amide, with an N-methyl group attached to a carbonyl carbon, which is linked through a methylene bridge to a sulfur atom. That sulfur is bonded to a phosphorus center bearing a double-bonded oxygen and two methoxy groups, giving a phosphonate-type ester arrangement. There are no rings or fused ring systems, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two methoxy groups are the only near-equivalent parts. Its many single bonds confer considerable rotational flexibility. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl and phosphoryl oxygens and the ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a 1,4-naphthoquinone core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a fully conjugated benzene ring is fused to a six-membered ring bearing two carbonyl groups at the 1 and 4 positions. The quinone ring carries a chlorine atom on one alkene carbon and an anilino group (an NH bonded to a phenyl ring) on the other, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The two rings are planar and rigid, with the phenyl ring attached through a single N–C bond that allows some rotation. The amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, fully unsaturated carbon chain built from three carbon-carbon triple bonds alternating with single bonds, with a nitrile group (carbon-nitrogen triple bond) capping each end. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no branching or substitution, so its skeleton is a straight rod-like scaffold. Each terminal nitrile nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors because the molecule has no N-H or O-H bonds. The molecule is highly rigid, with its linear geometry fixed by the sp-hybridized carbons, and it possesses a high degree of symmetry, being centrosymmetric about its central carbon-carbon bond.

The molecule is a single saturated lactam: a twelve-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom, with a carbonyl carbon directly bonded to that nitrogen, making it a cyclic amide. Apart from the amide carbonyl and the adjacent N–H, every atom in the ring is a methylene (CH2) group, so there are no aromatic rings, no fused ring systems, and no substituents hanging off the ring. The ring is large and unstrained, and its amide bond is planar, which introduces some local rigidity, while the many CH2 units allow considerable conformational flexibility elsewhere in the ring. The molecule has no symmetry beyond a rough pseudo-mirror relationship across the amide, since the nitrogen and carbonyl carbon are unique positions. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a phenanthrene scaffold, three benzene rings fused in an angular arrangement that gives it a bent, non-linear shape. An amino group (–NH2) is attached to one of the central-ring carbons, placing it on the middle ring where it sits adjacent to the fused junction. The aromatic framework is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core and very limited conformational flexibility. The amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the substituent position onto itself, so its substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is built around a phosphoramidate-type core: a central phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded oxygen, two ethoxy groups (each an ethyl chain attached through oxygen), and a nitrogen that links to a carbon of a five-membered ring. That ring is a 1,3-dithiolane, containing two sulfur atoms and two methylene carbons, with the exocyclic C=N double bond placing the nitrogen at the ring's 2-position. The ring is saturated and non-aromatic, with no ring fusion, and the ethyl groups add some conformational flexibility around the P–O bonds.
