The structure lacks any symmetry element beyond the mirror-like arrangement of the two ethoxy arms. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N–H or O–H groups are present, while the phosphoryl oxygen, the ether oxygens, and the imine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a rigid, planar bicyclic aromatic system. A single ethyl group (a two-carbon saturated chain) is attached to one of the carbons on the fused-ring framework, placing it at a substitution position on one ring rather than at the ring-fusion atoms. The molecule contains no heteroatoms and no polar functional groups such as hydroxyls, amines, or carbonyls. Consequently, it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability. Its overall shape is largely rigid and flat, with only the ethyl substituent providing some conformational flexibility, and the substitution pattern breaks the symmetry of the parent naphthalene framework.

The molecule is a coumarin-type scaffold, consisting of a benzene ring fused to a six-membered α-pyrone (2H-chromen-2-one) lactone ring that contains an endocyclic ester oxygen and a carbonyl group. The fused bicyclic core is planar and largely rigid, with aromatic character across both rings. A hydroxyl group sits on the pyrone ring at the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl, giving an enol-type substituent. This OH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the lactone ring oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygen can each serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the approximate planar framework, since the substituent is located on only one side of the bicyclic system.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene rings sharing one edge in a fused bicyclic, fully aromatic arrangement. Two primary amino groups (–NH2) are attached to the same ring, on adjacent carbons, with one amine sitting at a peri-adjacent position relative to the fusion carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2-diamino on one ring, leaving the other ring unsubstituted. The fused framework is planar and rigid, while the amino groups can rotate about their C–N bonds. Each NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the aromatic system contributes little to hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a single saturated lactam: a nine-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom and a carbonyl carbon directly bonded to that nitrogen, forming an amide within the ring. The ring is monocyclic with no fused or bridged rings, and it has no substituents beyond the ring itself, so the structure is unsubstituted and carries no aromatic character. Apart from the amide carbonyl and the amide N-H, the remaining seven carbons form a flexible, all-saturated aliphatic chain that can adopt multiple conformations and has no meaningful internal symmetry. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a fatty acid methyl ester with a long, unbranched saturated hydrocarbon chain. It has no rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents or stereocenters, so its skeleton is a single linear carbon chain. The only functional group is a methyl ester, where a carbonyl carbon bridges the alkyl chain and an oxygen-linked methyl group. The chain is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds that allow it to adopt many conformations. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond its extended linear shape. The ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a short acyclic carbon chain with no ring systems, built from a central three-carbon unit that carries two nitrile groups at one end and one nitrile group on a terminal methylene. A primary amine sits on the central sp2 carbon, which is double-bonded to the adjacent carbon, creating an enamine-like alkene conjugated with the nitrile groups. The skeleton is essentially planar around the C=C unit, with the nitrile groups extending linearly, giving it limited conformational flexibility, though the terminal CH2 bond can rotate. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the two N–H bonds of the amine, while the three nitrile nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three nitrile groups are attached at different positions on the carbon framework.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazole ring bearing a methyl group on one carbon, an N-phenyl group on the adjacent nitrogen, and an arylamino substituent on the carbon next to that nitrogen. That amino group links through a sulfonamide (–NH–SO2–) to a para-aminophenyl ring, so the structure is a sulfonamide joining two aromatic systems. The molecule contains three separate benzene-type rings and one aromatic heterocycle, but no ring fusion, so each ring is attached through single bonds and the scaffold is largely planar within each ring with rotatable linkages between them. It has two hydrogen-bond donors, the sulfonamide N–H and the primary aromatic amine, and several acceptors at the sulfonyl oxygens and the pyrazole nitrogen. It lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core: a seven-membered 1,4-benzodiazepine-type ring joined to a benzene ring, with the two rings sharing an edge. The diazepine ring contains an N-methyl amide (lactam) nitrogen adjacent to a carbonyl, and a second, imine-type nitrogen that is double-bonded to a carbon in the ring. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon between the carbonyl and the imine. One pendant phenyl ring, carrying a chlorine atom at its ortho position, is attached to the imine carbon, while the fused benzo ring carries a second chlorine atom. The overall framework is largely rigid, with the fused system fixed in place and only the pendant aryl ring able to rotate. The molecule has no internal symmetry. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the imine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon built from four fused six-membered rings arranged in an angular, phenanthrene-like pattern with an extra ring fused onto a naphthalene core. Every ring is aromatic, and the fused framework is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the skeleton. A single methyl group is attached to one of the peripheral carbons at a position adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon, creating a bay-like environment that breaks any mirror symmetry. The molecule contains no heteroatoms, no hydrogen-bond donors, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since its only substituent is a simple alkyl group.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring, with no double bonds, aromatic character, or heteroatoms within the ring itself. Two chlorine atoms are attached to adjacent carbons of the ring, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern in which both substituents sit on neighboring positions. The ring is fully sp3-hybridized and can adopt chair-like conformations, so the molecule is conformationally flexible, though the vicinal substituents introduce a preference for relative orientation between them. The structure has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak acceptors, so its hydrogen-bonding capacity is minimal. Overall, the molecule lacks any higher symmetry beyond a local mirror relationship across the axis bisecting the two substituted carbons.

The molecule is a linear aliphatic diester built from a five-carbon dicarboxylic acid backbone with an ethyl ester group capping each terminus. The central chain contains three methylene units between the two carbonyl carbons, giving a straight, unbranched skeleton with no rings and no aromatic or fused ring systems. Each ester carbonyl carries a double-bonded oxygen acceptor and a single-bonded ether oxygen linked to an ethyl group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all heteroatoms are oxygen atoms bearing no hydrogens, but the four oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its high flexibility arises from numerous rotatable single bonds along the chain, and it possesses approximately two-fold symmetry about the midpoint of the central methylene.

The molecule is cyclopropyl methyl ketone, built on a three-membered cyclopropane ring bearing a single acetyl substituent. The core scaffold is a saturated carbocycle with no fused or bridged rings, so the structure is compact and small. A carbonyl group (C=O) sits between a methyl group and the ring carbon, making it a ketone whose carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The cyclopropane ring is strained and rigid, which constrains the orientation of the attached acetyl group. Apart from a local mirror plane through the ketone, the molecule is largely unsymmetrical, and its overall shape is fairly flexible at the single bond linking the ring to the carbonyl.

The molecule is a small, fully saturated acyclic haloalkane with a three-carbon chain, carrying a fluorine atom on one terminal carbon and a chlorine atom on the other. Its scaffold is a simple linear propane backbone with no ring systems or ring fusion. The two halogen substituents sit at opposite ends of the chain, giving a 1,3-disubstituted pattern, and there is no functional group beyond these carbon-halogen bonds. The molecule is flexible, since rotation about its single bonds allows several conformations, and its only mirror-symmetry is the approximate one arising from the two terminal halogens. It lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, and the halogens can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a phthalimide core, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imide ring bearing two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen atom. That nitrogen carries a CH2 linker leading to a dithiophosphate ester unit, where a central phosphorus is double-bonded to sulfur and bonded to two methoxy groups and a sulfur atom that connects to the methylene linker. The fused bicyclic aromatic-imide system is planar and rigid, while the CH2-S-P linkage provides rotational flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens and the phosphorus-bound sulfur and oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local symmetry of the methoxy groups.

The molecule is a sulfonamide built from a 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl group linked through an NH to a 2-amino-oxazole-type heteroaryl ring. The five-membered heterocycle contains one oxygen and one nitrogen and carries two adjacent methyl substituents on its carbon atoms. The benzene ring is para-disubstituted, with a primary amine opposite the sulfonyl group, giving a linear, elongated shape. Two rings joined through a sulfonamide linker make the structure fairly rigid, with some rotational freedom around the S–N bond. The primary aromatic amine and the sulfonamide NH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogen and oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a saturated, fully fluorinated cyclic scaffold built on a single five-membered carbon ring, with no ring fusion and no additional substituents beyond the halogens. Its ring contains one carbon-carbon double bond, which is flanked by two chlorine atoms, making that alkene a chloro-substituted site. The remaining ring carbons each carry two fluorine atoms, giving a geminal difluoro pattern at each position. The substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis passing through the midpoint of the double bond and the opposite carbon, and the structure is rigid because of the ring and the alkene. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no conventional hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the halogens are poor acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing one oxygen atom and one nitrogen atom, fused to nothing else and carrying no additional rings. The ring is a cyclic carbamate: an oxygen-bonded ester-like carbonyl sits beside an NH group, and an adjacent ketone-type carbonyl is attached next to the nitrogen, forming a cyclic imide-like arrangement. A single quaternary carbon at one ring position bears two ethyl substituents, which makes that position sterically crowded and gives the scaffold a non-planar, somewhat puckered shape. The molecule has no stereocenters and no rotational symmetry beyond what the two identical ethyl groups provide. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring, with no fused rings and no heteroatoms. An isopropyl group, a carbon bearing two methyl groups, is attached to one ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is monosubstitution. The overall framework is fully aliphatic with no double bonds or aromatic character, and no functional groups are present. Because the ring can adopt chair conformations and the isopropyl branch rotates freely, the structure is moderately flexible, with no element of symmetry beyond the local mirror plane through the substituent. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a linear, acyclic diester built on a flexible thiodipropionate backbone. Its central unit is a three-atom thioether bridge (a sulfur atom) flanked by two two-carbon chains, each terminating in an ester carbonyl. Each ester oxygen is bonded to a long, unbranched octadecyl chain, so the molecule is symmetric about the central sulfur. There are no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no aromatic groups. The two carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The long alkyl tails confer high conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a six-membered unsaturated lactone, a 2-pyranone ring, with the carbonyl carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, one on a carbon alongside the ring oxygen-bearing sp2 carbon and one at the other position, giving a 4,6-dimethyl substitution pattern on the pyranone core. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, so the scaffold is rigid with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl groups. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two methyl substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the lactone carbonyl oxygen and the ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-type tetracyclic scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, with the A-ring fully aromatic. The aromatic ring carries a single phenolic hydroxyl group, which acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The five-membered D-ring bears a secondary alcohol, providing a second donor and acceptor site. A quaternary carbon at the ring junction carries an angular methyl group, and the central ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond that breaks the otherwise saturated framework. The fused, largely rigid ring system limits conformational flexibility, while the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two hydroxyl groups sit on different rings.

This molecule is a benzoate ester built on a benzene ring that carries no other substituents, so the aromatic core is a simple, planar phenyl group. The ester carbonyl is attached directly to that ring and links through an oxygen to a single sp3 carbon. That carbon bears two nitro groups, making it a geminal dinitro center, and each nitro group contributes strongly electron-withdrawing character. The phenyl ring is monosubstituted and therefore has no symmetry-breaking pattern beyond its own ring symmetry. The ester and C–N bonds allow rotation, so the molecule is moderately flexible apart from the rigid aromatic ring. The carbonyl oxygen and nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a linear chain of four benzene rings joined by single bonds, making it a quaterphenyl scaffold with no fused rings. Each inner ring is attached at its ortho positions, so the chain bends into a non-linear shape rather than running straight. The two terminal rings are unsubstituted phenyl groups, and there are no functional groups or heteroatoms present. The molecule is largely hydrocarbon in character, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its aromatic biaryl linkages give it moderate rigidity, though rotation about the single bonds between rings remains possible.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Three of its six ring carbons bear iodine atoms and the other three carry hydrogen, so the ring has no other functional groups; the iodines occupy adjacent positions in one cluster, with a single iodine separated from them by one unsubstituted carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore unsymmetrical, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local arrangement. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the carbon-iodine bonds project outward from it with little conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no heteroatom acceptors, since the only heteroatoms are the halogen substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) attached directly to the ring, and the other is a sulfonic acid group (–SO3H), which is bonded to the ring through a sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens and one hydroxyl. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two acidic groups rotate fairly freely about their single bonds. Both acid groups provide hydrogen-bond donor capability through their hydroxyl oxygens and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through their carbonyl and sulfonyl oxygens. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are chemically distinct.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a two-carbon backbone. A carboxyl group, bearing a hydroxyl and a carbonyl oxygen, sits at one end, and the adjacent alpha carbon carries two bromine atoms on the same carbon, making it a geminal dihalide. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and fairly flexible about its single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two bromines are equivalent but the carboxyl end is distinct. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its oxygen atoms.

This molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated alkyl chain built from eighteen carbon atoms in a straight line, with no rings, double bonds, or other heteroatoms along the backbone. A single iodine atom sits on the terminal carbon, making it a primary alkyl iodide and the only functional group present. The scaffold is highly flexible, since rotation about each of the many carbon-carbon single bonds lets the chain adopt many conformations, and it lacks any symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the methylene units. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, because it carries no N-H or O-H groups. Its only potential acceptor site is the iodine atom, which is a weak, poorly polarized one.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic nitrile: a linear saturated hydrocarbon chain of twelve carbons terminated by a cyano group (C≡N) at one end. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents branching off the chain, so the scaffold is simply an unbranched alkyl backbone. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the trivial, since the two ends are chemically distinct, with the nitrile carbon-nitrogen triple bond being the only point of unsaturation. Its structure is highly flexible, as the single bonds along the alkyl chain can rotate freely. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an ester built around a short, unbranched carbon chain with no ring systems. On one side of the ester oxygen sits an acetyl group, a two-carbon unit ending in a carbonyl, and on the other side is a six-carbon alkyl group that carries a methyl branch at the carbon bonded directly to the oxygen. There are no aromatic rings or ring fusions, and the single stereocenter at that branch point is the only source of asymmetry. The chain is flexible, with several freely rotating single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small acyclic imide built around a single nitrogen atom bonded to two acetyl groups. Its skeleton is a linear chain of three atoms, carbon-carbon-nitrogen with a carbonyl on each side, and it contains no ring systems or ring fusion. The two carbonyl groups flank a central secondary amide-type nitrogen that carries one hydrogen, giving the characteristic diacyl-amine (imide) functionality. The structure is essentially symmetric, with the two acetyl arms mirror-related about the central nitrogen. Because the molecule is small and has few rotatable bonds, it is fairly compact and conformationally limited. The N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a very small acyclic structure built from a single carbon atom, the central carbon of a hydroxy-substituted formamidine-type unit. Two nitrogen atoms are attached to this carbon: one bears two hydrogens as a primary amino group, and the other is linked through a double bond and carries a hydroxyl group, giving an N-hydroxy imine arrangement. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no substitution pattern beyond these terminal groups, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two nitrogens bear different substituents. Its chain is short and conformationally limited, with restricted rotation about the carbon-nitrogen double bond. The amino group and the hydroxyl group can each donate hydrogen bonds, while the nitrogen and oxygen atoms can each accept them.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built on a short two-carbon chain, with an ethyl group bonded through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon. The carbonyl is conjugated to a diazo group (a carbon double-bonded to a nitrogen that is in turn bonded to a second nitrogen carrying a formal charge pair), so the scaffold is linear and contains no rings or ring fusion. It is essentially flat across the conjugated carbonyl-diazo unit and has no stereocenters, so it is highly symmetric in the sense that it lacks any chiral features, though the terminal ethyl group rotates freely, giving it moderate flexibility. The ester oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a glycerol triester built on a three-carbon propane backbone, with each of its three hydroxyl positions acylated by a straight-chain hexanoyl group (six carbons each). It contains no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and fully saturated, with three ester carbonyl groups as its only functional groups. The two terminal primary positions and the central secondary position carry identical acyl chains, giving the molecule a near-mirror symmetry about the central carbon, though the central carbon is itself a stereocenter in the asymmetric sense only if the acyl groups differ, which they do not here. The long, flexible alkyl chains confer considerable conformational freedom. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the three ester oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a phenyl ester built from a benzene ring attached through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which in turn bears a chloromethyl group, so the scaffold is an aryl ester with a single unsubstituted six-membered aromatic ring and no additional ring systems or fused rings. The ester functional group (–O–C(=O)–) links the flat aromatic ring to a short two-atom alkyl chain ending in a chlorine substituent on the terminal carbon. The benzene ring carries no substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ester linkage. Its overall framework is fairly flexible at the ester and chloromethyl bonds, though the phenyl ring itself is rigid. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the ester ether oxygen can accept weaker hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with fully delocalized pi electrons, and carries one iodomethyl group attached to one ring carbon. The substituent is a methylene unit bearing an iodine atom, so the functional group is a primary alkyl iodide, which makes the side chain the reactive part of the structure. Because only one position on the ring is substituted, the arrangement has no positional isomerism issues and the overall shape is nearly planar along the ring with a single flexible rotatable bond connecting the CH2 group to the aromatic core. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only lone-pair-bearing atom is the iodine, which offers at most weak acceptor character, so it has essentially no hydrogen-bonding capacity.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing two substituents at meta positions relative to each other. One substituent is an isopropyl group (a central carbon bonded to two methyl groups), attached to the ring through a single carbon-carbon bond. The other is a hydroxyl group, making it a phenol-type structure with an aromatic carbon bearing an –OH. The molecule has no stereocenters and only partial symmetry, with a mirror plane through the ring lying along the axis of the isopropyl and hydroxyl substituents. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the isopropyl group adds some conformational freedom around its single bond. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the oxygen lone pairs provide an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems. The ring nitrogen carries an acetyl group, so the nitrogen is an amide nitrogen rather than a basic amine, and the carbonyl oxygen is the only heteroatom functional group present. The remaining five ring carbons are all sp3 hybridized and unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule has no stereocenters. Its overall shape is largely fixed by the ring chair conformation, with some flexibility from the rotation of the acetyl group. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small acyclic tertiary amine built on a single nitrogen atom bearing two ethyl groups, one on each side, with no rings or fused ring systems present. The third substituent on the nitrogen is a cyano group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which makes the molecule an N-cyanamide, a nitrogen bonded directly to a nitrile carbon. The two ethyl arms are identical, so the structure has a mirror-plane symmetry through the central nitrogen and the cyano carbon. The chain is flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds, while the linear cyano group is rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H bonds, but it can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through the nitrile nitrogen and the amine nitrogen.

The molecule is a substituted malonic acid in which the central carbon bears a benzyl group, so its skeleton is a three-carbon chain with two terminal carboxylic acid groups. A phenyl ring is attached through a flexible methylene linker, giving an unfused benzene ring with no additional fused ring systems. The two carboxyl groups are equivalent and sit on the same carbon, and the molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric plane through the central carbon because that carbon is a stereocenter-bearing methine. Both carboxylic acid groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aromatic ring offers a hydrophobic, planar surface. Rotation about several single bonds makes the molecule fairly flexible overall.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group (–OCH3) and two amino groups (–NH2), arranged as a trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The two amino groups sit at adjacent positions on the ring, flanking one carbon, while the methoxy group is placed meta to one amine and para to the other, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis beyond the free rotation of the methoxy group. The ring itself is planar and rigid, though the methoxy group and amine hydrogens can rotate, adding modest flexibility at the periphery. The two primary amines and the ether oxygen supply hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, with the amines acting as both donors and acceptors and the methoxy oxygen acting as an acceptor only.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic framework. A single nitro group (–NO2) is attached to the carbocyclic benzene ring, at a position on the ring remote from the fusion carbons, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry. The rigid, planar bicyclic core allows essentially no conformational flexibility, with the nitro group lying roughly in the plane of the ring. The pyridine-type ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the nitro group's oxygen atoms also serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups.

The molecule is built on a linear fused polycyclic aromatic scaffold made of four six-membered rings joined edge-to-edge in a straight line, so it is a tetracyclic framework with no heteroatoms. Its ring fusion is continuous and planar, giving an extended, rigid, flat system with no rotatable bonds. A single methyl group is attached to one of the terminal rings, creating a simple alkyl substitution pattern at one position on the periphery. The structure lacks any functional groups beyond the methyl substituent, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its overall shape has only approximate mirror symmetry through the long axis, broken by the placement of the methyl group.

The molecule is a biaryl built from a phenyl ring bonded directly to the 2-position of a naphthalene unit, giving a fully aromatic, carbon-only scaffold with no heteroatoms. The naphthalene portion is a bicyclic system of two ortho-fused benzene rings, and the phenyl ring attaches as a single substituent at one carbon of this fused system. Because the two aryl rings are joined by a single C–C bond, they can rotate relative to each other, though the extended conjugated framework keeps the overall shape largely planar and rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited symmetry, since the phenyl attachment breaks the symmetry of the naphthalene core. It lacks hydrogen-bond donors and any heteroatom acceptors, so its hydrogen-bonding capability is essentially nil.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitro group, two chlorine atoms, and a hydroxyl group, giving it a substituted phenol scaffold. The hydroxyl and nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons, with the nitro group on one side and the hydroxyl immediately next to it, while the two chlorine atoms occupy the meta positions relative to each other on the opposite side of the ring. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the structure is planar and rigid, with the nitro group's N–O bonds and the hydroxyl bond able to rotate only slightly. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro group's oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and the adjacent carbon carries a tertiary amine nitrogen bearing two N-methyl groups, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. The nitrogen is trivalent and bonded to the aromatic ring, which lets its lone pair partially conjugate with the pi system and makes the nitrogen nearly planar. Overall the scaffold is compact and fairly rigid, with only modest rotational freedom around the aryl-nitrogen and methyl bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogen substituents are carbon, while the amine nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Four of the six ring positions carry bromine atoms, which are the only substituents, so the compound is a tetrabrominated benzene. Two positions remain bearing hydrogen, located meta to each other with one ring carbon between them. The bromine atoms are unevenly distributed around the ring, which gives the molecule a lower degree of symmetry than a fully or evenly substituted benzene would have. The structure is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bromine atoms can act only as weak halogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short, fully saturated, acyclic dicarboxylic acid built on a four-carbon chain: two carboxylic acid groups sit at the chain ends, and each carbon bearing a carboxyl group also carries a methyl branch, so the skeleton is a 2,3-dimethylbutanedioic acid framework. It contains no rings or aromatic rings, which makes it flexible, with free rotation about the central carbon-carbon bond. The two stereocentres at the branch points give it a symmetric substitution pattern, with the two carboxyl groups in a mirror-related arrangement across the central bond. Each carboxylic acid group offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens (the C=O and the hydroxyl oxygen), so the molecule as a whole has two donors and four acceptors.

This molecule is a biaryl compound built from a benzene ring joined by a single C–C bond to the 1-position of a naphthalene unit, so it contains three fused-free aromatic rings in total: one phenyl group and a bicyclic naphthalene system whose two rings share an edge. The scaffold is entirely aromatic and planar within each ring, though the bond between the two aryl units allows some rotation about the connecting axis. There are no functional groups beyond the hydrocarbon framework, so the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its substitution pattern is a single attachment point on each aromatic partner, giving it no overall rotational symmetry axis beyond that of the aryl bond itself. Overall the structure is rigid and rod-like across its aromatic core, with only modest flexibility at the inter-ring linkage.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three nitro groups, each attached to adjacent ring carbons, and a methyl group on a fourth carbon, so the substitution pattern is contiguous on one side of the ring. The three nitro groups sit next to one another, which makes the arrangement asymmetric overall, with the methyl group breaking any symmetry. The scaffold is planar and rigid, though the nitro groups can twist somewhat out of the ring plane. The nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a diaryl sulfone scaffold, in which two benzene rings are joined through a central sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens. Each aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered benzene ring. Each ring carries a primary amino group at the meta position relative to the sulfone linkage, so the two substituents are arranged symmetrically across the molecule. The sulfone group is a strongly polar, tetrahedral linker that makes the structure fairly rigid, although the two rings can rotate about the sulfur-carbon bonds. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic urea, with a carbonyl carbon bonded to two nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a methyl group and the other a primary amino group. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system, and the scaffold is simply a central C(=O)(N)N unit with a single methyl substituent on one nitrogen. The urea functional group gives the molecule a planar, conjugated amide-type arrangement around the carbonyl, which makes it fairly rigid about that core while the methyl group rotates freely. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two nitrogens bear different substituents. Each nitrogen carries N–H bonds that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a central quaternary carbon that carries an ethyl group, two hydroxymethyl arms, and a nitro group. Because the central carbon bears four different attachments with two identical hydroxymethyl branches, the skeleton has no rings and no ring fusion, and its only symmetry is a local mirror relationship between the two CH2OH arms. The two primary alcohol groups act as hydrogen-bond donors through their O–H bonds and as acceptors through their oxygen lone pairs. The nitro group, drawn as a charge-separated N+ with an O− and an =O, contributes two strong hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens and no donor capability. The chain is flexible, since the single bonds to the ethyl and hydroxymethyl groups allow free rotation about the central carbon.

This molecule is an azo compound built from two benzene rings joined through a central N=N double bond, with the trans (E) geometry drawn in the SMILES. Each benzene ring carries a single methyl group on the position directly adjacent to the azo linkage, giving an ortho-substitution pattern on both sides. The two ring halves are roughly mirror-related, so the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry about the central nitrogen-nitrogen axis. The azo linkage and the attached aromatic rings are largely planar and conjugated, which keeps the overall framework fairly rigid, though the rings can rotate about their bonds to the nitrogens. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. Its two azo nitrogens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no double bonds, heteroatoms, or fused rings. Two methyl groups are attached to adjacent carbon atoms of the ring, so the substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted. Because the two methyl groups sit on neighboring carbons, the molecule has no functional groups and no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, and it possesses a mirror-plane or mirror-free geometry depending on the relative orientation of the two substituents. The ring can adopt chair conformations that interconvert, giving the structure moderate flexibility, while the lack of polar groups means it cannot form hydrogen bonds in either direction.

The molecule is built on a single aromatic six-membered 1,3,5-triazine ring, with three nitrogen atoms alternating with carbon atoms around the ring. Two of the ring carbons carry diethylamino groups, each consisting of a nitrogen bonded to two ethyl chains, and the third ring carbon carries a chlorine atom. The substitution pattern is therefore symmetric about the ring in its two diethylamino positions, though the chlorine breaks full threefold symmetry. The tertiary amine nitrogens are not hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ethyl groups add conformational flexibility, while the planar aromatic core remains rigid.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a quinoline scaffold. A hydroxyl group is attached to the benzenoid ring at a position on the carbocyclic side, giving it a phenolic character. The fused ring system is fully aromatic and planar, so the molecule is rigid with no rotatable bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the pyridine-type ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry that would make its two faces or ring positions equivalent.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic fused scaffold in which a five-membered imidazole-type ring is joined to a six-membered pyrimidine-type ring, sharing a common bond. A methyl group sits on one of the nitrogen atoms of the five-membered ring, which fixes the substitution pattern and removes one potential hydrogen-bond donor. The six-membered ring carries an exocyclic amino group on the carbon between two ring nitrogens and a carbonyl group on the adjacent carbon, while an NH in the ring provides an additional donor site. Because the fused framework is flat and rigid, with only the methyl group and amino group free to rotate, the overall shape has little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry, and its combination of amino and carbonyl groups with ring nitrogens gives it several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor positions.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a bicyclic aromatic system. Two methyl groups are attached to the same ring, placed on adjacent carbons, which creates a 1,2-dimethyl substitution pattern on one side of the fused system. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond its planar framework, and its rigid, flat aromatic core allows only limited conformational flexibility from the methyl rotations. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor either.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, making it planar and rigid. The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated alkyl thiol built on a branched carbon skeleton. Its backbone is a chain of carbons in which one quaternary carbon carries three methyl groups and a neopentyl-type methylene linker, and the terminal carbon bearing the sulfur is also quaternary, bearing two methyl groups. The only functional group is a single sulfhydryl (–SH) group attached to a tertiary carbon, giving the molecule a single hydrogen-bond donor through the S–H hydrogen and a weak, sulfur-based acceptor capacity. There are no ring systems, no fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom substitution beyond the thiol. The molecule is highly flexible about its single bonds, though the bulky tert-butyl-like groups impose steric hindrance around the sulfur and limit conformational freedom at the branch points.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane, with no fused rings or heteroatoms within the ring itself. A quaternary carbon at the 1-position of the ring carries a methyl group and a hydroxyl group, making it a tertiary alcohol. The 4-position bears an isopropenyl group, a prop-1-en-2-yl unit with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond. Because the substituents sit on opposite sides of the ring, the substitution pattern is 1,4-disubstituted, and the molecule has no particular mirror or rotational symmetry, since the two substituents differ. The cyclohexane ring is conformationally flexible while the alkene is rigid. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkene provides no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its substituents occupy four of the six ring positions: a primary amino group, a carboxylic acid, and two chlorine atoms, with the chlorines sitting ortho to the amine and meta to each other, respectively. The carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the amino group offers two N–H donors and a lone-pair acceptor. The chlorines contribute only weak halogen-type interactions. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is rigid, though the carboxyl and amino groups can rotate about their bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Five of the six ring carbons carry chlorine atoms, leaving one carbon bearing a thiol (–SH) group, so the substitution pattern is fully crowded around the ring with the thiol flanked on both sides by chlorines. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the chlorine substituents lying in the ring plane and providing no rotational freedom beyond the thiol hydrogen. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry element that would make all positions equivalent, since the single thiol sets it apart from the pentachloro-substituted ring. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the thiol hydrogen can act as a weak donor, while the sulfur and chlorine atoms can only act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing an amino group, a hydroxyl group, and a phenyl ester, so it is an aromatic ester with two benzene rings joined through a carboxylate linkage. The first ring carries an amino group and an ortho-hydroxyl group relative to the carbonyl, making the substitution pattern 1,2,4 on that ring, while the second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl attached to the ester oxygen. The molecule has no stereocenters and is largely planar within each ring, though the ester linkage gives it moderate rotational flexibility between the two aromatic systems. The amino and hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen, ester oxygen, and hydroxyl oxygen provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

This molecule is captan, but I must describe only structure without naming it. It is built around a cyclic imide: a five-membered ring containing a nitrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups, fused to a six-membered carbocycle that contains one carbon-carbon double bond. The fused bicyclic scaffold is a cis-fused tetrahydrophthalimide-type framework, which makes the core relatively rigid, while the ring carbons adjacent to the fusion are sp3-hybridized. The imide nitrogen carries a sulfur atom that bonds to a trichloromethyl group, giving a three-atom substituent of sulfur bearing a carbon with three chlorines. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the sulfenyl substituent sits on an asymmetric imide nitrogen and the alkene breaks the ring symmetry. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is an azo compound built from two aromatic units joined by a nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) configuration. One half is an ortho-tolyl ring, a benzene ring carrying a methyl group adjacent to the azo linkage. The other half is a naphthalene ring system, a bicyclic fused scaffold of two benzene rings sharing an edge, bearing the azo group at one position and a primary amino group on the adjacent carbon of the same ring. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor and the azo nitrogens and amine nitrogen act as acceptors. The extended, largely planar aromatic framework makes the structure fairly rigid, with the only notable flexibility arising from rotation about the bonds linking the azo group to the rings.

This molecule is a bis-naphthalene scaffold in which two 2-hydroxy-3-naphthoic acid units are joined through a single methylene bridge at their 1-positions. Each naphthalene is a fused bicyclic aromatic system, with the ring fusion giving the rigid, planar core of each half. Each half carries a carboxylic acid group and an adjacent phenolic hydroxyl, arranged ortho to one another. The two halves are related by symmetry about the central CH2 linker, giving a roughly mirror-symmetric framework. The phenolic and carboxylic groups supply multiple hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the central methylene keeps the two aromatic systems flexible relative to one another.

The molecule is built on an anthraquinone-type tricyclic scaffold: two outer benzene rings joined through a central six-membered ring that carries two carbonyl groups at opposite positions, making it a fused, fully planar aromatic-quinone system. One of the outer benzene rings bears a single hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to a ring-fusion position, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks a mirror plane that would divide the two halves equally. The rigid, flat framework gives little conformational flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the phenolic hydroxyl can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries an acetamide group, a nitrogen-linked carbonyl with a methyl group attached to the carbonyl carbon, which contributes a secondary amide with both a hydrogen-bond donor (the N–H) and an acceptor (the C=O). The opposite side carries a primary sulfonamide, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to an NH2 group, providing additional hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amide and sulfonamide linkages add limited rotational flexibility. The para substitution gives the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring, though the two ends differ in functionality.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a phenol group, with the remaining two ring positions carrying tertiary alkyl substituents. Each substituent is a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups and an ethyl group, so the framework is a 2,4-di(tert-pentyl)-type arrangement on the phenolic ring. The two bulky groups sit adjacent to each other, with one flanking the hydroxyl and the other positioned para to it, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern without any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring itself is rigid and planar, while the alkyl chains add conformational flexibility at their peripheries. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, whereas the carbon framework contributes no further polar interaction sites.

The molecule is a small, single five-membered heterocyclic ring containing one carbonyl carbon, two nitrogen atoms, and two carbon atoms, specifically an imidazolidinone scaffold. The ring is saturated apart from the carbonyl, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to one nitrogen and the other nitrogen attached through a two-carbon chain, so there are no ring fusions or substituents beyond the ring atoms. The molecule is compact and rigid, with little conformational freedom, and it has a plane of approximate symmetry through the carbonyl and the opposite methylene bond. The amide N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the second, amine-type nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a symmetric diester built around a flexible linear chain of two ethylene-oxygen units, specifically a diethylene glycol core, capped at both ends by benzoate groups. Each terminus carries a phenyl ring bonded directly to a carbonyl carbon, so the two aromatic rings are unfused and connected only through the ester linkages and the central ether oxygen. The molecule possesses approximately mirror or two-fold symmetry about its central ether oxygen. The ester carbonyl oxygens and the central ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The aliphatic chain gives the structure considerable conformational flexibility, whereas the two aromatic rings remain rigid and planar.

The molecule is built from two substituted phenol rings joined by a single methylene bridge, so its scaffold is a diarylmethane. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring carrying a hydroxyl group ortho to the bridge, with a tert-butyl group adjacent to that hydroxyl and a methyl group in the para position relative to the bridge attachment. The two halves are mirror-related, giving the whole molecule approximate two-fold symmetry about the central CH2 carbon. Both phenolic oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the bulky tert-butyl groups add steric hindrance around them. The rings are rotationally flexible about the bridge, though the ortho substituents restrict their motion somewhat.

This molecule is an organophosphorothioate built around a diethyl thiophosphate core, with the central phosphorus double-bonded to sulfur and bearing two ethoxy groups. The phosphorus is linked through an oxygen to a six-membered pyridazinone ring, a diazine containing two adjacent nitrogens and a carbonyl on the ring. The ring nitrogen adjacent to the carbonyl carries a phenyl substituent, which adds a second aromatic system attached by a single bond. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a modest degree of symmetry, with the two ethyl arms on phosphorus being chemically equivalent. Its ring framework is rigid, while the ethoxy chains and the rotatable linkages to the phenyl and phosphate groups allow conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the carbonyl oxygen, ring nitrogens, and phosphate oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring with two carbonyl groups positioned para to each other, giving a 1,4-benzoquinone-type scaffold. Each of the four remaining ring carbons carries a chlorine atom, so the ring is fully substituted with halogens at a symmetric 2,3,5,6 pattern. The conjugated system of the ring and its two exocyclic carbon-oxygen double bonds makes the framework flat and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has high symmetry, with a two-fold axis and mirror planes passing through the carbonyl carbons. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two carbonyl oxygens, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a quinuclidine-based alkaloid built around a bicyclic bridged amine, the 1-azabicyclo[2.2.2]octane cage, which carries a vinyl group on one of its carbons. Attached to the cage through a carbinol carbon is a quinoline ring system, a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring, joined at the pyridine's 4-position. The secondary hydroxyl group sits at a single stereogenic center linking the two ring systems. The rigid, cage-like amine contributes a tertiary nitrogen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the hydroxyl serves as both a donor and an acceptor, and the quinoline nitrogen is an additional acceptor. The fused aromatic system and the bridged cage make the overall framework largely rigid, with flexibility confined mainly to rotation about the bond connecting the carbinol carbon to the quinoline ring.

This molecule is a phthalate diester, built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent ester groups at the 1 and 2 positions (an ortho-disubstituted pattern). Each ester carbonyl links to a flexible two-carbon ether chain terminating in a methoxy group, so the scaffold consists of one rigid aromatic core flanked by two long, conformationally mobile side arms. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the ring, since the two ester arms are identical. Each ester contributes two oxygen atoms, and the ether oxygens add further sites, so the molecule has several hydrogen-bond acceptors but no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a large, fully fused polycyclic aromatic diketone built from several benzene and naphthalene-like rings joined into a rigid, nearly planar cage-free sheet. Two carbonyl groups sit in six-membered rings, each flanked by an ortho-linked benzo ring, so the diketone units are bridged and locked in place by the surrounding fused framework. The skeleton contains many ring-fusion carbons, and the substitution pattern is entirely peripheral, with no pendant alkyl or heteroatom substituents apart from the two ketone oxygens. The structure is highly rigid with little conformational flexibility, and its overall shape is roughly centrosymmetric. The carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a diaryl sulfone: a central sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and bonded to two benzene rings, giving a rigid, non-planar scaffold with the sulfone geometry tilting the rings relative to each other. One ring carries a single chlorine atom at the position para to the sulfonyl group, giving it a symmetric substitution pattern. The other ring carries three chlorine atoms, arranged so that one sits ortho to the sulfonyl group and the remaining two sit on adjacent carbons further around the ring, producing an unsymmetrical pattern overall. The sulfone oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Aromatic rings provide the only flexibility-limiting, planar regions, and the overall framework is fairly rigid.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, with no aromatic rings and no ring fusion. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, which makes that position the main functional group, and the ring also carries three methyl substituents: one on a neighbouring carbon and two geminal methyls on the carbon opposite the hydroxyl-bearing position. Because the three methyls are asymmetrically placed relative to the hydroxyl, the overall shape lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The cyclohexane framework is conformationally flexible but its ring carbons are all sp3, so the bulky substituents bias the ring toward preferred chair arrangements. The single hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the remaining hydrocarbon portions are nonpolar.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated chain with no rings, built from ethylene-oxide-type repeat units joined through ether linkages. The backbone reads as an ethyl group, followed by three repeating –CH2–CH2–O– units, and ending in a terminal hydroxyl group on one end and an ethyl cap on the other. There are no aromatic or fused ring systems, and no substituents branch off the chain, so the molecule is essentially a flat, unbranched polyether. Its ether oxygens and terminal hydroxyl can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the single hydroxyl oxygen-bound hydrogen can donate one. Because every bond along the backbone is freely rotatable, the chain is highly flexible and has no fixed molecular symmetry beyond its approximate mirror arrangement along the chain axis.

The molecule is a linear, fully saturated acyclic ether with no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic or unsaturated groups. Its backbone is a chain of twelve carbon atoms and three oxygen atoms arranged as two butyl ends joined through a central ethylene-linked ether segment, so the ether oxygens sit at the internal positions separating carbon segments. The structure has no stereocenters and possesses an approximate mirror-symmetric arrangement about the central ether oxygen. Because every bond is a freely rotating single bond, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The oxygen atoms are hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since it contains no hydroxyl or amine functionality.

The molecule is a short, acyclic, fully saturated chain built from two 2-chloroethyl units joined through a central methylene-bridged ether linkage. Its backbone reads as Cl–CH2–CH2–O–CH2–O–CH2–CH2–Cl, so the scaffold is a flexible, unbranched chain with no rings and no ring fusion. The only functional groups are two primary alkyl chlorides at the chain termini and two ether oxygens, one of which sits in an acetal-type arrangement where it is flanked by two oxygen-linked carbons. The substitution pattern is symmetric about the central CH2 carbon, giving the molecule a mirror-like arrangement along its length. Because all bonds are single and rotatable, the chain is highly flexible and conformationally mobile. The oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic ether-alcohol with a flexible, unbranched carbon chain of seven carbons interrupted by a single oxygen atom. One end bears an ethyl group bonded to an ether oxygen, and the other end terminates in a primary hydroxyl group on a three-carbon propyl segment. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and conformationally flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds. The ether oxygen can act only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the terminal hydroxyl can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry, since the two ends differ in their functional groups.

This molecule is a small, acyclic ether built on a linear chain of carbons. One end carries a vinyl group, a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, bonded through an oxygen atom to a three-carbon propyl chain. The chain terminates in a chlorine atom at the far end, so the compound is a primary alkyl chloride with an enol-ether-type vinyl ether on the other side. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no stereocenters, and the molecule is highly flexible because every bond in the backbone is a freely rotating single bond. The only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the ether oxygen, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated aliphatic diester built from a single unbranched chain of carbons with no rings and no aromatic units. Two ester groups sit at the ends of the central segment, each formed from a carboxyl carbon bonded to a straight alkyl chain, so the scaffold is symmetric in its overall layout. Each ester contributes one carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the ester oxygens are weak acceptors and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The long alkyl tails and the four-methylene spacer give the molecule substantial conformational flexibility, with few rigid elements to constrain its shape.

This molecule is divinyl ether, built from a single oxygen atom bridging two terminal vinyl groups in a linear, open-chain arrangement with no rings. Each vinyl unit contains a carbon-carbon double bond at its end, so the molecule has two alkene functionalities joined through an ether linkage. The structure is symmetric about the central oxygen, and the skeleton is small and fairly flexible, with rotation possible around the single bonds flanking the oxygen. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since it lacks any O-H or N-H bonds.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built on a branched, saturated carbon chain. Its backbone is a six-carbon chain bearing methyl branches, and the ester group (an acetate unit attached through an oxygen) sits on one of the internal carbons, so the structure has no rings or ring fusion. Two methyl groups branch from the chain, giving a non-symmetric, flexible skeleton with many freely rotatable single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites because every heteroatom is an acceptor and all carbon-bound hydrogens are non-polar.

This molecule is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing three ring nitrogen atoms placed alternately with three carbon atoms, forming a symmetric 1,3,5-triazine scaffold. Each of the three ring carbons carries a hydroxyl group, so the substitution pattern is threefold and identical around the ring, giving the molecule a high degree of symmetry. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, which makes the overall structure rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds. Each hydroxyl oxygen can donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H group and each ring nitrogen can accept one, so the molecule has strong hydrogen-bonding capability. Because the hydroxyl groups sit adjacent to ring nitrogens, the structure can also tautomerize between hydroxy and keto-like forms, which affects how its donor and acceptor sites are presented.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 4, which places it in the piperazine family, with no ring fusion or additional rings present. Two methyl groups are attached to carbon atoms adjacent to the nitrogens, one on each side of the ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric about the ring's carbon framework. The ring is fully sp3-hybridized and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation that can interconvert, giving it modest rigidity. Both nitrogens are secondary amines bearing an N–H, so the molecule can act as two hydrogen-bond donors and, through the nitrogen lone pairs, as two hydrogen-bond acceptors. No other functional groups are present.

The molecule is a linear, fully saturated aliphatic diester built from a six-carbon dicarboxylic acid backbone capped at both ends by n-propyl groups. Its scaffold is an unbranched chain of six carbons, with two ester carbonyl carbons at the termini and four methylene units in between, so there are no rings and no ring fusion. Each ester group consists of a carbonyl oxygen double-bonded to the carbonyl carbon and an ether-type oxygen bonded to a propyl chain. The substitution pattern is strictly symmetric, with identical propyl ester arms at both ends, giving the molecule a mirror-like or two-fold symmetry along its midpoint. The chain is highly flexible due to freely rotating single bonds, although the ester planarity introduces some local rigidity. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its four oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a linear aliphatic diester built around a flexible six-carbon dicarboxylic acid core. The central chain is a straight run of four methylene groups flanked on each end by an ester carbonyl, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic character. Each terminus carries an unbranched n-butyl group bonded through an ester oxygen, giving a symmetrical molecule with a two-fold axis through the midpoint of the central chain. The many rotatable single bonds make the structure highly flexible rather than rigid. The two carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all of its hydrogens sit on saturated carbons.

This molecule is a symmetric peroxydicarbonate diester built around a central oxygen–oxygen single bond (a peroxide linkage). Each end of the chain bears a carbonyl group, and each carbonyl is bonded to an isopropyl ester group, so the two halves are mirror-identical about the O–O axis. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and fairly flexible, with rotation possible around the C–O and O–O bonds. The structure contains two carbonyl oxygens and four ether-type oxygens, all of which can accept hydrogen bonds, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors because every heteroatom is fully substituted and the only hydrogens sit on the saturated isopropyl carbons.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group, attached directly to the aromatic ring), and the other is a benzylic CH2 linked through an ester oxygen to an acetyl group, giving an acetate ester. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, and the para substitution gives the overall structure a roughly linear, two-fold symmetric outline. The ester linkage and the ether oxygen introduce some rotational flexibility, though the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H groups, but the two ether-type oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a disulfide bridge (S–S) linking two nitrogen atoms, with each nitrogen sitting in its own saturated six-membered heterocycle. Each ring is a morpholine unit, containing one nitrogen and one oxygen separated by two carbons on either side, so the two rings are identical and related by symmetry across the central S–S bond. The rings are fully saturated and non-aromatic, adopting flexible chair-like conformations, while the S–S linkage allows rotation around the bond. Each nitrogen is tertiary, bearing three substituents (two ring carbons and the sulfur), so there is no N–H donor. The ether oxygens in the rings can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the nitrogens offer weak acceptor character, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a linear aliphatic diester built from a straight eight-carbon dicarboxylic acid chain (a sebacate-type backbone) capped at both ends by ester linkages. Each ester oxygen is attached to a branched 2-ethylhexyl-type alkyl group, which carries an ethyl branch on the second carbon from the attachment point. There are no rings, aromatic systems, or heteroatoms beyond the two ester groups. The molecule is fully symmetric, with a mirror-like arrangement of the two identical halves around the central chain. It is highly flexible because of the many freely rotating single bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the four ester oxygens serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings and no heteroatoms. Three ethyl groups are attached to the ring at alternating positions, at carbons 1, 3, and 5, so the substitution pattern is symmetric (meta to one another). It contains no functional groups beyond these alkyl substituents, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while each ethyl group adds some conformational flexibility through rotation about its single bonds.

The molecule is an ester built from two benzene rings joined by a flexible linker. A phenylacetyl unit forms the acyl half: a benzene ring bearing a CH2 group that connects to the ester carbonyl. The alcohol half is a two-carbon ethylene chain ending in a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring, so both aromatic rings are monosubstituted and carry no ring fusion. The ester group, with its carbonyl oxygen and single-bonded ether-type oxygen, is the only polar functional group and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has no stereocenters and no significant symmetry, and its several rotatable bonds make it fairly flexible.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two secondary amine substituents placed opposite each other, at the 1 and 4 positions, so the substitution pattern is para. Each nitrogen is attached to a sec-butyl group, a four-carbon branched alkyl chain with a stereocenter at the carbon bonded to the nitrogen. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the two sec-butyl arms give the outer portions of the molecule considerable conformational flexibility. Overall the structure has approximate two-fold symmetry through the center of the ring. Each NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and each nitrogen lone pair can serve as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ring itself is electron-rich.

This molecule is an acetoacetanilide-type compound: a four-carbon acetoacetyl chain (a methyl ketone flanked by a methylene and an amide carbonyl) attached through an amide nitrogen to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered benzene ring carrying one chlorine atom para to the amide nitrogen, giving a 1,4-disubstituted, planar pattern with no internal symmetry axis beyond the ring's own. The ketone and amide carbonyls are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the secondary amide N–H serves as a single hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule is fairly flexible along the acyclic chain, with the amide linkage conferring partial rigidity near the aryl ring.

The molecule is a substituted urea built around a central carbonyl group flanked by two nitrogen atoms. One nitrogen carries two methyl groups, making it a tertiary amide-type nitrogen with no hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the other is an N-H attached directly to a phenyl ring. The phenyl ring is a simple, unsubstituted benzene ring, so the aromatic portion adds planarity and a lipophilic surface but no additional polar groups. The scaffold is therefore a single flexible linker joining a rigid aromatic ring to a small dimethylamino end. The carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the N-H acts as a single hydrogen-bond donor.

This molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries two carboxylic acid groups, each attached directly to the ring carbons, one at the position adjacent to the nitrogen and one at the position meta to it, giving a 2,5-disubstitution pattern. The molecule lacks any rotational symmetry because the two acid groups sit in different positions relative to the nitrogen. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, though each carboxyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The two acid groups each provide a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered carbocyclic ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems. The ring contains two carbon-carbon double bonds, so it is a partially unsaturated cyclohexadiene framework rather than a fully saturated cyclohexane. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and an isopropyl group sits on another, placed at a 1,4-relationship across the ring, giving a substitution pattern with no symmetry plane that maps the two substituents onto each other. The ring is fairly rigid because of its endocyclic double bonds, while the isopropyl group retains some rotational freedom. The molecule contains no heteroatoms and no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three substituents sit on the ring: a methyl group, a nitro group, and a hydroxyl group, with the hydroxyl adjacent to the methyl and the nitro group positioned para to the hydroxyl. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and planar, while the phenolic hydroxyl is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The methyl group adds a small nonpolar bulk. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogen and nitro oxygens to consider, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the aromatic plane.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring with no ring fusion, bearing one substituent at one position. That substituent is a two-carbon chain: a terminal methyl group attached to a tetrahedral stereogenic carbon that also carries a primary amine (-NH2) group. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted otherwise, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis through the chiral center. The side chain is rotatable and moderately flexible, while the phenyl ring is rigid and planar. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its two N-H bonds) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (through the nitrogen lone pair).

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to one carbon of this ring is a sulfonic acid group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and also bears a hydroxyl group. Positioned para to the sulfonic acid, on the opposite side of the ring, is a chlorine substituent, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern. The ring and its two substituents lie roughly in one plane, so the scaffold is rigid, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen able to rotate. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the long axis of the ring. The sulfonic acid group can donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds at its sulfonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, while the chlorine is a weak halogen acceptor.

The molecule is built from two substituted benzene rings joined through a single sulfur atom, forming a diaryl sulfide (thioether) linkage. Each ring carries a hydroxyl group and a tert-butyl group ortho to one another, and each also bears a methyl group, so the two halves are near-mirror-image copies. The aromatic rings are planar and rigid, while the C–S–C bridge gives the molecule some rotational flexibility around its two bonds to sulfur. The phenolic hydroxyl groups can act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the sulfur atom is a weak acceptor. The bulky tert-butyl groups sterically shield the hydroxyls.

The molecule is an acyclic three-carbon chain, a propane skeleton with no rings and no fused ring systems. The central carbon carries a bromine atom and is flanked by two methylene groups, one bearing a chlorine atom and the other a bromine atom, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane or axis of symmetry. The three carbons are sp3-hybridized, and the single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility through free rotation about each carbon-carbon bond. The molecule contains only halogen substituents and no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and the halogens can act only as weak acceptors, so it has essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring that contains both sulfur and nitrogen. The bicyclic core is fully aromatic and planar, which makes the framework rigid. At the 2-position of the thiazole ring, a sulfenamide linkage (an S–N bond) connects the heteroaromatic system to a cyclohexylamine unit. The cyclohexyl ring adopts a non-planar chair-like conformation and gives the molecule a bulky, flexible aliphatic region. The thiazole nitrogen and the sulfenamide nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the sulfenamide N–H can serve as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is a bicyclic hydrocarbon scaffold built on a norbornene-type framework, with two fused five- and six-membered carbon rings sharing a bridged arrangement. One ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond, which introduces rigidity and limits conformational flexibility across the cage-like core. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to a saturated bridgehead-adjacent carbon, serving as the only substituent. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.
