Its overall structure is asymmetric because the single nitrile substituent breaks the symmetry of the bicyclic framework.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a para-disposed substituent pattern: a hydroxyl group sits at one position and a two-carbon side chain at the opposite position, with no ring fusion. The side chain is a flexible ethanolamine-type unit, consisting of a secondary alcohol on the carbon adjacent to the ring, followed by a methylene linked to a secondary amine that carries an N-methyl group. The aromatic ring and phenolic hydroxyl are essentially planar and rigid, while the side chain contributes rotatable bonds and conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local two-fold arrangement of the para-substituted ring, because the side chain bears a stereogenic center. The hydroxyl oxygen groups and the secondary amine nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond donors, and all three heteroatoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic tertiary amine with a central nitrogen bearing three substituents: two carboxymethyl arms, each ending in a carboxylic acid group, and one 2-hydroxyethyl arm terminating in a primary alcohol. There are no rings, so the scaffold is a flexible, open-chain framework with no ring fusion or fixed geometry. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the hydroxyethyl arm differs from the two identical carboxymethyl arms. Its functional groups are two carboxylic acids, one primary alcohol, and one tertiary amine, giving it multiple hydrogen-bond donors from the O–H groups and several acceptors from the carbonyl oxygens, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the nitrogen lone pair.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two secondary amine (NH) linkers in a para arrangement, so the two nitrogens sit on opposite sides of the ring. Each NH connects that central ring to a naphthalene unit, which is a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene rings sharing an edge. The naphthyl groups are attached at the 2-position (beta carbon) of each naphthalene, leaving the fused rings unsubstituted otherwise. The overall skeleton is extended, nearly linear, and highly aromatic, giving it considerable rigidity with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation about the C–N bonds. Each NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen lone pairs offer weak acceptor capability, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through its central axis.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. Attached at the 2-position of this fused system is a para-substituted phenyl ring, which bears a primary amino group at the position opposite the linkage. A methyl group sits on the benzo portion of the fused bicyclic core, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused aromatic system and the directly bonded phenyl ring are essentially planar and rigid, with only limited rotational freedom about the single bond linking the two ring systems. The amino group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the thiazole nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is an acetoacetanilide-type amide built on a benzene ring bearing a methoxy group at the ortho position relative to the amide nitrogen. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, which is planar and rigid, while the attached side chain provides conformational flexibility. A secondary amide (N-H and C=O) links the aryl ring to a four-carbon chain containing a ketone, so the chain carries two carbonyl groups separated by a methylene. The ortho-methoxy ether oxygen and both carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amide N-H serves as a single hydrogen-bond donor. The substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted on the benzene ring, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two substituents are different.

This molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond with no fused ring system. The phenyl ring bearing the hydroxyl group carries a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the hydroxyl, so the substituents sit in a 1,2,4 pattern relative to the biaryl bond. The unsubstituted phenyl ring is unbranched and lacks any additional substituents. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single rotatable biaryl bond, so it is fairly rigid and planar in its ring framework. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine provides a weak halogen acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single bond, with no additional fused ring systems. Each ring carries an isocyanate group (N=C=O) and an adjacent methyl group, placing both substituents ortho to one another on each ring. The two rings are arranged in a para-linked, roughly symmetric fashion, so the molecule has approximate C2 symmetry about the central biaryl bond. The biaryl linkage allows some rotation, giving moderate flexibility, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid. The isocyanate carbons are electrophilic and the oxygen and nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with no fused ring systems. Each ring carries an amino group (–NH2) and a chlorine atom, and the two rings are substituted in a mirror-related pattern: the amine sits para to the biaryl bond on each ring, and each chlorine sits ortho to its amine, on the carbon adjacent to the amino group. The molecule is therefore approximately symmetric about the central biaryl axis. The biaryl bond allows rotation, giving some conformational flexibility, though the rings are fully aromatic and planar. Each amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-bond or acceptor character.

This molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with no ring fusion. Each ring carries a methoxy group ortho to the biaryl linkage and an isocyanate group (–N=C=O) para to that linkage on the opposite side, giving a symmetric 3,3'-dimethoxy-4,4'-diisocyanato pattern. The biaryl bond allows some rotation, so the molecule is moderately flexible, though the substituents limit how freely the rings twist. The isocyanate carbons are electrophilic and the oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups and isocyanates can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two benzene rings fused together along a shared edge to form a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic system. A single chlorine atom is attached to one of the carbon atoms on the fused system, placing the halogen substituent on the ring that is not fused to the other, in a position adjacent to the ring-fusion region. The compound has no stereocenters and lacks any rotatable bonds beyond the aromatic framework, so it is essentially planar and conformationally rigid. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the chlorine atom and the pi-electron system offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a tertiary amide built on a benzene scaffold: a single unsubstituted phenyl ring is bonded directly to a nitrogen atom that also carries an n-butyl chain and an acetyl group (C(=O)CH3). There are no fused or additional ring systems, and the phenyl ring carries no substituents, so the substitution pattern is simply monosubstituted. The amide carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitrogen has no hydrogen and therefore offers no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The molecule is largely flexible because of the rotatable n-butyl chain, though the amide C–N bond has partial double-bond character that restricts rotation around it. Overall the structure lacks any symmetry element beyond local planarity of the amide and aromatic groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons of that ring, forming an ortho-disubstituted pattern. One substituent is a methyl group, and the other is an aminomethyl group, meaning a CH2 linker bonded to a primary amine nitrogen. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair acting as an acceptor, while the aromatic ring and methyl group contribute no polar donor or acceptor character. The structure is fairly compact and has a rotatable bond between the ring and the methylene carbon, so it shows modest conformational flexibility, and it lacks any mirror-symmetry axis that would make its two substituents equivalent.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, and a nitro group, a nitrogen bearing two oxygen atoms with one formally charged, sits adjacent to one of them, giving a 1,4-dimethyl-2-nitro substitution pattern. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the nitro group breaks the mirror symmetry the two methyl groups would otherwise share. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add minor rotational freedom. The nitro group contains no hydrogen-bond donors, but its oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other): a primary amino group (-NH2) and a sulfonic acid group (-SO3H), which is attached to the ring through a sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens and one hydroxyl. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the sulfonic acid's oxygen atoms and hydroxyl provide several additional donor and acceptor sites. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, though the sulfonic acid group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is built on a five-membered lactam ring, a pyrrolidin-2-one core, in which a nitrogen atom sits in the ring alongside a carbonyl carbon adjacent to it. The nitrogen carries a vinyl substituent, a small unsaturated two-carbon group attached directly to the ring nitrogen, so the ring is not fused to any other ring system. The amide-type carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor because the nitrogen is fully substituted and no N-H or O-H groups are present. The ring is largely planar at the amide unit but the three methylene groups give it some conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror-like arrangement around the nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a hydroxyl group sitting directly on the ring, which is a phenolic OH and acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The other is an ester linkage: a carbonyl carbon attached to the ring and bonded through an oxygen to a two-carbon chain that ends in a terminal primary hydroxyl group. The flexible ethyl-linked side chain contrasts with the rigid planar aromatic core, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. Overall it offers three hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens from the ester and phenol and two donor hydroxyl groups.

The molecule is a tricyclic aromatic system built from a central furan ring fused on either side to benzene rings, forming a dibenzofuran scaffold. Both outer rings are fully aromatic and planar, and the fused arrangement makes the whole framework rigid and flat. A single bromine atom sits as a substituent on one of the outer benzene rings, away from the oxygen bridge. The ether oxygen in the central five-membered ring is the only heteroatom, contributing no hydrogen-bond donor capability and acting only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the bromine.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused pair of benzene rings sharing one edge, which makes the core rigid and planar. An amino group sits on one ring, and two sulfonic acid groups (–SO3H) are attached to the other ring at positions that are not symmetric with respect to each other, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The sulfonic acid groups are strongly polar and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the amino group contributes one donor pair and a lone pair acceptor. Overall the structure offers several hydrogen-bonding sites on a compact, flat aromatic framework.

This molecule is a urea derivative, specifically a tetrasubstituted urea in which a central carbonyl carbon is bonded to two nitrogen atoms. Each nitrogen carries an ethyl group and a phenyl ring, so the scaffold is built around a single C=O unit flanked by two N,N-diethyl-N-phenyl amide-like centers. Both aromatic rings are unsubstituted benzene rings, with no ring fusion and no additional substituents on them. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every nitrogen is fully substituted, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor. The two ethyl chains and the two phenyl rings give a fairly flexible, non-planar arrangement around the central urea core.

This molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two ester groups on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic core. One ester carbonyl attaches directly to the ring as an aryl ester, while the other ring-bound carbonyl is part of a butyl ester, which is joined through a flexible ether-like oxygen and a methylene linker to a second butyl ester chain. The two n-butyl chains and the glycolate-type linker give the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, in contrast to the rigid aromatic core. Four ester oxygens and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because the two ester arms differ in their connectivity.

The molecule is built on a quinuclidine-type bicyclic amine, a rigid cage in which a nitrogen sits at a bridgehead position and carries a vinyl group on an adjacent ring carbon. A ketone links this cage at a bridgehead-adjacent carbon to a 6-methoxyquinoline unit, a fused bicyclic aromatic system containing a pyridine-type nitrogen. The methoxy group sits on the benzo portion of the quinoline, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The scaffold is largely rigid, with the ketone and aryl bond providing limited rotational freedom. The tertiary amine nitrogen and the quinoline nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, so it is fully substituted with no unsubstituted ring positions. Going around the ring from the methoxy-bearing carbon, it carries a methoxy group, a tert-butyl group, a hydrogen on one carbon, a nitro group, a methyl group, and a second nitro group adjacent to the methoxy. The two nitro groups are positioned ortho to each other on one side of the ring, while the bulky tert-butyl group sits flanked by the methoxy and the ring hydrogen, which gives the scaffold an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, though the tert-butyl and methoxy groups add some conformational freedom. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the nitro oxygens and the methoxy oxygen act as acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a piperazine core, a six-membered saturated ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship. One nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine, while the other nitrogen bears a benzhydryl group, a carbon atom bonded to two separate unsubstituted phenyl rings. The two phenyl rings are not fused to each other or to the piperazine, so the scaffold consists of three distinct ring systems joined through a single tetrahedral carbon. The molecule has no stereocenter at that central carbon because its two phenyl groups are identical, and the piperazine ring can adopt flexible chair conformations, giving moderate overall flexibility. Both basic nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since no N-H or O-H bonds are present.

The molecule is a polycyclic aromatic dianhydride built around a naphthalene-type core in which two peri-related carbons are bridged by a second anhydride-containing ring system, giving a fused, largely planar framework. Two cyclic anhydride rings are present, each consisting of a five-membered ring containing a C(=O)–O–C(=O) unit fused onto the aromatic periphery. The aromatic carbons are arranged so that the anhydride groups sit on opposite sides of the central fused system, producing a symmetric substitution pattern with a centre of inversion. The rigid, fully fused ring system allows essentially no rotational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its four carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a diaryl sulfonate ester: a central sulfur atom in a sulfonyl group (S with two double-bonded oxygens) links one 4-chlorophenyl ring directly through a carbon-sulfur bond and another 4-chlorophenyl ring through an oxygen bridge. Both aromatic rings are simple benzene rings with no fused ring systems, and each carries a single chlorine atom at the para position relative to its attachment point. The structure is fairly symmetric, with the two rings arranged around the tetrahedral sulfur centre, though the rings can rotate about their single bonds, giving moderate flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined through a sulfonamide linker. One ring is a benzene ring carrying a primary amino group para to the sulfonyl group, giving a 1,4-disubstituted, flat, planar aromatic unit. The other is a six-membered pyridazine ring, a diazine containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, bearing a chlorine atom on the carbon next to one ring nitrogen. The sulfonamide nitrogen bridges the sulfonyl sulfur and the pyridazine ring, and it carries one hydrogen, so it acts as a hydrogen-bond donor. The two sulfonyl oxygens and the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amino group provides additional donor capacity. The molecule has no stereocenters and little internal symmetry, and its rigid aromatic rings give it limited conformational flexibility around the sulfonamide bonds.

The molecule is built from a single central tertiary carbon that bears a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and two identical para-chlorophenyl rings, so it is a 1,1-diarylethanol scaffold. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring with a chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, giving a symmetric para-disubstitution pattern, and the two rings are related by a mirror-like symmetry through the central carbon. The only hydrogen-bond donor is the hydroxyl hydrogen, while the oxygen atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The sp3 central carbon links the rings without fusion, so the molecule has a propeller-like, moderately flexible three-dimensional shape around that junction.

This molecule is built around a central quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups and two identical aryl rings, giving a propane-2,2-diyl bridge between two benzene rings. Each benzene ring is substituted with two chlorine atoms flanking a hydroxyl group, so each ring carries a phenol at the position opposite the bridge. The two halves are related by a mirror-like symmetry through the central carbon, making the molecule symmetric overall. The central sp3 carbon makes the scaffold non-planar and somewhat rigid, while the aryl rings themselves are planar and unfused. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the chlorine atoms add steric bulk and weak halogen-bonding potential.

This molecule is a small acyclic ester built on a single carbonyl carbon, so it has no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no stereocenters. The central carbon is double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to a methoxy group (a methyl attached through an oxygen) and to a chlorine atom, which makes it a chloroformate. The skeleton is linear and flexible, with free rotation about the C–O single bonds, and the molecule has limited symmetry because the two substituents on the carbonyl carbon are chemically distinct. The carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small saturated heterocycle built on an oxetane ring, a four-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and three carbon atoms. A single quaternary carbon sits at the 3-position of this ring and carries two identical chloromethyl substituents, each a CH2 group bonded to a chlorine atom. The two chloromethyl arms are equivalent, giving the molecule a local mirror plane through the ring oxygen and the quaternary carbon. The ring is strained and rigid, while the two chloromethyl groups provide some conformational freedom. The ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that bears a hydroxyl group and is attached to three aromatic rings: a para-chlorophenyl group linked through a methylene bridge, a para-tolyl group, and a para-substituted phenyl ring. This central tertiary alcohol carbon makes the scaffold a triaryl-type core with a branched, non-planar geometry. The phenyl ring carrying the alkoxy side chain is para-disubstituted, as are the chlorophenyl and tolyl rings, so each aromatic ring has a simple, symmetric substitution pattern. A flexible two-carbon ether linker connects an oxygen on the phenyl ring to a diethylamino group, which adds rotational freedom to the otherwise rigid aromatic framework. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ether oxygen and tertiary amine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the chlorine atom contributes a halogen substituent on one ring.

This molecule is built on a single quaternary carbon that serves as the central scaffold, bearing four identical arms, each ending in an oxygen linked to a nitro group. Each arm therefore consists of a methylene bridge, an ether-type oxygen, and a nitrate ester group, where the nitrogen is bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the framework is fully acyclic. The four nitrate ester groups are arranged with tetrahedral, highly symmetric substitution around the central carbon, giving the molecule near-equivalent arms. The structure is flexible through its many single bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its numerous oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, non-aromatic ester built around a single quaternary carbon that bears three butyl ester arms, an acetoxy group, and a CH2 linker. Its scaffold is a flexible, chain-like skeleton with no rings and no fusion. Three of the four substituents on the central carbon are butoxycarbonyl groups, and the fourth is an acetate ester, so the molecule carries four ester carbonyls in total. Each ester oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The many rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible, and its only symmetry is a rough pseudo-threefold arrangement of the three butyl ester arms.

The molecule is an acyclic compound built around a single quaternary carbon that carries two ethyl groups, a bromine atom, and a carbonyl group, giving it a branched, non-aromatic scaffold with no ring systems or ring fusion. The carbonyl carbon links to an N-acylurea unit, in which a secondary amide nitrogen joins a urea carbonyl that terminates in a primary amine (–NH2). The bromine sits on the quaternary center and acts as a halogen substituent, while the two ethyl arms add conformational flexibility through freely rotating single bonds. The local symmetry around the quaternary carbon is partial, since the two ethyl groups are equivalent but the remaining substituents are not. The N-acylurea group provides multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites from its NH and NH2 groups and several acceptor sites at its two carbonyl oxygens.

The molecule has a cyclic siloxane scaffold: an eight-membered ring alternating silicon and oxygen atoms, specifically a four-silicon, four-oxygen ring. Each silicon is tetrahedral and carries one methyl group and one phenyl group, so the ring is fully substituted and has no hydroxyl or N-H groups. The phenyl rings are unsubstituted benzene rings hanging off the silicon atoms, giving the molecule a high degree of substitution with pendant aromatic groups. The arrangement has approximate alternating symmetry, with methyl and phenyl groups repeating around the ring, and the Si–O backbone is relatively rigid while the pendant groups rotate. The oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid ester built on a bornane-type skeleton, a rigid fused bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane framework carrying three methyl groups on the bridgehead and gem-dimethyl positions. The ring system consists of two five-membered rings sharing a common edge, giving a compact, strongly constrained cage with little conformational flexibility. An acetate ester group is attached to one ring carbon, with its carbonyl oxygen serving as a hydrogen-bond acceptor while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric overall because of the single ester at one position, though the carbon framework retains a degree of local symmetry around the bridge. Its hydrocarbon-rich, sterically crowded framework limits access to the ester functionality.

This molecule is a short, fully saturated two-carbon chain built on a central C–C bond, with each carbon bearing two hydroxyl groups and one carboxylic acid group. There are no rings, no aromatic systems, and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and open. The structure contains two carboxylic acid groups at opposite ends and four hydroxyl groups on the central carbons, giving a symmetric substitution pattern in which the two halves are identical. The molecule is conformationally flexible about the central C–C bond. Its numerous hydroxyl and carboxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is a small acyclic haloalkane built on a two-carbon skeleton, with one carbon bearing three fluorine atoms and the adjacent carbon bearing two hydrogens and a chlorine atom. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no conjugated or aromatic system. Its only functional groups are carbon-halogen bonds, with the trifluoromethyl group as the dominant feature. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the local threefold axis of the CF3 group, and it has rotational freedom around the central carbon-carbon single bond. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a single carbon atom serving as the entire scaffold, with no rings or ring fusion present. The central carbon carries one chlorine atom and three fluorine atoms, arranged in a tetrahedral geometry with no stereocenters. Its substitution pattern is fully halogenated, leaving no carbon-hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has local threefold symmetry around the carbon-chlorine axis. Because it is a small, saturated structure with no rotatable bonds, it is essentially rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a single carbon atom bearing four halogen substituents: two fluorine atoms and two bromine atoms, which makes it a one-carbon tetrahalomethane with no rings or chain. Its scaffold is therefore just a tetrahedral sp3 carbon center with no ring fusion, no heteroatom functional groups beyond the halogens, and no stereocenters. The two fluorines are identical to each other, as are the two bromines, giving the molecule a pair of mirror planes and effectively C2v symmetry. Because there are no rotatable bonds, the structure is completely rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the halogens are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is propyne, a three-carbon chain with a carbon-carbon triple bond at one end, so it has no ring systems or ring fusion. Its skeleton is a short linear chain: a terminal alkyne carbon bonded to a second alkyne carbon, which is bonded to a methyl group. The terminal C-H on the alkyne end is weakly acidic in character, and the molecule carries no heteroatoms or other functional groups beyond the triple bond itself. The triple bond and the linear arrangement of the three carbons make the structure rigid along its axis, with no rotatable bonds. It has a local threefold axis of symmetry along the chain, and it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor, since its only polar C-H is a very weak donor, nor as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, since it has no lone-pair-bearing atoms.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement, so the core is a monosubstituted-style aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. One substituent is a nitro group, a strongly electron-withdrawing group attached directly to the ring. The other is a two-carbon side chain containing a secondary alcohol on the carbon next to the ring, followed by a CH2 linked to a secondary amine that carries an isopropyl group. The side chain is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds, while the aromatic ring stays rigid and planar. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local symmetry of the para-substituted ring, and it is chiral at the carbinol carbon. Its hydrogen-bonding profile includes two donors (the hydroxyl O–H and the amine N–H) and several acceptors (the hydroxyl oxygen, the amine nitrogen, and the two oxygens of the nitro group).

This molecule is a steroid-type tetracyclic scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene framework. The A ring carries an α,β-unsaturated ketone, with a carbonyl at one end and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to it, and the D ring bears a secondary ester oxygen linked to a cyclopentylpropanoyl chain. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring-fusion positions, which makes the fused core rigid and largely planar in shape, while the side chain adds flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ketone and ester oxygens act as acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a bridged bicyclic hydrocarbon skeleton, a norbornene-type cage built from a fused cyclopentane and cyclohexane framework joined by a shared bridgehead arrangement. It contains a single carbon-carbon double bond within one six-membered ring, flanked by two chlorine-bearing alkene carbons. The remaining saturated carbons are heavily substituted with chlorine atoms, giving a dense, highly regular substitution pattern across the cage. The rigid polycyclic framework limits conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since all heteroatoms are halogen substituents on carbon.

This molecule is 1,1-dimethylhydrazine, a small acyclic scaffold with no rings and no fused systems. Its skeleton consists of two nitrogen atoms joined by a single bond, with both methyl groups attached to one nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric: one nitrogen is fully substituted with two methyls while the other bears two hydrogens. The molecule is small and highly flexible, with free rotation about the nitrogen-nitrogen bond. The terminal NH2 group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary nitrogen can serve only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a small, fully acyclic structure built around a single central carbon atom that is bonded to three nitrogen-containing groups, giving it a branched, non-ring scaffold. Each of the three carbons on the core bears two nitrogen substituents, one of which is double-bonded (an imine-type nitrogen) and one of which is a bare amino group, so the chain of atoms forms a compact, highly polar framework. There are no aromatic rings, no ring fusion, and no stereocenters, and the molecule is fairly flexible about its single bonds while the C=N double bonds impose local planarity. The structure is essentially symmetric in its two terminal guanidine-like units, and it carries many hydrogen-bond donors through its NH and NH2 groups along with several nitrogen lone-pair acceptors.

The molecule is an azo compound built from two benzene rings joined through a central nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) configuration. One ring carries a methyl group at a meta position relative to the azo linkage, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern on that side. The other ring bears a dimethylamino group para to the azo bond, which adds an electron-donating tertiary amine. The two aromatic rings are unfused and connected through a planar, rigid azo bridge, so the overall framework is largely flat and conjugated. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens sit on carbon. The azo nitrogens and the tertiary amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a diaryl ether scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom, with no fused ring systems. The first ring carries a carboxymethyl group (an acetic acid side chain, CH2-COOH) para to the ether linkage's position, with two iodine atoms flanking the ether oxygen. The second ring bears a hydroxyl group and one iodine atom, positioned ortho to each other on the ring. The molecule has one carboxylic acid, one phenolic hydroxyl, and an aryl ether oxygen, giving it both hydrogen-bond donor sites (the acid and phenol OH groups) and several acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the ether oxygen). The rings are rigid, while the ether linkage and the CH2 group provide some conformational flexibility, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to one ring carbon, with four chlorine atoms occupying the remaining positions. Two of the chlorines sit on adjacent carbons and are flanked by the other chlorine substituents, so the ring is heavily halogenated on one side while the carboxyl-bearing carbon and one neighboring carbon are left with a single hydrogen between them. The scaffold is a single aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and it is essentially planar and rigid. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry in its overall arrangement.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring carrying two substituents on opposite positions. One substituent is a bulky 1,1,3,3-tetramethylbutyl group, a quaternary carbon framework attached to the ring through a tertiary carbon bearing two methyl groups. The other substituent is a 2-hydroxyethoxy chain, an aryl ether linked to a terminal primary alcohol. The aromatic core is a single unfused benzene ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the para arrangement gives the ring a pseudo-symmetric, elongated shape. The alkyl side chain is highly branched and sterically crowded, while the ether-linked hydroxyethyl tail is comparatively flexible. The terminal hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents in a 1,2,4,6 pattern. A dipropylamino group sits on one carbon, flanked on both sides by nitro groups at adjacent and ortho positions, and a trifluoromethyl group occupies the position across the ring. Its only ring system is the single aromatic six-membered ring, with no ring fusion. The two nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, while the tertiary amine nitrogen is a weak acceptor and offers no donor sites, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two propyl chains are flexible, but the ring and its bulky substituents limit overall conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three ethoxy groups (O-CH2CH3) at three ring positions, leaving the remaining two ring carbons as aromatic C-H. Attached to the ring at the one remaining substituted position is a four-carbon chain that contains a ketone carbonyl and terminates in a carboxylic acid group, so the chain is a 4-oxobutanoic acid unit linked directly to the aryl ring. The three ether oxygens and the ketone oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the carboxylic acid OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the chain and the three ethoxy groups are not arranged in a mirror-related or rotationally symmetric way about the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the ethoxy groups and the flexible aliphatic chain provide considerable conformational freedom.

The molecule is built around a fused bicyclic core: a six-membered pyridine-type ring fused to a five-membered ring containing an N-N bond, giving a pyridotriazinone-like heteroaromatic scaffold with a carbonyl on the five-membered ring. A flexible three-carbon linker extends from one ring nitrogen to a piperazine ring, which is a saturated six-membered diamine. The second nitrogen of that piperazine carries a 3-chlorophenyl group, a meta-substituted benzene ring. The carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is asymmetric and moderately flexible, with the rigid fused core and aryl ring contrasting with the rotatable alkyl linker.

This molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring carrying a methyl group on one side and a ketone-bearing side chain on the other. The ketone (aryl carbonyl) is attached to a branched carbon that bears a methyl group and a CH2 linker leading to a piperidine nitrogen. The piperidine is a saturated six-membered ring with a single tertiary amine nitrogen, making it a basic, flexible, non-aromatic heterocycle with no fused rings. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry overall, though the aryl portion is symmetric about its long axis. The carbonyl oxygen and the tertiary amine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule has a thiocarbamate core: a central carbon double-bonded to sulfur, bonded to an N-methyl nitrogen and an oxygen that links to a fused polycyclic aromatic-aliphatic system. The nitrogen also carries a meta-tolyl ring (a benzene bearing a methyl group at the meta position relative to the nitrogen). The oxygen-bearing ring is a benzene fused to a bridged bicyclic hydrocarbon framework, a norbornane-like cage, giving a rigid, three-dimensional scaffold with the bridged portion providing little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen is fully substituted, but the sulfur and oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall, the molecule is asymmetric because the two aromatic substituents differ in substitution pattern and the bridged framework is not symmetric about the thiocarbamate linkage.

The molecule is built around a thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, which is substituted at the 2-position by a propanoic acid side chain bearing an alpha-methyl group, and at the 5-position by a benzoyl group. The benzoyl unit links a phenyl ring to the thiophene through a ketone carbonyl, so the aromatic systems are connected by a single flexible carbonyl linker rather than being fused. Functional groups include a carboxylic acid, which carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and a diaryl ketone whose carbonyl oxygen is an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The alpha carbon is a stereocenter, so the structure is chiral, and the overall shape is asymmetric because the two substituents on the thiophene differ. The molecule has moderate conformational flexibility from the rotatable bonds around the side chain and the ketone linker.

The molecule is a benzamide built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. The amide carbonyl is attached to the ring at one position, with an N-H group linking it to a flexible two-carbon chain that terminates in a diethylamino group. Adjacent to the amide on the ring sits a methoxy group, and a methylsulfonyl group occupies a position meta to the amide on the opposite side of the ring. The molecule has no stereocenters and little overall symmetry, though the diethyl terminus has local two-fold symmetry. The ethylene linker and the tertiary amine make the side chain quite flexible, while the aromatic core and amide are comparatively rigid. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl, the sulfonyl oxygens, the methoxy oxygen, and the tertiary amine nitrogen can all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries a methylsulfonyl group (a sulfone bearing a methyl) at one position and a side chain at the para position. The side chain is a three-carbon unit: a secondary alcohol on the carbon attached to the ring, a primary hydroxymethyl group on the next carbon, and an amide nitrogen linking to a dichloroacetyl group. The benzene ring is flat and rigid, while the side chain contains several rotatable single bonds, giving the molecule moderate flexibility. There are two stereogenic centers in the side chain, so the molecule is chiral. Hydrogen-bond donors include the two hydroxyl groups and the amide N–H, while acceptors include the sulfone oxygens, the amide carbonyl oxygen, and both hydroxyl oxygens.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused or additional rings. The nitrogen carries a hydroxyl group directly attached to it, giving an N-hydroxy amine. Two geminal methyl groups sit on each carbon flanking the nitrogen, which creates a symmetric, sterically crowded pattern around the heteroatom. A single secondary alcohol hydroxyl group is located on the carbon opposite the nitrogen, at the position para to it in the ring. The overall framework is conformationally rigid because of the ring and the bulky methyl substituents, while the molecule has a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the axis running through the nitrogen and the hydroxylated carbon. Both hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ring nitrogen itself contributes only as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built around a diaryl sulfide core, with a sulfur atom bridging two para-substituted benzene rings. Each phenyl ring carries, at the position opposite the sulfur, an oxygen linked to a phosphorus center that is double-bonded to sulfur (a P=S thiophosphate unit) and bears two methoxy groups. The two halves are mirror-related, giving the whole structure a symmetric, roughly linear shape. Both aromatic rings are rigid, while the central sulfide linkage and the P–O–aryl bonds allow some rotational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H groups; its potential acceptors are the oxygen atoms of the ester-like linkages and methoxy groups.

The molecule is built on a 1,3,4-thiadiazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. At the 2-position of this ring sits an N-methyl amino group that is part of a urea unit, where a carbonyl bears an NH-methyl substituent, and the nitrogen attached to the ring also carries a methyl group. At the 5-position of the thiadiazole is a tert-butyl group, a bulky, sterically demanding, non-polar substituent with three methyl groups on a central quaternary carbon. The molecule has no stereocenters and no true rotational symmetry, though the tert-butyl group contributes local threefold symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the urea linkage and methyl groups allow some conformational flexibility. The secondary N-H of the urea acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the thiadiazole ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is an isopropyl thioether (a sulfur atom bonded to an isopropyl group), and the other is a two-carbon chain carrying a hydroxyl group on the carbon attached to the ring, followed by a secondary amine bonded to an n-octyl chain. The ring is aromatic and planar, while the aliphatic chains are flexible, with several rotatable bonds. The secondary amine nitrogen and the hydroxyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the thioether sulfur can serve as a weak acceptor. The molecule has two stereocenters, so it lacks an overall mirror plane, and its overall shape is elongated and asymmetric.

This molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing a primary aromatic amine at one position and a sulfonyl group at the para position, giving a 1,4-disubstituted, planar aromatic core. The sulfonyl group connects through a nitrogen to a carbonyl, forming an acyl sulfonamide linker that joins the first ring to a second, unsubstituted benzene ring carrying a benzoyl unit. The two rings are attached through a flexible linker that allows some rotation, though the aromatic rings themselves are rigid and flat. The amino group and the acidic N-H of the sulfonamide act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl and carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the two aromatic rings carry different substitution patterns.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic 1,3,5-triazine ring, with three nitrogen atoms alternating with three carbon atoms. Two of the ring carbons carry isopropylamino groups (–NH–CH(CH₃)₂), each attached through a secondary amine nitrogen, while the third ring carbon bears a chlorine atom, giving the ring a 2,4-diamino-6-chloro substitution pattern. The core is fully planar and rigid, and the two isopropyl groups are the only flexible, sp³-rich portions of the structure. The molecule has an approximate mirror-like symmetry across the axis passing through the chlorine-bearing carbon and the opposite ring nitrogen, since the two amino substituents are identical. The two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogens and the amine nitrogens provide acceptor sites.

The molecule is an anilide built from a single benzene ring bearing a propanamide group on one carbon and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, at the 3 and 4 positions relative to the amide nitrogen. The core scaffold is a planar aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is meta and para on the same side of the ring. The amide linkage, a secondary amide with an N-H donor and a carbonyl oxygen acceptor, connects an ethyl-terminated acyl chain to the ring. The two chlorine atoms are electron-withdrawing halogens that add lipophilic bulk but do not donate hydrogen bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are not arranged symmetrically around the ring, and it is moderately flexible through rotation about the ethyl and amide bonds, while the aromatic ring stays rigid.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, with a secondary alcohol and an isopropyl-substituted amine attached to a side chain at one ring position. The side chain begins at the aromatic carbon and runs through a hydroxylated carbon, then a CH2 group, to a secondary amine nitrogen bearing an isopropyl group. The aromatic system is planar and rigid, while the side chain contributes conformational flexibility through its rotatable single bonds. The hydroxyl group and the secondary amine each act as hydrogen-bond donors, and both the oxygen and nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituent sits on one ring at a single asymmetric position, and the hydroxylated carbon is a stereocenter.

The molecule is built around a biguanide-type backbone, a central chain of two guanidine-like units linked through an NH bridge. One terminus carries an isopropyl group attached to nitrogen, while the other terminus is bonded to a benzene ring bearing a chlorine atom at the position para to the nitrogen attachment, giving a 1,4-disubstituted aromatic pattern. The aromatic ring is a single unfused six-membered ring, and the rest of the molecule is acyclic, so overall flexibility comes mainly from the rotatable single bonds in the chain. The guanidine-like nitrogens bear multiple N–H groups and imine (C=N) functionalities, so the molecule offers several hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. Because the isopropyl end and the para-chlorophenyl end are different, the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with an acetamide group (an N-acylated amine, CH3C(=O)NH-) on one side and an ether-linked side chain on the opposite side. The side chain is a three-carbon unit containing a secondary alcohol and terminates in a secondary isopropylamine, giving a flexible, non-cyclic tail attached to the aromatic core through an aryl ether oxygen. The only ring system is the single benzene ring, which is unfused, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two ends are chemically distinct. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the amide N-H, the hydroxyl O-H, and the secondary amine N-H, while acceptor sites include the amide carbonyl oxygen, the ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the amine nitrogen. The chain's several rotatable bonds make the overall structure fairly flexible.

The molecule is built around a central piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. One nitrogen is bonded directly to a pyrimidine ring, an aromatic six-membered ring with two nitrogens in a 1,3 arrangement, attached through its carbon at the 2-position. The other piperazine nitrogen carries a benzyl-type CH2 group that links to a 1,3-benzodioxole unit, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered dioxole ring containing two oxygens joined by a methylene bridge. The aromatic portions are planar and rigid, while the piperazine core adds conformational flexibility. The molecule has no overall mirror or rotational symmetry because the two ends differ. Hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the pyrimidine nitrogens, the two dioxole oxygens, and the tertiary amine nitrogens, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a tricyclic fused scaffold in which a furan ring is fused to a benzene ring that is in turn fused to a coumarin-type lactone ring, giving a linear arrangement of three aromatic-containing rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH₃) sit on adjacent carbons of the central benzene ring, creating a contiguous substitution pattern on one side of the fused system. The lactone carbonyl and the ring oxygens of the furan and pyranone rings are the main hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The flat, fully fused polycyclic framework is rigid, with only the methoxy groups providing rotational freedom.

This molecule is built around a five-membered lactone ring, a saturated gamma-butyrolactone in which the carbonyl sits adjacent to the ring oxygen. An ethyl group is attached at the carbon next to the carbonyl, and a CH2 linker at the adjacent ring carbon connects to a second heterocycle. That heterocycle is an N-methylimidazole, a five-membered aromatic ring with two nitrogens, where the methyl sits on one ring nitrogen and the linker attaches at a carbon. The two ring systems are not fused but joined by a single methylene bridge, giving a moderately flexible scaffold with one stereogenic center per saturated ring carbon bearing substituents. Functionally, the lactone ester provides a carbonyl oxygen acceptor, the ring ether oxygen is an additional weak acceptor, and the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent, so it is a monosubstituted phenyl group attached to a two-carbon aliphatic chain. The chain carries a secondary alcohol on the carbon directly bonded to the aromatic ring and a primary amine on the adjacent carbon, which places an amino group and a hydroxyl group on neighboring sp3 centers. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the acyclic chain provides rotational flexibility, so the overall shape is only partly constrained. Both the hydroxyl and the amino group can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, giving the molecule two polar sites. The molecule has two stereocenters and no internal symmetry that would make it superimposable on its mirror image.

The molecule is an N-(2-hydroxyethyl) amide: a straight, unbranched saturated alkyl chain of sixteen carbons terminates in a secondary amide carbonyl, which is bonded to an ethanolamine unit ending in a primary hydroxyl group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. The long methylene chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, while the amide linkage is planar and relatively rigid. Because the molecule is not symmetric, it lacks any meaningful symmetry element. The amide N–H and the terminal hydroxyl O–H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a highly oxygenated, polycyclic diterpenoid-type scaffold built from fused carbocyclic and oxygen-containing rings, including a strained oxetane-like fused ether ring. Its core contains a bridged framework with several quaternary carbons, and it carries multiple ester groups: two acetate esters, a benzoate ester, and a side-chain ester linked to an N-benzoyl phenylisoserine-like unit bearing two phenyl rings. Hydroxyl groups are present at several positions, along with a ketone on the ring system, and an amide linkage in the side chain. The overall framework is conformationally rigid because of its fused and bridged rings, though the pendant side chain provides some flexibility. The molecule offers numerous hydrogen-bond acceptor sites at its carbonyl and ether oxygens and several hydrogen-bond donor sites from its hydroxyl and amide groups.

This molecule has a steroidal four-ring scaffold: three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, typical of a gonane skeleton. The A ring is an enone-containing ring, with a ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated within the fused system, while the D ring carries a tertiary alcohol and a terminal alkyne substituent at the same carbon, alongside an angular methyl group on the ring junction. The ring fusions are all trans-type, making the core rigid and largely planar in shape, with limited conformational freedom beyond the saturated ring puckering. The molecule is not symmetric, since the A and D rings differ in their functionalization. Its hydrogen-bond capability is limited to the hydroxyl group, which can act as both a donor and an acceptor, plus the ketone oxygen, which acts only as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a pyrazolone core, a five-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogens and a carbonyl group, which is fused to nothing else. An N-phenyl group is attached to one ring nitrogen, and the other ring nitrogen carries an N-methyl group, while a methyl substituent sits on the carbon adjacent to it. A third, exocyclic substituent on the ring carbon is an amide linkage connecting to a pyridine-3-carboxamide unit. The structure contains three aromatic systems (the phenyl ring, the pyridine ring, and the pyrazolone ring) joined through rotatable single bonds, giving moderate flexibility around the amide and aryl linkages. The amide N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygens and the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is a morphinan-type polycyclic alkaloid built on a rigid, fused pentacyclic framework containing a tertiary amine within a piperidine ring. An aromatic benzene ring carries a phenolic hydroxyl group and is bridged through an ether oxygen to the saturated core, creating a dihydrofuran-type fusion. A secondary alcohol sits on one of the partially unsaturated six-membered rings, which also contains a cis-alkene. The N-allyl group, a three-carbon chain with a terminal double bond, is attached to the nitrogen. The overall structure is largely three-dimensional and conformationally constrained, with few freely rotating bonds. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity comes from the phenolic and alcoholic hydroxyls, while the ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygens, and the tertiary nitrogen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is an ergoline-type scaffold: a tetracyclic system built from a fused indole unit joined to a partly saturated six-membered ring and a tetrahydropyridine ring, with an N-methyl on the indole nitrogen and a second N-methyl on the amine in the piperidine-type ring. The indole and the adjacent rings are fused, creating a rigid, largely planar aromatic core with limited conformational freedom, while the ring bearing the amide side chain adds some three-dimensional character. A carboxamide links the core to a branched side chain carrying a primary alcohol, which provides one hydrogen-bond donor and an additional oxygen acceptor. The amide carbonyl and the tertiary amine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the amide N-H serves as a donor. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its substitution pattern is asymmetric throughout.

This molecule is built on a central quaternary carbon bearing two phenyl rings, giving a diaryl scaffold. One branch is an ethyl ketone (a propanoyl group), and the other is a CH2 linked to a chiral carbon that carries a methyl group and a tertiary dimethylamino nitrogen. Both phenyl rings are unsubstituted benzene rings, so the aromatic portion is symmetric about the central carbon, but the stereocenter on the side chain removes overall symmetry. The ketone carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the tertiary amine nitrogen is a basic acceptor with no hydrogen-bond donor groups present. The structure has several rotatable single bonds and is therefore fairly flexible, although the bulky quaternary center restricts its conformations.

This molecule is a fully saturated-plus-enone steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene arrangement. Ring A is a cross-conjugated dienone, with two carbon-carbon double bonds conjugated to a ketone, while the other rings carry a ketone and an additional carbonyl on a two-carbon side chain. A tertiary hydroxyl sits at a ring-fusion-adjacent carbon, bearing the alpha-ketol side chain. Two methyl groups are attached at angular and ring positions, adding steric bulk. The fused framework is rigid, with only the side chain showing rotational freedom. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the single hydroxyl group, while the three carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a small acyclic tertiary amine, with a central nitrogen bearing one methyl group and two 2-chloroethyl arms, so its skeleton is a simple branched chain with no rings and no ring fusion. The two terminal chlorine atoms, each attached to a primary carbon at the end of an ethyl chain, are the only functional groups beyond the amine, and they sit in a symmetric arrangement across the nitrogen. The molecule has an approximate mirror-symmetric layout about the N–CH3 axis, and its many single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. The nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since it contains no N–H or O–H bonds.

Parsing the SMILES: a tricyclic-like fused system. A para-chlorophenyl ring is attached to a quaternary sp3 carbon bearing a hydroxyl group. That carbon is fused to a benzene ring (ortho-disubstituted), and also sits within a five-membered ring containing the carbon, the benzo carbons, an amidine-type C=N, and a nitrogen that is shared with a six-membered dihydropyrazine-like ring (N–CH2–CH2–N=C). So the scaffold is a fused benzo-imidazo-pyrazine-type polycycle with the hydroxyl-bearing carbon as a bridgehead-like junction.

Functional groups: one tertiary alcohol, one C=N imine (amidine character), one tertiary amine nitrogen, and a chlorine atom in a para position on the pendant phenyl ring. The molecule has no plane of symmetry because the fused rings and the aryl substituent break it. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the saturated two-carbon linker gives some flexibility. The hydroxyl group is a hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen and the imine nitrogen act as acceptors.

This molecule is a nitrosourea, built around a central urea-type carbonyl that links a cyclohexylamine-derived nitrogen to a nitrogen bearing both a nitroso group and a 2-chloroethyl chain. The cyclohexyl ring is a saturated six-membered carbocycle with no fusion or unsaturation, giving it a chair-like, conformationally flexible framework. The N-nitroso group (N=O) and the carbonyl oxygen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the single N-H on the cyclohexyl-bearing nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The chloroethyl side chain adds a flexible, non-aromatic tether with a terminal halogen. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the two substituents on the urea nitrogens differ fundamentally in character.

This molecule is built on a cyclohexanone scaffold, with a single ketone carbonyl on the six-membered ring. The ring carbon adjacent to that carbonyl is quaternary, carrying both a methylamino group (a secondary amine bearing one methyl substituent) and a 2-chlorophenyl ring attached through a single bond. The aromatic ring is a benzene with a chlorine atom on the carbon immediately next to the point of attachment, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the quaternary center carries four distinct groups. The saturated cyclohexanone ring is conformationally flexible, while the aryl-to-ring bond restricts rotation somewhat. The nitrogen-hydrogen group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen, the nitrogen lone pair, and the chlorine can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six substituents, so it has no fused ring system. The ring carries three iodine atoms placed at alternating positions, giving a symmetric pattern around the core. Two acetamide-type groups are present: one attached through a CH2 linker (an N-acetylaminomethyl group) and one attached directly to the ring as an N-acetyl amino group. The remaining ring position carries a carboxylic acid group, which together with the two amide NH groups supplies hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and the acid oxygens act as acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid, while the CH2 linker and the amide side chains add some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built around a central two-carbon backbone in which each carbon carries an ethyl group and a para-hydroxyphenyl ring, so it is a symmetric 3,4-diarylhexane skeleton. Both aromatic rings are unfused benzene rings, each bearing a single phenolic hydroxyl group at the position opposite the point of attachment. The molecule is essentially mirror-symmetric about the central carbon-carbon bond, with two identical halves. The two stereocenters on the backbone allow several stereoisomers, and the connecting sp3 chain gives moderate conformational flexibility. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, giving the molecule two donor and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a flavanone scaffold: a saturated six-membered oxygen heterocycle (a chromanone ring) fused to a benzene ring, with a ketone carbonyl at position 4 and a single stereocenter at the carbon bearing the aryl substituent. The aryl group is a phenyl ring carrying a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group in a 3-hydroxy-4-methoxy pattern. The fused benzo ring carries two additional hydroxyl groups, giving a 5,7-dihydroxy substitution pattern. Because the central heterocycle is saturated, the scaffold is moderately rigid but not planar, and the pendant aryl ring can rotate about its single bond. The phenolic hydroxyls and the ketone oxygen provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the ether oxygens add further acceptor capacity.

This molecule is a steroidal spirostan-type scaffold: a rigid, fused polycyclic core of four carbocyclic rings in a cholestane-like framework, terminating in a spiro-linked tetrahydropyran-type oxygen-containing ring that is joined at a single quaternary spiro carbon. The fused ring system is largely rigid, though the spiroketal side ring retains some conformational flexibility. A single secondary hydroxyl group sits on one of the saturated rings, and a ketone carbonyl is present on another ring, giving one hydrogen-bond donor and several acceptor oxygens, including the ether-type oxygens of the spiroketal. Methyl substituents are distributed at several ring-junction and ring positions, producing an asymmetric, stereochemically dense substitution pattern with no overall molecular symmetry.

This molecule is built around a thiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing both sulfur and nitrogen, which serves as the central scaffold. At the 2-position of the thiazole sits a guanidine group, attached through an N-aryl linkage. From the 4-position, a flexible chain runs through a thioether sulfur and two methylene units to an amidine-type carbon bearing a sulfonyl-amide (sulfamoyl) group on the imine nitrogen. The chain's several single bonds and the thioether give the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, while the heteroaromatic core is planar and rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry. It is rich in hydrogen-bonding capability, with multiple N–H groups acting as donors and the thiazole nitrogen, sulfonyl oxygens, and imine nitrogen acting as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzamide bearing an n-hexyloxy chain on the ring carbon adjacent to the amide, so the two substituents sit ortho to each other on a single benzene ring. The core scaffold is a six-membered aromatic ring carrying a primary carboxamide, which is planar and conjugated with the ring, while the hexyl ether tail is a flexible, unbranched alkyl chain of six carbons linked through an oxygen atom. The molecule has no stereocenters and no rings beyond the benzene ring, and its overall shape is asymmetric because the two substituents differ in size and character. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites on the nitrogen and one acceptor site on the carbonyl oxygen, and the ether oxygen provides an additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an acyclic organophosphorus compound built around a central methylene bridge that links two identical diethyl phosphorodithioate units through sulfur atoms, giving a symmetric S–CH2–S linker. Each phosphorus center is tetrahedral and bears a P=S double bond, two ethoxy groups, and a thioether sulfur connecting to the central carbon. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain. The structure is highly flexible, with many rotatable P–O, P–S, and C–S bonds allowing extensive conformational freedom. The two halves are related by a mirror or C2-type symmetry through the central methylene carbon. The molecule has no classical hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no O–H or N–H groups, but the sulfur and oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a pentacyclic triterpenoid built on a fused polycyclic skeleton, with five rings arranged in a largely linear-angular fashion typical of oleanane-type scaffolds. It contains a carboxylic acid group on a quaternary carbon at one end, a secondary hydroxyl group on a ring carbon near the opposite end, and an α,β-unsaturated ketone embedded in one of the central rings conjugated with a carbon-carbon double bond. Multiple angular methyl groups sit at quaternary centers, giving the molecule a bulky, rigid framework with little rotational freedom, and it lacks any overall symmetry. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups, while the carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, all linked in a rigid, cage-like framework. At one end of the five-membered ring sits a propanoate ester, formed from a propionic acid unit attached through an oxygen. A ketone sits in one of the six-membered rings, adjacent to a methyl-bearing carbon, and two additional methyl groups are attached at ring-fusion positions. The ester carbonyl and the ketone oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its oxygen-bearing sites lack acidic hydrogens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a rigid, planar aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The ring carries six substituents: a methyl group, a primary carboxamide, and two nitro groups, arranged so that the nitro groups sit meta to one another and the methyl and carboxamide occupy adjacent positions. The nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and are conjugated with the ring, while the carboxamide contributes a -C(=O)NH2 unit. Because the substitution pattern is asymmetric, the molecule has no internal symmetry. Its functional groups provide hydrogen-bond donor capability through the two amide N-H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through the amide carbonyl oxygen and the oxygens of both nitro groups.

The molecule is a steroid-type scaffold: four fused rings in the classic cyclopentanophenanthrene arrangement, with a cross-conjugated dienone in ring A and a fully saturated cyclopentane D ring. The two outer rings are fused with trans-configured junctions, giving the core a rigid, roughly planar-to-bowed shape. Substituents decorate the framework, including two fluorine atoms on the B and C rings, a tertiary hydroxyl near the C ring, a methyl group on the D ring, and a two-carbon ketone side chain at the D-ring junction that is esterified with a straight-chain pentanoyl group. The ester and ketone carbonyls, along with the ring ketone, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the single secondary alcohol offers one hydrogen-bond donor. The overall framework is largely rigid, with flexibility confined mainly to the pentanoyl ester chain.

This molecule is a nucleoside analogue built from a saturated five-membered oxolane (tetrahydrofuran) ring, bearing a hydroxymethyl group on one carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen and a purine-type heterocycle attached at the other adjacent carbon. The purine is a fused bicyclic system of a five-membered imidazole ring joined to a six-membered pyrimidine ring, with nitrogen atoms at several positions and a hydroxyl group on the six-membered ring, which can exist in a tautomeric lactam form. The sugar-like ring is flexible and puckered, while the fused aromatic base is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. The primary alcohol and the ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the purine nitrogens and the hydroxyl on the base provide additional hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

This molecule is a steroid, built on the fused four-ring cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene scaffold: three six-membered rings fused linearly-angularly to a five-membered ring. A saturated side chain of a methyl-branched butanoic acid unit hangs from the five-membered ring. Three ketone carbonyls sit on the ring framework, and a terminal carboxylic acid group sits at the end of the side chain. Two angular methyl groups are attached at ring-fusion carbons. The fused polycyclic core is rigid, while the side chain is flexible. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, and the three ketones act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-like fused polycyclic framework made of four rings, three six-membered and one five-membered, joined by shared bonds in a rigid, largely planar-to-puckered arrangement typical of the gonane skeleton. At one end, a five-membered ring carries a terminal alkyne substituent and a tertiary hydroxyl group on the same carbon, with two angular methyl groups on the ring junctions. The fourth ring is an isoxazole, an aromatic five-membered ring containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, fused onto the central six-membered ring, which contributes a conjugated double bond. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring oxygen and nitrogen of the isoxazole serve as acceptors. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because of its asymmetric heterocyclic fusion.

This molecule is a cardenolide-type steroid glycoside built on a fused four-ring tetracyclic skeleton, with three rings in a six-membered series and one five-membered ring carrying a substituent. The steroid core is rigid and largely saturated, with ring fusions that give it a bowl-like, angular shape. At one end of the framework sits an unsaturated five-membered lactone ring attached to the five-membered ring, and a formyl group projects from a ring-fusion carbon. Two tertiary hydroxyl groups are present on the core, and a sugar unit is attached through a glycosidic ether linkage. The sugar carries several free hydroxyls and a methyl group, providing multiple hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the lactone carbonyl and ether oxygens serve as additional acceptors. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry and is conformationally constrained by its fused rings, apart from the flexible glycosidic linkage.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a phenol group, with a 2,2,4,4-tetramethylbutyl-type tert-alkyl substituent (a bulky, sterically hindered aliphatic chain featuring two quaternary carbons) attached para to the hydroxyl. A second benzene ring, carrying chlorine atoms at the 2- and 4-positions, is connected to the phenol ring through a single methylene bridge at the position ortho to the OH. The two aromatic rings are not fused; they are linked by a flexible CH2 spacer, giving the scaffold a diarylmethane-type core. The phenolic hydroxyl serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor character. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two aryl rings are substituted differently, and its bulky alkyl groups add conformational constraint around the aryl–alkyl bond.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one cyclopentane ring, with a cross-conjugated dienone in ring A and a saturated, highly substituted ring D. The skeleton is rigid and largely planar in its fused core, though the 17-position ester and the chloromethyl ketone side chain add conformational flexibility. Functional groups include a propanoate ester, a ketone bearing an alpha-chlorine, a tertiary fluorine, a secondary alcohol, and two conjugated carbonyls in the dienone. Substitution is asymmetric, with methyl groups at several ring-junction positions and a methyl on the cyclopentane, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity comes solely from the single hydroxyl group, while the multiple carbonyl and ester oxygens, along with the fluorine, serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a quinuclidine-based alkaloid built around a bridged bicyclic amine, specifically a 1-azabicyclo[2.2.2]octane core bearing a vinyl group on one bridgehead-adjacent carbon. The bicyclic cage is rigid and three-dimensional, with a tertiary nitrogen at the bridgehead. A secondary alcohol connects the cage at the carbon next to the nitrogen to a quinoline ring, which is a fused bicyclic aromatic system of a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the vinyl group, hydroxyl carbon, and quinoline attachment break the cage's symmetry. The hydroxyl group and the pyridine-type nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary amine serves as an additional acceptor.

This molecule is built on a pyrimidine-2,4-dione (uracil-type) ring, a six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogens and two carbonyl groups. A fluorine atom sits on the ring carbon at position 5, and the ring is otherwise unfused, so the core is flat and rigid. On the nitrogen at position 1 there is an N-linked carboxamide, bearing an unbranched six-carbon alkyl chain that gives the molecule a flexible tail. The molecule has no symmetry, because the fluorine and the carbamoyl substituent break any internal mirror plane. Hydrogen-bond capability comes from one N-H donor on the ring, while the two ring carbonyl oxygens and the amide carbonyl oxygen act as acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic scaffold built from four rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, fused together in the classic cyclopenta-phenanthrene arrangement. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-junction carbons, and a secondary alcohol sits on one of the six-membered rings. A tertiary alcohol occupies a ring-junction position on the fused framework, and a six-membered unsaturated lactone (a 2-pyranone ring) is attached as a substituent on the five-membered ring. The fused core is largely saturated and conformationally rigid, while the pyranone ring is planar and aromatic-like. Hydroxyl groups and the lactone carbonyl and ring oxygen provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

This molecule is a fused tetracyclic heteroaromatic system built around a central triazole ring that is fused to a thiophene ring and to a seven-membered diazepine ring bearing an imine (C=N) linkage. The triazole carries a methyl group on one carbon, while the thiophene carries a bromine substituent on the carbon adjacent to sulfur.
