A 2-chlorophenyl group hangs off the diazepine carbon that is double-bonded to nitrogen, which gives the pendant aryl ring an ortho chlorine. The fused polycyclic core is largely planar and rigid, with only the chlorophenyl ring able to rotate about its single bond. Hydrogen-bond acceptor capability comes from the triazole and imine nitrogens, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a central sp3 methine carbon bearing three aromatic substituents: two para-substituted phenyl rings and one pyridin-2-yl ring, giving a diarylpyridylmethane scaffold. Each phenyl ring carries an acetyl ester group (an acetoxy substituent) at the para position, so the two ester groups are symmetric about the central carbon, though the pyridine ring breaks full mirror symmetry. The central carbon is tetrahedral, which makes the three-ring arrangement propeller-like and moderately flexible around the single bonds, while each aromatic ring is rigid and planar. The ester carbonyl oxygens and the pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered heterocycle containing a nitrogen, a sulfur, and a carbonyl carbon. The aromatic ring is ortho-disubstituted, with the amide-type carbonyl on one carbon and an NH nitrogen on the adjacent carbon, giving the fused system a largely planar, rigid character. The sulfur atom is in a sulfonyl (S(=O)2) oxidation state, bonded to the ring nitrogen and to a second nitrogen, and the lactam-type carbonyl sits alongside it. An isopropyl group is attached to the ring nitrogen that bears the carbonyl, which introduces a branched, non-planar substituent. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the isopropyl group and the benzo ring sit on opposite sides of the heterocycle. The NH group provides a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl and sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzazepinone scaffold: a seven-membered lactam ring fused to a benzene ring, with the lactam nitrogen bearing a carboxymethyl group. Attached at the saturated carbon adjacent to the lactam carbonyl is an amino linkage that connects to a phenylpropyl side chain ending in an ethyl ester. The aromatic rings are unsubstituted phenyl groups, giving the core a fused bicyclic framework with a fairly rigid bicyclic portion and a flexible tether. The molecule lacks any symmetry because of its distinct substituents on the ring nitrogen and the stereocentres. It contains a secondary amine N-H, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, along with several carbonyl oxygens and the carboxylic acid group that serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a large macrolide built on a fifteen-membered lactone ring, with an ester carbonyl embedded in the ring and multiple methyl branches along the backbone. Within that macrocycle sits a nitrogen-containing ring that is bridged into the framework, so the lactone and the amine-containing segment are linked rather than fused in a simple manner. Two appended sugar residues are attached through glycosidic linkages: one is a 2,6-dideoxy-type ring bearing a methoxy group and a free hydroxyl, and the other carries a dimethylamino substituent. Hydroxyl groups are distributed around the macrocycle, along with a tertiary amine and several ether oxygens, giving the molecule many hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The overall scaffold is asymmetric and conformationally constrained by its rings, with flexibility mainly in the alkyl side chains.

This molecule is built around a central sp2 carbon that links two identical 4-hydroxy-3-carboxyphenyl rings and a quinoid-type cyclohexadienone ring bearing a carboxylic acid and a ketone, giving a triarylmethane-like scaffold. The two outer benzene rings are each substituted with a phenolic hydroxyl and an ortho-positioned carboxylic acid, creating a salicylic acid motif on each arm. The central six-membered ring is a conjugated cyclohexadienone, with its carbonyl and carboxylic acid groups contributing to an extended planar π-system. The arrangement is propeller-like around the central carbon, with the three aryl-type units twisted out of a common plane, which limits overall rigidity. The molecule has no strict symmetry because the quinoid ring differs from the two phenyl arms, though the two phenolic arms are equivalent. Multiple hydroxyl and carboxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused scaffold, with three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring arranged in the familiar cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene pattern. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-fusion carbons, giving the framework its characteristic three-dimensional shape. The first ring carries a conjugated enone, a ketone adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond, while a second ketone sits on the five-membered ring. The fused, largely saturated ring system is rigid, though some puckering is possible. Oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an ester built around a central carbon bearing two phenyl rings, giving a diphenylacetic acid-derived scaffold. The acid carbonyl is bonded through an oxygen to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a diethylamino group, so the tertiary amine sits at the far end of a flexible ethyl linker. Both aromatic rings are unsubstituted benzene rings attached to the same tetrahedral carbon, which gives the two rings a propeller-like, non-coplanar arrangement and some rotational freedom. The ester oxygen and carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the tertiary nitrogen is a basic acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a pyrimidine-2,4-dione (uracil-type) ring, bearing an ethyl group at the C5 position and a sugar-like ring attached through a nitrogen at N1. The attached five-membered ring is a saturated tetrahydrofuran with no ring fusion to the pyrimidinedione, and it carries a secondary hydroxyl group and a hydroxymethyl substituent. The uracil portion has an N3-H donor adjacent to two carbonyl acceptors, giving several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, and its two ring systems are joined by a single bond, so it has moderate conformational flexibility, mainly in the sugar-like ring.

This molecule is an aryl ether ester built on a benzene ring that carries two chlorine atoms at the 2 and 4 positions relative to the oxygen-linked side chain. The side chain is an oxyacetic acid unit whose carboxyl group is esterified with a methyl group, giving a methyl ester bonded to the ring through a flexible ether oxygen and methylene linker. The aromatic core is a single benzene ring with no fused rings, and its two chlorines create an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The ester carbonyl and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The chain's rotatable bonds make the molecule moderately flexible, although the planar aromatic ring remains rigid.

This molecule is a phenoxyacetic acid built on a benzene ring, with an ether-linked CH2–COOH group attached to one ring carbon. The aromatic ring carries three chlorine substituents at positions that leave two adjacent ring hydrogens, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The benzene core is rigid and planar, while the oxymethylene linker and carboxylic acid tail provide some rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (its O–H) and acceptor (its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a disaccharide built from two six-membered pyranose-type rings and a five-membered furanose-type ring joined through a single glycosidic linkage. The first unit is a fully hydroxylated six-membered ring with a hydroxymethyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, and the second unit is a five-membered ring whose anomeric carbon also bears a hydroxymethyl group, so the two rings connect through an acetal-type bridge at both anomeric centers. Every ring carbon that is not part of the glycosidic bond carries a free hydroxyl group, and there are several primary and secondary alcohol groups in total. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its ring fusion is absent since the two rings share only the linking oxygen, which gives moderate conformational flexibility around the glycosidic bond. Its many hydroxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, with the ring oxygens also serving as acceptors.

This molecule is quinic acid, a saturated cyclohexane ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and four hydroxyl groups. The carboxylic acid and one hydroxyl are both attached to the same ring carbon, creating a tertiary alcohol adjacent to the acid. The remaining three hydroxyls sit on separate ring carbons, giving a densely oxygenated, non-aromatic scaffold with no fused or bridged rings. Because the ring is fully saturated, it is conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair-like forms, though the many substituents restrict some motion. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane, so its carbons are stereochemically distinct. Its five hydroxyl and carboxyl oxygen atoms make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is a two-carbon dicarboxylic acid with no rings, consisting of a short, unbranched backbone in which two carboxyl groups are directly bonded to each other. Each carboxyl group contains a carbonyl oxygen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and a hydroxyl oxygen that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The structure is fully symmetric, with the two carboxyl units mirror-related across the central carbon-carbon bond. Because the backbone has only a single bond between the two carboxyl carbons and no ring constraints, the molecule is comparatively flexible about that bond. Its functional groups are limited entirely to these carboxylic acid units, with no other substituents present.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain attached at one position. The side chain contains a secondary amine bearing a methyl group, linked to a carbon that also carries a hydroxyl group, so the chain has one stereocenter. The aromatic ring carries two adjacent hydroxyl groups, a catechol arrangement, located at positions meta and para relative to the side chain attachment. Because the ring is fully substituted in a 1,2,4 pattern, the molecule lacks any mirror symmetry overall. Its three hydroxyl groups and one amine nitrogen give it several hydrogen-bond donor sites and acceptor sites, while the aromatic ring and flexible side chain together provide moderate conformational freedom.

The molecule given by this SMILES is hydrogen cyanide's structural counterpart in the nitrile class, consisting of a single carbon atom triple-bonded to a single nitrogen atom with no additional substituents. It has no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no branching, so the scaffold is simply a linear two-atom unit. The carbon atom carries no hydrogen atoms, and the nitrile group is the only functional group present. Because the triple bond forces a straight, rod-like geometry, the molecule is completely rigid and possesses high axial symmetry. The nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is a three-carbon acyclic chain, with no rings, so its scaffold is simply a linear propane-based skeleton. One end carries an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, with the carbon also bonded to hydrogen), while the central carbon bears a hydroxyl group and the terminal carbon bears a second hydroxyl group, giving a primary alcohol. The substitution pattern is therefore unsymmetrical: the aldehyde end differs from the primary alcohol end, and the central carbon is a stereogenic center, so the structure is chiral as written. Because the chain is open and freely rotatable, the molecule is quite flexible. Its three oxygen atoms and the two hydroxyl hydrogens give it multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon chain with a terminal primary amine, forming an aminoethyl side chain attached to one ring carbon. Two adjacent hydroxyl groups sit on the ring, giving a catechol unit (a 1,2-dihydroxybenzene arrangement) at positions that flank the chain in a 1,3,4 substitution pattern. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no additional ring fusion, so the core scaffold is simple and planar. The ethylamine tail is flexible, with free rotation about its two sigma bonds, while the aromatic core remains rigid. The primary amine and both phenolic hydroxyls act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the molecule lacks any stereocenters or symmetry element beyond a local mirror-like arrangement of the catechol.

This molecule is built around a saturated five-membered cyclic urea, an imidazolidin-2-one ring containing two nitrogen atoms flanking a carbonyl group. The ring carries a methyl group on one carbon adjacent to a nitrogen, and a flexible six-carbon chain bearing a terminal carboxylic acid is attached to the adjacent ring carbon. The ring is non-aromatic and has one stereogenic centre pair, so the scaffold is compact and fairly rigid while the alkyl chain adds considerable conformational flexibility. The cyclic urea provides two N–H hydrogen-bond donors and a carbonyl acceptor, and the carboxylic acid contributes an additional donor and two acceptor oxygens. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the methyl and chain substituents are placed asymmetrically on the ring.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated chain of six carbons, with a carboxylic acid group at each end and a hydroxyl group on each of the four interior carbons. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is a simple linear backbone. The two terminal carboxylic acids and four secondary alcohols give the structure a dense array of functional groups, arranged in a regular pattern along the chain. The molecule is symmetric about its central bond, since the substitution pattern reads the same from either end. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. Each of the six oxygen-bearing groups can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the structure a high capacity for hydrogen bonding.

SMILES N#CO corresponds to a very small molecule with a linear arrangement of three heavy atoms: a nitrogen triply bonded to a carbon, which is singly bonded to an oxygen. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution pattern to describe, and the molecule carries no symmetry beyond its linear geometry. Its structure is essentially a nitrile group attached to a terminal hydroxyl-type oxygen, giving it a rigid, linear backbone with very little conformational flexibility. The terminal oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitrogen of the nitrile offers a weaker acceptor site, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

This molecule is a four-carbon, acyclic amino dicarboxylic acid built on a linear chain with no rings. It carries an alpha-amino group on the carbon adjacent to one carboxylic acid, and a second carboxylic acid group at the chain terminus, so the two acid groups sit at opposite ends of the backbone. The alpha-carbon is a stereocenter, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the amine and the two acid groups are placed asymmetrically along the chain. Its flexible, unbranched backbone allows free rotation about the single bonds. The amino group and both carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, giving the molecule several polar sites.

The SMILES string "S" denotes a single sulfur atom with no attached atoms, which corresponds to a bare sulfur atom (as in a sulfur species in its elemental or ionic form) rather than a molecule with a carbon skeleton. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no functional groups, so there is no scaffold, substitution pattern, or internal symmetry to describe beyond the trivial spherical arrangement of a lone atom. The structure is completely rigid in the sense that there are no rotatable bonds to produce conformational flexibility. Because the atom carries no hydrogen atoms, it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and it offers no lone-pair-bearing heteroatom substituents beyond its own valence electrons, so any acceptor character is limited to that single sulfur centre.

This molecule is a disaccharide built from two six-membered pyranose rings joined through a glycosidic linkage. Each ring is saturated and carries a hydroxymethyl group and several hydroxyl groups, so the scaffold is a pair of fused-by-linkage cyclic polyol units rather than a flat aromatic system. The two rings are connected by a single oxygen bridge at an anomeric carbon, giving a flexible connection that allows rotation about the linkage. The substitution pattern is dense and asymmetric, with eight free hydroxyl groups and two exocyclic CH2OH groups distributed around the rings. Because of this many hydroxyls, the molecule can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor at numerous sites.

Carbon dioxide is a small linear molecule consisting of a single central carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms through double bonds. It has no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no substituents, so the scaffold is simply the O=C=O backbone itself. The molecule possesses high symmetry, with the two oxygen atoms related by a mirror plane through the central carbon, and its geometry is rigid and linear with no rotatable bonds. Because it has no N–H or O–H groups, it cannot donate hydrogen bonds, but its oxygen atoms carry lone pairs and can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a cyclic nucleotide built on a purine scaffold, specifically an adenine core in which the nitrogen at position 9 is bonded to a sugar. The fused bicyclic purine system contains a six-membered and a five-membered aromatic ring sharing an edge, bearing an exocyclic amino group on the six-membered ring. The sugar portion is a ribose-type furanose ring that is bridged to a phosphate through a second fused ring, creating a rigid, bicyclic cyclic phosphate. The molecule has several hydroxyl and phosphate oxygens, so it can donate hydrogen bonds from the hydroxyl and P–OH groups and accept them at the ring nitrogens and phosphoryl oxygen. The overall structure is largely rigid, with limited flexibility confined mainly to the bond rotations around the glycosidic linkage.

This molecule is a phosphate diester built around a central phosphorus atom bearing one double-bonded oxygen, one free hydroxyl group, and two aryloxy substituents. Each aryloxy arm is a benzene ring, so the scaffold is symmetric about the phosphorus center. Each benzene ring carries a nitro group (–NO₂) positioned para to the oxygen linkage, giving a linear, 1,4-disubstituted pattern on both rings. The two aromatic rings are rigid and planar, while the P–O–C linkages provide rotational flexibility that lets the arms adopt different spatial orientations. The free P–OH and the P=O oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitro oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a four-carbon acyclic chain, so its scaffold is an open-chain (aliphatic) backbone with no rings and no ring fusion. The chain carries a carboxylic acid group at one terminus and a primary carboxamide group at the other, with a primary amine sitting on the carbon between them, so the amine is attached to the alpha position relative to the acid. The substitution pattern is therefore linear with a single branching amine. Because the chain is flexible and has no stereochemical constraints imposed by rings, it can adopt many conformations. Its functional groups give it several hydrogen-bond donor sites (the amine and the amide and acid N-H and O-H hydrogens) and several acceptor sites (the carbonyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen).

This molecule is a four-carbon-free, two-carbon dicarboxylic acid backbone: a short saturated chain of two carbon atoms, each bearing a carboxylic acid group at one end, with a hydroxyl group attached to each of the central carbons. Its scaffold is entirely acyclic, so it contains no ring systems or ring fusion and is conformationally flexible about its single C–C bond. The two carboxyl groups and the two secondary alcohol groups are placed symmetrically across the chain, giving the molecule a plane of symmetry through the central C–C bond. Each carboxylic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and each hydroxyl can likewise act as a donor and acceptor, so the molecule has four hydrogen-bond donors and up to eight acceptor sites in total.

The molecule is an unbranched carbon chain with a terminal alkyne at one end and a carboxylic acid at the other, giving a linear, open-chain scaffold with no ring systems or ring fusion. The triple bond between the first two carbons is a rigid, linear unit, while the remaining saturated methylene segment is flexible and can adopt many conformations. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, and the terminal alkyne C-H can also act as a weak donor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because its two ends differ in functionality, and no substituents branch off the main chain.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane ring, a saturated six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings and no aromatic character. A tert-butyl group, a carbon bearing three methyl groups, is attached at one ring carbon, and an acetate ester (an acetyl group bonded through an oxygen) is attached at the carbon directly across the ring, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern. Because both substituents sit para to each other on the ring, the molecule has a fairly symmetric shape. The ring is conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair forms, while the bulky tert-butyl group tends to favor an equatorial position. The ester oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A nitro group sits on one ring carbon, ortho to a secondary amine bearing a 2-hydroxyethyl chain, and a tertiary amine bearing two 2-hydroxyethyl arms sits meta to the nitro group on the opposite side. The ring is aromatic and planar, while the three hydroxyethyl chains are flexible and can rotate freely. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the three hydroxyl groups and the secondary amine N–H provide several donor and acceptor sites. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

This molecule is a tetrachlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxin, built from two benzene rings fused to a central six-membered 1,4-dioxin ring bridged by two oxygen atoms. The fused tricyclic scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Four chlorine atoms sit on the two outer benzene rings in a symmetric 2,3,7,8-type arrangement, giving the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with a twofold axis and mirror planes through the central ring. The ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every carbon-bound position is either aromatic C-H or C-Cl.

The molecule is a tricyclic scaffold in which two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms, creating a dibenzo-p-dioxin core. The central ring is a 1,4-dioxin unit bridging the two aromatic rings, so the ring system is essentially planar and rigid. A single chlorine atom is attached to one of the outer benzene rings, adjacent to a ring-fusion ether oxygen, which breaks the symmetry of the otherwise symmetric core. The two ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall, the structure is a compact, flat, aromatic framework with limited conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a tetrahydroisoquinoline, a bicyclic scaffold in which a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring is fused to a benzene ring. The nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but not a donor. Two adjacent hydroxyl groups sit on the aromatic ring, forming a catechol unit that provides two hydrogen-bond donors and two acceptors. The substitution pattern is 1,2 on the benzene ring with the fused ring occupying the remaining positions, giving the molecule no internal symmetry. The saturated ring adopts a rather flexible half-chair-like conformation, while the fused aromatic portion remains planar and rigid.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three iodine atoms, an acetamido group, and an ether-linked side chain. The aromatic core is fully substituted in a pattern where the iodines sit at three positions and the acetamido nitrogen occupies a fourth, leaving the oxygen-bearing carbon as the attachment point for a flexible two-carbon ether linker. That linker connects to a branched aliphatic chain ending in a carboxylic acid, with the branch point bearing an ethyl group. The amide NH and the carboxylic acid OH serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygens act as acceptors. The aromatic ring and amide are rigid, whereas the ether-linked tail is conformationally flexible, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group and a sulfonamide nitrogen attached to a trifluoromethanesulfonyl group. A second benzene ring is connected to the first through a sulfone linkage, so the aromatic system is a diaryl sulfone with a para relationship to the sulfonamide nitrogen. The molecule has no fused ring systems, and the two aromatic rings are joined by a single flexible sulfur bridge. The trifluoromethyl sulfonyl portion is strongly electron-withdrawing, and the sulfone and sulfonamide oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The sulfonamide N–H provides one hydrogen-bond donor site.

The molecule is a tetrachlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxin, built from two benzene rings joined through a central six-membered 1,4-dioxin ring that contains two oxygen atoms, giving a flat, tricyclic, fused scaffold. One outer benzene ring carries a single chlorine substituent, while the other carries four chlorine atoms on adjacent positions, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any higher symmetry axis. The aromatic framework and fused ring system make the structure rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds within the core. The two ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all remaining positions are substituted by chlorine or aromatic hydrogen.

This molecule is built around a single central phosphorus atom bearing one double-bonded oxygen and three ester-type oxygens, making it a phosphate triester. Each of the three ester oxygens connects to a 1,4-dichlorobutan-2-yl-type fragment: a two-carbon unit where one carbon carries a chlorine atom and the adjacent carbon chain terminates in a second chlorine atom. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and branched around the phosphorus center. The three arms are chemically identical, giving the molecule approximate threefold symmetry about the P=O axis. Its many single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility. The phosphoryl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries a methoxy group and a methyl group on adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern with the carbonyl attached para to the methoxy. The second ring bears a single methyl group at the meta position relative to the carbonyl attachment. Each aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, while the carbonyl linkage allows some rotational freedom between the two rings. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor capability comes from the ketone oxygen and the ether oxygen of the methoxy group.

The molecule is a diaryl-type urea built from a para-tolyl ring and a 2-phenylpropan-2-yl (cumyl) group, linked through a central N,N'-disubstituted urea unit. The p-tolyl ring carries a methyl group para to the nitrogen, giving a 1,4-disubstitution pattern on a benzene core. The other nitrogen bears a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups and a phenyl ring, so the scaffold is two separate benzene rings joined by a flexible urea linker with no ring fusion. The urea carbonyl and its two N–H groups provide hydrogen-bond acceptor and donor sites, while the rest of the molecule is hydrophobic aromatic and alkyl surface. The urea linkage and the sp3 quaternary carbon give moderate conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern. One substituent is an acetamide group (an acetyl carbonyl attached to an NH bridging to the ring), another is a methyl group, and the third is a sulfonamide in which the NH is attached to a sulfonyl group carrying a trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule is largely planar and rigid at the ring, with some rotational freedom at the amide and sulfonamide linkages. It lacks any element of symmetry, since the substituents are not arranged to mirror one another. Two NH groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and sulfonyl oxygens act as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one methoxy group and three chlorine atoms, giving a fully substituted aromatic core with no fused rings. The methoxy group (an ether, –O–CH3) occupies one ring position, and the three chlorines sit at the remaining positions, with two chlorines adjacent to one another and the methoxy flanked by one chlorine on each side. The aromatic system is planar and rigid, while the methoxy methyl group can rotate about the C–O bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the whole structure onto itself, because the substituent pattern is asymmetric around the ring. The ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a five-membered oxazolidinedione ring, a saturated heterocycle containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom along with two carbonyl groups. The carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen is quaternary, bearing both a methyl group and a vinyl (ethenyl) group, which gives that position a stereogenic center. The ring nitrogen carries a 3,5-dichlorophenyl substituent, placing two chlorine atoms meta to each other on an otherwise unsubstituted benzene ring that is attached to the nitrogen. The molecule is largely rigid around the fused-ring-and-aryl core, with only the vinyl and methyl groups providing limited flexibility, and it has no internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the aryl chlorines. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its two carbonyl oxygens and ring oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on an aniline-type scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a nitrogen substituent at one position, with methyl groups at both ortho positions flanking that nitrogen, giving a 2,6-disubstituted, non-fused aromatic ring. The nitrogen is tertiary, carrying a 2-methoxyethyl chain and an acyl group, which places a chloromethyl ketone-type amide (a carbonyl bonded to a CH2 bearing chlorine) on it. The amide carbonyl and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its flexible methoxyethyl and chloroacetyl side chains contrast with the more rigid, twisted aromatic core, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ortho methyls and the two side chains differ.

The molecule is an ester built from a straight, unbranched chain on each side of a central carbonyl-oxygen linkage. One side is a nine-carbon acyl unit ending in a terminal methyl group, and the other side is a four-carbon alkyl unit attached through an oxygen atom. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic groups, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. The only functional group is the ester, which contains a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule is highly flexible because of its many rotatable single bonds, and it has no meaningful symmetry since the two chains differ in length.

The molecule is built on a dibenzo-p-dioxin-type skeleton, but here the central ring is a furan rather than a dioxin, making it a dibenzofuran core: two benzene rings are fused on either side of a central five-membered oxygen-containing ring, giving a planar, rigid, fully aromatic tricyclic system. Three chlorine atoms are attached at the periphery, two on one outer ring and one on the other, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and no mirror or rotational symmetry is present. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are on aromatic carbons. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the ring oxygen of the central furan, which is weakly basic because its lone pair is partly delocalized into the aromatic system.

The molecule is a polycyclic terpenoid-like scaffold built from a fused carbocyclic core bridged by an ether oxygen, which creates a cage-like, rigid framework with several stereocenters. One six-membered ring contains an α,β-unsaturated ketone, with a methyl-substituted alkene conjugated to the carbonyl. A tetrahydrofuran-type ether ring bridges the core, and a fused three-membered epoxide (oxirane) is spiro-attached to the framework. Hydroxyl groups sit on two carbons, and a hydroxymethyl group is attached at a ring-fusion carbon, while the remaining methyl groups are placed at quaternary centers. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, and its fused ring system limits conformational flexibility. Its several hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the ketone, ether, and epoxide oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing one methoxy group and four chlorine atoms, giving a fully substituted aromatic core with no remaining aromatic hydrogens. The ring is a single six-membered aromatic system with no fusion, and its substituents occupy five of the six positions in a pattern of two adjacent chlorines, then a third chlorine separated by one carbon, with the methoxy group sitting next to a chlorinated carbon. The ether oxygen of the methoxy group can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all attached hydrogens are on the methyl carbon. The substituents are rigid and planar with the ring, and only the methyl rotation of the methoxy group adds conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring and its substituents.

The molecule is built on a fluorene-type tricyclic scaffold, in which two benzene rings are joined through a five-membered ring that also carries a single sp3 carbon bearing both a hydroxyl group and a butyl ester. That quaternary carbon sits at the bridging position between the two aromatic rings, so the three rings are fused and largely planar, giving the core a rigid character. The ester group, a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries an unbranched four-carbon chain, extends from this carbon and adds some conformational flexibility to the side chain only. The hydroxyl group and the ester carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl hydrogen can serve as a hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because of the asymmetric substitution at the bridging carbon.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fusion to other rings. Its substitution pattern places an amino group on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by chlorine atoms at the adjacent positions, while a carboxylic acid group sits at the position across the ring from the amine. The carboxylic acid is the primary polar functional group, and together with the amine it gives the molecule both hydrogen-bond donor capability (from the N–H and O–H groups) and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability (from the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the amine nitrogen). The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the carboxylic acid able to rotate slightly about its single bond to the ring. The overall arrangement lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis because the two chlorines and the amine and acid groups occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is built on a dibenzofuran scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a central five-membered furan ring that contains a single oxygen atom, giving a fully aromatic, planar, rigid tricyclic core. Four chlorine atoms are attached to the ring carbons, distributed across both outer benzene rings in a pattern that leaves the molecule without a mirror or rotational axis of symmetry beyond the planar framework. The molecule has no hydroxyl, amine, or carbonyl groups, so it carries no hydrogen-bond donors. The furan oxygen is its only potential hydrogen-bond acceptor, and it is sterically and electronically modest because it sits within the aromatic system. Because the fused ring system is rigid and lacks rotatable bonds, its conformation is essentially fixed.

This molecule is a tetrachlorinated dibenzofuran: two benzene rings joined by a central furan ring that shares a C–C bond with each benzene ring, giving a flat, fully fused tricyclic aromatic scaffold. Four chlorine atoms are attached to the outer benzene rings, two on each, at positions that are not symmetrically equivalent, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The molecule has no stereocenters and is essentially rigid and planar, with little conformational flexibility. The central ether oxygen is its only heteroatom and can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors since no N–H or O–H groups are present.

The molecule is a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused six-membered aromatic rings sharing a common edge, giving a flat, rigid, planar framework. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring, and a primary amino group sits on the adjacent ring, with the two substituents placed in a 1,4-relationship across the same ring. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the nitrile nitrogen acts only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks rotational flexibility and has no internal symmetry beyond the planar aromatic framework.

The molecule is a dibenzofuran core, meaning two benzene rings fused on either side of a central furan ring that contains one oxygen atom. The scaffold is fully aromatic and planar, with the three rings sharing edges to form a rigid, flat tricyclic system. Four chlorine atoms sit on the outer benzene rings at positions that break the symmetry of the parent ring system, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The ether oxygen in the central ring is the only heteroatom apart from the halogens and can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a single sulfur atom, forming a diaryl thioether, with the rings placed at adjacent (ortho) positions relative to that sulfur bridge. One ring carries an aminomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a primary amine), and the other carries a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to an OH), giving the molecule two flexible side chains. Neither ring is fused to another, and the sulfur linkage allows rotation about its bonds, so the structure is fairly flexible and lacks any internal symmetry. The primary amine and the alcohol each provide hydrogen-bond donor capability through their N–H and O–H groups, and both also serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the sulfur atom acts only as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a dibenzofuran core, meaning two benzene rings joined through a central five-membered furan ring that contains a single oxygen atom. The structure is fully aromatic and planar, so it is rigid with no rotatable bonds. Four chlorine atoms sit on the outer benzene rings at positions adjacent to the ring fusion or the furan oxygen, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The chlorines are weakly electron-withdrawing substituents that add steric bulk around the periphery. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, while the furan oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a tetrachlorinated dibenzofuran: a dibenzofuran scaffold in which two benzene rings are fused to a central five-membered furan ring that contains one oxygen atom. The fused tricyclic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Four chlorine atoms sit on the outer rings at symmetric positions, two on each benzene ring, so the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis through the furan oxygen. The ether oxygen is the only heteroatom besides the halogens, and it can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an N-acylurea built from a central urea unit, with one nitrogen bearing a 2-chlorobenzoyl group and the other nitrogen bearing a para-substituted phenyl ring. The aryl ring carries a trifluoromethoxy group opposite the urea nitrogen, giving a linear, para-disubstituted pattern. The 2-chlorobenzoyl ring is ortho-substituted, which introduces a twist relative to the carbonyl plane. Both aromatic rings are benzene rings with no fused ring systems, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two halves differ. The acylurea core provides two N–H hydrogen-bond donors and several carbonyl and ether-type oxygen acceptors, while the trifluoromethoxy and chloro substituents add lipophilic character.

This molecule is built around a benzoxazole ring, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to an oxazole through a shared carbon-carbon bond, with the oxazole containing both oxygen and nitrogen. A chlorine atom sits on the benzo portion of this fused system, at a position remote from the ether linkage. The benzoxazole is attached through its C-2 position via an aryl ether bond to a second, para-disubstituted benzene ring. That central ring carries, on its opposite side, an ethoxy-carbonyl ester group linked through an alpha-methyl ether, giving the molecule a flexible propanoate tail. The ester carbonyl and the ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is elongated and largely aromatic, with rigidity concentrated in the fused and linked aryl rings and flexibility in the ether and ester side chain.

The molecule is a dibenzo-p-dioxin core, meaning two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms positioned opposite each other. The overall scaffold is planar and fully aromatic, with the central dioxin ring fused to both outer rings, giving a rigid, flat tricyclic system. Four chlorine atoms are attached directly to the aromatic carbons, with three clustered on one benzene ring at adjacent positions and one on the other ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks the full symmetry of the unsubstituted parent. The ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because every remaining hydrogen sits on carbon.

The molecule is built from a 2,6-dimethylphenyl ring bearing an amide-type nitrogen at one ortho position, with both ortho positions blocked by methyl groups that sterically crowd that nitrogen. The nitrogen carries two further substituents: a CH2 linker leading to a pyrazole ring attached through one of its nitrogen atoms, and a chloroacetyl group, which is a carbonyl bonded to a CH2 bearing a chlorine. The aromatic benzene ring and the five-membered pyrazole are the two ring systems, joined by the flexible methylene linkage rather than fused. The molecule is largely non-planar and conformationally flexible around the amide and linker bonds. The amide carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogen and carbon positions are substituted.

The molecule is a fused tetracyclic aromatic system built on a dibenzofuran core, in which two benzene rings are joined through a central furan ring containing one oxygen atom. Four chlorine atoms are attached directly to the aromatic rings, with two substituents on one outer ring and two on the other, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fully fused ring system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. The ether oxygen in the furan ring can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a straight four-carbon saturated alkyl chain (butyl group) attached to a sulfur atom that carries two double-bonded oxygens and one hydroxyl group, making it a sulfonic acid. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and the backbone is highly flexible, with free rotation about each C–C and C–S single bond. The sulfonic acid group is the sole functional group, with the sulfur in its highest oxidation state, tetrahedrally coordinated by the two sulfonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen. The molecule is unsymmetrical, since the alkyl end and the polar sulfonic acid end differ entirely. The hydroxyl hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a push-pull azo dye built on an aromatic scaffold with two para-substituted benzene rings joined by a central N=N azo bridge in the trans configuration. The left-hand ring carries a tertiary amine nitrogen bearing an n-butyl chain and a 2-cyanoethyl group, placing a strong electron-donating group para to the azo linkage. The right-hand ring carries a nitro group para to the azo bond, an electron-withdrawing substituent that completes the conjugated system. The molecule is largely planar and rigid through the extended aromatic and azo framework, while the butyl and cyanoethyl arms add flexibility. Its hydrogen-bond donor capacity is nil, since no N-H or O-H groups are present, but the nitrile, nitro oxygens, azo nitrogens, and tertiary amine nitrogen can all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a 1,3-diketone whose two carbonyl carbons are linked by a single methylene group, with each carbonyl bearing a para-substituted benzene ring. One ring carries a methoxy group at the para position, which contributes an electron-donating ether oxygen, while the other carries a tert-butyl group, a bulky alkyl substituent that adds steric bulk at the far end of the molecule. Both aromatic rings are planar and fully unfused, so the scaffold is a flexible linear chain connecting two rigid aryl units. The central methylene can tautomerize to an enol form, giving the diketone an intramolecular hydrogen-bond donor site. The two carbonyl oxygens and the methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule lacks any strong hydrogen-bond donor apart from that enolizable position.

The molecule is a dibenzofuran scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings fused to a central five-membered furan ring that contains a single oxygen atom, giving a planar, rigid tricyclic core. Four chlorine atoms are attached as aryl substituents at fixed positions on the two outer benzene rings, leaving the arrangement asymmetric, since one ring carries one chlorine while the other carries three. The oxygen atom in the furan ring is an ether-type acceptor for hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it bears no N–H or O–H groups. Overall the structure is aromatic, fully conjugated, and conformationally fixed, with essentially no rotatable bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzamide-type scaffold: a benzene ring bearing an N-acylsulfonamide group (a C=O linked to an NH that is attached to a methylsulfonyl group) on one side. The central benzene ring carries a nitro group ortho to the amide carbonyl and an aryl ether linkage meta to it, connecting to a second benzene ring. That second ring is substituted with a chlorine atom ortho to the ether oxygen and a trifluoromethyl group para to it. The two aromatic rings are joined by a flexible oxygen bridge, giving the molecule moderate conformational freedom around the diaryl ether. The acyl sulfonamide NH is a strong hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl, sulfonyl, nitro, and ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is a dibenzofuran core, consisting of two benzene rings fused on either side of a central five-membered furan ring that contains a single oxygen atom. The fused tricyclic system is essentially planar and rigid, with the aromatic rings locked in a single plane. Two chlorine atoms are attached as substituents on the outer benzene rings, one on each ring, at positions that break the symmetry of the scaffold, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the two halves identical. The ether oxygen in the furan ring can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since all its hydrogens are aromatic C-H bonds.

This molecule is built around a 1,2,4-triazole ring attached through a nitrogen atom to a tert-butyl-substituted carbon chain that bears a secondary alcohol. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, branched alkyl unit, and the carbon framework connects it to a benzyl-type linker leading to a phenyl ring carrying two chlorine atoms at the 2 and 4 positions. The aromatic triazole and phenyl rings are unfused, and the chain between them contains several rotatable single bonds, so the overall shape is moderately flexible. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the triazole nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry because the substituents on the chain differ from one another.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries four chlorine atoms on adjacent positions, and two of its neighboring positions bear a carboxylic acid group and a carboxamide group, making it a 1,2-disubstituted phthalamic acid pattern. The amide nitrogen is attached to a second benzene ring that carries chlorines at its 2, 3, and 5 positions, so it is an asymmetric anilide with no internal symmetry. Both rings are aromatic and planar, and the amide linkage connecting them restricts rotation, giving the overall framework moderate rigidity. The carboxylic acid OH and the amide N–H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. Chlorine atoms add steric bulk and lipophilic character around both rings.

This molecule is a sulfonylurea built around a benzene ring bearing a methyl ester group and a sulfonylurea bridge at the ortho position. The ortho-disubstituted benzene carries a methoxycarbonyl (methyl ester) substituent and a benzylic CH2 linked to a sulfonyl group, which connects through an N-H to a urea carbonyl and then to a second N-H. The other terminus of the urea is attached to a pyrimidine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with two nitrogens, bearing two methoxy groups at the 4 and 6 positions. The structure has no fused ring systems, and the two aromatic rings are joined by a flexible chain, giving it moderate conformational freedom. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the two sulfonylurea N-H groups, while the ester and sulfonyl oxygens, the urea carbonyl, the pyrimidine nitrogens, and the methoxy oxygens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a dibenzofuran scaffold, a tricyclic system in which a central five-membered furan ring is fused between two benzene rings, making the whole framework planar and rigid. Four chlorine atoms are attached to the aromatic rings, with three on one benzene ring at positions adjacent to the fusion and one on the other ring near the oxygen-bearing carbon, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The only heteroatom is the ring oxygen, which acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. The lack of rotatable bonds and the extended aromatic surface make the structure highly rigid.

The molecule is a dibenzo-p-dioxin core, two benzene rings joined through a central six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms in a para (1,4) arrangement. Each benzene ring is fused to the central dioxin ring, giving a tricyclic, largely planar, rigid scaffold. Both outer rings carry a single bromine substituent placed adjacent to one of the ring oxygens, so the two bromines sit on the same side of the fused system and the overall framework has approximate two-fold symmetry. The ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks N–H or O–H groups. The aromatic framework is rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond minor ring puckering.

This molecule is a 2-phenoxybutanoic acid, built from a four-carbon saturated chain bearing a carboxylic acid at one end. The alpha carbon, adjacent to the carboxyl group, carries an ether oxygen that links to an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the phenyl group is attached through a flexible C–O–C linkage rather than directly. The molecule has a single stereogenic center at the alpha carbon, and its benzene ring has no substituents, giving it no additional symmetry beyond that. The carboxylic acid group is both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as an acceptor. The aliphatic chain and ether linkage provide considerable conformational flexibility, in contrast to the rigid aromatic ring.

The molecule is built on a dibenzo-1,4-dioxin scaffold: two benzene rings fused on either side of a central six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms positioned para to each other. Each benzene ring is fused to the central dioxin ring, giving a tricyclic, fairly planar and rigid framework. A single iodine atom sits on one of the outer benzene rings, providing a substituent that breaks the otherwise symmetric arrangement. The two ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since all its hydrogens are attached to carbon.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing three ring oxygen atoms alternating with three ring carbons, forming a 1,3,5-trioxane scaffold. Each of the three ring carbons carries a single methyl substituent, giving a symmetric 2,4,6-trimethyl substitution pattern on the ring. The ring contains no double bonds or aromatic character, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors because every heteroatom is an ether oxygen with no attached hydrogen. The three oxygen atoms can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The chair-like ring is conformationally flexible yet constrained by its acetal linkages, which hold the molecule compact and rigid compared with open-chain analogues.

The molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a six-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle, with the nitrogen carrying an N-methyl group. At the 4-position of this ring sits a quaternary carbon that bears both an ethyl ester (CO2-ethyl) and a phenyl ring. That phenyl ring carries a single hydroxyl group at the meta position relative to the point of attachment, giving a meta-substituted phenol. The piperidine and phenyl rings are not fused but joined through the shared quaternary carbon, so the scaffold is non-planar and moderately rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane because of the asymmetric arrangement of the ester and aryl groups. Hydrogen-bond capability is mixed: the phenolic OH can act as both donor and acceptor, the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen are acceptors, and the tertiary amine nitrogen is an acceptor.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built from a linear, unbranched carbon chain with no rings or fused systems. Its central feature is a single ester group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to one oxygen double-bonded and one oxygen single-bonded to an alkyl chain. Both sides of the ester carry straight four-carbon chains, so the molecule is symmetric about the ester linkage. The chains are fully saturated and highly flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds. The ester oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which is a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, making this an ortho-disubstituted pattern: one is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), and the other is an ester in which an acetyl group is attached through an oxygen to the ring. The ester carbonyl and the ether oxygen are both hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ring is rigid and planar, but the single bonds to the two substituents allow some rotational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond what the substitution pattern allows.

The molecule is an aryl amine in which a nitro group is attached to the nitrogen rather than to the ring, giving an N-nitroaniline scaffold built on a single benzene ring with no ring fusion. The nitrogen bears one hydrogen and is bonded to the phenyl ring and to the nitro group, which carries a formal positive charge on nitrogen and a negative charge on one oxygen. The benzene ring is unsubstituted apart from this amino linkage, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the ring retains local symmetry about the axis through the substituted carbon and its para position. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is relatively rigid overall because of the planar aromatic ring, though the bond to the nitro nitrogen allows some rotational freedom.

The molecule is an acyclic, flexible chain built from a 2-ethylbutyl group, an ether oxygen, a two-carbon linker, and a terminal carboxylic acid. The branched 2-ethylbutyl end contains a tertiary carbon bearing two ethyl substituents, which gives the hydrocarbon portion a bulky, asymmetric shape. An ether linkage (C–O–C) connects this branched alkyl group to a short ethylene spacer, which then leads to a propanoic acid unit. The terminal carboxylic acid group (–COOH) can both donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygen atoms, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. Because there are no rings and many rotatable single bonds, the molecule is conformationally flexible and lacks any overall symmetry.

This molecule is a biaryl compound built from two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, so there is no ring fusion. One ring carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the biaryl linkage, and a chlorine atom sits on the neighboring carbon, giving a 1,2-substitution pattern on that ring. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group, so the molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry. The biaryl bond allows rotation between the two rings, which gives moderate conformational flexibility. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine is a weak acceptor and the aromatic π systems are weak acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzimidazolone core, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl group. The benzimidazolone nitrogen not part of the carbonyl is substituted by a piperidine ring, which is attached through its C4 position, while the other ring nitrogen carries an N-propanoyl (propionyl) amide group. The piperidine nitrogen is tertiary and bears a flexible chain ending in a nitrile-substituted quaternary carbon that also carries two phenyl rings. The molecule has no internal symmetry overall, though its two phenyl groups are equivalent. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the carbonyl oxygens and nitrile nitrogen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a central quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, linking two identical aromatic rings, so it is a diaryl-propane (bisphenol-type) scaffold with two-fold symmetry. Each benzene ring carries three bromine atoms and one allyloxy group (an O-CH2-CH=CH2 ether), arranged so the substituents are placed symmetrically on each ring. The molecule has no fused ring systems and no polar hydrogen-bond donors, since all oxygens are ether-type and there are no hydroxyl or amine groups. Its two ether oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The bulky central carbon and the rotatable allyl and aryl-carbon bonds give it moderate conformational flexibility around the core.

The molecule is an ethyl ester of a naphthalene-bearing acetic acid, built on a bicyclic aromatic naphthalene core with a single substituent. The naphthalene unit consists of two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic scaffold. Attached at the 1-position is a CH2 linker leading to a carboxylate ester, where the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the ester oxygen provides a second acceptor site, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors. An ethyl group caps the ester oxygen, adding a small flexible tail. Overall the molecule has little symmetry because the substituent breaks the naphthalene's symmetry, and the aromatic core is rigid while the side chain rotates freely.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl thiol: a linear, unbranched saturated carbon chain of eleven carbon atoms terminated at one end by a sulfhydryl group (-SH). There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so the scaffold is simply an open, flexible aliphatic chain. The chain has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror-like arrangement along its length, and its many rotatable single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. The terminal thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S-H bond, while the sulfur atom can serve as a weak acceptor, and the rest of the molecule contributes no polar hydrogen-bonding functionality.

This molecule is an acyclic ester with no rings, so its skeleton is a single unbranched chain. A seven-carbon alkyl group (heptyl) is joined through an oxygen atom to a carbonyl carbon, which carries a three-carbon straight chain on the other side, giving a linear, symmetry-free structure. The ester functional group (–C(=O)–O–) is the only polar feature, with the carbonyl oxygen able to accept hydrogen bonds and the ester oxygen acting as a weaker acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen sits on carbon. Its many single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility, and it has no aromatic or fused ring systems to add rigidity.

This molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, with no fused ring systems. Every ring carbon not involved in the linkage bears a chlorine atom, so the molecule is a polychlorinated biphenyl with five chlorines in total: three on one ring at the 3, 4, and 5 positions relative to the bond, and two on the other ring at the 2 and 4 positions relative to the bond. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the two rings are not equivalent. Rotation about the central bond is hindered by the bulky ortho chlorine, which makes the molecule relatively rigid and gives the rings a twisted, non-coplanar arrangement. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, since its only heteroatoms are chlorine substituents on an aromatic framework.

This molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, and it carries six chlorine substituents distributed across both rings with no other functional groups. One ring bears three chlorines at positions that leave one aromatic hydrogen between them, while the other ring is substituted with four chlorines, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern without a mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The ortho-chlorines flanking the inter-ring bond sterically hinder rotation around that axis, so the molecule is relatively rigid and nonplanar rather than fully flat. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, since the only heteroatoms are halogens, which are weak acceptors at best.

The molecule is built on a quinazolinone scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered pyrimidinone ring that contains a carbonyl group, giving a bicyclic core. A second, separate phenyl ring is attached to one of the ring nitrogens, so the structure carries three aromatic rings in total. The other ring nitrogen bears an acyl group, a carbonyl linked through a CH2 to a morpholine ring, which is a saturated six-membered ring containing both nitrogen and oxygen. The molecule has no stereocenters and considerable conformational flexibility from the N-CH2 and N-C(=O) linkages, though the fused core is largely planar. It has two carbonyl oxygens and the morpholine oxygen and nitrogen as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and no hydrogen-bond donors since no N-H or O-H groups are present.

The molecule is an organophosphorus compound built around a central phosphorus atom that is double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to a methyl group, a fluorine atom, and an ester-type oxygen. That oxygen connects to a cyclohexane ring, a saturated six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings or unsaturation. The phosphorus center is tetrahedral in geometry and carries no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only N-H or O-H sites are absent. The phosphoryl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the fluorine and ester oxygen can also weakly accept hydrogen bonds. The cyclohexyl ring is conformationally flexible, able to interconvert between chair forms, while the phosphorus substituents add modest local rigidity around the attachment point.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type alcohol built on a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) scaffold. Its skeleton carries three methyl groups, two on one bridgehead-adjacent carbon and one on the other bridgehead carbon, with a hydroxyl group on the carbon bridging the two bridgeheads in the two-carbon arm. The ring system is fused in a bridged, cage-like fashion, which makes it rigid and conformationally restricted rather than flexible. The molecule has no stereochemical symmetry elements beyond the bicyclic framework itself, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical. The single hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is saturated hydrocarbon.

The molecule is built from an alpha-substituted acrylate ester: a terminal vinyl group bearing a phenyl ring sits on the carbonyl carbon of an ester whose alkoxy partner is a bicyclic amine. That amine is a tropane-type scaffold, a bridged bicyclo[3.2.1] system in which a six-membered piperidine-like ring and a five-membered pyrrolidine-like ring share a bridging nitrogen, which carries an N-methyl group. The ester oxygen is attached to the bridgehead-adjacent carbon of the six-membered ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric, though the bicycle itself is conformationally constrained and rigid. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and attached directly to the vinylic carbon. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen and the tertiary amine nitrogen act as acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic system built on a coumarin-type lactone core: a six-membered pyranone ring carrying a carbonyl and an endocyclic ester oxygen is fused to a benzene ring. A furan ring is fused onto that benzene ring, giving an angular, roughly planar tricyclic framework with extensive conjugation across all three rings. A single hydroxyl group sits on the aromatic carbon at the junction between the benzene and furan portions, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The rigid, flat scaffold allows little conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the lactone carbonyl oxygen and the ring oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a para-aminobenzoyl amide of glutamic acid, built from a benzene ring bearing an amino group and a carbonyl-amide linkage, with the amide nitrogen attached to a five-carbon chain ending in two carboxylic acid groups. The benzene ring is para-disubstituted, giving it a symmetric, elongated shape, while the aliphatic chain adds rotational flexibility. The amide bond links the aromatic and aliphatic portions and contributes a planar, relatively rigid region. Functionally, the aniline-type amino group, the amide N–H, and the two carboxylic acid OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and carboxyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a fused tricyclic aromatic heterocycle built from three linearly or angularly joined six-membered rings, with two nitrogen atoms incorporated into the ring system. Two methyl groups sit on carbons adjacent to the ring nitrogens, giving a symmetric substitution pattern across the scaffold. The fully conjugated, planar framework is rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two methyl substituents. Each ring nitrogen is an sp2 pyridine-type center that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring carbons bear hydrogens or methyls rather than hydroxyl or amine functionality.

The molecule is an acyclic two-carbon compound: a ketone carbonyl group flanked on one side by a dibromomethyl-substituted carbon and on the other side by a carbon bearing three bromine atoms. The carbon framework is short, flexible, and open-chain, with no rings or ring fusion present. Every carbon-bearing position beyond the carbonyl is fully substituted with bromine, giving a dense halogenated pattern with little hydrogen remaining on the carbon skeleton. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two halogenated termini carry different numbers of bromine atoms. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the carbonyl oxygen, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built around a six-membered 1,3,2-oxazaphosphinane ring, a saturated heterocycle containing one phosphorus, one nitrogen, and one oxygen. The phosphorus carries a double-bonded oxygen (a phosphoryl group) and is bonded to the ring oxygen and ring nitrogen, while also bearing an exocyclic nitrogen that is substituted with two 2-chloroethyl chains. The ring nitrogen carries a third 2-chloroethyl arm, so three chloroethyl groups are attached in total. Because the ring is saturated and the phosphorus-containing core is not fused to any other ring, the scaffold is conformationally flexible apart from the ring itself. The molecule has no internal symmetry element that maps the three chloroethyl arms onto one another, since the ring nitrogen differs from the exocyclic amine. The phosphoryl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the ring oxygen and nitrogen are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an anthraquinone scaffold: three fused rings in which a central quinone-type ring with two carbonyl groups sits between a benzo ring and a fully aromatic ring bearing substituents. Two amino groups sit on the same ring, one on each side of the fused system, and two chlorine atoms occupy the two remaining adjacent positions on that ring, giving a contiguous substitution pattern. The fused tricyclic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with limited conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two primary amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and can also accept hydrogen bonds at their nitrogen lone pairs. The molecule lacks any significant symmetry because the chlorine and amino substituents break the symmetry of the aromatic ring.

The molecule is built around a central two-carbon ester linker that connects a para-chlorophenyl ether to a pyridine-3-carboxylate ester. On one end, a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups is bonded to an oxygen that links to a benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom para to the ether oxygen. The other end is a nicotinic-acid-type aromatic ester attached through a flexible ethylene glycol bridge, with the pyridine nitrogen placed meta to the carbonyl. The molecule contains two separate aromatic rings, a benzene and a pyridine, which are not fused and are joined only through the flexible chain, giving it an extended, moderately flexible shape with no internal symmetry. It has two ester carbonyl groups and two ether oxygens that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the pyridine nitrogen adds a further acceptor site, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a three-carbon chain, with no rings or ring fusion. The terminal carbon bears a trichloromethyl-type carbon: a single carbon carrying three chlorine atoms, which forms the most electron-poor, bulky end of the chain. Adjacent to it sits a secondary carbon bearing a hydroxyl group, and beyond that a terminal methyl group. Its hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms can only weakly accept hydrogen bonds. The chain is flexible and lacks any internal symmetry, since the two ends carry very different substituents.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries an ethyl group, a methyl group, and two para-hydroxyphenyl rings, giving a 2,2-diarylbutane scaffold. Both aromatic rings are unfused benzene rings, each bearing one hydroxyl group at the position opposite the attachment point, so the substitution pattern is para on each ring. The two aryl groups are related by a mirror-like arrangement through the central carbon, though the ethyl and methyl groups break full symmetry. Its only flexible parts are the ethyl chain and rotation around the bonds to the central carbon, while the aromatic rings remain rigid. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated aliphatic structure built on a central quaternary carbon bearing an ethyl group and three identical CH2-O-NO2 arms. Each arm is a nitrate ester, with the oxygen linked to a nitrogen that carries two oxygens, one formally charged, forming a nitro-type group. The arrangement is highly symmetric, with three equivalent substituents radiating from one carbon, so the scaffold has no ring systems or ring fusion. The molecule is flexible because all bonds are single and rotatable, while the ethyl group adds a small hydrocarbon tail. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen sits on carbon, and its oxygen atoms in the nitrate groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzoic acid core: a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group. At the ortho position relative to that acid, a single sp3-hybridized carbon links to two separate para-hydroxyphenyl rings, so the central carbon carries one hydrogen and two aryl groups. The two phenol rings are each substituted at the para position with a hydroxyl group, giving the molecule three benzene rings joined around one tetrahedral center. The structure has no fused ring systems, but the single sp3 junction allows rotation, so it is fairly flexible while the aromatic rings remain planar. Its hydrogen-bond capability is strong: the carboxylic acid and the two phenolic hydroxyls can each donate hydrogen bonds, and their oxygens can accept them.

This molecule is built on a five-membered succinimide ring, a saturated heterocycle containing a nitrogen atom flanked by two carbonyl groups. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the imide nitrogen, so the nitrogen is an N-substituted imide with no free N-H group. The two ring carbonyls make the imide an acceptor for hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two methylene carbons of the ring form a flexible CH2–CH2 linkage, whereas the planar aromatic ring and the imide are rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited internal symmetry, with a single bond connecting the two ring systems.

This molecule is a 3-methylchromone, built on a benzopyran-4-one scaffold. A benzene ring is fused to a six-membered pyranone ring that contains a ring oxygen and a carbonyl carbon at the 4-position, with the fused bicycle essentially planar. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl within the pyrone ring. The aromatic benzene portion is unsubstituted. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ring oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid fused system gives it little conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon scaffold with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on adjacent ring carbons, forming an ortho pattern: a hydroxyl group directly on the ring and a carboxamide-type group bearing an N-hydroxy (oxime-like hydroxylamine) unit. The hydroxamic acid group contains a carbonyl oxygen, an amide nitrogen, and an N-bound hydroxyl, giving it several hydrogen-bond donor sites and acceptor sites. The phenolic hydroxyl adds further donor and acceptor capability, and the two groups can engage in intramolecular hydrogen bonding because of their proximity. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the side chain has some rotational freedom around the bond linking it to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an amino group, a chlorine atom, and a carboxylic acid, arranged on adjacent and meta-related carbons of the aromatic core. The carboxylic acid sits at one position, the amino group directly beside it, and the chlorine located across the ring in a meta relationship to the amine and para to the acid. The scaffold is a single fused-free aromatic ring with no additional ring systems. Its substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid and aromatic amine are conjugated with the ring, which limits rotation about those bonds and makes the core fairly rigid, with only the carboxyl group able to rotate slightly.
