The compound carries both hydrogen-bond donor sites (the N–H and O–H groups) and hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the nitrogen lone pair).

This molecule is a tricyclic fused heteroaromatic system built around a thiazole-type five-membered ring fused to a pyrimidine ring, with an additional saturated six-membered ring that links the two through a nitrogen atom. The fused core is largely planar and rigid, while the 2-hydroxyethyl side chain attached to the five-membered ring is flexible. Two methyl groups sit on the aromatic framework, one on the five-membered ring and one on the pyrimidine ring, which breaks any overall symmetry. The primary alcohol offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, and the several ring nitrogen atoms serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit para to each other on that ring: a hydrazinyl group (–NH–NH2) attached through one nitrogen, and a sulfonic acid group (–SO3H) attached through sulfur. The hydrazine unit contributes three N–H bonds that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, along with lone pairs on its nitrogens that can accept hydrogen bonds. The sulfonic acid group supplies a strongly polar acidic O–H donor and multiple oxygen acceptors. The para arrangement gives the molecule a roughly linear, elongated shape with a C2-type symmetry axis through the two substituents, and the rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the single bonds to the substituents still allow some rotation.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no additional ring fusion. Three substituents are attached around the ring: one amino group (-NH2) and two carboxylic acid groups (-COOH). The two carboxylic acids sit at the 1 and 3 positions relative to each other, and the amino group sits between them at the 5 position, giving a symmetric meta-disubstituted arrangement with a mirror plane through the amino-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxyl and amino groups each contribute rotational freedom at their attachment bonds. The amino group and the two carboxylic acid groups together provide several hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens of the acids, along with the amino nitrogen, serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para arrangement. One substituent is a sulfonic acid group, attached directly to the ring through sulfur, which carries a hydroxyl and a double-bonded oxygen. The other substituent is a chlorine atom located on the carbon opposite the sulfonic acid group. Because the two groups sit at opposite positions of a single aromatic ring, the molecule has a flat, rigid framework with an approximate two-fold axis of symmetry running through both substituents. The sulfonic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the chlorine atom is a weak halogen acceptor.

The molecule is an ester built from a long, straight, saturated eighteen-carbon acyl chain attached through a carbonyl group to the oxygen of a cyclohexane ring. The carbonyl carbon sits at one end of the chain, so the molecule has a clearly amphiphilic-looking linear tail with a single polar ester junction. The cyclohexyl ring is fully saturated and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, bearing only the single ester oxygen as a substituent, so there is no meaningful substitution pattern or stereochemical complexity beyond that. The ester group contributes one carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is highly flexible because of its many rotatable single bonds, and it has no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the cyclohexane ring.

This molecule is a symmetric disulfide built from two identical halves joined through a central S–S bond. Each half is an O-isopropyl dithiocarbonate unit, in which a thiocarbonyl carbon is bonded to a sulfur atom, an oxygen atom carrying an isopropyl group, and the disulfide sulfur. The structure contains no rings, so it is fully acyclic and comparatively flexible about its single bonds, though the C=S bonds are rigid. The two isopropyl groups are arranged mirror-symmetrically across the disulfide axis. The molecule has no classical hydrogen-bond donors, since it bears no N–H or O–H groups, but its thiocarbonyl sulfur atoms and ether oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated chain built from an eighteen-carbon acyl unit joined through an ester linkage to a polyether tail. The long alkyl segment is highly flexible and free of rings, unsaturation, or branching. The ester carbonyl sits at one end of that chain, and its single-bonded oxygen connects to a series of repeating two-carbon ether units, four ethylene oxide units in all, terminated by a free primary hydroxyl group. The molecule has no stereocenters and no rotational symmetry beyond the trivial, and its molecular framework is largely unbranched and conformationally mobile. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated at the terminus: the terminal hydroxyl can act as both a donor and an acceptor, while the carbonyl and the ether oxygens serve as acceptors only.

This molecule is an acyl chloride built on a straight, unbranched fourteen-carbon chain. The carbon skeleton is entirely saturated and acyclic, with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. Its defining functional group is the acyl chloride, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded both to a double-bonded oxygen and to a chlorine atom, sitting at one terminus of the chain. Because the chain is linear and flexible, rotation about its many single bonds gives it considerable conformational freedom, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a rough mirror-like arrangement of the alkyl tail. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a bicyclic indane-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, with the five-membered ring bearing a gem-dimethyl group at one carbon and a quaternary carbon carrying a second gem-dimethyl pair. The aromatic ring carries a methyl group and two nitro groups, placed on adjacent-to-methyl and meta-related positions, giving a non-symmetric substitution pattern. The fused ring system is rigid, while the saturated portion is fairly bulky and sterically crowded. Nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygens but provide no hydrogen-bond donors, and the molecule has no N–H or O–H groups, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, forming an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a methylamino group (a nitrogen bonded to a methyl group and to the ring), which acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and an acceptor through the nitrogen lone pair. The other is a carboxylic acid group, which contributes a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The benzene core is fully aromatic and planar, giving the molecule a rigid framework, while the single bonds to the substituents allow limited rotation. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two adjacent functional groups are chemically distinct.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents at the meta positions relative to each other. One substituent is a primary sulfonamide group, where a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to an NH2 group, and the other is a nitro group, consisting of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formal charge separation. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid and flat. The sulfonamide contributes two N–H hydrogen-bond donors and two sulfonyl oxygen acceptors, while the nitro group adds two oxygen acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local pseudo-mirror plane through the substituent axis, and its rotational freedom is limited mainly to the sulfonamide and nitro bonds.

This molecule is an anthraquinone scaffold: three fused six-membered rings in which the central ring carries two ketone (quinone-type) carbonyl groups. The two outer rings each bear an amino group and a sulfonic acid group, and each also carries a hydroxyl group adjacent to the sulfonic acid. The substitution pattern is positioned so that the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry across the central axis. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with limited conformational flexibility. The amino and hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens, sulfonyl oxygens, and hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated aliphatic chain with no rings, so its scaffold is a flexible, unbranched hydrocarbon tail attached to a polar head. A twelve-carbon acyl chain terminates in an ester linkage, which connects it to a short ether-containing spacer of the form diethylene glycol. The terminal end is a primary alcohol, so the molecule carries one free hydroxyl group in addition to the ester carbonyl and the two ether oxygens. These oxygens and the hydroxyl make the head group a good hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the terminal hydroxyl can act as both a donor and an acceptor. The structure has no internal symmetry and is highly flexible because of its many rotatable single bonds.

The molecule is a fully aromatic, planar, fused polycyclic system built from four six-membered rings that share edges in a compact arrangement. Two of the rings contain nitrogen atoms, one in each terminal pyridine-like ring, and the nitrogens sit on opposite sides of the framework, giving the molecule a centrosymmetric, C2-type symmetry. There are no substituents or exocyclic functional groups, so the only chemical handles are the ring nitrogens. Because the scaffold is rigid and flat, it has no rotatable bonds, and each nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair while offering no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is a single saturated six-membered ring containing six atoms in total, with four carbon atoms and two sulfur atoms... wait, let me correct that: parsing C1SSCSSS1 gives a ring of six sulfur atoms interleaved with one carbon, so the ring contains one carbon and five sulfur atoms, closed back onto itself. The scaffold is a simple monocyclic, fully saturated heterocycle with no ring fusion, no pendant substituents, and no additional functional groups beyond the ring itself. Because every atom in the ring is either a sulfur or a single methylene-type carbon joined by single bonds, the structure is essentially unsubstituted and lacks any stereocenters, giving it a high degree of local symmetry around the ring. The chain of consecutive sulfur–sulfur bonds gives the ring considerable conformational flexibility rather than rigidity. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the lone pairs on the sulfur atoms, which are weak.

This molecule is a fully fluorinated, acyclic branched alkane built on a short carbon chain. Its backbone consists of a linear run of three carbons, each bearing two fluorine atoms, followed by a fourth carbon that carries a single fluorine and two trifluoromethyl branches, with a terminal trifluoromethyl group completing the chain. The structure contains no rings and no heteroatoms other than fluorine, so it has no ring fusion, no hydrogen-bond donors, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors in the conventional sense. The fluorine substitution is dense and essentially saturates every carbon, while the branching at the central carbon introduces a bulky, asymmetric arrangement. Because it is a flexible chain with free rotation about its single bonds, the molecule can adopt many conformations, though the bulky trifluoromethyl groups restrict some rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused ring systems. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon and a trifluoromethyl group sits on the carbon directly across the ring, giving a para (1,4) substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the two substituents. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. The trifluoromethyl group contributes a bulky, strongly electron-withdrawing carbon center bearing three fluorine atoms, which can accept weak hydrogen bonds but does not donate any.

The molecule is a small acyclic haloalkane built on a propane-type skeleton: a central carbon bears two methyl groups and two fluorine atoms, with the remaining methyl group completing the three-carbon chain. Because the molecule contains no rings or ring fusions, its scaffold is entirely open-chain and sp3-hybridized. The functional groups are carbon-fluorine bonds, located on a single internal carbon, which gives a geminal difluoro substitution pattern. The arrangement has local symmetry around that carbon, with the two fluorines and two methyls in a tetrahedral geometry, but the overall structure lacks a higher symmetry element beyond a mirror plane. The skeleton is flexible through rotation about its single bonds, though the bulky, electronegative substituents restrict conformational freedom somewhat. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, since it carries no O–H or N–H groups, and its fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is an ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain), and the other is a single fluorine atom attached directly to the ring. The aromatic core is a flat, fully conjugated six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the ethoxy tail adds some conformational flexibility while the ring itself remains rigid. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the ring's para positions and the two substituents.

The molecule encoded by this SMILES is a very small, acyclic species built from a single carbon atom bonded to two nitrogen atoms. The central carbon carries one double bond to a nitrogen, which bears only a hydrogen, and one single bond to a second nitrogen, which bears two hydrogens. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution pattern beyond these simple terminal groups. The structure is essentially a one-carbon scaffold with an imine-type C=N unit and a primary amino group, so it is fully flexible in the sense that it has no rotatable ring constraints to speak of. Both nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H bonds, and both carry lone pairs that allow them to serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around two benzene rings joined by an ester linkage, so it is a diaryl ester with a central C(=O)O bridge. The first ring carries a methyl ester, a methyl group, and a hydroxyl group in a crowded arrangement, while the second ring carries a methyl group, a hydroxyl, an aldehyde (formyl) group, and a second hydroxyl adjacent to the aldehyde. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the two halves differ in their functional groups. Each ring is rigid and planar, but the ester bridge gives the overall structure some rotational flexibility. The phenolic hydroxyls and the aldehyde provide several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the ester carbonyls add further acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic scaffold: a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine-type ring, which is in turn fused to a furan ring, giving a linear-to-angular aromatic framework in which every ring is planar and aromatic. A single methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) is attached to the central ring at a carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal mirror plane beyond its overall flat outline. The entire fused core is rigid, with only the methyl group of the methoxy substituent able to rotate. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the furan oxygen and the methoxy oxygen can each serve as weaker acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered carbocyclic ring with a cyclohexadiene-dione core: two carbonyl groups sit at opposite positions (para-related) on the ring, separated by two carbon-carbon double bonds. Each of the four remaining ring carbons bears one bromine atom, so the substitution pattern is fully symmetric, with all four halogens on the sp2 carbons flanking the carbonyls. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and it contains no fused ring systems. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The conjugated, cross-linked arrangement of the double bonds and carbonyls makes the scaffold electron-poor overall.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two adjacent hydroxyl groups (a catechol unit) and a long, unbranched saturated alkyl chain of fifteen carbons attached to the ring. The aromatic core is fully unsaturated and planar, while the pendant chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The substitution pattern is 1,2,3 on the ring: the alkyl group sits next to one hydroxyl, which in turn neighbors the second hydroxyl, leaving the molecule without any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two phenolic groups can cooperate in intramolecular or intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The molecule therefore combines a rigid, polar aromatic head with a flexible, nonpolar hydrocarbon tail.

The molecule is a meta-substituted phenol, with a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a straight, unbranched fifteen-carbon alkyl chain on the carbon two positions away around the ring. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so there are no additional ring systems or ring fusion. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkyl chain contributes only nonpolar, carbon-hydrogen character. The molecule lacks any symmetry that would make its two sides identical, because the long chain sits on one side of the ring while the hydroxyl is positioned differently. The saturated chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, whereas the benzene ring is rigid and planar.

This molecule is an acyclic ether with no rings, built from a linear chain of carbon atoms joined through two oxygen atoms. It consists of a propyl group attached to an oxygen, which is bonded to a methylene carbon that bridges to a second oxygen, followed by an ethyl-capped two-carbon chain ending in a propyl-like terminus. The two ether oxygens are the only functional groups, each bearing two carbon neighbors and no hydrogens. The skeleton is fully saturated and flexible, with many rotatable single bonds, so it can adopt numerous conformations. The molecule lacks symmetry overall, though its carbon chains are roughly mirror-related about the central acetal-type carbon. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no hydrogens sit on oxygen or nitrogen, and it has two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites at the ether oxygens.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing one edge. Two carboxylic acid groups are attached at the peri positions, carbons 1 and 8, which sit on the same side of the ring junction and are held close together. Each carboxyl group contributes a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and ether-like oxygen). The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the peri substitution introduces steric crowding that forces the carboxyl groups slightly out of the ring plane. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the long axis of the naphthalene core.

This molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl group bridges two benzene rings. One ring carries two adjacent hydroxyl groups at the 3- and 4-positions (a catechol unit), giving it a 1,2-dihydroxy-substituted pattern. The other ring bears three hydroxyl groups at the 2-, 4-, and 6-positions, arranged symmetrically around the ketone attachment. The two aromatic rings are not fused to each other, though they are connected through the planar carbonyl linker, which allows some rotational freedom about the single bonds. Together, the eight hydroxyl oxygens and the ketone oxygen provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites and acceptor sites, with intramolecular hydrogen bonding possible between the ortho hydroxyl and the carbonyl.

The molecule is built on an anthracene scaffold, three fused benzene rings arranged linearly. Two bromine atoms are attached at the 9 and 10 positions, the two central carbons of the middle ring, which are para to each other across that ring. The bromines sit on sp2 carbons, so they add no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors beyond the weak halogen contributions. The fused aromatic framework is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Its symmetry is high, with a two-fold axis and mirror planes passing through the bromine-bearing carbons, so the two outer benzo rings are equivalent.

The molecule is built from two naphthalene units joined through a single secondary amine nitrogen, giving a diarylamine with an N–H group. Each naphthalene is a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene-like rings sharing an edge, and the nitrogen is attached to a carbon on the second position of each ring system, a substitution pattern that gives the molecule an extended, roughly linear shape. The scaffold is largely planar and rigid, with the aromatic rings and the nitrogen conjugated through the lone pair, though the C–N bonds allow some rotational freedom about the amine. The molecule has no stereocenters and only approximate two-fold symmetry about the central nitrogen. The N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen lone pair is a weak acceptor, and the aromatic faces offer π-stacking capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings, so its scaffold is a simple monocyclic phenyl core. Two substituents sit on the ring at opposite positions, giving a para (1,4) substitution pattern: one side carries a two-carbon chain ending in a tertiary dimethylamino group, and the other carries a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring as a phenol. The molecule has a plane of symmetry running through both substituents, and the flexible ethyl linker gives it some conformational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary amine nitrogen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor since it carries no hydrogen.

The molecule is a small saturated carbocycle: a three-membered cyclopropane ring, with no fused or additional rings and no double bonds. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) is attached to one of the ring carbons, so the ring bears a single ether substituent and the remaining ring carbons are unsubstituted CH2 groups. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The strained, rigid ring contrasts with the more flexible, freely rotating methoxy group, and the structure lacks any mirror-symmetric plane that would make the carbons equivalent.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a sulfonamide bridge, with each ring bearing a sulfur-containing group at the para position relative to the bridge. One ring carries a primary amine (an aniline-type NH2) on the carbon opposite the sulfonyl attachment, while the other carries a primary sulfonamide (SO2NH2). The central linkage is a secondary sulfonamide, SO2-NH, connecting the two aromatic rings. The skeleton is essentially linear and symmetric in its overall layout, with both aromatic rings flat and rotationally constrained by the sulfonyl groups. The molecule has several hydrogen-bond donors (the amine and the two NH groups) and multiple acceptors (the sulfonyl oxygens and the nitrogen atoms).

The molecule is a fused bicyclic aromatic system built from a quinoline scaffold, with a pyridine ring fused edge-to-edge to a benzene ring. An amino group is attached to the pyridine-type ring at the carbon position adjacent to the ring fusion, on the same side as the aromatic nitrogen's neighboring carbon. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor hydrogens and an additional acceptor site. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the substituent sits on only one ring.

This molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a simple three-carbon chain. The central carbon is quaternary, bearing two methyl groups, a chlorine atom, and the carboxyl carbon, so the chlorine sits on a tertiary carbon alpha to the acid. There are no rings and no ring fusion, and the scaffold is essentially a compact branched aliphatic framework. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the chlorine adds a weak polar, halogen-type acceptor site. The molecule is small and flexible about its single bonds but lacks any stereocenters, and its two methyl groups make the substitution pattern nearly symmetric around the quaternary carbon.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two ester groups on adjacent (ortho) carbons, giving it a phthalate-type scaffold. Each ester carbonyl is attached to the ring and connected through an oxygen to a flexible chain of two-carbon units interrupted by an ether oxygen, ending in an ethyl group. The molecule has no stereocenters and a roughly mirror-symmetric arrangement of its two identical arms. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the four ether-linked side chains are highly flexible. The two carbonyl oxygens and the four ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a ketone built on a three-carbon chain, with a carbonyl group flanked by a phenyl ring on one side and a CH2 linked to a CH carbon on the other. The terminal CH carbon bears two phenyl rings, so the scaffold contains three separate benzene rings, all unfused and attached through sp3 carbons, giving the molecule a propeller-like, fairly flexible shape. The only functional group is the aryl ketone carbonyl, which can accept hydrogen bonds at its oxygen but has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. The two phenyl rings on the same carbon make the arrangement partly but not fully symmetric, and the aromatic rings are unsubstituted.

The molecule is an N,N-diphenylformamide: a single formyl group (an aldehyde-type carbonyl carbon bearing one hydrogen) is bonded to a central nitrogen, and that nitrogen carries two unsubstituted phenyl rings. The scaffold is therefore a tertiary amide built around one nitrogen, with two separate benzene rings and no fused ring systems. Each phenyl ring is monosubstituted at the position attached to nitrogen and otherwise unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and the two rings are equivalent. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the N–C=O axis, though the rings can rotate about their N–C bonds, giving it moderate conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen is fully substituted.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring at adjacent carbons. The bromine-bearing carbon sits at the 2-position of the pyridine-type ring, adjacent to the ring nitrogen. That carbon carries three bromine atoms, giving a bulky, electron-poor trihalomethyl group that is attached directly to the aromatic system. The fused aromatic framework is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituent is placed asymmetrically on one ring.

This molecule is an acyclic acetal-type compound built around a central sp3 carbon bearing a furan ring and two acetoxy groups. The furan is a five-membered, fully aromatic oxygen heterocycle attached directly to that central carbon, which makes it a monosubstituted, unfused ring with no additional ring systems. Each acetoxy substituent is an ester group in which an acetyl unit is bonded through oxygen to the central carbon, so the molecule contains two ester carbonyls that act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the ring oxygen offers a further weak acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two ester arms are not identical in environment relative to the furan, so it lacks any strict symmetry. The sp3 central carbon and the single bonds to the ester oxygens give the chain considerable conformational flexibility, in contrast to the rigid planar furan ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two carboxylic acid groups, each a carbonyl bearing a hydroxyl, are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 3, meta to one another, and a phenolic hydroxyl sits at position 5, so the three substituents are spaced symmetrically around the ring. The arrangement has an approximate mirror plane passing through the hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it, giving the framework a high degree of symmetry. The ring and its directly attached planar groups are rigid, while the rotation about each carbon-to-carbon bond linking a carboxyl group to the ring gives limited conformational freedom. Each carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the phenolic hydroxyl adds one further donor and acceptor.

The molecule is a saturated carboxylic acid with a single carboxyl group at one end of a long aliphatic chain. The carboxyl carbon is attached to a branched carbon that carries two straight eight-carbon alkyl arms, giving a 2-octyldecanoic-type scaffold with no rings, no double bonds, and no aromatic groups. The only functional group is the carboxylic acid, which contains one hydroxyl donor and one carbonyl acceptor and can form hydrogen-bonded pairs. The molecule is largely flexible because of its many rotatable single bonds, and its branching at the alpha carbon makes it asymmetric, with the two alkyl arms being chemically equivalent but the carboxyl end distinct from the tail.

The molecule is phenyl azide, consisting of a single benzene ring bearing one azido group attached directly to a ring carbon. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, with no ring fusion and no additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The azido group is linear in arrangement, a chain of three nitrogen atoms that carries a formal charge distribution across its terminal and central nitrogens. The overall framework is rigid and flat, with the only rotational freedom arising from rotation about the bond joining the ring to the azide. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the terminal nitrogens of the azido group can weakly act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a carbonate diester built around a single central carbonyl carbon bonded to one double-bonded oxygen and two single-bonded ether-type oxygens. Each of the two oxygens connects to a flexible two-carbon ethyl chain that terminates in a chlorine atom, so the molecule is fully acyclic with no ring systems or ring fusion. The structure is symmetric about the central carbonate unit, with both halogenated arms identical and joined through the same connectivity. The molecule is highly flexible because of the freely rotating single bonds in each chain. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the three oxygen atoms, while it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic diester built on a flexible two-carbon ethylene glycol linker. Each terminus of the linker is capped by an ester group, with a long straight saturated alkyl chain of roughly eleven carbons extending from each carbonyl carbon, so the two chains are identical and the molecule is symmetric about the central C–C bond of the linker. There are no ring systems, no aromatic rings, and no stereocenters. The ester carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The long alkyl chains give the structure considerable conformational flexibility, with the ester linkages providing limited rotational constraint.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built on a straight-chain scaffold with no rings or fused systems. One side of the ester linkage is an eight-carbon acyl chain (an octanoyl group), and the other side is an n-propyl group attached through an oxygen atom. The ester carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because all of its hydrogens sit on saturated carbon. The structure is linear and highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds and no meaningful symmetry beyond the simple chain arrangement. Its only substitution pattern is the terminal alkyl chains flanking the central ester group.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic compound built on a branched five-carbon chain, with an isopentyl-type skeleton in which one terminal carbon bears two methyl groups. Its only functional group is a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one drawn as a charge-separated N-oxide form) attached at the end of the chain, so there are no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local equivalence of the two terminal methyl groups, and its carbon chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The nitro group contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since all of its hydrogens are attached to carbon.

This molecule is a straight-chain hydrocarbon built from six carbons, with no rings, branching, or heteroatoms. Both ends of the chain carry a terminal alkyne, a carbon-carbon triple bond bearing a single hydrogen, so the molecule is symmetric about its central methylene (CH2) units. Its scaffold is entirely sp and sp3 hybridized carbon, giving a linear, rigid alkyne termini separated by a flexible two-carbon saturated core. Because it contains no oxygen or nitrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, and the only acidic sites are the terminal alkyne hydrogens.

The molecule is an acyclic urea in which both nitrogen atoms of the central carbonyl carry acetyl groups, so it is a diacetylated urea with a linear, open-chain skeleton. Its core is a single carbonyl carbon bonded to two nitrogen atoms, and each nitrogen is connected to a separate acetyl unit, giving a symmetrical arrangement in which the two acetyl branches mirror one another about the central urea carbon. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, and no substitution beyond the methyl groups of the acetyl units. The molecule has three carbonyl groups total, with two imide-like N-acyl linkages flanking the central urea, which gives it considerable conformational flexibility around the C–N bonds. Each nitrogen bears one hydrogen, so the molecule offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the three carbonyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a salicylanilide-type scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a phenol group (ortho to a carboxamide) is joined through an amide linkage to a second benzene ring. The first aromatic ring carries a hydroxyl group and a chlorine atom positioned meta to the amide carbonyl and para to the hydroxyl, while the anilide ring carries two adjacent chlorine substituents at the 3 and 4 positions. The amide N–H and the phenolic O–H act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and phenolic oxygen serve as acceptors, with the phenol and amide carbonyl able to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond. The two aromatic rings are planar and conjugated through the amide, giving a fairly rigid, largely flat framework with limited rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the chlorine substitution patterns on the two rings differ.

This molecule is an acid anhydride built from two identical straight-chain saturated acyl units joined through a central C(=O)–O–C(=O) linkage. Each side carries a twelve-carbon alkyl chain, giving a long, flexible hydrocarbon tail at both ends of a compact, polar core. There are no rings and no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is fully symmetric about the central oxygen. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The long alkyl arms rotate freely, so the structure is highly flexible overall, with rigidity limited to the planar anhydride unit.

This molecule is an acetyl-substituted pentafluorobenzene, built on a single six-membered aromatic benzene ring. Five of the six ring positions carry fluorine atoms, and the remaining position bears an acetyl group, a two-carbon unit consisting of a carbonyl attached directly to a methyl group. The ketone carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fluorine substituents are arranged contiguously around the ring, so there is no molecular symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the acetyl group and the opposite ring carbon. The rigid aromatic core limits flexibility, although the acetyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring.

The molecule is a saturated two-carbon chain, a short acyclic skeleton with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. Each carbon is fully substituted with halogens: the first carbon carries two fluorines and one chlorine, and the second carbon carries two chlorines, while the terminal carbon bears two fluorines and one chlorine. Because all substituents are halogens, the molecule has no functional groups beyond the carbon-halogen bonds, and it contains no hydrogen atoms at all. It lacks any hydrogen-bond donor and has no lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms that could act as acceptors in the conventional sense. The chain can rotate freely about its central carbon-carbon single bond, so it is flexible rather than rigid, and its substitution pattern is asymmetric overall.

This molecule is a fully fluorinated, unbranched carbon chain (a perfluoroalkyl chain) attached at one terminus to a two-carbon hydroxyethyl unit, with a primary alcohol group at the far end. The chain consists of eight carbon atoms in total, each bearing two or three fluorine atoms, with no rings or ring fusion present. Because the backbone is linear and saturated, the molecule is highly flexible about its single bonds, although the bulky fluorine atoms give the chain a stiff, rod-like appearance. The terminal hydroxyl group is the only hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry because the non-fluorinated end differs from the perfluorinated tail.

The molecule is a short, fully fluorinated acyclic hydrocarbon skeleton built from a chain of four carbon atoms joined by a central carbon-carbon bond. It contains two carbon-carbon double bonds, one at each end of the chain, with the central single bond connecting them, so it is a conjugated diene. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms other than the fluorine atoms, which occupy every remaining position on the carbon backbone. Each terminal carbon bears two fluorines, and each internal sp2 carbon bears one, giving a fully substituted pattern. The molecule is nearly planar around its conjugated core and has a degree of symmetry, since the two halves of the chain are related by a center of inversion. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptors are the fluorine atoms, which are weak.

This molecule is an acyclic diester, specifically a diethyl ester of a two-carbon dicarboxylic acid backbone. Two ethyl ester groups flank a central tetrahedral carbon that carries a single bromine substituent, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric about that stereocenter. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, and the chain is highly flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds. Each ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens sit on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with four substituents arranged around it: a methoxy group, a hydroxyl group, an aldehyde (formyl) group, and a second methoxy group. The hydroxyl and the aldehyde sit next to each other on the ring, so they can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, and the two methoxy groups occupy the remaining positions, giving a 1,3,5-trisubstituted-type pattern with the hydroxyl and aldehyde adjacent. The ring carries no fused partners, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic aromatic core. Overall the structure is fairly rigid, with only the methoxy and aldehyde groups providing some rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the oxygens of the two methoxy groups, the hydroxyl, and the aldehyde carbonyl all serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused aromatic six-membered rings sharing one edge. Attached at the alpha position of one ring is an ether oxygen linking to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a primary hydroxyl group, so the substitution pattern is a single 1-naphthyl ether bearing a 2-hydroxyethyl arm. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ethoxy side chain adds conformational flexibility. The terminal hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any stereocenters or internal symmetry beyond the naphthalene framework.

This molecule is a symmetric diarylcarbodiimide built around a central N=C=N unit, with each nitrogen bonded to a para-tolyl ring. Each aromatic ring is a simple benzene ring bearing a single methyl group positioned opposite the carbodiimide attachment, so the two halves are mirror images across the central carbon. The linear, cumulated C=N=C arrangement makes the core rigid and extended, while the rings can rotate around their bonds to the nitrogens. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H positions are absent, but the nitrogen atoms of the carbodiimide can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems. Its only functional group is a hydroperoxide, an –O–OH unit attached directly to one ring carbon, and the ring carbons carry no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The cyclohexane ring can adopt chair and boat conformations and the peroxide bond allows rotation, so the molecule is flexible rather than rigid. Its overall structure lacks any symmetry element beyond the local mirror plane through the substituted carbon, since the stereocenter at the attachment point is the only chiral feature. The hydroperoxy group supplies one hydrogen-bond donor through its terminal O–H and two acceptor oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms and one sulfur atom in a 2,1,3-benzothiadiazole arrangement. The fused ring system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. A single primary amine group (-NH2) is attached to the benzene ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any significant symmetry. The amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as an acceptor through its lone pair, while the ring nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small, fully saturated acyclic haloalkane built on a two-carbon backbone, with one carbon bearing a single fluorine and two chlorines and the adjacent carbon bearing a single chlorine. The skeleton is a simple ethane-type framework with no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no multiple bonds. Halogen atoms are the only functional groups, arranged as a geminal trihalo pattern on one carbon and a monohalo substitution on the other. The molecule has no stereocenters or internal symmetry, and its single C–C bond allows free rotation, so it is conformationally flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its halogen substituents can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated aliphatic chain with no rings, so it has no ring fusion or aromatic character. A terminal vinyl group (CH2=CH-) is attached through an ether oxygen to a long unbranched run of methylene units, giving a single ether linkage as its only heteroatom functional group. The structure is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many C-C bonds, and it has no stereocenters or internal symmetry beyond the chain's overall linear shape. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic heterocycle built from a fused pair of six-membered rings, forming a quinoline-type scaffold in which one ring contains a nitrogen atom and the other is a benzene ring. The two rings share an edge, so the system is planar and rigid with no rotatable bonds. Two methyl groups are attached as the only substituents, one on the benzenoid ring and one on the nitrogen-containing ring, giving the molecule no internal symmetry. The ring nitrogen has a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic saturated hydrocarbon skeleton with no rings and no double bonds. Its backbone is a central quaternary carbon bearing a tert-butyl group on one side, with a second quaternary carbon carrying two methyl groups and a chlorine atom. The only functional group is a single carbon-chlorine bond, which sits on a fully substituted carbon with no attached hydrogen. The structure is highly branched and compact, with several methyl groups radiating around the two quaternary centers, giving it a roughly tetrahedral, bulky shape. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine is only a weak acceptor, with no other heteroatoms present.

The molecule is tert-butyl vinyl ether, built on a simple acyclic scaffold with no rings. A vinyl group (a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, CH2=CH-) is bonded through a single ether oxygen to a quaternary carbon that carries three methyl groups, giving a compact, highly branched tert-butyl unit. The only functional groups are the alkene and the ether linkage, and the bulky tert-butyl group makes the arrangement sterically hindered around the oxygen. The molecule has no stereocenters and is fairly flexible about its single bonds, though the tert-butyl group restricts rotation nearby. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small heterocycle built around a single five-membered ring containing one sulfur atom at position 1 and a second sulfur atom at position 3, with two carbon-carbon double bonds in the ring, making it an aromatic-like 1,3-dithiole core. The ring is fused to nothing else and carries an exocyclic thiocarbonyl group (C=S) at the carbon between the two ring sulfur atoms, which is the principal functional group. The ring framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the sulfur atoms can each act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a propanoyl group (a three-carbon chain attached through a ketone carbonyl), a methyl group, and a hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl sits ortho to the ketone, so the two groups are adjacent on the ring, while the methyl group is positioned meta to the ketone and para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic core is a flat, rigid, fully conjugated six-membered ring, and the acyl chain adds only modest flexibility through its single bonds. The phenolic OH can donate a hydrogen bond, and both the ketone oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen can accept one. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane in its planar arrangement.

The molecule is an aryl ketone built from a benzene ring bearing a carbonyl group directly attached to one ring carbon. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbon ring with alternating double bonds, and it carries no fused rings and no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The carbonyl carbon connects the ring to a straight, unbranched five-carbon alkyl chain, giving an open, flexible tail. The overall shape has no internal symmetry beyond the local mirror plane of the benzene ring and the free rotation of the alkyl chain. The ketone oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule has a single silicon atom at its center, bonded to three methyl groups and one hydrogen, giving a silane skeleton with no rings or fused ring systems. Its only functional group is the silicon-hydrogen bond, and there are no heteroatoms, double bonds, or aromatic features. The structure is highly symmetric, with the three methyl groups arranged around the central silicon in a tetrahedral geometry, so the molecule is effectively a compact, rigid, and non-polar framework with minimal conformational flexibility. It carries no hydrogen-bond donor capability, since the only hydrogen is bonded to silicon rather than to an electronegative atom, and it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites either.

The molecule is a saturated five-membered heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, specifically a sulfolane ring with the sulfur bearing two double-bonded oxygen atoms, making it a cyclic sulfone. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring carbons flanking the sulfone group, one on the carbon adjacent to sulfur and one on the carbon in the position beta to sulfur, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is fully sp3-hybridized and non-aromatic, giving it a puckered, moderately flexible conformation rather than a flat one. The sulfone oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring at adjacent carbon atoms. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with the nitrogen atom located in the pyridine-type ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion. A two-carbon hydroxyethyl side chain (–CH2CH2OH) is attached to the carbon next to that nitrogen, making the substitution pattern asymmetric. The terminal primary alcohol provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H group and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. The ring nitrogen also serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the flexible ethyl linker gives the molecule some conformational freedom relative to the otherwise rigid aromatic core.

The molecule is a small heteroaromatic ring system built on a single six-membered ring containing four nitrogen atoms and two carbon atoms, with the nitrogens arranged in a 1,2,4,5 pattern typical of a triazine-type scaffold. It is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion and no saturated or sp3-hybridized atoms, which makes the framework rigid. A single primary amino group is attached to one of the ring carbons, giving the only substituent and the only functional group present. Because the substitution pattern is asymmetric, the molecule lacks any meaningful rotational symmetry beyond its planar outline. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H hydrogens, while the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a barbiturate-type scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidinetrione ring containing two ring nitrogens flanked by three carbonyl groups. The carbon at position 5 is quaternary, bearing both an isopropyl group and a furan-2-ylmethyl substituent, which makes the core non-planar about that center and gives it a branched, asymmetric substitution pattern. The attached furan is an aromatic five-membered oxygen heterocycle linked through a flexible methylene bridge, adding some conformational freedom. The imide-like N–H groups on the pyrimidine ring act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the three carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the furan oxygen can accept a further hydrogen bond.

This molecule is built on a six-membered, partially saturated nitrogen-containing ring, a 1,4-dihydropyridine scaffold. The ring carries two methyl groups on the carbons flanking the nitrogen and two ethyl ester groups on the carbons at the 3 and 5 positions, giving a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The C=C double bonds conjugate with the ester carbonyls, and the ring has a single sp3-hybridized carbon at the 4-position, which places it out of plane and gives a puckered, moderately rigid shape. The ring N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the four ester oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a quinoline scaffold. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon that bears the nitrogen-adjacent position, so the oxygen and the ring nitrogen are positioned for intramolecular interaction. A bromine atom occupies the position para to the hydroxyl group on the carbocyclic ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern across the fused framework. The fully aromatic, planar, and rigid core leaves little conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the pyridine-type nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane ring that carries two substituents on the same carbon, one of them being a tertiary alcohol, and a phenyl group on the carbon across the ring, so the ring is 1,4-disubstituted. Attached to the carbinol carbon is a side chain containing a stereogenic alpha-carbon bearing an ethyl group and a terminal carboxylic acid. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, and the cyclohexane ring is saturated and non-fused, giving it chair-type conformational flexibility, while the aromatic ring adds planar rigidity. The structure has no overall symmetry because the two ends of the scaffold differ. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the tertiary hydroxyl adds a further donor and acceptor.

This molecule is built around a substituted benzamide core: a benzene ring bearing an amide carbonyl, a sulfonamide group bearing an N-methyl substituent, a primary aromatic amine, and a methoxy ether, arranged so that the ring carries four distinct substituents. The amide nitrogen connects through a methylene linker to a pyrrolidine ring, which is itself N-substituted with an allyl (prop-2-enyl) group, giving a flexible tertiary amine. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the pyrrolidine and allyl portions add conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. Hydrogen-bond donors include the amide N–H, the sulfonamide N–H, and the aromatic NH2, whereas the carbonyl oxygen, sulfonyl oxygens, methoxy oxygen, and tertiary amine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated aliphatic chain with no rings, fused systems, or aromatic groups. A single terminal aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing one hydrogen) caps one end of the straight carbon backbone, and the other end is a terminal methyl group. Because the chain has no substituents or branching, the molecule is essentially symmetric only in its linear arrangement and is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms and a sulfur atom, forming a 1,2,4-benzothiadiazine-type ring system with the sulfur bearing two oxygen atoms (a sulfonyl group). The benzene ring carries a primary sulfonamide group and a chlorine atom on adjacent positions, while the saturated portion of the heterocycle bears a trichloromethyl substituent on the carbon between the two nitrogens. The fused ring system is largely rigid, with only the trichloromethyl group offering rotational freedom. The sulfonyl oxygens and the sulfonamide nitrogen-bound hydrogens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor and donor sites, and the ring NH group adds further donor capability.

The molecule is built from two phenyl rings linked through a central one-carbon-bridged hydrazine unit. One benzene ring is attached directly to a sp3 carbon that also carries a methyl group, giving a 1-phenylethyl fragment. This carbon bonds to one nitrogen of a hydrazine, and the second nitrogen is acylated by a benzoyl group, forming a hydrazide with a carbonyl oxygen acceptor. The two benzene rings are unfused and separated by flexible single bonds, so the structure is conformationally flexible and lacks any internal symmetry. The two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a diacylurea built around a central urea unit, with one carbonyl bearing a 2,6-difluorobenzoyl group and the other nitrogen attached to a 2,6-dichloro-substituted phenyl ring. The aromatic ring on the urea side carries a polyfluorinated alkoxy group, a 1,1,2,3,3,3-hexafluoropropoxy chain, located para to the urea nitrogen and flanked by the chlorine atoms. Both benzene rings are planar and there are no fused ring systems, but the molecule as a whole is flexible because of the rotatable amide and urea bonds. The urea and amide N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and ether oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single quaternary carbon that serves as a central scaffold, carrying four substituents: two hydroxymethyl groups (–CH2OH) and two chloromethyl groups (–CH2Cl). There are no rings and no fused ring systems, so the structure is entirely acyclic and saturated. The two primary alcohol groups are functional groups capable of acting as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the two primary alkyl chlorides are polar but are not hydrogen-bond donors and only weakly accept hydrogen bonds. The arrangement is highly symmetrical, with the two hydroxymethyl arms and the two chloromethyl arms each pairwise equivalent around the central carbon. Because all linkages are single bonds about a tetrahedral center, the molecule is flexible, with free rotation about its C–C and C–O bonds.

This molecule is built on an imidazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 arrangement. The ring carries a methyl group on the carbon between the two nitrogens, a nitro group on one ring carbon, and a 2-hydroxypropyl chain attached to the ring nitrogen. The nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent that is conjugated with the aromatic system. The side chain contains a secondary alcohol, giving the molecule a hydroxyl that can donate a hydrogen bond, while the ring nitrogen, the nitro oxygens, and the hydroxyl oxygen can all accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule is asymmetric because of the unsymmetrical substitution pattern and the stereocenter-bearing side chain, and it has moderate flexibility from the rotatable propyl linkage.

The molecule is a secondary ester built around a branched carbon chain: an isopropyl group bonded to a carbon that carries both a para-chlorophenyl ring and an ester oxygen. The ester links this carbon to a pyridine-3-carboxylic acid unit, so the scaffold combines two aromatic rings joined through a flexible sp3 linker. The benzene ring carries a single chlorine substituent at the para position, while the pyridine ring contains one nitrogen atom at the meta position relative to the carbonyl. The molecule has no fused ring systems and no internal symmetry axis because the two aromatic rings differ. The ester carbonyl oxygen and pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from a linear three-carbon chain bearing a carboxylic acid at one end, with the middle carbon bonded to a cyclohexane ring. The ring carbon attached to the chain also carries a hydroxyl group, making it a tertiary alcohol, so the ring is a simple saturated six-membered carbocycle with no fusion or unsaturation. The scaffold is fully saturated and sp3-hybridized throughout, lacking any aromatic rings or double bonds apart from the carbonyl of the acid group. The carboxylic acid and the hydroxyl group together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and up to three acceptor sites. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, with the stereocenter at the alpha carbon of the acid and the substituted ring carbon, and the molecule has considerable conformational flexibility due to its open chain and rotatable bonds.

The molecule is built around a cyclopentane ring that carries two identical substituents on the same carbon, a quaternary center bearing two CH2 groups. Each of those CH2 groups is bonded through an oxygen to a carbamate carbonyl, and each carbamate nitrogen is attached to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the two arms are symmetric. Each carbamate unit has one N–H that can donate a hydrogen bond and a carbonyl oxygen plus an ether-type oxygen that can accept one. The two phenyl rings are unsubstituted and attached through nitrogen, giving the molecule a mirror-symmetric, moderately flexible shape built from aromatic and saturated segments.

The molecule is built on a six-membered pyridazinone core, a diazine ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl group at one position. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons of this ring, one of them directly beside the carbonyl, giving a dense, electron-poor substitution pattern. A phenyl ring is attached to one of the ring nitrogens, so the two aromatic systems are joined by a single N–C bond and are not fused. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, and the overall scaffold is largely planar and rigid, with limited rotational freedom about the N–phenyl bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the remaining ring nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic carboxylic acid with a terminal carboxyl group at one end. A long, unbranched methylene chain runs from the acid group to a single five-membered carbocyclic ring at the other end. The ring is a cyclopentene, containing one carbon-carbon double bond, so it is partially unsaturated and not fully aromatic. There are no ring fusions and no additional substituents, so the scaffold is simple and lacks any symmetry beyond the local ring geometry. The long saturated chain gives considerable conformational flexibility, while the ring and its double bond add some local rigidity. The carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the remaining hydrocarbon framework contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a 2-(2-chlorophenoxy)propanoic acid, built from a three-carbon chain bearing a carboxylic acid at one end and an aryl ether at the alpha carbon. The benzene ring is ortho-disubstituted, with an ether oxygen and a chlorine atom on adjacent carbons, giving an aromatic scaffold that is planar and rigid. The alpha carbon is a stereocenter, so the molecule is chiral, and its rotatable bonds around the ether linkage and side chain give it moderate conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the OH) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor and the chlorine as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a dibenzofuran scaffold, a tricyclic system in which a central five-membered furan ring is fused to two benzene rings, making the framework essentially planar and rigid. A single nitro group (–NO2) is attached to one of the outer benzene rings, at a position that breaks the symmetry of the parent scaffold. The aromatic system has no rotatable bonds and no sp3-hybridized carbons, so its conformation is fixed. The furan oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitro oxygens are stronger acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built around a 1,3,5-triazine ring bearing a methoxy group and a methyl group at two of its carbons, with the third carbon linked to a urea-type nitrogen. That urea connects through a carbonyl to a sulfonyl group, which is attached to a benzene ring. The benzene ring carries an ortho substituent consisting of an ether oxygen followed by a three-carbon chain ending in a chlorine atom. The aromatic triazine and benzene rings are joined through a flexible sulfonylurea bridge, giving the molecule moderate conformational freedom around its linking bonds. Hydrogen-bond donors come from the two N-H groups of the urea-sulfonyl unit, while the triazine nitrogens, carbonyl oxygen, sulfonyl oxygens, and ether oxygens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two chlorine atoms in a meta-relationship, with a third substituent at the remaining position. That substituent is an oxetane-like small ring: a carbon bearing the aryl group is part of a three-membered epoxide (oxirane) ring, since the ring closure contains only one oxygen and two carbons, linking the quaternary carbon to a CH2 that bears an oxygen bridge. Attached to the same quaternary carbon is a two-carbon chain ending in a trichloromethyl group. The aryl ring is planar and aromatic, while the epoxide introduces strain and rigidity at the junction. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the aryl ring. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor: the ether oxygen of the epoxide, with no hydrogen-bond donors present.

The molecule is built around a 1,2-oxazole (isoxazole) ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms. At one carbon of this ring sits a quaternary carbon bearing two ethyl groups and a methyl group, creating a bulky, branched alkyl substituent. The ring's other carbon carries an amide nitrogen, which links through a carbonyl to a benzene ring bearing two methoxy groups flanking the amide attachment point, a 2,6-disubstitution pattern. The aliphatic branch and ortho-methoxy groups give the molecule considerable steric bulk and restricted rotation around the amide bond. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the two methoxy oxygens, and the ring nitrogen and oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single quaternary carbon that serves as the central atom of a simple acyclic scaffold, with no rings and no fused systems. Four identical iodomethyl groups (–CH2I) radiate outward from this central carbon, giving the molecule a tetrahedral arrangement and a high degree of symmetry. Each arm terminates in a carbon–iodine bond, which is the only functional group present. Because the structure contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms capable of accepting hydrogen bonds, its hydrogen-bonding capability is essentially nil. The molecule is highly flexible, since all of its bonds are single bonds around sp3 carbons that can rotate freely.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene-like bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming an isoquinoline core. The fused system is fully aromatic and planar, so the framework is rigid with no rotatable bonds. A primary amino group is attached to the carbon in the pyridine ring adjacent to the ring nitrogen, which places it at the position next to the heteroatom. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the amino group supplies two hydrogen-bond donor sites and can also accept hydrogen bonds through its nitrogen lone pair. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the planar framework because the single substituent breaks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to one ring carbon is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a chlorine atom, and on the adjacent carbon sits a hydroxyl group, giving a 1,2-disubstituted, ortho-patterned arrangement. The molecule lacks any rotational symmetry beyond a planar mirror plane through the ring, and its small size and lack of flexible chains make it fairly rigid. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as an acceptor, and the acyl chloride carbon is a reactive electrophilic center.

The molecule is a naphthalene derivative in which a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached to one of the carbon atoms of the fused bicyclic aromatic system. The two six-membered aromatic rings share an edge, giving a flat, rigid, fully conjugated scaffold with no rotatable bonds within the core. The substituent sits at a position on one ring, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern that lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis. The single primary alcohol group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. Apart from that hydroxyl, the molecule contains no other polar functional groups.

The molecule is a single, unbranched hydrocarbon chain with a terminal alkene: one carbon-carbon double bond sits at one end, and the rest of the structure is a straight run of saturated methylene units. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or other functional groups, so the scaffold is purely aliphatic. The molecule has no stereocenters and no substitution pattern to speak of, and its only symmetry is the loose constitutional symmetry of a linear chain. It is highly flexible, since rotation about the many single bonds lets the chain adopt many conformations. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, because it consists only of carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring containing two nitrogen atoms separated by one carbon, with no ring fusion. The nitrogen at position 1 carries a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group, so the substitution pattern is a simple N-alkyl imidazole with no other ring substituents. The ring is planar and aromatic, and the ethyl linker adds some conformational flexibility to an otherwise rigid core. The terminal alcohol is both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the unsubstituted pyridine-type nitrogen on the ring serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the ring itself.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Going around the ring, a methyl group and a hydroxyl group sit on adjacent carbons, and an isopropyl group sits on the carbon para to the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The phenolic hydroxyl is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkyl groups are nonpolar and contribute only steric bulk and lipophilic character. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with the isopropyl group providing a small degree of rotational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the mirror plane of the ring framework, since the three substituents are all different.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned meta to each other across the ring. It carries three substituents: a methyl group on one ring carbon and a chlorine atom on each of the two carbons flanked by the ring nitrogens. Because the ring is fully aromatic and planar, the scaffold is rigid with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the methyl sits on a different carbon than the two chlorines. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched carbon chain of ten carbons with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple linear skeleton. One end carries a carboxylic acid group, where a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl oxygen, and the carbonyl carbon sits directly next to a carbon-carbon triple bond, making it an alkynoic acid. The triple bond is located at the second position from the acid carbon, creating a rigid, linear segment in an otherwise flexible chain. The remaining hexyl tail is an unbranched alkyl group that adds conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry, since the acid end and the alkyl end differ. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is built on a fused polycyclic aromatic scaffold made of four six-membered rings, with three rings fused in an angular, phenanthrene-like arrangement and an additional ring fused onto it. The core is fully aromatic and planar, giving it a rigid, flat framework with no rotatable bonds. A single primary amino group (–NH2) is attached to one of the terminal outer rings, which is the only functional group present. That amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the nitrogen lone pair. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the amino group sits at an asymmetric position on the fused framework.

This molecule is a symmetric diester built around a central oxalate (ethanedioate) core, with two carbonyl groups bonded directly to each other. Each carbonyl carbon is attached to an ester oxygen that links to an isopentyl (3-methylbutyl) chain, so the two halves are identical and the molecule has a mirror-symmetric, C2-like arrangement about the central C–C bond. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and fairly flexible, with free rotation about the C–C and C–O single bonds. The four carbonyl and ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all N–H and O–H groups are absent. Each terminal end carries a branched methyl-substituted alkyl group, which adds steric bulk at the periphery.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by a single methylene linker: a benzene ring bearing a CH2 group that connects to the nitrogen of a pyrrole ring. The pyrrole is a five-membered, electron-rich aromatic heterocycle with its nitrogen fully substituted, so it has no N-H and cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, with no polar functional groups, and the two rings are not fused, so the scaffold is a simple N-benzylpyrrole arrangement. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks rotational symmetry overall, though the benzyl linker gives it moderate conformational flexibility. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor capability is weak, arising from the pyrrole nitrogen's lone pair, which is delocalized into the aromatic system.

This molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered cyclic imide, meaning two carbonyl groups flank a nitrogen atom within the ring. The nitrogen is substituted with a benzyl group, a methylene linker attached to a second, unfused phenyl ring. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the benzyl arm adds some rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The imide carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen carries no hydrogen. Two aromatic systems give the molecule a largely flat, aromatic character overall, with no stereocenters and only limited overall symmetry.

The molecule is an ester built from a long, unbranched saturated acyl chain joined to a short linear alkyl group. The acid portion contains sixteen carbons in a straight chain ending in a carbonyl carbon, which is bonded through an oxygen atom to a three-carbon propyl group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. The only functional group is the ester linkage, which provides one carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and one ether-type oxygen that is a weak acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. Its high flexibility arises from many freely rotating single bonds along the chain, and it lacks any element of symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the alkyl groups.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a bicyclic system of two fused benzene rings sharing one edge. A hydrazinyl group (–NH–NH2) is attached to one of the carbons on the fused ring junction side, at an alpha position adjacent to the ring fusion. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with the substituent extending from it giving limited conformational flexibility. The hydrazine unit provides two adjacent nitrogen atoms with hydrogen-bond donor capability through its N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through the lone pairs on nitrogen. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the single substituent breaks the symmetry of the parent ring system.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries a nitro group (-NO2) at the meta position relative to the carbonyl attachment point, giving a 3-substituted phenyl ring. The scaffold is non-fused, with no ring fusion, and the two aromatic rings can rotate about the single bonds connecting them to the carbonyl carbon, so the molecule is moderately flexible. The overall shape lacks any internal symmetry because the nitro substituent breaks the symmetry between the two rings. The carbonyl oxygen and the nitro group's oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond between their para-positions relative to each other's substituents.
