Each ring carries three methyl groups and one hydroxyl group, arranged so that each hydroxyl sits flanked by two ortho-methyl groups. The two rings are related by a symmetry plane through the inter-ring bond, giving the molecule a mirror-symmetric, C2-like overall shape. The biaryl bond allows rotation, so the molecule has some conformational flexibility, though the bulky ortho-methyl groups restrict that rotation. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two oxygen atoms are the only heteroatoms present.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing a bond, giving a flat, rigid, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A dimethylamino group, a nitrogen bearing two methyl substituents, is attached to one carbon of the naphthalene ring at a position beta to the ring fusion. The only functional group is this tertiary amine, which has no N-H bond. Because the nitrogen lacks a hydrogen, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, although the nitrogen lone pair can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the two rings equivalent, aside from the local symmetry of the two methyl groups.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic amine built on a single straight chain of eighteen saturated carbon atoms, with a methyl-substituted nitrogen attached at one terminus. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic groups, so the scaffold is entirely linear and unbranched. The only functional group is a secondary amine, in which the nitrogen carries one hydrogen and one methyl group in addition to the alkyl chain. The molecule is highly flexible, since its many carbon-carbon single bonds allow free rotation, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond the approximate linearity of the chain. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the hydrocarbon portion contributes no polar interaction sites.

Parsing the SMILES: a phenol ring (OH on a benzene ring) fused via a CH2 bridge and a direct biaryl bond to a second benzene ring, forming a fluorene-type tricyclic core (a 9H-fluorene skeleton). The hydroxyl sits on one of the outer aromatic rings, making the molecule a hydroxyfluorene with substitution at a single position on one ring. The central five-membered ring contains an sp3 CH2 carbon, so the framework is largely planar and rigid, with only modest flexibility from the methylene bridge. The molecule lacks a mirror-plane or rotational symmetry because the hydroxyl breaks the symmetry of the fused system. The phenolic OH provides one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor site at the oxygen, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak, non-directional interaction surfaces.

The molecule is an acyclic secondary amine built from two straight, unbranched alkyl chains of seven carbons each, joined through a single nitrogen atom at the center. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or other heteroatom-bearing groups beyond that one amine nitrogen, so the scaffold is simply a long linear hydrocarbon framework interrupted by a single N-H center. The two chains are identical, giving the molecule a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the nitrogen. Because every bond is a single rotatable bond along a flexible chain, the structure is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The nitrogen carries one hydrogen, so it can act as one hydrogen-bond donor and, through its lone pair, as one hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents spread around the ring: an ethyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is attached to an ethyl chain), a methyl group, and two hydroxyl groups. Taking the ester-bearing carbon as position one, the methyl sits at position two, and the hydroxyls sit at positions four and six, giving a 1,3-relationship between the two phenolic oxygens. The ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester tail adds some conformational flexibility. The two phenolic hydroxyls can each donate a hydrogen bond, and together with the ester oxygens they provide several hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. The overall arrangement is asymmetric, since the substituents are not evenly distributed around the ring.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic acetal, built from a long, unbranched sixteen-carbon chain in which the terminal carbon of the chain is bonded to a single carbon bearing two identical methoxy groups. The carbon framework is fully saturated, containing no rings, no double bonds, and no aromatic systems. Its only heteroatoms are the two ether oxygens, which sit on the same acetal carbon and each carry a terminal methyl group. The structure is substituted only at that one acetal center, so there is no stereocenter and the molecule has a plane of symmetry running through the acetal carbon and the chain. It is highly flexible because of the many freely rotating single bonds along the alkyl chain. The oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that serves as the central atom of a neopentane-type scaffold, with four identical two-carbon arms radiating outward. Each arm consists of a methylene group bearing one bromine atom, so the structure contains four primary alkyl bromide functional groups and no rings or ring fusion. The substitution pattern is fully symmetric, with all four bromomethyl units attached to the same central carbon, giving the molecule high tetrahedral symmetry. Because every bond is a single sigma bond with free rotation, the framework is flexible, though the bulky central carbon restricts the arms to a compact, roughly spherical shape. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no O-H or N-H groups, and the bromine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, placing them in an ortho relationship. One substituent is an isocyanate group, consisting of a nitrogen double-bonded to a carbon that is itself double-bonded to oxygen, attached directly to the ring. The neighboring ring carbon carries a chlorine atom. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the isocyanate group is linear and has no hydrogen-bond donors, though its oxygen and nitrogen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring and substituents, and its only significant flexibility lies in rotation about the bond joining the isocyanate to the ring.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single sulfur atom, forming a diaryl sulfide (thioether) scaffold. Each ring carries one bromine atom at the position para to the sulfur linkage, so the two halogens sit on opposite ends of the molecule. The overall structure has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the sulfur atom, with both halves identical. Both aromatic rings are planar and rigid, while the C–S–C linkage allows some rotational flexibility around the bonds to sulfur. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom is only a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a pyridine-3-carboxamide, meaning a six-membered aromatic nitrogen-containing ring bearing a carboxamide group at the position meta to the ring nitrogen. The ring is unsubstituted apart from this single amide attachment, so the substitution pattern is simple and the ring itself is flat and rigid. The amide nitrogen carries a hydroxymethyl group, giving a flexible N-CH2-OH arm that can rotate relative to the planar aromatic system. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the substituent sits on one side of the ring. The ring nitrogen and the amide carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amide N-H and the terminal hydroxyl O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an anthracene-type tricyclic core, three fused benzene rings in a linear arrangement, and the central ring carries two benzyl groups on its 9 and 10 positions, which are the para-related carbons across the middle ring. Each benzyl unit consists of a methylene linker joining the central ring to a separate unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the molecule contains five aromatic rings in total. The substitution pattern is symmetric about a central axis through the two substituted carbons, and the structure is largely rigid because of the fused aromatic framework, though the methylene linkers permit rotation of the outer phenyl rings. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or heteroatoms, so its only interactions are as a weak acceptor through the pi-electron systems.

This molecule is a small acyclic sulfur-centered compound built around a sulfinyl (S=O) group flanked by two dimethylamino nitrogens. Each nitrogen carries two methyl substituents, so the scaffold is symmetric about the central sulfur, with no rings and no fused systems. The sulfur is bonded to two tertiary amine nitrogens and one oxygen, which is the only electronegative atom that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the nitrogens have no hydrogens to donate. Because all bonds are single or the single S=O double bond and there are no rotationally restricted units, the structure is comparatively flexible.

This molecule consists of two benzene rings joined by a single ether oxygen, forming a diaryl ether scaffold with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ether linkage, giving it an ortho substitution pattern, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The ether oxygen is the only heteroatom and functional group present, and it can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The two aromatic rings can rotate about the C–O–C bonds, so the structure is moderately flexible, and it lacks any overall symmetry because of the asymmetric methyl placement.

The molecule is an acyclic, flexible chain built from two-carbon units, with no rings and no aromatic systems. Its backbone is a linear sequence of ethylene segments joined by secondary amine nitrogens, so the skeleton consists of two terminal hydroxyethyl arms bridged by a central ethylene-amine-ethylene linkage. Each end carries a primary alcohol group, and the two secondary amine nitrogens sit at the interior positions of the chain. The arrangement is symmetric about the central nitrogen, which lies at the midpoint of the chain. Because there are many single bonds and no ring constraints, the molecule is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and each secondary amine can also donate and accept hydrogen bonds, giving the molecule several polar sites.

The molecule is a straight-chain, fully saturated alkane scaffold of seven methylene units, with a bromine atom bonded to each terminal carbon, giving a symmetric 1,7-dibromoheptane pattern. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the two carbon-bromine bonds at either end. The two halogen substituents sit at equivalent positions on opposite termini, so the molecule has a centre of symmetry along the midpoint of the chain. The chain is highly flexible, as its many single bonds can rotate freely and adopt numerous conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, since the bromine atoms are weak halogen acceptors rather than classical hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic amino alcohol built on a short two-carbon ethanol chain, with no ring systems and no aromatic rings. The nitrogen carries a tert-butyl group, a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, which provides a bulky, symmetric end to the structure. A secondary amine links this tert-butyl group to a two-carbon spacer that terminates in a primary alcohol. The skeleton is highly flexible because all bonds are single and free to rotate, and the molecule lacks any stereocenters. The secondary amine N–H and the hydroxyl O–H can each act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen and oxygen lone pairs serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a xanthine-type bicyclic scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidinedione ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, sharing a common C–C bond. Two N-methyl groups sit on the pyrimidinedione nitrogens, and a carbonyl sits at each of the two positions flanking them. The imidazole ring carries a CH2 linker bearing a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the morpholine ring adds conformational flexibility at its tether. Carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the morpholine oxygen and the imidazole nitrogen add further acceptor sites, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a linear, unbranched aliphatic diester-acid built from a four-carbon chain. One end carries a butyl ester, formed from a straight n-butyl group bonded through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon. The other end terminates in a free carboxylic acid, separated from the ester carbonyl by a two-carbon methylene linker. The molecule contains no rings, no aromatic systems, and no stereocenters, so it is highly flexible with freely rotating single bonds. Its polar termini provide two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites at the ester and two carbonyl-type oxygens at the acid, while the carboxylic hydroxyl serves as a hydrogen-bond donor.

This molecule is a fully fluorinated saturated carbocycle, a six-membered ring built entirely from sp3 carbons. Every ring carbon carries fluorine atoms, and there are no hydrogens on the skeleton. One ring carbon bears a trifluoromethyl group, and another ring carbon, adjacent to it, is substituted by a second trifluoromethyl group, which lies in the ring's first-carbon position relative to the chain. The ring has no fused partners, no heteroatoms other than fluorine, and no polar functional groups, so there is no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability beyond the weak fluorine lone pairs. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, the ring is conformationally constrained with limited flexibility, and the overall framework is rigid and compact.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexene-type scaffold with one carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to a ketone, making it a cyclic enol-ketone system. A methyl group sits on one alkene carbon and an isopropyl group sits on a saturated ring carbon, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is fully carbocyclic and single-ring, so it is relatively rigid around the alkene and conjugated core, while the isopropyl group and the remaining saturated carbons allow some conformational flexibility. The enol hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a five-membered furanose-type ring (containing one ring oxygen) is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, with an acetal-type carbon linking the two oxygens. Three secondary hydroxyl groups are attached to the carbocyclic positions, giving the structure a clearly asymmetric substitution pattern across its stereocenters. The fused ring system is relatively rigid, while the hydroxyls add conformational freedom at their attachment points. Each hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ring oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors, making the molecule highly polar in its hydrogen-bonding capacity.

This molecule is a bicyclic tropane-type scaffold: a seven-membered bridged system in which a nitrogen-containing bridge spans a cyclohexane-like ring, creating a rigid, compact three-dimensional framework. The bridgehead nitrogen carries a methyl substituent, making it a tertiary amine. A ketone group sits on one of the carbon bridges, adding a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring system is conformationally constrained, so the molecule shows little flexibility. The nitrogen lone pair and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all nitrogen and carbon valences are satisfied by alkyl or carbonyl groups.

This molecule is an acyclic tetraester built on a four-carbon chain, with each of the four carbons bearing a carboxylate group as an ethyl ester. The central two carbons each carry one hydrogen and link the two inner ester carbonyls, giving a flexible, unbranched backbone with no ring systems or ring fusion. Four ethoxycarbonyl groups are arranged symmetrically about the central C–C bond, so the molecule has a two-fold symmetry in its constitution. The skeleton is highly flexible because of many freely rotating single bonds. Each ester group offers a carbonyl oxygen and an ether oxygen as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all acidic hydrogens have been replaced by ethyl groups.

The molecule is built on a saturated five-membered sulfur-containing ring, a sulfolane (tetrahydrothiophene 1,1-dioxide) scaffold. The sulfur atom carries two double-bonded oxygen atoms, forming a sulfone group that is strongly polar and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens, while it has no hydrogen-bond donors. A single methyl group is attached to a ring carbon adjacent to the methylene next to the sulfone, giving a monosubstituted, non-symmetric pattern with one stereocenter. The ring is fully saturated with no aromatic or fused rings, so it is conformationally flexible, adopting puckered envelope-like shapes.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond with no ring fusion between them. Each ring carries one sulfonic acid group (–SO3H) attached at the para position relative to the inter-ring bond, giving a linear, symmetric 4,4'-disubstituted arrangement. The two aromatic rings are conjugated through the central bond and can twist relative to one another, so the framework is fairly rigid overall. Each sulfonic acid group contributes both hydrogen-bond donor capacity through its acidic O–H and multiple acceptor sites through its sulfonyl oxygens.

The molecule is benzophenone hydrazone, built around a single sp2 carbon that is double-bonded to a hydrazone nitrogen (N=C) and singly bonded to two phenyl rings. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the substitution pattern is simple and symmetric about the central C=N axis. The terminal NH2 group of the hydrazone unit gives the molecule a hydrogen-bond donor site, while the imine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The two aryl rings can rotate about their single bonds to the central carbon, so the scaffold is moderately flexible, though the conjugated C=N bond itself is rigid.

The molecule is an acyclic thioether built from a linear chain of carbon and sulfur atoms, with no rings and no aromatic systems. Two sulfur atoms sit at the centre of the chain, each flanked by two-carbon ethyl and ethylene segments, so the sulfur atoms are separated by a two-carbon bridge. The structure has no functional groups beyond the thioether linkages and possesses approximate mirror symmetry through the central CH2 group. Because all bonds are single and the chain has many rotatable bonds, the molecule is highly flexible. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, so it has no ring fusion or aromatic systems. The carbon skeleton consists of a long run of sp3 methylene units terminated at one end by a methyl group and at the other by a nitrile group, which is a carbon-nitrogen triple bond. Its only functional group is that terminal nitrile, and there are no substituents along the chain, so the substitution pattern is simple and linear. The molecule has a mirror-like, linear symmetry along its long axis, and the many single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic sulfonic acid built on a small aliphatic skeleton: an isopropyl group (a central carbon bearing two methyl groups) is bonded directly to a sulfur atom. That sulfur carries two double-bonded oxygens and one hydroxyl group, forming a sulfonic acid functional group, so there are no rings and no ring fusion. The substitution pattern is simple and branched, with the sulfonyl group sitting at one terminus of the branched carbon chain. The molecule has a local two-fold symmetry about the C–S axis because the two methyl groups are equivalent, and its flexibility is limited to rotation about single bonds. The hydroxyl hydrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the three oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a flexible linker, with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, placing the methyl and the amine linkage in an ortho relationship. The two aryl rings are connected through a secondary amine nitrogen that bears one hydrogen, and a methylene (CH2) bridge separates that nitrogen from the second aromatic ring. Because the molecule contains only aromatic carbocycles, a single N-H group serves as the hydrogen-bond donor, and the nitrogen lone pair offers modest acceptor capability. The rotatable benzylic and aryl-amine bonds make the scaffold fairly flexible, and the molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two rings differ in substitution.

The molecule is built around a piperazine core, a six-membered saturated ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions (1,4-relationship). Both ring nitrogens are fully substituted, each bearing an ethoxycarbonyl group, so the molecule is a symmetric 1,4-bis(ethyl carbamate)-type derivative with an identical substitution pattern on each side. The two carbamate units each contain a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The piperazine ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, and the ethyl ester tails add conformational freedom, giving a moderately flexible, centrosymmetric structure overall.

The molecule is a linear polysulfide chain of four sulfur atoms, with each terminal sulfur bonded to a tert-butyl group. Each tert-butyl unit is a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, giving the structure a compact, bulky, and roughly symmetrical arrangement about the central S–S–S–S axis. There are no rings and no fused ring systems, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. The only functional groups are the sulfur–sulfur bonds of the polysulfide linkage, with no hydroxyl, carbonyl, amine, or other heteroatom-bearing groups. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, and its sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its flexibility comes from rotation about the S–S bonds, which is partly restricted by the bulky tert-butyl ends.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with no ring systems and no aromatic rings. Its skeleton is a straight, unbranched chain of thirteen carbon atoms, with a single carbonyl group (C=O) located at the centre, so that the chain is split into a seven-carbon arm and a six-carbon arm. The only functional group is this ketone, which contains a polar carbon-oxygen double bond with no hydrogen bond donor capability; the oxygen can act only as a hydrogen bond acceptor. The chain is highly flexible, free to adopt many conformations through rotation about its single bonds. The molecule is nearly symmetric, since the two arms are almost identical in length apart from the one-carbon difference.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon chain, with a nitro group attached at the far end of that chain. The aromatic ring is a single unfused six-membered carbon ring, and it is monosubstituted, so there is no regiochemical substitution pattern to consider and the ring carries no other substituents. The nitro group, with its formally charged nitrogen and two oxygens, is the only polar functional group, and it can accept hydrogen bonds at its oxygen atoms while offering no hydrogen-bond donors. The ethylene linker between the ring and the nitro group gives the molecule some conformational flexibility, while the phenyl ring remains planar and rigid, and the overall structure has no symmetry axis beyond the ring's local symmetry.

This molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing two chlorine atoms at the 2 and 4 positions, relative to the carbon bearing the side chain. A two-carbon linker joins that ring to a 1,2,4-triazole ring attached through one of its nitrogen atoms, giving an aromatic five-membered heterocycle with three nitrogens and two CH positions. The side chain also carries a tetrafluoroethyl ether, an oxygen bridging a CH2 group to a CF2H–CF2 unit, which is fully fluorinated except for one terminal hydrogen-bearing carbon. The molecule has no stereocentres in its ring systems but contains one tetrahedral carbon in the linker, so it is conformationally flexible around its single bonds. Hydrogen-bond capability is modest: the triazole nitrogens and the ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the only donor is the weakly acidic CF2H hydrogen.

This molecule is an unbranched saturated alkyl chain of twenty carbons with a primary alcohol group on one terminus, so it is a straight-chain aliphatic alcohol with no rings or fused ring systems. The scaffold is a single linear skeleton of methylene units ending in a terminal hydroxyl group, and there is no substitution along the chain or branching to break its symmetry. Its only symmetry is the approximate mirror relationship along the carbon backbone, with no stereocenters present. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating carbon-carbon single bonds that allow it to adopt numerous conformations. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar and hydrocarbon in character.

The molecule is built around a single, acyclic four-carbon chain: a central C=C double bond flanked on each side by a carbon that carries two ester groups. Each of the four carbons bears a carboxylate ester in which the carbonyl is attached to an ethyl-oxygen unit, so there are four ethyl ester groups in total. The skeleton is therefore a tetra-substituted alkene, with all four substituents being ethoxycarbonyl groups arranged symmetrically around the double bond. The molecule has no rings, so it is flexible about its single bonds, although the conjugated alkene and carbonyls restrict rotation somewhat. Its carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a 2,3-dimethylanthraquinone-type scaffold: three fused six-membered rings in a linear arrangement, with the central ring bearing two carbonyl groups at opposite positions. The two outer rings are benzene rings, and the terminal ring carrying the two adjacent methyl substituents forms the fused aromatic framework alongside the central quinone-like ring. The two methyl groups sit on adjacent carbons of one outer ring, giving that ring an asymmetric substitution pattern relative to the unsubstituted outer ring. The core is largely planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the ring system, though the methyl groups can rotate freely. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxyl group, a methyl group, and an n-butyl chain, forming a trisubstituted phenol. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon, the butyl group occupies the ortho position relative to it, and the methyl group sits para to the hydroxyl, giving a 2,5-type pattern across the aromatic core. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, while the four-carbon alkyl chain is flexible and can adopt multiple conformations. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane in the ring framework, because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically.

This molecule is a straight-chain primary amine built on an unbranched, fully saturated skeleton of eleven carbon atoms. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no double or triple bonds, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and aliphatic. Its only functional group is a primary amine (–NH2) located at one terminus of the chain, with no substituents along the carbon backbone. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror relationship of its linear alkyl framework, and the long chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through rotation about its single bonds. The nitrogen atom can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is built around a single tertiary amine nitrogen that serves as the central atom of a compact, acyclic scaffold. Three identical two-carbon arms radiate outward from this nitrogen, and each arm terminates in a nitrile group, giving the molecule three cyano substituents arranged in a threefold, propeller-like pattern. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, so the framework is entirely open-chain. The molecule has high local symmetry, with the three arms equivalent, and the arms provide moderate conformational flexibility around their single bonds. The nitrogen lone pair and the nitrile nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a 1,1-diarylethylene core, with one aryl group being a para-substituted benzoic acid ring and the other a bicyclic tetralin-type system. That second aryl is a 1,1,4,4,6-pentasubstituted tetralin, where a saturated six-membered carbocycle is fused to the aromatic ring, bearing two gem-dimethyl groups on each of the two aliphatic bridgehead-adjacent carbons and an additional methyl on the aromatic ring. The carboxylic acid on the phenyl ring is the sole hydrogen-bond donor and provides two acceptor oxygens, while the remaining framework is entirely hydrocarbon. The overall structure is bulky and sterically crowded around the ethylene linker, with limited conformational flexibility arising from the fused rings and the rigid carbon-carbon double bond, and it lacks any internal symmetry axis because of the asymmetric placement of the carboxyl and methyl substituents.

The molecule is a urea derivative in which one nitrogen is attached to a naphthalene ring system, specifically at the 2-position of the fused bicyclic core. The naphthalene scaffold consists of two benzene rings sharing a common edge, giving a rigid, planar, fully aromatic framework. The urea group, with its carbonyl flanked by an NH2 and an NH, is the only polar functional group and provides two hydrogen-bond donors and one hydrogen-bond acceptor. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the urea sits on one side of the fused system, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the planar aromatic core. Overall the structure is largely rigid, with limited rotational freedom mainly around the bond linking the urea nitrogen to the ring.

The molecule is built on a xanthine-type bicyclic scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidinedione ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, with the two ring nitrogens of the pyrimidinedione each carrying a methyl group. Both carbonyl groups sit on the six-membered ring, and the imidazole ring retains one unsubstituted aromatic CH. The nitrogen on the imidazole ring bears a two-carbon ethyl linker that ends in an ester, which connects to a pyridine-3-carboxylic acid unit, so the pyridine ring is a flat aromatic substituent. The fused core and pyridine ring are rigid, while the ethyl ester linker provides the main conformational flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens and the pyridine nitrogen and ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a thiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group on one carbon, a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon, and a propanoyl amide group attached to the carbon between the sulfur and nitrogen. The amide links an ethyl-substituted carbonyl to the ring through an NH group, which can donate one hydrogen bond while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen can each accept one. Because the thiazole core is planar and fully aromatic, the scaffold is rigid, with only the ethyl tail and the amide bond offering rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since each ring position bears a different group.

This molecule is a substituted phenethylamine-type structure, built on a single benzene ring with no fused rings. The aromatic core carries three substituents: two methoxy groups (–OCH3) and one methyl group, arranged so that the ring has a 2,5-dimethoxy-4-methyl style pattern across its six positions. A two-carbon chain attached to the ring bears a methyl branch and ends in a primary amine (–NH2), which serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The two ether oxygens act only as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry because the substituents are unevenly placed and the side chain contains a stereocenter. The alkyl side chain gives moderate conformational flexibility, while the benzene ring remains rigid and planar.

The molecule is built around a para-disubstituted phenyl ring that carries an aryl ether linkage on one side and an aryloxypropanoate ester chain on the other. The ether oxygen connects this ring to a quinoxaline bicycle, a benzene ring fused to a pyrazine ring, which carries a single chlorine substituent on the benzo portion. The ester is attached through a two-carbon ethylene spacer to an oxime ether, a dimethyl-substituted C=N–O unit. Several rotatable single bonds in the ether, ester, and oxime linkages give the chain considerable flexibility, while the fused aromatic systems remain rigid and planar. Nitrogen atoms in the quinoxaline ring and the oxime, along with the oxygen atoms of the ethers and ester carbonyl, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic 1,2,4-triazole ring, a heterocycle containing three nitrogen atoms and two carbon atoms. At one carbon of this ring sits a thioether linkage that connects to a CH2 group, which is then bonded to an ethyl ester, giving a flexible side chain. A tert-butyl group occupies the other carbon of the ring, adding bulky, nonpolar character. The ring nitrogen that is not part of the thioether bears an N,N-dimethylcarbamoyl group, a urea-like amide attached through a carbonyl. The ring itself is unfused and planar, while the ester and carbamoyl groups provide conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent because there are no N-H or O-H groups, whereas the carbonyl oxygens and ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a 1,3-thiazole ring bearing a methyl group at one carbon adjacent to the sulfur and nitrogen, and a trifluoromethyl group on the neighboring carbon, which sits next to the ring nitrogen. A carboxamide links the thiazole to an aryl ring through its amide nitrogen, forming a secondary amide that is largely planar and relatively rigid. The aniline-derived phenyl ring carries two bromine atoms flanking the amide nitrogen, plus a trifluoromethoxy group positioned para to the amide attachment, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the thiazole nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a cyclopropane ring, a three-membered carbocycle that is highly strained and therefore rigid. One carbon of this ring carries two substituents: an ethyl ester group (an ethoxycarbonyl unit, with a carbonyl oxygen and an ether oxygen) and a sulfonyl group. The sulfonyl is attached to a para-tolyl ring, a benzene ring bearing a methyl group opposite the sulfur-bearing carbon, which gives it a symmetric 1,4-substitution pattern. The sulfone's two oxygens and the ester's oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a cyclopropane ring, a three-membered carbocycle that is highly strained and therefore rigid. One carbon of this ring carries two substituents: a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that bears a methyl group) and a sulfonyl group. The sulfonyl group is attached to a benzene ring, which is substituted at the position opposite to the sulfonyl linkage by a bromine atom, giving a para-disubstituted aromatic system. The sulfonyl group contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen add further acceptor sites. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its overall shape is only partly flexible, since the aryl sulfone and ester rotate about single bonds while the cyclopropane core stays fixed.

This molecule is a bicyclic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered saturated carbocycle, forming a tetralin-type scaffold. The non-aromatic ring carries a ketone carbonyl directly adjacent to the fused benzene ring, and the carbon next to that carbonyl bears an acetyl group, so the molecule contains two carbonyl functionalities in a 1,3-dicarbonyl-like arrangement. The fused rings are rigid and planar in the aromatic portion, while the saturated ring adds some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry element that maps it onto itself. Both carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type structure built from a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring through a single shared quaternary carbon, forming a spiro-type junction. The six-membered ring contains an α,β-unsaturated ketone (an enone), with a methyl group on the alkene carbon and a methyl group on the adjacent sp3 carbon. The five-membered ring carries an exocyclic isopropylidene group (a C=C bearing two methyl substituents), which adds a branched, nonpolar substituent. The scaffold is largely hydrocarbon, with only the ketone oxygen available as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and no hydrogen-bond donors. Several sp3 centers and the fused ring junction give the skeleton a moderately rigid framework.

The molecule is built around a central three-carbon-derived backbone: a tertiary carbon bearing a dimethylamino group, flanked by two identical CH2 arms. Each arm carries a sulfur-sulfur linkage (a disulfide-type S–S bond) attached to a sulfonyl group, so each terminus is a benzenesulfonyl unit, the phenyl ring being unsubstituted. The two phenyl rings are monocyclic aromatics with no fusion, and the molecule is largely flexible because of the sp3 carbons and S–S bonds, though the rings add some rigidity. The structure has an approximate mirror-type symmetry through the central carbon, although the central carbon is a stereocentre. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the tertiary amine nitrogen and the sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, a tert-butyl group, and a second methyl group. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon and makes the compound a phenol, which can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond. The tert-butyl group is bulky and branched, with a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups. Because the substituents occupy positions that break the ring's symmetry, the molecule has no mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the bulky tert-butyl group adds steric hindrance next to the phenolic oxygen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: a methyl group, two chlorine atoms, and one hydroxyl group, so it is a substituted phenol. The ring is a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, giving a planar, rigid scaffold. The two chlorines sit on adjacent carbons flanking the methyl group, and the hydroxyl is positioned para to one chlorine, creating a substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The phenolic hydroxyl acts as one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors. The methyl group is the only nonpolar, rotatable substituent.

The molecule is an aliphatic ketone built from a single unbranched chain of carbon atoms, with no ring systems present. A long saturated hydrocarbon tail of fifteen carbons runs into a carbonyl group, which is attached on its other side to a two-carbon ethyl group, so the carbonyl sits near the end of a long chain. Apart from the carbonyl oxygen, the molecule contains no heteroatoms or additional functional groups, and the substitution pattern is simple and linear. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds. The molecule has no symmetry, since the two groups flanking the carbonyl differ greatly in length. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain aliphatic diol: a saturated carbon backbone of fourteen methylene units, with a hydroxyl group bonded to each terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. Its only functional groups are the two primary alcohol groups at opposite ends of the chain, which makes the structure symmetric about the midpoint of the carbon chain. The long methylene segment is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, so the molecule can adopt numerous conformations. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two such sites at its termini.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built from a straight, unbranched chain: a six-carbon n-hexyl group bonded through an oxygen to the carbonyl carbon of a two-carbon acyl unit, which is a propanoyl (ethyl-substituted carbonyl) fragment. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is simply a linear alkyl-ester framework. The only functional group is the ester linkage, with its C=O carbonyl and single-bonded ether-type oxygen. Because the chain is flexible and unbranched, the molecule lacks any stereocenters and has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the linear arrangement. Its hydrogen-bond capability is limited: it has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the two ester oxygens serve only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a biphenyl in which one iodine atom sits on one of the two benzene rings, at the meta position relative to the bond joining the rings. Both rings are simple unsubstituted-otherwise benzene rings, so the scaffold is a fully aromatic, planar-leaning biaryl system with no fused rings. The single carbon–carbon bond linking the rings allows some rotation, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited symmetry: the unsubstituted ring retains local mirror symmetry, while the iodinated ring is asymmetric. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the only heteroatom is the halogen, which is a weak acceptor at best.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl ester (a carbonyl carbon bonded to an oxygen that carries a methyl group), a hydroxyl group, and a methyl group. The hydroxyl and the ester sit on adjacent ring carbons, so the ring is ortho-disubstituted with a pendant ester, while the methyl group occupies a position para to the hydroxyl, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the ester and hydroxyl groups are largely coplanar with it, with the terminal methyl of the ester being the main source of conformational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the carbonyl and ester oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small aromatic amide built around a 3-methylfuran ring, whose carbonyl carbon is attached at the 2-position. That carbonyl links through an amide nitrogen to a phenyl ring, giving a planar, fairly rigid scaffold made of two aromatic rings joined by a single amide bridge. The furan ring is a five-membered oxygen heterocycle carrying a methyl substituent adjacent to the carboxamide, while the benzene ring is unsubstituted. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen and the furan oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited conformational freedom around the amide and aryl–amide bonds.

This molecule is a tricyclic diterpenoid-type scaffold built from three fused six-membered carbocycles, with a perhydrophenanthrene-like arrangement. It carries an isopropyl group on one of the ring alkenes, giving a conjugated-looking but isolated trisubstituted double bond, along with a second, non-conjugated ring alkene. A carboxylic acid is attached to a quaternary carbon at one ring junction, alongside a methyl group, and two additional angular methyl groups sit on adjacent ring-fusion carbons. The fused ring system is largely rigid and bulky, with limited conformational freedom beyond the saturated cyclohexane portions. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the hydrocarbon framework offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule centers on a single quaternary carbon bearing two phenyl rings, a 1,2,4-triazol-1-yl group, and a 3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl ring, giving a propeller-like three-dimensional shape. The trifluoromethyl group sits at the meta position of one aryl ring, leaving that ring with an asymmetric substitution pattern. The two unsubstituted phenyl rings are equivalent, so the molecule has a partial mirror-type symmetry around the central carbon. The central carbon is sp3-hybridized, so the rings are rigidly fixed around it while still allowing some rotation about the bonds to the rings. The triazole's nitrogen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing a common edge. It carries four chlorine atoms as its only substituents, each attached directly to an aromatic carbon, so there are no alkyl chains, carbonyls, or other functional groups. The chlorines sit at four of the eight peripheral positions, distributed across both rings in an uneven pattern that leaves the molecule without a mirror or rotational symmetry axis passing through the whole framework. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Because it contains no hydrogen-bond donors and only weakly polarized carbon-chlorine bonds as potential acceptors, its hydrogen-bonding capability is minimal.

This molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, and it bears five chlorine substituents with no other functional groups. One ring carries three chlorines at the positions meta and para to each other and the ring junction, leaving two aromatic hydrogens, while the second ring carries three chlorines clustered on one side adjacent to the linkage. The aromatic rings are fully conjugated and planar, but the bulky chlorines flanking the bond between the rings force a substantial twist, making the molecule conformationally restricted rather than flexible. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors and has no lone-pair acceptors beyond the halogen atoms, so its polar interaction capacity is minimal, and its overall symmetry is low because the two rings carry different substitution patterns.

This molecule is an organothiophosphate ester built around a central phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded sulfur and two methoxy groups. The phosphorus is linked through a single oxygen to a benzene ring, giving an aryl phosphorothioate scaffold. The aromatic ring is substituted with two chlorine atoms and one methyl group, placed in a 2,6-dichloro-4-methyl pattern relative to the oxygen attachment, which makes the ring asymmetric overall. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the P–O bonds allow some rotational flexibility around the phosphorus center. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors; the oxygen atoms and the thiono sulfur act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a trisubstituted urea: a central carbonyl carbon bonded to one nitrogen that carries a phenyl ring (an N-aryl amide-type NH) and a second nitrogen that is fully substituted, bearing a cyclopentyl ring and a para-chlorobenzyl group. The two aromatic rings are monocyclic benzene rings with no fused systems, and the cyclopentane is a saturated, non-planar five-membered ring. The para-chloro substitution on the benzyl ring is the only halogen, and the phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The molecule has no symmetry axis because its two nitrogen substituents differ. The benzyl and phenyl linkages allow considerable rotational freedom, though the planar urea core restricts it somewhat. The single N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, giving a flat, rigid aromatic framework. A carboxylic acid group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring-fusion position, next to the nitrogen-bearing ring, so the acid and the ring nitrogen are positioned close together. Two chlorine atoms are attached at separate positions on the carbocyclic ring and on the pyridine-side carbon, making the substitution pattern asymmetric. The carboxylic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the aromatic nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built from a pyridazinone core, a six-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl group, which is substituted with a chlorine atom on the carbon next to the carbonyl. The ring nitrogen bears a bulky tert-butyl group, and a thioether linkage (a sulfur atom bonded to a methylene) connects the ring at the carbon opposite the chlorine to a para-tert-butylphenyl ring. The two tert-butyl groups are sterically demanding and contribute to the three-dimensional bulk of the structure, while the aromatic and heteroaromatic rings are planar and relatively rigid. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogens can act as acceptors, but there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution around the pyridazinone ring.

The molecule is a trisubstituted urea in which a central carbonyl carbon is bonded to two nitrogen atoms. One nitrogen carries a methyl group and an unsubstituted phenyl ring, while the other nitrogen is attached to a tertiary carbon that bears two methyl groups and a second phenyl ring, giving a bulky, sterically crowded alkyl-aryl substituent. Both phenyl rings are simple benzene rings with no further substitution, so the scaffold has no fused ring systems. The urea group provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the N–H) and one hydrogen-bond acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the tertiary nitrogen contributes no donor capability. The molecule is fairly flexible around its single bonds, though the gem-dimethyl substitution restricts rotation near the central carbon. It lacks any symmetry element that would make the two halves identical.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, with alternating hydroxyl and chloro groups around the ring, so it is a tetrachlorohydroquinone-type scaffold in which two hydroxyls sit para to each other and two chlorines occupy the remaining positions. Its aromatic core is a single fully substituted six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The two hydroxyl groups each serve as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the chlorines contribute only weak halogen-bonding and steric bulk. The substitution pattern gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with a two-fold axis passing through the ring, and the rigid planar ring leaves little conformational flexibility beyond hydroxyl rotation.

The molecule is an acyclic ether-alcohol with no ring systems, built on a short saturated carbon chain. A tert-butyl group, consisting of a central quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, is attached through an ether oxygen to a three-carbon chain. That chain carries a secondary hydroxyl group on its middle carbon, so the molecule contains one ether oxygen and one alcohol oxygen. Its lack of rings and aromatic character makes it highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry because the two ends differ, with the bulky tert-butyl group on one side and the hydroxylated chain on the other.

This molecule is built on a six-membered glutarimide-type ring, a saturated heterocycle containing one nitrogen and two carbonyl groups that form an imide unit, with a phenyl ring attached directly to a carbon on that scaffold. A diethylaminoethyl side chain hangs from the adjacent carbon, introducing a flexible tertiary amine with two ethyl substituents. The imide N-H and two carbonyl oxygens give hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the tertiary amine nitrogen acts as an additional acceptor. Because the molecule has two stereocenters on the ring and no internal symmetry, it is chiral and lacks a mirror plane. The saturated ring is conformationally flexible, while the phenyl group provides a rigid aromatic region.

This molecule is built around a central methine carbon bearing two identical aryl groups plus a short alkyl linker, giving a flexible, non-fused skeleton with no fused ring systems. Each of the two terminal rings is a benzene ring carrying a hydroxyl group, a tert-butyl group, and a methyl group in a 2,4,6-type pattern relative to the attachment point. The two aryl arms are constitutionally identical, so the molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry about the central carbon, though the single stereocenter means it is chiral. Each phenol OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bulky tert-butyl groups sterically shield the hydroxyls. Overall the framework is conformationally flexible around its sp3 linkers.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic diol built on a straight carbon chain of five carbons, with no rings or fused ring systems present. Its skeleton is a linear pentane-type backbone bearing two primary and secondary hydroxyl groups: one hydroxyl sits on the terminal carbon and the other on the adjacent internal carbon, giving a 1,2-diol arrangement at one end. Because every carbon is sp3-hybridized and no bonds are constrained, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The two hydroxyl groups each function as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the hydroxyls occupy non-equivalent positions. Overall, the structure is a small, unbranched, polar-functionalized alkane chain.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold bearing no ring fusion. Two tert-butyl peroxy groups (–O–O–C(CH3)3) are attached to the same ring carbon, forming a geminal bis(peroxide) motif, while the ring also carries one methyl group on an adjacent carbon and two methyl groups on a third carbon, giving a trimethyl substitution pattern that is not symmetric. The ring is fully sp3-hybridized and conformationally flexible, though the bulky substituents restrict its movement. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H bonds, but the four oxygen atoms of the two peroxide linkages can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and two chlorine atoms, arranged so that the methyl sits between the two halogens on adjacent positions while a single bond links the aromatic core to a second ring at the opposite side. That second ring is a six-membered pyridazinone, a diazine containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl group, with one nitrogen carrying a hydrogen atom. The two rings are joined directly without a linker, giving a rigid, nearly planar biaryl-type scaffold with limited conformational freedom. The chlorine and methyl substituents create an asymmetric substitution pattern on the phenyl ring, so the overall molecule lacks a mirror plane of symmetry. The pyridazinone portion offers a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen.

This molecule is built on a cyclobutane ring, a four-membered carbocycle, with one carbon bearing two substituents: a methyl ester group (a carbonyl attached to an oxygen that carries a methyl group) and a phenylsulfonyl group. The sulfonyl unit is a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the aromatic portion is a simple phenyl with no ring substitution. The quaternary carbon sits at a single stereocenter-free junction, and the two groups attached to it are not symmetry-equivalent, so the overall molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis. The cyclobutane ring is strained and fairly rigid, while the bond to the sulfonyl group allows some rotational freedom. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ester and sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a short carbon chain with no rings, so its scaffold is entirely open-chain and flexible. The core is an acrylate unit: a terminal vinyl group (CH2=CH-) attached directly to a carbonyl carbon that forms an ester linkage to a secondary carbon bearing a methyl branch. The remaining hydroxyl-bearing primary carbon completes the chain, placing a free alcohol group at one end. The structure lacks any symmetry because the ester oxygen and the hydroxyl sit at different positions along an unbranched backbone with a single methyl branch. Hydrogen-bond capability is asymmetric: the hydroxyl group can act as both a donor and an acceptor, while the carbonyl and ester oxygens serve only as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two carbamate-type substituents at meta positions (1,3-disubstitution). One substituent is an O-aryl carbamate in which the carbonyl is attached to a nitrogen that carries both an ethyl group and a second phenyl ring, giving an N,N-disubstituted, diaryl-containing carbamate linkage. The other substituent is an N-aryl carbamate formed with an isopropyl ester group. The molecule contains three aromatic rings in total, connected through flexible carbamate linkages, so it is not fused into a rigid polycyclic system and has no internal symmetry. Each carbamate N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl and ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is N,N'-diphenylformamidine, a small acyclic scaffold built around a central amidine-type carbon bearing one carbon-nitrogen double bond and one carbon-nitrogen single bond. Each nitrogen carries a phenyl ring, so the two aromatic rings are unfused and not fused to any other ring system. The structure is symmetric about the central carbon in its connectivity, with the two phenyl groups unsubstituted. The C=N linkage and the flanking nitrogens make the central unit fairly rigid, while rotation around the single bonds to the phenyl rings allows some conformational flexibility. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the imine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carbon chain, so it has no ring systems and no ring fusion. Its backbone is a four-carbon skeleton carrying a tertiary alcohol and a terminal carboxylic acid on the same quaternary-adjacent carbon, which makes it an alpha-hydroxy acid. The central carbon bears a hydroxyl group, a methyl group, an ethyl group, and the carboxyl carbon, so the substitution pattern is branched and lacks any internal symmetry plane. Its single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility around the chain. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and three hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

This molecule is a substituted pyrimidinetrione, built on a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms and three carbonyl groups arranged as a barbiturate-type scaffold. The quaternary carbon at position 5 carries two alkyl substituents, an allyl group and an isopropyl group, which creates a tetrahedral center and breaks any mirror symmetry across the ring. One ring nitrogen bears a methyl group while the other remains an N-H, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is largely planar and rigid, with the carbonyls conjugated to the nitrogens, while the allyl chain offers some conformational flexibility. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor from the remaining N-H and three hydrogen-bond acceptors from the carbonyl oxygens.

The molecule is a bicyclic hydrocarbon-based alcohol built on a norbornene-type scaffold: a seven-carbon bridged framework containing one carbon-carbon double bond. Two of its carbons are bridgehead atoms joined by three bridges, one of which is the alkene, giving a rigid, cage-like three-dimensional shape with limited conformational flexibility. A single hydroxyl group is attached to a saturated carbon on one of the bridges, so the only functional group is an alcohol. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkene and the carbon framework contribute no additional polar sites. The structure has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry because the hydroxyl substituent breaks the symmetry of the bicyclic core.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic core: a benzene ring fused to a pyridone-type ring containing a nitrogen bearing an N-methyl group, which is in turn fused to a five-membered oxygen-containing ring (a dihydrofuran). A methoxy group sits on the benzenoid ring adjacent to the ring-fusion nitrogen-bearing carbon, and a carbonyl group is part of the central six-membered ring. The fused framework is largely planar and rigid, while the isopropyl substituent on the saturated furan ring adds a small degree of conformational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all nitrogen and oxygen positions are substituted. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the methoxy, methyl, and isopropyl groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, flexible chain built on a short backbone with no rings. An acetamide group (an acetyl unit bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the central carbon, which also carries a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid and an adjacent carboxylic acid group, giving two carboxyl groups in total. The stereocenter at the substituted carbon means the molecule is chiral, and it lacks any internal symmetry. The amide N-H and both carboxylic acid O-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, giving the structure strong hydrogen-bonding capacity.

This molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, so there is no aromaticity and no ring fusion. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, an isopropyl group, and an oxyacetic acid side chain (an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 that terminates in a carboxylic acid). The substitution pattern is 1,2,4-trisubstituted, which removes any overall symmetry, so the molecule is chiral with several stereocenters. The cyclohexane core and the flexible ether and acetic acid linkage give moderate conformational freedom. The carboxylic acid group offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the OH) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen provides an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is an ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain), and the other is an amide nitrogen connected to a carbonyl carbon. That carbonyl carries a side chain with a secondary alcohol, making it a 2-hydroxypropanamide unit. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ethyl and hydroxypropyl portions add some conformational flexibility. The amide N–H and the hydroxyl O–H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, whereas the amide carbonyl oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the ether oxygen act as acceptors. The para arrangement gives the aromatic ring a linear, elongated overall shape.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic carboxylic acid with no rings, so its scaffold is a saturated eight-carbon chain running from a terminal methyl group to a carboxyl carbon. A bromine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the carboxyl group, which is the alpha position, giving a single halogen substituent with no further branching. The carboxylic acid group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms. Apart from the alpha-carbon stereocenter, the molecule lacks symmetry and is conformationally flexible because of the rotatable single bonds along the alkyl chain.

The molecule is a spiro compound in which one carbon atom joins two ring systems: a 1,3-dihydroindole (indoline) unit bearing an N-methyl group and a gem-dimethyl group at the 3-position, and a 2H-chromene (benzopyran) unit whose ring oxygen is bonded to the spiro carbon. The chromene portion carries a nitro group on its benzene ring, and a C=C double bond links the spiro carbon to the pyran ring. Both bicyclic halves are fused benzene-containing systems, giving a largely rigid, three-dimensional framework with the two ring planes meeting roughly perpendicularly at the spiro center. The nitro group acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the ring oxygen and tertiary nitrogen can serve as weak acceptors, and no hydrogen-bond donors are present.

This molecule is built around a para-disubstituted benzene ring whose two oxygen-linked substituents are an aryl ether and an alpha-aryloxy propanoate ester. One side carries a 4-chlorophenoxy group, so the structure is a diaryl ether with a chlorine atom para to the ether linkage on the distal ring. The other side bears an O-linked 2-methylpropyl (isobutyl) ester of 2-aryloxypropanoic acid, which contains a chiral center at the alpha carbon. The molecule has three aromatic and flexible linkers, with several rotatable bonds across the ether and ester chain, giving it considerable conformational flexibility. Its hydrogen-bond capacity is limited: the ester carbonyl and the three ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a sulfonylurea built on a benzene ring bearing a methyl ester ortho to the sulfonyl group, so the two substituents sit on adjacent carbons. The sulfonyl group links through an N-H to a urea carbonyl, which connects to an aminopyrimidine ring, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogens. That pyrimidine carries two difluoromethoxy groups at the 4- and 6-positions, giving it a symmetric pattern about the ring. The molecule is fairly flexible at the sulfonyl-urea linker, with rotation possible around several single bonds. Its N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl and carbonyl oxygens, the ester oxygens, and the pyrimidine nitrogens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a fully fluorinated saturated carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring in which every ring carbon bears two fluorine atoms (or one fluorine plus one ring bond and one substituent). The ring carbon at the start of the SMILES carries a fluorine and a trifluoromethyl group, and the carbon closing the ring carries a fluorine and another trifluoromethyl group, so the two trifluoromethyl groups sit on adjacent ring atoms. The skeleton is a single six-membered ring with no fused or bridged rings, no double bonds, and no heteroatoms other than fluorine. Its substitution pattern is ortho-disubstituted with trifluoromethyl groups, which gives the molecule only modest symmetry. The ring is conformationally constrained, though it can still interconvert between chair forms. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors in the usual sense, since the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is a fused polycyclic amine built around a central tertiary nitrogen that sits at a ring junction. Two benzene rings are each fused to a saturated six-membered ring, and those saturated rings are linked through the nitrogen and a shared carbon, giving a compact, bridged-looking tetracyclic framework. The only heteroatom is that single nitrogen, which carries no hydrogen and so acts purely as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, with no hydrogen-bond donor present. The aromatic rings are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple, and the overall shape is rigid and largely planar in its aromatic portions with a puckered aliphatic core, offering limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a quinuclidine-type bicyclic amine scaffold, a saturated cage in which a nitrogen sits at a bridgehead position, and it carries an ethyl group on one of the carbons of that cage. A secondary alcohol carbon links this bicyclic core to a quinoline ring system, a bicyclic aromatic made of a pyridine ring fused to a benzene ring. The quinoline is attached at its pyridine-side carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, so the aromatic portion is planar while the cage is rigid and three-dimensional. The tertiary amine nitrogen and the pyridine-type ring nitrogen can each accept hydrogen bonds, and the hydroxyl group can both donate and accept them. The structure has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern and several stereocenters.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered imidazoline ring, a saturated-at-C4/C5 heterocycle containing two nitrogens, one of which carries a hydrogen and one of which is part of a C=N double bond. The ring carries a phenyl group on the sp2 carbon at position 2, which is conjugated with the ring's imine nitrogen, and two additional phenyl groups on the adjacent sp3 carbons, placed on adjacent carbons that are bonded to each other. Overall the framework has three benzene rings attached to a central non-aromatic heterocycle, with no ring fusion. The 4,5-diphenyl substitution gives the molecule a chiral centre pair and only partial symmetry, while the attached rings add considerable bulk. The ring NH acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and the imine nitrogen as an acceptor.

The molecule is an acyclic saturated hydrocarbon skeleton of six carbons, specifically a hexane-type chain bearing two chlorine substituents on adjacent internal carbons. Each chlorine is attached to a carbon that also carries a hydrogen, and the two substituted carbons sit next to one another along the chain, with an ethyl branch at one end and a methyl branch at the other. The structure contains no rings, no double bonds, and no other functional groups, so it is built entirely from sp3 carbon centers. Because the two stereocenters are present and the chain is flexible, the molecule can adopt many rotameric conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, so its capacity for hydrogen bonding is minimal.

This molecule is a four-carbon acyclic chain with no rings, built as a diester-diacid type backbone. One end carries an ethyl ester group (an ethoxy group attached to a carbonyl), while the other end carries a free carboxylic acid. Two adjacent secondary hydroxyl groups sit on the two central carbons, giving the chain a vicinal diol arrangement. The molecule is flexible because of its unbranched sp3 carbon framework, and it has no internal symmetry because the two ends differ, with an ester on one side and an acid on the other. It can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two hydroxyls and its carboxylic acid OH, and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its multiple carbonyl and ether oxygens.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic carboxylic acid with ten carbons in total, the terminal carbon of the chain being a carboxyl group. A linear alkyl tail of eight carbons extends from the alpha carbon, which carries a single bromine substituent, so the substitution sits directly adjacent to the carbonyl. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic groups, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the bromine breaks any potential mirror plane along the chain. The backbone is flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds along the alkyl portion. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit around that ring: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a nitro group. The methyl and nitro groups are located meta to one another, with the bromine positioned between them, giving a 1,3,5-substitution pattern. Because the three substituents are different, the molecule lacks any rotational symmetry axis beyond a single mirror plane through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the nitro and methyl groups add little conformational flexibility. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a short, acyclic four-carbon chain with no rings, so its scaffold is a linear, flexible backbone. Its terminal carbons carry an amide group (a carbonyl bonded to a nitrogen bearing two hydrogens) at one end and a carboxylic acid group at the other. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the acid, creating a stereocenter, so the molecule can exist in mirror-image forms. Overall it has no meaningful internal symmetry, and its several polar groups give it multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites (the amide NH2, the hydroxyl OH, and the acid OH) and multiple acceptor oxygens.

The molecule is a fully saturated bicyclic amine built from two six-membered rings sharing a common edge, giving a decahydroquinoline-type scaffold (a fused cyclohexane and piperidine system). The ring fusion is cis or trans-capable at the two bridgehead carbons, which constrains the overall three-dimensional shape. The only heteroatom is a single secondary amine nitrogen in the piperidine ring, which carries one hydrogen and therefore acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. There are no other functional groups, no aromatic rings, and no substituents, so the molecule has no stereocenter-bearing side chains and only modest symmetry. Its rigid fused framework limits conformational freedom compared with an open-chain analogue.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, with no fused or additional rings. The nitrogen atom carries an acetyl group, making it an amide, so the ring nitrogen is part of a planar, conjugated amide unit rather than a basic amine. A methyl substituent sits on a ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen-bearing carbon, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with a stereocenter and no internal symmetry. The ring is conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair-like arrangements, while the amide bond restricts rotation locally. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small saturated cyclic ketone built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring with no fused or bridged rings and no aromatic character. The ring carries a single carbonyl group, placing a ketone at one ring carbon and making the ring's alpha-carbon adjacent to it. Three alkyl substituents sit on the ring: one methyl group on the carbon next to the carbonyl and a geminal pair of methyl groups on the carbon two positions away from it. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the methyl groups are not equivalent, and the ring is conformationally flexible but restricted by its gem-dimethyl substitution. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor is the carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para arrangement: a tertiary amine nitrogen carrying a 2-acetoxyethyl chain and a 2-cyanoethyl chain, and an azo linker (–N=N–) in the trans configuration leading to a second aromatic unit. That second unit is a benzothiazole, a bicyclic fused system in which a benzene ring is merged with a five-membered thiazole ring, and it carries a nitro group on the benzo portion. The molecule is extended and conjugated across the azo bridge, giving it a largely planar, rigid aromatic core flanked by flexible aliphatic arms. Hydrogen-bond acceptor sites include the ester carbonyl and ester oxygens, the nitrile nitrogen, the nitro oxygens, and the ring nitrogens, while it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic scaffold: a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring (an indoline-type system) and that ring is further bridged to a saturated tetrahydrofuran ring through a shared quaternary carbon and an adjacent aminal-type carbon. Its principal functional group is an N-methylcarbamate ester attached to the aromatic ring, which contributes both a carbonyl oxygen and an N-H donor. The aromatic ring carries this carbamate at one position, with the remaining positions unsubstituted, giving a single, asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused ring system is largely rigid, while the saturated oxolane ring adds some conformational puckering. The molecule has one N-H hydrogen-bond donor and several acceptors, including the carbonyl oxygen, the ester oxygen, the ring ether oxygen, and the tertiary nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom.
