An amino group sits on one ring carbon, while chlorine atoms occupy two other positions, one adjacent to the ring nitrogen and one on the opposite side of the ring, giving a trisubstituted, non-symmetric pattern with no fused rings. The planar aromatic core is rigid, with the substituents lying in the same plane and only the amino group's hydrogens offering limited rotational freedom. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, and the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The chlorine substituents contribute electron-withdrawing character to the ring but are not themselves hydrogen-bond participants.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. A methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) sits on one ring carbon, and directly adjacent to it, on the neighboring carbon, is a side chain consisting of a carbon bearing both a methyl group and a hydroxyl group. This ortho-disubstitution pattern gives the aromatic ring a lower symmetry, with no mirror or rotational symmetry across the whole molecule. The side chain contains a stereocenter at the carbinol carbon, so the molecule is chiral. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a lactone core: a five-membered oxygen-containing ring (a gamma-butyrolactone) carrying a carbonyl and bearing two side chains on adjacent carbons. One side chain is a benzylic secondary alcohol, with a free hydroxyl group attached to a carbon that also bears an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The other side chain is a CH2 linker to a 1-methylimidazole ring, where the N-methyl sits on one nitrogen and the imidazole's other nitrogen is a basic, unsubstituted acceptor. The molecule has one stereogenic center on the lactone ring plus the carbinol carbon, so it is non-symmetric and has several rotatable bonds, giving it moderate flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability includes one donor from the hydroxyl group, while the lactone carbonyl, lactone ether oxygen, hydroxyl oxygen, and the imidazole nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered lactone ring, a gamma-butyrolactone-type scaffold containing one ring oxygen and a carbonyl carbon adjacent to it. The ring carbon bearing the side chain sits next to a quaternary carbon that carries two methyl groups, so the ring is substituted at adjacent positions and has no internal symmetry. Attached to the ring is a flexible acetic acid side chain, a CH2 linked to a terminal carboxylic acid group. The ring is a single fused-free unit, and the lactone ester and the carboxylic acid together provide two carbonyl oxygens that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the acid's hydroxyl group can both donate and accept them. The molecule is otherwise fairly compact, with the gem-dimethyl group adding steric bulk near the lactone oxygen.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built on a straight, unbranched chain of carbons. An ethyl group is attached through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon, which forms the ester functional group, and the carbonyl is linked to a five-carbon saturated alkyl chain that terminates in a bromine atom at the far end. There are no ring systems or fused rings, so the scaffold is entirely open and linear. The molecule has a single polar ester group that can accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and ether-type oxygens but cannot donate any, while the terminal bromine adds a polarizable halogen site at the opposite end. Its many rotatable single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility, and its overall structure lacks any symmetry because the two ends carry different functionality.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing an edge, with no heteroatoms or polar functional groups present. A linear nine-carbon n-nonyl chain is attached to one of the carbons at the alpha position, adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the saturated alkyl tail is flexible and can adopt many conformations. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since its only atoms are carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is a biaryl built on a pyridine core, with two phenyl rings attached at adjacent positions: one phenyl at the 3-position and the other at the 2-position of the pyridine ring, giving a 2,3-diphenylpyridine scaffold. It contains three aromatic six-membered rings in total, all fully aromatic and unfused to one another, connected by single C–C bonds. The nitrogen in the pyridine ring is the only heteroatom and has a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the two phenyl groups sit ortho to each other, steric crowding forces them to twist out of the plane of the pyridine ring, so the overall shape is non-planar and the molecule is relatively rigid with restricted rotation about the biaryl bonds.

The molecule is built on a 1,3-indandione-type core, specifically a 2-substituted 2-phenyl-indane-1,3-dione: a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing two ketone carbonyls flanking a single quaternary carbon. That central sp3 carbon carries both a phenyl ring and a CH2 linker that bears a morpholine ring, a saturated six-membered ring with oxygen and nitrogen at opposite positions. The two carbonyls are conjugated with the fused aromatic ring, and the ring system is largely rigid, though the morpholine and the CH2 linker add some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. It has hydrogen-bond acceptor capacity at the two carbonyl oxygens, the ether oxygen of morpholine, and the tertiary amine nitrogen. It has no overall molecular symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution at the quaternary carbon.

The molecule is a pyrimidine-2,4-dione (uracil-type) ring bearing a bromine atom at the 5-position, with the ring nitrogen at position 1 attached to a saturated tetrahydrofuran ring. That sugar-like ring is a five-membered oxygen heterocycle carrying a hydroxymethyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, and it lacks any hydroxyl at the 2' or 3' positions. The pyrimidinedione core is planar and aromatic-like, while the furanose ring is flexible and adopts puckered conformations, linked through a single C–N bond. The molecule is asymmetric, since the two sides of the scaffold differ substantially. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the ring N–H and the primary alcohol's O–H, while acceptor sites include the two carbonyl oxygens, the ring oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygen.

This molecule is a five-membered cyclic imide, the succinimide ring, with an N-iodo substituent on the nitrogen atom. The ring contains two carbonyl groups flanking the nitrogen, and the two methylene carbons form the saturated backbone between them. The ring is small, planar-leaning, and rigid, with no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the mirror plane passing through the nitrogen and the midpoint of the CH2-CH2 bond. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no N-H or O-H donors because the nitrogen is fully substituted by the iodine atom.

This molecule is an acyclic, flexible chain with no ring systems. Its backbone is a short aliphatic framework containing two ether oxygens, one linking a propyl group to a branched carbon and another linking that carbon to a second branched carbon bearing a terminal hydroxyl group. Each branch carries a methyl substituent, giving a non-symmetrical substitution pattern with a secondary alcohol at one end. The single free hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two ether oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Because all bonds are single and rotatable, the molecule is highly conformationally flexible.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain amino acid built from a three-carbon backbone bearing a sulfoxide. A terminal vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond) is attached to a methylene that connects to a sulfur atom carrying a single oxygen, making it a sulfoxide with a stereogenic sulfur center. The sulfoxide links through a methylene to an alpha-carbon bearing a primary amine, which is adjacent to a terminal carboxylic acid. The molecule contains no rings, so it is highly flexible with free rotation about its single bonds. The primary amine and the carboxylic acid OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfoxide oxygen, the carboxyl oxygens, and the nitrogen lone pair serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on an azulene-type scaffold, a fused bicyclic system in which a five-membered ring and a seven-membered ring share a bond, giving it a polarized, non-benzenoid aromatic character. The seven-membered ring carries an isopropenyl group (a 1-methylvinyl substituent) and the five-membered ring carries an aldehyde (formyl) group, while a methyl group sits on the seven-membered ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused core is planar and rigid, with only the isopropenyl and formyl groups providing limited rotational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small unsaturated carboxylic acid built on a linear chain of six carbons, with no ring systems present. A carbon-carbon double bond sits between the second and third carbons, and that alkene is trisubstituted, carrying a methyl group on each of the two sp2 carbons. The terminal carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl, is conjugated with the double bond, and the molecule has no rings or stereocenters to fix its shape. Because the chain is fairly flexible and the alkene's substituents define its geometry, the structure lacks any significant symmetry. The carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two acceptor sites through its oxygen atoms.

The molecule is an acyclic amide built on a two-carbon chain, bearing an azidomethyl group (–CH2–N3) attached to a carbonyl. The amide nitrogen connects to a carbon carrying a hydroxymethyl group, which is bonded to a benzylic carbon that bears a secondary hydroxyl. This benzylic carbon is attached to a benzene ring carrying a nitro group in the para position relative to the chain, giving a 1,4-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The molecule has two stereogenic centers and substantial conformational flexibility from its rotatable single bonds, while the hydroxyl and amide N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and the carbonyl, hydroxyl oxygens, nitro oxygens, and azide nitrogens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a symmetric diester built from a linear two-carbon ethylene glycol core, with a butyryl group attached to each oxygen. Each ester unit is an acyclic C(=O)O linkage bearing a straight three-carbon alkyl chain, so the molecule contains no rings and no aromatic systems. The ester carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks any N-H or O-H groups. The structure is fully flexible, with multiple rotatable single bonds along the chains and the central ethylene linker, and its two halves are related by a mirror-type symmetry through the central C-C bond.

The molecule is a bicyclic saturated hydrocarbon built from two fused six-membered carbocyclic rings that share a common bond, giving a decalin-type bridged or fused scaffold. Every ring atom is sp3-hybridized and bears only hydrogens, so there are no functional groups, heteroatoms, or unsaturation. Because the two rings share a bridgehead arrangement, the framework is conformationally constrained, with limited flexibility compared with an open-chain alkane. Having no donors or acceptors, the molecule cannot form hydrogen bonds in either role, and its overall shape lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axes that would make it highly symmetric.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent-to-each-other positions: an ethoxy group (a two-carbon chain attached through an oxygen atom) and a fluorine atom, placed meta to one another on the six-membered aromatic ring. The aromatic core is a single fused-free benzene scaffold, so there is no ring fusion, and the ring is planar and rigid, while the ethoxy chain adds a modest degree of conformational flexibility around its C–O and O–C bonds. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry in its substituent arrangement. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the fluorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a linear, unbranched hydrocarbon chain of six carbon atoms, with a methyl group at each end. The two central carbons are joined by a cumulated double bond, so the carbon skeleton contains an allene unit, with the two C=C bonds sharing a single central carbon. There are no rings, no heteroatoms, and no functional groups such as alcohols, carbonyls, or amines. The molecule is highly symmetric, possessing a two-fold axis through the central carbon, and it is rigid around the allene core while the terminal methyl groups can rotate freely. Because it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a very small acyclic haloalkane built on a two-carbon ethane backbone, with one chlorine atom attached to one terminal carbon and one iodine atom attached to the other. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the two halogen substituents. The two carbons are sp3-hybridized and the halogens sit at opposite ends of the chain, giving a simple, unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry element beyond the free rotation about the central carbon-carbon bond. Because of that free rotation the molecule is highly flexible, adopting multiple conformers. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, with two methyl groups and four fluorine atoms arranged around the aromatic core. Looking at the substitution pattern, the two methyl groups sit at positions 1 and 4, which are para to each other, while the fluorines occupy the remaining four positions in pairs flanking each methyl. This gives the ring a highly symmetric arrangement, with a mirror plane and a two-fold axis running through the two methyl-bearing carbons. The scaffold is a single aromatic ring with no ring fusion and no other functional groups beyond the C–F bonds and the alkyl substituents. Because the ring is rigid and the substituents are small and directly attached, the molecule is conformationally inflexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the fluorine atoms, which are weak.

This molecule is a symmetric anhydride built from two identical acyl units joined through a central carbonyl-oxygen-carbonyl linkage. Each half consists of a carbonyl carbon bonded to a tetrahedral methine carbon that carries two separate, unfused phenyl rings, so the structure contains four benzene rings in total and no fused ring systems. The two diphenylacetyl halves are related by a mirror-like symmetry through the central oxygen, giving the molecule a pseudo-C2 arrangement. The anhydride group acts as the only polar, reactive core, providing two carbonyl oxygens as hydrogen-bond acceptors and no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule is fairly flexible around its single bonds, while the four phenyl rings are rigid planar units.

This molecule is an acyclic, saturated hydrocarbon built around a central branched chain: a three-carbon unit bearing a methyl branch on the middle carbon, with each terminal end attached to a cyclohexane ring. The two cyclohexane rings are simple, fully saturated six-membered carbocycles with no ring fusion and no heteroatoms, and they are joined through a flexible CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2 linker. The structure is essentially symmetric about the central methine carbon, though the methyl branch breaks perfect mirror symmetry. It contains no functional groups, no double bonds, and no aromatic rings. Because it has only C–C and C–H single bonds, it is conformationally flexible, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule is a single silicon atom acting as the central scaffold, bonded to one isopropyl group and three chlorine atoms, giving a tetrahedral arrangement with no rings or ring fusion. The isopropyl group is a branched three-carbon alkyl chain attached through its central carbon, which places two methyl groups on one end of the bond to silicon. Three identical chlorine substituents sit on the silicon, so the substitution pattern is highly symmetric around the Si–C axis, with local threefold symmetry at the silicon center. The structure is fairly rigid at the silicon center, while the isopropyl group retains some rotational freedom about the Si–C bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a branched, fully saturated hydrocarbon built on a single carbon chain with no rings and no heteroatoms. Its one double bond is terminal, sitting between the first two carbons as a 1,1-disubstituted alkene bearing a methyl group on the second carbon. The adjacent carbon carries a sec-butyl-like branch made of an ethyl and a methyl arm, which gives the skeleton an asymmetric, highly branched shape. Because it has no ring systems, its only rotational freedom comes from single bonds, so it is flexible rather than rigid. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it is composed solely of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an acyclic acetal built on a single quaternary carbon bearing an ethyl group and two methoxy groups, with the central carbon also linked to a third oxygen that is attached to a terminal methyl group. The scaffold is entirely saturated and open-chain, containing no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. Its functional groups are three ether oxygens, all connected to the same carbon, so the molecule is a fully alkylated orthoester-type framework. The arrangement is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and it lacks any stereocenter, so no meaningful chiral or rigid symmetry element is present. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no hydrogens sit on oxygen or nitrogen, but its three oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered hydantoin ring, a saturated heterocycle containing two carbonyl groups and two nitrogens. The carbon at the 5-position of this ring bears two phenyl groups on the same atom, giving a bulky, geminal diphenyl substitution pattern that creates a rigid, non-planar region. The ring nitrogen at position 3 carries a CH2 linker attached to an ester, where a straight-chain pentanoyl group is bonded through an oxygen atom. The two aromatic rings and the hydantoin core restrict conformational freedom, while the flexible alkyl ester chain adds some mobility. The hydantoin NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens and ester oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered saturated carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems. Carbon 1 of the ring carries two nitro groups (–NO2) attached to the same carbon, making it a geminal dinitro substitution pattern. The remaining five ring carbons are plain methylene units with no further substituents, so the molecule has a local mirror plane through the substituted carbon and the ring is conformationally flexible, with the chair form dominating. Nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a cyclopentane ring whose carbon bearing the substituents is quaternary, meaning it carries both a sulfonyl group and an isopropyl ester group. The sulfonyl group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens, links that ring carbon to a para-tolyl ring, a benzene ring with a methyl group opposite the sulfonyl attachment. The ester is an isopropyl carboxylate, a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that bears an isopropyl group, which adds flexible branching. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the saturated cyclopentane and isopropyl portions add conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the two ends differ, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all heteroatoms are oxygens acting only as acceptors in the sulfonyl and ester groups.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying an aryloxy-propanolamine side chain. The aromatic ring is para-disubstituted: one position bears a hydroxyl group and the other is linked through an ether oxygen to a three-carbon chain. That chain contains a secondary alcohol on the middle carbon and terminates in an isopropylamino group, a secondary amine attached to a branched isopropyl unit. The phenyl ring is flat and rigid, while the aliphatic chain is flexible, with several rotatable bonds. The molecule has no stereocenter-based symmetry across its full length, but the para pattern gives the ring a local mirror symmetry. The phenolic OH and the alcohol OH can each donate and accept hydrogen bonds, the secondary amine can donate one and accept one, and the ether oxygen acts as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring that carries an ester side chain through an ether linkage: a two-carbon ethyl ester of an acetic acid unit attached via oxygen to the aromatic ring. The benzene is substituted with a chlorine and a fluorine, and it bears a pyrazole ring attached directly to the aromatic carbon, so the two ring systems are linked by a single bond rather than fused. The pyrazole is N-methylated and carries a difluoromethoxy group and a chlorine atom on its remaining carbons. Overall the molecule is a polyhalogenated biaryl-type scaffold with an ester carbonyl and several ether oxygens acting as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The single biaryl bond and the flexible ester chain give it moderate conformational freedom, while the molecule lacks any symmetry element.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four chlorine atoms and two carbonyl-containing groups on adjacent positions, making it an ortho-disubstituted, tetrachlorinated aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a free carboxylic acid and the other is an ethyl ester, so the two groups sit next to each other on the ring and can interact sterically. The four chlorines occupy the remaining ring positions in a contiguous run, giving a highly substituted and electron-poor aromatic core with no molecular symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ester–acid axis. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester chain adds some conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas the ester oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a nitroguanidine derivative: a central guanidine carbon bears a methylamino group, an imine nitrogen linked to a CH2 group, and a nitro-substituted nitrogen. The side chain attached through the imine nitrogen is a tetrahydrofuran ring connected via a methylene bridge, with the ring oxygen providing an ether functionality. The nitro group (N(=O)O on an amino nitrogen) is strongly electron-withdrawing and conjugated with the guanidine core. The molecule has no symmetry, and its flexibility comes mainly from the rotatable single bonds linking the saturated five-membered ring to the guanidine unit. Hydrogen-bond donors are the NH groups on the guanidine, while acceptors include the ether oxygen, the nitro oxygens, and the imine nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. Each substituent is a dimethylmethylene carbon, meaning a quaternary carbon carrying two methyl groups, which is bonded to an oxygen-oxygen linkage terminating in a hydrogen atom, so each arm is a hydroperoxyalkyl group. The molecule has a high degree of symmetry, with a two-fold axis passing through the centre of the ring and the two arms mirror-related. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the peroxide-bearing arms can rotate about their single bonds, giving some conformational flexibility. Each hydroperoxy group contains two hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites (the O-H donor and the oxygen lone pairs as acceptors), so the molecule can participate in hydrogen bonding at both ends.

The molecule is built around a silicon atom bonded to a para-tolyl ether oxygen and to a bicyclic silatrane cage. The aromatic ring is a benzene bearing a methyl group and the aryloxy linkage in a 1,4 (para) arrangement, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis through the two substituents. The silatrane core consists of three fused five-membered rings sharing a central silicon and a central tertiary amine nitrogen, with three ethylene-oxy arms linking them, giving a rigid, cage-like three-dimensional framework. The nitrogen is a tertiary amine and the ring oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the aryl portion is planar and the silatrane cage is conformationally rigid.

The molecule is built around a silicon atom bonded to an oxygen from a 4-chlorophenyl ring and to three further oxygens, which together with a central nitrogen form a tricyclic silatrane cage. Each of the three arms from the silicon through the nitrogen contains a two-carbon bridge, so the cage consists of three fused five-membered rings sharing the Si–N axis, giving a rigid, highly symmetric, three-fold framework. The aromatic ring is a benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom para to the oxygen linkage, a simple para-disubstituted pattern. The tertiary amine nitrogen sits at the cage apex and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ring oxygens are weaker acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a fully acetylated disaccharide built from two sugar rings joined through a glycosidic linkage at an anomeric carbon. One ring is a six-membered pyranose and the other is a five-membered furanose, with the furanose ring's anomeric carbon bearing a quaternary center that carries a hydroxymethyl-derived ester side chain. Every free hydroxyl position on both rings is capped with an acetyl ester, giving the molecule many carbonyl oxygens as acceptors and no hydroxyl donors. The two ring systems are linked through a single oxygen bridge, so each ring retains its own stereochemical framework and considerable conformational flexibility. The acetate groups are arranged asymmetrically, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule has a steroid scaffold: four fused rings arranged as three six-membered rings followed by one five-membered ring, with the typical trans ring fusions of the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene core. A carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with a ketone sits in the first ring, creating an α,β-unsaturated enone system. The five-membered ring carries a secondary hydroxyl group, and an angular methyl group occupies a ring-fusion position. The four-ring framework is largely rigid, though the saturated portions allow some conformational flexibility. The ketone oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl hydrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built on a fused four-ring steroid-type scaffold of three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, arranged in the classic tetracyclic fashion. The A ring is an unsaturated cyclohexenone, containing a ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with it. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-fusion carbons, one on the A/B junction and one on the C/D junction. A side chain on the five-membered ring carries a ketone and a primary hydroxymethyl group, adding one hydrogen-bond donor and several acceptor sites. The ring fusions make the core fairly rigid, while the side chain remains flexible. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered aromatic furan ring, which carries four phenyl substituents, one on each carbon of the ring. Two of these phenyl groups sit on the two carbons flanking the oxygen atom (positions 2 and 5), while the other two occupy the adjacent 3 and 4 positions. The compound contains no hydroxyl, carbonyl, amine, or other heteroatom-bearing functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors and offers only the furan oxygen as a weak acceptor. The four phenyl rings are rotatable, but steric crowding among adjacent aryl groups restricts their rotation, giving the structure a propeller-like, rather bulky three-dimensional shape. Overall the molecule is fully aromatic, with no fused ring systems and only limited symmetry because the two substitution patterns differ.

The molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, joined in a cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene arrangement. The rings are fused trans-to-trans at the ring junctions, giving a rigid, nearly flat core with two angular methyl groups projecting above the plane. A branched alkyl side chain, containing a 1,5-dimethylhexyl-type tail, extends from the five-membered ring. One ring carries a single secondary hydroxyl group, and there is one carbon-carbon double bond in the ring system. The only hydrogen-bond donor is the hydroxyl oxygen-bound hydrogen, which can also accept hydrogen bonds through its oxygen. The overall structure lacks any internal symmetry, and its flexibility is confined mainly to the terminal side chain.

This molecule is a glycoside built around an iridoid-type bicyclic core: a cyclopentane ring fused to a dihydropyran ring, with a fused unsaturated lactone embedded in the framework. The ring system is fairly rigid and fused, with a carbon-carbon double bond within the pyran portion and an enol ether linkage. An acetoxymethyl group (an acetate ester) sits on one alkene carbon, while an O-linked hexopyranose sugar, a six-membered ring bearing several hydroxyl groups and a hydroxymethyl arm, is attached at the anomeric position. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its many oxygen atoms provide numerous hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the sugar's hydroxyls supply several hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a fully protected sugar derivative built on a bicyclic fused scaffold: a furanose-type five-membered ring fused to a 1,3-dioxolane ring through a shared carbon pair, with the dioxolane carbon bearing two methyl groups as an acetonide. The sugar side chain carries three benzoate ester groups, one on the ring oxygen-adjacent carbon, one on the exocyclic chain, and one on the ring carbon, each attached to a phenyl ring. The structure is rigid across its fused core but flexible in the benzoyloxy side chain. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydroxyl is esterified or ketalized, while the ring oxygens and carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an adenine-type purine scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidine ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, bearing a primary amino group on the six-membered ring. The nine-nitrogen bicyclic core is planar and aromatic, while the fused system is rigid. At the imidazole nitrogen sits a saturated, oxygen-containing sugar-like ring with a ring oxygen, several secondary hydroxyl groups, and two hydroxymethyl arms, making the appendage stereochemically complex and conformationally more flexible. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity comes from the amino group and multiple hydroxyls, while the ring nitrogens and oxygens serve as acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the purine base and the attached ring are structurally distinct.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that bears a hydroxyl group, one benzyl group (a phenyl ring joined through a CH2 linker), and two directly attached phenyl rings. This gives a tertiary alcohol scaffold with three aromatic rings radiating from one central sp3 carbon. The three benzene rings are unfused and simply unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is uniform and no ring fusion is present. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the benzyl arm differs from the two diphenyl arms, while the two directly bonded phenyl rings are equivalent. The rings can rotate about their single bonds, so the framework is fairly flexible, though the bulky crowding around the central carbon restricts rotation. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic rings offer only weak pi-system interactions.

The molecule is built on a purine scaffold: a fused bicyclic system in which a six-membered pyrimidine-type ring shares an edge with a five-membered imidazole-type ring, giving four nitrogen atoms within the fused core. An amino group sits on the six-membered ring, adjacent to a ring nitrogen, making it a primary aromatic amine. The five-membered ring nitrogen bears a saturated sugar-like ring through a single bond. That ring is a five-membered oxolane (tetrahydrofuran-type) with a hydroxymethyl substituent on one carbon next to the ring oxygen and a secondary hydroxyl on the carbon beside the attachment point, and it lacks the 2-position hydroxyl typical of ribose. The aromatic core is flat and rigid, while the saturated ring adds limited flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donors include the amino group and two hydroxyl groups, and the ring nitrogens and oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule consists of a purine-type bicyclic heteroaromatic system, specifically a fused pyrimidine-imidazole framework, attached through a nitrogen to a saturated five-membered sugar ring. The ring is a furanose-type oxolane bearing three hydroxyl groups, two on adjacent carbons and one on a hydroxymethyl arm extending from the carbon next to the ring oxygen. The glycosidic linkage connects the sugar's anomeric carbon to one of the imidazole nitrogens, giving the molecule a rigid aromatic base joined to a flexible, polyhydroxylated ring. Multiple nitrogen atoms in the fused heteroaromatic core act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the three hydroxyl groups serve as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the sugar and base are attached asymmetrically.

This molecule is a fused polycyclic steroid-like scaffold containing four rings in a rigid, nearly planar-fused arrangement typical of a cyclopenta-phenanthrene framework. A lactone ring is fused onto the A-ring region, incorporating a ring ester oxygen and carbonyl within a six-membered oxygen-containing heterocycle. The D-ring carries a tertiary hydroxyl group and an angular methyl substituent, while another angular methyl sits at the ring junction. The structure is largely saturated, with no double bonds, and its fused polycycle is conformationally constrained. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the lactone carbonyl and ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built from a five-membered saturated furanose-type ring (a tetrahydrofuran) bearing three acetoxy ester groups, one on the exocyclic CH2 carbon and two on adjacent ring carbons. The ring carbon bearing the nitrogen is attached to a six-membered 1,2,4-triazine-type heterocycle that carries a ketone and an N–H amide-like unit, giving it a dione character. The three ester carbonyls and the triazine oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the single ring N–H provides one hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents differ in position and character, and the fused-free sugar-like ring with its linked heterocycle confers moderate conformational flexibility around the glycosidic-type bond.

The molecule consists of a benzene ring bearing a single substituent at one position, a benzyl group, which is a CH2 linker attached to a nitrogen atom. That nitrogen is part of a saturated six-membered morpholine ring, which contains one oxygen atom opposite the nitrogen, so the two heteroatoms sit at the 1,4-positions of the ring. The aromatic ring is unfused and monosubstituted, while the morpholine ring is non-planar and adopts a chair-like conformation. The tertiary amine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the ether oxygen is a weaker acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure has a mirror-plane symmetry through the benzyl axis and is moderately flexible around the CH2 linker.

This molecule is a tropane-type bicyclic amine, specifically an N-methyl azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane skeleton, in which a nitrogen bridges two carbons of a cyclohexane-like ring and a five-membered ring shares that bridgehead framework. The bridged, cage-like scaffold is conformationally rigid, and the bridgehead nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine that can accept a hydrogen bond. Attached to the carbon skeleton is a carboxylic acid group, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and a secondary alcohol on an adjacent ring carbon, which adds another donor and acceptor site. The substituents sit on different carbons with no mirror symmetry, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane and carries several stereocenters.

The molecule is built on a quinolin-2(1H)-one scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring bearing a carbonyl group adjacent to the nitrogen. The nitrogen carries an N-methyl substituent, and the fused ring system is largely planar and rigid. Two methoxy groups are attached, one on the carbon adjacent to the ring junction and one on the benzenoid ring, while a side chain at the third ring position carries a secondary alcohol flanked by an isopropyl group, which adds conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the secondary hydroxyl can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the planar core, since the side chain breaks any mirror relationship.

The molecule is a symmetric hydrazine derivative built from two para-tolyl rings joined through a central N–N bond. Each aromatic ring is a benzene carrying a methyl group para to the nitrogen attachment, so the two halves mirror each other across the central hydrazo linkage. There are no fused ring systems, and the aryl rings can rotate about the N–aryl bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The two nitrogen atoms each bear one hydrogen, so they can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while their lone pairs make them weak acceptors. The methyl groups contribute only nonpolar bulk to the otherwise aromatic framework.

This molecule is a glycoside built from a single six-membered sugar ring linked through an oxygen atom to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is para-disubstituted, carrying a nitro group on one side and the glycosidic ether oxygen on the other, which gives it a linear, symmetric arrangement. The sugar portion is a fully saturated pyranose-type ring bearing four hydroxyl groups and an exocyclic hydroxymethyl group, all of which can donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen contributes a further weak acceptor site. The molecule has a flexible glycosidic linkage connecting its rigid aromatic and cyclic sugar components.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring is fused to a six-membered benzene ring along a shared carbon-carbon bond. The nitrogen atom of the pyrrole ring carries an ethyl group, so the ring nitrogen is substituted rather than bearing a free N-H. The fused aromatic system is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds apart from the terminal ethyl chain. Because the nitrogen is alkylated, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the pyrrole nitrogen's lone pair is part of the aromatic system and only weakly accepts hydrogen bonds. The overall shape is asymmetric, since the ethyl group sits on one side of the fused framework.

This molecule is a highly oxygenated steroid-like scaffold built from four fused rings, consistent with a cardenolide-type framework. Three of the rings are saturated six- and five-membered carbocycles in a fused tetracyclic arrangement, and the fusion stereochemistry locks the core into a rigid, angular shape. A fifth, separate unsaturated five-membered lactone ring is attached at the terminal position of the skeleton, bearing a conjugated carbon-carbon double bond adjacent to a carbonyl. The structure carries multiple hydroxyl groups at several ring positions, along with a hydroxymethyl substituent, creating a strongly hydrogen-bonding surface. Because the substitution pattern is asymmetric, the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is built on a purine scaffold, a fused bicyclic system in which a six-membered pyrimidine-type ring is joined to a five-membered imidazole-type ring through a shared edge. The six-membered ring carries an exocyclic primary amine at one position, while the five-membered ring bears, at its nitrogen, a saturated tetrahydrofuran ring attached through its anomeric carbon. That furanose-like ring carries a hydroxymethyl group on the carbon adjacent to its ring oxygen, giving it a stereochemically defined, non-planar sugar-like appendage. The fused aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the saturated ring and hydroxymethyl arm add some conformational flexibility. The amine and the ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the hydroxyl group adds further donor and acceptor capacity.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The nitrogen sits in the pyridine ring, so the ring system is an aromatic, planar, fully conjugated framework with no sp3 centers, making it rigid. A nitrile group (carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the pyridine-ring carbon at the position adjacent to the fused ring junction, serving as the only substituent. The ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen is a weaker acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall, the structure has no symmetry beyond its planar outline and is essentially inflexible.

The molecule has a flexible saturated chain of six carbons, with a single sp3 carbon at one end bearing two phenyl substituents, so the two benzene rings sit on the same carbon in a diphenylalkane arrangement. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene, with no fused ring systems and no heteroatoms. The structure contains no functional groups beyond the aromatic rings and alkyl chain, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The two aryl groups are chemically equivalent and the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the central carbon, though the long alkyl chain removes overall symmetry. The aliphatic chain gives the scaffold substantial conformational flexibility, while the two rings remain rigid planar units.

This is a fused tetracyclic steroid-type scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring joined in a rigid, mostly trans-fused arrangement typical of cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-junction carbons, and a secondary hydroxyl group is located on one of the six-membered rings. A tertiary hydroxyl sits at a ring-fusion carbon, and the five-membered ring carries a substituent that is an unsaturated five-membered lactone (a butenolide), attached through a saturated carbon. The lactone contains a carbonyl with an adjacent carbon-carbon double bond and an ester oxygen in the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because its substituents are placed asymmetrically around the fused skeleton. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the two hydroxyl groups, while the lactone carbonyl and ring oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a tetracyclic, saturated alkaloid-type scaffold built from fused and bridged aliphatic rings containing two nitrogen atoms: a tertiary amine nitrogen and an amide nitrogen. The amide carbonyl sits within a ring that is fused to the rest of the framework, so the carbonyl is part of a lactam. The rings are fully saturated and share several bonds, forming a compact, cage-like three-dimensional structure with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any substituents beyond the ring atoms and has no aromatic rings, and its arrangement is asymmetric. Its hydrogen-bond profile is limited: it has no N–H or O–H donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the tertiary amine nitrogen can act as acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic saturated hydrocarbon with no rings, heteroatoms, or functional groups. Its skeleton is a single branched chain: a central carbon bears two long straight-chain alkyl arms, one of ten carbons and one of thirteen, and a third arm of ten carbons attached at the same branch point, giving a tertiary-centered, asymmetric framework. The molecule has no ring fusion and no substitution pattern beyond this one branch point, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability because it contains only carbon and hydrogen. Its long methylene chains make it highly flexible, with many free rotations about its single bonds.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a six-membered piperidine-type ring and a second six-membered ring share a nitrogen atom and one adjacent carbon, forming a quinolizidine-type bridged system with the nitrogen at the ring junction. A hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached to the carbon at the ring fusion adjacent to the nitrogen, giving a primary alcohol side chain. The only heteroatoms are the tertiary amine nitrogen, which carries no hydrogen and is part of both rings, and the hydroxyl oxygen. The saturated, all-sp3 framework is conformationally flexible, able to adopt several chair-like arrangements, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the off-center hydroxymethyl substituent. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary nitrogen can serve only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a steroid built on the four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold, with three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring. The rings are fused in a trans-anti arrangement typical of sterols, giving a rigid, angular framework. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, and a branched alkyl side chain of eight carbons with two methyl branches projects from the five-membered ring. A single secondary hydroxyl group is attached to one of the six-membered rings, and a carbon-carbon double bond sits within the central ring system. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar hydrocarbon, and the overall shape is asymmetric because of the side chain and the single polar substituent.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, arranged in a rigid, roughly planar-fused framework. The ring junctions are fused, with several angular methyl groups projecting from the ring system. A single alkene sits in the second ring, and one secondary hydroxyl group occupies a position on the A ring. A long, branched, flexible alkyl side chain extends from the five-membered D ring and contains multiple stereocenters and a methyl branch. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is essentially hydrocarbon and offers no other polar sites.

The molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene arrangement. The ring fusions are largely trans-type, which gives the core a fairly rigid, flat-sided shape, while the side chain at C17 is a flexible branched alkyl chain ending in a trisubstituted alkene. The only polar group is a single secondary hydroxyl on one ring, which can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, and the ring system also carries a double bond and several angular methyl groups. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because of the asymmetric side chain and the hydroxyl position.

The molecule is built on a five-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopentene, with a carbon-carbon double bond between two ring atoms. One alkene carbon carries a methyl group, while the other bears a carboxylic acid substituent, so the double bond is trisubstituted and the acid is conjugated with it. The adjacent sp3 ring carbon is quaternary, carrying two methyl groups in a gem-dimethyl arrangement that adds steric bulk on one side of the ring. The ring is fairly rigid because of the double bond, though the saturated positions allow some puckering. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the substitution pattern is asymmetric. Its only hydrogen-bond donor is the carboxylic acid hydroxyl, and the carboxyl oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a symmetric acid anhydride built from two identical phenylacetyl units joined through a central C(=O)–O–C(=O) linkage. Each half consists of a benzene ring attached through a single methylene carbon to a carbonyl group, giving two monosubstituted phenyl rings with no ring fusion. The two halves are related by a mirror-like symmetry across the central oxygen, so the overall framework is highly symmetric. The anhydride carbonyls are electrophilic and the central ether-type oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The flexible methylene linkers allow considerable rotational freedom, though the aromatic rings and anhydride group remain relatively planar.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated six-carbon chain whose backbone bears a terminal aldehyde at one end and a primary alcohol at the other, with an amino group on the carbon adjacent to the aldehyde. Four carbons along the chain each carry a hydroxyl group, and one of them also carries the amine, so the skeleton is decorated with five hydroxyl oxygens, one nitrogen, and one carbonyl oxygen. The chain has no ring systems or ring fusion, and its substitution pattern is asymmetric because the amine and aldehyde sit at one end only. Because every carbon is sp3 apart from the carbonyl carbon, the molecule is highly flexible with many rotatable bonds. It is a strong hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and amino hydrogens and a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen and nitrogen atoms.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with no fused ring system. One ring carries an ethoxy group (–O–CH2–CH3) attached to the carbon adjacent to the biaryl linkage's ring, placing the ether substituent meta to the phenyl connection on that ring. The unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached directly to this position, so the scaffold is a 3-substituted biphenyl. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aromatic rings can rotate about the central bond, giving moderate flexibility, and the ethyl tail adds limited conformational freedom.

This molecule is a bicyclic iridoid-type glycoside built on a fused cyclopentane-pyran skeleton, with the six-membered dihydropyran ring fused to a five-membered ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. A lactone (cyclic ester) is embedded in the framework, and an enol ether double bond sits in the ring system. A vinyl group hangs off one ring carbon, and a glucose-type sugar unit is attached through a glycosidic linkage, bringing several hydroxyl groups and a hydroxymethyl group. The sugar and aglycone portions give many hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fused ring system is fairly rigid and the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on an isoflavan-type scaffold: a chroman (benzopyran) ring system in which a benzene ring is fused to a saturated oxygen-containing six-membered ring. A second phenol ring is attached at the 3-position of the saturated heterocycle through a single carbon-carbon bond, giving two aromatic rings joined by a partly flexible linker. Two phenolic hydroxyl groups are present, one on each aromatic ring, both in para-related positions relative to the connection point or ring oxygen. The ring oxygen of the chroman unit acts as an ether, and the stereocenter at the 3-position makes the molecule chiral. Both hydroxyl groups can serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ether oxygen can serve only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built around a saturated six-membered oxygen heterocycle, a tetrahydropyran ring containing one ring oxygen, with no aromatic or fused ring systems. Two carboxylic acid groups are attached to the ring, one at a quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group adjacent to the ring oxygen and the other on a carbon two positions away, while a gem-dimethyl group sits on the carbon next to the oxygen on the other side. The substitution pattern is therefore dense and asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is conformationally constrained, though the sp3 framework allows some chair-type flexibility. The two carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ring ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is morphinan-type: a rigid, polycyclic, fused framework built from four rings, with a phenolic aromatic ring fused to a cyclohexene-type ring and a bridging ether. The aromatic ring carries a hydroxyl group, and a second ring bears an ether oxygen linking it through a bridge, creating a cage-like ring fusion. A secondary alcohol sits on a saturated ring, next to a carbon-carbon double bond. A basic tertiary-to-secondary nitrogen is embedded in a fused piperidine-type ring. The phenol and alcohol provide hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygens, and the nitrogen serve as acceptors. The overall skeleton is highly rigid with few rotatable bonds, and it is asymmetric.

This molecule is a tertiary amide built around a central nitrogen that carries three substituents. One is a benzylic-type CH2 linking to a 3-methoxythiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic ring containing sulfur with a methoxy group on one carbon adjacent to the sulfur-bearing carbon. Another is a 2,6-dimethylphenyl ring attached directly to the nitrogen, with methyl groups flanking the point of attachment, which restricts rotation around that bond. The third is a chloroacetyl group, a carbonyl bearing a CH2Cl unit, giving an electrophilic alkyl halide terminus. The aromatic rings are unfused and connected through flexible single bonds, so the overall shape is moderately flexible. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond local ring mirror planes. It has no N–H or O–H groups, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds, but the carbonyl oxygen, ether oxygen, and thiophene sulfur can act as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid built on a fused four-ring framework: three six-membered rings followed by a five-membered ring, typical of the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton. The A ring is a cross-conjugated cyclohexadienone, containing two carbon-carbon double bonds and a ketone, which makes that portion relatively planar. A fluorine atom sits at a ring-fusion position, and the ring system carries several hydroxyl groups along with a two-carbon ketol side chain attached to the five-membered ring. A methyl group is present on the five-membered ring and additional angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions. The fused rings are largely rigid, with the side chain providing the main conformational flexibility. The molecule has no overall symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern and multiple stereocenters. Its hydroxyl groups and carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is an aryl alkyl ether built from a benzene ring bearing a single oxygen substituent. The oxygen links the aromatic ring to an unbranched six-carbon alkyl chain, so the scaffold consists of one planar six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The benzene ring is monosubstituted, meaning the ether oxygen is the only group attached to it, which gives the ring a simple, unsubstituted substitution pattern with no meaningful symmetry breaking beyond the single attachment point. The hexyl tail is flexible, with several freely rotating single bonds, while the aromatic ring is rigid. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a para-substituted toluene derivative, with a methyl group and a dichloromethylsilyl group on opposite positions of a single benzene ring. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and there are no fused ring systems. The silicon atom is tetrahedral, carrying one methyl group and two chlorine atoms in addition to its bond to the ring. Because the two ring substituents sit at opposite positions, the molecule has a high degree of symmetry about its long axis. The aromatic core and the rigid silicon center make the structure fairly rigid, though the Si–C bond to the ring allows some rotation of the silicon fragment. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring containing one ketone group, making it a cyclohexenone-type scaffold with no fused or bridged ring systems. A carbon-carbon double bond sits within the ring, conjugated with neither the carbonyl nor any other unsaturation, and a single methyl group is attached to one of the alkene carbons, creating a simple, unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The ring is partially rigid because of the endocyclic double bond, while the remaining saturated carbons allow limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic decalin-type scaffold, with two six-membered saturated rings sharing a single bond at a quaternary ring-fusion carbon that carries an angular methyl group. Each ring bears a tertiary alcohol: one on a side chain attached to the first ring, which also carries a vinyl (ethenyl) group, and one directly on the second ring. The second ring also carries a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern, and the ring carbons are otherwise fully saturated. Because the fused system is rigid while the side chain is flexible, the molecule has no overall symmetry. The two hydroxyl groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the remaining carbon skeleton contributes no additional polar functionality.

This molecule is a fused tetracyclic steroid-type scaffold made of three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring joined by shared edges, forming the classic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene framework. It carries two angular methyl groups at ring-fusion carbons, and its two hydroxyl groups sit at the ring positions shown in the SMILES, one on a saturated six-membered ring and one on the five-membered ring. A single carbon-carbon double bond sits within one of the six-membered rings, adding some rigidity to that part of the fused system. Overall the framework is largely rigid with limited flexibility, and both hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused framework: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring. The A ring is a cross-conjugated cyclohexadienone, containing a ketone and two carbon-carbon double bonds that create an extended conjugated system with the ketone as the principal carbonyl feature. The D ring is a five-membered carbocycle bearing a tertiary alcohol and an angular methyl group at the ring junction. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring fusions, giving the molecule its rigid, roughly planar-with-bulk shape, while the ketone oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors and the hydroxyl hydrogen as a hydrogen-bond donor.

This molecule is a saturated tricyclic terpenoid-like skeleton built from fused all-carbon rings, with no aromatic rings and no double bonds. Ring A is a cyclohexane bearing a methyl substituent, fused to a second ring that carries a gem-dimethyl group, and a bridging carbon framework creates a compact bicyclic bridge across the core. The only heteroatom is a single tertiary hydroxyl group on a quaternary carbon that also bears a methyl group, which makes the molecule a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor at one site. The fused and bridged cage makes the scaffold quite rigid, though some ring carbons allow limited conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a m-tolyl ether of a silatrane, with the aryl oxygen bonded to a silicon atom at the center of a tricyclic cage. The silicon is coordinated by three oxygen atoms and one nitrogen in a bridged bicyclic framework of three fused five-membered rings sharing the Si–N axis. The aromatic portion is a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and the Si–O–aryl linkage in a meta (1,3) relationship. The cage contributes three-fold pseudo-symmetry around the N–Si axis, while the aryl ring rotates relatively freely about the C–O bond. The oxygen atoms of the cage can accept hydrogen bonds, the tertiary amine nitrogen is a weak acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a complex, highly oxygenated sesquiterpenoid-type scaffold built on a fused polycyclic carbon framework. It contains a cyclohexene ring fused to a larger oxygen-bridged ring system, with an embedded epoxide (a three-membered oxygen ring) attached at a quaternary spiro-like carbon. Its functional groups include three acetate-type ester linkages, an isovalerate ester, a free secondary hydroxyl group, and an ether oxygen bridge. The substitution pattern is dense and asymmetric, with several quaternary carbons and methyl branches creating a rigid, three-dimensional architecture. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is limited to the single hydroxyl group, while the multiple ester, ether, and epoxide oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-like polycyclic framework built from four fused rings, with an angular methyl group at each ring junction. Ring A is a cyclohexenone, containing a conjugated ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond, while ring D is a five-membered ring bearing a tertiary alcohol and an angular methyl. Two thioacetate groups (S-acetyl units) are attached at separate positions on the ring system, and they are the only heteroatom-containing substituents besides the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The scaffold is largely rigid because of its fused ring junctions, with the thioester side chains providing some conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes only from the single hydroxyl group, while the ketone and the two thioester carbonyls serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused scaffold: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, all fused together in a rigid, largely planar-tracking framework. The ring A portion contains a conjugated enone, a cyclohexenone with a carbon-carbon double bond adjacent to a ketone, which introduces an electron-poor, planar region. At the D-ring carbon bearing a quaternary center, there is an ethynyl group and an acetate ester oxygen, giving the molecule a linear alkyne projection and an ester carbonyl that can accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule has only one ring-embedded carbonyl oxygen and one ester carbonyl oxygen as hydrogen-bond acceptors, with no hydrogen-bond donors, and it lacks symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring arranged in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene framework. The fusion is trans-type at the ring junctions, giving the core a rigid, bulky shape with two angular methyl groups projecting from the ring junctions. A single carbon-carbon double bond sits in one of the six-membered rings. Two propanoate ester groups are attached at the ring positions remote from each other, each consisting of a carbonyl bonded to an ethyl chain through an oxygen linkage. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all oxygen atoms are part of ester groups, and the two carbonyl oxygens serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its overall shape is largely rigid, with flexibility limited to the two ethyl ester side chains.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered oxygen heterocycle, a tetrahydropyran ring, with no fused rings and no aromatic character. The ring contains one oxygen atom and five sp3 carbons, and it carries four substituents: a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, plus three hydroxyl groups on the remaining ring carbons. Three of the hydroxyls sit on adjacent carbons, giving a contiguous polyol arrangement along one side of the ring, and the methyl and hydroxyl groups create several stereogenic centers. Because the ring is saturated, it is conformationally flexible, adopting chair-like arrangements whose substituents can be axial or equatorial. The four oxygen atoms, three hydroxyls and one ring ether, together provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites and several acceptor sites.

The molecule is a single tetrahedral carbon atom with no ring systems, so its scaffold is simply one sp3 carbon at the center. That carbon carries four halogen substituents: three chlorine atoms and one iodine atom, arranged around it in a tetrahedral geometry. There are no hydrogen atoms bonded to the central carbon, and no other functional groups are present. Because the four substituents are not all identical, the molecule has no rotational symmetry beyond the local threefold axis through the carbon-iodine bond, which is shared by the three chlorines. The structure is rigid, since there are no rotatable bonds, and the halogen atoms can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, with no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene-like bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a partially saturated six-membered ring containing one carbon-carbon double bond. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached directly to an sp2 carbon of that non-aromatic ring, conjugated with the adjacent alkene. The benzene ring is unsubstituted apart from the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is limited to this single carboxylic acid group. Because the partially saturated ring contains sp3 methylene carbons and a fused geometry, the framework is moderately rigid with some conformational flexibility in the saturated portion. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, and the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered saturated carbocycle, with the fusion occurring at two adjacent aromatic carbons. A linear n-hexyl chain is attached directly to the aromatic ring at a position meta to the ring fusion, creating a single substituent on the benzene portion. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the fused cyclopentane ring adopts a slightly puckered conformation and the hexyl chain is highly flexible. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, approximate symmetry, since the substituent breaks the symmetry of the aromatic ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, as it consists solely of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

Its ring is a 2-pyrone-free, fully conjugated cyclohexane-type skeleton bearing a carbonyl (C=O) in place of one ring carbon, giving a non-benzenoid quinonoid-style scaffold. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis and is essentially rigid because the ring is planar, though the hydroxyl and acid groups can rotate. Together the carboxylic acid and the hydroxyls provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites and several oxygen-based acceptor sites.

The molecule is a bicyclic scaffold built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered nitrogen-containing lactam ring, giving a dihydroisoquinolinone core.
