The fused ring system is largely planar and rigid, with only the saturated CH2 units in the lactam ring providing modest conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond an approximate mirror through the aromatic ring.

This molecule is built around a flexible acyclic backbone: a tert-butyl group bonded to a secondary alcohol carbon, which connects to a second carbon bearing a para-chlorobenzyl substituent and a 1,2,4-triazole ring attached through a ring nitrogen. The benzene ring is a monosubstituted-at-two-positions aromatic system, with chlorine para to the benzylic CH2, giving a symmetric 1,4-substitution pattern on that ring. The 1,2,4-triazole is a five-membered, fully aromatic heterocycle containing three nitrogen atoms, and its N1-linkage leaves the remaining nitrogens available as acceptors. The hydroxyl group provides one hydrogen-bond donor and an additional acceptor site, while the triazole nitrogens serve as further acceptors. Overall the molecule has several rotatable single bonds and only one stereocenter-bearing carbon region, so it is moderately flexible, with the aromatic rings providing localized rigidity.

This molecule is a fully saturated tetracyclic steroid-type scaffold built from three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, arranged in the classic gonane framework. Several ring-fusion junctions carry angular methyl groups, which lock the rings into a rigid, three-dimensional shape. Hydroxyl groups sit at multiple positions on the ring system, and the side chain at the five-membered ring ends in a ketone flanked by a primary alcohol, giving an α-hydroxy ketone. The hydroxyls and carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and the stereocentres create an asymmetric, non-planar surface.

This is a steroid-type tetracyclic scaffold: three fused six-membered rings and one fused five-membered ring, with the five-membered ring carrying an acetyl side chain at one end. The A ring is an α,β-unsaturated ketone (a cross-conjugated enone with a ring carbonyl and a C=C double bond), and a second ketone sits on the C ring. Two angular methyl groups are attached at ring-fusion carbons, which imparts a rigid, bulky, three-dimensional shape with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry and contains only carbonyl oxygens as hydrogen-bond acceptors, with no hydrogen-bond donor groups present.

The molecule is a short, straight-chain four-carbon acid with no ring systems or fused rings, so its scaffold is simply an open aliphatic backbone. A carbon-carbon double bond sits between the second and third carbons, which makes the chain conjugated with a terminal carboxylic acid group at one end. The carboxylic acid carries a carbonyl oxygen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and a hydroxyl group that can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule lacks any symmetry, since the methyl end and the acid end differ, and its rigidity is limited to the planar region around the double bond, with the single bonds elsewhere allowing rotation.

This molecule is a short, unbranched three-carbon acid built on a linear skeleton with no ring systems. Its terminal carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl, is conjugated to a carbon-carbon double bond, and a chlorine atom sits on the far end of that alkene, giving a vinyl halide. The alkene is locked in a fixed geometry, so the molecule is quite rigid with little conformational flexibility around the double bond. Overall the structure has no meaningful symmetry because the chlorine and carboxyl groups occupy different ends of the chain. The hydroxyl hydrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a four-carbon linear chain with a carbon-carbon double bond between the second and third carbons, so it has no rings and no fused ring systems. A bromine atom is attached to each terminal carbon, making it a symmetric 1,4-dibromo-substituted alkene. The central C=C bond is planar and rigid, which fixes the geometry of the two bromomethyl arms relative to one another, while the single bonds at the chain ends allow some conformational flexibility. The compound contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms capable of accepting hydrogen bonds other than the halogens, which are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a short, unbranched carbon chain built around a carboxylic acid group at one end, with a branched isopropyl group at the other end. The backbone contains a single carbon-carbon double bond located between the second and third carbons from the acid, and this double bond has a trans (E) geometry, which keeps the chain extended and fairly rigid. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and symmetry is absent because the two ends of the chain are chemically distinct. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the rest of the skeleton is purely hydrocarbon and contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a six-carbon straight-chain hydrocarbon, with its skeleton built entirely from sp2 and sp3 carbons and no rings or heteroatoms. It contains two carbon-carbon double bonds, located at positions 2 and 4 of the chain, and both are in the trans (E) configuration, which places the two alkyl ends on opposite sides of each double bond. The conjugated diene unit gives the central portion of the molecule a largely planar, extended geometry, while the terminal ethyl and methyl groups provide some rotational freedom. The molecule has a near-linear, approximately C2-symmetric shape, since its two terminal ends are chemically equivalent. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, because it carries only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

Parsing the SMILES: a carbamate (N-methyl, O-linked to an aryl ring) on a benzene ring that is fused to an indoline-type five-membered ring bearing an N-methyl group, and that five-membered ring is fused to a saturated six-membered N-methyl piperidine ring, giving a tricyclic, fully fused scaffold. A quaternary carbon at the ring fusion carries a methyl group, and a second stereocenter sits at the adjacent carbon, which makes the framework rigid with defined three-dimensional shape. The aromatic ring has a single carbamate substituent, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. The carbamate N-H is the only hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl and ester oxygen and the two tertiary amine nitrogens provide acceptor sites.

The molecule is a substituted thiourea in which one nitrogen is attached to a benzene ring bearing a methoxy group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho-substitution pattern on an otherwise unfused aromatic scaffold. The thiourea unit, consisting of a central thiocarbonyl carbon flanked by an NH group and a terminal NH2 group, is the principal functional group, and the aryl ether oxygen adds a further acceptor site. The structure has no rings beyond the single benzene ring, and its rotatable bonds around the thiourea and the aryl-nitrogen linkage give it moderate conformational flexibility, though it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. Its hydrogen-bond capability is pronounced: the two NH groups act as donors, while the sulfur and methoxy oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a thioacetanilide: a single benzene ring bearing one N-substituent, with the nitrogen attached directly to the aromatic ring. The benzene ring is unfused, monosubstituted, and planar, giving the aromatic core rigid geometry. Extending from the nitrogen is a thioamide group, in which a carbon is double-bonded to sulfur and single-bonded to a methyl group. The molecule has a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the axis through the nitrogen, the carbonyl-like carbon, and the para position of the ring, though the methyl and thiocarbonyl groups make the overall shape asymmetric. The amide-like N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom acts as a relatively weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The C–N bond has partial double-bond character, which limits rotation and adds conformational rigidity around the thioamide linkage.

This molecule is a symmetric cross-conjugated dienone: a central ketone carbonyl flanked on both sides by a trans-configured C=C double bond. Each alkene terminates in a furan ring attached at its 2-position, so the two furan rings are identical and mirror each other across the carbonyl. The furans are five-membered aromatic oxygen heterocycles, unfused and unsubstituted beyond that single linkage. The ketone carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the furan ring oxygens provide additional weak acceptor sites, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The extended conjugated framework makes the structure largely planar and rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the bonds connecting the furans to the alkenes.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing a single substituent, which is a three-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group. The aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered carbocycle with no heteroatoms, and the substitution pattern is monosubstituted, so the ring carries no additional functional groups. The chain contains a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated directly with the ring, which makes the overall framework largely planar and fairly rigid, with the nitrile as a linear, electron-withdrawing terminus. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure has no stereocenters and only one substituent on the ring, so it has a single axis of approximate symmetry through the ring and chain.

This molecule is an open-chain secondary amide built from a cinnamoyl unit linked to a 2-hydroxyethyl group. The core is a trans (E) alkene conjugated directly to a phenyl ring, giving a planar, rigid styryl segment attached to the carbonyl carbon. The amide nitrogen carries an N-H and bears a flexible two-carbon chain ending in a primary alcohol. Hydrogen-bond capacity is substantial: the amide N-H and the terminal hydroxyl act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen act as acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the aromatic ring.

This molecule is an acyclic, symmetric bis-amide-type scaffold built around a central two-carbon unit in which both carbons bear a thiocarbonyl group, so it is best described as an oxalyl-type backbone with each carbonyl oxygen replaced by sulfur. Each end carries a secondary thioamide nitrogen attached to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a primary hydroxyl group. The molecule has no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or stereogenic centers, and the two halves are mirror-related, giving it a symmetric substitution pattern. Its chain segments are conformationally flexible, though the thioamide C–N bonds have restricted rotation. Each thioamide N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two terminal hydroxyl groups provide both donor and acceptor capability, and the sulfur atoms serve as weaker acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic thiourea-type scaffold built around a central carbon that bears a sulfur atom and two nitrogen atoms, with one nitrogen double-bonded to that carbon in an imine-like tautomeric arrangement. One nitrogen carries an allyl group (a three-carbon chain ending in a terminal alkene), while the other carries a 2-hydroxyethyl chain terminating in a primary alcohol. The molecule contains no ring systems and no ring fusion, so it is fully open-chain and conformationally flexible. Its functional groups include a terminal alkene, a thiocarbonyl-derived unit with a free thiol or thione character, and a primary hydroxyl group. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the hydroxyl hydrogen and the N–H and S–H positions, while acceptor capability is provided by the oxygen, the nitrogen atoms, and the sulfur.

The molecule is a symmetric N,N'-diarylthiourea: a central thiocarbonyl group (C=S) flanked on each side by an NH linked to a para-substituted benzene ring. Each phenyl ring carries an ether oxygen at the para position, which connects to a flexible 3-methylbutyl (isopentyl) chain, so the two halves are mirror-related. The two aromatic rings are rigid and planar, while the alkyl tails add conformational flexibility. The thiourea NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur and ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a very small acyclic species built around a single thiocarbonyl-containing carbon. Its skeleton is just one carbon atom bonded to an amino group on one side and to a sulfur atom joined by a double bond on the other, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution pattern beyond these two heteroatom attachments. The thiocarbonyl group (C=S) and the amine nitrogen together form a compact thioamide-type functional unit. Because the structure is so small and has no rotatable bonds of significance, it is essentially rigid, and the molecule carries no internal symmetry beyond its local planarity around the central carbon. The nitrogen-bound hydrogens serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur atom can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a steroid built on the classic four-ring fused framework of three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring. The A ring is an enone, a cyclohexenone in which a ketone is conjugated with a carbon-carbon double bond, and the C ring carries a ketone adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon. The D ring is five-membered and bears a tertiary hydroxyl group at a ring-fusion position, together with a two-carbon side chain ending in a ketone and a primary alcohol. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, which makes the fused skeleton rigid and bulky. Overall, the molecule has several hydrogen-bond acceptors from its three carbonyl oxygens and two hydrogen-bond donors from its hydroxyl groups.

The molecule is an ester built from a long, straight, saturated fourteen-carbon acyl chain joined through a carbonyl group to a benzyl alcohol-derived unit. The acid portion is a fully saturated, unbranched alkyl chain that ends at the carbonyl carbon, giving the molecule a highly flexible, rod-like backbone with many freely rotating single bonds. The alcohol portion carries a single benzene ring, an aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings and no substituents on the ring itself, connected to the ester oxygen through a one-carbon methylene linker. The ester functional group, with its carbonyl oxygen and single ether-type oxygen, is the only polar feature in the structure. Overall, the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond local planarity of the ester and aromatic groups, and its only hydrogen-bond capability is acceptance at the two oxygen atoms, since it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic thiocarbamate built around a single central carbon. That carbon is bonded to an ethoxy group (an ethyl chain attached through oxygen), a primary amino group (NH2), and a sulfur atom joined by a double bond, so it is a thiocarbonyl. Because there are no rings, the scaffold is entirely open-chain and quite flexible, with free rotation about the single bonds. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the local arrangement around the central carbon. Its hydrogen-bond capability is clear: the NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two hydrogens, while the oxygen and sulfur atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a thiourea core, a central carbon double-bonded to sulfur and bonded to two NH groups, with each nitrogen attached to a 1-naphthyl ring system. Each naphthalene is a bicyclic aromatic scaffold of two fused benzene rings, and it is attached through an alpha position adjacent to the ring fusion, giving a bulky, planar aromatic unit on each side. The two naphthyl groups are related by a near-mirror arrangement about the thiourea, giving the overall molecule an approximately symmetric, elongated shape. The aromatic rings make the structure fairly rigid, while rotation about the C–N bonds of the thiourea core provides some conformational flexibility. The two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a steroid-type scaffold built from four fused rings in the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene arrangement, with three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, and the five-membered ring carries a tertiary alcohol with an adjacent methyl. Ring A contains an enone, with a hydroxymethylene group conjugated to a ketone, which adds a planar, electron-poor region to an otherwise saturated and rigid framework. The molecule is largely rigid because of its fused ring system, though some conformational flexibility remains in the saturated portions. The hydroxyl group and the enol-type hydroxymethylene oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ketone and hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The overall structure lacks any symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is a small five-membered heterocycle built around a single saturated ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen, forming an oxazolidine-type scaffold. The ring carries a thiocarbonyl group (a C=S double bond) on the carbon between the nitrogen and the oxygen, making it a cyclic thiocarbamate. A vinyl (ethenyl) substituent sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, which provides a small region of unsaturation outside the ring. The ring is compact and only partly flexible, with the vinyl group able to rotate freely. The nitrogen bears one hydrogen and can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur and oxygen atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry because the vinyl group occupies only one side of the ring.

This molecule is a small acyclic haloalkane built on a two-carbon chain, with no rings or fused ring systems. One carbon is fully substituted by two fluorine atoms and one chlorine atom, while the adjacent carbon is a methylene group carrying a bromine atom at its terminus. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the two carbons bear different halogen sets, so the molecule lacks any significant internal symmetry. Its flexible single-bond backbone allows free rotation about the central carbon-carbon bond, giving it conformational freedom rather than rigidity. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built from a quinoline core, a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring. At the 4-position of the quinoline, an ether oxygen links the core to a second benzene ring that carries a single fluorine atom at the para position relative to the ether linkage. The quinoline portion bears two chlorine substituents on the carbocyclic ring, at positions that leave it asymmetric overall. The fully aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with the diaryl ether linkage allowing only limited rotation between the two ring systems. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is nitrogen dioxide, a tiny three-atom species with no carbon skeleton and no ring systems. A single nitrogen atom sits at the center, bonded to two oxygen atoms, and the SMILES notation shows it with one formal positive charge on nitrogen and one double bond to each oxygen, which makes it an odd-electron, bent-type structure rather than a closed-shell linear one. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution pattern, since the entire structure is a single central atom flanked by two terminal oxygens. Because it is so small, the molecule is highly rigid with essentially no conformational flexibility to speak of. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, but both oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a glycoside built from a substituted benzaldehyde aglycone linked through an ether oxygen to a six-membered pyranose sugar ring. The aromatic benzene ring carries an aldehyde group and a methoxy group positioned ortho to one another, with the sugar attached at the carbon para to the aldehyde, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The sugar portion is a fully saturated tetrahydropyran ring bearing four hydroxyl groups and a hydroxymethyl side chain, creating a stereochemically rich, polar scaffold. The molecule is largely flexible around the glycosidic bond, while the aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and it lacks any meaningful internal symmetry. Hydroxyl groups on the sugar act as strong hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aldehyde and methoxy oxygens serve as additional acceptors.

This molecule is a dipeptide-like structure built from a proline ring linked by an amide bond to an alanine-type unit, which is in turn attached through an amine to a 2-amino-4-phenylbutanoic acid residue. The pyrrolidine ring of the proline portion is a saturated five-membered ring fused to nothing else, and the phenyl group is a single unsubstituted benzene ring attached to the end of a flexible ethyl-linked chain. The molecule contains two carboxylic acid groups, one on the proline ring and one at the terminus of the phenylbutanoic segment, along with a tertiary amide and a secondary amine. These groups give it several hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the multiple rotatable bonds make the overall backbone fairly flexible, with the pyrrolidine ring contributing some local rigidity. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since its three segments are chemically distinct.

This molecule is a salicylaldehyde glycoside, built from a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group and an ether-linked sugar. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with two adjacent substituents, so the substitution pattern is ortho. The aldehyde carbonyl is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the glycosidic oxygen and the ring oxygen of the sugar add further acceptor sites. The attached pyranose unit is a saturated six-membered ring carrying four hydroxyl groups and a hydroxymethyl arm, which together make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor and give it considerable conformational flexibility. The aromatic ring and the sugar are joined only through a single ether linkage, so the molecule has no fused ring systems and no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a benzotriazole core: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered triazole ring, so the two rings share an edge and form a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic scaffold. The triazole portion contains three adjacent nitrogen atoms, with one nitrogen bearing a saturated cyclohexyl group, which is attached through a single carbon-nitrogen bond. The cyclohexyl ring adopts a nonpolar, flexible chair-like geometry that projects out of the otherwise planar framework. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, since the cyclohexyl group sits on only one side of the triazole. The aromatic nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single central carbon atom that is doubly bonded to one nitrogen and singly bonded to two others, giving it a guanidine-type core. One of the nitrogens bears a hydrazinyl group, meaning a second nitrogen that carries a free NH2 terminus. Another nitrogen is attached to a nitro group, with the nitrogen bearing a formal positive charge and two oxygens, one double-bonded and one carrying a negative charge. The structure contains no rings, so it is acyclic and fairly flexible around its single bonds. It has several hydrogen-bond donors from the amine and hydrazine NH and NH2 groups, and several acceptors from the nitrogen lone pairs and the nitro oxygens. It lacks any internal symmetry, since the substituents on the central carbon are chemically distinct.

The molecule is built around a single sp3-hybridized carbon that bears an ethyl group and two identical para-hydroxyphenyl rings, giving a central methine-linked diaryl scaffold with no ring fusion. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring carrying one phenolic hydroxyl group at the position opposite the point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is para on both rings. The two halves are related by a mirror plane through the central carbon, so the molecule is symmetric about that axis. The aryl rings and the ethyl chain can rotate about their single bonds, so the molecule is moderately flexible rather than rigid. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites overall.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a primary sulfonamide group, where a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to an NH2 group. The opposite side carries a thioether linkage, a sulfur atom bonded to a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group. The aromatic core is a flat, rigid scaffold, while the thioether-ethanol side chain is flexible because of its rotatable single bonds. The sulfonamide contributes two hydrogen-bond donors (the NH2 protons) and several acceptors (the sulfonyl oxygens), and the terminal hydroxyl adds further donor and acceptor capability. The para pattern gives the molecule an approximate elongated, linear shape with a degree of mirror symmetry through the ring axis.

This is a steroid-type fused polycyclic framework made of four rings, with a cross-conjugated dienone unit in one of the six-membered rings and a cyclopentanone fused to the other end. An exocyclic methylene group sits on one ring, and two angular methyl groups project from ring-fusion carbons. The molecule is largely rigid because of its fused ring system, with limited flexibility only from the saturated portions. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two carbonyl oxygens, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a fused polycyclic natural-product-like scaffold built from several rings sharing edges. On one side sits a dimethoxy-substituted benzene ring, with two methoxy groups placed adjacent to each other, and the aromatic system is linked through an oxygen-containing bridge to a saturated ring. A hydroxyl group sits on a quaternary carbon, and a ketone is conjugated into an adjacent aromatic ring. The other end contains a dimethyl-substituted pyran fused to a benzene ring, with a cis-type alkene in the pyran ring. The molecule is largely rigid because of the fused ring system, with little rotational freedom, and it lacks symmetry. It has one hydroxyl group that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ketone, ether oxygens, and methoxy oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small six-membered carbocyclic ring bearing two ketone carbonyls and an enol-type hydroxyl on adjacent positions, with a methyl group on one of the sp2 ring carbons. A three-membered epoxide ring is fused across two adjacent sp3 carbons of the six-membered ring, creating a bicyclic, epoxide-fused cyclohexenedione scaffold. The double bond within the six-membered ring is conjugated with both carbonyl groups and the hydroxyl, which makes the core largely planar and rigid, while the strained epoxide adds local three-dimensional character. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the epoxide oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a fused bicyclic decalin-type framework, consisting of two six-membered carbocyclic rings sharing a common edge, with one ring carrying a conjugated diene unit. A side chain extends from one ring and terminates in a lactone, a six-membered cyclic ester that also bears a hydroxyl group on its ring. The ester linkage connects a bulky, branched 2,2-dimethylbutanoyl group to the ring system, which is a pronounced steric feature. Several methyl substituents are distributed around the carbocyclic core, breaking any overall symmetry and creating several stereocenters. The fused ring system and conjugated double bonds confer substantial rigidity, while the side chain provides some flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited to one hydroxyl group acting as both donor and acceptor, with the carbonyl and ring oxygens of the ester and lactone serving as additional acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single four-membered beta-lactam (azetidin-2-one) ring, a strained cyclic amide, bearing three aryl-containing substituents. The nitrogen of the lactam carries a 4-fluorophenyl group, and the adjacent ring carbon carries a 4-hydroxyphenyl group, making the core substitution pattern para-disubstituted on both aryl rings. A three-carbon chain branches from the other ring carbon and ends in a secondary alcohol that is attached to a second 4-fluorophenyl ring. The molecule has no fused ring systems, and its two fluorophenyl rings are related by a near-mirror arrangement, though the stereocenters break full symmetry. The aryl groups and the lactam ring limit flexibility, while the side chain adds some conformational freedom. Hydrogen-bond capability comes from the phenolic and secondary alcohol hydroxyl groups, which act as donors, and from the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygens, which act as acceptors.

This molecule is a disaccharide-like structure built from two five-membered furanose-type rings joined through an acetal linkage at an anomeric carbon. The first ring is a fully saturated tetrahydrofuran-type ring bearing a hydroxymethyl group, a hydroxyl, and a chloro-substituted carbon, while the second ring is a six-membered pyranose-type ring with a chloromethyl group and multiple hydroxyl substituents. Chlorine atoms appear at several positions as alkyl halides, and the molecule carries numerous hydroxyl groups as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The two ring systems are connected by a glycosidic oxygen bridge, giving the scaffold moderate conformational flexibility, and the many stereocenters lack any internal mirror symmetry.

This molecule is built on a flavonol scaffold: a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core fused to a second, pyranone-type ring, with a 3-hydroxy group on the heterocycle. A catechol-type phenyl ring (two adjacent hydroxyls) hangs off the 2-position, while the fused benzo ring carries two additional hydroxyls in a meta arrangement. The fused ring system is essentially planar and rigid, with the pendant aryl ring able to rotate only slightly. Its numerous hydroxyl groups and ring oxygens make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a 4H-chromen-4-one (chromone) scaffold, a benzopyranone in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring. A para-methoxyphenyl group is attached at the C3 position of the pyranone ring, making the substituent sit on the five-membered-looking heterocycle's neighboring carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. A hydroxyl group is located on the fused benzene ring, para to the ring-fusion oxygen region, and a methoxy ether group sits at the para position of the pendant phenyl ring. The core is largely planar and conjugated, with the aryl substituent able to rotate about a single bond, giving limited flexibility. The ketone oxygen and ring ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenolic hydroxyl acts as both a donor and an acceptor.

This molecule is a benzopyranone, specifically a coumarin scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered lactone ring containing an unsaturated ring-embedded ester (a 2H-chromen-2-one core). The fused bicyclic system is planar and largely rigid, with little conformational flexibility. Two substituents sit on the benzenoid ring: a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho-relationship between them. The lactone carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the phenolic hydroxyl can serve as both a donor and an acceptor, and the methoxy oxygen is an additional acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic coumarin-type scaffold: a 2H-chromen-2-one core, in which a six-membered lactone-containing pyranone ring is fused to a benzene ring. The pyranone ring carries a carbonyl at the position adjacent to the ring oxygen, giving an α,β-unsaturated lactone. Two adjacent hydroxyl groups sit on the benzenoid ring, forming a catechol-type pattern that places them next to the ring fusion. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core. Hydrogen-bond capability is clear: the two hydroxyl groups act as donors and acceptors, while the lactone carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is an open-chain polyunsaturated compound built on a linear fourteen-carbon backbone, with no rings at all. Its skeleton contains an alternating sequence of carbon-carbon double bonds (three conjugated C=C units) followed by two consecutive triple bonds forming a diyne segment, which makes the chain highly rigid and rod-like across its central region. Hydroxyl groups sit at both ends of the chain, one on a secondary carbon near the propyl terminus and one on a primary carbon at the opposite end, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry and the two terminal alkyl segments differ in length and substitution. Because the chain is largely unsaturated and linear, conformational flexibility is limited to the saturated ends. Both hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the unsaturated core contributes only weak, non-directional interactions.

The molecule is built around a 2-pyranone (α-pyrone) ring, a six-membered unsaturated lactone containing an endocyclic ester oxygen and a conjugated carbonyl. This ring carries a methoxy group on the carbon meta to the lactone oxygen, placing an ether oxygen on the scaffold. At the 6-position of the pyranone, a trans-configured vinyl linker connects to a para-methoxyphenyl ring, which is itself a simple benzene ring bearing a methoxy group opposite the alkene attachment. The whole framework is largely planar and conjugated, with the two aromatic systems joined through the rigid double bond, so rotation is restricted. Hydrogen-bond acceptor sites include the carbonyl oxygen, the lactone ring oxygen, and the two methoxy oxygens, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a flavonol, built on a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core fused to a second benzene ring, with a phenyl ring attached at the 2-position of the pyranone. The central chromone system is planar and largely rigid, with the pendant aryl ring able to rotate only slightly about its single bond to the core. Three hydroxyl groups sit on the scaffold: one on the fused benzo ring, one at the 3-position of the pyranone, and two adjacent (catechol-type) hydroxyls on the pendant ring, while the ketone carbonyl at the 4-position acts as an acceptor. Collectively, the hydroxyls supply several hydrogen-bond donors and the carbonyl and ring oxygen supply acceptors, giving the molecule considerable hydrogen-bonding capability. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the hydroxyl substitution pattern differs across its rings.

This molecule is an isoflavone, built on a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core with a phenyl ring attached at the 3-position of the heterocyclic pyranone ring. The fused bicyclic system contains a benzene ring joined to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone, which makes the core largely planar and rigid. Substituents include a methoxy group on the benzo ring, a phenolic hydroxyl adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing ring fusion, and a para-hydroxyl on the pendant phenyl ring, so the substitution is asymmetric overall. The carbonyl oxygen and ring ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two phenolic hydroxyls serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central methylene-bridged diaryl scaffold, with two phenolic rings joined by a single CH2 linker. One ring is a polyhydroxyacetophenone-type aromatic bearing an acetyl group, a methyl substituent, and multiple hydroxyl groups positioned ortho to one another. The other aryl unit is fused to a dihydropyran ring that carries a gem-dimethyl group, giving a chromene-type bicyclic core. A conjugated cinnamoyl (enone) side chain, consisting of a carbonyl linked to a styryl group, extends from the second aromatic ring. Multiple phenolic hydroxyls and carbonyl oxygens provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is an ester built from a cyclopropane-carboxylic acid core bearing a gem-dimethyl group and a 2-chloro-3,3,3-trifluoropropenyl side chain, linked through a CH2 group to a benzylic position. The benzylic ring is a biphenyl unit, with a phenyl ring attached to a methyl-substituted benzene ring in an ortho-related arrangement that creates a twisted biaryl geometry. The cyclopropane ring is fused to nothing else but carries three contiguous substituents, which gives the core a compact, strained, and fairly rigid character. The ester carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor of note, since the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is asymmetric and moderately flexible at the ester and benzylic linkages, while the aromatic and cyclopropane units are rigid.

This molecule is built around a tetrasubstituted benzene ring bearing four fluorine atoms and one methyl group, giving it a highly substituted, electron-poor aromatic core. A benzylic CH2 links that ring through an ester oxygen to a cyclopropane carboxylate, where the cyclopropane carries a gem-dimethyl group and a vinyl side chain. The vinyl group is a trisubstituted alkene bearing a chlorine atom and a trifluoromethyl group, which adds further halogenated bulk. The ester carbonyl is the sole hydrogen-bond acceptor site on the oxygen-rich portion, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall it is a rigid, sterically compact scaffold with the aromatic and cyclopropane units fixed relative to one another, and little internal symmetry beyond the ring's local pattern.

The molecule is built on a tricyclic scaffold: two benzene rings are fused to a central seven-membered ring that contains a sulfur atom, giving a dibenzothiepine-type framework. The central ring bears an exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond that links it to a flexible three-carbon chain ending in a dimethylamino group. The tertiary amine is the only basic, hydrogen-bond-accepting center, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The tricyclic core is non-planar and somewhat flexible because of the puckered seven-membered ring, while the side chain adds conformational freedom. The arrangement lacks any symmetry element, since the two fused rings differ in their connectivity to the sulfur atom and the exocyclic substituent.

The molecule is built around a tri-substituted alkene (C=C) that carries a para-tolyl ring, a 2-pyridyl ring, and a CH2 linker leading to a pyrrolidine nitrogen. The p-tolyl group is a benzene ring bearing a methyl substituent positioned opposite the point of attachment, giving it a symmetric para pattern. The 2-pyridyl ring contains an aromatic nitrogen adjacent to the carbon bonded to the alkene, which serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The pyrrolidine is a saturated five-membered ring with a tertiary amine, a basic site that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall, the structure is only partly rigid: the aromatic rings and alkene are planar, while the CH2 and pyrrolidine portion adds conformational flexibility.

This molecule is an unbranched aliphatic carboxylic acid with a carbon chain of about twelve atoms, containing a single carbon-carbon double bond located near the middle-to-acid end of the chain. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and has no ring fusion or aromatic character. The only functional groups are the terminal carboxylic acid, which carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, and the isolated alkene. The molecule has no substitution pattern or stereocenters, and its overall shape is essentially linear, with the double bond introducing a local kink in the chain. The long saturated segment makes the structure highly flexible, with many rotatable bonds.

The molecule is a straight-chain unsaturated carboxylic acid with no ring systems. Its skeleton is a ten-carbon chain: a saturated pentyl tail is followed by two carbon-carbon double bonds in conjugation with a terminal carboxyl group. The two alkene units are arranged in a conjugated diene pattern adjacent to the acid, which makes the carbonyl side of the chain planar and rigid. The saturated end of the chain remains flexible and has no symmetry. The carboxylic acid group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched aliphatic chain of seven carbons with no ring systems and no fused rings. Its backbone is a linear sequence in which a terminal ethyl group is followed by two carbon-carbon double bonds arranged in a conjugated diene pattern, and the chain terminates in an aldehyde group at one end. Because every carbon is in a straight chain, the molecule has no stereocenters and possesses no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror-line of its linear shape. The conjugated double bonds and the single bonds between them confer considerable rigidity to the central portion, while the terminal ethyl segment retains some rotational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen of the aldehyde can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully unbranched carbon chain of nine carbons, with an aldehyde group at one terminus, so it has no rings and no ring fusion. Three carbon-carbon double bonds lie in conjugation with one another and with the terminal carbonyl, forming an extended planar polyene-aldehyde system, and a terminal methyl group caps the opposite end. The chain is largely rigid and flat because of the conjugated double bonds, though the single bonds still allow some rotation and conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the methyl and aldehyde ends differ. The aldehyde oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a steroid built on the familiar four-ring fused scaffold, with three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring joined together. The ring system contains a single internal carbon-carbon double bond within the fused core. A hydroxyl group sits on one of the six-membered rings, and two angular methyl groups project from the ring junctions. A long, flexible side chain attached to the five-membered ring carries a trans double bond and several branched alkyl groups. The fused rings are conformationally rigid, while the side chain is flexible. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is largely hydrophobic and offers few other hydrogen-bonding sites.

This molecule is a secosteroid-type scaffold built from a fused tetracyclic core with a seco B-ring, meaning one ring is opened so that two separate ring systems are joined by a conjugated diene bridge. One six-membered carbocycle carries an exocyclic methylene group and a hydroxyl group on the ring carbon, giving it a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site. The other ring system is a fused polycyclic framework with angular methyl substituents at ring junctions, which makes the core rigid and sterically congested. A flexible, unsaturated side chain extends from the five-membered ring, containing a trans double bond and several methyl branches. The molecule has no overall symmetry, and its single hydroxyl group is the only polar functional group.

This molecule is built on a bridged bicyclic tropane-type scaffold: a seven-membered-to-six fused framework in which a nitrogen atom bridges two carbons of a cyclohexane ring, with an N-methyl group on that nitrogen. The ring system is conformationally rigid, with the bridging nitrogen locking the two fused rings into a fixed geometry. A methyl ester is attached to one ring carbon adjacent to the bridgehead, and a benzoate ester (a benzene ring bonded through a carbonyl-oxygen linkage) is attached to a neighboring carbon, giving a specific, non-symmetric substitution pattern with defined stereocenters. The two ester carbonyl oxygens and the tertiary amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because all nitrogen and oxygen atoms are fully substituted.

This molecule is an aurone, a benzofuranone in which a five-membered furanone ring is fused to a benzene ring and bears an exocyclic benzylidene group at the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. The exocyclic C=C bond, conjugated with the ketone and the aryl ring, gives the scaffold a largely planar, rigid geometry. The benzofuranone core carries a hydroxyl group on its fused benzene ring, while the pendant phenyl ring carries two adjacent hydroxyl groups in a catechol arrangement. The molecule has no symmetry, as the two aromatic rings are substituted differently. Its three hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ketone carbonyl and ring ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic aliphatic oxime with a straight carbon chain. A two-carbon ethyl group is bonded to a carbon that is double-bonded to a nitrogen, and that nitrogen carries a hydroxyl group, giving the C=N–OH oxime functionality. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, and its substitution pattern is simply linear. The molecule is essentially flexible, with rotation possible about its single bonds, though the C=N double bond fixes local geometry. The hydroxyl oxygen and hydroxyl hydrogen allow hydrogen-bond donation, while the nitrogen lone pair and oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a flavonol glycoside built on a fused bicyclic aromatic core, with a chromone-type benzopyranone scaffold carrying a 3-O substituted ring and a 4-hydroxyphenyl group attached at the 2-position of the central pyran ring. The A ring bears two hydroxyl groups and a further sugar linked through an oxygen, while the B ring is a para-hydroxylated phenyl. Attached to the flavonoid oxygen are two sugar units: a branched disaccharide of hexose and deoxyhexose residues joined by a glycosidic linkage, plus a terminal deoxyhexose. The many ring hydroxyls and ring oxygens make the molecule a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the glycosidic linkages add conformational flexibility to an otherwise planar aromatic core.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered thiophene ring bearing a methyl group on one carbon adjacent to the sulfur, with a vinyl linker at the neighboring position. That linker is a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond connecting the thiophene to a six-membered cyclic amidine ring, which contains an endocyclic C=N double bond and an N-methyl nitrogen. The two aromatic and heterocyclic ring systems are not fused, so the scaffold consists of three separate units joined in a linear arrangement. The rigid C=C and C=N unsaturation limits conformational freedom, while the saturated tetrahydropyrimidine methylene carbons add some flexibility to the ring. The sulfur atom and the imine nitrogen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are fully substituted or part of a double bond.

This molecule is an acyclic amino alcohol built on a long, unbranched chain of roughly eighteen carbons. A trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond sits near one end, adjacent to a secondary alcohol carbon, which is followed by a carbon bearing a primary amine and a terminal primary hydroxymethyl group. Because the skeleton is linear and carries no rings, it is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds along the hydrocarbon tail. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the long alkyl tail and the polar head group differ entirely in character. It has three hydrogen-bond donor sites (the hydroxyl and amine hydrogens) and three acceptor sites (the oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs).

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent, a four-carbon chain with a carbon-carbon double bond placed between its second and third atoms. The aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered carbon ring with no heteroatoms, and the substitution pattern is monosubstituted, so the ring has a single attachment point. The alkenyl side chain carries a methyl group on one end of the double bond and an ethyl-type terminus on the other, creating a trisubstituted alkene with a terminal methyl group. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen atoms. Its side chain has some conformational freedom around the single bond joining it to the ring, while the planar aromatic ring and the rigid alkene segment limit overall flexibility.

This molecule is an aliphatic oxime with a straight, unbranched seven-carbon chain, containing no rings and no fused ring systems. The chain terminates in a carbon-nitrogen double bond, forming a C=N-OH group, which is the defining oxime functionality. The hydroxyl oxygen on the nitrogen can donate a hydrogen bond through its O-H group and accept one through its lone pairs, while the imine nitrogen can also act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any meaningful internal symmetry beyond the linear chain, and its flexible alkyl tail allows considerable conformational freedom, while the C=N-O unit is comparatively rigid.

This molecule is a bicyclic pyrrolizidine alkaloid-type scaffold, built from two fused five-membered rings sharing a bridgehead nitrogen and a bridgehead carbon. One ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond, and the scaffold is substituted by a tertiary amine nitrogen at the ring fusion. An unsaturated ester side chain, a 2-methyl-2-butenoate group, is attached through an ester oxygen at a ring carbon, while a second ester linkage connects a branched hydroxylated acyl unit through a methylene bridge to the ring system. The branched acyl portion carries multiple hydroxyl and ether oxygens and several methyl groups, creating a sterically crowded, stereochemically defined region. The molecule is largely rigid in its bicyclic core but flexible in its side chains, lacks any internal symmetry, and features several hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens alongside two hydroxyl groups that act as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an unbranched, four-carbon-backbone diacid with two carboxylic acid groups, one at each terminus, joined by a central carbon–carbon double bond system. Both internal C=C double bonds have E (trans) geometry, which makes the chain fully extended and essentially planar. The molecule has no rings, so there is no ring fusion or substitution pattern to describe beyond the linear arrangement. It possesses a two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoint of the central C–C single bond, since the two halves are mirror-related. The rigid conjugated backbone limits conformational flexibility, while each carboxylic acid group provides two hydrogen-bond oxygen acceptors and one hydrogen-bond donor hydroxyl, giving the molecule four acceptor sites and two donor sites overall.

This molecule is a secosteroid-type scaffold built from a fused tetracyclic-like framework in which one ring has been opened, leaving a conjugated triene linking two ring systems. One terminus is a cyclohexane ring bearing an exocyclic methylene group and a secondary hydroxyl group on the opposite side of the ring. The other terminus is a fused bicyclic system containing a quaternary carbon bearing an angular methyl group, a side chain of the form CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH2CH(CH3)2 attached to a five-membered ring, and several saturated carbocycles. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and one hydrogen-bond acceptor (the oxygen atom), and it is largely hydrocarbon in character. Its overall shape is elongated and only partly rigid, since the conjugated triene constrains the central region while the saturated side chain and ring junctions add flexibility. It lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring systems and the substituents differ in size and placement.

The molecule is a short, linear four-carbon chain built around a central carbon-carbon double bond with a defined trans (E) geometry, which makes it rigid and planar at the alkene. It carries two terminal carbonyl-bearing groups: one end is a primary amide (–C(=O)NH2) and the other is a carboxylic acid (–C(=O)OH), so the molecule is unsymmetrical. Because there are no rings, the scaffold is entirely acyclic, and the only substituents are these two functional groups at opposite ends of the alkene. The amide contributes two N–H hydrogen-bond donors and a carbonyl acceptor, while the carboxylic acid offers an O–H donor and two oxygen acceptors, giving the molecule substantial hydrogen-bonding capability overall.

This molecule is a triacylglycerol-type structure built on a three-carbon glycerol backbone, with each of its three hydroxyl groups esterified to a long unbranched C18 monounsaturated fatty acyl chain. Each chain carries a single cis-configured carbon-carbon double bond near its midpoint, which introduces a characteristic kink along an otherwise extended hydrocarbon tail. The molecule contains no rings and no aromatic groups, and its three ester carbonyls are the only polar functionalities. Because the three acyl chains are identical and attached symmetrically at the primary and secondary glycerol positions, the molecule has a mirror-related arrangement at its ends but a chiral center at the central glycerol carbon. Its long flexible chains give substantial conformational freedom, while the ester groups can accept hydrogen bonds at their carbonyl oxygens but cannot donate any.

The molecule is built around a central imino-ester carbon that is double-bonded to an oxime-type nitrogen bearing an ethoxy group, and single-bonded to an oxygen that connects to a benzoyl group. That central carbon is also attached to a substituted benzene ring carrying two methoxy groups and a chlorine atom, placed at positions that make the arrangement asymmetric. The aromatic rings are flat and rigid, while the ethyl chain and the ester linkage give the molecule some rotational flexibility. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered methylenedioxy ring, giving a 1,3-benzodioxole scaffold. Attached to the aromatic ring is a conjugated diene chain that terminates in a carboxylic acid, so the carbon framework is largely planar and rigid, with the two C=C double bonds held in a fixed geometry. The substitution pattern is 1,3,4 on the benzene ring: the dioxole oxygens occupy two adjacent positions and the extended chain sits at a third, meta-related position. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the side chain is attached asymmetrically. The carboxylic acid group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the two ether oxygens of the dioxole ring act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single two-carbon ethylene unit, with one carbon bearing a chlorine atom and a phenyl ring and the other carbon bearing a phenyl ring, so the core scaffold is a 1,2-diphenylvinyl skeleton. It contains two separate benzene rings, each unfused and monosubstituted, attached to opposite ends of the central alkene. The only functional groups are the carbon-carbon double bond and the vinylic chlorine. Because the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and only the weakly polarized chlorine as a potential acceptor, its hydrogen-bonding capability is minimal. The two phenyl rings give the structure a fairly rigid, planar-leaning framework, with limited conformational freedom around the double bond.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic core: a pyranone ring (a six-membered ring containing a lactone-type ester oxygen and a ring carbonyl) fused to a second six-membered oxygen-containing ring, giving a chromanone-like scaffold. A propenyl (prop-1-enyl) side chain is attached to the aromatic-like pyranone carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, adding a conjugated C=C unit. The second ring carries a ketone, a secondary hydroxyl group, and a methyl-bearing stereogenic carbon next to the ether oxygen, which introduces a chiral center and a non-planar, partly flexible saturated region. Hydroxyl hydrogen is a donor, while the carbonyl oxygens and ring oxygens act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around an indane-1,3-dione-type core, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered carbocycle bearing a ketone. The five-membered ring carries a hydrazone (C=N–NH2) at one position, with the adjacent carbon attached to an acyl group that links to a carbon bearing two unsubstituted phenyl rings, giving a diphenylmethyl unit. The fused benzene ring is unsubstituted, and the phenyl groups are attached at a single carbon, so the molecule has no internal symmetry axis. The fused bicyclic core is rigid, while the acyl linker and the diphenylmethyl group add conformational flexibility. The terminal NH2 group and the ring N–H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ketone oxygens and imine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a five-membered thiazolidinone ring containing one sulfur atom, one nitrogen atom bearing a methyl group, and a carbonyl at the adjacent position. An exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond at the ring carbon next to sulfur carries an ethyl ester group, creating a conjugated, planar acrylate-like unit. The ring's remaining saturated carbon bears a piperidine ring attached through its nitrogen, which adds a flexible six-membered saturated component. Overall the structure is moderately rigid around the fused core but has rotational freedom in the ethyl and piperidinyl groups. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond acceptor-rich region from the two carbonyl oxygens and the ester oxygens, and no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all nitrogens are fully substituted.

This molecule is a coumarin (2H-chromen-2-one) core, a benzene ring fused to an unsaturated six-membered lactone ring, giving a flat, largely rigid bicyclic scaffold. The benzene portion carries two adjacent hydroxyl groups, which act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the lactone carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen serve as additional acceptors. At the 4-position of the pyranone ring sits a CH2 linker attached to a morpholine ring, a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing both nitrogen and oxygen. The tertiary amine nitrogen of the morpholine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen adds further acceptor capacity. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its flexibility is limited to rotation about the single bonds connecting the methylene linker and the morpholine ring.

The molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built on a six-carbon chain with two carbon-carbon double bonds in the main backbone and a third terminal double bond on a branch. The chain contains one trans-configured internal double bond (the /C=C/ unit) flanked by two methyl-substituted vinyl ends, so the scaffold is a conjugated diene carrying a methyl group at each terminus. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or polar functional groups beyond the alkene units. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the two ends carry different branching, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. It is flexible through its single bonds but its internal double bond fixes local geometry. Having no oxygen or nitrogen, it offers no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a very small acyclic hydrocarbon skeleton containing just two carbon atoms joined by a carbon-carbon double bond, with one iodine atom attached to each carbon. It has no ring systems, no fused rings, and no heteroatom functional groups beyond the two halogen substituents. The two iodines sit on opposite ends of the double bond, and the arrangement of these halogens relative to the double bond determines whether the molecule is cis or trans, though the stereochemistry is not specified in this SMILES string. Because of the rigid planar alkene unit, the scaffold is fairly restricted in conformation, and the molecule has a degree of symmetry that depends on the stereoisomer. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the iodine atoms are poor acceptors and there are no hydrogens bonded to electronegative atoms.

This molecule is built around a central benzene ring bearing two substituents in an ortho relationship. One substituent is a methyl oxime ether group, in which an O-methylated oxime carbon also carries a methyl ester. The second substituent is a benzyloxymethyl-type linker, a CH2 bridging the central ring to an ether oxygen that connects to a second benzene ring. That terminal ring carries an ortho methyl group, giving it a defined substitution pattern. The structure contains three aromatic rings joined by flexible single bonds, so it is conformationally flexible rather than rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the ether, oxime, and ester oxygens and nitrogen act only as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two outer rings differ in their substituents.

The molecule is built around a single two-carbon unit: a nitrile carbon bonded to a carbon that carries both a phenyl ring and an oxime group, where the oxime is a C=N double bond to a nitrogen bearing a hydroxyl. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, a plain benzene ring with no ring fusion and no substituents on its carbons. The core is fairly compact, with the linear nitrile and the planar C=N–OH arrangement giving limited conformational freedom, though the bond between the central carbon and the phenyl ring can rotate. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated at the oxime: the hydroxyl oxygen-bound hydrogen can act as a donor, while the oxime nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local planarity of the phenyl ring.

This molecule is a long, unbranched saturated hydrocarbon chain of thirteen carbons connected through an ether oxygen to a three-membered epoxide (oxirane) ring. The epoxide carries a single CH2 linker, so the ring sits at one terminus of the molecule and is substituted at a single carbon, with no ring fusion or additional rings present. The only heteroatoms are the ether oxygen and the epoxide oxygen, which act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The alkyl tail is highly flexible with free rotation about its many single bonds, whereas the strained epoxide ring is rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a five-membered lactam ring, a pyrrolidin-2-one (gamma-lactam), in which the ring nitrogen carries a long, unbranched twelve-carbon alkyl chain. A methyl ester group, a carbonyl bearing an oxygen-linked methyl, is attached to the ring carbon at the 4-position, next to the methylene adjacent to the lactam carbonyl. The scaffold is a single saturated ring with no fused or aromatic rings, so the core is compact and relatively rigid, while the dodecyl tail adds substantial conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the substituents sit at distinct positions on the ring. For hydrogen bonding, the molecule has no donor groups, since the nitrogen is fully substituted, but it offers two acceptor sites: the lactam carbonyl oxygen and the ester carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is a thiocarbamate built around a central carbonyl carbon bonded to a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen carries two isopropyl groups, making it a fully substituted, acyclic amide-type nitrogen with no N–H bond. The sulfur links the carbonyl to a 2,3-dichloroallyl chain, in which a methylene group is followed by a carbon–carbon double bond bearing one chlorine on each alkene carbon. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and conformationally flexible about its single bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors; the carbonyl oxygen is its only notable acceptor, while the sulfur and nitrogen contribute only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a large glycosylated polyketide built on a tetracyclic aromatic core. The aglycone contains a fused tricyclic system: an aromatic ring bearing a methyl group and two phenolic hydroxyls, fused to a partially saturated ring that carries a ketone and a cyclohexane-like ring bearing the side chain. Its side chain is a branched, polyhydroxylated fragment with a methoxy group, a ketone, and several secondary and tertiary alcohols. Attached to the core are three oligosaccharide chains of deoxysugars, linked through ether bonds, with many free hydroxyl groups. The molecule is therefore highly stereochemically complex and rich in both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, with substantial conformational flexibility in its sugar chains.

The molecule is built around a central carbon-carbon double bond that carries two ethyl groups, one on each alkene carbon, and each alkene carbon is also bonded to a para-methoxyphenyl ring, so the skeleton is a 1,2-diarylbut-1-ene scaffold. Both aromatic rings are benzene rings, each bearing a methoxy (aryl ether) group at the position opposite the point of attachment, and the two ends of the molecule are therefore identical. The arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis through the central alkene. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor, since the two ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds while there are no donor groups. The central double bond and the attached aryl rings limit rotation somewhat, while the two ethyl chains and methoxy groups remain relatively flexible.

The molecule is built around a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring with two nitrogens in a 1,4 arrangement, which gives it a fairly flexible, chair-capable core. One nitrogen carries an ethyl ester group joined through a methylene linker, while the other is acylated by an α,β-unsaturated amide whose alkene is in the E configuration and links to a phenyl ring. That aromatic ring bears three adjacent methoxy substituents at the 3, 4, and 5 positions, giving a trimethoxyphenyl pattern. The overall arrangement lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the substituted ring. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N–H or O–H groups, while the carbonyl oxygens, ester oxygens, methoxy oxygens, and the tertiary piperazine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This is an acyclic, straight-chain polyunsaturated C15 alcohol with no ring systems and no ring fusion. The backbone contains a conjugated diene, a conjugated diyne, and a further alkene, giving a largely linear, rigid, rod-like scaffold with limited conformational freedom at the unsaturated segments. Two secondary and primary hydroxyl groups sit at opposite ends of the chain, one at the terminal allylic position and one as a secondary alcohol near the butyl end. Both hydroxyls can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the two ends differ in their substitution and in the saturation of the chain.

The molecule is built on a five-membered furan ring, an aromatic oxygen-containing heterocycle. A nitro group (–NO2) is attached to one carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, and a short side chain sits on the opposite alpha position. That side chain is a single CH=N–OH unit, an oxime, which links the ring to a hydroxyl group through a C=N double bond. The scaffold is essentially planar and fully conjugated, with the ring, nitro group, and oxime largely in one plane, so the structure is quite rigid with only the oxime hydroxyl free to rotate. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two ring substituents differ. The oxime OH and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the oxime OH can also act as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built around a central amide linker connecting two aromatic units. One side is a 4-nitrobenzoyl group, a benzene ring bearing a nitro group para to the carbonyl, which makes that ring strongly electron-poor. The other side is a fused bicyclic benzotriazole system, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered triazole ring, and the triazole nitrogen carries a cyclohexyl substituent. The amide NH and carbonyl oxygen, together with the nitro oxygens and triazole nitrogens, give the structure several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The molecule is largely planar and rigid across its aromatic and amide portions, with the cyclohexyl ring as the most flexible region, and it has no internal symmetry because the two ends differ.

The molecule is built on a 2-methyl-2H-benzotriazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a triazole ring bearing an N-methyl group on one of the nitrogens of the five-membered ring. A secondary amide links the benzotriazole core, through its benzene ring, to a para-nitrophenyl group, so the substitution pattern is elongated and roughly linear. The molecule is largely planar and conjugated, with the fused bicyclic system, amide, and nitro-substituted phenyl ring contributing to a rigid framework with limited conformational freedom. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen, the nitro group oxygens, and the triazole nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl-substituted triazole and the nitro-substituted ring are positioned asymmetrically.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system. It consists of a long saturated hydrocarbon segment interrupted by a single carbon-carbon double bond near the middle, and terminated at one end by a nitrile group (a carbon-nitrogen triple bond). The double bond introduces a local kink in an otherwise linear skeleton, and the molecule as a whole is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds. It has no symmetry beyond its approximate linear shape. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a hydrazone formed from a 2-butanone-derived ketone unit: an ethyl and a methyl group sit on a carbon that is double-bonded to a nitrogen, which in turn is single-bonded to a second nitrogen attached to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered benzene system bearing two nitro groups, placed at the positions ortho and para to the hydrazine linkage, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The C=N–NH linker is largely planar and conjugated with the aryl ring, which limits rotation and makes the core fairly rigid, while the terminal ethyl group adds some flexibility. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the nitrogen atoms of the hydrazone and the oxygen atoms of the two nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built around a linear acyclic chain connecting a nitrofuran ring to a urea-type unit. A five-membered furan ring carries a nitro group on the carbon opposite the point of attachment, giving an electron-poor aromatic heterocycle with a single, unfused ring system. The chain runs from the furan through a hydrazone-type C=N linkage, then to a nitrogen bearing a 2-hydroxyethyl arm and a carboxamide (urea) group. The molecule lacks any symmetry, and the C=N double bond fixes the geometry of the linkage while the hydroxyethyl arm adds conformational flexibility. The primary amide NH2 and the hydroxyl group act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, the nitro oxygens, the furan oxygen, and the imine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built around a central sp3 carbon bearing two nitrogen-containing arms, with three furan rings attached in total. Parsing the SMILES, one furan-2-yl group is bonded to a terminal imine carbon (a C=N unit), and the central carbon is attached to a second furan ring and to an aminal-type nitrogen that leads into a second C=N imine bearing a third furan-2-yl group. The three furans are unfused, each connected through a single or conjugated bond, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule carries no stereochemical symmetry beyond what the sp2 imine geometry imposes. Its key functional groups are the two imine (C=N) linkages and the furan oxygens, which act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule offers no hydrogen-bond donors since the nitrogens carry no N–H. The conjugated imine and furan units give the framework considerable rigidity, though the central sp3 carbon allows some rotational flexibility between the two halves.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,2,4-triazinone-type ring containing two adjacent nitrogens, one of which carries a methyl group on a carbon double-bonded to nitrogen, giving a hydrazone-like C=N linkage within the ring. A carbonyl group sits in the ring adjacent to a ring nitrogen, forming a cyclic amide-like (urea-type) unit. The second ring nitrogen bears an exocyclic N-N=CH substituent that connects to a pyridin-3-yl ring through an imine (azomethine) bond. The overall scaffold is non-fused, with one saturated-looking ring system linked to one aromatic pyridine by a flexible hydrazone chain. Because of the unsymmetrical substitution, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. The ring and the conjugated hydrazone linker give moderate rigidity, while the amide-type carbonyl and ring NH can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built around a two-carbon core: an N-methyl amide carbonyl bonded to an sp2 carbon that carries an O-methyl oxime ether (C=N-O-CH3). That central carbon also bears a phenyl ring, which carries a phenoxy group (a diaryl ether linkage) at the ortho position, giving two separate benzene rings joined through an oxygen atom. The aromatic rings are unfused and freely rotating about the ether bond, so the structure is moderately flexible, though the C=N double bond fixes the oxime geometry. The amide N-H is the only hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen, the oxime nitrogen, the oxime oxygen, and the diaryl ether oxygen all act as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions: a ketoxime ether unit (a C=N double bond carrying an O-methyl group and a methyl group), an aryl ether linkage, and a methyl ester. The aryl ether connects the benzene to a pyrimidine ring, which is substituted with two methoxy groups in a 4,6-pattern. The benzene and pyrimidine rings are joined through a single oxygen bridge, so they are not fused, and the overall structure is fairly flexible around the ether and oxime bonds. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the nitrogen atoms of the oxime and pyrimidine ring, along with several oxygen atoms, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.
