The other side bears a sulfone linked through a two-carbon chain to a secondary amine, which in turn carries a branched isobutyl group. The para arrangement gives the aromatic core a symmetric, rigid geometry, while the saturated chain adds some conformational flexibility. The sulfonamide NH2 can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and both sulfonyl oxygens as acceptors, and the secondary amine provides an additional donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic aromatic core: a benzene ring fused to a 1,2,3-triazole ring, which bears a cyclopentyl group on one of its ring nitrogens (a benzotriazole scaffold). The aromatic benzene ring carries a single pivalamide substituent, meaning a secondary amide NH linked to a carbonyl that is attached to a bulky tert-butyl group, placed para-like to the fused junction. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, while the cyclopentyl ring and the tert-butyl group add three-dimensional bulk. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen along with the unsubstituted triazole nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element that would make it highly symmetric, since the substituents are attached asymmetrically.

The molecule is an ester built from a benzoic acid unit linked through a glycolamide-type spacer to a tertiary amide nitrogen bearing two isobutyl groups. The aromatic core is a single unsubstituted benzene ring, so the substitution pattern is simply monosubstituted at the carbonyl-bearing carbon, with no ring fusion. Functional groups present are an aryl ester, a tertiary amide, and an ether-type oxygen linking the two carbonyl-containing segments. The two isobutyl chains are branched, flexible alkyl groups attached symmetrically to the nitrogen, giving the molecule a partial local symmetry around the amide, while the ester and amide linkages add rotatable bonds and conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since there is no N–H or O–H, but it offers several acceptors through the two carbonyl oxygens, the ester oxygen, and the amide nitrogen's lone pair, which is largely delocalized.

The molecule is built around a thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic sulfur heterocycle, bearing two substituents at positions 2 and 5. One substituent is a primary sulfonamide (–SO2NH2) and the other is a sulfone (–SO2–) linked through a flexible three-carbon chain to a methoxyacetate ester, with the ester carbonyl and ether oxygen providing additional polar character. The ring is planar and fully substituted at the 2 and 5 positions, giving the core a rigid, elongated shape, while the propyl linker and methoxyethyl ester tail add conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents differ. The sulfonamide NH2 group offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the sulfonyl oxygens, ester carbonyl, ester oxygen, and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two ortho substituents: an acetoxy group (an ester formed from acetic acid and a phenolic oxygen) and a carboxylate ester. The second ester links to a two-carbon glycolate-type unit that terminates in a tertiary amide, where the nitrogen carries a methyl group and a CH2 that leads to a primary carboxamide. The benzene ring is the only ring system, with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is 1,2 (ortho). Apart from the aromatic ring, the chain is flexible, with several rotatable single bonds. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the aromatic core. Hydrogen-bond capability is present: the primary amide provides two N–H donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of the esters and amide, along with the ester ether oxygens, serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine-type ring carrying a nitroxide-like N-hydroxyl group flanked by two geminal dimethyl-substituted carbons, giving a sterically shielded, non-planar heterocyclic core. A second ring carbon bears a urea linkage, in which one nitrogen is attached to a phosphoryl group. That phosphorus center is bonded to two aziridine rings, each a strained three-membered nitrogen heterocycle fused to nothing but attached through their nitrogens. The ring system is not fused; the aziridines and the piperidine are connected through the urea and phosphoramide linkages, so the scaffold is modular with several independent rotatable bonds. There is no overall molecular symmetry, although the two aziridine groups are chemically equivalent. The N-hydroxy group and the urea N-H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the urea carbonyl, phosphoryl oxygen, and ring nitrogens act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a diacylhydrazine core: two carbonyl groups are attached to a central nitrogen-nitrogen bond, with one nitrogen also bearing a bulky tert-butyl group. One carbonyl is attached to an ortho-methylated benzene ring, and the other to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the two aromatic rings are not symmetric with each other. Both rings are simple benzene rings with no fused ring systems, and the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk that restricts rotation around the adjacent nitrogen. Each amide-like carbonyl carries a hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygen, while the single remaining N–H on the hydrazine offers one hydrogen-bond donor site. The molecule is fairly flexible overall, aside from the rigidity imposed by the aromatic rings and the hindered nitrogen.

The molecule is built around a single para-substituted benzene ring bearing a methyl group, opposite a carbonyl-bearing carbon, so the aromatic ring is the central scaffold. The carbonyl attached to that ring forms an amide with a nitrogen that is also bonded to a tert-butyl group, and this nitrogen carries a second nitrogen that is acylated by a benzoyl unit, giving a 1,2-diacylhydrazine core. A second unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached through its carbonyl, so the molecule contains two aromatic rings with no ring fusion. The bulky tert-butyl group and the N-N linkage give the structure considerable steric shape and moderate conformational flexibility, with no internal symmetry between the two aryl halves. Two amide N-H or carbonyl-type groups are present as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, with the carbonyl oxygens serving as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a 1,8-naphthyridin-4-one core, a bicyclic scaffold in which two fused six-membered rings each contain nitrogen atoms, with the carbonyl carbon of the pyridone ring sitting at the fused junction region. The ring system is fully aromatic and planar, giving it a rigid framework, while the side chains attached to it are flexible. On the nitrogen of the pyridone ring sits an N-ethyl group, and a methyl group is positioned on the adjacent pyridine-type ring. At the third position, a carboxamide links to a glycine-derived ethyl ester chain, adding conformational flexibility at its end. The molecule has no internal symmetry. Hydrogen-bond capability is present: the amide N-H serves as a donor, while the ring carbonyl oxygen, the amide carbonyl oxygen, the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen, and the ring nitrogen act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a 1,8-naphthyridin-4-one scaffold: a bicyclic system of two fused six-membered aromatic rings, each containing one ring nitrogen, with the nitrogens positioned on opposite ring-fusion sides. An N-ethyl group sits on the nitrogen of the pyridone-type ring, and a methyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the other ring nitrogen. Off the ring, a carboxamide links through an amide bond to an alanine-like unit whose terminal carboxylic acid is esterified with methanol. The fused aromatic core is essentially planar and rigid, while the side chain offers several rotatable single bonds. The amide N-H is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the ring carbonyl oxygen, amide carbonyl, ester carbonyl, and ring nitrogen act as acceptors.

This molecule is a diacylhydrazine built around a central N–N bond, with one nitrogen bearing a tert-butyl group and the other carrying a benzoyl (phenyl carbonyl) unit. Its acyl substituents are both aromatic: one is an unsubstituted phenyl ring attached through an amide-type C=O, and the other is a meta-chlorophenyl ring attached through a second C=O on the tert-butyl-bearing nitrogen. The two benzene rings are not fused and are connected to the hydrazine core only through carbonyl linkages, so the scaffold is non-fused and moderately flexible around the N–N and C–N bonds. The tert-butyl group is bulky and sterically dominant, lacking any symmetry axis that spans the whole molecule. The molecule has two N–H or carbonyl-type hydrogen-bond features: one N–H donor on the unsubstituted nitrogen, and two carbonyl oxygen acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing one edge. The fused ring system is fully aromatic and planar, which makes the core rigid. One ring carries a chlorine atom on a carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, while the other ring carries four oxygen-containing substituents: two methoxy groups and two acetoxy (acetate ester) groups, all placed on adjacent positions of the same ring. The substitution pattern is therefore dense and unsymmetrical, with no mirror or rotational symmetry in the overall structure. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the four oxygen atoms of the ether and ester carbonyl groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a 1,2-diacylhydrazine in which the central nitrogen-nitrogen bond links two amide-type carbonyl units. One nitrogen bears a tert-butyl group, while the other nitrogen carries an unsubstituted benzoyl group, and the first nitrogen is also acylated by a 2-bromobenzoyl group. The scaffold therefore consists of two separate benzene rings, each attached through a carbonyl linker, with no fused ring systems. The bromine sits ortho to the carbonyl on one ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The bulky tert-butyl group and the two amide planes restrict conformational freedom around the N-N bond. Two N-H or carbonyl-oxygen sites can participate in hydrogen bonding, but the molecule has only one N-H donor.

This molecule is built around a single nitrogen-nitrogen bond that links two acyl groups in a 1,2-diacylhydrazine arrangement. One nitrogen carries a bulky tert-butyl group, which sterically shields that side of the scaffold, while the other bears a hydrogen atom. Two aromatic rings sit at the ends: an unsubstituted benzene ring attached through a carbonyl, and a para-cyanobenzene ring attached through a second carbonyl, with the nitrile functioning as a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. The molecule has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and its amide-type linkages give it a fairly rigid central region flanked by rotatable aryl bonds. The NH and two carbonyl oxygens provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the nitrile nitrogen offers an additional acceptor site.

This molecule is built around a single nitrogen-nitrogen bond, forming a 1,2-diacylhydrazine-type core in which one nitrogen carries a bulky tert-butyl group. The second nitrogen bears a benzoyl group, a plain phenyl ring attached to a carbonyl, while the first nitrogen carries a 2,6-difluorobenzoyl group, an aromatic ring with fluorine atoms flanking the carbonyl attachment point. Both aryl rings are unfused benzene rings, so the scaffold has no fused ring system and no internal symmetry, since the two aroyl halves differ. The two carbonyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the single N–H on the benzoyl-bearing nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The bulky tert-butyl group and the ortho-fluorines restrict rotation around adjacent bonds, giving the molecule a moderately constrained conformation.

The molecule is an amide built from two aromatic rings joined by a short flexible linker. One ring is a 3,4-dimethoxyphenyl group attached through a two-carbon ethyl chain to a secondary amide nitrogen. The other ring is a catechol, a benzene bearing two adjacent hydroxyl groups, and it connects to the amide carbonyl through a rigid trans carbon-carbon double bond. The two aromatic rings are each unfused and monosubstituted at distinct positions, so the overall scaffold lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The conjugated alkene and amide make the central region relatively planar, while the ethyl linker adds rotational freedom. The two phenolic hydroxyls and the amide N-H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen, the two methoxy oxygens, and the phenolic oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a 1,8-naphthyridin-4-one scaffold, a bicyclic system of two fused six-membered rings each containing one nitrogen atom. An N-ethyl group sits on the nitrogen of the pyridone-type ring, and a methyl group is attached to the adjacent pyridine-type ring. At the 3-position, a carboxamide links to a valine-derived unit whose alpha-carbon carries a methyl ester and whose side chain is isopropyl. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the amino acid ester tail adds conformational flexibility. The amide N-H is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens of the ketone, amide, and ester, together with the ring nitrogen, act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a para-tolyl sulfonamide: a benzene ring carrying a methyl group opposite a sulfonyl group, which connects through an NH to a second aromatic system. That second system is a benzotriazole, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing three nitrogen atoms, and the fusion makes the bicyclic core largely planar and rigid. The triazole nitrogen bears a cyclopentyl substituent, which adds a non-planar aliphatic ring that is somewhat flexible. The sulfonamide NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfonyl oxygens and the triazole nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two aromatic halves and the substitution positions differ.

The molecule is built around a sulfonamide linker joining two aromatic systems. One end carries a para-aminophenyl ring, a benzene bearing a primary amine opposite the sulfonyl group. The other end is a benzotriazole, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered triazole ring, with the sulfonamide nitrogen attached to the benzo portion. The triazole nitrogen at position 2 carries a cyclopentyl substituent, so the fused system is N-alkylated. The aromatic rings are rigid and planar, while the S–N bond and the cyclopentyl group add some conformational flexibility. The primary amine and the sulfonamide N–H act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfonyl oxygens and triazole nitrogens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central dithiocarbonimidate-type carbon bearing two sulfur substituents and a double bond to a nitrogen, which in turn connects to a pyridine ring at its 3-position. One sulfur carries a straight four-carbon n-butyl chain, while the other links to a benzyl group whose phenyl ring is substituted at the para position with a tert-butyl group, giving a clearly asymmetric arrangement. The aromatic pyridine and benzene rings are separate, unfused, and joined through the flexible thioether and imine linkages, so the molecule has considerable conformational freedom. The pyridine nitrogen and the imine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens sit on saturated carbons.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents: two nitro groups and a trifluoromethyl group, with a secondary amine linking the benzene to a pyridine ring. The aromatic core is a substituted aniline-type scaffold, with the two nitro groups in meta-like positions relative to one another and the trifluoromethyl group adjacent to the amine. The attached pyridine ring is fully aromatic and bears two chlorine atoms, one on the ring carbon next to the nitrogen-bearing carbon and one further around the ring. The NH linker is flexible enough to allow some rotation, though the overall framework is largely planar and rigid. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes solely from the single N–H, while the nitro oxygens, the pyridine nitrogen, and the fluorine atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a 1,2-diacylhydrazine in which both nitrogens are substituted: one nitrogen carries a tert-butyl group and an aroyl group, while the other is an NH bearing an unsubstituted benzoyl group. The central N–N bond links two amide-type carbonyls, giving a flexible, non-fused core built from three separate benzene rings rather than any fused ring system. The first benzoyl unit is ortho-substituted with a trifluoromethyl group, which adds a bulky, strongly electron-withdrawing substituent that twists that ring out of plane. The bulky tert-butyl group on the adjacent nitrogen adds steric crowding and restricts rotation around the N–N bond. The molecule has no symmetry, and it offers one N–H donor and two carbonyl oxygen acceptors.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine-type ring carrying an N-hydroxyl group (a nitroxide-precursor hydroxylamine) and four methyl substituents on the carbons flanking the nitrogen, giving a sterically crowded, non-aromatic scaffold. A urea linkage (NC(=O)N) connects the ring's carbon at position 3 to a phosphoramide center bearing two identical 2,2-dimethylaziridine rings, each attached through its ring nitrogen. The aziridines are strained three-membered rings, making that region rigid, while the ring-to-urea and urea-to-phosphorus bonds leave the molecule moderately flexible. Hydrogen-bond donor sites include the N-OH, the urea N-H groups, and the N-H on the piperidine linkage, while acceptors include the urea and phosphoryl oxygens and the tertiary ring nitrogens. The two aziridine groups are constitutionally identical, though the overall molecule lacks a symmetry element that would make the piperidine ring's two halves equivalent.

The molecule is built around a benzotriazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing three nitrogen atoms, and that fused unit bears a cyclopentyl group on one of its triazole nitrogens. A sulfonamide linker, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to an NH group, connects the fused bicyclic system to a second benzene ring. That second ring carries a nitro group para to the sulfonyl attachment, which gives it a strongly electron-poor, linear substitution pattern. The molecule has no overall symmetry, and its aromatic framework is rigid, while the saturated cyclopentyl ring and the sulfonamide bonds allow some conformational flexibility. The sulfonamide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfonyl oxygens, the nitro oxygens, and the triazole nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

Let me parse the structure. The core is a 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine ring bearing an N-hydroxy group (a nitroxide-type hydroxylamine on the ring nitrogen), with the 4-position attached to a urea nitrogen. The urea carbonyl is bonded to a phosphoramide-type phosphorus that carries two aziridine rings, each with gem-dimethyl substitution on the three-membered ring. The piperidine ring is saturated and sterically crowded by four methyl groups flanking the nitrogen and the adjacent carbons. The molecule has no rings fused to one another, but it links three separate ring systems through a flexible urea-phosphoryl chain. Hydrogen-bond donors are the N-H of the urea and the N-OH hydroxyl; acceptors include the urea carbonyl oxygen, the phosphoryl oxygen, and the piperidine ring nitrogen.

The molecule is built around a pyridine ring bearing a nitro group, with a secondary amine (NH) linking it to a benzene ring. The pyridine carries a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the linking nitrogen, and a nitro group on the ring carbon meta to the nitrogen. The aniline-type ring carries two nitro groups and a trifluoromethyl group, all in a 2,4-dinitro-6-(trifluoromethyl) pattern relative to the amine. Both aromatic rings are planar and fully conjugated, while the NH bridge gives the overall structure some rotational flexibility around the two C–N bonds. The molecule has no symmetry, since the two rings carry different substituents. The NH group is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the nitro oxygens, the pyridine nitrogen, and the amine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused pair of benzene rings, with four substituents around the bicyclic core. Two adjacent positions on one ring carry methoxy groups (–OCH3), and the remaining two positions on that ring each bear a pivalate ester, where a bulky tert-butyl-type carbonyl group is attached through an oxygen. The benzo ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric overall but has a partial mirror-like arrangement across the ring. The fused aromatic system is rigid and planar, while the bulky ester groups are sterically crowded and add some conformational freedom around the C–O bonds. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, whereas the four oxygen atoms of the ethers and carbonyl esters can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a large macrocyclic lactone built around a polycyclic core, with a 16-membered-type macrolide ring bridged by a spiroketal system. Several rings are fused and bridged together, giving the scaffold a rigid, three-dimensional character in its central region. The structure contains a lactone ester, a free secondary hydroxyl group, and a tertiary hydroxyl at a ring-fusion carbon, along with an ether oxygen within the bicyclic framework. Multiple carbon-carbon double bonds sit in the macrocycle and in the adjacent fused ring, adding conformational constraint. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, and its two hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors while the ester, ether, and ketal oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a macrocyclic polyketide-type lactone built around a fused polycyclic core. A spiroketal system, in which a tetrahydropyran ring and a second cyclic ether share one carbon, sits at one end of the framework. The macrocyclic lactone ring contains an ester linkage and several trans-configured alkene units, which add rigidity along parts of the chain. A fused bicyclic ether, bearing a hydroxyl group and a methyl-substituted ring alkene, closes the opposite end of the structure. Hydroxyl groups provide hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the ether oxygens and ester carbonyl act as acceptors, and the scaffold is largely asymmetric with several methyl and ethyl branches.

This molecule is a fully conjugated, flat, polycyclic aromatic system built from four fused or linked five-membered heteroaromatic rings, each containing a pyridine-like nitrogen, arranged in a macrocyclic framework. The four nitrogen atoms sit at inward-facing positions, so the core resembles a porphyrin-type tetrapyrrole skeleton with the inner ring bearing four aza atoms, and there are no sp3 carbons or substituents hanging off the periphery. The molecule has high symmetry, with the four pyrrolic units related by a four-fold or near-four-fold arrangement, and it is essentially rigid and planar because every atom is part of the conjugated ring network. Its only hydrogen-bond capability comes from the imine-type nitrogens, which can act as acceptors, while there are no N-H or O-H donors present.

The molecule is a small acyclic organophosphorus compound built around a single phosphorus center bearing a methyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a phosphoryl oxygen, with one additional hydroxyl group. Because there are no rings or ring fusions, the scaffold is simply a short, flexible-free chain of one carbon attached to a tetrahedral-like phosphorus core. The phosphorus is double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to a hydroxyl oxygen, giving it a phosphinic-acid-type functional arrangement, and the molecule has no stereocenters or internal symmetry beyond a local rotational freedom about the carbon-phosphorus bond. It is rigid around the phosphorus-oxygen unit but otherwise compact. The hydroxyl group and the phosphoryl oxygen together make it capable of both hydrogen-bond donation and hydrogen-bond acceptance.

This molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a nitrogen-nitrogen double bond in the trans (E) configuration, giving an extended, rigid, mostly planar scaffold. The first ring is a 1,2,4-trisubstituted benzene bearing two hydroxyl groups at positions ortho and meta to the azo linkage, so the two OH groups sit adjacent to each other on the same ring. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached to the azo bridge. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two aromatic rings carry different substitution patterns. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the azo nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-type tetracyclic framework: three six-membered rings fused to a five-membered ring, with one additional bridging ether ring formed by a cyclic acetal-like oxygen linkage across the lower portion of the skeleton. The A ring is an unsaturated cyclohexenone bearing a ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to it. A hydroxyacetyl side chain, containing a second ketone and a primary alcohol, is attached to the five-membered D ring. A hemiacetal hydroxyl sits on the bridged carbon, and a quaternary methyl group anchors the ring junction. The fused, polycyclic rigid core contrasts with the flexible side chain, and the molecule offers several hydrogen-bond acceptors from its carbonyl and ether oxygens and two hydrogen-bond donors from its hydroxyl groups.

This molecule is built on a fused tetracyclic scaffold of four six-membered rings, with three rings sharing edges in a linear-angular arrangement and the fourth ring fused to the aromatic system. The aromatic ring is a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group and a chlorine atom, and it is fused to a ketone-containing ring. The remaining rings carry multiple enol and tertiary alcohol groups, a primary carboxamide, a ketone, and a dimethylamino group on a saturated stereogenic carbon. The substitution pattern is highly asymmetric, with many contiguous stereocenters, so the framework has no meaningful symmetry. The fused polycyclic core is fairly rigid, while the dimethylamino group and carboxamide offer some conformational freedom. Hydroxyl, enol, and amide groups make the molecule a strong hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl and ring oxygen atoms serve as multiple acceptors.

The molecule is a flexible, acyclic diester built on a linear polyether chain. Two 2-ethylbutyl ester groups, each with a branched alkyl carbon bearing two ethyl substituents, sit at opposite ends of a central chain containing three ether oxygens separated by ethylene units. Because the molecule has no rings, it adopts many conformations and is highly rotatable. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two carbonyl oxygens and three ether oxygens, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is approximately symmetric about its central ether oxygen.

The molecule is an azo compound built from two benzene rings joined by a nitrogen-nitrogen double bond (an N=N linkage), giving an extended, conjugated aromatic skeleton with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a single methyl group ortho to the azo linkage, while the other ring carries an amino group para to the azo bond and a methyl group ortho to it, so both substituents are placed asymmetrically across the two rings. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry axis because the two rings bear different substitution patterns. The azo bridge and the two aryl rings are largely planar and rigid, though the rings can rotate about their single bonds to the nitrogen atoms. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the amine nitrogen and the azo nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a flavonol-type glycoside built on a fused bicyclic chromone core, in which a benzopyran-4-one ring system is fused to a second aromatic ring. A catechol-substituted phenyl ring is attached at the position adjacent to the ring oxygen, which is part of the pyranone ring. The aromatic core carries two free phenolic hydroxyl groups on the fused benzo ring and two additional hydroxyls on the pendant phenyl ring, giving a 1,2-diol pattern there. A sugar unit is linked through an oxygen at the 3-position of the pyranone ring, and this sugar bears a further glycosidic chain with multiple free hydroxyl groups. The molecule is largely rigid in its aromatic portion but flexible in the sugar side chain, and it contains many hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic ester built around a central chain that carries two phenyl rings on adjacent carbons. A propanoate (propionate) ester group is attached to one benzylic carbon, while the neighboring carbon bears the second phenyl ring and a branched methyl group that leads into a dimethylaminomethyl side chain. The two benzene rings are unfused and separated by sp3 carbons, so the scaffold is flexible, with several rotatable bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two phenyl groups sit in different chemical environments. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the tertiary amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an open-chain polyol linked to a six-membered cyclic sugar-like ring through an ether oxygen. The acyclic portion is a straight carbon chain bearing multiple secondary and primary hydroxyl groups, giving it a flexible, extended shape. The ring is a saturated pyranose-type scaffold with one ring oxygen, a hydroxymethyl substituent, and several hydroxyl groups attached at different positions, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. Overall, the molecule has no internal symmetry, many rotatable single bonds, and a high capacity to act as both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its numerous hydroxyl and ether oxygen atoms.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated carbon chain with no rings, and it carries a terminal alkyne at one end (C#C-). Along the backbone are four methyl branches on alternating carbons, giving a branched aliphatic skeleton, and two adjacent secondary alcohol groups (-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-) sit near the opposite terminus, followed by a short ethyl tail. The substitution pattern is irregular, so the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry. Its many single bonds make it highly flexible, with no rigid ring or planar scaffold to restrict conformation. The two hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the terminal alkyne offers only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a small, acyclic dioxime built on a four-carbon chain. The central carbon atom is bonded to a methyl group, and it carries two oxime groups, each formed by a carbon double-bonded to a nitrogen that bears a hydroxyl group. One oxime sits at the terminal carbon of the chain, and the other sits on the carbon adjacent to the methyl group, so the two C=N-OH units are conjugated through the carbon backbone. The structure contains no rings, so its scaffold is entirely open-chain and fairly flexible, with rotation possible around the single bonds. Each oxime hydroxyl can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and each oxime nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the molecule two donor and two acceptor sites overall. It has no clear internal symmetry because the two oxime groups occupy chemically different positions on the chain.

This molecule is an organophosphate ester built around a central phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded oxygen and two methoxy groups. The phosphorus is linked through a third oxygen to a vinyl carbon that carries a chlorine atom on its terminal position, forming a chlorovinyl unit. That vinyl carbon is attached to a benzene ring bearing chlorine substituents at the 2 and 4 positions, giving a 2,4-dichlorophenyl scaffold. The structure has a flexible phosphate linker connecting a rigid aromatic ring and the alkene, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, with several oxygen atoms acting as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the substitution on the phenyl ring is unequal.

This molecule is an ester built from a linear nine-carbon alkyl chain bonded through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon, which in turn is attached to a benzene ring. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fusion, and it carries two substituents at opposite positions (para), giving the ring a symmetric 1,4-pattern. One substituent is the ester carbonyl and the other is a primary amino group on the far side of the ring. The long saturated alkyl tail is highly flexible and adds considerable conformational freedom, while the aromatic core and ester linkage are comparatively rigid. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the ester carbonyl oxygen and ester oxygen, along with the amine nitrogen, can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered thiazolidine-type ring containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom within the ring, with the carbon framework bearing exocyclic imine linkages. Two of the ring carbons carry exocyclic C=N double bonds, each connected to a trifluoromethyl group through the nitrogen, so the core is a diimine-substituted thiazolidine. A third exocyclic imine links to a phenyl ring, and the ring nitrogen bears a second phenyl group, giving two unsubstituted benzene rings attached to the scaffold. The molecule has no stereocentres, but its double bonds are fixed in defined geometry, which makes the core fairly rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the imine nitrogens and the ring sulfur and nitrogen can act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a coumarin-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered α-pyranone (2H-chromen-2-one) lactone ring, giving a bicyclic aromatic core. A hydroxyl group sits on the pyranone ring at the carbon adjacent to the fused benzene, and the adjacent carbon bears a saturated tetralin-type unit, a partly hydrogenated naphthalene in which one ring is aromatic and the other is a cyclohexane-like ring. The aromatic portion of that unit carries a para-biphenyl substituent, a phenyl ring attached to a second phenyl ring. The molecule is rigid across its fused and biaryl regions but has some flexibility at the single-bond linkage to the saturated ring. It lacks any symmetry because the substituents are unevenly placed. The hydroxyl group and lactone carbonyl oxygen give it hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a 2,2-dimethyl-2,3-dihydrobenzofuran (a benzene ring fused to a five-membered oxygen-containing ring that carries a gem-dimethyl group on the carbon next to the aromatic ring). On the benzene ring, a sulfonate ester group is attached, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to an ethoxy group, positioned adjacent to the ring fusion. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, while the ethyl chain of the sulfonate ester is flexible. The ring ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, the sulfonyl oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a propyl chain, a nitrile group, a 1,2,4-triazol-1-ylmethyl arm, and a para-chlorophenyl ring. The triazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing three nitrogen atoms, attached through one of its ring nitrogens, and it is unfused. The benzene ring is para-disubstituted, with the chlorine on the carbon opposite the quaternary attachment point, giving the aromatic portion a symmetric arrangement about its long axis. The nitrile is a linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the unsubstituted ring nitrogens of the triazole also serve as acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its quaternary center gives it a three-dimensional, moderately flexible framework.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents: an ethyl ester (CCOC(=O)) and a sulfonyl group that links to a hydrazine-type nitrogen. That nitrogen carries both a formyl group (N-C=O) and a pyrimidine ring attached through a carbon atom, so the pyrimidine ring is substituted with one chlorine and one methoxy group at positions that sit on opposite sides of the nitrogen-containing core. The molecule has no ring fusion, and its three ring systems (benzene and the single pyrimidine, plus the flexible linker) give it moderate conformational freedom around the sulfonyl-nitrogen and nitrogen-pyrimidine bonds. It lacks any molecular symmetry, since the substituents on each ring are placed asymmetrically. The sulfonamide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ester and sulfonyl oxygens, the formyl oxygen, the methoxy oxygen, and the pyrimidine nitrogens act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered pyrazoline-type ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a methyl group, while the carbon framework bears a methyl ester and a chlorine on a double bond within the ring. A sulfonyl group links the ring to a urea unit, which in turn connects to a pyrimidine ring substituted with two methoxy groups, giving an asymmetric, moderately flexible structure. The sulfonylurea linkage and the ring NH provide hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the sulfonyl oxygens, carbonyl oxygens, methoxy oxygens, and pyrimidine nitrogens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a six-membered cyclohexane-type ring that carries two ketone groups, placing them in a 1,3-relationship within the ring. A carboxylic acid group hangs off the ring carbon between the ketones on the opposite side, and the ring's adjacent carbon bears an exocyclic enol bearing a cyclopropyl group attached to the carbon bearing the hydroxyl. The ring is non-aromatic and not fused to any other ring, though the cyclopropane is a separate small ring attached by a single bond. The structure has no meaningful symmetry, and its exocyclic enol and acid groups give it moderate conformational flexibility around the single bonds. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the carboxylic acid and enol hydroxyl groups, while the carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen act as acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic scaffold built from a thiophene ring fused to a six-membered sulfone-containing ring, giving a thieno-thiopyran core. The aromatic thiophene carries a primary sulfonamide group (–SO2NH2) on the carbon adjacent to the ring sulfur, while the other ring fusion carbon connects to a saturated sulfone (–SO2–) within the fused ring. The two CH2 groups in the saturated ring provide flexibility, whereas the fused aromatic–heterocyclic system is largely planar and rigid. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the sulfonamide and sulfone groups sit at distinct positions. The sulfonamide NH2 offers hydrogen-bond donor capability and the four sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a saturated six-membered oxane (tetrahydropyran-type) ring, with no aromatic rings and no ring fusion. The ring carries four nitrate ester groups, each an oxygen attached to a nitro group, distributed around the ring at positions that give a non-symmetric substitution pattern. A propoxy group, a three-carbon chain linked through oxygen, sits on the anomeric carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, while a nitrate-bearing CH2 arm extends from the ring carbon opposite it. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its stereocenters create a defined three-dimensional arrangement, though the bulky substituents limit conformational freedom of the ring. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent because there are no N–H or O–H groups, and the many oxygen atoms in the nitrate and ether functions serve only as acceptors.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered sugar-like ring, a tetrahydropyran bearing an ethoxy group at the anomeric carbon, so its scaffold resembles a glycoside skeleton. Four of the ring and side-chain oxygens each carry a nitrate ester group (O-NO2), with one such group on a exocyclic CH2 and three on adjacent ring carbons, giving a densely and asymmetrically substituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is fully saturated and contains only single bonds, with no ring fusion, so it adopts a chair-like conformation, though the bulky nitrate groups restrict its flexibility. The ring oxygen and the ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because every hydroxyl has been converted to an ester.

Here is a structural description of the molecule, based on the SMILES given. The core is a six-membered 1,3-oxazinan-type ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen, bearing a ring carbonyl adjacent to the nitrogen, which makes it a lactam. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon next to the oxygen, and a phenyl ring is attached to the neighboring alkene-type carbon, giving a conjugated, partly unsaturated ring. The lactam nitrogen carries a bulky tert-alkyl group, a carbon bearing two methyl groups that is linked to a 3,5-dichlorophenyl ring, so the substitution is meta on that aryl ring and gives it a symmetric pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters in the ring, while the rotatable bonds and the bulky substituents give moderate rigidity overall. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the carbonyl oxygen and the ring ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a short aliphatic carboxylic acid with no ring systems, so its scaffold is a single two-carbon chain. The carbon bearing the carboxyl group also carries two iodine atoms, making it a geminal diiodo substituent pattern on one carbon. The carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is the only polar functional group, and it can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the chain, and its acyclic framework is fairly flexible, with rotation possible about its single bonds.

The molecule is built on a quinoxaline-type bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered pyrazine-like ring that contains two nitrogen atoms, both of which carry N-oxide oxygens. A carbon of the heteroaromatic ring bears an exocyclic hydrazone linkage (C=N–NH) that connects to a methyl carbamate group (–C(=O)OCH3). The bicyclic core is fully aromatic and planar, so the ring system is rigid, while the hydrazone-carbamate side chain offers some rotational freedom. The N-oxide oxygens and carbamate carbonyl act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the NH of the hydrazone serves as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is a symmetric, nearly linear scaffold built around a central carbon-carbon double bond joining two para-substituted benzene rings. Each terminal ring carries an amidine group (C(=NH)NH2) at the position opposite the vinyl linkage, and one of the two rings also bears a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the vinyl attachment, breaking the otherwise mirror-like symmetry. The stilbene-type central linkage gives the molecule a rigid, extended, planar-leaning shape with little conformational flexibility. Each amidine group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the phenolic hydroxyl adds a further donor and acceptor site.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic scaffold built from four rings, three six-membered and one five-membered, with the five-membered ring fused to the lower right edge. It carries a conjugated cross-ring dienone in the A ring (a 1,4-dien-3-one arrangement) and a secondary hydroxyl group on the C ring. A fluorine atom sits on the B ring, and methyl groups are placed at several ring-fusion and side positions. A butyl α-ketoester side chain is attached to the five-membered ring, contributing an ester carbonyl and an adjacent ketone. The hydroxyl and ketone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the single hydroxyl serves as the only hydrogen-bond donor. The fused ring system is rigid, while the butyl ester tail is flexible, and the overall substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is a 1,4-naphthoquinone core bearing a hydroxyl group on one quinone carbon, so the quinone ring carries both a ketone and an enol-type OH. The fused benzene ring of the naphthoquinone is unsubstituted, giving a planar bicyclic aromatic-quinonoid scaffold. At the other quinone carbon sits a trans-1,4-disubstituted cyclohexyl ring, which links to a para-chlorophenyl group, so the chain is rod-like and elongated. The OH and the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl group also acts as a hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, and its rigid fused core contrasts with the more conformationally flexible cyclohexyl linker.

The molecule is built on a 1,4-naphthoquinone-type scaffold, in which a fused bicyclic system pairs a benzene ring with a six-membered ring bearing two carbonyl groups in a para-like arrangement. The benzo ring is unsubstituted, while the quinone ring carries two adjacent substituents on one side: a hydroxyl group on one sp2 carbon and a 3-methylbut-2-enyl chain on the neighboring carbon. The prenyl side chain contains a trisubstituted alkene and a gem-dimethyl terminus, adding some conformational flexibility to an otherwise planar, rigid core. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution pattern. The enolic hydroxyl can donate a hydrogen bond, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single carbon atom at its center, a one-carbon tetrahedral scaffold with no rings and no fused systems. Bonded to that carbon are one fluorine atom, two chlorine atoms, and one iodine atom, so the substitution pattern is a mixed tetrahalomethane in which all four positions carry a different halogen or a repeated one. The structure contains no conventional functional groups beyond the carbon-halogen bonds themselves. Because the central carbon is tetrahedral and the substituents are monatomic, the molecule has only a limited degree of symmetry, a local threefold arrangement of the two chlorines around the C-F and C-I axis, and it is essentially rigid with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic organic peroxide built on a single quaternary carbon bearing three ethyl groups, giving a 3-ethylpentan-3-yl scaffold. That central carbon is bonded to an oxygen-oxygen linkage, so the terminal oxygen carries a hydrogen, making the group a hydroperoxide. The structure contains no rings and no ring fusion, and its substitution pattern is fully symmetric about the central carbon, with the three ethyl arms interchangeable. Because it consists only of freely rotating single bonds, it is conformationally flexible. The hydroperoxy group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its two oxygen lone pairs.

This molecule is a substituted imidazole, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. The ring carries a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to one nitrogen, a nitro group on the carbon at the opposite side of the ring, and a 1-hydroxyethyl chain attached to the other ring nitrogen. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen acceptor sites, while the terminal hydroxyl on the side chain acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the side chain offering rotational flexibility, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry.

This molecule is built on a macrocyclic germacranolide-type skeleton, with a ten-membered carbocycle that is fused to a five-membered lactone ring at one edge. The lactone carries an exocyclic alpha-methylene group, a common reactive feature in such systems, and an ester linkage connects the macrocycle to a branched side chain bearing a second methylene-substituted acrylate unit. Several trisubstituted and disubstituted ring alkenes are present, along with hydroxymethyl and hydroxyl groups that add polarity. Because of the large fused ring system and multiple alkene constraints, the framework is relatively rigid, though the macrocycle retains some conformational flexibility. Multiple hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the hydrocarbon portions of the scaffold remain nonpolar.

This molecule is 1,1-difluoroethylene, a very small acyclic alkene built on a two-carbon skeleton with no rings or ring fusion. Its only functional group is a carbon-carbon double bond, and both fluorine atoms sit on the same terminal carbon, giving a geminal substitution pattern. The molecule is planar at the double bond, rigid with no rotatable single bonds, and has no meaningful stereocenters. Fluorine is a poor hydrogen-bond acceptor and carbon-bound hydrogens are weak donors, so it has essentially no classical hydrogen-bond donor capability and only very weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a fully fluorinated cyclopentane ring, with every carbon bearing two fluorine atoms and no hydrogens present. The scaffold is a single saturated five-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, no additional substituents, and no functional groups beyond the carbon-fluorine bonds. The structure is highly symmetric, with the ring carbons arranged so that the fluorine substitution pattern is uniform around the entire ring. The saturated ring confers limited conformational flexibility, with puckering being the main motion available. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a two-carbon acyclic compound, built on a single carbon-carbon bond as its entire skeleton, with no rings and no aromatic systems. Each carbon carries two fluorine atoms and one chlorine atom, giving the two halves identical substitution patterns. The arrangement is highly symmetric, with a two-fold axis relating the two carbon centers, and the molecule is only modestly flexible because rotation about the central C–C bond is possible. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since no O–H or N–H groups are present, and its only potential acceptors are the halogen atoms, which are weak.

This molecule is a perfluorinated linear alkane built on a four-carbon backbone, with every carbon bearing only fluorine substituents: the two terminal carbons each carry three fluorines (a trifluoromethyl group) and the two internal carbons each carry two. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no heteroatoms other than the fluorines. The structure is achiral and highly symmetric, with the backbone presenting a mirror-like arrangement end to end. Because the carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds and the chain is unbranched, the skeleton is flexible in principle, though the bulky fluorine atoms restrict rotation. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine atoms can only act as very weak acceptors.

The molecule is built from two cyclohexane rings joined by a single methylene bridge, giving a bis(cyclohexyl)methane skeleton with no fused or aromatic rings. Each cyclohexane ring carries one primary amino group, and both amines sit at the 4-position relative to the bridge, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the central carbon. Because the rings are saturated, the framework is largely sp3 and conformationally flexible, though the chair conformations of the rings impose some rigidity. The two terminal primary amines each act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H bonds and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their nitrogen lone pairs, while the hydrocarbon core contributes no polar acceptor or donor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: a primary amine (-NH2) on one ring carbon, a methoxy group (-OCH3) on the adjacent carbon, and a methyl group (-CH3) positioned para to the methoxy group, so the pattern is 1,2,4-trisubstituted. The amino and methoxy groups are both electron-donating, while the methyl adds a further weak donor. The primary amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, and the ether oxygen of the methoxy group is a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The structure has no internal symmetry beyond the planar ring, and its rigidity comes from the aromatic core, with only the methoxy and methyl groups contributing rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methyl groups and one chlorine atom are attached to the ring, giving a trisubstituted benzene with the chlorine positioned ortho to one methyl group and meta to the other. The substituents are arranged asymmetrically, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one. The ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add only minor rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only heteroatom is the chlorine, which can act as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents. One aromatic carbon carries an N-allyl sulfonamide group, where the nitrogen is attached to a CH2-CH=CH2 chain and the sulfur bears two double-bonded oxygens. A second sulfonamide group, with a free NH2 on the sulfur, sits on the ring meta to the first, and a chlorine atom occupies the position between them on one side. The third substituent is a nitrogen-linked unsaturated chain, an imine (N=CH) connected to a conjugated alkene bearing a methyl group and terminating in a hydroxyl-bearing carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the allyl and enol-type chains add flexibility. Both sulfonamide groups provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the hydroxyl adds further donor and acceptor capacity.

The molecule is built around a five-membered saturated ring containing one sulfur atom, a thiolactone (a cyclic thioester) in which the carbonyl carbon sits directly next to the sulfur. Adjacent to that carbonyl carbon is a carbon bearing an O-acyl hydroxylamine group, where an acetyl group is attached through an oxygen to a nitrogen that links back to the ring. The ring is non-aromatic and fairly rigid, with the sp2 carbonyl fixing one portion of it, while the remaining ring carbons can pucker. The molecule has no internal symmetry and only one stereocenter at the substituted ring carbon. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the single N–H, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ester-type oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no fused rings and no aromaticity. Every ring carbon carries one chlorine atom, so the substitution pattern is fully uniform, with six C–Cl bonds distributed evenly around the ring. The stereocenter labels indicate defined relative configurations at each carbon, which gives the ring a fixed three-dimensional arrangement of its substituents. The chlorines are not hydrogen-bond donors, and their electronegativity makes them weak acceptors at most, so the molecule has no classical hydrogen-bond donor sites and only very limited acceptor capability.

This molecule is built on a porphyrin-type macrocycle, a large, nearly planar scaffold of four pyrrole-derived rings linked by methine bridges into a fully conjugated ring system. Two of the pyrrole positions carry propanoic acid side chains, each ending in a carboxylic acid group that can donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The other substituents are methyl groups and two 1-hydroxyethyl groups, which add secondary alcohol functionality. The macrocycle is rigid and flat, while the side chains provide some conformational flexibility. The two free carboxylic acids and two hydroxyl groups make this a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the central nitrogen atoms add further acceptor capability.

This molecule is a steroid built on a fused four-ring tetracyclic scaffold of three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring. The A ring is an α,β-unsaturated cyclohexenone, with a ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to it. The C ring carries a secondary hydroxyl group, while the D ring bears a tertiary hydroxyl at a ring-fusion carbon that also links to a two-carbon side chain ending in a ketone and a primary hydroxyl. Two angular methyl groups sit at the ring junctions, giving the framework a rigid, mostly sp3 character. Its hydroxyl and carbonyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the molecule has no overall symmetry.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing one methyl group and three chlorine atoms, giving a 1,2,3,5-tetrasubstituted aromatic scaffold. The three chlorines occupy three adjacent ring positions, while the methyl group sits on the carbon separated from them by one unsubstituted position, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the only conformational freedom lies in the rotation of the methyl group. The chlorine atoms are weakly electron-withdrawing substituents with no hydrogen-bond donor capability. Because the molecule lacks N–H or O–H groups, it has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, the chlorine atoms being poor acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring with alternating double bonds, forming a cyclohexadienone-type scaffold. One ring carbon bears a ketone oxygen (C=O), and the carbon directly across the ring, at the para position, bears a thiocarbonyl group (C=S), so the two exocyclic double bonds sit on opposite sides of the ring. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, with no sp3 carbons, which makes the framework rigid and flat. The molecule has a two-fold axis of symmetry passing through the two carbonyl-type carbons, so the two halves of the ring are mirror-related. The ketone oxygen and thiocarbonyl sulfur are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built around a central amidine-type unit in which a nitrogen bears a methyl group and links two N-aryl imine branches, giving a formamidine-like backbone with two C=N double bonds. Both terminal nitrogens are attached to separate benzene rings, each carrying a methyl substituent, with one ring bearing a methyl group in the meta position and the other bearing methyl groups at ortho and para positions relative to the nitrogen. The two aromatic halves are not symmetric, since their methyl substitution patterns differ. Because the central unit contains conjugated C=N bonds and rotatable N-aryl bonds, the scaffold is moderately flexible. The imine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring in a para (1,4) arrangement: a phenolic hydroxyl group, which is an aromatic alcohol that can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, and an allyl group, a three-carbon chain ending in a terminal carbon-carbon double bond. The allyl side chain is flexible and can rotate freely about its single bonds, while the aromatic core is planar and rigid. The para-disubstituted pattern gives the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring's long axis, with the polar hydroxyl end contrasting with the nonpolar hydrocarbon allyl end.

The molecule is a small, saturated diepoxide built from a four-carbon chain in which the two central carbons each bear an oxygen that closes a three-membered ring. The two epoxide rings are linked directly by a carbon-carbon single bond, giving a bis-oxirane scaffold with no other rings, heteroatoms, or substituents. Each strained oxirane ring contains one oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is essentially symmetric about the central bond, and the rigid, strained three-membered rings make the framework comparatively inflexible, though rotation about the linking bond remains possible.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing one amino group and five fluorine atoms, giving a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The amino group sits on one ring carbon, and the remaining five ring positions each carry a fluorine, so the substitution pattern is the same around the ring with the amine flanked by two fluorines on adjacent carbons. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the fluorine atoms making the ring electron-poor. The primary amine supplies two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair that can act as an acceptor, while the fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has only a loose approximate mirror symmetry through the amine and the opposite carbon, with the rest of the framework fixed in place.

This molecule is a small acyclic compound built around a central carbon atom bearing one hydrogen and one methyl group, which connects two acetoxy units through oxygen atoms. Each side of the structure contains an ester linkage, where a carbonyl group is bonded to a single-bonded oxygen that joins to the central carbon, giving two ester functional groups in total. There are no ring systems or fused rings, and the chain is flexible because all connections are single bonds apart from the two carbonyl double bonds. The molecule has a roughly mirror-symmetric arrangement, with the two acetyl ester arms attached to the same central carbon. The four ester oxygens and the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it lacks any O–H or N–H bonds.

The molecule is a substituted aniline built on a single benzene ring, with an amino group (–NH2) attached to one carbon. Two ethyl groups (–CH2CH3) sit on the ring carbons flanking the amino-bearing carbon, one at each ortho-adjacent position, producing a 2,6-disubstituted pattern. Because the two ethyl groups are identical and positioned symmetrically about the amine, the substitution pattern gives the aromatic core a mirror-symmetric arrangement, with the amino group lying along the symmetry axis. The ring is fully aromatic and rigid, while the two ethyl chains add some conformational flexibility. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a methyl group, and a nitro group. The methoxy group (an ether linked through oxygen to a methyl) and the methyl group sit para to one another, while the nitro group occupies a position ortho to the methyl and meta to the methoxy, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic core. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and planar with the ring, which makes the scaffold rigid and flat, with only the methoxy and methyl rotors offering modest flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are different and arranged asymmetrically. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygens of the methoxy and nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring in a para (1,4) relationship: an ethyl group, a two-carbon saturated chain, and a nitro group, in which a nitrogen is bonded to two oxygens with one formal positive charge on nitrogen and one negative charge on an oxygen. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing functional group, while the ethyl group is a flexible alkyl substituent with rotatable single bonds. The overall framework is largely planar and rigid, apart from the freely rotating ethyl chain. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, but the nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a three-carbon chain, with no rings or ring fusion present. Its skeleton contains a terminal vinyl group, where one alkene carbon carries a chlorine substituent, and the other end of the chain bears a nitrile group, which is a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen. The chlorine and the nitrile are both electron-withdrawing, giving the alkene a highly substituted, unsymmetrical pattern, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element. Because it contains only a double bond and a triple bond with no rotatable single-bond framework beyond the attached groups, the structure is quite rigid and compact. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. An acetyl group (a ketone with a methyl attached to the carbonyl carbon) is attached directly to one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group sits on the ring carbon para to it, so the two are on opposite sides of the ring. A methyl group occupies the position adjacent to the acetyl group, making the substitution pattern 1,2,4 around the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the acetyl and methyl groups contributing limited rotational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl can donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen can each accept one, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because its three substituents differ.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is an ethyl group, a two-carbon saturated chain that adds a small amount of conformational flexibility. The other is a nitro group, a nitrogen atom bonded to two oxygens with one formal positive and one negative charge, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and planar with the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, with the ethyl chain as its only flexible element. The molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the substituents. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds delocalized across all six carbons. Each ring carbon carries one substituent, with five fluorine atoms and two bromine atoms attached, and the two bromines sit on adjacent carbons next to each other. The sequence of substituents around the ring is fluorine, fluorine, fluorine, bromine, bromine, fluorine, so the substitution pattern is highly crowded and lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since no hydrogen is bonded to a heteroatom, and the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors. The rigid aromatic ring leaves little conformational flexibility, with the halogen atoms lying in the ring plane.

The molecule is a small aromatic compound built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent attached at one ring carbon. That substituent is a two-carbon chain: a secondary carbon carrying a methyl group, with a terminal carbon that bears a bromine atom, so the bromine sits on a primary carbon one step removed from the ring. The benzene ring is unfused and monosubstituted, so it has no ring fusion and retains a plane of symmetry through the ring and the attached chain. The side chain has a stereogenic center at the branching carbon, and rotation about its single bonds makes the chain moderately flexible while the aromatic ring stays rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom, the bromine, offers weak acceptor character, while the aromatic pi system provides a modest acceptor region.

This molecule is an acetal-type structure built around a single benzene ring bearing one substituent at the carbon that is directly attached to it. That benzylic carbon carries two acetoxy groups, each an ester formed from an acetyl unit linked through an oxygen, so the scaffold is a phenyl group joined to a central sp3 carbon that bridges two ester functionalities. The benzene ring is monosubstituted and unfused, and the overall framework is flexible because of several rotatable single bonds linking the ring to the central carbon and the ester oxygens to their acyl groups. Each ester oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since all of its hydrogens sit on carbon atoms.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three primary amino groups (-NH2) are attached to the ring at positions 1, 2, and 4, giving a 1,2,4-triaminobenzene substitution pattern in which the amines are not symmetrically placed, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the three amine substituents are small and flexible only in their N-H bond orientations. Each amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair, making the molecule highly capable of hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a tetrasubstituted aromatic compound with no fused rings. The ring carries a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and two tert-butyl groups (each a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyls), arranged so the hydroxyl sits between one tert-butyl group and an open ring position. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the scaffold is composed of nonpolar alkyl and aromatic carbon framework. Ethyl ester of a fused polycyclic lactone. This molecule is built on a central thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. The molecule is built around a saturated five-membered cyclic sulfamidate: a ring containing one nitrogen, one oxygen, and a sulfur atom bearing two sulfonyl oxygens, with the remaining ring carbons forming the backbone. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor capacity comes from the two nitrogen atoms, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens sit on carbon.

The aromatic ring carries a single methoxy group (an aryl ether oxygen acting only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor) at a position para-like to the ring fusion. This molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazole ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The ring is fully substituted: one nitrogen carries an N-acyl group linking to a meta-tolyl benzoyl unit, a carbon adjacent to that nitrogen bears a methyl thioether (S-methyl), another ring carbon carries a methyl group, and the remaining ring carbon is attached to an ethyl ester. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and ring nitrogen act as acceptors. The biaryl bond allows some rotation, though the bulky ortho-chlorine adjacent to the linkage restricts it, and the molecule is largely hydrophobic and planar-leaning in its aromatic regions.

The molecule is built on a six-membered pyrimidine-type ring containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 with a carbonyl at position 2, which together form a cyclic acylurea-like scaffold. At the quaternary carbon (position 5) sits a sp3 center bearing both an ethyl group and a phenyl ring, which breaks the planarity of the core and makes the molecule somewhat three-dimensional. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and monocyclic, attached directly to that quaternary carbon. The two hydroxyl groups on the ring carbons adjacent to the nitrogens are present as enol-type tautomers, and the ring contains conjugated C=N and C=O functionalities. Overall, the molecule has no symmetry because the ethyl and phenyl groups differ, and it offers multiple hydrogen-bond donors (the hydroxyl and ring NH-type sites) along with several carbonyl and nitrogen acceptors.

This molecule is built on a quinuclidine-type bicyclic amine fused to a 6-methoxyquinoline ring system, the same scaffold as the cinchona alkaloids. The bicyclic cage is fully saturated and rigid, containing one tertiary nitrogen that serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. A vinyl group sits on one bridgehead-adjacent carbon, and a secondary alcohol bridges the cage to the quinoline at the 4-position. The quinoline's pyridine nitrogen is an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The methoxy group on the benzo ring adds an ether oxygen acceptor, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because of its multiple stereocenters.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three oxygen-containing substituents: two methoxy groups and one free hydroxyl group, arranged so that the hydroxyl sits between the two methoxy groups on adjacent positions. At the opposite side of the ring, a para-positioned acrylic acid chain extends outward as a conjugated C=C double bond terminating in a carboxylic acid. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the trans-configured double bond keeps the side chain largely extended and flat. The substitution pattern gives the ring a mirror-plane arrangement through the ring carbons, so the overall framework is nearly symmetric apart from the carboxylic acid end. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl and ether oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a steroid-type fused polycyclic scaffold built from four rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring, arranged in the characteristic fused tetracyclic pattern. The A ring is an enone, containing a ketone at one position and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to it, which makes that portion of the framework relatively planar. Two angular methyl groups sit at ring-fusion carbons, and the five-membered ring carries a bulky ester substituent in which a phenylacetyl group is joined through an oxygen atom. The molecule has no internal symmetry, is conformationally constrained by its fused rings apart from the flexible ester side chain, and offers one ketone oxygen and one ester carbonyl oxygen as hydrogen-bond acceptors while lacking any hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a central alpha-carbon bearing a para-dimethylaminophenyl group, a tert-butyl amide, and a tertiary N-methyl amide nitrogen that carries a four-carbon acyl chain ending in a large fused polycyclic aromatic system. That aromatic unit is a pyrene-type framework of four fused benzene-like rings, giving a flat, rigid, highly conjugated region, while the rest of the chain is flexible. The dimethylamino group and the tertiary amide oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the secondary amide N-H is the only hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the substituents differ at each branch.
